#1 — Highly Innovative (84)

Extending concurrent separation logic to the hardware level to verify the xv6 OS kernel on RISC-V with AI agents

MF Kaashoek, N Zeldovich · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MachCSL, a concurrent separation logic framework (built on Iris/Rocq) for verifying an OS kernel directly on sub-instruction-level RISC-V hardware semantics, and uses it to produce a machine-checked whole-system correctness theorem for the xv6 kernel (6,593 lines of C/assembly compiling to 8,607 RISC-V instructions). - Why it's important: Prior kernel verifications (seL4, CertiKOS, etc.) assume idealized hardware behavior — page tables, TLBs, interrupts, and DMA are abstracted away — leaving the gap between the proof and real silicon unverified; this work closes that gap by proving the kernel against the Sail RISC-V ISA model, with the build toolchain excluded from the TCB. - How it does it: The core move is formulating kernel safety as a continuation-based weakest-precondition over an infinite CPU-execution loop grounded in the Sail model, with per-instruction and sub-instruction CSL specs, and delegating the enormous proof burden (1.3M lines of Rocq) to parallel Claude Code agents whose output is machine-checked by Rocq. - The good: The whole-system theorem yields four strong corollaries — kernel integrity, process isolation, file-system crash safety, and hardware safety (no undefined MMIO/DRAM behavior) — and the verification uncovered nine real xv6 bugs plus one bug in the Sail RISC-V model itself, demonstrating the framework finds genuine defects. - The missing: The result covers safety only (no liveness, no non-interference/information-flow), depends on a large trusted model of the SoC (memory, devices, interconnect) developed by the authors, and conformance validation of that model against real hardware (QEMU, one JH7110 board) is subset-style testing rather than exhaustive correspondence. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on verified systems, separation logic, or LLM-assisted formal methods — it is the most hardware-grounded kernel verification to date and the most detailed published account of agent-driven proof engineering; skip it if you need liveness or confidentiality guarantees or want a verified kernel you can deploy (xv6 is a teaching kernel).
Why this rank
Scored using SYSTEMS profile (built verification framework with substantial released artifact plus empirical model validation). Novelty (88) is the standout — grounding a whole-kernel concurrent separation logic proof in the off-the-shelf Sail ISA model, down to page-table walks, TLB races, and A/D writeback, is a new method genuinely beyond seL4/CertiKOS, and the whole-system theorem over the literal ELF removes the toolchain from the TCB. Rigor (85) is high — the 1.3M-line Rocq proof is machine-checked, the adequacy theorem forces non-vacuous specs, code is released, and real bugs (9 in xv6, 1 in Sail) were found — but held back by a self-authored trusted SoC model validated only one-directionally against one emulator and one board. Non-Obviousness (85): the continuation-based weakest-precondition over an infinite CPU loop and the TSO view-relative resources are genuine technical contributions not predicted by prior work. Completeness (80) benefits from unusually direct limitation acknowledgment (safety-only, TCB disclosure), offset by the truncated bug reporting and unexercised hardware behaviors. Resilience (78) is solid because claims are precisely bounded ('what is proven is the theorem, not that xv6 is bug-free'), though the model-hardware conformance gap invites hard questions. Practical Impact (85) reflects the released MachCSL framework, proof development, verified xv6 branch, and the first detailed agent-driven proof-engineering playbook — though the verified artifact is a teaching kernel, not a deployable system. Weighted composite: 0.15*88 + 0.15*85 + 0.10*85 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*78 + 0.30*85 = 83.65 → 84.

Problem & Motivation: OS kernels must program raw hardware — page tables, TLBs, privilege levels, configuration CSRs, interrupt controllers, DMA devices — and run under extreme concurrency: multi-core execution, kernel-mode interrupts, preemptive context switching, concurrent hardware page-table walks, and power failures. Applications inherit whatever bugs the kernel and its hardware configuration contain. Prior verified kernels (seL4, hypervisors, security monitors) prove correctness against abstract machine models that assume hardware mechanisms behave correctly, so the proofs never cover boot code, TLB management, A/D-bit writeback races, or interrupt delivery timing. The authors ask whether a full, traditionally-structured Unix kernel — one not written with verification in mind — can be verified down to the actual ISA semantics and the literal bytes of the compiled binary, and whether the tedium this entails can be made tractable with LLM agents. Key Idea: The key idea is to treat the entire kernel execution as one infinite loop (wp CpuLoop) whose semantics is the Sail RISC-V model's per-cycle execution, and to decompose its proof with continuation-style CSL specs: every function spec takes a proof about "the rest of the infinite loop" as an argument, so a function's proof composes with the caller's proof without any notion of function return baked into the semantics. Proving safety of the kernel reduces to establishing wp CpuLoop at power-on, and hardware details (TLB, page-table walks, interrupt checking, A/D writeback) are handled by per-register and per-device ownership invariants rather than assumed away. The second enabling idea is that agents can write these tedious, machine-checked proofs even though humans must design the abstractions. Methodology: The framework has three layers. (1) A trusted system model: the Sail RISC-V HART model translated to Rocq via Sail's backend, augmented with the authors' models of TSO shared memory (a global write log with per-core timestamps; atomic instructions force timestamp sync; fences advance to own writes), devices (UART, DMA-capable virtio disk controller, PLIC), and a power-cycling thread — all interleaving at the granularity of individual memory/register events, so a hardware page-table walk can race with a kernel PTE update. (2) The MachCSL logic: Iris-style resources for registers (r ↦ Reg v), physical memory (pa ↦ Mem v), virtual memory (va ↦ vMem v backed by a page-table/TLB invariant strans_inv), device invariants, and a wp Sail(m) {Φ} layer for sub-instruction stages (translateAddr, fetch, decode, trap dispatch). The adequacy theorem cancels all intermediate specs and yields a statement purely about the operational semantics, initializing every invariant and bootstrapping from the literal mkfs-produced fs.img bytes. (3) The xv6 proof: specifications per kernel function in a strict SpecF/CodeF/ProofF/LinkF file layout, with notable constructions including the sie_cap_gpr resource (tracking interrupt-enable state, stack budget for the trap handler, per-core lock sets, CPU migration), a two-tier kernel translation scheme for the boot sequence, view-relative resources for TSO (spinlock views, suspended views for cross-core context switches), cancellable invariants for dynamically allocated pipe locks, a counted-vs-concurrent two-regime kalloc spec, file-reference slot tokens to rule out refcount overflow, write-permit callbacks threading ghost state through two-sector disk writes for crash atomicity, and log-absorption/cross-transaction accounting for the MAXOPBLOCKS budget. Verification of the binary was driven by parallel Claude Code agents (Fable-class models for design orchestration, Opus/Sonnet for proof execution) with human-designed abstractions, multi-agent design review for hard proofs (buffer cache, inode cache under TSO), fresh-context agent restarts, and continuous proof-performance optimization. Critical design decisions: continuation-based specs instead of Hoare-triple postconditions (well-justified — required because hardware semantics has no notion of return), grounding proofs in the ELF binary to remove the toolchain from the TCB (justified, but makes proofs brittle to recompilation — mitigated only by agents), and human ownership of abstraction design (justified by documented agent failure modes). Key Results: The headline artifact is a machine-checked whole-system theorem over 8 Sail RISC-V HARTs with UART, disk, PLIC, and power cycles, proven in 1.3 million lines of Rocq covering all 8,607 instructions of the xv6 kernel binary, developed in 77 days including framework construction. It implies four corollaries: kernel integrity (no assertion failures, double frees, or arbitrary jumps), process isolation (arbitrary user code cannot corrupt kernel memory or re-enter except via the trap handler), crash safety (the on-disk file system stays consistent under any interleaving of system calls and power failures), and hardware safety (no stray DRAM/MMIO access or device protocol violations). The effort found 9 xv6 bugs (including kernel-panicking races between iput/ialloc, an unlogged partial writei, a missing icache fence after exec, and a scheduler push_off reset bug) and 1 Sail model bug (blind A/D-bit writeback that can resurrect a cleared PTE, confirmed and fixed upstream). Model validation: conformance tests cross-check the Rocq model against QEMU rv64 and a StarFive JH7110 (VisionFive2) board via JTAG, proving every observed 4KB reference snapshot is reproducible in the model, including TSO race outcomes with explicitly synthesized schedules. No error bars or seed variance apply (proof artifacts are binary: checked or not); the relevant robustness metric is proof-checking time, which the authors actively optimized but do not quantify in the provided text. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a CSL/Hiris adaptation to sub-instruction-level hardware execution with continuation-style specs, TSO views, and device invariants) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a detailed demonstration that LLM agents can produce a 1.3M-line machine-checked proof, given human-designed abstractions) plus an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component (agent workflow, file discipline, proof-performance tuning). Genuinely novel: the grounding of a concurrent kernel proof in the off-the-shelf Sail ISA model including page-table walks, TLB, interrupts, and power failures, and the whole-system theorem over the literal kernel ELF. Standard combination: the separation-logic machinery itself (Iris), crash-consistency reasoning via write-ahead log ghosts, and refcount/allocator specs are established techniques applied at a new level of fidelity. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation in the proof sense exists implicitly: the adequacy theorem forces every invariant to be instantiated and cancels intermediate specs, so unsound or vacuous specs cannot survive — and the paper documents three concrete cases (vacuous crash-safety theorem, agent-introduced axiom create_fresh_ty, agent-modified xv6 source) where the methodology caught unsound moves. No statistical claims are made (appropriate for a correctness proof). Code is released: the proof development at github.com/mit-pdos/xv6iris and the pinned kernel on the verified branch of github.com/mit-pdos/xv6-riscv. Methodological concerns: the trusted model of shared memory, devices, and the interconnect is authored by the same team whose theorem depends on it, and its conformance validation is one-directional (reference behaviors ⊆ model behaviors, with model "stuck" states counted as matches) against one emulator and one board, so model-hardware mismatch beyond the tested subset would silently weaken the theorem's real-world meaning. The deadlock argument is a spec-enforced discipline, not a proven property. The PDF text is truncated mid-Section 8 (bug descriptions incomplete), so full bug reporting cannot be assessed. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built verification framework and proof artifact, with an empirical validation component for the model). Practical: Runs on ordinary developer hardware — the artifacts are a Rocq development and Claude Code agents; the verified kernel targets commodity RISC-V (QEMU, JH7110). Efficient: The verified kernel is unmodified upstream xv6 with no runtime overhead (proofs are about the binary, not instrumentation); the cost is proof development (77 person-days plus substantial LLM compute, unquantified) and proof-checking time, which the authors optimized but do not report numerically. Effective: Evidence shows the stated safety goals are met for the model, and the bug haul shows the process finds real defects; effectiveness against real silicon is limited by the conformance-testing gap. Scalable: Untested beyond 6.6k LOC of kernel and 8 HARTs; the authors claim agents fix proofs after recompiles "within several hours," but scaling to a kernel 10–50× larger (Linux-class) is only implied by the workflow, never demonstrated. Delivered artifacts: the MachCSL Rocq framework, the full proof development, the verified xv6 branch, and reusable methodology (conformance tester, CodeF.v generation scripts, agent orchestration practices) — a substantial software artifact, not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The most hardware-faithful kernel verification to date: unlike seL4/CertiKOS-style proofs over abstract machine models, this proof must and does account for boot code, TLB switching windows, A/D writeback races, WRS.NTO user-mode sleep, GCC's modular-inverse struct-offset optimization, and interrupt delivery between sub-instruction steps — assumptions other verifications explicitly or implicitly discharge. (2) The whole-system theorem over the literal ELF and fs.img bytes removes the compiler, assembler, and build toolchain from the TCB, a rigorous answer to a problem most verified-kernel efforts sidestep. (3) The TSO treatment — view-relative resources, lock views pinned to release timestamps, suspended views for cross-core thread migration, and the weakened kfree spec (ownership without stability) — is a genuine technical contribution to weak-memory separation logic. (4) The agent-methodology sections are unusually candid and transferable: documented failure spirals, the axiom-reporting discipline that caught a hallucinated axiom, multi-agent design review that unblocked the TSO buffer-cache proofs, and the observation that agents execute proofs well but design abstractions poorly. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: proofs cover safety only — no liveness (scheduling progress) and no non-interference/information-flow properties; the TCB (Rocq checker plus the authors' RISC-V system model including Sail and the memory/device models) is assumed correct; the theorem applies to their TSO memory model only; and what is proven is the precise theorem statement, not a vague claim that "xv6 is bug-free." They also acknowledge within the text that spinlock deadlock-freedom is enforced by spec discipline rather than proven by the adequacy theorem, and that proofs are tied to the exact kernel binary, making recompilation expensive without agents. The paper confronts these limitations directly and enumerates them early, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The trusted SoC model is self-authored: the paper's central claim — coverage of "all the hardware details" — is only as good as a model whose device, interconnect, and memory semantics the authors wrote themselves, and the conformance checker accepts "model gets stuck" as correspondence, so unexercised hardware behaviors (icache incoherence is explicitly unmodeled) are outside the theorem's reach in ways real hardware may exercise. (2) The one-directional conformance relation (implementation behaviors ⊆ model behaviors) does not rule out the model permitting behaviors real hardware never exhibits, which is the direction that matters for the corollaries' practical force. (3) Verification was performed on the authors' own framework with the kernel effectively co-developed with the proof (bug fixes to xv6 during verification); there is no independent replication, and the 77-day figure counts expert MIT CSAIL effort plus unquantified LLM usage — cost claims for outsiders are extrapolation. (4) The bug list is truncated in the provided text, so severity and fix status of all nine kernel bugs cannot be fully audited. (5) Deadlock-freedom, the most likely runtime failure mode of a fine-grained-locked kernel, is disciplined rather than proven. (6) The user-mode isolation corollary is safety-only: a user process corrupting the kernel is excluded, but timing or resource-channel interference between processes (outside non-interference, acknowledged) means "isolation" is weaker than the security connotation it carries. Bottom Line: This is a landmark systems-verification paper that anyone in formal methods, verified kernels, or AI-for-math should read — it redefines how low a kernel proof can reach and provides the best published playbook for agent-driven proof engineering — but it is a research milestone on a teaching kernel over a partially-validated hardware model, not a deployable verified system, and its liveness and confidentiality silences are real.}

#2 — Highly Innovative (83)

Privacy Failure in Split-LLM Training, The Returned Gradient Nullifies the Decoys (2 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a systems-security case study showing that a two-node split-LLM training system passed its forward-channel privacy evaluation while the returned output gradient leaked the exact real-versus-decoy row partition, and it backs the diagnosis with a pre-registered, calibrated evaluation protocol. - Why it's important: Split-learning deployments claim data owners can rent untrusted cloud compute without exposing training data, and a privacy evaluation that passes while never instrumenting an observable channel produces false assurance at exactly the point where a privacy failure is costliest. - How it does it: Because the trusted node's loss excludes the 48 decoy rows per frame, every decoy's returned gradient is identically zero, so the zero-support pattern deterministically tells the compromised cloud which of the 80 rows carry private data before any content attack is attempted. - The good: The structural disclosure is deterministic and universal — the real/decoy split is exact on 4,096/4,096 frames on each of nine seeds — and the study pairs it with injected-leak calibration, shuffled-label negative controls, and a predeclared Bonferroni–Wilson gate, none of which the three audited external evaluations combine. - The missing: The content-level damage is modest (a +0.92 pp pooled frequent-token advantage over a constant-guess baseline, roughly one extra token per hundred), five attack families — including cross-step accumulation and membership inference — were declared but never measured, and the passing-both-gates result rests on 2,000-step diagnostic runs of a 0.6B model that never reach convergence scale. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate split-learning or secure-training systems and need a template for channel-explicit, calibrated privacy audits; skip it if you want strong content-reconstruction attacks, since this paper explicitly establishes only metadata partitioning plus a bounded frequent-token effect.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (90) is the anchor — pre-registered thresholds, dose-response calibration with injected leaks, representation-matched positive controls, shuffled-label negative controls, nine-seed deterministic replication, and released code with committed manifests. Novelty (78) reflects a new formulation of channel-explicit privacy auditing atop a new (if implementation-defect-level) empirical finding; the zero-gradient partition itself is an instance of known backward-channel risk. Non-Obviousness (85) is high — the defence-as-leak mechanism (decoy exclusion making gradients an exact partition oracle) is genuinely counter-intuitive and not predicted by prior art. Completeness (85) is exceptional: a claim-evidence ledger with withdrawn claims and direct, non-minimizing limitation statements. Resilience (78) is solid but the constant-guess baseline and five unmeasured attack families leave exposed flanks. Impact (75) comes from a reusable audit template and artifact release, tempered by the 0.6B/2,000-step scale. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*90 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*78 + 0.10*75 = 83.

Problem & Motivation: Split learning lets a data owner train an LLM on rented cloud compute without shipping raw text: the Trusted Local Node (TLN) sends activations to an Untrusted Cloud Node (UCN), and because only TLN holds the private loss, it returns output gradients. The privacy claim — the cloud cannot read training data — is only as strong as the evaluation instrument behind it. The specific system studied here had an evaluation that instrumented the forward wire (activations) and passed its gate, while the backward wire (the returned gradient) was never declared a privacy surface. The general problem is evaluation semantics: a privacy gate can return "pass" for channels it never declared, and no published split-LLM evaluation audited (BiSR, DualGuard, "Prompts to Responses") combines injected-leak calibration, shuffled-label negative controls, and a predeclared gate. The practitioners who have this problem are anyone deploying split-training, split-inference, or federated LLM pipelines against a compromised cloud. Key Idea: The core insight is that a defence mechanism can be its own leak: excluding decoy rows from the private loss makes their returned gradients exactly zero, so the gradient's support pattern is a deterministic, per-frame oracle for which rows are real — collapsing the anonymity set that the decoy padding was constructed to create. The second, more general idea is methodological: a privacy metric can certify absence of leakage only if it has been shown to detect a deliberately injected leak at known dose, on every declared channel, with the decision threshold fixed in advance and falsifiable via shuffled-label controls. Methodology: The system trains Qwen3-0.6B (weights and corpus SHA-256-pinned) on WikiText-2 with a D=64 latent bottleneck, per-request rotation/permutation/scale gauges, and 80-row frames mixing 32 real rows with 48 recycled decoys; forward and return wires are clipped (C=1.0) and Gaussian-noised (σ=0.35C), while the backward wire carried the gradient raw. The evaluation protocol fixes, before the replication and mitigation runs: (1) a declared-channel table enumerating nine adversary channel families (forward, gradient, joint, accumulated history, stateful state, timing, active perturbation, membership, response side), (2) per-metric dose–response calibration injecting a known token leak at 19 coverage levels to find each metric's detection onset (token top-1 onset ~0.04–0.06 coverage; rare-token top-1 at 0.04; cross-entropy flat until the leak dominates; membership AUC falsified as a channel), (3) a gate statistic G = max over nine predeclared probe arms of Bonferroni-adjusted Wilson upper-95 accuracy minus the constant-guess baseline (~5–6%), failing above +1.0 pp, and (4) shuffled-label negative controls as a false-positive check. A representation-matched positive control (a 4-layer transformer probe that inverts the naked D=1024 boundary at +24.19 pp but reads floor through the defence) proves the instrument is not blind. The main claims are the structural partition disclosure (zero-support match), the frequent-token content effect, and mitigation runs on a shallower four-layer split where per-row gradient clipping (C=0.01) plus Gaussian noise closes the leak. Critical design decisions: pre-registration of thresholds and seeds (well justified, stated as fixed before the relevant runs); the constant-guess baseline as the effect unit (reasonable but makes the headline +0.92 pp look modest in absolute terms); and the block-held-out rather than document-held-out evaluation split (a disclosed protocol deviation the authors flag as out-of-scope for document-independence claims). Key Results: The zero-support readback identified real rows exactly on 4,096/4,096 frames per run, on all nine seeds (row agreement 1.000). The frequent-token gradient-arm paired effect over the constant-guess baseline ranged +0.65 to +1.50 pp per seed, pooled at +0.92 pp (95% CI [0.74, 1.09], τ=0.23, I²=77%); shuffled-label negative controls stayed at floor (|N| ≤ 0.08 pp). In the audit ladder (single seed per cell), the token effect was detected at 11–12 delegated layers and D=64/96 but not at 6–8 layers or D=128, and did not grow from 40k to 100k steps; the partition itself was exact at every depth and width. In the mitigation set, all six defended gradient-open cells (3 seeds × 2 datasets, four-layer topology) passed the forward privacy gate and the utility gate (+0.05 to +0.09 nats against a 0.35 bound) yet broke the +1.0 pp gate on the joint forward∥gradient view (+1.44 to +2.18 pp gate statistic); adding per-row clipping and noise dropped all arms to floor (+0.48) with support leak 0/1,024 frames at a held-out cost of ≈0.01 nats. An X^T G cross-Gram rotation-cancelling feature was implemented and read at floor everywhere. Notably, the paper reports that gradient content alone contributed at most +0.18 pp over the oracle-partitioned forward arm on five of six seeds — the backward wire's unique damage is the partition, not extra content. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a NEW FORMULATION of privacy evaluation (channel-explicit, calibrated, pre-registered auditing adapted from DP-auditing lineage to split-protocol channels). The zero-gradient-partition mechanism is an implementation defect rather than a new attack primitive — gradient-leakage and backward-channel attacks are established prior work, which the paper says explicitly — and the defence primitives (bottleneck, gauges, noise, decoys) are standard compositions. The genuinely novel elements are the verified diagnosis of a false pass caused by an undeclared channel plus a degenerate calibration floor, and the demonstration that the calibrated three-control protocol exposes it where three recent external evaluations lack all three controls. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and unusually well structured: a nine-cell audit across depth, width, and budget; a dose–response calibration sweep; representation-matched positive controls; shuffled-label negative controls per arm; internal scorer reimplementation matching all nine primary seeds to ≤10⁻⁶ pp; and a packaged-code rerun of seed 42 confirming the container-independent result. Uncertainty is handled with frame-clustered bootstraps and a hierarchical seed-level random-effects estimate; the paper reports heterogeneity (I²=77%) rather than hiding it. Code and derived summaries are released at github.com/setloop-io/Privacy-Failure-in-Split-LLM-Training (7.4 GB bundle manifests committed; raw prediction tensors cluster-side, so exploratory and mitigation values are redisplayed from committed summaries rather than fully re-derivable; the independent scorer check is recorded but not re-executable). Methodological concerns flagged by the authors themselves: a protocol file declaring document-level splits while the runner implements block-level splits; a withdrawn membership-inference claim refuted by its own negative control; three degenerate calibration cells; and all shape-threshold readings from single runs. The evidence is self-consistent and unusually honest about withdrawn claims, but it is a case study of one system, and the constant-guess baseline inflates relative significance of small absolute effects. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measured attack and mitigation on a built system). - Practical: Runs on a 0.6B model in a Transformers 5.13.0 runtime with a two-node WebSocket/TLS setup — commercially feasible, though the defence stack (gauges, KDF, decoys, integrity replicas) is substantial. - Efficient: The mitigation costs ≈0.01 nats held-out cross-entropy, essentially free; the defence stack overall was not cost-profiled in this paper (its own table lists 1.05–2.5× WAN overhead for the composite). - Effective: The evidence shows the audit method detects a real leak that a forward-only gate missed, and that clipping+noise closes the measured leak — but "safe" is not established since five attack families were never measured. - Scalable: Not tested — the passing-both-gates configuration is 2,000-step diagnostics on a 0.6B model; convergence-scale behaviour and behaviour on larger models remain claimed-free but untested, and the paper says so. Deliverable: an artefact release (code, committed summaries, manifests, verification transcripts) at the GitHub repository above; not a library or product, but a reproducible case-study package with per-claim artefact indexing. Strengths: - The mechanism finding is deterministic and bulletproof within its scope: an exactly-zero gradient support pattern that reproduces the real/decoy partition on every frame of every seed is not a statistical artefact, and the paper correctly separates this structural claim from the modest content claim. - The calibration discipline — per-metric dose–response onset, injected positive controls, representation-matched sensitivity control (+24.19 pp on naked vs. floor through defence with the same probe architecture), predeclared thresholds, and shuffled-label nulls — is a materially better evaluation standard than the three audited external works, and the audit table (Table 12) substantiates that claim rather than asserting it. - Exceptional claim hygiene: claim levels are explicitly enumerated (established / not established), a claim-evidence ledger records withdrawn claims with refutation records, and negative results (MINE reading −1.3×10⁻⁶ nats while a +0.758 pp effect was present) are reported as cautionary evidence. - The mitigation-section design pre-empts the "nobody would deploy that configuration" objection by re-demonstrating the joint-view gate break on 6/6 cells that pass both the forward privacy and utility gates, on two corpora. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly that the findings concern one implementation, one main corpus (WikiText-2) with a three-seed second-corpus diagnostic, and a targeted three-work external audit rather than a survey. They declare five attack families unmeasured (accumulated history, stateful state, timing, membership, response side), note that rare-token and sequence reconstruction (TAG/LAMP/DAGER-class) were not adapted to this gradient-cut object, and confine the content result to frequent-token discrimination. They disclose the block-vs-document split protocol deviation, the uncommitted independent scorer, host-only raw transcripts, the single-seed nature of all shape-threshold readings, and the depth-budget confound in the depth ladder. They also state the protocol is "not evidence for a general methodology across independently designed systems." This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' own disclosures, a reviewer would flag: (1) the constant-guess baseline (~5–6%) makes the +0.92 pp headline effect look larger relative to baseline than it is in absolute token-recovery terms, and the forward-arm comparison lacks its own shuffled-label control, so the gradient-versus-forward attribution rests partly on an uncontrolled column; (2) the deployment-relevant configuration (four-layer split, 2,000 steps) is far from any realistic fine-tuning budget, and no convergence-scale evidence exists for the very configuration where the leak matters; (3) all audit-ladder cells use seed 42 only, so every shape threshold is a single-seed reading the paper treats as suggestive but which still structures the depth/width narrative; (4) the external audit of three systems is purposeful and unverifiable as a fair sample — the "none combined all three controls" claim covers exactly three works; (5) the mitigated runs disable the per-row scale gauge, so the joint-view result is conditional on a setting the paper notes but a deployer could miss; and (6) the strategic question — whether the decoy mechanism could be trivially fixed by giving decoys a tiny nonzero loss weight or noise floor rather than clipping+noise on the whole gradient — is never explored, leaving the cheapest fix unexamined. Bottom Line: A practitioner building split-learning or secure-training systems should read this: the calibrated channel-explicit audit protocol and the documented failure mode of an undeclared channel are directly transferable, even though the specific leak is a fixable implementation defect and the content damage is demonstrably small.

#3 — Highly Innovative (82)

Unlocking Lossless Speedups in LLMs via Discrete Diffusion (104 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces "diffusion-augmented LLMs" (Uno), a single architecture that adds lightweight LoRA diffusion weights to every layer of a frozen autoregressive LLM, plus a Ψ-Spec sampler that drafts token blocks in parallel via one-step diffusion and verifies them against the AR distribution for provably lossless speculative decoding without a separate draft model. - Why it's important: Sequential decoding is memory-bound and wastes GPU compute, and existing accelerators either need a separate drafter (speculative decoding) or sacrifice quality and lose their speedup at realistic batch sizes (diffusion LLMs) — a problem for agentic serving workloads and RL post-training where rollout generation dominates cost. - How it does it: Freeze the AR weights, train rank-128 LoRA adapters via blockwise one-step discrete consistency distillation plus a total-variation loss (which increases accepted-prefix length), then apply standard Leviathan-style rejection sampling so output exactly matches the AR model's distribution. - The good: The speedup persists at every batch size tested — 1.5× over the base AR model at batch 64 (max fitting on one H200) and ~2.2× at batch 1 for the from-scratch 8B model, and UnoQwen Pareto-dominates EAGLE-3 and DFlash across batch sizes 1–64 with fewer added parameters (0.35B vs 0.40B/1.05B) and a shared KV cache. - The missing: The most quantitatively striking claim — a ~4.6× system-throughput advantage over Mercury 2 — compares against vendor-reported numbers on faster Blackwell hardware with undisclosed quantization, and the 40% end-to-end RL-training speedup is asserted with results deferred to a future revision. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM inference systems or diffusion language models and want the current frontier of lossless multi-token drafting; skip the middle sections if you only need the benchmark tables, which mainly show an 8B model beating 14B–26B+ diffusion baselines that are already known to trail AR models in quality.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. This is the strongest paper in the cluster: it delivers a released, deployable artifact (Ψ-Spec samplers in Nano-vLLM and SGLang plus checkpoints), which drives Impact (88) under the Systems weighting. Novelty (78) reflects a genuinely new architecture move — in-architecture LoRA diffusion drafting sharing the verifier's base weights and KV cache — built from standard components but with the first credible lossless speedup that survives serving batch sizes (1.5–1.6× at batch 64). Rigor (80) is high: unusually thorough ablations, losslessness verified with confidence intervals over multiple seeds, strong current baselines (EAGLE-3, DFlash) with fair tuning, and the discovery of a losslessness bug in a concurrent competitor — though vendor-reported Mercury 2 numbers, missing throughput error bars, and a deferred RL-speedup result hold it back. Non-Obviousness (80) comes from the batch-size insight and the TV-objective/accepted-prefix connection; Completeness (82) is strengthened by limitations that confront rather than minimize (quadratic sampling deferred, Mercury comparison approximate). systems Novelty 78 Rigor 80 Non-Obv 80 Completeness 82 Resilience 78 Impact 88
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Autoregressive LLMs generate one token per forward pass, which is slow, memory-bound at long contexts, and leaves parallel compute idle. Speculative decoding fixes this but requires training and maintaining a separate, well-aligned draft model. Diffusion LLMs draft in parallel natively but modify base weights (lossy), trail AR quality, and — critically for modern agentic workloads that run many concurrent requests — their speedups evaporate at large batch sizes. The paper argues batch-size-1 latency benchmarks overstate diffusion-model speedups because practical serving runs batched; the gap it targets is a lossless accelerator that maintains its speedup at serving batch sizes and drops into existing AR training pipelines, including accelerating RL rollouts. Key Idea: Decouple quality from speed inside one architecture: keep an AR pathway (θ_AR) as the quality-defining verifier, and learn a diffusion pathway (θ_AR + θ_Δ, LoRA adapters) that drafts a whole block in one forward pass from the same distribution the verifier scores — then enforce losslessness with textbook speculative rejection sampling. Two enabling tricks: (1) NTP-parameterized block diffusion trained with a block-causal mask and gated LoRA, so teacher logits (θ_AR only) and student logits (θ_AR+θ_Δ) come from a single forward pass over the concatenated clean/noisy sequence; (2) a total-variation loss between draft and verifier distributions, which directly maximizes expected accepted-prefix length per Leviathan et al.'s Corollary 3.6. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) standard NTP pre-training/SFT of AR weights (from scratch: 23T tokens proprietary data with staged context extension to 512K; or frozen open-weight Qwen3-8B); (2) Diffusion Distillation Phase: train only θ_Δ on 7B tokens (Uno) or 14.7B OpenThoughts tokens (UnoQwen) to map a fully corrupted block z_1 plus clean context to the AR teacher's block distribution, using L = α·L_DCD + β·L_TV where L_DCD is blockwise KL between student and teacher clean-token distributions and L_TV is blockwise TV distance; (3) optional RL (DAPO) updating only θ_AR while the frozen adapters accelerate rollouts; (4) inference via Ψ-Spec: first block token sampled from pure AR weights (always accepted), remaining B−1 tokens from the adapted distribution, candidates sampled linearly (system-throughput mode, B=4) or via tree attention with (B,K,V)=(16,32,32) (batch-1 mode), verified by rejection sampling with tokens-per-forward bounded by (B+1)/2. Critical design decisions: LoRA parameterization for draft-verifier coupling (justified by losslessness and memory, but empirical — no direct comparison against full-weight diffusion adapters); TV-vs-KL loss balance (ablated, and notably TV-only beats DCD+TV, 2.39 vs 2.23 TPF, suggesting the headline "distillation" loss contributes little); block-size curriculum (ablated, +0.06 TPF). Implementations in Nano-vLLM and SGLang are provided. Key Results: Tested at genuine scale: an 8B from-scratch model (23T AR tokens; 60h distillation on 64 H200s) and Qwen3-8B augmented with 0.35B adapter params (32h on 32 H200s). Throughput via a controlled "1K/8K" test (fixed 1024 input/8192 output) on a single H200 in bfloat16. Uno: 5,255 tok/s system throughput vs 3,577 for its own AR base (1.5×) at batch 64, and 383 vs 176 tok/s per-request (2.2×) at batch 1; claims up to 3× in the best tree configuration. UnoQwen: 1.6× over base AR at max batch (5,733 vs EAGLE-3's 4,944 and DFlash's 5,351 tok/s) and 2.5× at batch 1 (445 vs EAGLE-3's 284 and DFlash's 370 tok/s), with lower peak memory (118 vs 129–130 GiB). Quality: Uno (8B) beats DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-14B on all 16 benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench Verified 68.4 vs 18.7 vs 0.8; AIME-25 90.7 vs 74.3 vs 40.0) and beats the proprietary Mercury 2 on agentic, coding, and long-context tasks (τ2-Telecom 90 vs 71; AA-LCR 68 vs 36), trailing only on AA-Omniscience (14.3 vs 20). RL adapters trained on the SFT checkpoint retain speedup after RL post-training (TPF 2.25→2.10, a 6% drop); 40% end-to-end RL training speedup claimed. Lossy diffusion baselines (SDAR, Fast-dLLM v2, etc.) degrade accuracy relative to their parents while Uno does not. Baselines are current and strong for the lossless comparison (EAGLE-3, DFlash 2026 checkpoints), with careful fair-tuning of baseline sampling configs including preserving DFlash's thinking mode. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (diffusion-augmented LLM: in-architecture LoRA diffusion drafting on a frozen AR base with NTP-parameterized one-step block diffusion) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (Ψ-Spec samplers integrated into Nano-vLLM/SGLang). The genuinely novel moves are the gated-LoRA teacher/student single-pass training trick and the demonstration that the same-distribution, single-KV-cache drafting wins at serving batch sizes. The rejection-sampling machinery, DCD, tree attention, and Medusa-style candidate pruning are all existing components; the empirical finding that speedups survive RL post-training with only 6% TPF decay is a valuable and non-obvious contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for a systems paper: loss terms (TV-only vs KL combos), block-size curricula, LoRA rank/α/adapter placement, and sampler configurations, each with per-benchmark numbers. The lossless property is verified empirically against the AR distribution on Qwen3 with 95% confidence intervals over 2–10 seeds in the I-DLM comparison, and the authors catch a genuine losslessness bug in a concurrent competitor's sampler (greedy drafting without adjusted rejection sampling) — a credibility positive. Code and checkpoints are released (s-sahoo.com/uno), and all lossless baselines use public checkpoints. Concerns: (1) the Mercury 2 comparison mixes self-reported vendor numbers on Blackwell hardware with the authors' own H200 measurements; (2) the from-scratch Uno's AR base is proprietary, so its benchmark table lacks a same-size public AR reference row in the main comparison; (3) the 40% RL speedup is asserted with "detailed results in the next revision"; (4) many throughput numbers lack error bars or seeds (Table 18 medians of 3 repetitions being the exception); (5) the throughput test, while fairer than prior work, is still a synthetic workload (1024 input/8192 output) rather than measured agentic traces. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL / SYSTEMS (built samplers in two open inference engines, released checkpoints). - Practical: Yes — runs on commodity H200 nodes with standard vLLM-family serving; needs only LoRA adapters appended to existing open-weight models. - Efficient: 0.35B–0.7B added parameters and a shared KV cache beat EAGLE-3 (0.40B, separate cache) and DFlash (1.05B) on peak memory; distillation cost is small (60h/64 GPUs or 32h/32 GPUs) relative to AR pre-training. - Effective: The evidence shows the exact mechanism claimed — verified lossless speedup at all batch sizes with matching accuracy — though "up to 3×" is a best-case batch-1 tree configuration, not the serving-regime number (1.5–1.6×). - Scalable: Tested to batch 64 on one H200 and 8B scale; behavior at 100× scale (larger models, multi-node serving) is claimed via the drop-in argument but not measured, and fixed B saturation (TPF plateauing at ~2.3 for B≥16 linear) suggests drafting gains taper. Delivers a concrete software artifact: code, sampler integrations in Nano-vLLM and SGLang, and released UnoQwen/Uno checkpoints. Strengths: - The core architectural insight — that a diffusion drafter sharing the verifier's base weights and KV cache beats separate-draft-model speculative decoding at high batch sizes — is a real, actionable idea, and the 1.5–1.6× speedup at the device's max batch size is the first credible demonstration of this in the lossless setting. - Directly optimizing the TV distance between draft and verifier distributions, tied to the accepted-prefix-length theory of Leviathan et al., is a well-motivated objective choice; the ablation honestly revealing that the DCD/KL term contributes little is more informative than hiding it. - The evaluation methodology fixes a real flaw in prior diffusion-LLM comparisons (throughput measured on variable-length task traces favors short-trace models) with a controlled fixed-length test, and the grid-searched, thinking-mode-preserving baseline tuning avoids strawman comparisons. - The discovery that a concurrent method's (I-DLM R-ISD) "lossless" sampler actually breaks losslessness, plus a corrected Ψ-Spec evaluation of it, adds genuine scientific value beyond the headline method. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that quadratic sampling (merging draft and verify into one pass) needs custom kernels and is left to future work; that systematic exploration of inference-time scaling via extra denoising steps (Sec. 4.3) is deferred; that detailed RL-speedup results are promised for a next revision; that combining Uno with MTP-style architectures is unexplored; and that Mercury 2's parameter count and quantization are undisclosed, making its comparison approximate. They confront these directly rather than minimize them, which strengthens the paper's credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evidence on the quality of the from-scratch Uno's AR base relative to a strong public 8B AR model in the main comparison table — "Uno matches the qualitative performance of Base AR" is supported by losslessness in principle, but the base model itself is never benchmarked head-to-head against Qwen3-8B-class peers in Table 1, so the benchmark wins over DiffusionGemma/Mercury 2 partly reflect base-model data quality, not the method. - The DCD ablation (TV-only ≥ DCD+TV) undercuts the paper's own framing that discrete consistency distillation is the engine of the method; a reviewer would want the "diffusion distillation" story reconciled with the evidence that a plain TV-matching objective suffices. - Losslessness is verified against sampling randomness at temp=1, but hardware non-determinism in tree-attention verification across batch sizes and kernels is not analyzed; throughput-vs-exactness interactions under concurrent batching in the Nano-vLLM implementation are likewise unexamined. - The inference-time scaling claim (extra denoising steps at fixed context could exceed AR quality) is raised as motivation but never tested, even in a small pilot. - All throughput claims are single-GPU (H200); multi-node tensor-parallel serving, where the KV-cache savings argument would be stressed differently, is untested. Bottom Line: For anyone building or deploying LLM inference systems, this is currently the strongest published recipe for lossless multi-token drafting that survives real batch sizes, and it meaningfully advances the AR-plus-diffusion-hybrid design space despite the headline 3× number being a best case and the Mercury 2 comparison being apples-to-oranges.

#4 — Highly Innovative (79)

One Form to Transfer Them All: Pretraining Multilingual Language Models Beyond Native Orthography

M Zhang, A Jencks, K Badikela, Y Tsvetkov, S Kumar · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows, via controlled from-scratch pretraining of autoregressive LMs at three scales (467M/709M/1.03B) on eight languages, that romanizing all training text yields stronger cross-lingual transfer than both native orthography and IPA transcription, and that the popular recipe of fine-tuning a text-pretrained model on romanized data actively harms languages the model already covers. - Why it's important: Multilingual LMs transfer poorly across writing systems because shared-subword vocabulary — the main channel of cross-lingual transfer — collapses when scripts differ, and the field currently applies romanization as a post hoc fix whose benefits the paper shows are largely illusory for modern multilingual models. - How it does it: The core move is holding architecture, data, vocabulary size, and training procedure constant while swapping only the surface form of the pretraining corpus (Uroman romanization vs. Phonemizer IPA vs. native script), then measuring downstream transfer across prompting and fine-tuning regimes, on seen and unseen languages. - The good: The counter-intuitive, well-controlled finding that Text→Romanized fine-tuning regresses seen-language performance (e.g., MASSIVE macro-F1 drops from 69.81 to 45.25 at the small scale and from 82.94 to 64.01 at large), while the same intervention reproduces prior positive results on an English-only GPT-2 baseline — cleanly isolating when the recipe helps (no script coverage) and when it hurts. - The missing: The largest pretrained model is 387M non-embedding parameters (vs. 7B–100B+ production multilingual models), and the trend of the romanization advantage widening with scale is extrapolated rather than demonstrated at deployable scale; IPA results are also confounded by known Phonemizer quality issues on low-resource languages. - Read it or not: Read it if you pretrain or adapt multilingual models, especially for non-Latin-script languages — it directly overturns the standard romanization-as-finetuning recipe and gives the first head-to-head comparison of romanization vs. phonemization in decoder-only pretraining; skip it if you only work with monolingual or Latin-script systems.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (85) is the anchor: three-scale controlled pretraining with representation as the only variable, significance tests, a GPT-2 reproduction that resolves the contradiction with prior work, and unusual transparency (post-hoc quantification of a tokenizer bug). Novelty (80) is strong for the field — the Text→Romanized regression finding is a new empirical result that overturns a standard recipe, not just an application. Non-Obviousness (80) is high: the coverage-dependent account of when romanization helps was not predicted by prior work. Completeness (80) benefits from direct, extensive limitation acknowledgment; Resilience (72) is dented by the unresolved confound that romanized models see ~3× more documents per token budget, and the IPA arm is tool-dependent. Impact (70) reflects the released code but no model weights, and a 387M-parameter ceiling limits deployable relevance. Problem & Motivation: Multilingual language models transfer knowledge across languages primarily through shared subword vocabulary, a mechanism that fails when related languages use different writing systems — e.g., Hindi and Urdu are mutually intelligible in speech but share essentially zero tokens in native script. Prior work attacks this "script barrier" via script equalization (romanization with Uroman, or phonemization to IPA), but these two mechanisms have almost never been directly compared, the literature is dominated by encoder-only models adapted post hoc to off-the-shelf checkpoints pretrained on orthographic text, and it was unknown whether the reported gains from romanized fine-tuning (e.g., Husain et al. 2024 on Llama 2) survive when the base model is already multilingual. The paper closes the gap by asking which input representation should be chosen at pretraining time for autoregressive multilingual LMs, and whether romanization's benefits can be recovered downstream without romanized pretraining. Key Idea: Treat input surface form as the only experimental variable in autoregressive multilingual pretraining: convert the identical 8-language corpus (~21.7B words from FineWeb-2, organized into four typologically motivated pairs — English–Spanish, Russian–Polish, Hindi–Urdu, Tamil–Malayalam — spanning the space of orthographic-vs-phonological overlap) into orthographic text, IPA (with diacritics/stress stripped to maximize overlap), or Uroman romanization, and pretrain matched models on each. The insight that emerges is that romanization helps by aligning the input with lexical structure internalized during pretraining — so its gains are captured at pretraining, not retrofitted — and that fine-tuning-time romanization disrupts script-specific representations the model already has while supplying overlap when it lacks them. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) corpus construction — pair-balanced FineWeb-2 subsampling preserving within-pair resource imbalance, sized to match OpenWebText per pair (~21.7B words total; 50B text tokens vs. 33B IPA/romanized tokens after tokenization, so the non-text models are actually compute-disadvantaged, making their gains conservative); (2) representation conversion — Phonemizer (modified to preserve digits and out-of-script characters; stress, length, tone, and nasalization diacritics stripped) for IPA and Uroman for romanization; (3) tokenization — a shared 100K ByteLevel BPE tokenizer per representation, with a frequency-weighted, corpus-size-normalized Jaccard overlap analysis (Appendix A) quantifying cross-lingual subword overlap before training; (4) pretraining — modded-nanogpt causal LMs at three scales (83M/197M/387M non-embedding parameters), dual-optimizer setup (AdamW β1=0.8/β2=0.95 for embeddings/head/scalars, Muon momentum=0.95 for hidden matrices), linear cooldown LR schedule, 524,288 tokens per step on 8×H100, 3 epochs; (5) evaluation — zero/few-shot likelihood scoring on XStoryCloze and XCOPA, plus fine-tuning on XNLI/IndicNLI, MASSIVE intent classification, and XL-Sum summarization, on the eight seen languages and four unseen ones (Arabic, French share scripts with pretraining data; Bengali, Greek do not). Statistical significance is tested with an approximate randomization test (p<0.05). Critical design decisions: using Phonemizer over higher-accuracy G2P tools like Epitran for throughput (acknowledged trade-off, justified at corpus scale); keeping vocabulary size constant at 100K across representations (well-justified for controlled comparison); and diacritic stripping, which roughly doubled cross-lingual overlap in early experiments (justified empirically but heuristic). Notably, the loss function is standard causal LM cross-entropy; the contribution is the experimental design, not an algorithmic innovation. Key Results: (1) Romanized pretraining wins in every evaluation regime at every scale: e.g., XNLI macro-F1 at the large scale is 81.60 (romanized) vs. 81.16 (IPA) vs. 79.67 (text); MASSIVE macro-F1 is 84.93 vs. 84.45 vs. 82.94; unseen-language MASSIVE fine-tuning macro-F1 is 70.42 vs. 67.53 vs. 61.42; unseen XNLI macro-F1 is 74.48 vs. 69.21 vs. 68.14; XL-Sum ROUGE-L macro is 25.33 vs. 24.95 vs. 21.96. The gap over text widens with scale. (2) IPA beats text in most settings but matches romanization only on Hindi–Urdu, the pair with maximal phonological and minimal orthographic overlap, and lags romanization badly on transfer to unseen languages. (3) Text→Rom fine-tuning of the multilingual checkpoints regresses all seen languages across all benchmarks (MASSIVE small macro 45.25 vs. 69.81 for matched text) and helps only on unseen languages lacking script coverage (Bengali, Greek), with margins far below full romanized pretraining. (4) The prior-work claim is reproduced in its original regime: English-only GPT-2 (small/medium/large) fine-tuned on romanized multilingual data gains 20–30 F1 on MASSIVE for Hindi, Urdu, Tamil, Malayalam, confirming the recipe helps only when the base model lacks script coverage. (5) Sequence-length analysis on FLORES: Hindi, Tamil, and Malayalam inflate ~3× under native-script tokenization versus romanized, so equalization also closes a tokenization-fairness gap. (6) Overlap analysis shows romanization and IPA are not interchangeable: romanization lifts Russian–Polish and Tamil–Malayalam overlap to English–Spanish levels, while IPA produces its highest overlap on Hindi–Urdu. Baselines (text and IPA pretraining, Text→Rom, bilingual reference models) are current and the setup is a serious mid-scale stress test (up to 1.03B parameters, 33–50B tokens), not toy scale, though still below production multilingual models. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (primary) plus NEW METHOD-adjacent recommendation — the genuinely novel contributions are (a) the first direct controlled comparison of romanized vs. phonemized vs. orthographic pretraining for decoder-only autoregressive LMs, and (b) the demonstration that the standard Text→Romanized fine-tuning recipe regresses multilingual models that already cover the target scripts. The individual components (Uroman, Phonemizer, BPE tokenization, nanogpt-style pretraining) are all standard tools competently combined; the novelty lies in the experimental design and the resulting qualification of prior work, not in new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive: three model scales, four shot counts (k=0–4), intermediate-pretraining-checkpoint evaluation showing the representation ranking is stable throughout training, bilingual reference models isolating per-pair effects, and a GPT-2 reproduction of the prior recipe to explain the contradiction with Husain et al. (2024). Significance is tested with approximate randomization tests (p<0.05) for fine-tuning results. Single-seed runs appear to be the norm (no error bars or multi-seed variance reported), though the consistency of rankings across scales, tasks, and shot counts partially compensates. Code is released at https://github.com/skai-research/one-form-transfer. Two methodological transparency positives stand out: the authors disclose an integer-overflow bug in the HuggingFace BPE trainer discovered after submission and show in Appendix E that retraining with the fix shifts MASSIVE macro-F1 by ≤0.46 points and zero-shot accuracy by ≤0.007, preserving every pairwise ordering (though XNLI/XL-Sum were not re-run due to compute budget); and they explicitly caution that bits-per-character values are not comparable across representations. Concerns: the IPA arm is evaluated with a known-noisy tool (Phonemizer/eSpeak) on low-resource languages, so IPA's second-place ranking may partly reflect tooling rather than the representation; and the corpus conversion applies the same Phonemizer/Uroman pipelines to downstream data, so evaluation inputs share preprocessing artifacts with training inputs. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (controlled pretraining experiments, no deployed system). - Practical: Yes — models up to 1.03B parameters train on 8×H100, well within commercially available hardware, and the representation conversion uses freely available rule-based/libraries (Uroman, Phonemizer). - Efficient: Romanization/IPA actually reduce cost for non-Latin scripts — Hindi, Tamil, Malayalam documents compress ~3× in tokens versus native script, cutting training compute per document, inference latency, and API cost — and the non-text models trained on fewer tokens (33B vs. 50B) still win, so the gains are if anything understated. - Effective: The evidence shows strong transfer gains on seen and unseen languages, but effectiveness in user-facing generation is unresolved: the authors did not evaluate phoneme/grapheme-to-text conversion back to native orthography, so a romanized-native model cannot directly serve users who read Devanagari, Arabic, or Tamil script. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 387M non-embedding parameters; the claim that the romanization advantage widens with scale is supported only up to that point and explicitly flagged as needing future work at 7B–100B+ scale, and no logographic writing systems (e.g., Chinese) were covered, so extension to those is speculative. Deliverable: code repository and training/evaluation recipes; no pretrained model weights are mentioned as released. Strengths: - The Text→Rom negative result is the paper's most valuable contribution: by reproducing prior positive results on English-only GPT-2 and showing reversal on multilingual checkpoints, it converts an apparent contradiction with Husain et al. (2024) into a coherent coverage-dependent account, directly changing practice for anyone adapting existing multilingual models with romanized data. - The controlled design is genuinely rigorous for this literature: identical data, vocabulary size, architecture, and optimizer across representations, with the non-text arms trained on ~34% fewer tokens yet still winning, making their advantage conservative under FLOP-matched comparison. - The typologically motivated pairing (English–Spanish as a shared-script control through Hindi–Urdu as maximal phonological/minimal orthographic overlap) lets the paper explain when IPA matches romanization rather than just reporting aggregate wins. - Unusual transparency: disclosing and quantifying the tokenizer integer-overflow bug post-submission (Appendix E), and explicitly refusing to compare bits-per-character across representations, both exceed field norms. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a credibility positive). They acknowledge: (1) scale — 387M non-embedding parameters versus 7B–100B+ production models; (2) language coverage — only alphabetic/abugida scripts, no logographic systems (e.g., Chinese), and no systematic study of how language-family distance or loanwords modulate the effects; (3) transcription quality — Phonemizer/eSpeak support is incomplete for some languages, diacritic stripping and digit-preservation are simple heuristics, and Unicode is likely a poor representation for phonemes, so better phonemization could change IPA results; and (4) no evaluation of converting romanized/IPA output back to orthographic text for generative use, with both conversions being lossy and potentially irreversible. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-seed pretraining: each (representation, scale) cell appears to be trained once; with no seed variance reported, scale-dependent interactions (e.g., the claimed widening gap) rest on one run per cell, though cross-task consistency mitigates this. - The romanized models' advantage partly confounds representation quality with effective data coverage: because non-Latin documents consume ~3× fewer tokens under romanization, romanized models see ~3× more documents per language within the fixed token budget, so part of the gain could reflect effective data augmentation rather than subword overlap per se; no FLOP- or token-matched control isolates this. - IPA's second place is entangled with Phonemizer quality, which the authors acknowledge, but no upper-bound experiment (e.g., Epitran on a subset, or gold phoneme transcripts) establishes whether better phonemization would close the gap to romanization — the headline "romanization beats IPA" claim is thus tool-dependent. - The i64 tokenizer fix was re-verified only on MASSIVE and zero-shot prompting; XNLI and XL-Sum conclusions rest on the buggy-tokenizer runs, justified by the small measured deltas but not directly confirmed. - No perplexity-based or linguistic-analysis evidence for the proposed mechanism ("romanization aligns with internalized lexical structure") — the mechanistic claim is plausible but supported only indirectly through behavior; the authors note representational analysis as future work. - In-context learning gains are small and few-shot prompting adds little over zero-shot (visible in Table 12), so the prompting-regime evidence for romanization is thinner than the fine-tuning-regime evidence, though the ordering is consistent. Bottom Line: For anyone pretraining or adapting multilingual LMs — particularly for Indic, Cyrillic, or other non-Latin-script languages — this is worth reading as the first controlled evidence that input surface form is a first-order pretraining design decision and that the popular romanized-fine-tuning recipe backfires on already-multilingual models; its ~1B-parameter ceiling and tool-dependent IPA arm mean it sets the agenda for scale-up rather than settling it, but no comparable head-to-head study exists.

EvoSafeHarness: Evolving Model- and Domain-Specific Harnesses for Securing Agents (11 ▲ )

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EvoSafeHarness, an automated search framework that synthesizes a deployable safety harness (natural-language policy plus executable code logic) for a specific frozen LLM in a specific application domain, rather than applying one fixed expert-designed defense. - Why it's important: Agent failures carry real-world consequences (payments, credential leaks, deleted data), and existing fixed defenses either over-block strong models (CaMeL drops DeepSeek benign utility to 0.0% on AgentDyn) or under-protect weak ones (ASR stays at 29.3% for GLM-5), so the safety-utility trade-off is currently chosen badly for most deployments. - How it does it: It runs a Designer-Criticizer-Analyzer loop over an archive of candidate harnesses, scoring each with a staged cheap-to-expensive evaluation cascade that separately measures benign utility, direct-attack ASR, and indirect-injection ASR, and screens candidates with a fresh-context adversarial review that rejects rules keyed to benchmark artifacts (filenames, tool names, literal strings). - The good: On the 15-cell DecodingTrust-Agent grid it cuts average ASR from 45.6% to 10.0% for a 3.3-point utility cost, winning 14 of 15 cells with paired McNemar significance in 13 (pooled p ≈ 2×10⁻⁷⁸), and the AgentDojo-searched harness transfers unchanged to unseen AgentDyn suites at 75.0% utility and 0.0% ASR — above the undefended agent. - The missing: Baselines are all fixed, frozen designs while EvoSafeHarness gets a per-cell search with expert-curated domain specifications and a security warm start, so the paper cannot separate the gain from per-deployment search per se from the gain from simply tuning any defense to the test distribution; no searched-variant of a baseline is compared. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or deploy agent guardrails — it is currently the clearest quantitative case that harness design should be deployment-specific, and the released mechanism inventories and failure-trace analyses are independently useful; skip it if you only want new attack techniques or theoretical guarantees, as it offers neither.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents act through tool calls, so unsafe behavior spans both indirect prompt injections (adversarial content in tool results, emails, files) and direct harmful user requests. Model-level defenses alone provide no system-level enforcement boundary, motivating harness-level defenses such as CaMeL, DRIFT, Progent, and SafeHarness. The gap: all of these are designed once by experts and applied unchanged across heterogeneous models and domains. The paper argues (and measures) that the optimal harness is deployment-dependent on two axes — the model determines how much external enforcement is tolerable before utility collapses, and the domain determines which safety relations, state, and lifecycle enforcement points are even relevant (filesystem threats need command/path/dataflow checks; finance needs trade-vs-egress routing and a transaction ledger to catch wash trading). No prior work searches a defense per model×domain deployment. Key Idea: Treat harness construction as a constrained search problem — maximize score = U − ASR over all programs H = (P, C) valid under a deployment adapter — and make that search safe by closing the three shortcuts open-ended security search would otherwise take: (1) a scalar score that never rewards refuse-all behavior because utility and ASR are always paired; (2) a fresh-context Criticizer plus an explicit generalization mandate ("would this rule still fire if the attacker renamed the path or rephrased the instruction?") that rejects rules keyed to benchmark artifacts before evaluation budget is spent; and (3) a three-channel evaluation signal (benign / direct / indirect) so the Designer can attribute each failure to the right control to revise. The search itself is a trace-driven agentic loop warm-started from distilled experience of existing defenses (CaMeL, DRIFT), which serve as guidance, not templates. Methodology: The system is a four-component loop (Algorithm 1) around a frozen victim model M and domain D: (1) a domain specification fixes the victim, tools, judges, threat semantics, immutable adapter (a Python Defense object with system_prompt_transform, on_pre_tool_call, on_post_tool_call hooks on DTAP; pipeline elements on AgentDojo), train-only cascade, and anti-overfit robustness check; (2) the Designer reads an explicit archive (source, parent, hypothesis, cascade scores, Criticizer verdicts, per-task traces) and applies any free-form edit to the (P, C) pair, changing one mechanism at a time when possible; (3) a fresh-context Criticizer — an independent LLM exempt from the frozen-model constraint — attempts to construct the cheapest intent-preserving evasion before any cascade run; (4) a four-stage nested cascade (static import check → smoke prefix → bootstrap confidence gate stopping only candidates whose one-sided 95% upper bound is >δ points below the no-defense reference → full search extension of the same evidence stream) scores survivors with score(M,H,D) = 100·(U − ASR); (5) the Analyzer distills failed traces into reusable design experience. Held-out splits are never read by the Designer or Criticizer. Critical design decisions: the anti-artifact Criticizer (justified by a controlled ablation showing its removal leaves search score unchanged or higher but costs up to 31 held-out points); the conservative confidence gate (justified by a replay showing zero score regret versus full evaluation while saving 43.6% of evaluation tokens); and warm-starting from eight distilled security experiences (justified by a 9.5–11.9 point held-out score gain in all three domains when present). Key Results: - DecodingTrust-Agent (primary): 15-cell grid (5 victims × 3 domains; per cell 30 benign / 35 direct / 35 indirect held-out tasks). EvoSafeHarness achieves 79.8% utility at 10.0% ASR versus no-defense 83.1%/45.6%, CaMeL 69.7%/37.7%, DRIFT 77.1%/42.4%, Progent 56.4%/10.5%. Best score in 14 of 15 cells; the single loss (Sonnet 4.6/finance) starts at 2.9% undefended ASR. McNemar significant in 13/15 cells; pooled 385 attacks neutralized vs 11 newly opened. Baselines are ported once and frozen — current and representative of the 2025–2026 system-level defense landscape. - Agent-SafetyBench (240 held-out tasks × 6 conditions, 1 rollout): only defense that lowers both unsafe-behaviour rate (24.6%→12.3%) and ASR (17.2%→7.4%) while raising utility under attack (61.6%→63.4%), averaged over three victims; best per-victim result in every block against CaMeL, DRIFT, Progent, SafeHarness. - AgentDojo→AgentDyn transfer: 82.8% utility at 0.0% ASR on AgentDojo (CaMeL: 41.0% at 0.0%); frozen transfer to unseen AgentDyn suites gives 75.0% utility at 0.0% ASR, above the undefended 73.3%. CaMeL completes zero AgentDyn tasks; Progent drops to 9.7% utility. - Adaptive attacks (AgentCanary): frozen harness holds 9.7% ASR at PAIR budget 0, rising to a 16.7–25.0% range (mean 19.5%) at refinement budget 16 across three attacker models — still below the 23.6% undefended static-prompt rate. - Ablations: the outer search model matters mainly for ASR (5.24–17.62% across four designers at comparable utility); removing the security warm-up costs 9.5–11.9 held-out points per domain; removing the Criticizer costs 18.6–31.0 held-out points while leaving search score unchanged or better. Residual failures concentrate in risk types lacking an observable runtime invariant (client-targeted scams stay at 60.0%, options solicitation at 30.0%, telecom finance fraud at 16.7%). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (automated per-deployment security-harness synthesis with anti-overfitting review) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (deployment-dependence of the harness optimum, with a concrete taxonomy: domain semantics determine which safety relations and state to protect; model and runtime behavior determine how and where to enforce them). The constituent techniques — trace-driven agentic code search (from Meta-Harness), natural-language policy surfaces (NLAH), multi-fidelity evaluation cascades (VeRO/AHE) — are existing ideas; the genuinely new elements are the threat-stratified scoring, the fresh-context adversarial reviewer targeting benchmark-artifact overfitting, and the demonstration that this regime transfers zero-shot and survives adaptive attack. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for this area. Ablations isolate the outer model, warm start, Criticizer, and cascade; per-cell statistics use exact McNemar tests and 95% Wilson intervals with an honest treatment of near-boundary zero counts; the nested-cascade cost replay is built on process-attributed token/dollar telemetry rather than estimates; utility and security are always reported jointly, refusing the trivial refuse-all solution. Code and the candidate archive are released (github.com/SaFo-Lab/EvoSafeHarness; project page andylinx.github.io/EvoSafeHarness). Concerns: (1) the structural asymmetry — EvoSafeHarness is searched per evaluation cell while every baseline is frozen — is the point of the paper but means headline numbers conflate method and adaptivity; (2) per-cell held-out sets are small (30 benign tasks), so utility costs are within noise, as the authors themselves note; (3) ASB uses a single rollout per condition; (4) search runs are not replicated per cell, so variance of the stochastic search itself is unmeasured (the outer-model ablation on one victim partially mitigates this); (5) this is an arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a search framework plus the harnesses it produces, evaluated extensively). - Practical: Yes — victims are commercially served models (Claude, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen) and the output is an ordinary Python Defense object or pipeline element; no special hardware. - Efficient: Search is expensive (inner evaluation envelope of 58,874 victim calls / $328.74 plus 40.5M fresh outer tokens per grid), but the nested cascade cuts evaluation cost 43.6% with zero selection regret, and 4 of 15 returned bundles need no runtime auxiliary LLM calls at all; per-deployment cost is the dominant economic question and is honestly ledgered rather than hidden. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem on the tested benchmarks, including a zero-shot transfer test and an adaptive-attack test — both are the right stress tests and both pass. - Scalable: Tested at 15 deployments plus three transfer suites; the framework parallelizes naturally (4–8 concurrent episodes), but the paper has not demonstrated per-deployment search cost at 10–100× the domain count, and the manual curation of each domain specification (including risk taxonomies, worth 9.5–11.9 points) is a human cost that does not obviously scale. The work delivers a real software artifact (code, search archive, per-cell harness bundles, telemetry) rather than stopping at paper form. Strengths: - The most rigorous evaluation protocol this reviewer has seen in the agent-defense literature: paired per-task statistics, sealed held-out splits the search components provably cannot read, joint reporting of utility with every safety number, and an exact cost ledger — most of this is absent from the CaMeL/DRIFT/Progent papers it compares against. - The anti-overfitting mechanism is a genuine contribution: the Criticizer ablation (Table 4a) shows search-set score unchanged or better without review while held-out score drops 14–31 points, with a code audit identifying the specific token-keyed rules responsible — a clean, mechanistic demonstration of Goodhart risk in automated defense search. - The qualitative analysis (§7) is unusually substantive: the progression from open-world content classification to closed-world action relations, order-independent two-legged coupling for wash-trading, and the concurrency-safe pre-hook cap are reusable design patterns, and the residual-risk audit honestly names the regime where the method fails (harms with no observable runtime invariant). - The discovered asymmetry — six of fifteen bundles omit the NL policy and four need no runtime LLM judge — is a surprising, actionable finding that contradicts the LLM-judge-heavy default in this space. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them: residual failures concentrate in five risk types (54 of 105) and three risk types show zero measured reduction because no destination, ownership, or trajectory invariant can certify truth or intent without also rejecting legitimate advice; the hook interface cannot inspect a tool-free final answer (the telecom value-distortion traces); small fixed test sets mis-rank candidates (38.2% of comparable mutations do not improve the search score; seven of fifteen returned bundles are not the small-stage maximum in their lineage); and they explicitly recommend train-only adaptive probes and an evidence-aware pre-response hook as future work. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central comparison never includes a searched baseline: running the same per-deployment optimization loop on Progent's policy format, or even scalar-score-only search without the security stack, would isolate how much gain comes from per-deployment search versus EvoSafeHarness's specific components. The ablations cover the latter but not the former. - The "automatic" framing undersells the human input: the domain specification includes a curated risk taxonomy, rules, and examples that the ablation shows are worth 9.5–11.9 held-out points; writing these specifications is expert labor the paper does not cost or scope. - Transfer is demonstrated for exactly one benchmark family (AgentDojo→AgentDyn); the fifteen DTAP harnesses are never cross-applied to show that their domain-specific mechanisms would fail elsewhere, which would be the direct experimental confirmation of the paper's core thesis. - The Criticizer reviews code and policy text; it never executes adversarial probes against the live candidate, so its review power is bounded by what an LLM can spot by reading — the authors' proposed train-only adaptive red-teaming is the missing stronger version. - Single search run per cell with no seed variance; per-cell utility differences of 3 points cannot be resolved with 30 benign tasks, so the headline "3.3-point utility cost" carries wide uncertainty the authors acknowledge but do not resolve with more benign tasks. - ASB evaluation uses one rollout per condition, and utility-under-attack differences of ~1–2 points between EvoSafeHarness and DRIFT/CaMeL rest on that single measurement. Bottom Line: This is the strongest evidence yet that agent safety harnesses should be searched per deployment rather than designed once — the evaluation rigor alone raises the bar for the field — but practitioners should read it as a well-instrumented existence proof whose headline comparison (searched vs. frozen) inflates the apparent advantage, and whose per-deployment search cost and expert-written domain specifications remain the open engineering problems.
