Problem & Motivation: Practitioners post-training LLMs with verifiable rewards (RLVR/GRPO) face a credit-assignment bottleneck: outcome rewards assign one scalar per response, so gradients cannot distinguish helpful reasoning tokens from harmful ones. On-policy distillation (OPD) fixes this with per-token teacher distributions, but the teacher question is unresolved: external stronger models degrade on the student's novel prefixes (distribution mismatch), and on-policy self-distillation with privileged conditioning (e.g., conditioning on a correct solution) is limited by the model's in-context learning capacity. Prior remedies (token gating, divergence mixing, DAgger-style rollouts, trajectory refinement) all accept a flawed teacher as given. RISE asks instead what the teacher should be, targeting labs and engineers running RLVR who cannot or do not want to field a separate stronger teacher. Key Idea: The model's own RLVR training trajectory contains a usable teacher: since post-training updates are dominated by a low-rank subspace and evolve approximately linearly (top-3 principal components capture ~87% of displacement variance in the authors' runs), linearly extrapolating the displacement from an anchor checkpoint through the current post-RLVR checkpoint (β > 1) yields a synthetic "future" policy that is closer to the convergence point π* than the student is — and distilling that teacher's token-level distribution converts a sparse outcome-driven parameter update into dense supervision. Because the displacement is refreshed every iteration, this becomes a recursive improvement loop rather than one-shot compression. Methodology: Each iteration has two phases on the same rollouts. (1) RLVR phase: GRPO-style clipped policy-gradient update from π_θn to θ′n+1 using outcome rewards. (2) OPD phase: construct the teacher π_future and distill it via a top-(K+1) Jensen–Shannon divergence loss (K=100, or 20 for code), with π_future held under stop-gradient. Two instantiations of the representation map φ: logit-space (geometric mixture π_future ∝ π_θn^(1−β)·π_θ′n+1^β, computed on the post-RLVR checkpoint's top-K support plus a tail bucket — no extra model needed) and weight-space (task arithmetic θ_future = θ_anchor + β·(θ′n+1 − θ_anchor), materialized and evaluated with one teacher forward pass per step). Supporting machinery: a monotonically decaying β schedule (β_n = 1 + (β₀−1)(1−n/N)) justified by a linear-trajectory analysis showing the safe range (1, 2α*/α_n − 1) narrows as training converges; an EMA anchor (η) to smooth noisy displacement directions; and a reverse-KL trust-region decomposition (Remark 1) where the loss repels from the anchor and regularizes toward the post-RLVR checkpoint. Theoretical support includes a performance-difference-based suboptimality decomposition (Theorem 2) and a contraction corollary, both explicitly framed as directional mechanism analyses rather than tight certificates. Critical design decisions — distill rather than adopt θ_future directly, require RLVR grounding for the direction, decay β — are each validated empirically (§4.3), which is above-average justification discipline. Key Results: Tested on Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B, Qwen2.5-3B, and OLMo3-7B across math (DAPOMath, OpenR1-Math-46K), multi-domain STEM, code (Skywork-OR1-Code), and agentic tasks (ALFWorld, WebShop). Baselines are GRPO plus three privileged-conditioning OPSD methods (GRPO+SDPO, SDAR, RLSD) sharing the same teacher; external-teacher OPD is excluded. Highlights: OLMo3-7B AIME'24 improves from 30.2 (GRPO) to 46.9 (RISE logit, +16.7) and Math Avg 47.6→56.4 (+8.8); Qwen3-1.7B Math Avg 45.4→50.2 (+4.8); Qwen3-8B Math Avg 60.0→62.7 (weight-space; multi-seed 62.4±0.2 vs. 60.1±0.2). Multi-domain (Qwen3-4B-Base): Math Avg 44.8 vs. GRPO's 40.2. Agentic (Qwen2.5-3B): ALFWorld +9.4, WebShop accuracy +10.9 over GRPO. Code shows faster convergence but only comparable final accuracy (e.g., matches GRPO's HumanEval+ at step 50 vs. 90). A compute-matched GRPO-2× control gains only +0.5 to +1.9, versus RISE's +2.7 to +4.8, attributing gains to supervision quality rather than extra gradient steps. Removing RLVR grounding collapses training within 60 steps (MATH-500 → 2.4%, length explodes to the 8K cap); removing OPD forfeits the gains (60.0→60.3 at 8B). pass@16 improves alongside avg@16 (+9.6 vs. +6.3 at 1.7B on AIME'24), indicating broadened coverage rather than mere sharpening. Direct checkpoint extrapolation (Fig. 6) empirically confirms the narrowing safe-β range (β=2.0 gives +7.3 at step 50 but −15 at step 100). These are preprint, self-reported numbers; scale is standard (1.7B–8B, single node of 8 GPUs), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING). The genuinely novel move is constructing the OPD teacher by extrapolating the student's own RLVR trajectory, converting model-merging linearity results (task arithmetic, linear mode connectivity, rank-1 RLVR dynamics — all prior work) from an interpolation tool into a recursive teacher-generation mechanism. The components — GRPO, top-K KL/JSD distillation, task arithmetic, geometric mixtures — are standard; the combination and, especially, the refresh-every-iteration recursion with a decaying β are new. The closest prior work, ExOPD's reward extrapolation, shares the geometric-mixture form but uses a static external teacher; the authors' distinction (non-stationary teacher, no external model) is fair though they note a direct comparison is inapplicable. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above average for this area. Ablations cover β₀, decay schedule, anchor dynamics (η), rollout reuse vs. resampling, compute-matched controls, and phase removals; three-seed runs with reported standard deviations (≤0.6 on Math Avg, gains of +2.2 to +4.5) establish the margins exceed seed noise; the top-K bias is analyzed explicitly (Appendix A.4) and the trajectory dimensionality is measured on the authors' own checkpoints, not just cited. Concerns: (a) η and β defaults are tuned per model family (η=0.1 helps Qwen but costs −6.3 on OLMo), so the method carries per-deployment hyperparameter sensitivity; (b) no external-teacher OPD baseline, justified but leaving the central "is the extrapolated teacher actually better than a strong external teacher?" question untested; (c) Theorem 2's T-prefactor bound is admittedly loose and Proposition 3 assumes an exactly linear trajectory — the authors are candid about this; (d) preprint, not peer-reviewed; no code or model release is mentioned in the provided text. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a training method run by the authors across six model configurations). - Practical: Yes — VeRL on a single 8-GPU node; no teacher model beyond the policy itself. - Efficient: 1.3–1.6× GRPO wall time (rollout generation shared; OPD adds one gradient phase plus an anchor forward pass), with no additional sampling cost — a favorable trade for the measured gains. - Effective: Evidence covers math, STEM, code, and agentic tasks with OOD checks and pass@k coverage analysis, but gains shrink with model scale (+4.8 at 1.7B, +2.7 at 8B on Math Avg) and vanish on saturated code benchmarks, so effectiveness at the high end is less certain. - Scalable: Only claimed by extrapolation from 1.7B→8B trends; nothing tests whether the low-rank linear-trajectory premise and modest β₀≤1.5 safe range hold at 70B+, where the method's value would matter most. Deliverable: method and analysis only — no released library, weights, or dataset are mentioned, so it currently stops at paper form. Strengths: - The core reframing — treat the OPD teacher as a design variable and synthesize it from the training trajectory — is a genuinely new answer to a question the field has been patching around, and it cleanly eliminates both the external-model dependency and the privileged-conditioning pathology. - The negative controls are unusually informative: the no-RLVR collapse (reward → 0, length explosion within 60 steps) and the no-OPD null result together pin down the mechanism, showing distillation (not longer steps) and grounding (not raw extrapolation) are each load-bearing. - Fig. 6's direct checkpoint-extrapolation experiment converts the theoretical safe-β claim into measured evidence (β=2.0: +7.3 pts at step 50, −15 pts at step 100), providing rare direct validation of a training-dynamics assumption. - Honest accounting of scale sensitivity: the paper reports that gains shrink at 8B and that η must flip between Qwen and OLMo, rather than hiding configuration-dependent tuning. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that RISE depends on the trajectory being sufficiently low-dimensional for linear extrapolation to remain meaningful at modest β; that principled detection of when extrapolation becomes unreliable is open (decay and EMA are empirical patches); and that RISE inherits and potentially amplifies any RLVR reward biases — a hackable reward gets its spurious direction extrapolated. They also concede in-text that the theory is directional, not a tight certificate, and that β₀=2.0 diverges. This is direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The strongest omitted baseline is a strong external-teacher OPD run at matched compute. The exclusion argument (RISE's premise is eliminating the external model) is legitimate for the no-external-model setting, but a practitioner with access to a strong teacher needs to know which option wins; the paper cannot answer this. - Configuration-dependent hyperparameters (η=0.1 vs. 1.0 flips sign across model families; K=20 for code) suggest the method needs per-run tuning that the single recommended default does not capture, and no guidance is given for a new model family. - The gain shrinks monotonically with base-model strength (+4.8 at 1.7B, +2.7 at 8B, ~0 on saturated code), and the 1.7B-Base (non-instruct) margin is only +1.2 — consistent with the method having limited headroom on strong or weak-extremes policies, which the paper notes but does not probe. - Related concurrent work on rank-1 RLVR trajectory extrapolation (Wei et al., 2026, cited) suggests cheap checkpoint extrapolation for capability gain is being discovered in parallel; the paper does not empirically compare against that simpler recipe (e.g., extrapolating a single RLVR run's final checkpoint), so the incremental value of the full recursive loop over one-shot extrapolation is not isolated. - All evaluation is on math/STEM/code/agentic benchmarks with objectively checkable rewards; the recursive loop's behavior under noisy or subjective reward models — the regime where the amplification risk the authors flag bites hardest — is untested. Bottom Line: A practitioner running RLVR post-training should read and try this: the extrapolated-teacher construction is simple, cheap (1.3–1.6× wall time), mechanistically well-validated, and likely to transfer, even though the shrinking gains at scale, per-family hyperparameter tuning, and missing external-teacher comparison mean it is an improvement to GRPO pipelines rather than a demonstrated replacement for stronger-teacher distillation.

Unifying Conformal Language Tasks with In-Context Ensembles (5 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Conformal Relevance, a framework that replaces task-specific hand-engineered LLM scoring prompts in recall-oriented conformal content selection with a fixed mean ensemble of four in-context-learning (ICL) example-selection strategies (Ens4), plus a theoretical characterization of when score ensembling raises the conformal floor. - Why it's important: Conformal coverage guarantees on content selection (summarization, QA, PII detection, legal clause scoring) are only as useful as the scoring function's conciseness, and prior state-of-the-art scoring required labor-intensive, brittle, per-task prompt engineering. - How it does it: Four mechanistically distinct ICL example retrieval strategies (anchor-DPP, pattern-DPP, BM25, random) each induce an LLM relevance scorer on a common [0,1] scale; Problem & Motivation: Many NLP tasks reduce to selecting relevant content spans from documents under two constraints: coverage (retain enough pertinent content) and conciseness (drop irrelevant content). Conformal prediction supplies a finite-sample, distribution-free recall-style coverage guarantee (P[|ŷ∩y|/|y| ≥ β] ≥ 1−α), but conciseness depends entirely on the quality of the relevance scoring function R(c;x). Prior work (conformal factuality, conformal importance, conformal agent error attribution) instantiated R as an LLM with a manually crafted, task-specific prompt — expensive to write, brittle, and unscalable across the many instantiations of content selection. The gap this paper closes: a single, task-agnostic scoring mechanism that maintains the coverage guarantee while improving conciseness with minimal manual input. Key Idea: Replace the definition of relevance written in natural language by demonstrations of it: curate a small labeled ICL pool, retrieve examples via four deliberately diverse strategies so that the resulting scorers' failures on positive spans do not coincide, and average their scores. The theoretical core is a complementarity condition — for K=2, the ensemble floor decomposes as S(2) = ½(Smax + Smin + Comp), and ensembling beats both individual scorers iff Comp > Smax − Smin — meaning designers should seek scorers whose lowest-scoring positives differ. Score-level (rather than set-level) ensembling preserves the 1−α guarantee without the 1−2α degradation of majority-vote set merging. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) split data into an ICL pool Π (50 examples, or 20/intent), a calibration set C (n=100), and a test set; (2) for each input, each of K=4 selection strategies σj draws k=2 ICL examples (anchor_dpp: nearest-document anchor then conditional DPP over cosine-Gram kernels; pattern_dpp: DPP over positive-minus-negative span-centroid "relevance direction" vectors; bm25: lexical top-k; random: uniform, serving as a regularizer); (3) each induces a Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite scorer Rj ∈ [0,1]; (4) the mean R̄ is used to compute the recall-oriented conformal score Sβ (the r-th order statistic of positive-span scores), the threshold q̂ is calibrated as the ⌊α(n+1)⌋-th order statistic, and test spans with R̄(c) ≥ q̂ form the prediction set. Coverage validity holds because each Rj is a deterministic function of x once ICL examples are fixed, with per-sample retrieval handled by conditioning on the pool and the tower property (Appendix B). Critical design decisions: fixed (non-data-driven) mean aggregation to avoid breaking exchangeability — justified and contrasted with Ochoa Rivera et al.'s two-stage calibration; mechanistic (retrieval) rather than stochastic (temperature) diversity — supported by controls; and a small k=2 per scorer — supported by the k-ablation showing degradation at k≥5. Extensions to β<1 replace the minimum with the r-th order statistic; proofs of all lemmas/propositions are in Appendix C. Key Results: On seven sentence-level relevance datasets across five domains (ECTSum, SubSumE, PUMA, PhysioNet, HotpotQA, Evidence Inference, ContractNLI; 1,482–59,922 test spans; docs of 14–461 sentences), Ens4 (Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, k=2, K=4) achieves MAP of 0.516 (ECTSum), 0.304 (Evidence Inf.), 0.839 (HotpotQA), 0.879 (PhysioNet), 0.814 (PUMA), 0.464 (SubSumE), 0.828 (ContractNLI) — versus ICL0 hand-crafted prompts at 0.206–0.764 and the post-hoc Best Single strategy, with gains over ICL0 of +0.090 to +0.170 MAP (+12% to +59%), all CIs excluding zero. Ens4 also beats Best Single on all seven (+5% to +43%). At fixed coverage (α=0.2, β=0.8), conciseness gains over ICL0 range from +0.083 (ECTSum) to +0.540 (SubSumE), with the paper claiming up to ~50% reduction in retained length. Empirical coverage stays within 1 pp of target over 400 random calibration/test splits. Mean-ensembling beats majority vote (which under-covers by −1.4 pp at α=0.2), COLA, and union-of-sets on coverage deviation and conciseness (0.711 vs 0.586 average conciseness for averaged single scorers). Notable secondary findings: no single selection strategy dominates (random is best on PhysioNet); Ens4 beats a supervised logistic-regression classifier trained on the full pool on 6/7 datasets (classifier wins on ECTSum, 0.615 vs 0.516); serial latency multipliers vs ICL0 range from 2.3× to 18×. Cross-model checks on Llama3-8B, Qwen3-8B (4 datasets) and GPT-5.6-terra (7 datasets, 500-sample subsets) largely hold, though Ens4 vs ICL0 on Llama3-8B/HotpotQA is a tie (−0.002). Baselines are reasonable for the conformal-LLM subfield (Mohri & Hashimoto-style prompting, Kuwahara et al. conformal importance), though no comparison to fine-tuned task-specific rerankers is given. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a task-agnostic ICL-ensemble scoring function for recall-oriented conformal content selection) plus NEW FORMULATION (a mathematical characterization — complementarity decomposition and O(1/K) diminishing-returns bound — of when score-level ensembling improves recall-oriented conformal scores). The ingredients are individually standard: split conformal prediction (Vovk et al.), score-level aggregation (Ochoa Rivera et al. 2025, established for classification/regression), ICL example selection with DPPs (Ye et al. 2023), and BM25 retrieval. The genuinely new parts are (a) porting score aggregation to recall-style coverage for language tasks with an exchangeability-preserving fixed mean, (b) the Comp condition and its β<1 generalization, and (c) the empirical demonstration that retrieval-induced diversity, not extra labels or stochasticity, drives the gain. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Ablations cover ICL count k (5 values), ensemble size K (all 11 non-singleton subsets), task hints (3 regimes), intent stratification, windowed ICL, and three cross-checks isolating complementarity (equal-ICL-budget at k=8, supervised classifier, temperature-diversity ensembles with matched compute — Ens4 wins 12/16 with overlapping CIs in the rest, and beats compute-matched ICL0×4 on 6/7). Theory is validated empirically: the Lemma 1 condition co-occurs with observed advantage 99.5%+ of the time over 471,378 pooled samples, with residuals attributed to floating-point ties. Statistics: 400 random calibration/test splits, 95% bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples); the authors honestly note the 7/7 pattern shares a model/template/seeds and should not be read as seven independent trials. Code is released at github.com/layer6ai-labs/conformal-relevance, with full prompt templates, retry logic, and dataset reformulation details in appendices. Concerns: (1) the primary metric (MAP) is measured on the same split structure the method is tuned on for defaults (k=2 chosen from observed behavior across these datasets — mild Goodhart risk since the default configuration is described as "untuned" but was selected after development experiments); (2) four of seven datasets were reformulated by the authors into binary sentence relevance, so the evaluation tests a proxy construction; (3) the ICL0 baseline prompts were written by the same authors, and prompt-engineering effort for ICL0 ("written once without empirical tuning" on 6/7 datasets) may under-represent what skilled prompt engineering achieves; (4) hosted-API inference introduces irreproducible server-side variation, which the authors flag. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — released code). Practical: Yes — needs only API access to a small LLM (Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite), a 22M-parameter embedding model, and BM25; no training. Efficient: 4× the scoring LLM calls of a single prompt (input-token ratio approaching 4×), with measured serial wall-clock multipliers of 2.3×–18× (calls are parallelizable, which mitigates latency but not cost); label budget of 150–440 examples per task is modest but nonzero. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem — better conciseness at guaranteed coverage across seven tasks — though the guarantee is marginal, not conditional (per-intent/stratum coverage is not assured; Mondrian methods would be needed). Scalability: Not tested beyond 10,000-sample test sets and documents of ≤461 sentences; behavior with drifted distributions or much larger pools is untested, and per-sample ICL retrieval over a growing pool adds negligible-but-unquantified cost. Deliverables: released code and processing scripts, a reusable theoretical framework (complementarity condition, β<1 extension), and a recipe (Ens4 configuration); no trained model weights. Strengths: - The complementarity condition (Lemma 1) is a clean, checkable characterization — and the authors actually verify it per-sample at scale (471,378 spans, 99.5% agreement), which is rare for a theory-motivated LLM paper. - The controls in Section 5.3/App. I genuinely isolate the claimed mechanism: equal ICL budget (k=8 single vs 8 spread over 4 scorers), equal labels (supervised classifier), and equal compute with stochastic diversity (temperature ensembles, ICL0×4) each rule out a mundane alternative explanation. - A single fixed configuration (Ens4, k=2, one-line hint) transfers across seven tasks and three model families, directly supporting the "minimal manual input" claim; the no-single-winner heterogeneity finding (random wins on PhysioNet) independently motivates ensembling. - Honest statistical hygiene: shared-configuration caveat on the 7/7 pattern, coverage-vs-target within 1 pp with proper bounds, and an unusually candid Limitations section. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length: required labeled data (150–440 examples) and a static, non-drifting relevance criterion for exchangeability; the optional one-line task hint (PhysioNet collapse from 0.879 to 0.549 without it); a limited and already-surpassed model set; 4× test-time compute cost; irreproducible server-side variation from the hosted LLM (replicate aggregate MAP, not per-sample scores); only marginal (not conditional) coverage; and sparse-positive pools limiting ICL informativeness. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Four of seven evaluation datasets were reformulated by the authors into sentence-level binary relevance (e.g., ECTSum positives defined by ROUGE alignment to a human summary; ContractNLI positives = gold evidence spans), so the "unification" claim is evaluated on the authors' own constructed proxies rather than native task metrics (no downstream ROUGE, exact-match, or legal-review accuracy is reported). - The ICL0 baseline's strength depends on authors' own prompt-writing effort; no comparison against a stronger externally-validated prompt, a fine-tuned reranker, or non-conformal selective-summarization baselines, so the cost of the framework relative to the best non-conformal alternative is unknown. - The Ens4 default (k=2, these four strategies) was presumably selected through development experimentation on these same datasets; the "untuned" framing is in tension with the observed k-ablation landscape, and no fully held-out new task tests the framework zero-shot at deployment time. - Ensemble diversity is heuristic — the theory says what property (non-coinciding minimizers) helps but the method offers no procedure to search for complementary scorers beyond the four hand-picked strategies; whether a learned or adaptive aggregator (which the authors defer to future work) would dominate is unexplored. - Latency measurements (up to 18×) are confounded by provider-side effects the authors acknowledge, but the 4× token-cost multiplier is itself significant for high-throughput deployment and is only analyzed structurally, not benchmarked in dollars. - β<1 ensembling lacks the concavity guarantee of β=1 (Compβ can be negative, so averaging can lower the score), yet the headline conciseness results use β=0.8 — the paper shows this is benign empirically but the failure regime is not characterized. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing uncertainty-quantified content selection should read this: the Ens4 recipe, released code, and validated complementarity theory offer a real, cheap-to-adopt alternative to per-task prompt engineering, and it is a stronger and better-controlled contribution than prior conformal-LLM work it builds on, despite the caveat that the cross-task evidence rests substantially on the authors' own dataset reformulations.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Discovery Certification Protocol (DCP), a three-gate, preregistered audit framework that converts an AI research agent's claimed result into executable tests of utility, alternative-route recoverability, and feedback-policy effect, yielding two explicit decisions (Core and Evidence) from a deterministic verifier. - Why it's important: Scores on sealed tests cannot distinguish genuine research contribution from memorization, trivial recombination, or contamination; as LLM agents claim discoveries (FunSearch-style search, AI-Scientist-style pipelines), funders and reviewers lack any rigorous way to certify that the agent's outcome reflects research rather than available information. - How it does it: The core trick is an information-provenance boundary: matched challenger agents receive all starting information K, initial observations E0, and the exact observed Web bytes Wobs, but the target run's history L* is withheld; any challenger reaching the target score − ε supplies a recovery witness that vetoes certification, and zero recoveries over n episodes yields a finite-sample bound on recovery probability. - The good: The protocol is fully exercised end-to-end — two complete audits (SQLite index selection, virtual catalyst optimization) plus three calibration cases covering recovered and audit-incomplete decisions, with a frozen, LLM-free verifier that replays decisions offline from machine-readable evidence bundles. - The missing: Both headline audits use small, synthetic, fully-sealable tasks with deterministic scoring; no evidence is given that the protocol works (or is affordable) for genuinely open-ended, noisy, real-world research where the sealed-evaluation and information-boundary assumptions are hardest to satisfy. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate AI research agents and need a concrete, statistical template for contamination-resistant discovery claims; skip it if you want evidence the method survives contact with realistic scientific tasks — the paper only calibrates the protocol on controlled testbeds.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Novelty (82) is the cluster's strongest — the E0/L* information-provenance boundary, the recovery-witness veto separated from the binomial recovery bound, and the outcome-recovery audit formulation are a genuinely new way to make 'the AI discovered X' falsifiable, and no prior agent benchmark attempts it. Rigor (75) is high for this literature: preregistered thresholds, itemized error budgets, deliberately included refuted (knapsack) and underpowered (affine) calibration cases, positive controls with recall lower bounds, a deterministic LLM-free verifier, released PyPI packages and evidence bundles, and itemized per-audit costs; it is reduced for being a preprint validated entirely on author-constructed, fully-sealable tasks with no external adversary attempting to break the boundary. Non-Obviousness (75) comes from the witness-vs-bound evidential distinction and the provenance decomposition. Completeness (75) is strengthened by honestly scoped decision records and self-reported issued=false; Resilience (65) is capped because Gate 3's neutral-feedback linchpin and the challenger-distribution Q_B are untested outside registered null families. Practical Impact (75) reflects real, cheap ($56–61), reusable audit infrastructure that agent evaluators could adopt tomorrow. Weighted composite: 0.15*82 + 0.15*75 + 0.10*75 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.30*75 = 74.55 ≈ 75.

Problem & Motivation: AI research agents (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, AI Scientist, co-scientist) report discoveries as numerical outcomes, but a high score conflates three different questions: is the artifact useful, could any agent reach the same score from the starting information alone (making the 'discovery' recoverable), and did truthful experimental feedback causally help? The authors point to known evaluation fragility (Melis et al. 2018, Musgrave et al. 2020, their own 'implementation lottery' work) and to contamination/memorization concerns: an agent may reproduce a known solution rather than discover one. Who has this problem: anyone claiming, reviewing, or funding AI-generated discoveries, and the benchmark ecosystem (MLE-bench, PaperBench, DiscoveryWorld, FIRE-Bench) that scores agents without testing alternative routes. DCP closes the gap between score-based evaluation and outcome-level attribution. Key Idea: Treat a discovery claim as falsifiable via registered counterfactual experiments: admit every valid route to the same number as a refutation. The single reconstructible insight is the E0/L* information-provenance split plus the rule "any valid challenger artifact scoring ≥ x − ε is a qualified recovery witness that vetoes the Core certificate," combined with a binomial fixed-sample bound (zero recoveries in n episodes ⟹ p_upper = 1 − α^(1/n)) for the probability that one fresh registered episode recovers the target. Feedback attribution is then isolated by a randomized paired design (truthful vs. neutral feedback from a shared checkpoint) with TOST-style null calibration — a competent transfer of preregistration, equivalence testing, and Rubin-style causal pairing into agent auditing, rather than a new algorithmic primitive. Methodology: DCP is a preregistration-and-testing pipeline, not a learning method. (1) Registration precedes the run and fixes task, model, information packet, tools, budgets, baseline, validity predicate P, selection/stopping rules, tolerance ε, thresholds δ_min/δ_evidence/δ_sham, and an error budget (0.05 total, itemized allocations). (2) Gate 1 validates utility on a sealed evaluation via a lower confidence bound on µ(A) − µ(b) ≥ δ_min (exact mean for enumerated finite workloads). (3) Gate 2 runs fresh matched challenger agents under the registered distribution Q_B with K, E0, and full observed Web bytes but no run history L; the recovery rule is Valid(a) ∧ score(a) ≥ x − ε; Core requires zero qualified witnesses, adequate controls (e.g., 45/45 positive controls, recall lower bound ≥ 0.8), and p_upper ≤ ρ. (4) Optional Gate 3 estimates Δ_feedback = E[u(A_truthful) − u(A_neutral) | c] from fresh paired branches at a frozen checkpoint, requiring the effect LCB ≥ δ_evidence + δ_sham after a 60-pair null calibration inside an equivalence band. Critical design decisions: (a) E0/L* provenance split — well-motivated and clearly defined; (b) best-of-k counts as one episode, so the full search budget sits inside one episode — justified and conservative; (c) the neutral feedback policy must preserve timing/schema/length while withholding direction — the trickiest design element, calibrated only on specific null-task families, which the authors acknowledge (calibration applies "to that family"). Web access goes through a byte-recording gateway; a threat model treats claimants as strategic, with tamper-evident ledgers, though formal issuance requires external countersigning the paper only describes. Key Results: Five audit cases across two models: (1) SQLite-Web (DeepSeek-v4-flash): agent plan scored 0.8855 on the sealed workload (88.55% traffic-weighted VM-step reduction; baseline 0); 96 challenger episodes yielded 0 recoveries, best challenger 0.6734 vs. recovery line 0.8805, p_upper = 0.0468 < ρ = 0.05; decision Core + Evidence. (2) Virtual catalyst (DeepSeek-v4-pro, 5 controls × 8 levels = 32,768 recipes): final recipe 1.0 vs. baseline 0.5990; 0/96 recoveries, best challenger 0.8146 vs. line 0.95, p_upper = 0.0468; Core + Evidence. (3) Device calibration (constructed information deficit): 0/80 recoveries, p_upper = 0.0477; Core. (4) Multidimensional knapsack: one episode produced two solutions (0.9363, 0.9356) above the 0.9329 recovery line — Core refuted by recovery witness, as designed. (5) Affine low-N case: correctly returned audit-incomplete on inadequate controls. Both Gate 3 studies: 30/30 truthful vs. 0/30 neutral recoveries, effect 1.0 with exact paired 99% CI [0.6379, 1.0] exceeding the required 0.51 margin; 60-pair null contrasts 0 with CI [−0.095, 0.095] inside ±0.17. Costs: $61.17 (507 sessions) and $56.40 (435 sessions) per complete audit. All baselines are author-constructed (no external agent baselines exist for this decision problem), and the tasks are small, sealed, and synthetic — standard-scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the outcome-recovery audit as an information-boundary refutation test for AI discovery claims, the clean separation of witness-based veto from probability-bound certification, and the pairing of this with a randomized feedback-effect estimand in one preregistered protocol. Standard components: Clopper–Pearson bounds, TOST equivalence testing, paired randomization (Rubin 1974), preregistration (Nosek 2018), and capture/replay infrastructure are all off-the-shelf; the contribution is their composition and the provenance-based task decomposition, applied to a new setting (agent discovery auditing). Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong on internal rigor: preregistered thresholds and error budgets, exact CIs, separate statistical units for candidate/episode/feedback uncertainty, positive controls with recall lower bounds (0.889–0.916), deliberately included negative (knapsack recovery) and underpowered (affine) calibration cases covering the full decision space, and a deterministic LLM-free verifier that replays every decision from frozen bundles. Reproducibility artifacts are concrete: PyPI packages dcp-audit and dcp-harness, GitHub repo, named certificate JSON files with content identifiers, and per-audit cost figures. Concerns: the protocol is developed and evaluated on the authors' own constructed tasks (no independent task suite or external red-team attempt to break the information boundary); the authors themselves are the claimant, evidence producer, and local registry in all reported audits — formal issuance (independent countersigning) is described but marked issued=false; no multiple-seed variation on the primary audits is reported beyond the registered episode counts. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built protocol, harness, verifier, and evidence bundles, evaluated by execution). Practical: Yes — runs on commercial LLM API endpoints via Claude CLI with task adapters; total audit cost was $56–61 per complete three-gate audit. Efficient: The expensive unit is the registered generation episode (~400–500 sessions); verification is offline and free, a favorable cost asymmetry for auditors vs. claimants. Effective: The evidence shows the protocol separates recoverable from non-recoverable outcomes on constructed tasks with known information deficits, but only a proxy for auditing real discoveries — the catalyst environment is virtual, deterministic, and fully sealed by design. Scalable: Not tested; the paper claims portability to other domains and retrospective audits but presents no case with noisy real-world measurements, large action spaces, or adversarial claimants beyond the threat-model discussion. Delivers a real software artifact: installable packages, reusable harness, evidence bundles, and figure-generation scripts. Strengths: (1) The E0/L* provenance decomposition is a crisp, checkable reframing that cleanly separates "what the agent was given" from "what the agent did," something score-based agent benchmarks (MLE-bench, PaperBench, DiscoveryWorld) do not attempt. (2) Distinguishing a recovery witness (constructive refutation) from a binomial recovery-probability bound (statistical certification) is a genuinely careful evidential design choice — most audit proposals would conflate them. (3) Including deliberately refuted and underpowered calibration cases and reporting a neutral-recovery upper bound (0.1619 at 30 episodes) alongside positive feedback effects shows the decision rule is tested against its own failure modes, not just demonstrated on positives. (4) End-to-end artifact discipline: frozen bundles, deterministic verifier, named content hashes, and itemized dollar costs make the numbers unusually checkable for this literature. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that null calibration applies only "to that family" of null tasks, that local bundles are not formally issued (formal issuance requires independent provenance verification and countersigning, marked issued=false throughout), that Core/Evidence decisions are scoped to the registered model, information, budget, and evaluation population, and that historical priority is explicitly not assessed. They confront scope limits directly and repeat the scope qualification in the decision records — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) All audited tasks are small, deterministic, and artificially sealable; the hardest practical obstacles — stochastic real-world measurements, incompletely capturable information environments, and claimed discoveries too expensive to re-seal — are unaddressed empirically. (2) The authors built the tasks, ran the agents, produced the evidence, and operate the local registry; no independent adversary attempted to break the E0/L boundary (e.g., extracting L content through the neutral channel or Web capture), so the threat model is untested against a strategic claimant. (3) The neutral feedback policy is the linchpin of Gate 3, and its non-directionality is verified only within registered null families on tasks whose answers are fixed by E0 — no evidence it stays non-directional on novel tasks. (4) The recovery bound conditions on the registered challenger distribution Q_B; a claimant or auditor choosing a weak Q_B can trivially certify Core, and the paper does not empirically probe how sensitive decisions are to this choice. (5) Several cited works (DeepSeek-v4 models, Ning et al. 2026a–e, FIRE-Bench) postdate or coincide with this submission; the literature positioning could not be verified as peer-reviewed context — this is a preprint (arXiv:2609.09219) and all results are self-reported. Bottom Line: This is the most concrete and statistically disciplined attempt yet to make "the AI discovered X" a falsifiable, replayable claim, and its harness plus evidence format are worth adopting by anyone auditing research agents — but until someone independent runs it on a noisy, real-world discovery task with an adversarial claimant, it remains a well-calibrated protocol validated on its own training ground.

#14 — Highly Innovative (75)

Beneath the Surface of Chains-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Reasoning Operations in LLMs (10 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that functionally distinct chain-of-thought reasoning operations (extraction, decomposition, recall, deduction, arithmetic, etc.) are linearly separable in the hidden representations of reasoning LLMs, peaking in middle layers, and that this geometry depends on preceding context. - Why it's important: As reasoning traces become direct optimization targets in RL-trained reasoning models, understanding whether the model internally represents the reasoning operations in those traces (beyond surface tokens) is a prerequisite for latent-space diagnosis, failure detection, and activation steering of reasoning. - How it does it: The authors annotate reasoning traces with a Pólya-derived eight-operation taxonomy (GPT-5, human-validated on 84 spans), then fit PCA+LDA probes on hidden states, validate separability with held-out AUROC/AUPRC, and rule out lexical, positional, and notation confounds with matched controls and attention-masking interventions. - The good: The confound-control suite is unusually thorough: hidden-state probes beat the best text-only baseline by +0.041 to +0.097 macro AUROC, survive lexically-matched pairs, competing-operation vocabulary, digit-density and position-stratified tests, and replicate across Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma4-31B, and Llama-3-8B plus cross-task transfer to GPQA-Diamond (0.938 AUROC) and MATH-500 (0.948). - The missing: The operation labels themselves come from GPT-5 annotating surface text with human validation on only 84 spans, so the probes may partly recover the annotator's text-based decision function rather than an internal cognitive operation; no application (steering, error detection) is evaluated. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on mechanistic interpretability of reasoning or want to build probe-based diagnostics over CoT; skip it if you need causal or intervention evidence that these operations matter for downstream correctness — the paper is explicitly diagnostic only.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) is anchored by a genuinely new empirical finding — operation-level geometric structure of CoT reasoning tied to a functional taxonomy rather than correctness — even though the probing machinery (PCA+LDA, centroid vectors) is standard. Rigor (80) is the paper's backbone: text-only/lexical/positional/adversarial controls, bootstrap CIs, 96 permutation tests, cross-family replication across four vendors, and a targeted attention-masking intervention with a matched discourse control; the preprint status, 84-span human validation, and annotation circularity keep it below 85. Non-Obviousness (70) comes from the dissociated error-execution result and context-dependence, though a linearly-decodable-structure finding is not shocking to interpretability practitioners. Completeness (80) benefits from an unusually candid limitations section; Resilience (75) reflects claims that are explicitly bounded as diagnostic-only. Practical Impact (60) reflects a released code/data artifact but no demonstrated operational payoff (no steering or error detection). Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*80 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*75 + 0.10*60 = 75.

Problem & Motivation: Reasoning-oriented LLMs are increasingly trained (via RL and process supervision) to produce structured reasoning trajectories, and prior work has shown that hidden states encode answer-correctness signals and that reasoning involves latent dynamics. But it was unknown whether the distinct functional operations that a CoT trace explicitly performs — extracting problem information, decomposing the problem, recalling a formula, deducing a conclusion — correspond to organized geometric structure in representation space, whether that structure generalizes across problems, tokens, and model families, and whether it survives when execution is factually wrong. The paper targets interpretability researchers and anyone building process-level monitors for reasoning models. Key Idea: Treat a reasoning trace as a sequence of operation-labeled chunks (per a Pólya taxonomy), learn a one-vs-rest "reasoning vector" per operation from held-out-probed hidden states, and characterize when/where/how these vectors organize representations — including testing whether the structure is causal (via attention masking of preceding context) rather than merely correlational. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) generate correct traces from Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma4-31B on DAPO-MATH-17K and TheoremQA (500–700 traces per model/dataset; correctness via LLM judge Qwen3.6-27B, not exact match); (2) segment traces into spans labeled with one of eight operations using GPT-5, human-validated (96.4% majority agreement on 84 spans, Fleiss' κ = 0.666; GPT-5–human exact agreement 76.2%, Cohen's κ = 0.715); (3) extract per-layer hidden states (residual stream), pool spans (middle-token, mean, first, last), L2-normalize, PCA to 128 dims, fit supervised LDA (7 dims), and define normalized one-vs-rest operation vectors as class-centroid differences; (4) evaluate held-out one-vs-rest AUROC/AUPRC with 5,000-replicate bootstrap CIs and 1,000 permutation tests. Confound controls: text-only (BoW/TF-IDF) classifiers, lexically matched pair analysis, competing-operation vocabulary subsets, 50–75% digit-density subsets, position-only baselines and position-stratified evaluation, PCA-only (no LDA) checks. Interventions: re-run the model masking attention from a chunk's first token to the preceding 30 tokens (plus preceding-chunk and random-block controls) and measure Δ in operation alignment. Error analysis: probes trained on correct traces applied to factual-error vs matched non-error spans in incorrect traces. Key design decisions: entropy-centered 50-token windows for long spans (reasonable but heuristic), GPT-5 annotation with only 84-span human validation (a material weakness, acknowledged), and analysis restricted to correct traces in main experiments (justified for clean labels but limits scope). Key Results: Held-out separability is high and middle-layer-peaked across all three models (e.g., Qwen3-8B mean-pooled macro AUROC/AUPRC 0.937/0.742 vs. 0.849/0.549 for the best text-only baseline; position-only baseline 0.718/0.279). PCA-only (no LDA) evaluation retains 0.872–0.938 AUROC. Probes transfer to Llama-3-8B (0.958/0.840) and, without retraining, to GPQA-Diamond (0.938/0.764) and MATH-500 (0.948/0.799). Intra-span variance analysis shows early-layer signals are token-local while middle-layer signals are distributed across spans; identical surface tokens (mostly function words like "the", "to", "is") acquire operation-dependent representations in middle layers. Masking the preceding 30 tokens reduces target-operation alignment (aggregate Δ = −0.4356, p < 0.0001), while a literary-discourse control (Harry Potter discourse functions, best-layer AUROC 0.665) shows no such reduction — supporting reasoning-specific context dependence. On incorrect traces, operation geometry persists but attenuates on factual-error spans (mean-pooled 0.955/0.877 vs. 0.971/0.901 non-error), with Deduction and Arithmetic Computation most affected and Recall unaffected. Scale is standard interpretability scale (7B–31B models, ~600–1,000 spans per operation), not stress-scale. A counter-intuitive nuance: some sustained late-layer signals onset before early-layer signals for several operations, and the authors correctly flag this exploratory analysis as detector-dependent. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (operation-level geometric organization of CoT in hidden states, with context-dependence and error-robustness) plus a NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK component (the Pólya-derived operation-span annotation methodology with human validation). The probing machinery (PCA+LDA, centroid difference vectors, AUROC evaluation) is standard interpretability technique; the genuinely new element is connecting a functional taxonomy of observable reasoning operations — rather than correctness, sentiment, or trajectory-level behaviors — to representation geometry, and systematically excluding lexical/positional confounds. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation/confound coverage is extensive and unusually honest: text-only, position-only, lexically-matched, adversarial-vocabulary, digit-density, PCA-only, random-label and random-position baselines, bootstrap CIs, and permutation tests (all 96 permutation tests p < 0.001). Statistical reliability is reported with 95% CIs throughout. Methodological concerns: (1) labels are GPT-5-generated with human validation on only 84 spans and no boundary validation — the probe's target is itself a text-level annotation function, creating a circularity risk that controls mitigate but cannot eliminate; (2) the train/test split is not strictly question-disjoint (14 of 608 Qwen3-8B questions appear in both splits); (3) correctness filtering relies on an LLM judge rather than exact match; (4) trace generation is not seeded, so the corpus is not bitwise reproducible. Code and project materials are released at https://github.com/naver-ai/beneath-cot. The paper is an arXiv preprint (dated 2026) and does not state peer-review status. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (probing and intervention experiments actually run; no deployed system). Practical: Yes — probing requires only hidden-state extraction on commodity GPUs; the annotation stage requires GPT-5 API access, which is a real cost for applying the method to new models. Efficient: Linear probes on 128-dim PCA projections are essentially free at inference; the expensive parts are trace generation (up to 4,096 tokens/problem on 8× V100) and GPT-5 annotation. Effective: The evidence supports the diagnostic claim (operations are represented and context-dependent), but the paper does not demonstrate any operational payoff — no steering, error detection, or decoding-time control is evaluated, so usefulness is currently a proxy/analogy rather than a demonstrated capability. Scalability: Untested; the annotation bottleneck (LLM segmentation plus human validation) and per-model probe fitting suggest cost grows with every new model and task, and the paper does not claim otherwise. Deliverable: a software artifact (code, probe pipeline, annotated span data) on GitHub; no trained model weights or packaged library beyond the repo. Strengths: - The confound-control battery is the paper's real contribution to rigor: four independent lexical controls plus positional controls plus a non-reasoning discourse control, each reported with per-operation detail in the appendix — most probing papers stop at a text-only baseline. - Cross-model, cross-task replication (four model families across three vendors, transfer to two unseen benchmarks without probe retraining) substantially strengthens the claim that operation geometry is a property of reasoning-trained LLMs generally, not one checkpoint. - The attention-masking intervention with a matched non-reasoning discourse control (reasoning probe drops, discourse probe does not) converts a correlational finding into a targeted causal claim about preceding-context dependence. - The error-execution analysis yields a non-obvious, dissociated result: operation identity survives factual errors overall, but attenuates for Deduction and Arithmetic Computation while remaining intact for Recall. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly state that (1) GPT-5 annotations are approximate labels of textual reasoning functions, not ground-truth latent states, validated on only 84 spans and not at span boundaries; (2) experiments cover only mathematical/theorem reasoning and four models, so geometry may differ for commonsense, planning, code, or interactive tasks; (3) the work is diagnostic, not interventional — no evaluation of whether the operation vectors improve model behavior (steering, failure detection, decoding control). This is a candid limitations section that confronts the weaknesses head-on rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central circularity the authors underweight: the probe's target label is defined by a procedure (GPT-5 reading surface text) that is itself an operation classifier. Even with controls, a hidden-state probe outperforming a text baseline does not establish the model represents the operation — only that hidden states encode more than the lexical features of the annotation function. A probe distilled from GPT-5's labels on text the same model generated (i.e., states conditioned on the model's own intended next chunk) could inherit annotation artifacts. - Generated traces are the model's own CoT under a fixed "solve step by step" prompt; there is no test on paraphrased, perturbed, or adversarially reworded traces, so robustness to trace style/formatting is unmeasured. - The judge (Qwen3.6-27B) shares lineage with two analyzed models, an unexamined contamination vector for the correctness filter and hence the retained span corpus. - Only aggregated Δ alignment is reported for the masking intervention; no per-operation effect sizes in the main text and no direct effect-magnitude comparison across controls (the authors disclaim this, but it leaves the causal dose-response story qualitative). - The human validation sample (84 spans, three authors among seven annotators) is too small to estimate label noise per operation, and per-operation noise plausibly correlates with the per-operation AUROC variation reported. Bottom Line: This is a careful, well-controlled empirical study that convincingly establishes operation-level geometric structure in reasoning LLM hidden states and belongs on the reading list for anyone building CoT-level interpretability or process-monitoring tools — but its circularity between GPT-5 annotation and probing, and its explicitly diagnostic-only scope, mean it is groundwork rather than a demonstrated technique for improving reasoning.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OpenWAM, an open modular research stack (infrastructure + controlled ablation studies + a pretrained model, OpenWAM-α) that turns World–Action Model (WAM) pretraining into a controlled experimental program and delivers an open WAM competitive across eight simulation benchmarks and real-robot platforms. - Why it's important: WAMs — policies that inherit generative video priors — currently exist only as monolithic systems whose coupled design choices make it impossible to tell which components matter, blocking systematic progress in an area where robot data is scarce and expensive. - How it does it: It factorizes WAM design into interchangeable modules (visual encoder, stream backbones, visibility attention masks, denoising schedules) under a single joint flow-matching objective sampled over the full 2-D (video, action) noise plane, then ablates each axis and composes the winning recipe into a 5B+1B dual-system model pretrained on 518.5M frames (~6,400 hours) of co-trained egocentric and robot data in an 80-D unified action space. - The good: The controlled studies yield actionable, quantified findings — e.g., embodied pretraining lifts OOD success on RoboTwin2.0-Clean2Random from 14.5% to 26.62% while barely moving ID (+0.68pp), and pretraining flips the preferred attention mask from one-way to mutual visibility — and the resulting model ranks top-tier across simulation and real robots. - The missing: The controlled studies (Questions 1–3) are run entirely on a single benchmark (RoboTwin2.0), with no error bars or seed variance reported, so the distilled 'principles' may be benchmark-specific; skip it if you only care about VLA-side methods, as the WAM components are assembled from known techniques (flow matching, DiT backbones, action chunking).

Problem & Motivation: Embodied agents must learn both how the world evolves and what actions cause that evolution. Videos of the world are abundant but robot trajectories with action labels are scarce, motivating WAMs that warm-start from video generation priors. The community's problem is that existing WAMs (and VLAs) are monolithic: the generative backbone, visual representation, architecture, cross-stream information flow, inference procedure, and data mixture are tightly coupled, so (a) the codebases are hard to extend and (b) controlled comparison is impossible — nobody knows which design choices actually transfer world knowledge, create world–action synergy, or scale across domains. Robotics researchers building generalist policies lack the kind of open modular ecosystem (OpenVLA, StarVLA) that already exists for VLAs. Key Idea: Factorize the WAM design space into a composition C(E, S, M) of pluggable visual encoders, stream backbones, and visibility attention masks, train every composition with one joint flow-matching loss where video and action timesteps are sampled independently (covering the full joint noise plane so any inference denoising schedule stays in-distribution), and use this substrate to answer three questions by controlled ablation: what world knowledge to inherit, how to create world–action synergy, and how to consolidate it across domains. The single most load-bearing trick is independent per-stream timestep sampling, which makes synchronized and asynchronous joint denoising interchangeable at inference without retraining. Methodology: OpenWAM-Infra (Section 3) defines three interchangeable module classes — visual encoders (Wan2.2-VAE, FLUX.2-VAE, DINOv3, V-JEPA 2.1, plus an S-VAE dimension-contraction adapter), stream backbones (five pretrained video DiTs from 1.3B to 14B parameters, an ActionDiT, an optional VLM stream), and visibility masks (mutual / action-sees-video / video-sees-action / isolated) — assembled by parameter-free composition rules into Single-, Dual-, and Tri-System families. Training uses a joint flow-matching objective: L = λv·E[w(tv)‖v̂z − (z−εv)‖²] + λa·E[w(ta)‖m⊙(v̂a − (a−εa))‖²], with per-dataset index maps scattering native actions into an 80-D unified action space (two mirrored 34-D arm blocks + 12 reserved slots) and a validity mask restricting gradients to populated slots. A single policy server serves all checkpoints with configurable inference mode (sync/async) and denoising schedule (sync diagonal, variance-shift, or linear-offset paths through the joint noise plane), plus serving accelerations (torch.compile under CUDA graphs, DiT velocity caching, prompt-embedding cache, VAE-decode skip). OpenWAM-Study (Section 4) runs controlled ablations on RoboTwin2.0 (2,500 clean + 25,000 randomized demos for ID; clean-only training for the OOD Clean2Random proxy), including a 600-hour pretraining budget comparison of robot-only vs. two-stage vs. one-stage ego+robot co-training from EgoDex and RoboCOIN. OpenWAM-α (Section 5) composes the resulting recipe: frozen Wan2.2-VAE encoder, pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B world DiT + 1B ActionDiT bridged at all 30 layers via joint self-attention under mutual visibility, bell-shaped timestep weighting, synchronized 10-step denoising at deployment, pretrained on 518.5M frames from five sources (30% egocentric, 40% real-robot, 30% synthetic) with a two-level vision/signal curation pipeline. Key Results: Backbone scaling is monotonic on RoboTwin2.0-Full: 90.14% (Wan2.1-VACE-1.3B) → 91.64% (Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B) → 92.39% (Wan2.2-TI2V-5B) → 93.79% (Wan2.1-I2V-14B); the 5B model trails the 14B by only 1.40 points. Architecture ablation: dual-system joint self-attention reaches 92.36% average vs 85.50% for single-system vanilla; tri-system peaks at 92.60%. Information-flow ablation: masks denying the action stream access to world features lose ~5 points (Isolated 87.41% vs Action-Sees-Video 92.39%); synchronized denoising (93.0%) beats every asynchronous schedule tested (α up to 32, offsets up to 0.8). Pretraining with a fixed 600-hour budget: OOD success on Clean2Random rises from 14.50% (scratch) to 26.62% (ego+robot co-train, +12.12pp) while ID moves only 14.50→87.68 range (+0.68pp for co-train); post-pretraining, mutual visibility consistently beats one-way (e.g., +0.72pp OOD C2R). OpenWAM-α at scale: LIBERO 99.3%, VLABench 58.9, RoboTwin2.0-Full 93.6%, RoboTwin2.0-C2R 69.0% (best WAM; Qwen-RobotManip leads at 77.1%), EBench 49.4 SR (new best, +3.8 over Qwen-RobotManip), RoboCasa-GR1 60.5%, RoboCasa365 38.2%, RoboDojo 11.92 SR, but LIBERO-Plus only 69.2% vs 89.0% for Qwen-RobotManip, collapsing specifically on camera (33.8) and noise (39.8) perturbations. Real robots: 82.5% average over six Franka single-arm tasks (vs LingBot-VA 77.5%, π0.5 55.0%); tops the RoboDojo-Real bimanual leaderboard at 37.6 Score / 24.4% SR; on an unseen dexterous-hand embodiment (30 tasks, 9-D EEF + 21-DoF hand action space absent from pretraining), it beats π0.5 on all four tasks (e.g., 100% vs 60% SR on Put Away Clothes ID). Baselines are current and strong (π0.5, Qwen-RobotManip, StarVLA, ABot-M0.5, Fast-WAM, LingBot-VA). Serving: ~170ms per chunk on a single RTX 5090, 2.0–2.6× speedup from cache+compile. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the open modular WAM infrastructure with unified training/serving/evaluation across eight benchmarks and real robots) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the quantified principles: pretraining buys OOD generalization not ID fit; the mutual-visibility reversal after pretraining; synchronized joint denoising beating all tested asynchronous schedules). The individual components — flow matching, DiT video backbones, action chunking, attention masking, MoE routing, S-VAE contraction — are standard; the genuine novelty is the systematic controlled-experiment methodology applied to WAMs (in the tradition of Cambrian-1 and the 'designing as empirical science' line) and the release of the first open WAM research ecosystem, not any single algorithmic mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the paper's core and are well structured: backbone size (4 points), encoder type (6 configurations), architecture (7 variants), training-time masks (4), inference schedules (17 configurations across two families), and pretraining data strategy (4 budgets), each changing one factor while holding others fixed — and the study even re-tests its mask conclusion after pretraining, catching a reversal. However, no error bars, seed counts, or significance tests are reported anywhere; single-run results are the norm. Code (github.com/OpenWAM-Official/OpenWAM), model weights and data (huggingface.co/OpenWAM), and full per-benchmark tables are released, plus detailed hyperparameters (128 H200 GPUs, ~7 days, batch 3,072). Methodological concerns: all three controlled studies run on RoboTwin2.0 alone, so Finding 1–3 generalize from one bimanual benchmark; several leaderboard baselines (e.g., Qwen-RobotManip, ABot-M0.5) were trained on substantially larger and more relevant pretraining data, and while the authors honestly analyze this for LIBERO-Plus, cross-model comparisons remain confounded by data; the VLA-vs-WAM paradigm comparison in Section 5.3.2 juxtaposes models differing in data, architecture, and training simultaneously, so it is suggestive rather than controlled. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong SYSTEMS component — the released infrastructure is itself a deliverable). - Practical: Yes — inference runs on a single consumer RTX 5090 (~170ms/chunk), though pretraining required 128 H200s for ~7 days. - Efficient: Serving is 2.0–2.6× faster with cache+compile, and the 5B backbone is within 1.4 points of the 14B at ~3× less compute, an explicit efficiency choice; training cost is comparable to other 5–6B-scale embodied pretraining efforts. - Effective: Evidence spans eight simulation benchmarks plus three real-robot embodiments including an unseen dexterous hand, and it solves the stated problem (a strong open WAM baseline) — with the notable LIBERO-Plus camera/noise failure showing pixel-latent prediction remains brittle under visual disturbance. - Scalable: Not directly tested: the paper claims more/diverse data remedies both paradigm deficits, but no experiment above the 6,400-hour pretraining budget is shown, and backbone scaling is only demonstrated to 14B on one benchmark. The work delivers a substantial software artifact: modular codebase, policy server, benchmark adapters, pretrained weights, and data recipes — not paper-only. Strengths: - The independent per-stream timestep sampling construction is a genuinely useful design: because training covers the full (tv, ta) noise plane, every inference schedule (sync, variance-shift, linear-offset) is in-distribution, making the denoising-schedule study meaningful and the deployment stack trivially aligned with training. - The discipline of re-testing the mask ablation after pretraining (and reporting the reversal from one-way to mutual visibility) is exactly the kind of conditional, sequenced experimentation most ablation sections lack; findings are presented as a recipe where each decision is validated under the conditions created by the previous one. - Honest negative analysis: the LIBERO-Plus failure is decomposed per-perturbation and attributed to single-arm pretraining data deficit plus pixel-latent sensitivity, corroborated by three other WAM baselines showing the same signature — the paper diagnoses its own weakness with data rather than hiding it. - Ecosystem value: first open modular WAM stack with an 80-D slot-semantics unified action space, a WebSocket client–server evaluation protocol that makes new benchmark integration a thin adapter, and self-contained checkpoints that hard-fail on normalization mismatch — real engineering against silent evaluation drift. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The appendix (Section A) explicitly lists: (1) only the pretraining phase is studied — post-training/adaptation methods are unexplored; (2) modality fusion is limited to cross-attention and hard-routed MoE, with early fusion and soft MoE left to future work; (3) no UMI-style data in the pretraining mixture, which the authors argue is a crucial OOD-generalization ingredient; (4) the chosen Wan2.2-VAE is 'the best trade-off currently available rather than an optimal solution' — pixel-reconstruction latents are admittedly not robust to viewpoint, noise, and scene variation. The authors confront limitations directly and concretely, which strengthens credibility; the LIBERO-Plus breakdown in Section 5.3.1 extends this honesty into the results themselves. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - All controlled 'principles' are derived from RoboTwin2.0 bimanual simulation; no cross-benchmark validation of Findings 1–3 is reported, yet they are presented as general WAM design principles and baked into OpenWAM-α. A practitioner cannot tell whether, e.g., 'synchronized denoising is best' holds on single-arm or mobile embodiments. - No variance reporting anywhere: every table entry appears to be a single run, and success-rate differences of 0.5–2 points (e.g., the mutual-vs-one-way reversal margins of +0.16 to +0.72pp) are within plausible seed noise, which undercuts the precision of several 'findings'. - The VLA-vs-WAM 'advantage region' analysis compares models with uncontrolled differences in pretraining data scale and composition (the authors' own Takeaway 1 concedes data dominance); the paradigm-level conclusion that 'neither prevails' may be an artifact of per-model data choices rather than a property of the paradigms. - The egocentric data source is the authors' own newly constructed 71.6K-video dataset with no action labels; its contribution is never isolated from RoboCOIN in the 600-hour study beyond the robot-only vs mixed comparison, and its curation quality is not independently evaluated. - Real-robot single-arm fine-tuning uses only 100 demonstrations per task with 20 trials each — small sample sizes where a 5% swing equals one trial; confidence intervals are absent. - Backbone scaling conflates parameter count with differing pretraining data and objectives (acknowledged in passing), so 'capable generative backbone' is not decomposed into size vs. prior quality. Bottom Line: For anyone training or evaluating robot foundation models, this is currently the reference open WAM stack and the most rigorous public ablation program in the WAM literature — its released infrastructure and data recipe alone justify reading — though its headline 'principles' should be treated as single-benchmark, single-run observations rather than established science, and VLAs still hold the OOD edge it does not close.

Mitra-v2 Technical Report

Y Tao, X Zhang, X Liu, B Han, D Maddix, H Fang… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Mitra-v2, a 77M-parameter tabular foundation model trained entirely on synthetic data that matches the 1.6B-parameter TabFM on TabArena and TALENT while beating TabPFN-3 by roughly 137 Elo (TabArena overall). - Why it's important: It shows that accuracy at the top of the tabular foundation-model leaderboard can be bought with a wider synthetic task distribution and a better optimizer rather than a 21× larger model, and it ships as a fully open Apache-2.0 release with zero imputed cells on both benchmarks. - How it does it: The trick is scaling the synthetic pretraining prior — adding a Hybrid SCM generator that composes MLP, tree, GP, and autoregressive mechanisms inside one causal DAG, with 10× longer contexts and 3× wider feature ranges — plus a Muon/AdamW optimizer stack and deployment-time fine-tune-and-bag with an 8-fold ensemble. - The good: The evaluation is unusually candid and controlled: a frozen pool, per-task sign tests (Mitra-v2 beats TabPFN-3 on 31/38 datasets, p=0.0001), negative-result and lever-ablation appendices, and an independent out-of-protocol check on 274 TALENT datasets with matched context policies. - The missing: The paper changes context length, feature range, prior mixture, optimizer, and checkpoint simultaneously and concedes it cannot isolate which change drove the gains, and the regression board (13 datasets) has bootstrap intervals of ±95–223 Elo that swallow most claimed separations. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or deploy tabular ML systems or study foundation-model scaling — the synthetic-prior-scaling result and the deployment-lever analysis are directly actionable; skip it if you want a clean scientific ablation of what made the model better, which the paper does not provide.
