Problem & Motivation: Tabular foundation models (TabPFN lineage) perform amortized in-context inference on new tables, and a small set of industrial-scale releases (Google's 1.6B TabFM, LG's EXAONE Tabular) has raised the question of how much capacity these models actually need. Practitioners also need coverage beyond typical pretraining caps: wide tables (hundreds to thousands of columns), targets with more than ten classes, and large-sample datasets with tens of thousands of rows. Mitra-v1 showed that mixing synthetic priors (SCMs plus tree generators) helps, but was capped at 512 support rows, 16 features, and trailed the field badly on regression (imputed on 46% of TabArena regression datasets). The open question this paper pursues is how far the prior-scaling recipe can be pushed without deepening the backbone. Key Idea: Scale the diversity and envelope of the synthetic task distribution, not the network: keep the 12-layer, 512-wide, factorized 2D-attention (row-axis + column-axis) backbone frozen in size, but (1) add a Hybrid SCM prior — a variant of O-prior with vector-valued nodes, random per-node mechanisms (MLPs, trees, ExtraTrees, random forests, 1D convolutions, GP via random Fourier features, VAR), random parent projections and aggregation operators creating residual-like paths, pretraining on 160–5,120 support rows, 1,280 query rows, and 1–50 features — and (2) replace uniform AdamW with Muon (Gram Newton–Schulz) on 2D weight matrices plus AdamW elsewhere. Deployment-time wrappers (train-only 256-feature reduction, hierarchical ≤10-class decomposition, raised inference-time support caps) extend the frozen checkpoint past its pretraining caps. Methodology: Pretraining minimizes masked-label cross-entropy over a task distribution G drawn from an outer mixture (configured weights: 0.35 base TabPFN/SCM, 0.35 new Hybrid SCM, 0.30 across five tree-based generators, hand-chosen and admitted as unoptimized). Regression is cast as 1,000-bin classification over the target range with a distributional head (the only architectural change vs. Mitra-v1 regression), replacing the v1 MSE head. Training runs on 4 nodes × 8 H200s, bfloat16, ~14,000 updates at an effective batch of 2,048 tasks (~28.7M nominal synthetic tasks; count is approximate because not fully logged). Deployment is the AutoGluon bagged fine-tuning system: 50 fine-tuning steps per bag child (250 s cap), 8-fold bagging, "heldout-in-support" prediction, support caps of 16,384–32,768 rows at prediction, SelectKBest(k=256) for wide classification tables and 256-component truncated SVD for wide regression tables, both fit on the training split only, and a balanced hierarchical class decomposition for >10-class targets (root routes to one of ≤10 groups, leaf predicts within group, recursing for >100 classes). Critical design decisions: (a) keeping depth at 12 — justified only by citing v1 saturation observations, not re-ablated here; (b) hand-set prior mixture weights — acknowledged as suboptimal, with the authors' own reweighting experiments showing little effect; (c) the fine-tune-and-bag deployment rather than zero-shot inference — well characterized but a substantial compute concession. The paper explicitly uses one uniform configuration for every dataset and refuses per-dataset tuning, calling it oracle benchmark tuning. Key Results: On TabArena (51 datasets, 816 units, one-hour per-unit budget, frozen 43-method pool): Mitra-v2 scores 1,774.6 Elo overall, statistically tied with TabFM (1,773.5, fits up to 5,886 s that exceed the budget) and EXAONE Tabular (1,749.4), and ~137 Elo above TabPFN-3 (1,637.5); the only higher entries are four-hour AutoGluon portfolios and the TabFM+ ensemble. Per-task, it beats TabPFN-3 on 31/38 classification datasets (sign test p=0.0001, median 2.1% relative error reduction, geometric mean +6.2% error for TabPFN-3), is at chance vs. EXAONE (22/38, p=0.42), and trails TabFM at the task level (13/38, p=0.07). Against Mitra-v1 in the same pool: 1,756.3 vs. 1,350.2 (classification) and 1,985.6 vs. 1,265.2 (regression), lower error on 26/26 classifiable datasets (p<10⁻⁷), with imputation falling from 32–46% to 0%. On TALENT main274 (274 datasets, 15 seeds, no time limit), it is statistically inside the leading group (1,479.7 train-only vs. TabFM 1,503.2, intervals ±~60) and ranks first outright on the 12 many-class datasets (2,070.1 vs. TabPFN-3's 1,850.3) despite never seeing >10 classes in pretraining; TabFM cannot run that slice at all. Deployment ablations show the support cap alone is worth +87.5 Elo on regression (1,848.4 → 1,935.9) and the two levers stack to ~+64 Elo on classification; the support-cap sweep shows error falling monotonically with context (airline-satisfaction, n=87k: −66% error from cap 512→32,768), with the model remaining support-limited, not capacity-limited, on the largest tables. Unit cost is a median ~8.8–9.6 minutes of fine-tuning plus bagged prediction — well above the seconds-per-fit forward-pass baselines. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the vector-valued Hybrid SCM variant with random parent projections — though adapted from the O-prior framework), plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a 12-layer, 77M model with a 10× wider synthetic prior matches a 1.6B competitor) and a substantial ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component (Muon stack, deployment wrappers, heldout-in-support). The genuinely novel element is the demonstrated primacy of synthetic-task-distribution scaling over parameter scaling; the architecture, regression-via-binned-classification, bagged fine-tuning, and feature-selection wrappers are competent recombinations of existing ideas (the Hybrid SCM is explicitly credited to O-prior). Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a technical report. Ablations are present and unusually informative: lever-level Elo attribution (Table 6), a support-cap sweep with an internal control (bit-identical errors at non-binding caps), a per-task sign-test diagnostic, and a full negative-results appendix (HL-Gauss/CRPS heads, continued pretraining, prior reweighting, log-uniform row sampling, stratified support selection — all reported as failures). Bootstrap intervals are reported throughout and the authors refuse to over-read close gaps. Weights, inference/fine-tuning code, and per-unit evaluation results are released under Apache-2.0 (huggingface.co/autogluon/mitra-classifier-2, -regressor-2, -finetune); the pretraining pipeline is not released. Methodological concerns: (1) the authors concede the confounded v1→v2 comparison — context, features, prior, optimizer, and checkpoint all changed at once with no isolation; (2) the primary benchmark (TabArena) is a living benchmark with substantial author overlap (Amazon/AutoGluon team), partially mitigated by the independent TALENT evaluation; (3) the regression board's 13 datasets yield intervals of ±95–223 Elo, so the "level with TabFM" regression claim rests on point estimates; (4) TabFM's leaderboard artifacts exceed the one-hour budget (up to 5,886 s fits), an asymmetry the authors disclose but cannot remove; (5) no error bars over training seeds — a single training run per task type. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model with extensive benchmark evaluation; a release, not a production deployment study). - Practical: Yes — 77M-parameter weights run on single-GPU hardware (H100 in the cost analysis; a community ONNX port runs on CPU), and all deployment levers are environment variables. - Efficient: Unfavorable at release defaults — ~9 minutes of fine-tuning plus 8-fold bagged prediction per dataset versus seconds for forward-pass models, a concession the paper states plainly rather than hiding; a cap-8192 preset recovers ~93% of the accuracy gain at near-baseline cost. - Effective: Yes for the stated benchmark regime — 0% imputation on 51 TabArena and 274 TALENT datasets, including regimes outside its pretraining caps (1,024-feature QSAR, 35-class targets), though evidence is benchmark-level, not from controlled field A/B deployments. - Scalable: Partially tested — inference support caps were swept to 32,768 rows with accuracy still rising on the largest tables, but the paper has not trained a deeper/wider variant or tested >100k-row contexts, and the fine-tuning cost grows linearly with deployment scale. The artifact is real and reusable: two model checkpoints, a fine-tuning/inference package with the benchmark configuration as defaults, and per-unit evaluation results. The pretraining generators and distributed trainer are not released, which limits reproduction of the training side. Strengths: - The central empirical result is clean and consequential: on a fixed 12-layer backbone, enlarging the synthetic prior (10× rows, 3× features, Hybrid SCM) plus a geometry-aware optimizer moves Elo from ~1,350 to ~1,774 in a frozen pool — direct evidence that prior diversity, not depth, is the binding constraint in this regime. - Evaluation discipline exceeds typical technical-report standards: matched context policies on TALENT (re-running TabFM and EXAONE under both policies and showing the context effect is symmetric across models), explicit refusal of per-dataset oracle tuning, disclosure of the TabFM budget asymmetry, and a documented negative-results appendix that saves others the compute. - The >10-class hierarchical wrapper is a well-executed idea that converts a hard pretraining cap into a state of first place on the many-class slice (2,070.1 Elo, 12 datasets) with zero additional training, in a regime where TabFM structurally cannot compete. - The deployment-lever analysis (support cap and train-only feature selection as free, tunable axes worth 64–88 Elo) gives practitioners actionable, zero-training-cost knobs with measured accuracy/time trade-offs. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The limitations section is candid and directly confronts the weak points: the top-of-board results are a statistical tie inside overlapping bootstrap intervals ("state-of-the-art level" should be read as such); the system is fine-tuned and bagged, much slower than forward-pass models, and not Pareto-dominant; the training-provenance is incomplete and the v1→v2 changes are confounded with no isolating ablation; regression rests on 13 datasets with wide intervals; large tables retain headroom (two of three largest still improving at cap 32,768); prediction time is not separately instrumented; and both benchmarks are frozen snapshots whose future rankings may differ. This degree of self-scrutiny is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' own list: (1) no ablation or even discussion of why Muon specifically was necessary — the optimizer change is bundled into the confound and never attributed; (2) the Hybrid SCM is evaluated only end-to-end, so the report cannot say whether the new prior or the 10× context/feature envelope drove the gain; (3) the outer mixture weights are hand-set and the paper's own reweighting experiment suggests insensitivity, which quietly undercuts the "wider prior" narrative as the mechanism — the context-length expansion may be doing most of the work; (4) the accuracy–time comparison mixes recorded times across hardware (acknowledged for TabFM, but the cross-method plane is still not hardware-controlled); (5) TALENT, while a different suite, is scored by the authors themselves rather than by the independent maintainers, and Elo computed by the submitting team on both benchmarks leaves no third-party verification; (6) single training runs per checkpoint mean run-to-run pretraining variance is unmeasured; (7) the TabArena ecosystem overlap (AutoGluon authors both fielding Mitra and maintaining the benchmark's harness) is not discussed as a conflict-of-interest risk. Bottom Line: This is the most informative tabular-foundation-model report of its generation for practitioners — the open release, the synthetic-prior-scaling finding, and the measured deployment levers are genuinely useful — but readers should treat the headline "matches a 1.6B model" as a statistically tied, confounded, self-evaluated claim whose causal mechanism (prior diversity vs. context length vs. optimizer) remains unisolated.

A Blind Trust, the Bloody Thrust: When Attacker-Controlled Hook Updates Steer AI Agent Harnesses towards Malicious Behaviors

P Li, L Zhang, J Hou, S Wu, S Li, Z Kang, X Zhang · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HOOKPRY, a fully automated attack framework that trojanizes benign versioned plugins in AI agent harnesses (Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex CLI, etc.) by smuggling malicious lifecycle-hook configurations through trusted plugin updates, achieving oracle-verified end-to-end attack success rates of 77.0% across 1,000 runs on 7 harnesses × 5 LLM backends. - Why it's important: Agent harnesses execute lifecycle-hook commands with host privileges outside the LLM's reasoning path, so prompt-layer defenses and model alignment are structurally blind to this supply-channel compromise — meaning every user of plugin-based coding/agent harnesses is exposed to a vector that current tooling largely cannot detect. - How it does it: The core trick is temporal decoupling: a plugin earns trust as a benign v1, then a later update under the same identity adds hook bindings that the harness executes without re-authorization; a 'Least Common Interface' compiler portably translates the attack semantics into each harness's native hook schema, while 'Adversarial Manifest Optimization' tunes metadata for multi-intent marketplace retrievability. - The good: The strongest evidence is the model-independence result plus the paired comparison: three harnesses show cross-backend E2E-ASR standard deviations ≤2.5pp, and native hooks reach 92.0% success vs. 56.0% for mechanically translated MCP tool-description poisons (p = 7.09×10⁻¹²), cleanly isolating the harness-layer execution path from model-mediated attacks. - The missing: The defense evaluation leans on a strawman baseline (Microsoft Defender, an endpoint AV scanning configuration files, at 0% recall) and an author-built 8-rule tool (HookPolicy, 50%), with no dynamic-analysis or commercial agent-scanning defenses tested, and the marketplace acquisition stage is never measured against real installation or update-adoption behavior. - Read it or not: Read it if you build, secure, or deploy agent harnesses or plugin marketplaces — the threat model and defense recommendations (per-hook re-authorization, manifest-payload signature binding, least privilege) are directly actionable; Problem & Motivation: AI agent harnesses (Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex CLI, and similar frameworks) expose lifecycle hooks: manifest entries binding runtime events (session start, tool call, file edit) to shell commands that the harness dispatches directly with host privileges, without the LLM interpreting or selecting them. Prior work has studied malicious plugin code, tool-description poisoning, skill manipulation, and prompt injection — all of which act through the model's decision path — but nobody has isolated harness-managed lifecycle hooks as an independent, remotely deliverable attack target. The paper poses the question: can hooks be attacked via the supply chain and ported across heterogeneous harnesses? The stakeholders are the rapidly growing population of developers and enterprises using agent harnesses with plugin ecosystems, and the gap is that defenses (prompt filtering, model alignment, endpoint AV) are architecturally positioned on the wrong side of the post-trigger execution boundary. Key Idea: Exploit the temporal gap between when a plugin earns trust and when it exercises hook privileges — trust acquired at installation is not re-validated per-hook-entry at update time — combined with compiling attack semantics into each harness's minimal shared hook interface rather than relying on harness-specific syntax. The paper formalizes the target boundary selection as maximizing a 'trust gap' G(b) = O(b)·(λr·R(b) − λv·V(b) − λa·A(b)): the boundary granting the highest runtime privilege under the weakest validation and per-entry authorization, gated by payload capability requirements and probe observability. Methodology: HOOKPRY chains three components. (1) Adversarial Manifest Optimization (AMO) optimizes only plugin metadata (name, description) against a parameterized multi-intent surrogate objective J(m) = α·mean similarity + β·min similarity + γ·centroid similarity over a proxy query set, with an ε-constraint for instance distinctiveness from benign reference plugins; weights are selected on development categories with preregistered non-inferiority tolerances and frozen before held-out evaluation. The benign hook is never altered — AMO changes only the retrieval representation. (2) Temporal Decoupling (TD) instruments candidate trust boundaries with benign probes that write randomized markers, measures four quantities per boundary (validation strength, per-hook authorization, runtime privilege, observability), selects the weakest boundary satisfying the payload's capability set and an observability threshold, then specializes the payload with a conditional predicate χ(s) so it activates only at that boundary and stays benign otherwise. (3) Least Common Interface (LCI) computes the intersection of normalized semantic capabilities across the target harness set, minimizes the capability subset needed for a given attack's effect and preconditions (Eq. 10), selects the native event with fewest trigger dependencies, and compiles a native (event, command, configuration) triple per harness. Attacks are operationalized as ten objectives derived from a three-dimensional taxonomy (target asset × victim consumer × communication pattern) mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics. The design decisions are mostly well-justified: probe-based differential measurement for boundary selection is sound; the ε-constraint and preregistered weight selection in AMO show unusual methodological care for an attack paper; the attacker weights λr, λv, λa are stated as 'predetermined' but their calibration is not detailed. Key Results: Across 1,000 end-to-end runs (40 abstract case seeds × 7 harnesses × 5 backends, ephemeral environments with synthetic assets, external oracles, partial outcomes receiving zero credit), HOOKPRY achieves 77.0% micro-averaged verified E2E-ASR (770 pass / 34 partial / 196 fail, zero blocked), peaking at 92.5% on Hermes and dipping to 52.5% on Claude Code. Privilege Escalation (93.5% macro) and Resource Hijacking (93.4%) transfer best; Command & Control (41.7%) and Persistence (55.3%) are limited by network and filesystem policy. Mechanism utility (83.9%) exceeds E2E-ASR, localizing most failures post-trigger. Model independence holds strongly for three harnesses (cross-backend SD ≤2.5pp for Codex CLI, OpenClaw, Claude Code) but degrades to 7.1–9.6pp where event generation depends on tool-use patterns. In the paired RQ2 experiment, native hooks reach 92.0% vs. 56.0% for mechanically translated malicious MCP descriptions (50 targets from MCPTox, one-sided exact binomial p = 7.09×10⁻¹²). Ablations (Claude Code + DeepSeek-V4-Flash): removing AMO drops E2E-ASR 16.4pp to 75.6% (an analytical estimate, not measured); removing TD or LCI yields 0% by structural construction. Defense evaluation on a sanitized 40:40 corpus: Microsoft Defender 0/40 recall, author-built HookPolicy 20/40 (50.0%, Wilson CI 35.2–64.8%), Semgrep with five generic rules 19/40 (47.5%), union miss rate 47.5%, all with 0/40 false positives. Note this is an arXiv preprint (v2), not peer-reviewed, and several cited works and CVEs are dated 2026. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM + NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel contribution is isolating the lifecycle-hook update path as an independent attack surface with a precise threat model (attacker controls only plugin metadata and hook configuration, no prompt injection, no implementation bugs, no sandbox escape) — prior disclosures demonstrated individual hook-execution primitives, and prior taxonomy work (DyMalSkill, DDIPE, MCPTox) targets model-mediated channels. AMO, TD, and LCI are individually constructed from standard ingredients (retrieval optimization, differential probing, capability-set intersection) applied to a new target; the three-part chain and the cross-harness compilation are new, the underlying primitives are not. Rigor & Reproducibility: Unusually rigorous for an attack paper: preregistered external checks, oracle-verified effects rather than self-reported success, partial outcomes receiving zero credit, Wilson CIs and exact binomial tests, a paired comparison design, frozen defense artifacts with mechanically sanitized corpora, and preregistered AMO parameter selection with non-inferiority constraints. Ablations exist but are asymmetric — the w/o AMO number is explicitly an 'analytical estimate' rather than a run, and w/o TD / w/o LCI produce 0% by construction (blocking the mechanism), so they demonstrate the dependency chain rather than quantify graceful degradation. Per-cell sample sizes in the main matrix are small (12–16 for most categories, 18–28 for two), and no multi-seed error bars are reported for the headline 77.0%. Code is released via an anonymized repository (anonymous.4open.science/r/HookPry-2EBD) with a staged-release plan. Methodological concerns: the defense baselines are weak by design — Defender is an AV scanning configuration semantics it was never built to assess, and the only hook-aware baseline (HookPolicy 0.1.0) is the authors' own eight-rule tool; the acquisition stage measures retrieval opportunities only, never actual marketplace deployment or update-adoption rates; and disclosure to vendors was still pending response at writing, so no CVE confirmation appears in the paper. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (attack framework actually executed in isolated environments; no primary theoretical claims). Practical: Yes — the attack requires only marketplace account access and standard harness installations; the defensive recommendations (per-hook authorization, signature binding, least privilege) are implementable in existing harnesses. Efficient: The attack is configuration-only and carries negligible compute cost, which is exactly what makes it dangerous; no expensive infrastructure is needed. Effective: The evidence supports the stated mechanism within the threat model — oracle-confirmed effects on all seven harnesses — but effectiveness is conditional on installation, update adoption, and event occurrence, none of which is measured against real users. Scalable: Not tested beyond 7 harnesses / 5 backends / 40 cases; cross-OS, cross-shell, enterprise-policy, and future-version generalization is acknowledged as untested. The work delivers a software artifact (open-source framework, case definitions, synthetic assets, oracles, defense rules) rather than stopping at paper form, with deliberate capability reduction on the released payloads. Strengths: (1) Clean threat-model discipline — excluding prompt injection, implementation bugs, and sandbox escape makes the configuration-layer contribution legible and prevents the result from being dismissed as a known primitive; the RQ2 paired design (92.0% native vs. 56.0% translated MCP, same targets, same oracles) is the crispest demonstration that the harness execution path, not the model, is the differentiator. (2) The benign-probe methodology for characterizing trust boundaries is a reusable technique: measure validation/authorization/privilege asymmetry differentially across boundaries without executing anything malicious, then target the max-gap boundary. (3) Ten-attack-objective taxonomy grounded in asset/consumer/pattern triples and MITRE ATT&CK gives the community a shared vocabulary beyond ad-hoc case studies. (4) The model-independence analysis is honest — the authors report where it fails (tool-use-dependent events on OpenHarness, Hermes, WorkBuddy at 7.1–9.6pp SD) rather than overclaiming. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that AMO measures retrieval opportunity, not installation or update-adoption rates; experiments use ephemeral environments with synthetic assets and cover only 7 harnesses, 5 backends, 40 cases, without exhausting OSes, shells, enterprise policies, network conditions, or future versions; the attack excludes implementation bugs and sandbox escapes and depends on event occurrence, hook authorization, and subprocess permissions (reflected in low C2/Persistence rates); RQ4 evaluates only two generic scanners plus one researcher-configured static baseline with synthetic benign controls, no dynamic analysis or commercial specialized products. They confront these limitations directly and map each to future work — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits: (1) the RQ4 defense comparison is largely a strawman construction — 0% recall from Defender against configuration-file attacks is the expected outcome, not evidence of a defense gap, and the absence of any dynamic/behavioral detection baseline means the claim 'defenses are insufficient' is only established for static scanning; (2) HookPolicy, the only hook-aware defense, is authored by the same group, so the 50% figure should be read as a lower bound from a deliberately minimal artifact, not an independent measurement; (3) no real-world marketplace study — the entire acquisition premise (that an AMO-optimized plugin actually gets installed and updated by real users) is asserted via retrieval simulation; (4) the w/o AMO ablation is an analytical estimate rather than an executed run, weakening the only ablation that measures graded rather than structural impact; (5) no repeated-seed variance for the headline 77.0% and small per-cell N, so harness-level rankings (e.g., Hermes 92.5% vs. Claude Code 52.5%) may be noisy; (6) vendor disclosure was pending with no confirmed CVEs, so real-world exploitability claims rest solely on the authors' own harness. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or securing agent harnesses should read this — the lifecycle-hook update path is a real, systematically characterized, currently under-defended attack surface with actionable mitigation requirements — but the defense-evidence half is weak enough that security teams should treat the 'defenses fail' conclusions as a starting point for their own dynamic-detection evaluation, not an established result.

From Zero to Hero: An Open LLM Ecosystem for Armenian

E Arakelyan, K Avetisyan, M Davtyan, H Grigoryan… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a complete open Armenian LLM ecosystem — the 4.37M-document ArmWeb news corpus, the 373K-pair verified English–Armenian STEM corpus ArmSTEM, and arm-gemma-e4b, a Gemma-4-E4B continued-pretrained model that beats all existing open Armenian models — released with full data, recipe, and code. - Why it's important: Armenian is a morphologically rich, low-resource language whose existing open models are unauditable weight-only releases trained on undisclosed, partially contaminated corpora, so no one can reproduce, audit, or build on prior Armenian LLM work. - How it does it: The core move is a continued-pretraining mixture (69% curated news / 6% answer-preserving verified translated STEM / 20% English replay / 5% code) where a small share of translated STEM data — verified by blind re-solving with exact-match answer checking — reverses the catastrophic forgetting that news-only adaptation causes. - The good: The paper isolates the effect with a controlled swap (identical trainer, seed, budget, and replay streams; only 6% of the news share changes), showing news-only CPT costs −21.2pp on Belebele while the STEM swap ends +2.2pp above the unadapted base, and a scaling ladder extrapolates to a held-out 1.3B model within 0.47%. - The missing: Each headline CPT run is a single seed, the evaluation relies partly on machine-translated benchmarks (Okapi-translated m-MMLU/ARC/HellaSwag-hy), and the paper cannot yet separate whether the STEM benefit comes from content, QA format, or verification. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on low-resource language adaptation, corpus curation, or benchmark contamination — the controlled forgetting/reversal study and the contamination audit of FineWeb-2/HPLT/CulturaX Armenian slices generalize beyond Armenian; skip it if you only want large-scale pretraining methods.

Problem & Motivation: Armenian has no open LLM ecosystem: its open text exists only as uncurated slices of multilingual web crawls (CulturaX, HPLT-v2, FineWeb-2), its open models (HyGPT-10b, tweety-7b-armenian, ArmenianGPT-1.0-3B) are released as weights without training data or recipes, no math or science training data with worked solutions exists at training scale, and evaluation infrastructure that recently appeared (ArmBench-LLM, INCLUDE, SynDARin) has no corresponding open training data. Practitioners building Armenian NLP therefore cannot reproduce or audit any existing open model, and the paper shows the public crawl slices overlap Armenian evaluation panels at 7.9–17.4% of documents — including FineWeb-2's own Armenian test split leaking into its training split — so prior perplexity-style results are inflated. Key Idea: The central technical insight is that verified translated knowledge data acts as a third lever against catastrophic forgetting in continued pretraining — unlike English replay, which only slows the loss, swapping just 6% of the news share for answer-preserving verified STEM translations reverses it, turning the fluency-for-knowledge trade into a net gain. A supporting insight is functional verification of translation: since STEM problems have machine-checkable answers, translation quality can be gated by whether an independent solver reproduces the gold answer from the Armenian translation, rather than by fluency judging. Methodology: Three stages. (1) ArmWeb curation: a 2011–2026 single-operator crawl of 19 Armenian news outlets stored as structured records (nearly eliminating boilerplate), minimal cleaning, GlotLID language filtering (98.3% retained), exact dedup plus MinHash LSH (word 5-gram shingles, 112 permutations, 14×8 bands, Jaccard ≈0.72 — deliberately below the standard 0.8 to catch news syndication reprints), global dedup before splitting, three held-out 20K splits with hard-assertion leakage gates (zero exact cross-split collisions; near-duplicate rates 0.045%/0.010%/0.005%), and 13-gram decontamination against ten Armenian benchmarks (removing 147,101 documents, 3.3%). Final: 4.37M documents, 11.0 GB, 3.3B Gemma tokens. Validated via a 410M-parameter ablation grid (4.6B SP tokens) comparing against CulturaX-hy, HPLT-v2-hy, and FineWeb-2-hy in bits-per-byte, a repetition study (positive marginal gains through 8 epochs), and a Chinchilla-budget scaling ladder (70M–1B, 3 seeds per rung) fit to bpb(N) = 4.9×10⁵·N^(−0.795) + 0.439, extrapolating to a held-out 1.3B model with 0.47% error. (2) ArmSTEM: 373K GSM8K/AceReason-Math/OpenScience/OpenScienceReasoning-2 problems machine-translated to Eastern Armenian with placeholder masking of numbers/LaTeX before translation (Gemini-3.1-flash-lite chosen over GPT-5.5 by a pre-registered decision rule: 94.0% vs 96.5% pass, below the 5-point switch threshold), then three gates: placeholder integrity, language ID, and blind re-solving (o4-mini must reproduce the gold answer exactly; solver-limited items tagged when the English original also fails, 10.9% math / 27.6% science). Overall acceptance 96.6%. Two native speakers rated 299/300 sampled problems valid with perfect agreement (κ = 1.0). Dual-side decontamination against English benchmark origins (notably MMLU-Pro) and Armenian benchmark targets. (3) Adaptation: Gemma-4-E4B (best Armenian tokenizer fertility at 4.15 tokens/word vs Qwen3.5's 5.31 and Llama-3.1's 12.2) continued-pretrained for 10B tokens on the 69/4/2/20/5 mixture, lr 3×10⁻⁵ cosine; vocabulary extension was ablated and rejected (mean-initialized extension lands 40–45% above the base in bpb at 2B tokens). Critical design decisions: syndication-aware dedup threshold (justified with cross-implementation validation against datasketch and NeMo-Curator, 99.2% document-level agreement on a sample), pre-registered translator selection (well-justified), and the controlled News-CPT vs STEM-CPT swap design (well-justified — identical trainer, seed, budget, and replay/code streams). Key Results: On the six-task Armenian likelihood suite (LM Evaluation Harness, zero-shot), arm-gemma-e4b scores 0.500 mean vs 0.477 for the unadapted Gemma-4-E4B base, vs 0.44 for HyGPT-10b, 0.47 for ArmenianGPT-1.0-3B, and 0.35 for tweety-7b. The knowledge-task submean (m-MMLU/INCLUDE/Belebele) rises from 0.459 (base) to 0.503; Belebele reaches 0.716 (+9.7pp over base) after News-CPT at lr 10⁻⁴ cost −21.2pp. News-CPT at 3×10⁻⁵ recovers roughly two-thirds of the forgetting; the STEM swap fully reverses it. On ArmBench generative tasks: SynDARin 0.04→0.92, Belebele 0.66→0.90, MMLU-Pro-Hy 0.154→0.251, exam history 1.0→2.5 points, and a perfect 50/50 on Scientific MCQA (audited: zero shared 8-grams with ArmSTEM; base already at 0.86). Negative results are reported: POS tagging regresses 0.18→0.01 under CPT and exam math is flat at 1.75 for the released model. The corpus ablation shows ArmWeb beats crawl slices by ~10% bpb on held-out news while crawls win on web/wiki panels, with the ArmWeb+CulturaX union winning the mean (0.532 vs 0.545 best single corpus) — a ranking that transfers exactly to 1.3B confirmation runs. Scale tested: 70M–1.3B for corpus/ladder studies, ~4B effective parameters for the released model (~1,250 H100-hours per run). Baselines are the actual existing open Armenian models plus the base and its own base (Gemma-2-9B), but all competitor models are weight-only releases evaluated out of the box. This is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2609.03350, September 2026), not stated as peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (ArmSTEM is the first Armenian STEM corpus with step-by-step solutions at training scale; ArmWeb is the first curated open Armenian news corpus with verified leakage gates), NEW METHOD (blind re-solve answer-checking applied to translation verification, and verified translated STEM data as a forgetting-reversal lever in continued pretraining), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the fluency-for-knowledge trade pattern identified in existing Armenian models, and the 7.9–17.4% benchmark contamination of public Armenian crawl slices including FineWeb-2's internal train/test leak). The corpus curation pipeline itself (MinHash dedup, n-gram decontamination, datasheets) and the ecosystem-release pattern (following Latxa for Basque, Sherkala for Kazakh, PLLuM for Polish) are standard practice applied to a new language; the scaling-law-based validation is a competent application of known techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: Unusually strong for a language-resource paper. Ablations isolate the tokenizer choice (Table 6), learning rate (1×10⁻⁴ vs 3×10⁻⁵), and the STEM swap with everything else held fixed; the 410M grid is independently replicated by a separately-trained repetition run (0.559 vs 0.561 bpb); the scaling ladder uses 3/3/3/2 seeds per rung with spreads ≤0.003 bpb; per-task 95% binomial half-widths are reported for the likelihood suite; the dedup engine is validated against two independent implementations; the perfect Scientific MCQA score is proactively audited at n=5 and n=8; and negative results (POS regression, flat exam math) are explicitly reported. All data, models, code, per-stage reports, and training configurations are released (huggingface.co/COPA-AI, github.com/COPATeam/armenian_llm_ecosystem). Methodological concerns: each of the five headline CPT runs is a single seed (the authors acknowledge this); the likelihood suite's m-MMLU-hy, ARC-hy, and HellaSwag-hy are Okapi machine translations of English benchmarks, and discriminative signal concentrates in only three tasks since HellaSwag-hy and ARC-hy sit at chance and MultiBLiMP is near ceiling; the decontamination scan is defined against the authors' own chosen evaluation panels, though the contamination findings are about other corpora's leakage rather than their own. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained models and corpora with measured evaluations). Practical: Yes — the released model is a ~4B-parameter dense model runnable on a single commodity GPU, and the full training recipe needed 128 H100s for ~10 hours per run, accessible to well-funded academic labs. Efficient: Cheap relative to alternatives — 10B tokens of CPT versus HyGPT's ~10B-token undisclosed run at 10B parameters, with the paper arguing curation beats raw token count (ArmWeb is a third of HyGPT's corpus yet yields a better model). Effective: The evidence shows the model tops the available Armenian evaluations and beats its own base, but evaluation is MCQA/likelihood-heavy with no generation-quality or safety assessment, so real-world Armenian generation quality is only a proxy claim. Scalable: Partially tested — the scaling ladder reaches 1.3B with a clean power-law fit and the corpus ranking transfers from 410M to 1.3B, but the released model itself was not tested at larger scale and ArmWeb's 3.3B tokens will repeat ~2× in any larger run (repetition gains are measured to 8 epochs, so this is bounded but not unlimited). Delivers concrete software artifacts: two datasets, one model, evaluation forks, and full pipeline code; a competition-math ArmSTEM tranche and an instruction-tuned variant are announced as future releases. Strengths: - The controlled attribution design for the headline finding is exemplary: News-CPT and STEM-CPT runs share trainer, seed, budget, and the replay/code streams, so the 2.2pp-above-base reversal is attributable to the 6% STEM swap alone, and the paper shows English replay alone did not prevent forgetting. - Functional verification of translation (G2 blind re-solving with exact-match answer checking, plus a control distinguishing mistranslation from solver failure) is a genuinely stronger gate than standard LLM adequacy judging and is validated by a 299/300 perfect-agreement human evaluation. - The contamination audit produces a transferable, quantified community finding — 7.9–17.4% document-level overlap of three major public crawl slices with Armenian evaluation panels, including FineWeb-2's own internal train/test leak — and the paper's own comparisons are made fair by decontaminating those panels. - Predictive validation via the scaling ladder (power-law fit extrapolating to 0.47% error on a held-out 1.3B model) converts small-scale data-recipe conclusions into evidence rather than assumption. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that ArmWeb is news-domain-concentrated with limited register diversity and is about a third the size of HyGPT's undisclosed corpus; that within the 6-point mixture swap they cannot separate STEM content, QA format, and verification contributions (a format-matched run is future work, though STEM-CPT-full provides a repetition-matched one); that evaluation is MCQA-heavy with no generation-quality or safety assessment; and that the perfect Scientific MCQA score comes from a 50-item set where only an n-gram audit (not a paraphrase-level audit) has been done. They also note the tokenizer-extension ablation used a smaller model at a fifth of the final budget, so stronger initializers remain untested. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-seed CPT runs: the ±2.2pp headline margin is within the range of seed variance for 4B-parameter CPT, and the paper's own per-task 95% half-widths (up to ±0.041 on INCLUDE) show several task-level differences are not significant; only the aggregate claim is defensible. - The evaluation suite's three machine-translated benchmarks (Okapi m-MMLU-hy, ARC-hy, HellaSwag-hy) may share translationese with ArmSTEM's translated training data, a subtle train/test stylistic affinity the decontamination gates (n-gram based) cannot catch; the paper argues against translationese artifacts using natively authored evaluations but does not address this affinity on the translated panels specifically. - The strongest competitor comparison is structurally asymmetric: HyGPT-10b, tweety-7b, and ArmenianGPT are evaluated without any adaptation to the strict ArmBench output formats, and no instruction-tuned variant of arm-gemma-e4b exists yet, so the 0.62 vs 0.57 accuracy-mean comparison against the one instruction-tuned competitor (ArmenianGPT) is the only like-for-like generative comparison and rests on small per-task sets. - The forgetting-reversal result is demonstrated at one model scale (~4B) and one base model; whether the 6% verified-STEM-swap lever holds for other languages and bases is claimed ("no Armenian-specific machinery") but not tested. - STEM-CPT-full's split behavior (better exam math, worse format tasks, worse exam history) is explained post hoc while composition (15/85 vs 51/49 math/science) and repetition change together — the authors flag this confound but it is unresolved. Bottom Line: For anyone doing low-resource language adaptation, this is worth reading in full — the controlled forgetting-reversal experiment, the answer-preserving translation verification, and the contamination audit are directly reusable beyond Armenian, and the released ecosystem is the only auditable starting point for Armenian LLM work despite the single-seed and translated-benchmark caveats.

Knowing Before Answering: Decoding Language Models for Reliable RAG

SM Huq, C Child, T Weyde, P Madhyastha · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces a lightweight three-way "RAG triage" router — a logistic regression probe trained on a single hidden layer's activations — that classifies retrieved evidence as ANSWER, REFUSE, or CONFLICT before the model generates a response. - Why it's important: RAG systems currently hallucinate or confidently answer from contradictory documents, and existing prompting/abstention fixes either operate post-generation or collapse the problem to binary answer/refuse, missing the distinct conflict failure mode. - How it does it: It decodes the evidence state linearly from the model's internal representations — hidden states, MLP outputs, or attention-derived features extracted via forward hooks at the last prompt token — using a controlled counterfactual-substitution benchmark to prevent parametric-knowledge leakage. - The good: Across 16 models (90M–32B, dense/MoE/hybrid/quantized), the activation router reaches up to 0.91 accuracy and cuts the False Answer Rate by up to 75% relative to the strongest prompt baseline, with random-label controls (0.332 ± 0.013) and zero-shot transfer to RAGTruth (0.84–0.92 accuracy) supporting that the signal is real and not dataset-specific. - The missing: The benchmark is fully synthetic (Gemini 2.5 Pro entity substitution, BM25 distractors, fixed 5-document contexts), so the three-way result on naturalistic conflicting evidence is untested — the RAGTruth transfer is necessarily binary because RAGTruth lacks conflict annotations. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on RAG reliability, hallucination detection, or interpretability-driven routing; skip it if you only deploy systems with naturalistic, possibly adversarial retrieval, since the diagnostic-to-production gap remains open.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (78) is high: the three-way Answer/Refuse/Conflict pre-generation triage is a genuine problem reformulation backed by a leakage-audited counterfactual benchmark and causal patching evidence, not merely a probe applied to a dataset. Rigor (75) is strong on ablations (random-label control, binary-vs-three-way, prompt-robustness sweeps, layer analysis across 16 models) but is held down by fully synthetic labels verified largely by one LLM plus one co-author, in-domain-only headline evaluation, and preprint status. Non-Obviousness (72) — the linear decodability of evidence state at the last prompt token is a useful, moderately surprising finding. Completeness (75) and Resilience (70) are solid thanks to honest, quantified limitations, though naturalistic three-way evaluation and end-to-end RAG outcome measurement are missing, so the diagnostic-to-production gap weakens resistance to adversarial review. Impact (70) for a released code-plus-dataset artifact with zero marginal inference cost. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*75 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*70 = 74.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying Retrieval-Augmented Generation face a reliability problem: retrieval is imperfect, so retrieved documents may be insufficient to answer a question or may contain mutually contradictory answers, and models tend to generate unsupported or contradictory responses rather than acknowledging evidential gaps (per Niu et al. 2024, Joren et al. 2025). Prior fixes — prompting with refusal policies (Zhou et al. 2023), confidence-based abstention (Kadavath et al. 2022), retrieval-side relevance estimation (Yoran et al. 2024), external entailment (TRUE) — share two limitations: they operate on the output side of the model, and they frame the problem as binary answer/refuse. A model that confidently answers from contradictory documents fails in a qualitatively different way from one answering without support, and the authors argue this distinction matters for trust, downstream tasks, and system design. The gap they close is a pre-generation, three-way evidence-state decision that does not consume additional tokens or inference cost. Key Idea: The core insight is that the evidence state (answerable / insufficient / conflicting) is linearly decodable from the model's internal activations before generation begins — specifically from a single middle-layer hidden state at the last prompt token — so a trivial multinomial logistic regression on those activations can triage the request more reliably than any prompting-based policy, at essentially zero marginal cost. The supporting construction trick is a counterfactual entity-substitution benchmark (following Xie et al. 2024, executed with Gemini 2.5 Pro, globally consistent substitutions) that forces the model to rely on context rather than parametric memory, making the three labels well-defined and leakage-auditable via a NO-CTX condition (models score 0.24–0.36 without context). Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Benchmark construction: 2,391 question–answer–evidence triples sampled from TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and Natural Questions (797 each); each question yields three aligned 5-document instances — ANSWER (gold + 4 BM25 distractors), REFUSE (5 BM25 non-gold documents), CONFLICT (original gold + a conflicting version with a different substituted answer entity + 3 distractors) — totaling 7,173 instances, split 70/10/20 at the question level. (2) Feature extraction: forward hooks capture per-layer hidden states (H), MLP outputs (M), and attention-derived features (7 scalars from the last query token's attention row over document segments: top-1/top-2 mass, gap, entropy, retriever-score alignment, coverage, margin). (3) Router training: multinomial logistic regression with StandardScaler and sigmoid calibration is trained per layer per feature type; the layer/feature combination with the best validation accuracy is selected. Metrics are accuracy, Macro-F1, and False Answer Rate (fraction of REFUSE/CONFLICT instances predicted as ANSWER), with 95% bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples over 1,435 test instances). Critical design decisions: (a) counterfactual substitution with global consistency — well-justified and empirically audited via the NO-CTX condition; (b) last-token representation over pooling — justified by an ablation showing final-token beats Doc-end-mean and Doc-token-mean pooling (e.g., 0.858 vs. 0.637 at k=5 for Qwen3-4B-Instruct), though performance degrades at longer contexts; (c) treating CONFLICT as a separate class — justified by the binary-vs-three-way ablation (similar accuracy, 0.832 vs. 0.829, but three-way lowers FAR 0.127 → 0.104 and raises Macro-F1 0.811 → 0.829). Key Results: The activation router (RA) beats every prompt-based and specialized baseline on all 16 models: accuracies range from 0.69 (Falcon-H1-Tiny-90M) to 0.91 (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-27B), with FAR as low as 0.06. The strongest prompt-based competitor is gpt-oss-20b with ATTR at 0.80 accuracy, but on most models prompt baselines sit near chance (0.33); specialized RAG models Self-RAG (0.340) and ChatQA-1.5 (0.370) and surface-text baselines TF-IDF+LR (0.356) and NLI DeBERTa (0.369) are all near chance. Category-level results (Table 2) show the router's largest gains on CONFLICT (e.g., OLMo-3.1-32B-Instruct: 0.44 → 0.90) and REFUSE, while prompt baselines fail via two behavioral modes — small/non-instruction-tuned models always answer; large instruction-tuned models over-refuse. Mechanistic findings: hidden-state features beat MLP outputs and attention features in most models; best-probe layers concentrate in the middle-to-upper-middle network (inverted-U), stable across OLMo-2 post-training stages; exceptions include Falcon-H1-Tiny-90M (early peak, hybrid Mamba design) and OLMo-3.1-32B-Instruct (early decodability). Hidden-state patching (Meng et al. 2022 style, 100 source-target pairs, 11 models) shifts downstream router predictions at rates exceeding 0.70 for refuse→answer and conflict→answer in instruction-tuned models, and generation-level patching changes 63–83% of free-form outputs (Jaccard ≥ 0.30) with ≤0.01 degeneration rate. Selective abstention at 50% coverage yields 0.943 average accuracy with FAR 0.013. Zero-shot transfer to RAGTruth (MS MARCO portion, 4 model families) gives 0.84–0.92 accuracy but only 0.63–0.65 Macro-F1 and in a binary setting. Tested scale: 16 models, 90M–32B parameters, single NVIDIA A100 (80GB) experiments; the dataset itself is small (7,173 instances, 1,435 test). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (three-way Answer/Refuse/Conflict evidence-state triage decided before generation) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the controlled counterfactual three-way diagnostic) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (evidence state is linearly decodable from middle-layer activations across architectures, and the probed layer is causally active per patching). The router itself — logistic regression on hidden states — is a standard linear-probe technique (Alain & Bengio 2017); the novelty lies in the problem framing, the leakage-controlled benchmark, and the systematic cross-model layer-probing and causal analysis, not in any new decoding algorithm. Closest prior work (Probing-RAG, SeaKR, RedeEP, LLM Microscope) is binary, post-generation, or single-perturbation; the paper distinguishes itself on the three-way, pre-generation setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: random-label control (0.332 ± 0.013, near chance), binary-vs-three-way comparison, cross-model transfer within the OLMo-2 family (fine-tuned variants transfer; base does not), prompt-robustness sweep (P0–P5; stable under lexical variation, degrades under question-first ordering), feature-source and layer-aggregation ablations (Top3/All layers, H+M combination, MLP classifier), long-context ablation (k = 5→20 showing distribution-shift sensitivity), artifact-robustness via back-translation (0.80–0.83 accuracy retained), and activation-steering ablation. Bootstrap CIs are reported with a fixed seed; the NO-CTX condition doubles as a leakage audit. Code and dataset are released at https://github.com/SyedHuq28/Knowing-Before-Answering-Decoding-Language-Models-for-Reliable-RAG. Methodological concerns: (a) the benchmark is authored and verified largely by the same tool (Gemini 2.5 Pro) that generates the counterfactual substitutions — human verification was one co-author on a 10% stratified sample, self-reported at 100% agreement; (b) routers are trained per-model on this benchmark and evaluated on the same benchmark's test split, so the headline numbers measure in-domain probe accuracy, with only the binary RAGTruth transfer as an out-of-domain check; (c) some named models in the tables (e.g., "Qwen3.5", "OLMo-3.1") are newer than typical review-familiar releases, and the arXiv ID (2608.27661, dated Aug 2026) and COLM 2026 venue indicate very recent work — baselines are current published methods but several are reimplemented prompt adaptations rather than original systems. Single-seed training for the routers is not explicitly addressed beyond the random-label control's standard deviations. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavored artifact — a releasable router plus dataset). Practical: Yes — the router is a logistic regression over activations extractable via forward hooks on any open-weight transformer; experiments ran on single 80GB A100s. Efficient: Zero additional tokens or inference cost beyond one forward pass the model already performs, a decisive advantage over CoT-style prompting and specialized RAG models; per-model probe training is cheap. Effective: Strong evidence it solves the diagnostic triage problem (up to 0.91 accuracy, FAR down to 0.06, causal patching confirmation), but only proxy evidence for naturalistic RAG reliability — the RAGTruth transfer is binary and its Macro-F1 (0.63–0.65) is markedly weaker than its accuracy. Scalable: Not tested beyond 32B parameters or 20-document contexts; the long-context ablation shows accuracy dropping to 0.72–0.82 at k=20 with train-at-k=5 degradation, so longer production retrieval stacks are an open risk. The work delivers a software artifact (code + dataset at the GitHub URL) plus a reusable diagnostic methodology; it does not release trained router weights per se, and stops at paper form for the steering direction. Strengths: - Genuine problem reframing: elevating CONFLICT from a confound to a first-class prediction target, with the binary-vs-three-way ablation quantifying exactly what the extra class buys (FAR 0.127 → 0.104 at no accuracy cost). - The leakage-audit discipline: counterfactual substitution plus an empirically reported NO-CTX condition (0.24–0.36 across all 16 models, including 32B) directly tests the benchmark's central assumption rather than asserting it. - Breadth of the model sweep: 16 models spanning 90M–32B, dense/MoE/hybrid/quantized, base/SFT/DPO/instruct/reasoning, which turns the layer-probing analysis into a cross-family finding rather than a single-model anecdote — including honest reporting of exceptions (Falcon-H1, Granite's irregular profile) with plausible architectural explanations. - Causal validation beyond correlation: hidden-state patching shows the probed middle layer is a functional control point (>0.70 prediction shift in two directions), and generation-level patching confirms the signal propagates to free-form text, with the authors candidly noting it "does not provide a complete explanation." Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly label the benchmark "a diagnostic testbed rather than as a replacement for naturalistic RAG evaluation." They acknowledge (Appendix G) that RAGTruth lacks conflict annotations, so the transfer experiment is binary and does not test three-way transfer, calling for a fully annotated naturalistic three-way benchmark. They report prompt-structure sensitivity (P4 question-first ordering, P5 structured format affecting small models), context-length distribution shift at larger k, and that steering only "partially controls" behavior with late-layer interventions degrading performance (Granite). They also note prompt baselines' failures reflect model-level behavioral biases, and that generation-level patching does not fully explain generation. This is a credibility positive: limitations are confronted directly and in specific, quantified terms rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The benchmark's labels are manufactured by the same LLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) that performs substitutions and quality verification; the human check is one co-author, 10% of data, self-reported 100% agreement — a circularity risk if substitution artifacts are systematically detectable by probes, and no inter-annotator study is reported. - Every headline number is in-domain probe accuracy on the authors' own synthetic distribution; the only external check (RAGTruth) is binary and shows a large accuracy/Macro-F1 gap (e.g., 0.92 accuracy but 0.65 Macro-F1 for Granite), suggesting severe class-imbalance or refusal-distribution issues in transfer that the accuracy figures mask. - CONFLICT instances are constructed by a single counterfactual substitution in one gold document — a narrow operationalization of "conflicting evidence"; real conflicts arise from nuanced disagreement, temporal staleness, or partial overlap, none of which are represented, so decodability of the synthetic conflict pattern may not generalize. - Retrieval is fixed to BM25 with 5 fixed documents; no dense retrievers, no adversarial distractors, and no evaluation on the end-to-end RAG outcome (does routing to refusal actually reduce hallucinated answers in generation?), so the downstream utility claim is asserted, not measured. - Cross-model transfer is only tested within the OLMo-2 family; whether a router can transfer across families (eliminating per-model training) is unexplored, though the base-vs-finetuned transfer failure hints it may not. - The FAR reduction "up to 75%" claim is against the strongest prompt baseline on the best models; on near-chance baselines the relative improvement is trivially large, and per-model baselines for gpt-oss-20b (0.82 ATTR accuracy vs. 0.82 router accuracy) show the router does not win everywhere on accuracy. Bottom Line: A practitioner building reliable RAG should read this: the three-way framing, the leakage-audited diagnostic benchmark, and the cross-model evidence that middle-layer activations encode evidence state are directly useful and likely predictive of where the field is heading — but treat the headline accuracies as diagnostic-testbed results, not production-ready triage, since naturalistic three-way evaluation remains undone.

An Open Recipe for IMO Gold: Training Nemotron for Olympiad Mathematics (6 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an open, natural-language test-time-compute pipeline built on three post-trained variants of Nemotron 3 Ultra (550B-A55B MoE) that scored 30 out of 42 points at IMO 2026, above the gold-medal cutoff of 29, with no formal prover, external tools, or internet access. - Why it's important: Gold-level olympiad proof generation had previously been demonstrated only by closed frontier systems (Gemini Deep Think, an OpenAI model); this is the first open, fully reproducible recipe — checkpoints, data, code, proofs, and compute accounting all released — showing how post-training and inference design produce that result. - How it does it: Three checkpoints (general, SFT, RL) run an iterative generate-verify-refine search where candidate proofs are accepted only under a unanimous 16-judgment panel from two selective verifier checkpoints, followed by a separate high-compute IMO-style final-selection stage; gains come from checkpoint complementarity, not more samples from one model. - The good: The verifier audit (Table 3) is unusually rigorous — on 300 stratified proofs it shows the RL+SFT unanimous panel achieves a 1.1% false-accept rate (95% CI [0.0, 2.7]) at the cost of an 81.3% false-reject rate, with bootstrap intervals, and honestly reports the panel's failure mode (both accepted-but-wrong proofs received unanimous full scores). - The missing: The headline claim rests on a single competition run with no replication; all ablations use a 30-problem development set the authors themselves used for design decisions, and model-jury ground truth shares the ~2-point blind spot the paper admits on Problems 3 and 6. - Read it or not: Read it if you build reasoning/inference pipelines or study test-time scaling — the verifier precision/recall trade-off analysis, the attempt-budget-vs-checkpoint-diversity experiments, and the documented negative results (Appendix A) are more instructive than the medal itself; skip it if you only want the IMO score, which a blog post covers.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (with a strong systems component). Non-Obviousness (75) is the standout: the asymmetric-cost verification analysis and the measured finding that checkpoint diversity beats attempt scaling are transferable insights for any generate-verify-refine system. Completeness (80) and Resilience (78) benefit from radical openness (checkpoints, data, code, proofs, compute accounting) and candid negative results including the admitted 2-point verifier blind spot; Rigor (70) is solid (clustered bootstrap verifier audit, compute-isolated pooling experiment) but capped by the single-run headline, dev-set Goodhart risk, and preprint status. Novelty (60) is the limiting dimension — the recipe assembles known techniques, and the medal confirms rather than opens a new capability class: 0.20*60 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*78 + 0.10*80 = 73.
empirical Novelty 60 Rigor 70 Non-Obv 75 Completeness 80 Resilience 78 Impact 80

Problem & Motivation: Teams competing in events like the IMO — and, more broadly, practitioners building LLM systems for long-form natural-language mathematical proof — face a choice between formal-verifier pipelines (Lean-based, hard to scale, limited domain coverage) and pure natural-language pipelines whose correctness cannot be machine-checked. Prior natural-language gold-medal results (IMO 2025) came exclusively from closed frontier labs, leaving open whether the post-training and inference recipe behind such results can be reproduced, studied, and extended by the community. The paper targets researchers and engineers who need to know which levers — checkpoint choice, verification strictness, refinement, ensemble composition, final-solution selection — actually move performance on hard proof problems, at what compute cost. Key Idea: The core insight is an asymmetric-cost verification rule: a false accept terminates search on an invalid proof irreversibly, while a false reject merely delays, so the search-time verifier should be tuned for extreme precision (unanimous 16/16 score-1 judgments from the two most selective checkpoints, SFT at 4.5% and RL at 12.4% single-checkpoint false-accept rates, jointly reaching 1.1%) while generation budget is diversified across complementary checkpoints — the paper shows doubling one checkpoint's attempts from 128 to 256 yields one extra accepted problem, whereas spending the same tokens on 64 SFT attempts reaches problems the RL checkpoint cannot (7 of 18 accepted problems came from only one checkpoint). Methodology: The system has a training phase and a two-stage inference phase. (1) SFT: starting from Nemotron 3 Ultra GA, a 414,890-example proof corpus (58,543 generation, 67,971 refinement, 236,360 verification, 52,016 meta-verification traces) is built synthetically using DeepSeek-V4-Pro on 15,879 hard AoPS problems with up to three feedback-conditioned refinement rounds; training uses standard per-token cross-entropy in BF16 at 425,984-token context on 512 GB200 GPUs with AdamW, peak LR 1.5e-5, cosine decay. (2) RL: 9,597 problems filtered to a 1–3-of-4 solve band (graded by DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale) train proof generation with a DeepSeekMath-V2-style reward (self-analysis reward removed, α=1, β=0) via asynchronous RL (PipeLinERL-like, dynamic sampling, truncated importance sampling, entropy masking above 0.4) on 128+128+16 nodes of 4×GB200 each. (3) Inference search: per problem, round 1 draws 384 proofs (3 checkpoints × 8 strategy-diverse prompts × 16 samples); RL+SFT verifiers issue 8 judgments each (0/0.5/1 scale); unanimous-1 proofs are accepted, else up to 16 top-pool proofs get 192 refinement attempts per round, for ≤8 rounds. (4) Final selection: up to three finalists are scored 0–7 by all three checkpoints (16 judgments each, 48 total) under a reference-free IMO-style milestone rubric; the highest-mean proof is submitted. Notable design decisions: budget split across checkpoints rather than one model (justified by the round-1 pooling experiment, Table 4); unanimity over the two selective verifiers (justified by the audit showing GA's votes add only false vetoes); and a deliberately separate final-selection prompt from the search-time verifier prompt (motivated but not directly ablated). Key Results: Officially graded at IMO 2026, the system scored 30/42 (gold cutoff 29): full marks on Problems 1, 2, 4, 5 and 1/7 each on Problems 3 and 6. The submitted proofs consumed ~707M generated tokens and 1,464 GB200 GPU-hours; the full run including in-flight rounds reached 2.31B tokens and 4,800 GPU-hours. All four full-credit proofs cleared final selection within 76 minutes per session. On the 30-problem development set, the ensemble scored 188 with 25 internally accepted problems versus 180/23 for the best single checkpoint (RL), 165/21 for SFT, and 162/23 for GA (Table 2, jury = GPT-5.5 + Gemini 3.1 Pro + Claude Opus 4.8). The verifier audit (Table 3, 300 proofs, 2,000 clustered bootstrap resamples) gives the numbers quoted above; relaxing acceptance to 14/16 raises false accepts from 1.1% to 17.0%. A candid negative finding: both internal and independent model juries estimated ~32 points, two above the official 30, entirely from Problems 3 and 6 — evidence of a shared model-verification blind spot, not search noise. A post-cutoff continued run found a better Problem 6 solution (4/7 in an unofficial human regrade, would imply 33) after 8h25m and 610M extra tokens. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (with an accompanying NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, Nemotron-IMO-Bench). The genuinely novel elements are the first open, fully released gold-level natural-language IMO system; the precision-first unanimous-panel verifier analysis with quantified false-accept/false-reject trade-offs; and the documented evidence that checkpoint diversity beats attempt scaling. The generate-verify-refine loop, the reward design, and the judge rubric are explicitly adapted from DeepSeekMath-V2 and MathArena — competent application of known ideas to a new, harder, open setting rather than a new formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-targeted: single-checkpoint pipelines, a verifier audit with bootstrap confidence intervals and problem-clustered resampling, and a compute-isolated round-1 pooling experiment (Table 4). No multiple seeds or significance tests are reported for the headline ablation scores, and the ensemble run is explicitly not compute-matched to the single-checkpoint baselines (the authors handle this with the separate Table 4 experiment). Reproducibility is a stated central goal and is unusually strong: two checkpoints, SFT and RL datasets, Nemotron-IMO-Bench (CC BY 4.0), inference code in NeMo-Skills, the RL recipe in NeMo-RL, submitted proofs, and per-problem GPU-hour/token accounting are all released (Hugging Face collection nvidia/nemotron-labs-imo-2026). Methodological concerns: (a) the 30-problem development set was used both for design iteration (checkpoint selection at SFT step 1300, verifier rule choice) and for ablation evaluation — a Goodhart risk the authors do not quantify; (b) the audit's ground truth is the same three-model jury that itself exhibits the admitted 2-point blind spot on Problems 3 and 6, so false-accept rates are relative to a noisy reference, though the official IMO result independently corroborates the pipeline's precision; (c) results rest on one competition sitting with no reruns; (d) the paper is an arXiv/company technical report, not peer-reviewed, and the 4/7 continued-run grade is explicitly unofficial. The negative-results appendix (triage discarded ancestors of correct proofs in 44% of cases) is a credibility positive. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — the released pipeline is a working artifact evaluated by an actual deployment at IMO 2026). - Practical: No — reproducing the full recipe requires roughly 512 GB200 GPUs for SFT and 272 four-GPU GB200 nodes for RL, plus ~4,800 GPU-hours per competition-style run; only holders of very large GPU fleets can replicate end-to-end, though the released checkpoints are usable for inference at much lower cost. - Efficient: The authors show where compute pays: ~707M tokens and 1,464 GPU-hours produced all six submitted proofs, and Table 4 shows the marginal token is better spent on a second checkpoint than on doubled sampling of one; nevertheless the absolute cost per solved hard problem is very high (e.g., 650M tokens for Problem 6's single point). - Effective: Yes for the stated target — the 30/42 official grade against human graders is direct evidence, not a proxy; but the system leaves hard problems (P3, P6) essentially unsolved, and both internal and external model verification over-credited those proofs by ~2 points. - Scalable: Not tested beyond the competition configuration; the continued-run experiment shows extended search found a better Problem 6 proof (round 8, 8h25m), suggesting returns to more rounds, but 10× scale on problems or search budget is untested and unclaimed. The work delivers a substantial software/data artifact: two model checkpoints, two training datasets, a 200-problem benchmark, inference and training code, submitted proofs, and resource accounting. Strengths: - The verifier operating-point analysis (Table 3) reframes verification as an asymmetric-cost decision problem and quantifies it with clustered bootstrap intervals — a genuinely transferable insight for any generate-verify-refine system, not just olympiad math. - The checkpoint-diversity finding (Table 4: RL 128 + SFT 128 at 2.36B tokens beats RL 256 at 1.59B on accepted problems 18 vs 14, with only 6 of 18 accepted from both checkpoints) is a concrete, measured answer to how test-time budget should be allocated across models. - Radical openness: releasing post-trained checkpoints, training corpora, code, the benchmark, the submitted proofs, and full compute accounting makes this the first independently checkable gold-level result in this space. - The negative-results appendix (cross-proof context, zero-first ranking, diverse-proof synthesis, triage routing) documents failed variants with effect sizes, including the striking triage finding that 44% of eventual winners' round-1 ancestors would have been discarded — evidence that resists publication bias. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that "accepted" means internal-verification acceptance, not official correctness; they report the 2-point overestimate shared by both their search verifier and the independent model jury on Problems 3 and 6, attributing it to a shared model-verification blind spot; they note the 4/7 Problem 6 grade is an unofficial human regrade without official marking schemes; they acknowledge the ensemble ablation run is not compute-matched to single-checkpoint runs and address it with a separate experiment; and they concede that aggressive triage discards correct-proof lineage. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-run headline: the 30/42 result has no variance estimate; nothing is known about score stability across runs, problem instances, or GPU-allocation schedules (the three problems per day shared one allocation, an unexamined coupling). - The 30-problem development set serves as both design-tuning and ablation benchmark; the ablation deltas (e.g., 188 vs 180) come from this same set, and with 30 problems a few problems' worth of jury noise could plausibly reorder configurations — no seed or problem-level bootstrap on these comparisons is given. - The independent jury used as ablation ground truth contains the very models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8) whose grading calibrated the final-selection rubric design (via MathArena), so "jury score 7 = correct" is not a neutral reference; the admitted P3/P6 blind spot quantifies this at roughly 2/42. - No head-to-head against the strongest available general-purpose reasoning models under matched compute — the comparison set is Nemotron's own three checkpoints, so the reader cannot tell how much of the gold result comes from the pipeline versus the base model's frontier-adjacent capability. - The final-selection prompt's separation from the search verifier is motivated but never ablated; the eight generation prompts are hand-designed without evidence that their diversity (rather than mere prompt variation) drives decorrelation. - SFT and RL are evaluated only as a pair of specialists from one base model at one scale (550B-A55B); the claim that the recipe generalizes to other models or sizes is untested. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating LLM reasoning systems this is essential reading — the quantified verifier trade-offs, the diversity-beats-sampling result, and the honest negative results are worth more than most benchmark papers in this area — even though the medal itself merely confirms what closed frontier labs already demonstrated, at a compute cost only a handful of organizations can bear.

#21 — Innovative (73)

Selective Forgetting

arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a knowledge-graph memory pipeline for LLM agents with an explicit importance-based forgetting module, and shows experimentally that graph-structured retrieval loses to flat vector RAG on LongMemEval while selective pruning removes ~10% of a persistent 27,021-node graph with no measurable quality loss (Δ F1 = +0.001, 95% CI [−0.015, +0.016]). - Why it's important: Long-term agent memory grows unboundedly in deployed assistants, and the field's assumption that graph-based memory beats flat retrieval is largely untested head-to-head; a negative result plus a bounded-cost retention mechanism directly informs memory-system design choices. - How it does it: Each turn is extracted by GPT-4o-mini into typed nodes/attributed edges with cosine de-duplication, questions are answered from a 2-hop subgraph of top-5 retrieved roots, and every 400 turns nodes are pruned when a weighted score of recency, access frequency, degree centrality, and age falls below 0.10. - The good: Honest, statistically careful negative result — a paired bootstrap over 500 questions shows the graph baseline is significantly worse than flat RAG (ΔF1 = −0.050, CI [−0.085, −0.016]), with a clear mechanistic diagnosis (entity decomposition destroys verbatim assistant-turn recall: judge accuracy 0.607 vs 0.911). - The missing: No matched-compression control (e.g., random pruning of 9.8% of nodes) to show the importance function matters, only one benchmark, one small extraction model, and a single un-swept operating point on the compression–quality curve. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building agent memory systems who assumes GraphRAG-style structure is a free win — this is one of the few controlled experiments showing where it fails — but skip it if you want a validated forgetting algorithm, since the retention module is evaluated only once, on one benchmark, at modest compression.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (70) and statistical hygiene are a standout — paired bootstrap with 95% CIs, Wilson intervals, released code — and the controlled negative result (graph significantly worse than flat RAG, ΔF1 = −0.050) with per-type failure localization is a genuinely valuable NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (Novelty 70, Non-Obviousness 68). Completeness (85) and Resilience (85) are excellent thanks to unusually candid scope discipline that pre-registers its own top follow-up. The composite is held back by Rigor gaps (no matched random-pruning control, no HippoRAG/Mem0 baselines, generator-judge coupling) and modest Impact (60) from a 9.8% compression proof-of-concept on one benchmark. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*85 + 0.10*60 = 73.
