Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Developers of personal AI assistants need long-term memory that persists across months of interaction. The dominant approach is flat retrieval-augmented generation over vector stores; a growing line of work (GraphRAG, HippoRAG, Mem0) assumes that representing conversation as knowledge graphs improves recall and multi-hop reasoning. The authors argue two gaps exist: (1) the graph-over-flat assumption is rarely tested directly at matched retrieval budgets, and (2) existing graph memory systems address writing and consistency but not unbounded memory growth — the need for selective forgetting. The paper targets both: does graph structure help, and can a persistent graph be pruned cheaply without hurting recall? Key Idea: The core move is not an algorithmic breakthrough but a controlled adversarial audit of a popular assumption, paired with a simple score-and-prune retention rule: node importance = 0.35·recency + 0.25·frequency + 0.20·centrality + 0.20·age-decay, with nodes below 0.10 removed every 400 turns together with incident edges. The key insight is analytical: the graph's failure on verbatim recall questions is caused by extraction decomposing turns into entities, discarding surface form — an insight the paper surfaces with per-question-type breakdowns. Methodology: Three-stage pipeline. (1) Update: each turn is processed by a GPT-4o-mini extraction call against a fixed 9-label ontology (Person, Organization, Location, Event, Concept, Artifact, Preference, Goal, Skill), returning strict JSON; assistant turns are processed in two modes (user-related facts and assistant-stated facts). Node descriptors are embedded with nomic-embed-text (local via Ollama) and de-duplicated by an O(1) title index followed by a cosine check at threshold 0.92. (2) Retrieval: query entities are extracted and embedded; nodes above cosine 0.75 are ranked, the top 5 seed a BFS 2-hop expansion capped at 15 nodes, and the subgraph is serialized into the answer prompt. (3) Retention: every 400 turns, the weighted importance score prunes nodes below 0.10. Evaluation uses LongMemEval (500 questions, ~33-month haystacks, 6 question types). Experiment 1 builds a fresh graph per question vs. a flat top-5 chunk baseline; Experiment 2 ingests all 500 haystacks into one persistent graph (27,021 nodes, 440.6 MB) with forgetting applied once. Critical design decisions: matched candidate budget of 5 (justified, isolates representation from hit count); hand-fixed, unswept retention weights and thresholds (acknowledged as unjustified beyond priors); extraction model choice GPT-4o-mini (budget-driven, limits generality). No explicit objective function beyond the heuristic importance score. Key Results: Experiment 1: baseline RAG beats the graph overall — token F1 0.468 vs 0.417, judge accuracy 0.536 vs 0.454 (ΔF1 = −0.050, 95% CI [−0.085, −0.016], significant; Δjudge = −0.082, CI [−0.128, −0.034], significant). The graph wins only on temporal-reasoning judge accuracy (0.293 vs 0.278). The largest deficit is single-session (assistant) questions: judge 0.607 vs 0.911. Experiment 2: one-shot forgetting removes 2,653 nodes (9.8%), 2,560 edges (5.5%), and 9.5% of bytes (440.6→398.6 MB) with F1 unchanged (0.292→0.293) and judge accuracy down 1.6 points (CI [−0.038, +0.006], not significant). Note the persistent-graph absolute performance (F1 ≈ 0.29) is far below the per-question setting (0.42–0.47), attributed to cross-conversation interference. Baselines are a straightforward flat-RAG control rather than strong tuned systems (no HippoRAG/Mem0 comparison at matched budget). Scale is modest: 500 benchmark questions, ~27K nodes, consumer GPU workstation. Surprising/counter-intuitive headline: the structured representation significantly underperforms flat retrieval at matched budget. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a controlled negative result on graph-vs-flat memory at matched candidate budget, with per-type failure localization) plus an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (the retention module integrated into the graph lifecycle). The individual components — LLM KG extraction, embedding de-duplication, BFS subgraph retrieval, Ebbinghaus/recency-weighted pruning — are standard combinations of existing ideas (closely following Generative Agents, MemoryBank, Mem0); the genuinely new contribution is the empirical characterization showing extraction-based structure hurts verbatim recall and the quantified cost bound of pruning. Rigor & Reproducibility: Unusually strong statistical hygiene for this area: paired nonparametric bootstrap (10,000 resamples), 95% CIs plus Wilson intervals for the binary judge metric, SEMs reported per condition, and paired comparisons explicitly separating significant from non-significant differences. Code is released (https://github.com/skhanzad/Selective-Amnesia). Ablations are weak: no component-wise ablation of the importance function, no sweep of the retention parameters (authors acknowledge a single operating point), and critically no matched random-pruning control — the authors name this themselves as their top follow-up. Methodological concerns: LLM-as-judge uses the same model family (GPT-4o-mini) as the generator, a self-judging bias risk not discussed; evaluation is confined to one benchmark (LongMemEval); the forgetting module is applied once rather than continuously during ingestion, so the periodic regime claimed in the architecture is never actually tested; the low persistent-graph F1 (0.292) makes the no-degradation claim easier to satisfy (floor effects). Baselines are current in concept but not tuned alternatives like HippoRAG. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — a working memory pipeline and released code). Practical: Yes — runs on a single consumer workstation (RX 7800 XT, 16 GB RAM) with local embeddings and a cheap API model. Efficient: Per-turn cost is O(Nd + M) due to exhaustive cosine scans (acknowledged as incidental; ANN indexing would remove it), plus one LLM extraction call per turn; forgetting is O(N+M) amortized over 400 turns. Effective: Mixed — the evidence shows the graph pipeline does not solve the recall-quality problem (it loses to flat RAG), and shows pruning is non-destructive at 9.5% compression; whether it remains non-destructive at meaningful compression (50%+) is untested. Scalable: Not tested — 27K nodes is small for a claimed long-term deployment; the linear-scan retrieval and one-shot pruning would need re-evaluation at 10–100× graph size. Delivers a code artifact (GitHub repo) but no packaged library, benchmark, or trained model. Strengths: - A genuinely useful negative result: the paper tests the graph-over-flat assumption head-to-head at a matched retrieval budget and reports a significant deficit with CIs, rather than burying it — rare and valuable for the field. - The per-question-type failure analysis is the intellectual core: localizing the graph's loss to verbatim assistant-turn recall (0.607 vs 0.911) and identifying extraction-induced information loss gives designers an actionable diagnosis, not just a score. - Statistical rigor (paired bootstrap, Wilson intervals, explicit significance marking) exceeds the norm for agent-memory papers. - Unusually candid scope discipline: the appendix explicitly states findings characterize "this extraction-based pipeline at this model scale, not graph-structured memory in general," lists budget constraints, and pre-registers the priority of a matched-compression control. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge: (1) a single small extraction model (GPT-4o-mini) and one benchmark, limiting generality; (2) no sweep of retention parameters, so Experiment 2 characterizes one point on the compression–quality curve; (3) no matched random-pruning control to isolate the importance function's contribution; (4) the conflict-resolution policy retains stale values on knowledge-update questions (proposing last-write-wins as a fix); (5) extraction/merging noise causes the smaller deficits on multi-session and user questions; (6) budget constraints limited them to four complete runs. They confront limitations directly and at the right granularity — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The judge metric is computed by GPT-4o-mini, the same model that generates answers; generator–judge coupling could bias condition comparisons, and no human evaluation validates the judge. - Forgetting is applied once after ingestion, so the paper's central architectural claim — periodic forgetting every 400 turns during a live deployment — is never exercised; cascading effects of repeated pruning (e.g., progressive loss of hub nodes) are unmeasured. - 9.8% compression is far too small to demonstrate the value proposition of forgetting, which is motivated by unbounded growth; the interesting regime (keeping memory bounded over long horizons) is untested. - No comparison to existing graph-memory systems (HippoRAG, Mem0, GraphRAG) or to FadeMem, the closest prior forgetting work — so the reader cannot tell whether the negative result is generic or specific to this pipeline's choices (extraction model, thresholds, subgraph cap of 15). - The four importance components are never ablated; the weights were fixed by convention, so the "importance function" is essentially unvalidated. - Floor effects in Experiment 2 (F1 ≈ 0.29 with heavy cross-conversation interference) make the no-degradation finding less demanding than it appears. Bottom Line: Read it if you build or evaluate agent memory systems — the controlled negative result and verbatim-recall diagnosis are worth more than many positive-result papers in this area — but treat the forgetting module as a modest, single-operating-point proof of concept rather than a validated retention algorithm, and wait for the promised matched-compression control before adopting the scoring rule.

#22 — Innovative (73)

Predict, Don't Iterate: Efficient Adaptive-Length Infilling for Diffusion Language Models

H Xu, S Chen, Y Bei, L Chen, Y Yan, D Fu, J He… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PILL, a training-free (backbone-frozen) decoding framework that lets fixed-length diffusion language models perform variable-length infilling by predicting the span length directly from a mask token's hidden state, decoding a small set of candidate lengths in parallel, and selecting the best candidate with a single-pass post-hoc coherence score. - Why it's important: Diffusion LMs must fix the number of masked positions before decoding, yet infilling quality is acutely sensitive to span length, and prior adaptive-length methods either need a sensitive preset initial length or pay large inference overheads (e.g., CAL: +94% wall-clock time on HumanEval-S), so this removes a practical blocker for code editing and text infilling with DLMs. - How it does it: The core trick is replacing iterative length search with a lightweight MLP probe that regresses log-length from the bidirectional hidden state of one mask token, then packing 2r+1 candidate lengths into one sequence via a slot-wise attention mask with linearly interpolated position IDs (which fixes an under-generation pathology caused by position-ID gaps), and scoring all candidates in one extra forward pass with causally-masked pseudo-likelihood probes over candidate-internal and suffix-continuation tokens. - The good: The evaluation is broad and honest — five DLM backbones (LLaDA-8B Base/Instruct, LLaDA-MoE, Dream-7B, Dream-Coder-7B) across eight code and text benchmarks, where PILL beats the strongest baseline CAL by +4.8 average pass rate on code and +6.0 BLEU-2 on text while running 1.82× faster with only 2 extra forward passes (+7% wall-clock over the fixed-length backbone). - The missing: There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests — all results come from a single deterministic run — and the largest failure mode (probe coverage, 24.3% of errors) plus the 10-point gap to the oracle selector show the selection headroom is quantified but not closed; experiments also stop at 7B/8B models on a single A40. - Read it or not: Read it if you deploy or build on diffusion language models and care about infilling or editing — it is a clean, well-ablated inference-time method with released code — but skip it if you work on autoregressive infilling or adaptive computation generally, as the techniques are DLM-specific.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (72) and Impact (65) pull the composite down: ablations are thorough and code is released, but every result is a single deterministic run with no seeds or error bars, experiments stop at 8B on one A40, and the deliverable is an experimental codebase rather than a packaged tool. Novelty (72) is solid — direct length regression plus the position-ID interpolation trick is a new inference-time recipe, not a new formulation — and Non-Obviousness (76) is the paper's best dimension: identifying that positional gaps cause under-generation was not predictable from prior work. Completeness (78) is helped by the oracle upper bound and explicit failure-mode breakdown. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*76 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*65 = 73.

Problem & Motivation: Diffusion language models (DLMs) with bidirectional attention are naturally suited to infilling — generating a middle span conditioned on both a prefix and a suffix — but decoding requires the number of masked positions L to be fixed in advance, while the correct length L* is unknown and content-dependent. The paper shows (Figure 1a) that a code infilling example is correct only at exactly the right length; one token too few or too many yields wrong completions. Existing adaptive-length methods have two flaws: (i) sensitivity to a preset initial length — CAL's final length and performance degrade sharply as the preset L grows (its MAE rises from 3.56 at L=4 to 24.13 at L=32); and (ii) inference inefficiency — methods like DAEDAL inject per-token length-changing operations, and CAL repeatedly probes denoising confidence, each costing extra forward passes. The audience is anyone running DLM inference for code editing, code infilling, or text-span completion. Key Idea: Predict the infilling length once from the frozen model's own bidirectional hidden state (the mask token's representation aggregates prefix and suffix context, making it a summary of how much content belongs in the gap), rather than searching for it iteratively — then hedge the prediction with a small parallel candidate set, exploiting a careful position-ID interpolation scheme so all candidates share the context in a single sequence without generation pathology. A key enabling observation is that DLMs anchor outputs to position IDs: leaving a positional gap between mask and context causes under-generation, so interpolating each slot's position IDs over a shared interval is what makes parallel multi-length decoding work. Methodology: Three stages over a frozen DLM backbone. (1) Length probing: run one forward pass on P ⊕ [M] ⊕ S, read the mask hidden state at the last layer, concatenate mean-pooled prefix/suffix neighbor states into a 3d vector, and regress log L̂ with a 3-layer MLP (trained per backbone on ~196k self-supervised spans from Py150/LeetCode/CodeContests/C4 with MSE loss, ~100 min on one A40; evaluation datasets are disjoint). (2) Multi-slot parallel decoding: expand L̂ into N = 2r+1 candidates (default r=2, so 5 slots) packed after a shared context region P ⊕ [M]^L̂ ⊕ S; a slot-wise attention mask lets each slot see only the shared context, and each slot's ℓ_j mask tokens get linearly interpolated position IDs across the fixed interval [p_P+1, p_S−1] (Eq. 2), so the suffix is anchored identically for all candidates. Slots denoise in parallel with the shared context's KV cached. (3) Post-hoc selection: since DLM probabilities at already-committed tokens are not predictive scores, the authors construct a single sequence containing all candidates with a block-wise mask; for each candidate, a visible block of candidate tokens plus selected suffix tokens is kept internally causal, and per-position mask "probes" sharing each token's position ID attend strictly to prefix and v_<k, yielding log p(v_k | P, v_<k) with no label leakage. Candidates are ranked by α·s_inner + (1−α)·s_suffix with α=0.5, where the suffix score uses only m ∈ [4,8] tokens (suffix head plus attention-salient tokens, capped at 32). Total extra cost: exactly two forward passes. Critical design decisions — position-ID interpolation (well-justified by Table 4: 51.6 vs 28.2/31.6 Avg Pass@1 for padding variants), the inclusive-causal visible block (justified by the leakage argument), and fixed radius r=2 (justified by ablation showing saturation) — are all ablated. Key Results: Across five DLMs and eight benchmarks (HumanEval-Infilling -S/-M, MBPP-S/-M, MultiPL-E Java and C/C++, WikiText, arXiv), PILL beats the strongest baseline CAL by +4.8 average pass rate on code (e.g., LLaDA-8B-Base Human-S: 71.35 vs 64.74) and +6.0 BLEU-2 on text (Wiki BLEU-2 29.29 vs 15.69). Efficiency on Human-S with LLaDA-8B-Base: PILL 71.35 Pass@1 at 1.18s (+7% over the 1.10s fixed-length backbone), versus CAL 64.74 at 2.13s (+94%) and DAEDAL 44.80 at 2.29s (+117%) — PILL is 1.82× faster than CAL and 6.6 points more accurate, with only 2 extra forward passes versus ~12–14. Baselines are recent and reasonably strong (CAL, DAEDAL, DreamOn), though DAEDAL was adapted rather than native, and DAEDAL actually degrades below the fixed-length backbone on text. The oracle-upper-bound PILL (Oracle) reaches 81.9 on Human-S, showing candidate coverage is good and selection is the main headroom. Failure analysis: probe coverage failures 24.3%, selection failures 11.4%, generation failures 3.6%. The probe itself achieves MAE 2.50 tokens with Acc@5 = 86.4% on Human-S, without any preset length, while CAL's MAE varies from 3.56 to 24.13 depending on initialization. Scaling study: 1→9 candidates raises time 0.82s→1.44s and memory 21.3→33.7 GB, with Pass@1 saturating at r=2. Experiments ran on a single NVIDIA A40 with models up to 8B (LLaDA-MoE variant), plus validation on the newer iLLaDA-8B and a multi-span extension (+4.86 over CAL at 2.6× its speed). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an element of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING in the position-ID/under-generation pathology). The genuinely novel pieces are (a) direct length regression from a frozen DLM's mask-token hidden state replacing iterative search, and (b) the position-ID interpolation scheme enabling parallel multi-length decoding in one sequence without under-generation. The components themselves — MLP probes on hidden states, block-wise attention masking, KV-cache reuse, pseudo-likelihood-style scoring — are standard machinery combined in a new setting, and the honest framing is a well-engineered inference-time recipe rather than a new modeling paradigm. No backbone retraining is involved (unlike DreamOn, FlexMDM, DDOT). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: probe input layer, candidate radius, scored-suffix length m, and score weight α are each varied (Fig. 4); position-ID design is compared against left/right padding and independent single-slot decoding (Table 4); selection strategies are ablated (Table 5, random 51.62 → inner+suffix 71.35); probe-training data scale (1k–100k samples), structural-complexity robustness, and per-stage overhead breakdown (probe 8.9%, multi-slot 3.4%, selection 9.4%) are reported. Code is released at https://github.com/Hsu1023/PILL. Weaknesses: all results are from a single run with deterministic decoding (explicitly stated, following prior adaptive-length work) — no seeds, error bars, or significance tests; the probe is trained per backbone, so there is a preparation cost that baselines partially share (CAL recalibrates per setting); probe-training corpora (LeetCode, CodeContests) have a topical relationship to code benchmarks even though evaluation instances are disjoint, and the authors address OOD concerns via the code-only-probe DreamOn comparison. The oracle-initialized CAL comparison (Table 16) is a fair self-critique — PILL loses to oracle CAL on HumanEval-S/M. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — released code). Practical: Yes — runs on a single NVIDIA A40 (~24 GB working memory at default settings), no backbone modifications or fine-tuning, probe trained in ~100 minutes on the same hardware. Efficient: Only 2 extra forward passes and +5–7% wall-clock over fixed-length decoding, versus +94–117% for CAL/DAEDAL at lower quality; memory grows with candidate count (1.58× from 1 to 9 candidates). Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on code and text infilling at ≤8B scale, but selection quality is the residual bottleneck (11.4% selection failures; PILL(Oracle) is ~10 points higher), so it solves most but not all of the length problem. Scalable: Only claimed implicitly — tested at 7B/8B on one GPU; the authors themselves flag that probe and selection behavior on substantially larger diffusion backbones is unverified, and multi-slot memory growth (~1.3 GB per extra candidate) could matter at 100B+ scale. Delivers a software artifact (public code repository) plus a per-backbone trained probe; not just paper form. Strengths: - The position-ID interpolation insight is the standout: identifying that DLMs anchor generation to position IDs and that any positional gap causes under-generation, then designing interpolation that makes parallel multi-length decoding nearly free (multi-slot stage costs only 3.4% overhead) — this is a non-obvious, reusable technique for any packed DLM decoding. - The replace-search-with-predict reframing cleanly removes the preset-initial-length dependency, backed by a direct length-prediction evaluation (MAE 2.50, Acc@5 86.4%) against CAL's initialization-sensitive MAE of 3.56–24.13. - The leakage-free single-pass causal scoring probe for DLM candidate selection is a careful solution to the real problem that DLMs cannot score sequences by next-token likelihood cheaply, and it is validated by ablation (random selection 51.62 vs 71.35). - Evaluation breadth and self-critique: five backbones, eight benchmarks, an oracle upper bound that localizes the headroom to selection, an explicit failure-mode breakdown, and an honest oracle-CAL comparison where the baseline wins on two benchmarks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (i) complex editing settings — nested spans and repository-level code patches — are not handled and left to future work, and (ii) experiments cover only DLMs up to ~7B/8B parameters on a single GPU, so scaling of the length probe and post-hoc selection to substantially larger backbones is unverified. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-run deterministic decoding with no variance estimates: for pass-rate metrics on code benchmarks with modest test counts, differences of a few points can be within run-to-run or sampling noise; the +4.8/+6.0 headline gains are large enough to likely survive, but per-benchmark comparisons (e.g., 57.49 vs 56.93 on MBPP-S) are not. - The probe is trained per backbone on code-heavy corpora; behavior on heavily non-English or highly templated text domains beyond Wiki/arXiv is untested, and the candidate radius r=2 and α=0.5 were tuned on benchmarks also used for headline reporting — a mild Goodhart risk for the exact operating point. - Only one adaptive-length baseline family (CAL, DAEDAL, DreamOn) is compared; FlexMDM and DDOT are cited as requiring fine-tuning but not empirically compared, so the frontier against fine-tuned adaptive-length methods rests on a partial DreamOn comparison the authors themselves caveat as a different adaptation regime. - The multi-slot layout grows sequence length with candidate count, so long-context infilling (contexts near the backbone's window) may force smaller candidate sets — no long-context stress test is reported. - Surprising result left somewhat unexplained: suffix-score-only selection underperforms random-adjacent levels (63.99 vs inner-only 69.02) even though suffix alignment is the stated motivation — the interaction deserves deeper analysis. Bottom Line: For anyone doing infilling or span-editing with open diffusion LLMs, PILL is now the obvious default — it dominates prior adaptive-length decoding on both quality and speed with a trivial integration cost and released code — and its position-ID interpolation trick alone justifies the read; the main open question is whether the probe-and-select recipe holds at frontier DLM scales.

#23 — Innovative (73)

Zero-Shot Conditional Forecasting and the Information Content of Central Bank Paths

VH Larsen, LA Thorsrud · ifo.de · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper reframes conditional macroeconomic forecasting as an input problem — a fixed, pre-trained multivariate foundation model (Amazon's Chronos-2, 122M parameters) reads a central bank's historical predictions and announced future paths alongside target histories, with no local re-estimation — and uses this to test whether published central bank paths are MSE-optimal summaries of their own information. - Why it's important: Central banks' published projection paths anchor private expectations and move asset prices, so whether they leave exploitable mean-square signal on the table matters for forecast users, and traditional conditional-VAR tools are bound by short macro samples that zero-shot mappings escape. - How it does it: The published path enters as a known-future covariate (via Chronos-2's group attention) rather than as a hard restriction inside an estimated system, and the framework nests Mincer–Zarnowitz and Granger–Ramanathan regressions as its parametric-linear special case, fixing how accuracy gains should be interpreted. - The good: The result is unusually well-defended: it replicates across three country panels (Norway, Sweden, New Zealand), survives asymmetric-loss (Elliott–Komunjer–Timmermann) rationalisations of the path, survives synthetic-only pretraining weights that rule out data contamination, and beats a rung-matched hard-conditioned VAR on rate and inflation at every horizon on all three panels. - The missing: The Diebold–Mariano tests never reject equal accuracy in the cells where the map beats Norges Bank, so the headline institutional inflation gains rest on average-MSE ratios (61–101 origins) rather than cell-level statistical rejection, and only one foundation model is evaluated. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on forecast evaluation, central bank communication, or applied time-series foundation models — it is the cleanest existing demonstration of input-based conditioning in macro; skip it if you need a production-ready forecasting tool, since no code or data release is stated.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (80) is the driver — a NEW FORMULATION (input-based conditional forecasting with a frozen foundation model) plus the MZ/GR nesting that licenses an efficiency reading, not just a new method. Rigor (72) is strong on ablations (contamination placebo, asymmetric-loss robustness, real-time vintages) but capped by the authors' own admission that DM tests never reject in the headline cells and by single-model, single-episode dependence. Non-Obviousness (78) is high — the credibility-gap identity and institution-specific efficiency finding reveal hidden structure. Completeness (78) benefits from unusually direct limitation acknowledgment; Resilience (68) is pulled down because the institutional inflation gains rest on average-MSE ratios over 61 origins. Practical Impact (55) is limited — no code/data release beyond the public Chronos-2 checkpoint. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*55 = 73.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Inflation-targeting central banks publish joint projection paths for the policy rate, inflation, and real activity as part of their policy communication, and these paths are constitutive of the policy stance (Svensson 2005; Woodford 2003). The question is whether a published path is an MSE-optimal summary of the information used to form it — a forecast-efficiency question in the Mincer–Zarnowitz tradition — or whether residual mean-square signal remains extractable. The operational obstacle: the standard remedy, conditional forecasting in the VAR lineage (Doan et al. 1984; Waggoner and Zha 1999; Bańbura et al. 2015), requires estimating a parametric system on the short local macro sample before conditioning, binding the exercise to data availability and treating conditioning as a property of the estimated equations rather than of the conditioning information itself. Forecast users with approximately quadratic loss (markets, analysts tracking central bank paths) face this problem in real time. Key Idea: Treat conditioning paths as inputs to a fixed, pre-trained predictive mapping g_θ*: (y_1:t, x_1:t, f_1:t, f_t+1:t+h) → ŷ_t+1:t+h, rather than as constraints imposed inside a locally estimated model. Because the producer's historical predictions enter alongside the announced path, the map's deviation from the path becomes a real-time, state-dependent signal — the "credibility gap" — whose directional content predicts where the institution's next miss will land. The nesting of MZ/GR regressions as the linear special case is the second key move: it converts an MSE comparison into a formal forecast-efficiency test. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) assemble a real-time country panel of published forecast vintages (Norges Bank MPRs late 2005–early 2026; Riksbank 2007–2025 via its API; RBNZ MPS 1995–2024) for policy rate, CPI inflation, and output gap, plus five monthly exogenous covariates (real oil price, Euro Area consumer sentiment, EPU, bilateral USD FX, US 3-month T-bill); (2) run Chronos-2 — an encoder-only transformer with alternating time attention (rotary embeddings) and group attention with a B×B mask M sending cross-group compatibilities to −∞, pretrained on the pinball loss with 21 quantiles — zero-shot along a six-rung input ladder (Noinfo → Uni → Multi rate-only → Multi → Multi+exog → Riksbank-augmented), evaluating 61 Norwegian origins (2010Q2–2025Q2), 57 Swedish, and 101 New Zealand origins at horizons h=1–4 with an expanding window; (3) cross-check with a recursively estimated Bayesian VAR under Chan's (2022) asymmetric conjugate prior, hard-conditioned via R·vec(Y) = r (Waggoner–Zha), sampled with the Chan–Jeliazkov precision sampler, matched rung-for-rung on the same imposed paths; (4) run the nested regression diagnostics — recursive Mincer–Zarnowitz recalibration, full-sample Granger–Ramanathan combination regressions (equation 4), EKT flex-loss GMM rationalisation, and credibility-gap MSE regressions (equations 6–9) plus an institutional-learning regression (equation 10). Critical design decisions: real-time output-gap vintages at each origin with final-vintage realisations; a hard-conditioning VAR baseline chosen deliberately for the cleanest contrast (the authors concede alternative VARs could narrow the gap); and synthetic-only Chronos-2 weights as a contamination placebo. All three are well-justified, though the last two are also acknowledged as potential weak points. Key Results: On Norwegian inflation, the input ladder improves accuracy near-monotonically: relative MSE vs Norges Bank moves from 1.02 (Noinfo) to 0.99 (Multi rate-only) to 0.79 at the Riksbank-augmented rung (~21% MSE cut); the Multi rung, reading nothing beyond the Bank's own published triple, beats the Bank at every horizon (~7% per-target average, >10% at h=2–3). On the policy rate and output gap the Bank dominates at every horizon (e.g., relative MSE up to 3.07 on the rate at h=1). New Zealand replicates the inflation result (Multi cuts MSE ~19%; up to 25% at the richest rung); Sweden does not — every rung's inflation relative MSE exceeds 1 (1.25–2.13). Against rung-matched conditional VARs, Chronos-2 attains lower MSE on rate and inflation at every rung and horizon on all three panels, often by wide margins (e.g., Norway h=1 rate: 0.25*, inflation: 0.42), with DM tests rejecting in most of these cells; output gap is mixed. The credibility-gap regressions show past own-target institutional MSE significantly predicts the squared gap, the map's predictive SD, the realised gain, and the alignment term in Norway (alignment ≈0.25) and New Zealand (≈0.70), while Sweden's alignment is zero (−0.01) and its gain coefficient flips negative (−0.94). The institutional-learning regression orders the inﬂation diagonals: Norges Bank 0.66, RBNZ 0.48, Riksbank 0.27 (all rejecting H0: γ=1), rationalising the Swedish failure as aggressive self-correction leaving no residual signal. Baselines are current and strong: Chronos-2 is the newest multivariate foundation model, the VAR follows Chan et al. (2025), and concurrent Guerrón-Quintana et al. (2026) and BIS work are discussed. Sample scale is modest-standard: 57–101 forecast origins per panel, three small open economies. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a NEW METHOD component. Genuinely novel: the input-based formalisation of conditional forecasting with a frozen pretrained multivariate map, the nesting of MZ/GR regressions that licenses the efficiency reading, and the cross-country finding that forecast inefficiency of published paths is institution-specific (concentrated on the externally-measured target and mediated by how aggressively the institution absorbs its own recent misses). Standard combinations: Chronos-2 itself is existing Amazon technology used unmodified; the conditional VAR, EKT loss framework, and DM tests are off-the-shelf. The contribution is the reframing and the evidence, not a new model. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are substantive: the input ladder itself isolates what each input group contributes; the synthetic-only weight rerun rules out pretraining contamination; the EKT exercise rules out the asymmetric-loss confound; the full-sample combination regression is transparently labelled an ex-post diagnostic, not a forecast; and window-W robustness (W=1..8) is reported as preserved. Inference uses Diebold–Mariano with Newey–West HAC throughout. Concerns: (i) the authors admit the DM tests never reject equal accuracy in the cells where the map beats Norges Bank — the headline institutional gains are average-MSE ratios, not statistically decisive rejections; (ii) the Riksbank-augmented rung carries a genuine timing-information advantage the authors flag, though conclusions do not rest on it; (iii) the credibility-gap and learning regressions are developed and evaluated on the same panels they interpret (small n, one episode — the post-2021 inflation surge — drives much of the realised gain); (iv) no code or data repository is stated as released (the Riksbank API and FRED tickers are named, aiding reconstruction); (v) no multiple-seeding issue arises (deterministic inference), which is fine. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — Chronos-2 is publicly released at 122M parameters and runs on commodity hardware; the institutional vintage panels require manual assembly but are public. Efficient: Zero-shot inference per origin (one forward pass) versus recursive VAR estimation plus MCMC sampling at each origin; the paper claims no numbers but the asymmetry favours the map, particularly in short samples. Effective: The evidence supports solving the stated problem on inflation for two of three institutions and against model-based conditioning broadly, but not for the institution's own instrument and construct, and not for Sweden. Scalable: Only claimed implicitly — three panels, 57–101 origins, horizons to four quarters; behaviour at richer input sets, other institutions (Fed, ECB), or longer horizons is untested. Deliverable form: paper only; no library, tool, dataset, or trained model release is stated beyond using the public Chronos-2 checkpoint. Strengths: - The nesting of Mincer–Zarnowitz and Granger–Ramanathan regressions inside the input-based mapping is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution: it converts an MSE horse-race into a formal forecast-efficiency statement and fixes the interpretation of every comparison in the paper. - The adversarial self-testing is unusually thorough for an applied macro paper: contamination placebo with synthetic-only weights, asymmetric-loss robustness of the combination weights, and a real-time vintage design that anticipates the obvious look-ahead objection on the output gap. - The credibility-gap decomposition (g = 2δ·e_NB − δ²) ties the Panels A–D regressions together by an exact accounting identity, so the state-dependence story is internally coherent rather than a collection of correlations. - The cross-country contrast is a real finding, not a replication nuisance: the Swedish failure is explained by the learning regression (γ=0.27, R²=0.03) rather than waved away, and the alignment-term split (0.25/0.70 Norway/NZ vs −0.01 Sweden) is sharp. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly flag: the Riksbank-augmented rung may carry a calendar-timing information advantage; DM tests do not reject equal accuracy against Norges Bank in the winning cells (they redirect inference to the regression diagnostics); the VAR contrast is necessarily specification-dependent and neither paradigm was optimised at the margin; output-gap VAR results are mixed; and the volatility counterfactuals in Appendix D are "descriptive rather than a causal decomposition." This is a credibility positive — the limitations are confronted directly rather than buried. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Only one foundation model is evaluated. Carriero et al. (2024) report that Moirai and TimesFM are unstable for macro forecasting; whether the result is a property of input-based conditioning generally or of Chronos-2 specifically cannot be determined from this paper. - The headline inflation gains are concentrated in the post-pandemic surge episode (Figure 4 shows the realised gain concentrated post-2020), when Norges Bank persistently underpredicted; with 61 origins and one such episode, the out-of-sample generalisation of the credibility-gap payoff is untested. - The full-sample Granger–Ramanathan regressions are ex-post diagnostics estimated on the same observations used to interpret them; no out-of-sample combination exercise is run despite the framework supporting one. - The five exogenous covariates are chosen from prior Norwegian evidence (Bjørnland et al. 2020); no covariate-set ablation shows the exogenous block's marginal contribution separately from the path triple. - The "zero-shot" framing is soft in one direction: the map reads the institution's full historical prediction record as input, so it is zero-shot in parameters but heavily conditioned on the task's own history; a reader comparing against genuinely history-blind benchmarks (e.g., unconditional foundation forecasts alone, which the Noinfo rung partially covers) should note the ladder starts near parity (relative MSE 1.02 on inflation). - No discussion of the Fed, ECB, or other large-economy institutions whose paths are the most consequential globally; all three panels are small open economies with similar external drivers. Bottom Line: A methodologically sharp and unusually well-defended paper that any macro-forecasting or central-bank-communication researcher should read for the input-based reframing and the institution-specific efficiency finding, though practitioners wanting a deployable conditional forecasting tool will need to supply the code and verify the gains outside three small open economies themselves.

E-Commerce Bench

arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces E-Commerce Bench, an open-source benchmark in which an LLM agent runs up to four simulated online stores for a 365-day year — sourcing inventory through multi-round supplier negotiation, pricing, fulfilling orders, handling returns, and managing cash flow — scored on end-of-year assets plus six capability dimensions. - Why it's important: Prior long-horizon business benchmarks force a trade-off: Vending-Bench-style negotiation uses stochastic LLM counterparts that are noisy and manipulable, while data-grounded retail benchmarks (MerchantBench, RetailBench) drop negotiation and adversarial dynamics entirely; this benchmark is the first to hold real platform data, deterministic counterpart economics, negotiation, fraud, and multi-store concurrency at once. - How it does it: Both market sides are deterministic — a fixed multi-factor demand model generates purchases/returns, and a rule-based negotiation kernel commits every supplier price, concession, and accept/walk-away decision, with an LLM used only to verbalize kernel decisions and a ±0.005 compliance check blocking renderer price tampering. - The good: Full determinism (seeded demand, kernel-fixed counterpart economics) makes outcome differences attributable to agent policy rather than sampling noise, and the seven-axis evaluation exposes real capability splits the asset leaderboard hides — the top earner (GPT-5.6 Sol, ¥1.43M, ~14.3× the ¥100k stake) ranks 16th of 18 on fraud avoidance. - The missing: Only 5 episodes per model with standard deviations as large as the means (GPT-5.5: ¥702k ± ¥616k), a single frozen environment seed/calendar, and the authors evaluating their own Qwen3.8-Max-Preview, which leads the open-weight tier. - Read it or not: Agent-benchmark builders and anyone designing negotiation or long-horizon evaluations should read it for the deterministic-kernel-plus-renderer methodology; readers wanting a trustworthy model ranking can skim Table 2 given the variance and conflict of interest.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Novelty (~75) is high — the deterministic-kernel-plus-LLM-renderer supplier design is a genuine methodological contribution to reproducible negotiation benchmarks, and the six-axis capability profile demonstrably changes conclusions. Impact (~78) reflects a fully open-source environment with unusually candid self-audit (Appendix B.5 discloses the authors' own data defects). Rigor (~70) and Resilience (~65) are held back by only 5 episodes per model with stds as large as means, a single frozen environment seed, and an unflagged conflict of interest — the vendor's own model tops the open-weight tier and is the sole model credited with learning. Weighted composite: 0.15*75 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*75 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.30*78 = 73.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents are increasingly asked to sustain competence over thousands of steps in continuing (non-episodic) tasks, where failures like loss of coherence and inability to learn from experience only surface over long horizons. Business operation is a natural continuing scenario with high-stakes irreversible decisions, but existing benchmarks cover it partially: Vending-Bench 1/2 rely on LLM-simulated suppliers (stochastic, manipulable, mock economics); YC-Bench is deterministic but has no supplier sourcing; MerchantBench and RetailBench use real data but drop negotiation and adversarial suppliers. Practitioners building autonomous business agents lack a reproducible evaluation that combines bargaining, fraud, dynamic demand, and cash-flow management, and no existing benchmark pairs a negotiating counterpart with reproducible supplier economics. Key Idea: Split each supplier into two layers: a deterministic negotiation kernel that commits every economic decision (price, concession size, accept/reject) via explicit bargaining-policy equations, and an LLM 'NPC renderer' that only converts kernel decisions into dialogue. This removes sampling noise and jailbreak exploitability from counterpart behavior while preserving naturalistic interaction — the trick that lets a year-long negotiation-heavy economy be fully reproducible. A secondary idea is scoring capability on six orthogonal axes (CSE+ bargaining, BadSpend% fraud cash, drawdown-over-peak solvency, ¥/tool-call efficiency, controllable return rate, AnchorRatio learning) rather than assets alone. Methodology: Four-layer architecture. (1) Agent loop: turn-based control where one model call yields a batch of tool calls; every tool but the day-jump costs simulated minutes out of a 600-minute day (e.g., 10 min balance check, 30 min supplier message); group-wise context eviction fires at 120,000 tokens releasing 60,000 (1,495 evictions across 90 episodes), plus a 20-entry persistent memory store outside the context. (2) Tool layer: 18 tools spanning market research, store operations, inventory, finance, negotiation, memory, time. (3) Environment: a deterministic demand model (Eq. 1) multiplying category base demand by price-elasticity response (four closed-form families per category), weekend, promotion, seasonality, event, and reputation factors, trimmed by two Michaelis-Menten capacity terms; a three-account deferred settlement (bank → escrow 9 days → platform wallet, explicit withdrawal) with bankruptcy after 10 consecutive negative-balance days; and the negotiation kernel extending TERMS-Bench's counterpart policy (reciprocal concession à la Faratin et al., logistic acceptance, walk-away hazard after round 5) to repeated cross-supplier bargaining, with 6 honest behavior templates and 5 scripted scam overlays (152 of 576 suppliers fraudulent; pre-deal scams inflate floors ~1.5×, post-deal scams short-ship 60–70% or deliver defectively). (4) Data layer: 6,886 SKUs, 60 categories, 576 suppliers desensitized/synthesized from a real e-commerce platform (Taobao & Tmall), plus a fixed calendar of 10 market events and 8 promotions. Evaluation: 18 models × 5 episodes (90 total), primary score end-of-year assets over the ¥100k stake. Critical design decisions: kernel-only economics (well justified — prevents benchmark degenerating into counter-jailbreaking); purchasing price discovery through free-form fenced negotiate blocks parsed deterministically (justified); LLM renderer identity and sampling left at provider defaults, introducing narrative variance on the fraud axis (acknowledged but only partially mitigated). Key Results: Eighteen frontier/open-weight models, five 365-day episodes each. GPT-5.6 Sol earns the most (¥1,431,425 mean, ~14.3× stake, std ¥314k); Fable5 second (¥805k, 8.05×) and most efficient (¥479/tool call vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's ¥363 on 59.9% fewer calls); Qwen3.8-Max-Preview leads open-weight at ¥416k (4.16×), 38% above GLM 5.2 (high) at ¥301k; Qwen3.5-Plus last (¥1.1k, 0.01×). A 1,264× spread separates top from bottom under a deterministic world. Ten of 90 episodes went bankrupt (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-Plus; two GPT-5.5 bankruptcies on day 17 before any revenue settled). No model bargains to the floor: CSE+ spans 0.596–0.811 versus 0.50 for accepting the opening quote. All 18 models lose money to fraud (BadSpend% spanning >160× in cash). On learning, 16 of 18 models' repeat-order prices are indistinguishable from or worse than a random shuffle of their own prices (AnchorRatio ≥ 1); only Qwen3.8-Max-Preview (0.834) and Gemini 3.5 Flash (0.918) beat their permutation null by >2σ, and Qwen3.8 alone shows a positive within-episode surplus trend. Error analysis derives ten detection rules and shows three commonly blamed failure modes (store churn, promotion neglect, uniform late-year collapse) do not survive the data. Baselines are current frontier models (2025–2026 generation) — strong, though self-selected by the authors. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW METHOD. Genuinely novel: the two-layer deterministic-kernel/LLM-renderer supplier design applied to repeated, cross-supplier, fraud-laden bargaining inside a data-grounded year-long economy, and the six-axis capability profile that decomposes a single asset score. Standard components reused: context eviction, persistent memory (MemGPT-style), the bargaining policy itself is an independent reimplementation of TERMS-Bench's counterpart, and the demand model composes known price-elasticity forms (Gallego & van Ryzin) — the contribution is their integration and calibration, not the pieces. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong on transparency: all kernel equations, parameters, prompts, metric definitions, and per-model tables are in appendices; code is released at https://github.com/QwenLM/E-CommerceBench; determinism is engineered and verified (same action sequence → identical money). Five-run means are printed with standard deviations, and the authors flag where variance swamps signal (fraud-share std exceeds its mean for 15 of 18 models; GPT-5.5's std is a population estimate). Unusually, Appendix B.5 audits the released data itself, disclosing four defects including a supplier-email local-part whose numeric suffix leaks the fraud label and 20 of 60 categories whose return-rate wording understates the numeric band. Concerns: five episodes per model is a small sample with no significance tests on the headline ranking; a single frozen environment seed and calendar mean all results are conditional on one world realization; the AnchorRatio null assumes equal cycle difficulty and the archive lacks the per-cycle opening quote needed to check it; the fraud axis carries renderer sampling noise on top of policy noise; and the benchmark was developed and evaluated by the Qwen team, whose own Qwen3.8-Max-Preview tops the open-weight tier. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, open-source benchmark environment evaluated by running 90 agent episodes). Practical: Runs anywhere with API access to the 18 models — the environment is a Python harness, not specialized hardware. Efficient: An episode costs up to 4,000 turns (~1,000–3,700 tool calls, e.g., GPT-5.6 Sol at 3,668 calls), so a 90-episode evaluation is nontrivial in tokens but routine compute. Effective: The evidence shows it discriminates among agents and localizes failure modes, but it measures performance against a synthetic demand model and scripted scams — a proxy for, not a demonstration of, real-market operation. Scalable: The 365-day horizon and 6,886-SKU catalog are already at the intended scale; longer horizons or more concurrent stores are untested, and the fixed seed means scale-up generalization is claimed implicitly, not measured. Deliverable: an open-source software artifact (environment, data layer, kernel, evaluation code); no trained models. Strengths: (1) The deterministic-kernel-plus-renderer decomposition is a real methodological contribution — it solves the reproducibility/manipulability dilemma of LLM-played counterparts without sacrificing dialogue, and the ±0.005 compliance check plus deterministic parsing closes the loophole convincingly. (2) The six-axis evaluation demonstrably changes conclusions: the profit leader is 16th/18 on fraud avoidance, and capability profiles are sharply divergent, which a single-score leaderboard would hide. (3) The learning analysis (AnchorRatio with a permutation null, 8,647 repeat orders) converts a vague claim ('agents should learn from experience') into a measurable, falsifiable statistic — and the negative result for 16/18 frontier models is a finding in its own right. (4) Rare candor: a self-audit appendix disclosing benchmark defects (email-label leakage, misleading return wording, an inert cost event) rather than burying them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: renderer sampling and out-of-seed delivery-day draws leave two sources of run-to-run variance (fraud detection reads vary); AnchorRatio's three scope limits (honest pairs only, unweighted by order size, excludes truncated episodes); five episodes is a small sample, so every mean carries its std; and the four data-layer defects of Appendix B.5, including that no tool reports the overdraft-day streak so agents cannot count it. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. They do not, however, flag the conflict of interest in ranking their own model. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single-world generalization: one seed, one calendar, one supplier roster means all rankings are conditional on a single realization; no experiment varies the environment to test whether conclusions (e.g., Qwen3.8's learning lead) transfer. (2) Conflict of interest: the benchmark's creators evaluate their own Qwen3.8-Max-Preview, which leads the open-weight tier and is the sole model credited with positive learning — no independent replication is reported. (3) The email-suffix fraud leak is disclosed but the paper's own check (§F.3) is cited rather than its result in the main narrative; if any model exploited it, the fraud axis is contaminated. (4) The demand model's realism is asserted via calibration to platform logs but never validated against held-out real sales data. (5) With stds equal to or exceeding means for several models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-Plus), rank orderings below the top few positions are statistically fragile, yet per-dimension ranks are reported to 18 places. (6) Possible benchmark overfitting vector: Qwen3.8's authors know the kernel design intimately; convergence to kernel-optimal concession behavior cannot be distinguished from general negotiation skill. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agent benchmarks or studying long-horizon negotiation gains a genuinely reusable methodology — deterministic counterpart kernels with LLM rendering, plus a multi-axis profiling template — that no prior benchmark provides, but the model rankings themselves should be treated as directional given the variance, single-world design, and vendor conflict of interest.

#25 — Innovative (73)

Rules as Executed

E Hotting, A Schuth · anneschuth.nl · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This position paper proposes that Dutch government bodies publish law execution as machine-executable specifications in a restricted, declarative format, under a binding regime where the published specification is the one that decides cases and every decision carries a signed attestation (specification digests, inputs, execution trace) that a recipient can re-execute to verify. - Why it's important: Opaque software has given the Dutch executive a practical monopoly on how operative law is applied — the structural blind spot implicated in the toeslagenaffaire, Robodebt, and Horizon — leaving Parliament, courts, and citizens unable to verify, review, or predict how law is actually executed. - How it does it: The core move is binding publication to execution: a restricted, termination-guaranteed declarative format whose every computed outcome is a default overridable by recorded, attributable authority, plus cryptographic attestation of the resolved dependency closure so that determinism makes any decision checkable by re-running the published rule. - The good: The paper convincingly shows that the one property no prior rules-as-code system provides — a guarantee that the published rule is the rule that runs — is precisely the property the constitutional argument requires, and it backs feasibility with a public reference implementation (20+ encoded Dutch regulations, three independent engines in Python, Go, and Rust/WASM). - The missing: The central claim that legal professionals can actually read and verify these encodings is explicitly a hypothesis, never tested; the translation pipeline's fidelity is unaudited; and the adversary model excludes a deliberately deceptive executive, whose evasion the design by its own admission cannot catch. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on rules-as-code, algorithmic government, computational law, or digital constitutionalism — it crisply reframes the field's gap as a binding/provenance problem rather than an encoding problem; skip it if you want empirical validation, which the paper itself defers to a research agenda.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. The composite rests on Novelty (80), Non-Obviousness (80), and Impact (70): the paper identifies — with a fair comparison table — that every prior rules-as-code system (OpenFisca, Catala, FLINT, RegelSpraak, STOP/TPOD) fails to guarantee the published rule is the executed rule, and then actually delivers the missing property via attested, deterministic re-execution, backed by a public reference implementation with 20+ encoded regulations and three independent engines. Rigor (60) is appropriate for a position paper with strong reproducibility artifacts but is pulled down by the untested load-bearing hypothesis (legal-professional readability), unmeasured LLM translation fidelity, and an informal multi-engine equivalence check. Completeness (75) and Resilience (75) are high because the authors confront their adversary-model limits, the freezing objection, and the enactment dependency directly, and route open questions to an explicit agenda. Impact (70) is capped at feasibility: the central institution — binding attestation — is unenacted, and no population-level verifier is named. Weighted composite: 0.15*80 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*80 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*75 + 0.30*70 = 72.5 ≈ 73.

Problem & Motivation: Dutch law execution runs on databases, spreadsheets, and bespoke software — sometimes vendor-locked — whose logic is published nowhere, often invisible even to the executing organization itself. The executive encodes its interpretations into systems only it can access; Parliament cannot assess the effects of statutes it passes (frustrating its Art. 42(2) and 68 Grondwet information duties), courts reviewing algorithmic decisions can only take the executive's account or reverse-engineer logic themselves (per van Amerongen & Schuurmans 2019, the SyRI judgment), and citizens cannot predict or verify decisions, making the nemo censetur ignorare legem fiction corrosive. Much of what decides cases is uitvoeringsbeleid and unpublished concretizations that never reach the beleidsregel publication duty. Existing substitute governance (Algoritmeregister, DPIAs, IAMA, proportionality committees) audits descriptions produced by the same system builders rather than the operative rules. The gap prior approaches leave: OpenFisca, Catala, FLINT, RegelSpraak/ALEF, and STOP/TPOD all support authoring or executing rules, but none guarantees that the disclosed rule is the rule the system runs — France's statutory disclosure duty has remained thin in practice, and the DSO's toepasbare regels keep published text, decision tree, and case system as three artifacts requiring manual alignment. Key Idea: Bind publication to execution via attestation: the specification is not documentation alongside a system but the artifact the deterministic engine runs, so publishing and executing are one act on one artifact; a cryptographic digest of each specification version in the resolved dependency closure, signed together with the inputs and full evaluation trace, plus the determinism of the restricted format, lets any verifier re-run the published rule and confirm the decision — turning constitutional oversight into a mechanical check, and interpretive departures into recorded, attributable overrides. Methodology: The paper is a constitutional-theoretical argument with an attached systems artifact, not an experimental study. The format (schema v0.5.6) fixes 25 operations in eight categories (arithmetic, selection, explicit rounding, comparison, logical combination, membership, guarded IF, calendar arithmetic), prohibits unbounded iteration, recursion, and collection aggregation (the Robodebt income-averaging shape is deliberately inexpressible), and follows the Bench-Capon/Coenen isomorphism principle of one provision mapping to one rule. Decisions record: content digests of every specification in the resolved closure, engine identity and binary digest, evaluation reference date, inputs, full trace, and any override (substituted value, ground, authority) — both lex specialis derogations declared in specifications and discretionary departures under Art. 4:84 Awb use the same substitution mechanism, and an automated batch override is marked as such. Version management treats Staatsblad publications as release tags with date-resolved dependency resolution (chronolexografie); four execution modes (active, reactive, generative, verificative) make triggers part of the published specification, including the Awb staged lifecycle. Translation at scale is assigned to LLM agents following published "skills," with a generate-validate-test loop, a reverse pass requiring every element to trace to statutory text, fidelity and drift audits, and a mandated untranslatable-annotation gate that blocks execution of articles containing constructs the format cannot express. Critical design decisions: (1) structured notation over controlled natural language — justified by multi-engine semantic equivalence, court-readable diff, and keeping the compiler out of the trust chain; (2) overrides-as-defaults — well-argued as the answer to the freezing objection (Hildebrandt) and to Waldron's argumentation requirement; (3) LLMs at translation and explanation edges only, never in evaluation — sound, but the paper concedes a first draft frames what reviewers see. Key Results: As a position paper, its results are artifact-based feasibility, not benchmarks. Concretely: a public reference implementation (github.com/MinBZK/regelrecht) with 20+ curated encoded Dutch regulations (Wet op de zorgtoeslag, Awb, Archiefwet) each paired with BDD test scenarios; 100+ further regulations drafted by the LLM pipeline and several thousand harvested awaiting translation; engines implemented in Python, Go, and Rust/WebAssembly, with an informal (explicitly non-rigorous) demonstration that independent engines produce identical results; a browser-runnable reading environment (editor.regelrecht.rijks.app); a demonstration explanation pipeline producing B1-level Dutch explanations from traces, citing Bos (2026) that trace-constrained explanations were substantially more faithful than unconstrained baselines though less readable. No accuracy metrics, no user study, no measured translation fidelity rates. Baselines are prior systems (OpenFisca, Catala, FLINT, RegelSpraak, OPA, Better Rules, STOP/TPOD) compared on properties, in Table 1, not on performance. The scale of the target corpus is stated (≈45,000 national regulations in >100,000 consolidated versions, >330,000 decentralized ones), but nothing near that scale has been encoded and human-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. Genuinely novel: the binding-to-execution property with per-decision cryptographic attestation of the resolved specification closure — the paper shows, with a fair comparison table, that no prior rules-as-code approach (OpenFisca, Catala, FLINT, RegelSpraak, STOP/TPOD, Better Rules) was designed to guarantee that the published rule is the deciding rule, and the derivation of data-access authorization from the published rule is likewise new. Standard combinations: the declarative restricted-rule format itself (a deliberate, well-motivated synthesis of known legal-knowledge-engineering principles), Git-style versioning applied to law, and LLM-based translation with reverse-tracing validation are competent applications of existing ideas; the supply-chain provenance analogy (SLSA-style attestation) is imported, not invented. Rigor & Reproducibility: Appropriate for a position paper but with real evidential limits. Ablations do not apply; the closest analogue — the operation-set governance story (no collection aggregation until needed, public version history) — is argued rather than tested. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests (nothing quantitative to attach them to). Reproducibility is a genuine strength: the reference implementation, schema, corpus, translation skills, and reading environment are all publicly released at named URLs, and the paper explicitly invites inspection of its own claims. Flagged concerns: (1) the key hypothesis — legal professionals can verify encodings unaided — is acknowledged as untested, which is honest but leaves the constitutional argument resting on an empirical assumption; (2) the multi-engine equivalence check is informal, and the paper itself names semantic equivalence as an open research problem; (3) the adversary model excludes a deliberately deceptive executive, so the security properties are conditional and self-acknowledged as such; (4) the proposal's central institution (binding attestation) has no empirical referent anywhere — it is a proposal about law that has not been enacted. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a designed format with a working reference implementation, wrapped in a normative argument, with no primary experimental claim). - Practical: Yes — the engine compiles to WebAssembly and runs in a browser; the format targets commodity hardware and plain-text artifacts. - Efficient: Deterministic evaluation of a small operation set is computationally trivial compared to the bespoke systems it would replace; the real cost is organizational (encoding, review, register infrastructure), not compute. - Effective: The artifact demonstrates feasibility of encoding and deterministic re-execution, but the stated problem — rebalancing constitutional power — is only solvable via statutory enactment of binding publication and attestation, which does not exist; current effect is a proof of concept plus an argument. - Scalable: Only partially claimed: the LLM translation pipeline is designed for the 45,000-regulation corpus and the marginal cost argument is plausible, but human review does not parallelize the same way, and nothing at that scale has been encoded, reviewed, or attested; verificative and generative execution modes have no implementation. Delivers: a public software artifact (format, engines, corpus, editor, translation skills), not a trained model or library at production maturity. Strengths: - The reframing of the field's gap as a binding/provenance problem rather than an encoding problem is the paper's real intellectual contribution: Table 1's observation that every prior system optimizes the writing/execution end while the constitutional deficit is at the reading end is an original, defensible analysis that recasts OpenFisca, Catala, and FLINT as solving adjacent but different problems. - The override mechanism is a genuinely well-designed legal-technical junction: one substitution primitive uniformly handling lex specialis, discretionary departure (Art. 4:84 Awb), and automated batch correction, while making withheld mercy countable — turning a classic objection to codified discretion (Hildebrandt's freezing worry) into a feature with an evidentiary trail. - Unusually strong intellectual honesty for a proposal paper: the authors flag their own adversary model's limits, concede that readability by legal professionals is an untested hypothesis, mark untranslatable constructs instead of approximating them, and route open questions to an explicit research agenda rather than asserting solutions. - The dependency-graph analysis of the Wet op de zorgtoeslag (Figure 4, including the interpretive, invisible link to the Penitentiaire beginselenwet via Art. 24 Zvw) is a concrete, checkable demonstration of the diagnostic value claim — encoding surfaces interpretive steps that today happen nowhere on the record. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which strengthens credibility: both are engineers reasoning on legal scholars' terrain; legal-professional readability is "a hypothesis to be tested, not a property we can assert"; semantic equivalence across engines is left open, with floating-point and temporal edge cases named; the attestation does not defend against an executive that sets out to deceive (double-signing, input selection) — no transparency logs or non-equivocation proposed; a specification's legal status (extension of beleidsregel vs. new instrument) is unsettled; whether recipients have a legal right to the trace is unsettled, including the partial-view problem for third-party data; the LLM translation step relocates the very silent-reinterpretation point the paper diagnoses into a first draft that frames reviewer attention; detection of semantic untranslatability is incomplete; Memorie van Toelichting examples decay as test oracles; verificative and generative execution modes raise open constitutional questions; and the proposal requires statutory enactment with consequences to matter at all. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No user study or expert evaluation of readability or verification accuracy by the intended audience (legislators, judges, caseworkers) — the load-bearing empirical claim of the whole constitutional argument, which the authors flag but do not attempt. - The translation pipeline's fidelity is never measured: no rate of hallucination caught by the reverse pass, no proportion of articles flagged untranslatable per corpus, no inter-reviewer agreement on adoption decisions — yet the paper claims translation-at-scale makes the transition affordable. - The enforcement/adversary gap is larger than acknowledged in one direction: even a non-deceptive but under-resourced agency could sign attestation digests routinely without anyone ever re-executing; the paper names no institution obligated or funded to be the population-level verifier, and audit capacity (Section 11.5 is truncated in the document) may be the true bottleneck. - Enforcement and risk-selection logic is deliberately kept unpublished (the gaming objection's scope rule), but that unpublished layer is exactly where high-stakes computational decisions (fraud detection à la toeslagenaffaire) now live — the proposal may inadvertently legitimize a growing opaque zone as long as the "decision logic" core is transparent. - Cross-organizational reliance on another body's signed decision reduces to provenance plus a duty to report gerede twijfel; the paper does not address systemic failure modes where a defective source besluit propagates through hundreds of downstream attested decisions, each individually verifiable yet all resting on the same unsound input. - No cost-benefit or transition-effort analysis beyond the qualitative phase sketch; the DSO precedent (a decade for a much narrower deployment, with ~90% municipal uptake of a voluntary scheme) is cited approvingly without reckoning with what its ten-year timeline implies for the proposal's far broader scope. Bottom Line: For anyone working on rules-as-code, computational law, or algorithmic-government accountability, this is essential reading — it names the binding gap everyone else leaves open and delivers a working artifact plus a sharp constitutional argument for closing it — but its claims are a research agenda and an unenacted proposal, not a validated system, so its numbers should be read as feasibility, not evidence of effect.

#26 — Innovative (72)

Verification-Aware Training for Speculative Decoding

G Gu, B Heo, HJ Jun, Y Kang, S Lee, S Yun, D Han · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Verification-Aware Training (VAT), a plug-in training objective for speculative-decoding draft models that simulates the target model's sequential verification at every training step and converts the resulting accept/reject patterns into two supervision signals: a verification head and sample-adaptive per-position loss weighting. - Why it's important: Speculative decoding is the dominant lossless inference-acceleration technique for LLMs, but draft models are trained by token-level imitation that ignores the verification process that actually determines speedup, leaving measurable speed on the table for every deployment that uses a drafter. - How it does it: At each training step, VAT compares draft and target predictions to locate each sample's first rejection point k, then (i) trains a lightweight binary head on whether each position survives sequential verification (gradients flow back into the draft) and (ii) keeps full per-position loss weight up to k and re-anchors the base decay schedule there instead of at position 1. - The good: The gains are consistent and reproducible across two drafting paradigms (autoregressive EAGLE-3, block-diffusion DFlash), three target models (Qwen3-4B/8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), and 8 benchmarks, with component-level ablations (Table 2) and an unusually thorough weighting-scheme ablation (Table A) showing the specific design choice — anchoring decay at the observed k* — beats six alternatives including GRIFFIN-style masking and D-PACE-style confidence weights. - The missing: All results are on target models of at most 8B parameters; there is no evidence the relative gains persist at 30B–70B+ scale where draft-target agreement distributions may differ substantially, and no error bars or significance tests are reported. - Read it or not: Read it if you train or deploy speculative-decoding drafters — it is a small, well-ablated change to a training loss with up to 8.7% free speedup and no inference cost; skip it if you only consume served models, since the contribution lives entirely in draft-training recipes.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (74) is moderate — a new training objective whose real contribution is the observation that the first-rejection point is observable at training time; the components (auxiliary head, positional weighting) are individually standard. Rigor (68) is pulled down by no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, a preprint status, code only 'promised,' speedup measured in the HF Transformers harness rather than a production server, and ablations confined to one configuration. Non-Obviousness (78) is high — re-anchoring the decay schedule at the simulated rejection point beats six alternatives and applies across autoregressive and diffusion drafters. Completeness (74) and Resilience (73) are supported by honest 8B-scale limitation acknowledgment and preemptive robustness checks; Impact (68) suffers from the not-yet-live code release despite a highly adoptable zero-inference-cost recipe. Weighted composite: 0.20*74 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*74 + 0.15*73 + 0.10*68 = 72.
