Problem & Motivation: Speculative decoding drafts K candidate tokens with a cheap draft model and verifies them against the target in one forward pass; speedup is governed by the average acceptance length τ — how many draft tokens survive sequential verification before the first rejection, after which every subsequent token is discarded. The training objective for draft models (in both EAGLE-3 and DFlash) is per-position cross-entropy against the target with a fixed, sample-agnostic positional decay (e.g., w_k = 0.8^(k−1)), which reflects neither that acceptance is determined by verification outcomes nor that a position's contribution is conditional on all preceding positions being accepted. Practitioners running EAGLE-3- or DFlash-style drafters inherit this train/inference misalignment. Related concurrent work (PARD-2, D-PACE, GRIFFIN) also touches this objective but with confidence-based proxies rather than the observed rejection point. Key Idea: Simulate the target's sequential verification inside the training loop: compute per-position acceptance indicators m_k via the speculative-sampling rule min(1, p_k(x)/p̂_k(x)) using the frozen target's distributions, derive the cumulative acceptance label v_k = 1[k < k] where k is the first rejection, and use v_k both as (i) an auxiliary binary-classification target for a head on the draft's hidden states (so acceptance outcomes become explicit gradient signal) and (ii) an anchor for the per-position loss decay, which starts at the sample's own k rather than at position 1. This one observation — that k is observable at training time and is the natural origin for the decay curve — reconstructs the whole method. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) generate a training corpus by sampling target-model responses (greedy, Perfectblend prompts) for 3 epochs of training; (2) at each step, run draft and frozen target to get p̂_k and p_k at all K draft positions, compute m_k, k, and v_k; (3) train with L = Σ_k ŵ_k(ℓ_soft_k + ℓ_hard_k) + β·L_VH, where ŵ_k = 1 for k < k and ŵ_k = w_{k−k+1} (the base schedule re-anchored) for k ≥ k, and L_VH is binary cross-entropy of a single dense-layer head predicting v_k from the draft's last hidden states. β = 1.0 throughout. The head is training-time only; the inference procedure is untouched, preserving losslessness. Critical design decisions: (a) full weight at k itself (it is the "nearest correctable failure") — justified by the hard-cutoff ablation showing zero-weighting from k collapses performance (τ 3.11 vs 6.03); (b) decayed rather than zeroed weight past k* — the unshifted-decay ablation shows re-anchoring accounts for a comparable margin (4.46×/5.75 vs 4.61×/6.03); (c) greedy-decoding simulation — Appendix B shows the greedy vs. stochastic verification rules correlate >0.92 and differ by ≤0.02 in downstream speedup/τ, so this simplification is well-validated. Training overhead measured: +1.2% step time for EAGLE-3, +6.1% (plus 7.7 GB memory) for DFlash, because DFlash must add an extra target LM-head pass. Key Results: On 8 benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME25, HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, MT-Bench, Alpaca) with temperature 0 on A100 80GB via HuggingFace Transformers: EAGLE-3+VAT on Qwen3-4B improves τ from 6.28 to 6.78 (+8.0%) and speedup from 4.07× to 4.39× (+7.9%); DFlash+VAT on Qwen3-4B improves τ 5.73→6.08 (+6.1%) and speedup 4.54×→4.81× (+5.9%). Largest single-gain: DFlash+VAT on Qwen3-8B, +11.4% τ (5.51→6.14) and +8.7% speedup. Gains hold at temperature 1 and for both model families. The full-factor ablation (τ 5.73→6.08) shows each component helps alone (head: 5.87; adaptive weighting: 5.91; soft+hard labels: 5.82) and compounds. A bonus inference use: the head predicts the first-rejection position with mean absolute error 1.18 (EAGLE-3) / 1.76 (DFlash) tokens, enabling early-exit drafting that recovers most of an oracle upper bound (e.g., DFlash Code 4.83×→4.97× vs oracle 5.20×). Baselines (EAGLE-3, DFlash) are current SOTA drafters, retrained by the authors on the same corpus for fairness. Notable counter-intuitive finding: the verification head keeps post-rejection token predictions stable through training while the baseline's degrade, even though its post-rejection region starts at deeper positions. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported. This is a preprint (arXiv 2608.30135), not peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (verification-simulating training objective with observed-first-rejection-anchored weighting) plus a modest NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (that conditioning loss weights on the simulated rejection point beats confidence-based surrogates). The components are individually simple — a binary auxiliary head is standard, and positional loss weighting existed — but the specific mechanism of deriving sample-adaptive weights from simulated speculative-sampling acceptance, applied across both autoregressive and diffusion drafters, is genuinely new; it distinguishes itself from concurrent PARD-2/D-PACE by conditioning on the observed rejection position rather than a confidence proxy. Combining soft and hard labels is standard knowledge distillation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong and go beyond the usual one-off: a factor analysis separating head/weighting/label-type, a six-alternative weighting-scheme comparison (including reimplementations of GRIFFIN masking and D-PACE weights inside the authors' framework), sensitivity analysis of the verification rule and corpus temperature (≤0.02 difference across all four combinations), measured training-time overhead, and training-dynamics plots. Missing: multiple seeds, variance estimates, and significance testing for any headline number. Code is promised at https://github.com/naver-ai/VAT but is only "will be available" in this preprint. Concerns: all ablations are on one configuration (DFlash + Qwen3-4B); evaluation uses the same Perfectblend-derived training corpus family as the EAGLE-3/DFlash baselines (fair, but single-corpus); speedup measured with the HuggingFace Transformers library rather than a production serving stack (vLLM/SGLang), so absolute speedup numbers may not transfer directly to deployed systems. The temperature-1 LLaMA results show DFlash performing poorly there (e.g., 1.23× on AIME25) and VAT's gains are comparatively smallest on LLaMA-3.1-8B (+2.5–3.8% τ), a heterogeneity the paper does not analyze. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (training method with wall-clock experiments). Practical: Yes — trains and evaluates on commodity A100 80GB GPUs, modifies only the loss, requires no architectural or serving-stack changes. Efficient: Training overhead is small and measured (+1.2% step time on EAGLE-3, +6.1% and +7.7 GB peak memory on DFlash due to an extra target LM-head pass); inference cost is unchanged unless the optional head-guided early exit is used, which saves drafting/verification compute. Effective: The evidence directly measures the deployment metric (wall-clock speedup and τ on 8 benchmarks), not just a proxy, though only under the HF Transformers harness and on ≤8B targets. Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B; the authors themselves flag this as the open question, and nothing in the method obviously breaks at larger scale but nothing confirms it either. Deliverable: a promised code release (repo URL stated, not yet verified as live), plus a reusable recipe applicable to any speculative-decoding trainer; no model weights or dataset released. Strengths: - The core insight is clean and generalizable: the first-rejection point k* is observable during training under speculative sampling, making it usable as both a classification target and a weighting anchor — a reframing of draft training that applies across drafting architectures, demonstrated on both EAGLE-3 and DFlash. - The ablation program is unusually complete for this area: the weighting-scheme table alone distinguishes re-anchoring from hard cutoff, from confidence surrogates (D-PACE), and from masking (GRIFFIN), attributing the gain to the adaptation mechanism rather than the decay functional form (Table 3: τ 6.09 vs 6.08 across two base schedules). - Deployability is respected throughout: inference stays lossless and unchanged, overhead is quantified per-baseline with an explanation of why they differ, and the head doubles as an optional inference-time early-exit signal validated against an oracle. - Robustness checks (verification-rule sensitivity, corpus-temperature sensitivity, temperature-1 evaluation) address the most obvious "greedy-only artifact" objection preemptively. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that evaluation is limited to models up to 8B parameters and that scaling verification-aware training to significantly larger models is a promising future direction. They also acknowledge the verification head's occasional false rejections when used for early exit (τ drop, e.g., 7.67→7.35 on DFlash Math). They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which is credible. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical rigor: single runs, no seeds, no confidence intervals — for gains of 2.5–3.8% (the LLaMA cases), run-to-run noise in draft training could be material. - Speedup is measured only under HuggingFace Transformers; acceptance-length gains are harness-independent, but wall-clock speedup ratios can shift substantially under batched/continuous-batching servers, where verification-pass amortization differs — the numbers most likely to be quoted in practice are the ones most sensitive to this. - The DFlash temperature-1 results (e.g., 1.23× on AIME25 for LLaMA-3.1-8B) reveal the baseline drafter nearly fails at high temperature on some tasks, yet the paper does not investigate why VAT's relative gains shrink in precisely those high-variance regimes or how simulated verification behaves when the target's greedy and sampled outputs diverge sharply. - Ablations are confined to one baseline/model pair; the component interactions under EAGLE-3 (where the target LM head is already computed) are not separately dissected, and the reported ablation budget differs (1 epoch in Table A vs 3 in main results), complicating cross-table comparison. - The verification head's early-exit threshold (p=0.5/0.6) is tuned on the evaluation benchmarks themselves, a mild Goodhart risk for that optional feature. Bottom Line: This is a well-ablated, zero-inference-cost training fix that any team training EAGLE-3- or DFlash-style drafters should adopt, and it currently has no stronger alternative for verification-aligned draft training — its main open question, scale beyond 8B, is the authors' own, not a reason to skip it.

Revisiting Complete Reasoning Traces for Post-Training (8 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Endpoint-based SFT (E-SFT), a training recipe that removes the middle ~20% of tokens from machine-generated reasoning trajectories, and shows this beats or matches standard full-trajectory SFT across AIME24, GPQA-D, and MATH500, and extends to GRPO and on-policy distillation. - Why it's important: Post-training on LRM-generated traces is now the dominant way to build reasoning models, and these traces are long, redundant, and expensive to train on; if the middle of a trace is dead weight, both data curation and training cost assumptions in the field need revisiting. - How it does it: Three converging analyses — averaged attention weights during answer generation, causal segment-ablation with answer-similarity scoring, and answer-perplexity under segment replacement — show intermediate segments are weakly attended, causally dispensable, and replaceable with model self-generated text, motivating a split-at-\n\n, keep-first-and-last-100/200-steps truncation. - The good: The finding generalizes beyond the SFT objective it was discovered in — masking the middle 20% under GRPO lifts Qwen3-1.7B-Base from 25.8 to 34.5 average across three benchmarks, and step-level masking improves on-policy distillation from 61.2 to 63.4. - The missing: No error bars, significance tests, or multi-seed training runs are reported, and headline deltas on AIME24 (30 problems) and MATH500 differences of under 1 point are within plausible noise; the "models internally infer missing steps" mechanism remains an interpretation, not a demonstrated result. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone doing reasoning-model post-training or data curation, since it directly challenges the default of training on complete traces with a recipe cheap enough to try immediately; skippable if you already work on CoT compression and only need the headline result.

Problem & Motivation: Labs and researchers post-training LLMs (roughly 1.7B–32B scale) on curated reasoning-trace datasets such as s1K-1.1 and OpenThoughts3 face a practical question: these LRM-generated trajectories routinely contain backtracking, repeated verification, and discarded exploratory paths, yet standard SFT optimizes negative log-likelihood over every token. Prior work (overthinking analyses, short-m@k, token-level CoT compression) treats length as the operative variable or relies on token-importance scorers and RL budget controllers, but none establishes which structural region of a trace carries the supervision signal. The paper targets the unexplored question of whether complete traces are even necessary supervision, and whether a principled, resource-free segment-level recipe can replace both naive fixed-limit truncation and expensive filtering pipelines. Key Idea: The core insight is that the supervision signal in a reasoning trace is concentrated at its endpoints — problem definition/planning at the start, answer consolidation at the end — while the middle is dominated by redundant deduction and backtracking that a competent base model neither attends to nor needs; deleting the middle span forces the model to interpolate missing steps from internal knowledge, which acts as a better training signal than the redundant original tokens. The operational trick is deliberately low-tech: split traces at double-newline boundaries, keep the first and last ~100–200 steps (~20% token removal), and train normally. Methodology: The paper proceeds in three phases. Phase 1 (diagnosis): (a) attention analysis — averaged and layer-wise attention from answer tokens over the trajectory, on the S1.1-32B model, showing U-shaped attention with layer-depth-dependent progression; (b) attention-knockout-style segment ablation — remove beginning/centered-middle/ending 10–20% spans from full trajectories of 100 GPQA-D problems and measure ROUGE-L/Jaccard/BLEU of regenerated answers against full-trajectory answers, finding middle removal is least disruptive; (c) segment replacement — swap in model self-generated text and measure answer perplexity, which drops only for middle replacement (PPL 1.56 full vs 1.58 begin-replaced vs 1.52 middle-replaced, approximately). Phase 2 (method): E-SFT minimizes the standard SFT loss L = −Σ log p(y, r | x) but on endpoint-retained traces; step counts are set to n=100 (s1K-1.1, avg 234 steps) and n=200 (OpenThoughts3, avg 461 steps), chosen to remove ~20% of tokens, with sensitivity analysis showing insensitivity to this ratio. Phase 3 (extension): for GRPO on DAPO-17k, middle-20% tokens remain in context and receive reward but are excluded from the per-token gradient; for on-policy distillation (Qwen3-8B teacher → 1.7B student), step-level masking outperforms token-level masking (+2.2 vs +0.7 average). Critical design decisions: the \n\n delimiter (validated via LLM-judged semantic-transition rates: 33.5%/28.0% across breaks vs 2.5%/1.0% within steps), the fixed ~20% trim ratio (shown to be a flat operating regime rather than a tuned hyperparameter), and keeping both endpoints rather than one (well-justified by the pilot study where prefix-only and suffix-only underperform). The objective functions are explicit and standard; the contribution is data transformation, not a new loss. Key Results: On s1K-1.1 with Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, E-SFT reaches 75.19 average (AIME24 68.89, GPQA-D 62.29, MATH 94.40) vs 73.51 for standard SFT (+1.68). On OpenThoughts3-100K, Qwen3-8B-Base improves 65.78 → 67.50 and Qwen3-4B-Base 58.97 → 60.04. Against filtering baselines on s1K-1.1 (32B), E-SFT (75.19) beats random step selection (70.92), Jaccard-similarity filtering (73.92), perplexity-based filtering (72.80–74.43), and LS-Mixture SFT (71.90); LLM-based compression with Claude Sonnet 4 collapses to 60.08 and Gemini to 49.55, a surprising result the authors attribute to disrupted reasoning structure. GRPO masking: Qwen3-1.7B-Base 25.8 → 34.5 average (mostly MATH500, 39.3 → 60.7), Qwen3-1.7B 51.2 → 52.4. OPD: 61.2 → 63.4 (step-level mask). E-SFT also better preserves general capabilities (e.g., TruthfulQA-MC1 33.17 vs 32.56 for SFT on Qwen3-4B). Appendix results extend to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (+1.34 average) and an inference-time middle-truncation decoding mode that cuts end-to-end GPQA-D evaluation time by 4.5% with flat accuracy across 25–75% removal ratios. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (published 2024–2025 filtering methods); evaluation is at standard, not stress, scale (100K of the 1.2M OpenThoughts3 examples; 32B largest model; training 20 hours on 16 H100s). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a NEW METHOD (E-SFT) that is an engineering-simple instantiation of it. The genuinely novel element is the region-level (not token-level, not length-level) localization of supervision signal in reasoning traces, validated by three complementary analysis methods and shown to transfer across SFT, GRPO, and OPD objectives. The method itself — delete a contiguous middle span and train — is a trivial combination of known ideas; the paper's value is the evidence that this suffices and that scorer-based and LLM-based compression alternatives underperform it, not algorithmic sophistication. Conceptually adjacent work (short-m@k, token-level CoT compression, Lost-in-the-Middle) is cited and differentiated. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and load-bearing: the pilot's four-way segment comparison, retained-step sensitivity (Figure B), step- vs token-level masking in OPD, and a model-capability threshold analysis (E-SFT gains appear only above ~60–65 base performance for s1K-1.1-scale data). However, no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported; each evaluation averages three generations at temperature 0.6, but training appears single-seed, and AIME24's 30 problems make deltas like +2.22 or +4.45 statistically fragile. Code is available (linked from the abstract); all datasets and models are public open-source artifacts. Methodological concerns: (1) the mechanism claim — models "internally infer" missing steps — is supported only indirectly by perplexity and LLM-judge evidence, not by a direct demonstration of interpolated reasoning; (2) the reasoning-quality claim rests on an LLM-as-judge (GPT-OSS-120B) preference study where 70% of comparisons are judged equivalent and the preference margin is 22% vs 19%; (3) the lower training perplexity under E-SFT is partly a selection effect (harder redundant tokens removed), which the paper acknowledges in spirit but does not disentangle; (4) middle-region functional labeling (Table A) uses LLM judges whose reliability for "deduction vs backtracking" taxonomy is unvalidated against humans. Deployability: EMPIRICAL profile (methods trained and evaluated by the authors; a small inference-time system extension in Appendix D). Practical: Yes — runs on open Qwen/Llama models with public frameworks (s1 repo, LLaMA-Factory, lm-evaluation-harness) on commodity H100 nodes. Efficient: Strictly cheaper than alternatives — it removes ~20% of training tokens, needs no auxiliary scorer (unlike perplexity filtering, which the authors report takes >2 hours on one H100 node, or LLM compression), and the inference-time variant cuts evaluation time 4.5% on GPQA-D under vLLM. Effective: Evidence shows it improves reasoning benchmark accuracy and preserves general language ability better than full-trace SFT, but effectiveness is bounded by base-model capability — the authors' own analysis shows no gain below ~60–65 base performance on s1K-scale data. Scalable: Not tested beyond 100K examples and 32B parameters; whether the ~20% trim heuristic holds at 1.2M examples, on frontier-scale teachers, or on traces from RL-distilled rather than SFT-derived teachers is claimed by implication only. Deliverables: code repository link, a reusable data-transformation recipe, and the inference-time truncation technique; no new trained model weights are stated as released. Strengths: - Three independent analysis methods (observational attention, causal ablation, replacement perplexity) converge on the same conclusion, which is unusually thorough evidential triangulation for a paper whose final method is a one-line data transform. - The generalization experiment across three distinct post-training objectives (SFT, GRPO, OPD) is the strongest result: it shows the finding is a property of reasoning traces, not an artifact of the cross-entropy objective, and the GRPO result on a 1.7B base model (+8.7 average) is a large effect. - The negative result on LLM-based compression (Claude: −13.43; Gemini: −23.96 average vs standard SFT) is a genuinely useful, counter-intuitive data point against the intuition that smarter compression helps. - Honest boundary analysis: the authors themselves map out when E-SFT fails (weak base models) and connect their phenomenon to, while distinguishing it from, Lost-in-the-Middle. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state (Appendix A) that E-SFT's effectiveness depends on base-model capability — gains emerge only above roughly 60–65 general performance on s1K-1.1 data, with the threshold lowered by larger/more diverse data — because weak models cannot reliably infer trimmed segments. They note performance sensitivity to the retained-step ratio exists (excessive truncation degrades), that \n\n is a proxy rather than an exact segmentation rule, that their functional-labeling analysis does not determine per-step redundancy, and that their mechanism differs from Lost-in-the-Middle while being potentially linked through data structure. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Statistical fragility: no seeds, no significance testing; several headline comparisons (e.g., GPQA-D +0.34, MATH −0.47 in some rows) are almost certainly within noise, and the paper's uniform-positive narrative would benefit from confidence-aware reporting. - The 20% trim ratio is a heuristic validated post hoc; the paper does not test whether the optimal trim depends on teacher model, domain (code vs math vs science), or trace length in a way that breaks the "near-universal regime" claim. - The "internal inference" mechanism is asserted more strongly than demonstrated — no experiment directly shows the model generating and using interpolated intermediate steps during training or at inference (e.g., probing what the model "would have said" in the gap). - All teacher traces come from one lineage (DeepSeek-R1-style traces in s1K/OpenThoughts); whether the endpoint structure generalizes to traces from other LRMs or from human-written CoT is untested. - The LLM-judge reasoning-quality evaluation (70–72% "equivalent") provides weak support and uses a judge that may itself prefer shorter, cleaner-looking text — a potential style bias rather than quality signal. - Code-generation results with E-SFT are only "comparable," and OpenThoughts3's code-heavy composition means the math-reasoning framing may not cover the dataset's actual use. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing reasoning-model post-training gains a cheap, immediately actionable finding — trim the middle of your traces, and the same trick helps GRPO and distillation — backed by the best triangulated evidence I have seen for a claim this simple, making it worth reading despite statistically soft margins and an under-proven mechanism story.

Modular Responsiveness Verification of Rust Async Runtimes

Y Li, I Beschastnikh, AJ Summers · liyz.pl · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LART, a core calculus for Rust async runtimes, together with modular static analyses whose verification conditions soundly imply the liveness property of eventual progression, and implements them in Jackdaw, a Rust compiler plugin that verifies pollable and reactor components of real runtimes (smol, futures, tokio). - Why it's important: Nearly all async Rust code implicitly trusts the runtime to eventually resume paused tasks, yet no prior work verifies this liveness guarantee, and Rust ships no canonical runtime, so a technique must cover a diversity of production implementations. - How it does it: It decomposes eventual progression into per-component conditions on pollables (P1–P3) and reactors (R1–R2), exploiting two abstractions — monotonic completion predicates and a novel notion of obligations — so each component can be checked in isolation by abstract interpretation over a small domain of predicate observations and symbolic obligations. - The good: The technique verifies real pollable and reactor implementations from smol, futures, and tokio with 4–11 lines of annotation per pollable (23% average annotation-to-code ratio) and sub-millisecond analysis times (10–152 µs per component), while rejecting seeded responsiveness bugs for every verification condition. - The missing: The MIR-to-LART lifting and the user-supplied annotations are trusted and unchecked — a mistaken annotation (e.g., triggering a monotonic event that never happened in real memory) silently voids the soundness guarantee, and the evaluation is a small handpicked component suite (9 pollables, 4 reactors) rather than whole runtimes. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on program verification of concurrency infrastructure, Rust tooling, or liveness reasoning; skip it if you want a formally connected end-to-end verified runtime, since the bridge from Rust to LART is heuristic and trusted.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Async runtimes (tokio, smol, and equivalents in Java, JavaScript, Python) manage graphs of inter-dependent user tasks: pausing tasks at await points, registering wakers, and resuming tasks when events fire. Users depend on a liveness property — eventual progression: assuming correct user code, OS, and compiler, every task a runtime manages eventually makes progress. Prior verification work targets user-level async code and treats the runtime as part of the trusted computing base; no prior work verifies the runtime itself. The problem is acute in Rust, where the language ships only an interface and users pick among many third-party runtime implementations, any of which must uphold the same guarantee. Verifying liveness of these libraries is hard because they are concurrent, highly optimized, and built from components that interleave and communicate. Key Idea: Three combined insights: (1) a task-centric view — it suffices to verify eventual progression for a single arbitrary task rather than a task collection; (2) component-boundary modularity — responsibility for a paused task transfers from pollable to reactor via waker registration, so each side can be checked against local contracts; and (3) monotonicity — runtime completion conditions (timer expiry, I/O readiness) are predicates that, once true, stay true, which makes observation-based branching decisions sound and lets a 4-valued observation domain (⊥, tt, ff, ⊤) with a refinement operator prune infeasible paths. The glue is the notion of an obligation (waker, predicate) pairs that must never be forgotten until discharged by wake or Ready — tracked symbolically in the abstract domain. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Modeling: a core language LART with small-step operational semantics captures the pollable/reactor programming paradigm; runtime states include a monotonic history Σ, a rescheduling queue Q, and a repository map R (an abstraction over how reactors store wakers). Obligations (w, p) ∈ Waker × P are created at each await and discharged only by a Ready return or a wake. Three trusted components are assumed: faithful Rust compilation, correct environment observations, and fair scheduling. (2) Analysis: an abstract-interpretation-style analysis over states σ = (S, bR, bL) — predicate observations, symbolic obligations in repositories, and locally held obligations. Pollables are analyzed twice (entry predicate ⊤ and tt) to check (P1vc) Ready implies condition held, (P2vc) condition-held implies Ready, and (P3vc) Pending discharges or transfers the obligation; reactors are checked per-iteration via (R1vc) obligations whose predicate holds at iteration start are woken that iteration and (R2vc) undischarge obligations are retained. Theorem 1 shows these local conditions imply global eventual progression (with a proof via Theorems 2–5). Two extensions handle real idioms: terminating reactors (e.g., one-shot channel send) via a precedes relation ≺ tracking strict temporal order of monotonic events (SOTvc), and pollable retry-loops via a least-fixpoint over the finite abstract lattice. (3) Tooling: Jackdaw (~5k lines of Rust, a rustc plugin) expands a macro annotation layer (mono_pred!, obs!, wake!, insert!, repo_for!, etc.) into no-op markers, lifts MIR control flow into LART models (heuristic, not formalized), and discharges the VCs. Critical design decisions: the monotonic-predicate abstraction (well-motivated by real runtime idioms but an assumption the tool cannot check), the per-iteration strengthening of (R1) (acknowledged as stronger than necessary but common in practice), and atomic sequential-consistency semantics for insert/take/wake (acknowledged as mismatched with tokio's weaker atomics). Key Results: Jackdaw verifies 9 pollables and 4 reactors drawn from smol, futures, and tokio, covering timers, I/O, and one-shot/MPSC channels. Annotation cost is 4–11 annotation lines per pollable (13–35% of code; 23% average for pollables); terminating reactors show 54–58% ratios due to very short bodies (≤13 lines). Per-component analysis runs in 9.9–152.2 µs (mean of 300 runs) on an Intel Core i9-9880H with 32 GB RAM under rustc 1.91.0-nightly — negligible relative to compilation. For each verification condition (P1/P2/P3, R1/R2, SOT), the authors seeded a violation in a real component and report Jackdaw rejects all of them, with no false negatives across the suite. Three cases required workarounds: post-join re-assertions when completion is carried in a boolean flag across control-flow merges, an ignore_path! annotation to prune tokio's cooperative-yield fairness code, and ghost annotations for cross-invocation invariants in tokio's one-shot receiver. Scale is component-level, not whole-runtime; the claim that verified components cannot cause hangs (Corollary 1) applies only to the verified subset. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (first work on verifying liveness of async runtimes themselves, as opposed to user async code), NEW FORMULATION (obligations in an operational semantics for runtime components; monotonic events and their orderings as first-class specification notions), NEW METHOD (the obligation-tracking abstract domain and modular VC decomposition), and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (Jackdaw). The individual ingredients — abstract interpretation, obligation-style specifications (Leino et al., Boström & Müller), and monotonic predicates (Hailpern & Owicki 1982) — are known; the novelty is their composition into a task-centric, component-local proof obligation set for the runtime pollable/reactor idiom, plus application to real code. The claim that reactor-style deferred discharge cannot be handled by Actor Services is asserted, not demonstrated with a head-to-head comparison. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation in the useful direction is present: every verification condition has a manually seeded violation that Jackdaw rejects, and a worked buggy-reactor example shows the analysis failing R1vc exactly as expected. Soundness is proved for the LART level (Theorems 2–6, with proofs sketched in the text and full semantics in appendices). No error bars beyond the mean-of-300-runs timing; no significance tests (not applicable to a verification result). No public code or artifact URL is stated in the paper. Methodological concerns: (a) the Rust-to-LART lifting is heuristic and trusted, so the end-to-end soundness claim rests on unverified translation plus user annotations the tool does not check; (b) the component suite is small and self-selected — no evidence of how many pollables/reactors in smol/tokio fall outside the model's coverage; (c) the bug-detection evaluation uses only seeded bugs rather than historically real responsiveness defects; (d) the expressiveness claim ('handles real-world components with two modest extensions') is difficult to falsify since the selection criteria for the component subset are not given. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL with a SYSTEMS artifact (a compiler plugin prototype). Practical: Yes — it is a rustc plugin running on commodity hardware (a 2019-era laptop sufficed), though adopting it requires annotating runtime source. Efficient: Extremely — sub-millisecond per component (10–152 µs), so the cost is essentially annotation authoring, not analysis time. Effective: Evidence shows it verifies the modeled components and rejects seeded bugs, but effectiveness at the stated problem (runtime-level responsiveness assurance) is only partial: coverage of an entire runtime is untested, and annotations/lifting are trusted. Scalable: Not tested beyond ~13–59-line components; whether the approach scales to complex pollables with heavy cross-invocation state (tokio's coop logic already required pruning) is unproven. The work delivers a prototype tool artifact (~5k lines of Rust), though no release URL is given, plus a reusable proof technique (obligation/monotonic-predicate decomposition) that stops at paper form for other settings. Strengths: - Genuinely first-mover problem framing: shifting liveness verification from user async code to the runtime layer itself, with a clean trusted-computing-base decomposition (compiler, environment, scheduler) that localizes blame (Corollary 1 is a practically useful attribution result). - The monotonic-predicate observation domain with a monotonicity-violating refinement mapping to ⊥ is a small, well-executed abstraction that buys real path pruning and makes the per-iteration reactor conditions checkable without a fixpoint in the base case. - The precedes-relation extension for terminating reactors is a non-obvious technical move: capturing 'obligation transferred strictly before completion predicate held' as an analyzable temporal ordering, which is exactly what one-shot channels require. - Honest, detailed accounting of where the tool needed workarounds (post-join re-assertions, ignore_path! pruning, ghost annotations), which is unusual candor for a tool evaluation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: missing wake-one primitive and cross-poll reasoning (needed for tokio's Mutex/Semaphore); the MIR-to-LART lifting and user annotations are trusted and unchecked, so annotation mistakes (e.g., triggering a monotonic event with no real-memory effect) undermine soundness; sequential-consistency assumptions that tokio's weaker atomics do not formally satisfy; no modeling of cancellation/task-drop and obligation revocation; panic-freedom and functional correctness out of scope; and eventual progression is unbounded liveness — no bounded latency, tail latency, or fairness guarantees. They confront limitations directly and at length (a full section plus a credibility-positive discussion of the trusted annotation gap), rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evidence about coverage: the paper never states what fraction of smol's, futures', or tokio's pollable/reactor implementations the model can express, so 'we verified various key components' may reflect cherry-picking; the components requiring workarounds (cooperative yielding, cross-invocation invariants) hint the friction rate on the long tail is unknown. - Bug detection is validated only against seeded bugs; no real-world responsiveness regressions (e.g., from tokio's issue tracker) are reproduced, leaving practical bug-finding value unproven. - The fairness assumption on the scheduler is exactly the kind of liveness property the runtime's own scheduler code would need verified — the paper punts this to 'well-studied' prior work, which leaves a hole in the end-to-end story for actual tokio/smold schedulers. - No comparison against any baseline (e.g., encoding a component in Verus/Anvil-style TLA or Prusti) to substantiate the 'lightweight' claim quantitatively — specification effort is reported only relative to the authors' own tool. - No artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of both the verification results and the seeded-bug experiments. - The soundness of the annotation layer is a dogs-not-barking omission in the evaluation: no experiment measures how often annotators introduce unsound annotations, even though the authors identify this as the main soundness threat. Bottom Line: A verification researcher or Rust runtime maintainer should read this: it opens a genuinely untouched problem with a well-crafted modular technique and credible early evidence, but practitioners wanting a deployable, end-to-end sound guarantee must wait for the trusted-annotation gap to close and for whole-runtime coverage to be demonstrated.

Marigold V2: Revisiting Diffusion Transformers for Monocular Depth Estimation (44 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Marigold V2, a two-stage fine-tuning protocol that converts the open-source Qwen-Image-Edit diffusion transformer into a single-step monocular depth estimator (and other dense regressors) trainable on one 32GB GPU in under a week. - Why it's important: Recent diffusion-based depth estimators oversmooth boundaries and lose fine detail, and adapting modern DiT backbones has become expensive (tens of GPU-days), locking out small labs; this recipe makes state-of-the-art depth accessible on a single consumer-grade GPU. - How it does it: The core trick is a two-stage recipe — Stage 1 aligns the DiT's internal representations to DINOv3 features computed on the ground-truth depth map (iREPA-depth, an unconventional depth-domain alignment target), and Stage 2 fine-tunes with SinkLoss, a block-wise Sinkhorn optimal-transport loss that supervises depth values as a set within K×K blocks rather than pixel-aligned, tolerating noisy ground truth on transparent/thin structures. - The good: The evaluation is unusually thorough for this price class: best zero-shot AbsRel among comparably-trained methods on all five standard benchmarks (e.g., 2.8 on ETH3D vs. 3.8 for the strongest baseline, 5.4 on KITTI vs. 6.5), best edge metrics (SEE3 0.352 vs. 0.404 for PPD), plus backbone-transfer ablations showing the losses generalize to Stable Diffusion 1.5 and FLUX.2 klein. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported (all results appear to be single runs), the edge-quality evaluation is confined to the synthetic HyperSim dataset, and SinkLoss hyperparameters (K, τ, iterations) receive no sensitivity analysis. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or fine-tune diffusion-based dense predictors and care about detail preservation or compute budgets; skip it if you need frontier metric depth at scale, where >5M-image discriminative models (π3, Depth Anything V2-62M) are excluded from the paper's rankings and still win on some benchmarks.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) is solid — SinkLoss (block-wise Sinkhorn OT matching for depth) is a genuinely new loss and depth-domain iREPA a new alignment formulation, though the overall recipe extends Marigold/Lotus. Non-Obviousness (75) is high: the insight that pixel-exact supervision on V-Ray-rendered transparent structures is actively harmful, and that set-matching within blocks fixes it, was not predicted by prior work. Rigor (70) is strong on baselines, backbone-transfer ablations, and verified cost claims, but reduced by absent seeds/error bars, edge metrics evaluated in-distribution on HyperSim, and no SinkLoss sensitivity analysis. Completeness (72) and Resilience (70) benefit from unusually honest self-reporting (iREPA benefit vanishing at 160K steps, π3 remaining better on NYUv2), while Impact (78) reflects a real single-GPU recipe with a demo release. Problem & Motivation: Monocular depth estimation is ill-posed and feeds computational photography, novel view synthesis, and 3D reconstruction. Discriminative regressors are bounded by scarce, sensor-noisy depth annotations and generalize poorly to non-Lambertian or adverse-weather inputs; diffusion-based repurposing of generative priors addresses this but suffers oversmoothed boundaries, flying pixels, and — since the community moved from U-Nets to large DiTs — prohibitive fine-tuning costs (DICEPTION: 96 GPU-days; Lotus-2: 8 GPUs). The paper targets practitioners and small labs who need sharp, detail-preserving, generalizing depth maps without multi-GPU infrastructure. Key Idea: Supervise where the ground truth is trustworthy and relax where it is not. Two mechanisms implement this: (1) iREPA-depth — representation alignment toward DINOv3 features extracted from the ground-truth depth map rather than the RGB input, giving a geometry-focused semantic regularizer with no inference-time dependency; and (2) SinkLoss — entropy-regularized optimal transport (Sinkhorn–Knopp) between predicted and ground-truth depths within non-overlapping K×K blocks (K=5, τ=0.1, 5 iterations, invalid pixels masked with a large cost B=10^6), which requires only that the prediction produce the right set of depth values per block, up to permutation. This is justified by the observation that rendering noise (e.g., V-Ray quasi-Monte Carlo sampling of transparent pixels) makes pixel-exact supervision on thin/ambiguous structures unattainable and even counterproductive. Methodology: The pipeline: (a) normalize metric depth to affine-invariant log-depth in [−1,1] using 2nd/98th-percentile clipping, replicated across three channels to mimic RGB; (b) initialize from Qwen-Image-Edit-2509, quantize DiT weights to 4-bit, train rank-128 QLoRA adapters with batch size 1; (c) Stage 1 minimizes L_DiT = L_latent (single-timestep t=0.5 rectified-flow velocity regression on latents, reducing to direct latent regression: target v = z_I − z_d, single forward pass at inference) + L_pix (L1 on decoded depth) + L_grad (L1 spatial gradients) + 0.2·L_iREPA, for 160K steps (~5 days on one 32GB GPU); (d) Stage 2 (30K steps, ~1 day) continues fine-tuning with SinkLoss (λ=1.0) and unfreezes the VAE decoder. Depth data: HyperSim (90% sampling weight) and vKITTI (10%). Design decisions: depth-domain (vs. RGB-domain) iREPA target — justified by ablation showing better AbsRel/δ1; log-depth parameterization — justified by ablation (AbsRel 4.72 vs. 5.04 linear, 5.28 disparity) and a first-order argument that L1 on log-depth approximates AbsRel; fixed-timestep single-pass regression — adopted from Lotus-2, well-motivated by latency but means the model never uses diffusion's iterative refinement capacity. Key Results: Zero-shot affine-invariant depth (RANSAC scale/shift alignment, PPD protocol), trained on 74K images: NYUv2 AbsRel 3.6/δ1 98.0, KITTI 5.4/97.4, ETH3D 2.8/99.2, ScanNet 3.7/97.9, DIODE 5.2/97.1 — best among methods trained on comparable data (59K–280K images), beating FE2E (3.8/6.5/3.8 on NYUv2/KITTI/ETH3D), Lotus-2, PPD (1024), DepthMaster, and InfiniDepth; the 16–26% AbsRel claim holds on KITTI (5.4 vs. 6.5) and ETH3D (2.8 vs. 3.8) versus the previous best. Edge-aware SEE3 on HyperSim: 0.352 vs. 0.404 (PPD) and 0.470 (InfiniDepth). Latency 1.9s/16.9GB at 1024² and 9.6s/29.3GB at 2048² on one 32GB GPU, where PPD, Lotus-2, and FE2E OOM at 2048². Transfers: depth completion via test-time rank-16 LoRA (100 Adam iterations, 21.2M params) achieves lowest RMSE on all four of iBims-1, NYUv2, KITTI-DC, DDAD among single-step methods (e.g., DDAD RMSE 5.32 tiled vs. 6.01 LDCM); see-through depth AbsRel 13.66→8.17 on LayeredDepth-Syn after targeted fine-tuning; normals MeanErr best on Sintel (28.7) with SinkLoss improving SAEE but slightly worsening MeanErr (18.53→18.84); albedo PSNR 20.78 vs. 19.28 (IID-in-the-wild). Baselines are current (2024–2026 venues), and several are re-evaluated under a common protocol rather than copied. Models trained on >5M images (Depth Anything V2-62M, MoGe, MoGe-2, π3) are shown but excluded from ranking — notably π3 still surpasses Marigold V2 on NYUv2 (2.9 vs. 3.6). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (SinkLoss, a block-wise Sinkhorn OT matching loss for depth) plus NEW FORMULATION (depth-domain iREPA alignment target, applied unconventionally in Stage 1) and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (4-bit QLoRA fine-tuning of a large editing DiT on one GPU). The overall framework — repurposing a generative model for dense prediction via single-step rectified-flow regression — is a direct extension of Marigold/Lotus/FE2E; the genuinely new pieces are the Sinkhorn-based set-matching loss and the depth-domain alignment target. The extension to normals/albedo/completion is competent application of the same recipe to new modalities. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: Stage-1 loss configurations at 30K and 160K steps, depth parameterization, backbone transfer (SD 1.5, FLUX.2 klein, Qwen), Stage-2 with/without SinkLoss, and a parameter-count-vs-quality frontier plot (Fig. 7). However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere — several headline margins (e.g., normals MeanErr 14.1 vs. 14.2 for FE2E on ScanNet; SinkLoss worsening Qwen AbsRel 4.10→4.12 while improving SEE) are within plausible run-to-run variance and are single numbers. The iREPA benefit shrinks at 160K steps (the authors show this honestly, retaining it as a convergence accelerator). No code release is stated beyond a project/HF Space demo URL; training data and hyperparameters are specified in enough detail to reproduce. Evaluation partly relies on numbers copied from the PPD paper for some baselines (reproduced for InfiniDepth, Lotus-2, FE2E, and their own method) — a mixed protocol, though disclosed. No Goodhart concern is present on the edge metrics since SEE is computed on HyperSim (a training dataset) — wait, this is a concern: SEE edge metrics are evaluated on HyperSim, which is 90% of the training mix, so edge-quality superiority is measured partly in-distribution. KITTI/ETH3D/NYUv2/DIODE/ScanNet evaluations are zero-shot, which mitigates this for AbsRel/δ1. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model plus measured benchmarks). Practical: Runs on a single 32GB GPU for both training and inference — the paper's central selling point and credibly demonstrated. Efficient: 1.9s and 16.9GB at 1024² is slower than InfiniDepth (0.2s) and Lotus-2-without-sharpener (1.1s), but uses far less memory than FE2E/Lotus-2 and is the only diffusion method here that runs at 2048² on 32GB. Effective: The evidence supports sharp, accurate relative depth on standard benchmarks, but edge-quality claims rest partly on in-distribution HyperSim, and the model is affine-invariant only — metric scale requires the completion extension. Scalable: Not tested beyond 2048² inference; the large image-editing backbone (tens of billions of parameters per Fig. 7) precludes real-time use, as the authors concede. Deliverable: a trained model with a demo Space; code/weights release is stated only via the project website link (https://hf.co/spaces/huawei-bayerlab/marigold-v2-web), not an explicit repository URL. Strengths: - SinkLoss is a genuinely new and well-motivated loss: the observation that V-Ray's stochastic sampling makes pixel-exact supervision on transparent/thin structures actively harmful, and that set-matching via entropy-regularized OT within blocks sidesteps this, is a clean insight with a correct masking construction (penalized rows/columns for invalid pixels). - The backbone-transfer ablation (SD 1.5, FLUX.2 klein, Qwen all improve under SinkLoss/iREPA) credibly attributes gains to the recipe rather than the specific Qwen prior — an ablation most competitors omit. - The cost claim is real and verified: one 32GB GPU, batch size 1, ~6 days total for a model that beats methods trained on 8 GPUs or 96 GPU-days. - Honest self-reporting in several places: the authors show iREPA's quantitative benefit nearly vanishing at 160K steps, SinkLoss slightly worsening mean AbsRel, and the model being non-real-time. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states the large image-editing backbone precludes real-time use, and that reflections, motion, and defocus blur remain ambiguous, suggesting uncertainty-aware or multi-layer extensions as future work. The paper also explicitly acknowledges the HyperSim ground-truth noise problem it designs SinkLoss around, and excludes >5M-image models from its rankings with a stated rationale. These limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No multi-seed variance or significance testing; several margins (ScanNet normals 14.1 vs. 14.2; albedo SSIM 0.811 vs. 0.819 for a baseline) look like noise, and the headline NYUv2 gap to π3 (3.6 vs. 2.9 among gray-listed models) shows the method does not actually dominate the strongest discriminative systems overall — the exclusion rule does real work. - Edge-quality evaluation (SEE/SAEE) is performed only on HyperSim, which dominates the training mix (90%); an edge metric on an unseen dataset is needed to rule out that SinkLoss's sharpness gains are partly in-distribution fitting. - No sensitivity analysis for SinkLoss hyperparameters (K=5, τ=0.1, 5 Sinkhorn iterations, B=10^6) — a single fixed configuration is used throughout, leaving robustness unknown. - The depth-completion comparison runs subsets (n=150) of KITTI-DC and DDAD rather than full evaluation sets, while NYUv2/iBims use full sets — the sampling protocol could favor either side. - The see-through depth result is trained and evaluated on the same dataset's (LayeredDepth-Syn) validation split, an in-distribution claim rather than a generalization claim. - Single fixed timestep t=0.5 and batch size 1 are used without ablation; whether other timesteps or larger batches (possible with more memory) would close the residual gap is unexplored. Bottom Line: A practitioner adapting diffusion transformers for dense prediction gains concrete, reproducible value here — the SinkLoss formulation, depth-domain alignment trick, and single-GPU recipe are all directly reusable — but for absolute best depth accuracy regardless of budget, π3/MoGe-2-class discriminative models remain competitive or better, so this is best read as the new reference for affordable, detail-preserving diffusion-based depth rather than an unconditional state of the art.

Foundation models for electricity price forecasting and battery arbitrage: Can they replace market-specific forecasting models?

A Lipiecki, R Weron · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper reports a large-scale empirical comparison of nine zero-shot foundation model variants (from Chronos-2, Moirai-2, TimesFM-2.5, TabPFN, and Mitra families) against two state-of-the-art market-specific electricity price forecasting (EPF) benchmarks on statistical and economic criteria. - Why it's important: Practitioners and vendors are being asked whether generic pretrained forecasters can replace bespoke per-market models, and forecast quality directly drives revenue in battery energy storage system (BESS) arbitrage — a multi-billion-euro application. - How it does it: It runs all models on identical data, context windows, and covariates across three structurally different European markets (Germany, Poland, Spain) over a five-year out-of-sample period (2021–2025), then evaluates both CRPS-type accuracy and realized profits from quantile-based and unlimited-bid BESS trading strategies. - The good: Only the TabPFN family significantly outperforms the DDNN-JSU benchmark across all three markets on all statistical measures (e.g., TabPFN-3 cuts CRPS by 14.5% in Germany, 12.3% in Poland, 12.4% in Spain), with significance confirmed by one-sided multivariate conditional predictive ability tests at the 1% level. - The missing: Statistical dominance does not translate into economic dominance — TabPFN wins only under riskier strategies, while DDNN-JSU is most profitable at low risk tolerance — and the authors do not disentangle why (e.g., tail calibration) or test ensembles/fine-tuning that could close the gap; test-set contamination for empirically pretrained FMs also cannot be excluded. - Read it or not: Read it if you forecast electricity prices or evaluate time series foundation models for trading applications; skip it if you want a new method — it is a benchmarking study with a clear negative/nuanced answer to its headline question.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (75) is the backbone: five out-of-sample years across three structurally distinct markets, fair information-set parity between FMs and benchmarks (fixing the main flaw of prior FM-EPF comparisons), one-sided multivariate CPA tests at the 1% level, and strong current benchmarks — docked modestly for no code release, a thin two-benchmark pool with one self-referential entry, and no runtime comparison. Non-Obviousness (75) comes from the genuinely non-obvious statistical-vs-economic decoupling finding: the CRPS-dominant model is never the profit-optimal one under risk-averse trading, a result most economic-evaluation papers elide. Novelty (70) reflects a well-executed new empirical finding rather than a new method, Completeness (70) benefits from direct limitation acknowledgment, and Resilience (75) is high because the nuanced answer ('components, not replacements') is well-bounded. Impact (60) is the limiter — no artifact released, though the guidance directly changes vendor/model selection behavior for traders and storage operators. Problem & Motivation: Day-ahead electricity prices are hard to forecast (spikes, heavy tails, negative values, strong seasonality, dependence on weather-driven load and renewable forecasts plus fuel/carbon prices), and forecast errors feed directly into operational and trading decisions, including BESS arbitrage. Vendors of time series and tabular foundation models (FMs) claim accurate zero-shot forecasting without task-specific training, and prior FM-vs-EPF studies are limited: single-year test periods, no exogenous variables, generic rather than EPF-specific benchmarks, point forecasts only, or no economic evaluation (e.g., Hornek et al. 2025; Marchesi et al. 2025; Lettner et al. 2026; Yu et al. PriceFM 2026; Ponyuenyong et al. 2026). No prior study jointly evaluates FMs against strong EPF-specific benchmarks on point accuracy, probabilistic accuracy, and economic value over a long test period across multiple markets. The market participants with this problem are power companies, traders, and storage operators deciding whether to adopt FMs or invest in market-specific models. Key Idea: The core move is not a new algorithm but a rigorous evaluation design: give zero-shot FMs a fair fight by feeding them the same exogenous information (day-ahead load and renewable generation forecasts, EUA/TTF/Brent/API2 futures with a 2-day lag) and context structures as the benchmarks, then test whether statistical gains survive translation into economic value under a battery-trading decision problem with an explicit risk-appetite parameter. The key empirical insight is the decoupling of statistical and economic rankings — TabPFN dominates CRPS everywhere but DDNN-JSU dominates risk-averse trading — showing that forecast quality and decision value must be evaluated separately. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) data assembly from ENTSO-E (day-ahead prices, load forecasts, wind/solar generation forecasts) and Investing.com (commodity futures) for 2017–2025, with DST handling and a 5-year out-of-sample test from 1 Jan 2021; (2) FM application in zero-shot mode — Chronos-2 variants natively multivariate with a 1,449-hour context (D=1449 days of daily 24-dim series); TimesFM-2.5 and TabPFN-TS-3 decompose the task into 24 univariate per-hour tasks with cross-hour lagged prices as exogenous features; Moirai-2 (no covariate support) uses univariate hourly multi-horizon forecasting with an 8,736-hour context; TabPFN-2/3 and Mitra+CP solve a tabular regression with explicit lags (prices at days 1,2,3,7; load/renewables at 0,1,7; day-of-week; market fundamentals at lag 2) via in-context learning on 1,449/1,449/1,085 observations respectively; (3) benchmarks: LEAR (Lasso per hour, averaged over four training windows of 56/84/728/1,092 days, area hyperbolic sine transform, 7-fold CV for λ) postprocessed with conformal prediction on a 1-year rolling calibration window, and DDNN-JSU (a 2-hidden-layer feedforward network whose output layer returns Johnson's SU distribution parameters per hour, tuned via 4×500-trial Optuna/TPE studies, retrained daily on 1,449 observations, four-model trimmed-mean ensembling); (4) evaluation via MAE/RMSE/CRPS (properly defined, not the half-CRPS pinball average the authors call out in the literature), one-sided multivariate Giacomini-White conditional predictive ability tests, and BESS arbitrage with a 1 MWh battery, η=0.95, C=25 EUR/trade, loop bids, quantile-based strategies at α ∈ {90,...,50}% plus unlimited-bid and Oracle (perfect foresight) scenarios. Critical design decisions: equalizing information sets across FMs and benchmarks (well justified — prior studies ignored covariates); using only zero-shot FMs (justified by the research question, but excludes fine-tuning); interpreting α as risk appetite (reasonable but heuristic); the loop-bid assumption that removes partial-execution settlement (a clean simplification, arguably more realistic than prior strategies). Key Results: TabPFN-3 achieves the lowest MAE, RMSE, and CRPS in Germany (12.59/22.59/9.15 vs DDNN-JSU's 14.58/24.96/10.70) and Poland (13.25/21.81/9.61), and TabPFN-2 the lowest MAE/RMSE in Spain (11.01/17.05) with TabPFN-3 the lowest CRPS (8.15 vs DDNN-JSU's 9.30). All three TabPFN variants significantly beat DDNN-JSU at the 1% level on all three metrics in all three markets. Chronos-2 and Chronos-2-synth significantly beat DDNN-JSU in Poland only; Moirai-2 and TimesFM-2.5 are consistently among the weakest and never significantly outperform the benchmark. Economically, TabPFN-TS-3 yields the highest profits at α=90–70% in Germany and Poland (e.g., 125,903 EUR in Germany at α=90%), while DDNN-JSU dominates at α=60–50% in all markets and at α=80–50% in Spain. Under unlimited bids, TabPFN variants lead narrowly (e.g., Poland: 106,685 EUR for TabPFN-3 vs 104,132 EUR for DDNN-JSU — a small margin). Best UB strategies capture 92.5% (Germany), 86.4% (Poland), and 83.3% (Spain) of Oracle profits (143,474 / 123,439 / 77,558 EUR respectively). QB strategies trade less often (max 1,346 of 1,826 days settled) but with higher mean/median profit per settled trade. A notable negative result: TabPFN-3 has the best CRPS in every market, yet TabPFN-TS-3 generates higher QB profits under every configuration — CRPS-optimal models are not profit-optimal. Tested at standard academic scale (3 markets, 1,826 test days each); no stress-scale claim is made. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING — the genuinely novel contribution is the first joint statistical-plus-economic evaluation of zero-shot FMs (both time series and tabular) against EPF-specific benchmarks over a five-year, three-market test period, yielding the non-obvious finding that the tabular TabPFN family (synthetic-pretraining) beats specialized models statistically while the economic winner depends on risk appetite. The individual components (existing FMs, established LEAR/DDNN benchmarks, standard trading strategies) are all prior art competently combined; no new method, dataset, or theory is introduced. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the three Chronos-2 variants (size, synthetic vs mixed pretraining) serve as an architecture/pretraining ablation, and univariate-vs-multivariate setups are compared, but there is no ablation of covariate inclusion for each FM (which prior work — Marchesi et al. — showed matters greatly), no fine-tuned FM baselines, and no ensemble of FM with benchmark. Significance is handled well: one-sided multivariate CPA tests at 10/5/1% levels are reported per model-market-metric. No error bars or multi-seed variance for the DDNN-JSU training runs (four hyperparameter realizations are ensembled, which partially mitigates this). Data are public (ENTSO-E, Investing.com); no code repository is mentioned in the text, which limits reproducibility of the exact FM context configurations. Methodological concerns: (i) possible test-period contamination for FMs pretrained on empirical time series (authors acknowledge; mitigated by TabPFN and Chronos-2-synth being synthetic-only); (ii) the LEAR benchmark is a modified reimplementation (shorter training windows due to data constraints) rather than the original specification, though the changes follow published recommendations; (iii) the DDNN-JSU benchmark comes from the authors' own research group (Marcjasz, Weron), so its strong showing is credible but self-referential; (iv) trading profits are acknowledged as not proper scoring functions. Overall, the benchmarking is honest and the strong-benchmark discipline is above average for the FM-comparison literature. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a large benchmarking experiment; no new system built). - Practical: Yes — all FMs run zero-shot on public data with modest parameter counts (11M–200M); no specialized hardware is indicated, and the small models (Moirai-2 at 11M, TabPFN-2 at 11M) run on commodity hardware. - Efficient: TabPFN-3 (58M) delivers the best accuracy; the paper notes (via Lettner et al.) that FMs carry substantially greater computational cost than task-specific models like NHITS+QRA, and TabPFN's in-context inference over 1,449 observations per forecast is nontrivial but does not report its own runtime comparison — not stated. - Effective: The evidence shows FMs (specifically TabPFN) solve the statistical forecasting problem, but only partially solve the economic problem — the effective answer depends on the risk configuration, and the paper demonstrates rather than assumes this dependency. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 3 markets and 1 MWh battery; the authors explicitly note conclusions may change with additional markets, battery specifications, and strategies; 10× scale (e.g., 30+ bidding zones, multi-asset portfolios) is unexamined. The paper delivers no software artifact, dataset release, or trained model — it stops at paper form (data sources are public, but no code URL is given). Strengths: - Long-horizon, multi-market evaluation design: five out-of-sample years across three structurally distinct markets is far more robust than the single-year test periods that dominate the prior FM-in-EPF literature, and it surfaces market-dependent rankings that short studies would miss. - Fair information-set parity: giving zero-shot FMs the same load/renewable forecasts and fundamentals as the benchmarks directly addresses the biggest flaw of earlier FM comparisons (univariate-only FMs), making the TabPFN result meaningful rather than an artifact of starved inputs. - The statistical-vs-economic decoupling finding is genuinely useful and non-obvious: the model with the best CRPS in every market (TabPFN-3) is never the most profitable under risk-averse trading, and the authors correctly flag that QB profits are not proper scoring functions — a subtlety most economic-evaluation papers elide. - Careful scoring hygiene: the paper explicitly distinguishes the proper CRPS from the mislabeled half-CRPS pinball averages common in the EPF literature and uses multivariate CPA tests rather than eyeballing point estimates. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: only three markets, one battery specification (1 MWh, η=0.95, C=25 EUR), and one family of trading strategies are considered; test-period contamination cannot be ruled out for FMs pretrained partly on empirical series (though not for synthetic-only TabPFN and Chronos-2-synth); small profit differences between leading models should be interpreted cautiously; and QB profits are not proper scoring functions. They confront limitations directly and conclude that FMs should be components of EPF systems, not universal substitutes — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No fine-tuned FM baselines: the headline question ("can FMs replace market-specific models?") is answered only for zero-shot FMs, yet fine-tuning is the obvious middle ground and prior work (Marchesi, Lettner) shows it materially improves calibration; the strict zero-shot framing may understate the FM ceiling. - No covariate ablation per FM: since the literature identifies covariate exploitation as the decisive FM weakness, showing each model's performance with vs. without exogenous variables would isolate which architectural choices matter; the paper varies context construction across models (multivariate vs. per-hour univariate vs. tabular), so FM rankings partly conflate model quality with input-pipeline choices. - No tail-calibration diagnostics: the economic reversal between TabPFN and DDNN-JSU at low α (extreme quantiles) begs for a pinball-loss-by-quantile-level or tail-coverage analysis; the mechanism behind DDNN-JSU's risk-averse profitability is asserted via violin plots but not statistically characterized. - No runtime/compute comparison despite the paper itself citing computational cost as a key FM drawback (via Lettner et al.); deployment decisions need the accuracy-per-EUR-of-compute trade-off. - No code or configuration release is mentioned, hindering exact replication of the FM context setups, which are the paper's most non-trivial engineering choices. - The benchmark pool is thin on the specialized-model side (two models, one from the authors' own lab); a third independent EPF benchmark (e.g., NHITS+QRA or a permutation-based DNN) would strengthen the "can FMs replace" claim. Bottom Line: For anyone deciding whether to deploy zero-shot foundation models in electricity price forecasting or storage trading, this is currently the most demanding and honest evaluation available — its answer (TabPFN yes for accuracy, no universal replacement for decision-making) is worth more than a dozen short-horizon FM papers, and there is no stronger alternative covering the same ground.

Unified Static–Dynamic Pruning for E icient LLM Inference

J Kim, Y Lee, J Do · vldb.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SPDP, a GPU inference framework with a new sparse weight format (Tiled-CBC) and two kernels that, for the first time, exploit unstructured static weight pruning and input-adaptive dynamic pruning together in a single execution path for LLM decoding and prefill. - Why it's important: Memory-bound autoregressive decoding dominates LLM serving cost—especially with test-time scaling and reasoning models—so combining weight compression with runtime activation skipping offers a way to cut latency and energy per token without the quality collapse that aggressive static or dynamic pruning alone causes. - How it does it: The key move is a joint format–kernel co-design: weights are stored in column-major bitmap-compressed micro-tiles with per-column metadata (ColInfo), so a CUDA-core spMspV kernel can skip activation-inactive columns at runtime while prefill reuses the same bytes as Tensor-Core-friendly SpMM tiles. - The good: The kernel-level evidence is solid: SPDP-spMspV beats the strongest static-sparsity baseline (SpInfer) by 1.24× average on A10G and 1.37× on L4, and hardware profiling (SM busy 66.0% vs 48.0/38.2%, bank conflicts 74 vs 3817/4491) directly explains why. - The missing: End-to-end gains are modest (×1.34 average TPOT speedup) due to Amdahl's law on non-sparsity-sensitive ops, and evaluation is confined to a single end-to-end model (Llama-2-7B), small-batch decode, and threshold-based DP (TEAL)—no variance reporting across seeds and no integration with a production serving stack with continuous batching. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate sparse LLM inference kernels or pruning systems—this is the first demonstrated practical SP+DP co-execution on GPUs; skip it if you need general sparse linear algebra (the authors show it loses to CSR-style kernels on SuiteSparse) or high-batch serving.
