Problem & Motivation: Small-batch LLM decoding is memory-bound: with batch size 1, linear layers reduce to skinny GEMV-like operations where data movement, not arithmetic, limits throughput—particularly on consumer GPUs with GDDR rather than HBM. Unstructured weight pruning preserves quality at moderate sparsity (30–60%) but existing sparse kernels fail to accelerate this regime because index overhead and irregular access erase the savings; recent LSCD systems (Flash-LLM, SpInfer) fix static-pruning acceleration but cannot adapt to input, while dynamic pruning (DP) methods (DejaVu, TEAL, CATS) exploit input-dependent activation sparsity only at coarse granularity, keep dense weights in memory, and were not implementable as fast kernels. The only prior SP+DP combination (DuoGPT) reported quality gains but no GPU kernel, so no realized speedup. The gap SPDP closes is making the theoretically multiplicative sparsity of joint SP+DP (total sparsity 1−(1−s_p)(1−s_d)) actually translate to GPU acceleration. Key Idea: Static and dynamic pruning act on orthogonal dimensions—SP removes weights row-wise offline (raising compression ratio), DP skips activation-inactive columns at runtime (raising effective compute intensity)—and a column-major tiled bitmap format with per-column offsets/counts lets a single compressed representation serve both a CUDA-core spMspV kernel that decodes and skips fragments on the fly (decode) and a Tensor-Core SpMM kernel that reorders the same tiles in shared memory (prefill). The paper's roofline analysis (CI = M·N / (M/CR + N·(1−s))) plus an empirical overlap study showing SP and DP prune largely independently (measured overlap ≈ s_p·s_d) substantiates why the sparsities compose rather than cancel. Methodology: The pipeline has three parts. (1) Tiled-CBC format: the statically pruned weight matrix is divided into GTiles of 256×16 column tiles (aligned to 64-bit words, four uint64 bitmaps per column); storage comprises TileOffset, column-major Values, Bitmaps, and a packed ColInfo array (16-bit start offset + 16-bit nonzero count per column) enabling O(1) column skipping; the paper gives an explicit storage formula. (2) SPDP-spMpV decode kernel: per iteration a thread block loads ColInfo and the dense activation XTile first (cp.async, LDGSTS.128), computes the DP mask by magnitude thresholding (TEAL ECDF quantiles, calibrated offline on 300 Alpaca samples), prefetches only activation-relevant weight columns, decodes them via HAD-SMBD (a DP-aware extension of SpInfer's SMBD using MaskedPopcount prefix ranks and a two-phase register unpacking), and performs CUDA-core GEMV accumulation, with a three-group fine-grained asynchronous pipeline (metadata / XTile / GTile+decode) double-buffered for latency hiding. (3) SPDP-SpMM prefill kernel: reuses the same format, adds a padding-based shared-memory layout-alignment stage (avoiding bank conflicts) before Tensor Core MMA, and drops the DP stage. Design decisions: CUDA-core rather than Tensor-Core decode (justified: mma.m16n8k16 CI drops up to 8× for GEMV, and Tensor-Core GEMV throughput is ~¼ of CUDA-core FP32 peak on these GPUs); column-major tiling (justified: matches DP's column-wise masks and 256-tile amortizes 16-byte padding); single shared format across phases (justified by avoiding duplicate storage/preprocessing, at the cost that prefill SpMM does not beat dense cuBLAS at large N). Key Results: On A10G and L4 GPUs (and L40S for end-to-end), against six kernel baselines (cuBLAS dense, cuSPARSE, Sputnik, SparTA, Flash-LLM, SpInfer) on SpInfer's weight-matrix shapes from OPT 13B–175B, LLaMA-2/3 7B–70B, Qwen/Qwen2 7B–72B, Mixtral-8×7B, Phi-2/3, and gpt-oss 20B/120B: SPDP-spMpV achieves 1.88× average (max 3.32×) over cuBLAS and 1.24× average (max 1.70×) over SpInfer on A10G; 2.11× (max 3.52×) and 1.37× (max 2.51–2.52×) on L4, at 30–50% static sparsity with 30% DP. Profiling: SM busy 66.0% vs SpInfer's 48.0% (30% SP) and 38.2% (50% SP); bank conflicts 74 vs 3817/4491. End-to-end on Llama-2-7B: average ×1.34 TPOT speedup over SpInfer; at matched perplexity SPDP sustains up to 25% more total sparsity than SpInfer (e.g., 65% total vs 50% SP at PPL ≈ 4.97–5.05); TPOT speedups saturate at high sparsity due to memory-bandwidth limits and non-sparse ops. Quality: downstream tasks (WikiText PPL, MMLU, GSM8K, CoQA, HumanEval on Qwen3-32B) show SPDP degrades less than Wanda-only or TEAL-only at ≥40% sparsity; 4-bit RTN quantization composes without PPL divergence. Baselines are current and strong (SpInfer is EuroSys'25 SOTA). Caveat: prefill SpMM does not beat cuBLAS at large N, and SPDP loses to cuSPARSE/Sputnik on ~85% of SuiteSparse matrices (>95% sparsity) — the authors honestly delimit the regime. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW FORMULATION component: the genuinely novel elements are (a) the first demonstrated GPU framework jointly executing unstructured static and dynamic pruning (prior work, DuoGPT, was algorithm-only), (b) the Tiled-CBC column-addressable format and HAD-SMBD decoding, and (c) the roofline-based quantification of SP–DP complementarity including the overlap-independence finding. The ingredients—LSCD (load-as-sparse, compute-as-dense) pipelines, bitmap compression, threshold-based DP (TEAL), magnitude/Wanda-style SP—are each standard; the contribution is their non-trivial co-design into one format and two kernels, which is competent and empirically validated combination rather than a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial but informative: a sparsity-regime sweep (SP 0–90% with DP fixed at 30%) delineates where SPDP wins and where it loses (very high sparsity), the overlap study independently justifies the multiplicative-sparsity assumption, and Nsight profiling ties throughput to hardware counters (SM busy, bandwidth, bank conflicts). The motivation experiments (Figures 2–3) test multiple SP methods (magnitude, SparseGPT, Wanda) against TEAL, though the system evaluation uses only Wanda+TEAL. Error bars/significance tests are not reported; end-to-end latency is a mean over 100 runs after 10 warm-ups with CPU overhead excluded via Nsight Systems. Code is publicly released at https://github.com/AIDASLab/SPDP, and the paper appeared at PVLDB Vol. 19 (peer-reviewed venue). Concerns: end-to-end quality/speed is evaluated on one model family at one scale (Llama-2-7B; Qwen3-32B only for HumanEval and quantization); no comparison against DuoGPT (the only other SP+DP work) or against Tensor-Core GEMV/CUDA-core dense GEMV baselines beyond cuBLAS_TC at the kernel level; the roofline model is a proxy that does not account for decode/DP runtime overheads, which the authors acknowledge. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (built kernels and format, evaluated by benchmark deployment on commodity GPUs). - Practical: Yes—targets consumer/inference GPUs (A10G, L4, L40S, all commercially available) with standard Ampere-era cp.async; no exotic hardware required. - Efficient: Kernel level it dominates alternatives (1.24–2.11× average over the strongest baselines at 30–50% sparsity), though Tiled-CBC's bitmap/ColInfo metadata makes it uncompetitive above ~95% sparsity and metadata dilutes stacking with 4-bit quantization. - Effective: The evidence supports the stated goal (lower TPOT at matched perplexity via joint SP+DP); the ×1.34 average end-to-end gain is real but bounded by Amdahl's law, and prefill acceleration is explicitly not achieved (dense cuBLAS wins at large N). - Scalable: Untested beyond 7B end-to-end and small-batch decode; batching with DP is not supported (SpMM is vector-per-batch only in decode; batched DP called future work), and multi-GPU/production serving integration is listed as future work—scalability claims beyond tested scale are not made, which is appropriate. The work delivers a software artifact (kernels + format, open-source on GitHub), reusable for threshold-based DP methods via a column-selection interface. Strengths: - First end-to-end demonstration that static and dynamic pruning compose on real GPUs; the overlap-sparsity measurement (observed ≈ s_p·s_d) is a genuine empirical finding that de-risks the whole approach, not just an implementation detail. - The Tiled-CBC/ColInfo design cleanly resolves the layout-mismatch problem—one compressed representation addressing both runtime column skipping (decode) and Tensor-Core tiles (prefill) without reformatting or duplicated storage. - Profiling-backed attribution: the SM busy/bandwidth/bank-conflict breakdown (Figure 9) explains the speedup mechanistically rather than leaving it as an end-to-end black box. - Unusually honest scope-setting: the authors show where their method loses (SuiteSparse extreme sparsity, large-N prefill, >70% static sparsity) rather than hiding it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: SPDP is a specialized LLM-decode kernel, not a general sparse library (loses on SuiteSparse); the prefill path does not beat dense cuBLAS at large N and mainly provides format compatibility and memory-footprint savings; quantization and sparsity are not multiplicative in practice because metadata (Bitmap, ColInfo, TileOffset, padding) does not shrink, making stacking beneficial mainly at high sparsity; batched DP is unsupported; and end-to-end gains are Amdahl-bounded by non-sparse operations. They confront limitations directly—this is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-model end-to-end evaluation (Llama-2-7B) limits external validity; no evidence the ×1.34 TPOT gain or the 25%-extra-sparsity-at-matched-PPL result holds for larger or newer models, despite kernel-level shapes covering up to gpt-oss-120B. - No variance across pruning seeds or calibration sets; perplexity differences between SPDP and baselines at moderate sparsity (Figure 2/6) are small and shown without error bars, so the quality-preservation claim at 40% sparsity is under-supported. - DP overhead accounting is thin: the mask-generation cost (loading activations, threshold comparisons per layer) is claimed near-zero via pipelining, but only indirectly; there is no end-to-end DP-on vs DP-off ablation of the full framework at fixed SP. - The efficiency comparison conflates two axes: SPDP(30%,30%) vs SpInfer(50%) compares different quality operating points; the cleanest matched-quality comparison (Figure 10) covers fewer configurations. - No comparison with orthogonal decode accelerators (speculative decoding, KV-cache methods, vLLM-style batching), so the practical end-to-end benefit relative to what a practitioner would actually deploy is unquantified. - Power/per-watt improvements are asserted from reduced byte movement but no direct energy measurements are reported. Bottom Line: For systems researchers and inference-infrastructure engineers, this is the reference point for joint static–dynamic sparsity execution on GPUs and worth reading for its format–kernel co-design lessons and honest evaluation; a practitioner seeking drop-in serving acceleration today gains less, since end-to-end gains are modest, batching is unsupported, and the quality curves would benefit from replication at larger scale.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OR-Clarify, a 100-case benchmark with 178 hidden slots for evaluating whether LLM agents ask the right clarifying questions before formulating an optimization model, plus InterOPT, a two-stage framework that tracks unresolved formulation gaps in a persistent ledger and uses them to decide what to ask and when to stop. - Why it's important: Real operations research requests are incomplete — a missing fact like whether routes are open or closed changes the mathematical program — and existing LLM-for-OR benchmarks assume complete specifications, so agents can silently build the wrong model without anyone measuring this failure. - How it does it: InterOPT separates monitoring from control: Stage 1 maintains a ledger of formulation-critical gaps discovered from public evidence, and Stage 2 anchors candidate clarification questions to open ledger entries, leaving the ask-or-stop decision to the tested model. - The good: In the choice-based protocol, InterOPT reaches 0.675 Core Exact versus 0.506 for the MC-D base protocol and 0.517 for ReadyGate, with diagnostics showing the gain comes from converting unresolved slots into fully recovered ones (617 yes vs. 253 no labels out of 890), not partial credit. - The missing: The headline choice-setting gain comes at roughly 3–4× the interaction cost (10.04 atomic questions vs. 2.35 for MC-D), and in the open-ended setting InterOPT does not beat strong baselines (0.538 Core Exact vs. ORPilot's 0.583), so the method's advantage is protocol-dependent; the benchmark also tops out at 100 cases and relies on an LLM judge. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate LLM agents for optimization modeling or interactive clarification more broadly — it defines a genuinely new evaluation target and releases code/data — but skip it if you want a clarification method that wins uniformly across interaction protocols.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners using LLM agents to convert natural-language business requests into optimization models face a failure mode prior work ignores: the agent formulates prematurely. Real requests omit objectives, hard-vs-soft constraint policies, or business rules, and an agent that silently assumes defaults (e.g., a closed tour when return-to-depot is unstated) changes the constraint structure without confirmation. Existing benchmarks (NL4Opt, OptiMUS, LLMOPT, ORLM) assume complete specifications and measure formulation/solving quality; interactive systems like ORPilot embed interviews but never isolate whether the agent recovers formulation-critical missing facts or knows when the specification is model-ready. The paper closes this gap by defining "pre-formulation clarification" as a standalone task: decide whether the public specification is formulation-complete (all plausible completions induce the same formulation structure) and, if not, recover missing formulation-critical facts with minimal interaction. Key Idea: Reframe OR assistance as a selective completeness decision — a fact is worth asking about only if its resolution could change the induced optimization formulation — and evaluate it by withholding benchmark-side "hidden slots" (grounded, masked facts) behind a strict information boundary. The method's enabling trick is a monitoring–control decomposition (borrowed from metacognition): a persistent, evidence-grounded gap ledger (Stage 1) decoupled from the action policy (Stage 2), so question generation stays anchored to diagnosed gaps while stopping remains a separate, fallible decision that the runner never blocks or forces. Methodology: OR-Clarify construction: (1) decompose fully specified OR task records into single-requirement facts; (2) screen out facts whose meaning is already determined by visible information (e.g., 15,000 production hours implies a capacity bound, but a 1,000-unit demand does not determine exact-satisfaction vs. backlogging); (3) mask ~half of eligible facts with a frozen, seeded pseudorandom procedure; (4) annotate each masked fact as a hidden slot with evidence, a fact-bounded simulated-user answer, acceptable-question examples, a semantic recovery rule, and a severity label (P0 blocking / P1 substantive / P2 secondary, assigned post-masking so severity cannot influence masking). The result is 100 cases and 178 slots (75 P0, 83 P1, 20 P2; mean 1.78 slots/case), human-audited. Evaluation: agent interacts with a simulated user that answers only the current question from private facts; a post-hoc judge scores exact slot recovery (partial credit excluded) against frozen rubrics, plus silent assumptions, stopping labels (premature/appropriate/over-questioning), and turn/question counts. InterOPT: Stage 1 runs a structured LLM call Φ updating a gap ledger (≤3 new gaps/turn across six categories, deduplicated, status Open/Asked); Stage 2 runs Ψ producing an ask/READY_TO_MODEL decision plus three gap-bound candidate state–question pairs (with A–C options under the Choice protocol), from which a selector picks one using a fixed priority (objectives/trade-offs first, mathematical detail downweighted). Main experiments: DeepSeek V4 Pro as tested model, K=5 runs/case, T_max=20, case as statistical unit, 95% case-level bootstrap intervals. Critical design decisions: masking rate fixed before evaluation (justified — prevents method-specific tuning); slot severity assigned after masking (well-justified); stopping left with the model rather than the ledger (explicitly justified as safe — an empty ledger does not imply completeness). Key Results: Off-the-shelf LLMs struggle: the best model (Opus-4.8) reaches only 0.583 Core Exact in both protocols, with 0.42–0.71 silent assumptions per run across DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM-5.1, GPT-5.5, and Opus-4.8 — confirming the benchmark is unsaturated. Choice protocol (Table 2): InterOPT 0.638 All-Slot / 0.675 Core Exact vs. ReadyGate 0.476/0.517, MC-D 0.474/0.506, MC 0.414/0.447, but at 10.674 turns and 10.036 atomic questions vs. ~3.3/2.4 for MC-D — a clear coverage–cost trade-off. Open protocol: ORPilot (adapter) is best at 0.546/0.583 with the fewest silent assumptions (0.268/run); InterOPT (0.492/0.538) is close but not dominant and leaves more silent assumptions (0.560/run) than ORPilot. Budget-matched curves show InterOPT keeps gaining after MC-D/ReadyGate plateau under Choice. Ablations (Core Exact): under Choice, removing Stage 1 costs 11.1 points (0.675→0.564) vs. 6.0 for removing Stage 2; under Open, w/o Stage 1 = 0.460, w/o Stage 2 = 0.506, full = 0.538 — gap discovery drives coverage, guided selection helps most under structured Choice. Diagnostics: in the open setting, 40.6% of 500 runs are flagged premature-stopping (agent declares ready in 98.8% of runs); multi-slot disclosures are rare (0.116/run), so recovery is not an artifact of generous answers. Scale: 100 cases, toy-to-standard OR problems, not industrial scale. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (pre-formulation clarification as a standalone OR task, with the formulation-completeness criterion of Eq. 3.1) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (OR-Clarify, first OR-specific framework jointly evaluating slot recovery, readiness, silent assumptions, and interaction cost), plus a NEW METHOD (InterOPT) that is a competent combination of known ideas — gap tracking is a structured scratchpad/memory, candidate generation plus selection is standard, and option-D choice protocols come from CAmbigNQ-style QA work. The genuinely new element is the evaluation target and information-boundary design, not the architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative, isolating both stages under both protocols with a plausible division-of-labor story. Statistical treatment is careful: K=5 runs per case, case-level aggregation and bootstrap CIs, protocol-audit failures retained in denominators, and temperature controls. Code (github.com/AIOR-Research/InterOpt) and data (huggingface.co/datasets/AIOR-Research/OR-Clarify) are released. Concerns: (1) the judge and simulated user are LLM-based and built by the authors; judge validation is described as human auditing of rubrics, but judge accuracy against human labels is not quantified; (2) open-setting baselines (GATE, ORPilot, Let's T-P-P) are task-aligned adapters, not full reproductions of the original systems, so "ORPilot wins in open setting" claims are about the adapters; (3) MC/MC-D are protocols the authors designed for this study, so the Choice comparison is partly self-referential; (4) the paper is an arXiv preprint (v2, September 2026), not peer-reviewed; (5) authors are affiliated with Cardinal Operations, a commercial OR vendor, which motivates the task but should be weighed when interpreting baseline framing. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus a prompt-level method run within a fixed harness; no training). Practical: Yes — training-free prompting on commodity LLM APIs, no special hardware. Efficient: Mixed — the full method costs 3–4× the questions of the base protocol under Choice (10.04 vs. 2.35 atomic questions per run) plus ledger-update calls, which the authors acknowledge as a coverage–cost trade-off. Effective: Partially — the evidence shows slot recovery improves, but downstream formulation or solver quality is never measured, so exact slot recovery remains a proxy for building the correct model. Scalable: Untested — the benchmark is 100 cases with 1–5 slots each; whether gap-ledger prompting degrades or the simulated-user fidelity holds on larger, messier, multi-stakeholder problems is claimed nowhere and shown nowhere. Deliverable: software artifact (code + benchmark dataset) in reusable form; the method itself is a prompt-level policy requiring no trained weights. Strengths: - The problem definition is sharp and consequential: formulation-completeness (Eq. 3.1) gives a precise, checkable criterion for when clarification matters, distinguishing the work from generic abstention and clarifying-question literature where any ambiguity counts. - The benchmark's information-boundary design is rigorous: hidden slots, fact-bounded user responses, a non-revealing protocol detector, and post-hoc rubric judging keep evaluation targets strictly outside the agent's context, and the masking/severity pipeline is auditable and frozen before evaluation. - Honest negative results are rare and valuable: the paper reports that InterOPT does not dominate open-ended baselines, that its choice-setting gain costs 3–4× interaction, and that 40.6% of open runs stop prematurely — the diagnostics section actively explains the failure mode (stopping, not question packaging). - The budget-matched recovery curves (Figure 4) complement endpoint metrics, addressing the obvious confound that asking more questions recovers more slots. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that gap-guided clarification does not uniformly dominate free-form baselines, that InterOPT can require substantially more interaction, that stopping remains imperfect, and that silent assumptions are not eliminated. They also flag that the D-option no-match rates are descriptive, not causal estimates, and that open-setting baselines are adapters rather than full system reproductions. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No end-to-end validation: the paper never shows that exact slot recovery translates into correct formulations or better solver outcomes, so the benchmark's central metric is validated only against its own rubrics — a proxy-validity gap the authors do not address. - Judge reliability is unquantified: human auditing is described for slot construction, but there is no reported inter-rater or human-vs-judge agreement on the yes/partial/no recovery labels, and the headline metric hinges on that LLM judge. - The simulated user is a constrained oracle that never volunteers facts and answers only the asked question; real users volunteer, misunderstand, and misremember, and no robustness to realistic user behavior is tested. - 100 cases derived from the authors' own source task collection (overlapping with their prior ORLM/OR-Space work) is small and possibly distribution-narrow; no external OR datasets are converted despite the construction pipeline being advertised as general. - The open-setting loss to the ORPilot adapter is underexplored — the paper does not test combining InterOPT's ledger with ORPilot's interview policy, which is the obvious next experiment. - Why stopping fails is diagnosed but not fixed: no calibrated-stopping baseline (e.g., a learned readiness threshold) is compared, leaving the identified dominant failure mode without a counterfactual. Bottom Line: For anyone building or benchmarking LLM optimization agents, OR-Clarify defines an evaluation target that existing benchmarks genuinely miss and the benchmark itself is worth adopting despite its small scale and unvalidated LLM judge; InterOPT is a useful but protocol-dependent starting point, not yet a method to deploy over strong free-form interview baselines.

DriveZero: End-to-End Driving Beyond Human Demonstrations (50 ▲ )

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DriveZero, a camera-only end-to-end driving system trained entirely without human trajectory supervision, built by distilling a privileged closed-loop RL teacher (DriveRL) into a visual planner whose backbone is pre-trained by distilling frozen vision foundation models (DriveVFM). - Why it's important: Imitation-based end-to-end driving is capped by the quality and coverage of human logs — single realized futures, rare recovery maneuvers, and compounding covariate shift — so a supervision source beyond demonstrations directly addresses the core scalability limit of the dominant paradigm. - How it does it: The system decouples perception and action: DriveRL trains a 5.7M-parameter privileged teacher with PPO in log-seeded mixed-agent simulation (~196,608 parallel worlds on 96 GPUs), DriveVFM agglomeratively distills DINOv3, SigLIP2, SAM, and Depth Anything V2 into one backbone from raw images, and DriveZero unifies them via winner-takes-all trajectory distillation on logged frames — with goal-conditioned teacher queries augmenting each scene into multiple valid supervision targets. - The good: The ablation isolating supervision source is the key evidence: DriveRL teacher trajectories alone score slightly below human supervision on NAVSIMv1 (93.61 vs. 93.92 PDMS), but adding goal augmentation lifts the same setup to 94.41 — a controlled demonstration that the RL teacher's behavior, not just any non-human data, exceeds human-log supervision. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported on the headline benchmark margins (e.g., 94.8 vs. 94.6 PDMS for DrivoR-Scale), and no code or model weights are stated as released despite a project page. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on end-to-end driving or teacher-student RL distillation — the zero-human-supervision recipe and goal-augmentation result are directly relevant; Problem & Motivation: End-to-end autonomous driving systems that map sensor input plus navigation intent directly to vehicle motion are almost universally trained by behavior cloning on human logs. This binds learned behavior to a single realized future per scene, omits safety-critical recovery maneuvers, and exposes the policy to compounding errors under its own induced state distribution (citing DAgger-style failure analysis). The practitioner with this problem is any team building a deployable camera-only driving policy. Prior privileged-RL-to-visual-distillation attempts (ROACH, GigaPixel, TerraTransfer) train closed-loop behavior but take the visual encoder off the shelf; the paper argues both perception and action need their own pre-training regimes — perception from massive diverse imagery, action from high-throughput closed-loop interaction — and no prior system pre-trains both before unification. Key Idea: Decouple the driving problem into an action model and a perception model, pre-train each in its best-suited regime (closed-loop RL on structured privileged state for action; foundation-model distillation on raw images for perception), then reunite them open-loop: the frozen RL teacher is rolled out at each logged frame to produce trajectories, and a camera-only student is distilled against those rollouts — no rendering or interactive visual training required. The multiplier is goal conditioning: because the teacher accepts arbitrary goal points, each logged scene can be queried under augmented driving intents, generating diverse, goal-consistent trajectories that a human log structurally cannot contain (the ablation shows goal augmentation, not RL supervision per se, is what beats human data). Methodology: Three stages. (1) DriveRL: a mixed-agent simulator converts nuPlan logs into interactive worlds where each background actor runs log replay, IDM, or a learned policy behind a common state–action interface; a 5.7M-parameter teacher (agent/map/ego token encoders, cross-attention to ego and map, Beta-distribution action head over longitudinal jerk and steering-rate, kinematic bicycle model) is trained from scratch with PPO on a scalar reward combining hard-event penalties, a one-time goal bonus, and a multiplicative product of six soft quality scores; an eight-channel decomposed critic supports GAE. A value-guided test-time search samples N policy candidates, scores them by short-horizon (L=5) discounted reward plus critic bootstrap, and switches from the modal action only if the margin δ=0.03 is exceeded. (2) DriveVFM: RADIO-style agglomerative distillation of four frozen teachers into one ViT, with asymmetric supervision (DINOv3: summary+patch; SigLIP2: summary only; SAM: patch only), PHI-S standardization to balance heterogeneous feature statistics, and a QK-Clip mechanism (weight rescaling when pre-softmax logits exceed 1,000, inspired by Kimi K2) for stability and FP16-safe deployment; two-stage progressive-resolution training (600K iters at 256², 200K at 512², batch 2,048) on a mixture of LAION-2B, ImageNet-21K, SA-1B, OpenDV, nuPlan, and Waymo. (3) DriveZero: DriveVFM (frozen, rank-32 Q/V LoRA) encodes four cameras; register tokens compress features; a 4-layer decoder emits 64 trajectory proposals trained with winner-takes-all L1 against the frozen teacher's 20-step rollout, plus a detached scoring branch predicting the six PDM score components via BCE. Key design decisions: Beta action heads (justified via CaRL for unimodality), scene-consistent late-actor insertion gating (well-motivated, addresses a real simulator artifact), and the conservative TTS margin (justified by noise in approximate rollouts). Notably, self-play background agents — used for their real-fleet deployment — gave no measurable benefit on nuPlan, which the authors honestly attribute to the benchmark's IDM-driven evaluation. Key Results: DriveRL on nuPlan: mean closed-loop score 93.01 across Val14, Test14-hard, and Test14-random in both reactive and non-reactive modes, beating the Log-Replay expert (mean 83.09 over the same six settings, e.g., 95.16 vs. 93.53 on Val14-NR and 89.97 vs. 85.96 on Test14-hard-NR) and beating CaRL and GigaFlow on every overlapping setting; TTS with N=64 raises the mean to 93.57 (+0.56). DriveZero on NAVSIMv1 navtest: 94.8 PDMS camera-only without human trajectories, equal to the Human Driver (94.8) and above the best prior camera-only method DrivoR-Scale (94.6) and camera–LiDAR DiffusionDrive (88.1); with 237K SimScale simulation scenes, DriveZero-Scale reaches 95.3. NAVSIMv2 navhard: 51.5 EPDMS (vs. GigaPixel's 50.1), 57.1 with SimScale scaling (vs. DrivoR-Scale's 54.6). HUGSIM zero-shot closed-loop: 46.6 average HD-Score vs. 38.5 for GigaPixel. Ablations (ViT-S, navtrain-only): DriveVFM beats DINOv3 ViT-S 94.41 vs. 93.88 PDMS; teacher models contribute cumulatively (+SAM +0.41, +Depth Anything +0.31); DriveRL trajectories 93.61 vs. human 93.92, DriveRL + goal augmentation 94.41. Backbone scaling: ViT-S→ViT-L yields 94.41→94.83. Baselines are current (2024–2026 methods), though the strongest comparisons on navtest rely on leaderboard-reported numbers. Scale is substantial for the RL stage (96 GPUs, 196,608 parallel worlds, ~21 hours) and moderate for the student (16×H20, 38 hours, 338M total/18.58M trainable parameters). Surprising finding: an imitation-free system matching and exceeding the human driver on a pseudo-closed-loop benchmark, with the largest closed-loop HUGSIM gains (+8.1 HD-Score) attributed to trajectory diversity on OOD SimScale data. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM (DriveZero as an end-to-end artifact) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (controlled evidence that goal-augmented RL-teacher supervision surpasses human-trajectory supervision) plus a modest NEW METHOD component (goal augmentation via goal-conditioned teacher queries). The genuinely new elements are the decoupled pre-training-then-distill architecture validated at leaderboard scale and the goal-augmentation supervision source. DriveVFM is essentially RADIO/PHI-S applied to driving with a driving-image corpus; value-guided test-time search follows known policy-and-value search principles; PPO with Beta heads follows CaRL; the privileged-to-visual transfer paradigm follows ROACH/GigaPixel/TerraTransfer. This is a strong competent system paper, not a fundamentally new learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-targeted: backbone substitution under fixed planner, cumulative teacher addition, and supervision-source comparison with components traced to specific PDM sub-metrics. However, no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests appear anywhere, and several headline margins (94.8 vs. 94.6; 93.61 vs. 93.92 for RL-only supervision) are within a range where run-to-run variance plausibly matters. No code or weight release is stated; only a project website with videos is given. Extensive hyperparameter tables (A1–A12) and controlled configurations (traffic-light ablations, goal-anchor layout, self-play variants, with caveats about non-comparable 32-GPU setups) are a reproducibility positive. Methodological concerns: (a) DriveZero's primary benchmarks are pseudo closed-loop (NAVSIM), and the true closed-loop result (HUGSIM) is zero-shot on reconstructed scenes rather than trained closed-loop; (b) the headline DriveZero-Scale uses 237K external SimScale simulation scenes, so the record scores are not achieved on navtrain alone — the paper does disclose this; (c) the nuPlan benchmark's scoring omits traffic-light violations, and the authors show a red-light reward lowers the aggregate score while cutting violations 3.88%→2.03% — a candid Goodhart acknowledgment, but it also means reported nuPlan/NAVSIM-style scores under-weight compliance; (d) the goal-augmentation ablation cannot have a human-data counterpart by construction, so "teacher > human" is only demonstrated in the augmented setting. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (built and run at benchmark scale, plus a small real-vehicle deployment). Practical: Yes for the teacher (5.7M parameters, structured inputs from autolabeled perception); the student requires a ViT-L backbone plus scoring head (~338M parameters) — plausible on automotive-grade hardware, and FP16-safe via QK-Clip, though vehicle-side latency is not reported. Efficient: TTS trades parallel compute for up to +0.56 nuPlan score with a fixed checkpoint; RL training consumed 96 GPUs (~21 h) and student training 16×H20 (~38 h) — nontrivial but realistic industrial budgets. Effective: Evidence is strong on benchmarks (surpasses log-replay expert and, with augmentation, human-trajectory supervision), but the real-world claim rests on one demonstrated deployment video with self-play training and degraded-input robustness described only qualitatively. Scalable: Partially tested — SimScale data scaling improved navhard Stage 2 by 8.3 points and HUGSIM by 7.0, and backbone scaling ViT-S→ViT-L shows a positive trend; beyond this, 100× scaling is claimed as a recipe, not demonstrated. Deliverables: a described system and training recipe; no released library, dataset, or weights are mentioned — the artifact currently exists in paper-plus-video form. Strengths: - The supervision-source ablation is a genuinely well-controlled experiment: same planner, data, and schedule across human vs. DriveRL vs. DriveRL+goal-augmentation, with the honest intermediate result that raw RL-trajectory distillation underperforms human data before augmentation fixes it. This converts a headline claim into causal evidence. - Goal augmentation is a clean, previously-unavailable supervision mechanism: only a goal-conditioned RL teacher can generate goal-consistent trajectories for counterfactual intents, and the paper correctly identifies this as the property human logs cannot match. - The mixed-agent simulation engineering is substantial and honestly reported — 196,608 parallel worlds, batched GPU rollouts, scene-consistent late-actor gating — and the self-play ablation showing no nuPlan benefit is reported rather than hidden, with a plausible benchmark-attribution explanation. - Candid negative-result reporting throughout: the traffic-light reward trade-off (violations down 1.85 pp, aggregate scores down ~2 points), the far-anchor goal sensitivity, and the Stage-1/Stage-2 score trade-off in DriveZero-Scale all strengthen credibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that self-play provides no measurable gain on nuPlan and attribute it to the benchmark's IDM-driven evaluation rather than to the method; that DriveRL-trajectory-only supervision slightly underperforms human trajectories (93.61 vs. 93.92); that TTS leaves Test14-hard reactive essentially unchanged (89.15 vs. 89.18); that DriveZero-Scale's Stage-1 navhard score drops 1.8 points while Stage-2 gains 8.3; that some ablations use non-comparable 32-GPU setups; and that the nuPlan aggregate does not capture red-light compliance. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Limitations they do not frame as such: the real-world deployment is a demonstration, not a measured study, and no sim-to-real gap quantification is offered. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: the 0.2–0.5-point margins that establish several headline claims (matching the human driver; DriveVFM over DINOv3; RL-supervision over human) carry no seed replication or significance testing, and the paper itself notes navtest is "highly saturated." - The distillation stage supervises the student with teacher rollouts in which background actors follow log replay — so the student never sees teacher behavior under reactive traffic, yet is evaluated in reactive and closed-loop settings; the interaction-distribution gap between distillation conditions and evaluation conditions is not analyzed. - DriveVFM's advantage over DINOv3 is demonstrated only through the downstream planner on one benchmark; no direct probing, geometry, or long-tail quantitative metric beyond qualitative PCA/prototype heatmaps (Figure 3) supports the representation-quality claim. - The HUGSIM comparison is zero-shot but benefits from SimScale data in DriveZero-Scale — the baseline methods' data budgets on HUGSIM are not stated, so the +8.1 HD-Score margin partially conflates supervision quality with extra training data. - No latency, memory, or real-time inference numbers for the ViT-L student, and no cost accounting for the 96-GPU RL stage relative to a behavior-cloning baseline of equal benchmark quality. - The teacher-student gap (DriveRL 95.8 vs. DriveZero 94.8 PDMS) is not decomposed into perception error vs. distillation error, leaving unclear where the next gains should come from. Bottom Line: For anyone building end-to-end driving systems, this is worth reading: it is the strongest published demonstration that an imitation-free pipeline — closed-loop RL teacher plus foundation-model distillation plus goal augmentation — can match or beat human-trajectory supervision on current benchmarks, and its honest ablation discipline makes the recipe actionable, provided one accepts that the evidence is benchmark-centric with only a demonstration-grade real-world footprint.

#34 — Innovative (71)

FlowBalance: Verifier-Grounded Self-Improvement from On-Policy Reasoning Experience (81 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FlowBalance, a post-training method that combines sparse verifier rewards with dense same-model privileged-hindsight scores inside a GFlowNet-style trajectory-balance objective, learning a normalized distribution over complete reasoning responses instead of a pointwise RL signal. - Why it's important: Verifier-only RL (GRPO) wastes dense information along long reasoning chains, while dense self-distillation can reinforce false confidence and collapse response length; a safer way to exploit self-generated dense signal directly affects the cost and stability of reasoning-model training. - How it does it: A frozen copy of the current policy, conditioned on training-only reference solutions, scores already-sampled tokens; these scores are sign-gated by the verifier's group-relative advantage (kept on successes, reversed on failures, disabled on ties), exponentially tilt a reference policy into a Gibbs target, and the policy is fitted with a profiled trajectory-balance loss using one log-partition estimate per rollout group. - The good: Five-seed results on Qwen3-4B/8B across AIME24/HMMT25/Minerva/MATH500/OlympiadBench show the best average of five methods (67.61 avg on 8B vs 65.49 for GRPO and 65.85 for FlowRL), plus 1.43× faster convergence to 0.5 AIME24 validation accuracy and stability over 400 steps where GRPO degrades after ~180. - The missing: Key hyperparameters (rollout group size, response-length cap) are listed as "pending release," the diversity evidence is a single-seed, single-checkpoint LLM-judged diagnostic, and the η_A ablation is non-monotonic in a way the paper does not explain. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM post-training or GFlowNet-style distribution matching for reasoning — it is one of the more careful attempts to make dense self-guidance verifier-safe; skip it if you need evidence outside math reasoning or require fully reproducible training recipes.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) is real — verifier sign-gated dense self-guidance inside a trajectory-balance Gibbs target is a new composition with an exact correction guarantee (Proposition 4). Rigor (70) benefits from five-seed results, appropriately scoped theory, and the right control (FlowRL minus guidance), but is reduced by 'pending release' hyperparameters that block reproduction, a single-seed LLM-judged diversity study, an unexplained non-monotonic η_A ablation, and preprint status. Non-Obviousness (74) is solid — the sign-gate insight that dense evidence may refine but never override the verifier's direction is conceptually crisp. Completeness (70) is helped by direct limitation confrontation but the math-only scope and never-run subtrajectory variant are real gaps; Resilience (68) holds within the stated scope. Impact (66) reflects referenced code/blog and a credible 1.43× convergence speedup, though no weights are released and privileged reference solutions limit transfer beyond math. Problem & Motivation: Labs training reasoning models with RL from verifiable rewards face a supervision sparsity problem: a response of thousands of tokens receives one terminal correctness bit, and group-relative methods attach that response-level signal to every token. Dense alternatives (on-policy self-distillation from a privileged view of the same model) provide token-level signal but demonstrably cause failure modes: response-length collapse, suppressed exploration, and self-confirmation of the model's own errors. The paper targets the inner loop of self-improvement — given on-policy experience, sparse verified outcomes, and imperfect dense self-guidance, what distribution should the next policy learn? The intended audience is post-training researchers; the gap it closes is that no prior work combines verifier grounding with dense same-model guidance inside a normalized distribution-matching objective over complete responses (RLSD adds dense guidance to an RL objective; FlowRL is outcome-only trajectory balance). Key Idea: Outcome-calibrated self-guidance via trajectory balance: use a privileged-hindsight view of the same frozen policy to compute a dense trajectory-level guidance score G_H, but let the verifier's group-relative advantage determine the sign of that guidance in the trajectory energy E = η_A·A + β_G·G_H·sgn(A), then fit the resulting reference-tilted Gibbs distribution with trajectory balance where the profiled log-partition absorbs only the common group offset. The sign gate is the crux — dense evidence refines which verified direction to prefer, but can never override the verifier's outcome direction. Methodology: The pipeline per iteration: (1) snapshot the policy, sample N responses per prompt without privileged context; (2) a rule-based verifier yields stopped group-relative advantages A_i (GRPO normalization); (3) a frozen privileged view π_H conditioned on training-only context c scores each sampled token; clipped token-level log-probability gains relative to π_ref are averaged into G_H; (4) the energy E = η_A·A + β_G·G_H·sgn(A) defines a target p* ∝ π_ref·exp(E/τ); (5) the policy minimizes the squared trajectory-balance residual with a profiled partition (mean of per-response implied log Z over the group), gradients only through πθ's log-probabilities. The framework is GFlowNet trajectory balance (Malkin et al.) applied to LLM reasoning, extending FlowRL with a guidance term in the energy. Critical design decisions: (a) sign gating by sgn(A) — well-justified theoretically (Proposition 4 gives an exact correction factor exp(2β_G·G_H(y−)/τ) on the success/failure probability ratio) and empirically (ungated shaping and stronger β_G both hurt); (b) profiling one scalar partition per group — justified by Proposition 1 showing all N−1 within-group contrasts are preserved, with an exact 34× local Gaussian risk reduction at N=32; (c) no separate token-level imitation loss — justified by the OPSD length-collapse contrast, though the subtrajectory-balance variant is described but never evaluated. Key Results: On Qwen3-8B at step 180 (five seeds), FlowBalance averages 67.61 across AIME24@16/HMMT25/Minerva/MATH500/OlympiadBench vs GRPO 65.49, OPSD 41.16, RLSD 64.12, FlowRL 65.85; on Qwen3-4B, 64.26 vs GRPO 62.31 and FlowRL 63.22. Against FlowRL (the closest baseline, same trajectory-balance family minus guidance), core-four averages improve by 1.67 (4B) and 1.98 (8B) points. Training dynamics: 0.5 AIME24 validation accuracy in ~100 steps vs ~143 for GRPO; stability to 400 steps vs GRPO degradation after ~step 180; no length collapse unlike OPSD. Ablations show β_G=1 > 2 > 3 (67.61/66.48/65.95) and η_A=15 best but η_A=10 (65.41) worse than η_A=5 (65.65) — non-monotonic and unexplained. HMMT25 standard deviations reach ±9.89, so per-benchmark gains there are noisy. The diversity diagnostic (correct-only Simpson diversity 0.2194 vs 0.1017 GRPO, 0.1456 RLSD) is one seed, one checkpoint, GPT-5.5-judged. Synthetic diagnostics quantify the mechanism (target success mass 0.900 vs 0.818 reward-only, 0.832 ungated). Baselines are current and appropriate; testing is at standard academic scale (4B/8B models, ~400 steps), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with elements of NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING). The genuinely novel piece is outcome-calibrated (sign-gated) dense self-guidance embedded in a reference-supported Gibbs target fitted by profiled trajectory balance — no prior work puts verifier-gated same-model guidance inside a distribution-matching objective. The components themselves are standard: GRPO-style group advantages, on-policy privileged self-scoring (RLSD/OPSD lineage), and trajectory balance (FlowRL/GFlowNets); the contribution is their composition plus the calibration mechanism and its analysis, not any single new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Theory is honest about scope — all four propositions are properties of the conditional target distribution, explicitly not claims of optimizer convergence, and proofs in Appendix B are complete and short. Ablations exist for both energy coefficients with per-benchmark breakdowns, but are one-dimensional sweeps, not a grid; the non-monotonic η_A result (10 < 5 < 15) is reported but not analyzed. Five seeds with sample standard deviations on all main-table entries is above average for this area; the diversity study is single-seed and LLM-judged, which the authors flag. Code is referenced (github.com/alexhuang13/FlowBalance) plus a blog. Concerns: rollout group size and max response length are "pending release" (Table 5), which blocks full reproduction now; the mechanism-validation synthetic diagnostics are the authors' own constructions; and the AIME24 Pass@16 entries with ±0.00 standard deviation (e.g., FlowRL 4B 80.00, FlowBalance 4B 80.00 on different methods) warrant a second look. No evaluation on the authors' own benchmark — all five are standard. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a THEORETICAL secondary component). - Practical: Yes — 4B/8B dense models, standard RL training infrastructure, rule-based verifier, no external scorer model beyond a frozen copy of the policy. - Efficient: Comparable to GRPO plus one extra scoring pass per rollout (no resampling from the hindsight view, no guidance gradients); claims 1.43× fewer steps to a fixed accuracy threshold, which partially offsets the overhead. - Effective: Evidence supports the claim on math reasoning (consistent gains over the strongest baselines at both scales), but effectiveness rests on Pass@1/Pass@16 accuracy proxies plus a one-seed diversity diagnostic; the causal story (calibrated guidance prevents self-confirmation) is validated only on synthetic enumerable distributions. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B and 400 steps; the per-group profiling cost and the requirement of training-time reference solutions make scaling behavior and applicability to domains without clean verifiers open questions — the paper claims no scale results. The paper delivers a method description and referenced code/blog; trained model weights are not stated as released. Strengths: - The sign-gating mechanism is a real conceptual contribution: it converts dense self-guidance from an unconditional imitation pressure into a verifier-controlled refinement, with an exact, checkable guarantee (Proposition 4's exp(2β_G·G_H(y−)/τ) correction) rather than a heuristic filter. - The ablation design isolates the claim well: FlowRL (same trajectory-balance machinery, no guidance) is the right control, and the consistent 1.67–1.98 point core-four gains over it at two scales credibly attribute the improvement to calibrated guidance rather than the distributional objective alone. - The theory is scoped correctly — the authors repeatedly distinguish target-distribution properties from optimizer-convergence claims, and the profiled-partition analysis (all N−1 contrasts preserved; 34× risk reduction at N=32) explains why the update is information-efficient in a way that connects to the observed training stability. - The failure-mode evidence is concrete: OPSD's length collapse, GRPO's post-step-180 degradation, and the β_G=3 accuracy drop (AIME24 89.33→86.00) all support the central thesis that uncalibrated dense signal is the problem being solved. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state four: (1) experiments cover only mathematical reasoning, leaving agentic/multimodal/long-horizon domains open; (2) the response-length comparison diagnoses a correlated failure mode but does not establish that longer responses cause accuracy; (3) the diversity analysis is one seed, one checkpoint, LLM-judged — not a population-level guarantee; (4) the method isolates the inner loop on a fixed prompt distribution and is not itself a self-evolving system. They confront limitations directly and scope their diversity conclusion to the single diagnostic — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The non-monotonic η_A ablation (average 65.65 at 5, 65.41 at 10, 67.61 at 15) suggests either high seed variance or an interaction the one-dimensional sweep design cannot see; the paper reports it without explanation. - The method requires training-time reference solutions or task feedback as privileged context c — the paper does not discuss cost, availability, or quality sensitivity of this supervision, which is a real deployment constraint outside math (where reference solutions are cheap) and is never ablated (e.g., noisy or partial contexts). - The claimed diversity benefit is measured with an LLM judge on 30 problems at one seed; given that diversity preservation is a headline motivation, a multi-seed or human-verified version is a conspicuous absence. - The subtrajectory-balance variant is formulated (Section 3.3) but never run, so long-response credit assignment — the stated motivation for trajectory balance — is only exercised at the complete-response granularity. - GFlowRL, which the related work cites as removing the partition network via in-batch estimates (the same trick FlowBalance uses for profiling), is not included as a baseline, leaving the distributional-RL comparison slightly incomplete. - "Pending release" hyperparameters in the reproducibility table mean the reported numbers cannot currently be independently regenerated from the paper alone. Bottom Line: A practitioner in LLM post-training should read this: the verifier-gated guidance mechanism is a genuinely useful and well-analyzed idea with credible two-scale evidence, and it is a stronger, more principled alternative to RLSD-style dense-guidance hybrids — though the missing hyperparameters, math-only scope, and single-seed diversity evidence mean the recipe is not yet turnkey.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a two-layer optimization formulation that jointly selects trust-domain partitions and within-domain credential-derivation trees to minimize credential blast radius subject to a measured post-quantum (PQC) authentication latency budget. - Why it's important: Architects deploying PQC face a real trade-off — segmenting services into independently rooted trust domains contains credential-compromise damage but pays a path-dependent latency penalty on every cross-boundary call, and existing zero-trust and microsegmentation guidance treats these decisions separately or fixes credential structure. - How it does it: The core move is a conservative linear blast-radius score (each service contributes its weight times the summed compromise probabilities on its root-to-leaf derivation path), which turns the joint design into a latency-constrained problem that decomposes into min-cut / metric-labeling / scheduling instances in restricted regimes. - The good: The theoretical treatment is unusually careful: coupled NP-hardness is proved (reduction from parallel-machine weighted completion time), exact polynomial regimes are identified, and 230 exhaustive small-instance comparisons show joint optimization beats a staged baseline in 195 cases, with mean regret up to 32.7% under chain delegation. - The missing: All quantitative risk results rest on synthetic compromise probabilities and weights applied to one public microservice benchmark (Train-Ticket, 32 services), so the headline 'up to 36% lower expected impact' is a property of invented scenario inputs, not observed deployments. - Read it or not: Worth a careful read for security architects and researchers working on IAM/zero-trust formalization or PQC migration planning; specialists in graph algorithms will find the reductions routine and can skim to Section 8's shared-issuer exactness conditions.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations operating many interacting services must decide where to place independently rooted credential issuers (trust boundaries) and how to structure credential delegation within each domain. More domains contain the damage from a compromised root but force more public-key crossings, and the PQC transition (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) inflates handshake bytes and crossing latency on constrained or lossy paths — measured crossing costs in this paper span 0.0338 to 15.5815 ms per call across five network profiles. Prior work either optimizes access structures with fixed credential authority (authentication-graph partitioning, IAM synthesis, microsegmentation) or optimizes key hierarchies with different objectives and no steady-state crossing cost; none jointly optimizes the partition, the derivation forest, and measured boundary cost. The authors are from a bank's lab (OP Pohjola, Finland), and the motivation is PQC-migration-era architecture planning. Key Idea: Express blast radius as a linear, additive score — for each service, its weight times the sum of compromise probabilities along its root-to-leaf path in a single-parent derivation arborescence — which (a) makes the derivation side solvable exactly in chain/star/depth-two regimes and (b) lets the domain-assignment side inherit cut and labeling machinery, with a latency constraint coupling the two layers. A companion structural result (the antichain condition) identifies exactly when shared-issuer risk can be scored additively rather than by explicit reachability tracing. Methodology: The model couples a directed service-interaction graph G with per-edge rates r, latency sensitivities ℓ, and calibrated crossing costs c_pqc to per-domain derivation arborescences H_i rooted at virtual issuers ρ_i, subject to partition, policy, fanout (∆), and depth (h) constraints. The objective minimizes the linear score BR_node subject to Lat(D) ≤ B (Eq. 10), with a normalized scalarization (Eq. 12) for candidate generation and ε-constraint refinement to recover unsupported Pareto points. On the theory side: chain optimization reduces to ratio ordering (exact, O(n log n)); depth-two reduces to a capacitated assignment with a greedy fill rule; k=2 direct issuance reduces to minimum s–t cut over O(n²) anchor pairs with a Gallo–Grigoriadis–Tarjan parametric sweep; bounded-treewidth graphs admit exact DP in O(n·k^(τ+1)); the coupled chain case is strongly NP-hard via reduction from Pk‖ΣwⱼCⱼ. Shared-issuer acceptance (M, J) is scored exactly by reachability when accepted targets form an antichain (Prop. 8.1), otherwise additively as an upper bound. The evaluation measures three TLS profiles (C0 classical, K1 hybrid KEM, A1 hybrid KEM+ML-DSA) over 12,000 observations across five shaped network paths, then replays a Train-Ticket trace-derived graph (32 services, 72 edges from 1,157 Jaeger traces) with synthetic risk scenarios, (∆,h)=(3,3), one fixed breadth-first derivation family, and k ∈ {1,…,6}. Critical design decisions: optimizing the conservative linear score instead of an assumed dependence model (validated by surrogate-regret checks, max 1.22% regret); a 5% budget reserve on block-maximum calibration (passes all 20 held-out path-budget checks); and zero root priors in replay, which the authors note isolates delegated-principal risk. Key Results: Joint optimization outperforms the staged (boundary-first) baseline in 195 of 230 exhaustive n=9, k=3 comparisons — 117/120 chain cases (mean regret 29.4–32.7%, max 66.4%) and 156/220 depth-two cases (mean regret 2.5–2.7%, max 14.7%), where the tie rule deliberately favors the baseline. In the trace replay on the unshaped path N0, risk-aware search achieves mean exact expected-impact ratios of 0.693 and 0.638 at budgets 0.10/0.20 ms versus 0.884 for latency-first search (up to 36% lower than the single-domain baseline). Higher crossing costs reduce the selected domain count: k=6 (the search cap, i.e., right-censored) on N0/N1 down to k=2 on the constrained-lossy N4 path. Budget compliance transfers to held-out measurement blocks in 20/20 checks with the 5% reserve; unreserved point estimates fail on some paths (e.g., 7/10). The additive issuer score ranks the best explicitly evaluated candidate in 11 of 12 comparisons (max miss 5.86%), and a reachability-aware shortlist of three recovers the best candidate in all 12. Scaling tests on synthetic clustered graphs up to n=1,000 show frontier-search runtime growing 8.7× for 20× more services (1.95→17.03 s). The N2 comparison between risk-aware search and traffic clustering remains unresolved (overlapping ranges over five runs) — an honest negative result. Baselines are the authors' own staged and latency-first variants; there is no external system to compare against, which is arguably appropriate for a new formulation. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD, with supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDINGS. The genuinely novel element is the joint decision problem itself — independent-root partition plus operational derivation forest plus steady-state crossing cost under a latency budget — together with the antichain condition for exact additive issuer scoring. The algorithmic machinery (min-cut, Potts/metric labeling, parametric flow, scheduling reduction, ratio ordering) is standard, competently repurposed; the paper is explicit that solver guarantees are inherited rather than invented. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a formulation paper. Ablations isolate each factor: exhaustive small-instance references (Table 2, 230 comparisons), budget-repair contribution (miss rate 51.7%→3.3%→0% with traffic starts, Table S1), solver-transfer diagnostics, surrogate-regret CIs (Table S2), and a solver-quality table showing local search hits only 43% exact assignments with up to 84.3% gap — an unusually candid self-report. Fixed seeds, pinned NumPy dependencies, SHA-256 manifests, and held-out validation blocks support reproducibility. However: no code or data release (only 'upon reasonable request, subject to organizational approval'), no significance tests beyond normal-approximation CIs in one table, and five-run comparisons with ranges rather than statistical inference. Methodological concerns: (p, w) inputs are constructed synthetic scenarios, not empirical estimates; the derivation family in replay is fixed and heuristic, so global optimality is unverified (the authors say so); and the whole evaluation runs on one benchmark workload. This is a preprint (arXiv 2609.04566v2), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: (EMPIRICAL profile, with substantial theoretical content):* Practical: Yes — the pipeline runs on commodity hardware (ARM64 host, OpenSSL 3.6.3, Python/NumPy) and consumes telemetry (Jaeger/OpenTelemetry) and control-plane metadata that most organizations already have. Efficient: Candidate generation on Train-Ticket takes 0.09× exact-DP time via α-expansion; frontier search stays in tens of seconds up to n=1,000, though exact bounded-treewidth DP explodes under scoped refinement (runtime ratios up to 3,992×). Effective: The evidence shows the method changes designs and beats staged selection on proxy and exact scores under synthetic risk inputs; whether it reduces real-world compromise impact is untested, as the authors concede. Scalable:* Tested to n=1,000 synthetic services and k=6 (right-censored); behavior on production graphs with tens of thousands of services, dense eligibility structures, or DAG derivations is claimed nowhere and unknown. Deliverable form: paper only — no library, CLI, or dataset is released; the practitioner checklist (Supp. S5.3) is the reusable artifact, plus a proof technique for when additive issuer scoring is exact. Strengths: - The joint formulation is a real gap-filler: prior segmentation, IAM-synthesis, and logical-key-hierarchy lines each freeze one of the two decision layers, and the paper delineates this difference precisely (Sec. 13). - Honest boundary-drawing between proved model-specific results and guarantees inherited from cited algorithms (Table 1), plus a hardness proof that cleanly maps chain-derivation blast radius to weighted completion time — this mapping itself (BR_node = ΣwⱼCⱼ/T under chains) is a neat observation. - The shared-issuer analysis addresses a deployment-relevant failure mode (JWT/OIDC issuers silently bypassing domain boundaries) with a checkable structural condition rather than blanket conservatism. - Measurement discipline: crossing costs are deployment-calibrated inputs, not algorithm benchmarks; held-out budget validation with a reserve rule is a sensible operational control, and the paper refuses to overclaim from finite held-out success. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Extensive and direct (Sec. 12) — propagation covers only credential authority (no verifier compromise, supply chain, or lateral movement); compromise probabilities are exogenous marginals, though segmentation may alter real exposure; single-parent derivation excludes multi-parent/threshold DAG issuance; the linearized latency model omits correlated loss, retries, queueing, and tail latency; replay uses one fixed derivation family and finite search budgets so global optimality is unverified; two public workloads plus synthetic families do not establish production generality; and k=6 is a search cap, not an optimum. The N2 ordering failure and the additive-score misranking risk are also conceded. This level of self-critique is a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The entire quantitative case rests on synthetic p(x) and w(v) (e.g., Train-Ticket weights from a log formula and compromise priors from service-name hashing for 'admin'/'payment' terms); no sensitivity analysis over the functional form of these scenario generators is shown, so the 36% headline could be an artifact of the chosen generator. - Only one real workload (Train-Ticket) drives the operational comparison; a second trace-derived graph would materially strengthen external validity. - The evaluation fixes a deterministic breadth-first derivation family, so the reported joint-vs-staged regret conflates assignment effects with a possibly suboptimal inner tree; the exhaustive chain/depth-two checks (n=9) partially cover this, but only at toy scale. - No comparison against any deployed segmentation or workload-identity tooling (e.g., SPIRE topology recommendations), so practitioner positioning against incumbent practice is unmeasured. - Domain-root compromise probabilities are zeroed in replay with a partition-invariance argument for homogeneous roots, but heterogeneous root risk — arguably the main reason to segment — is exercised only in the small synthetic Q1 study, not in the trace replay. - Code unavailability ('upon request, subject to organizational approval') limits independent verification of the 12,000-observation measurement pipeline. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous treatment I have seen of the trust-boundary/delegation co-design problem, and its theory, honest evaluation, and deployment checklist make it genuinely useful for security architects planning PQC-era segmentation — but practitioners should treat its numbers as scenario-conditional planning illustrations, not evidence of real-world impact, and wait for a tooling release or independent replication before betting an architecture on it.

Bringing Foundational Verification to Real-World Rust Code

A SHINNAR · iris-project.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper extends the RefinedRust deductive verifier with support for Rust traits, closures, iterators, and recursive types, so that foundational, machine-checked Rocq/Iris proofs can be produced for idiomatic Rust code that mixes safe and unsafe constructs. - Why it's important: Real safety-critical systems code pervasively uses iterators, closures, and unsafe raw-pointer manipulation, but until now no verifier combined foundational (tool-independent, machine-checked) guarantees with support for all of these features together. - How it does it: The core move is a separation-logic generalization of Prusti/Creusot-style iterator specifications (letting an iterator invariant carry Iris ownership consumed by unsafe closures), plus a redesigned caller-callee contract with trait-linking assumptions that reconciles polymorphic verification with Rust's monomorphization. - The good: The approach is validated on ~600 lines of real, security-critical code from IBM's ACE security monitor (page tokens and a tree-based page allocator), where it found two previously undetected bugs disclosed to the ACE authors. - The missing: Verification is 10-100× slower than SMT-based non-foundational tools (minutes vs. seconds), requires substantial manual Rocq proof effort (e.g., 191 proof lines for a 16-LOC function), and the evaluation covers only ~600 LOC of a single system. - Read it or not: Worth reading for PL verification researchers and anyone building or choosing Rust verifiers for high-assurance systems; practitioners wanting fast, automated verification of pure safe Rust can skip it and use Creusot.
Why this rank

Practical Impact (72) is the largest weighted contributor — the extended RefinedRust, case studies, and ACE verification are publicly released, and the tool verified ~600 LOC of real security-critical IBM code, finding two disclosed bugs. Novelty (75) reflects the ownership-carrying iterator invariant and the trait-linking caller-callee contract — a genuinely new method, though conceptually derived from Prusti/Creusot's iterator specifications — and Non-Obviousness (70) benefits from the clean solution to polymorphic verification of a monomorphizing language. Rigor (72) is helped by the released artifact and per-function cost accounting, but reduced by the partially self-evaluated case study (author overlap with ACE, unflagged) and a Creusot comparison that omits Creusot's inference strengths. Completeness (70) is a positive — limitations are confronted directly — while Resilience (65) is pulled down by the 600-LOC evaluation ceiling, the ~8-function sample behind the 'no proof overhead from higher-order features' claim, and the relative weakness of foundational guarantees for functional correctness of open modules.
