Miles v0.1: Production-Level Post-Training (44 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents Miles v0.1, an open-source full-stack system for frontier-scale LLM post-training that integrates SGLang-based rollout, a dual-backend trainer (Megatron-LM or PyTorch FSDP), three weight-synchronization transports, and token-exact trajectory handling into one asynchronous RL loop. - Why it's important: Frontier post-training (multi-turn agentic RL over trillion-parameter MoE models) requires reconciling latency-sensitive generation with throughput-oriented training while keeping the trainer's view of trajectories numerically faithful; mismatches silently corrupt gradients, and no single open system previously addressed fidelity, efficiency, and scale together. - How it does it: The core move is making rollout fidelity a first-class system contract: a session server owns tokenization so the trainer sees exactly the tokens sampled (TITO), recorded expert-routing assignments are replayed verbatim during training (R3), and rollout/training share a single bit-exact quantization path across supported precisions. - The good: The headline demonstration is credible and concrete — fully asynchronous agentic RL on GLM-5.2 (744B-A40B) across 64 GB300 GPUs with a median step time of 263 seconds and 96% prefix-cache hit rate, plus an 86.4% weight-transfer speedup over NCCL broadcast for Kimi K2 1T-A32B (53.28s → 7.23s via P2P RDMA). - The missing: There are no head-to-head comparisons against competing post-training systems (e.g., verl, AReaL, or slime itself) at matched scale, the reward improvement (0.438 → 0.556 over one 100-step run) is explicitly not separated from run-to-run variance, and the flagship run leaves R3 off. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or selecting an RL post-training infrastructure — it is the most candid systems report in its class — but skip it if you want algorithmic novelty or controlled benchmark comparisons, since its contribution is engineering synthesis rather than new learning methods.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Novelty (58) and Rigor (62) pull the composite down: this is an engineering synthesis of existing techniques with no head-to-head comparison against any competing post-training system, the flagship RL run is a single 100-step run the authors themselves refuse to interpret as improvement, and key low-precision evidence is outsourced to blog posts. Completeness (72) is a genuine bright spot — the claim-versus-measurement discipline and explicit 'not verified' labels are exemplary candor — and Impact (82) is high under the Systems weighting given the substantial open-source artifact demonstrated at 744B scale on 64 GPUs. Non-Obviousness (65) rests on the fidelity-by-construction architectural thesis, which is coherent but partially inherited from prior work. Weighted composite: 0.15*58 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*65 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*68 + 0.30*82 = 70.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations running RL post-training at frontier scale face three coupled problems. First, agentic rollouts (multi-turn, tool-using, environment-interacting episodes over trillion-parameter MoE models) make a lockstep generate-then-train schedule waste GPUs on stragglers. Second, the numerical gap between inference engines and trainers — different kernels, precisions, batching, and, for MoE, divergent expert routing — silently invalidates the RL objective: the trainer updates against log-probabilities for trajectories the policy effectively never produced, which Ma et al. report can end in catastrophic training collapse. Third, weight synchronization itself becomes a bottleneck (a full NCCL broadcast of Kimi K2 1T-A32B takes nearly a minute per step). The audience is research labs and enterprises that need frontier-scale RL without proprietary internal infrastructure. The gap closed is the absence of an open, verifiable, full-stack system where accuracy (fidelity), efficiency, reliability, and scalability are simultaneously engineered rather than traded off. Key Idea: The single organizing insight is that train–rollout mismatch in RL should be eliminated by construction at the system level, not merely corrected in the loss: a server layer that owns tokenization and checkpoints exact token IDs per turn (TITO), replay of recorded MoE expert-routing assignments instead of recomputation (R3), and a bit-exact shared quantization contract spanning checkpoint conversion, trainer forward pass, weight export, and rollout — with importance-ratio corrections (truncated importance sampling, clip-or-pop) reserved for whatever numerical remainder persists. Methodology: Miles implements a three-stage RL loop — rollout (SGLang engines behind a router with session-affinity routing), training (Megatron-LM or FSDP backend computing GRPO/GSPO/REINFORCE++/PPO losses), and weight update — which need not run in lockstep: a fully asynchronous mode runs generation and training on disjoint GPU pools, coupled by a bounded data buffer that filters groups on arrival (generation timeout, zero-advantage) and at collection (staleness, defined pessimistically as current trainer weight version minus the oldest version under which any token in the group was generated), with per-step observability metrics. Environment integration uses three nested plug-in layers (agent function, generate function, rollout function) so frameworks from Harbor to Prime Intellect Verifiers can attach at whatever layer they own; sandbox backends (Daytona, E2B, Modal, AgentENV) are orthogonal. Low-precision support covers FP8 blockwise (production), MXFP8 and NVFP4 (Beta), with the invariant that both rollout and training run identical quantization logic; NVFP4 additionally offers dequantized backward and four-over-six block scaling applied identically in both Transformer Engine and FlashInfer kernels. Memory mechanisms include allocator-level actor eviction (to host RAM or node-local disk) and per-bucket streaming of FP32 master weights plus Adam moments (12 bytes/param) to disk, optionally with BF16 moments. Weight sync offers three transports over one bucketed preparation pipeline (512 MB default): NCCL broadcast, peer-to-peer RDMA writes using a CPU-resident SGLang replica to re-shard into target layouts, and disk-delta updates (XOR or idempotent overwrite encodings against a shared base checkpoint, checksummed per-tensor). Critical design decisions: (1) session affinity + least-loaded placement for cache reuse — well-justified by the 96% measured hit rate; (2) failing loudly on unkeyed requests rather than silently falling back to load-based routing — well-justified for debuggability; (3) making R3 a per-recipe choice rather than default — reasonable but leaves the flagship run unexercised by this mechanism. The paper also extends the same architecture to LoRA RL (adapter as the unit of sync, multi-LoRA against one base), on-policy distillation (per-token reverse-KL estimate folded into advantages, with a top-K variant), true-on-policy alignment (bitwise-identical log-probabilities via FlashAttention-3, batch-invariant GEMMs, deterministic modes), and diffusion models (Miles-Diffusion with Flow-GRPO/DiffusionNFT recipes and explicit evidence-level labels). Key Results: The evidence is mostly single-configuration system measurements, with no baselines from competing systems. Headline numbers: GLM-5.2 744B-A40B agentic RL (terminal-bench-2 tasks, OpenEnv/Daytona sandboxes, 65,536-token sessions) on 64 GB300 GPUs — median step 263 seconds over the first 30 measured steps, prefix-cache hit rate 96%, train–inference KL divergence mean 0.0369 over 100 steps, raw reward 9-step moving average rising 0.438 → 0.556, which the authors themselves decline to call a measured improvement given a single run. Weight transfer: P2P vs. NCCL broadcast on H100 clusters — Kimi K2 1T-A32B at 32 nodes/side: 53.28s → 7.23s (−86.4%); GLM-5 744B at 16 nodes/side: 58.30s → 8.48s (−85.5%); Qwen3-30B-A3B at 2 nodes/side: 2.67s → 2.16s (−19.1%); P2P is up to 70% slower than broadcast on single nodes. Optimizer streaming on Qwen3-30B-A3B cuts actor offload 24s → 5.2s and reload 8.9s → 1.3s. On-policy distillation (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, teacher = same model after 5 RL steps): response length 14,070 → 6,132 tokens (−56%) with accuracy 84.0% → 85.2%, inside the ~1.6-point standard error — the authors honestly frame this as length reduction with no reliable accuracy change. Miles-Diffusion on LTX-2.3: rollout time 157.4 → 87.6s per step, total step 321.9 → 252.1s from streaming deserialization/reward. True-on-policy alignment achieves exactly zero log-probability difference for dense Qwen3 0.6B/4B. Low-precision recipes (MXFP8, NVFP4) report reward curves tracking BF16 baselines, but no tables of numbers are given in this paper (deferred to separate blog reports). Baseline strength is the report's weakest dimension: the comparison set is internal (BF16 vs. quantized, broadcast vs. P2P), not competitive. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely novel elements are the three-layer environment connector taxonomy with per-layer responsibility assignment, the end-to-end bit-exact quantization contract enforced across four pipeline stages, the CPU-resident replica trick for P2P RDMA weight re-sharding, and the per-recipe evidence-level scheme (fully gated / proxy gated / verified / not verified). The rest is competent integration of existing published techniques — TITO extends the authors' prior LMSYS blog work, R3 is taken from Ma et al. (2025), the RL loop builds on slime, and the advantage estimators, LoRA, and on-policy distillation are all established methods re-implemented in a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present in places (group vs. sample granularity replacement, three transport comparisons across three fleet widths, three evaluation modes, streaming vs. non-streaming offload timings) but absent where they matter most: no comparison against any external post-training system, no seed replication, no error bars or significance tests anywhere, and the flagship reward trend is a single 100-step run the authors explicitly refuse to interpret as improvement — a candor positive, but also an admission the case study is a demonstration, not an evaluation. Code is open source at https://github.com/radixark/miles with launch scripts for the reference run, CI-enforced metric gating against historical values, and bit-exact end-to-end tests for deterministic recipes. Methodological concerns: several quantitative claims (FP8/MXFP8/NVFP4 reward tracking, INT4 QAT) are deferred to self-published blog reports rather than evidenced in the paper; low-precision validation covers only a handful of models per format (Table 5); the true-on-policy zero-difference guarantee covers two small dense models only. The system is developed and evaluated on its own workloads, so Goodhart risk is low but generalization evidence is thin. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, open-source tool evaluated by operation rather than by benchmark comparison). Practical: Yes — runs on NVIDIA A100 through GB300 and natively on AMD MI300X–MI355X, installable from the public repo with validated launchers. Efficient: Strong measured wins where it counts — 86% weight-transfer reduction at wide fleets, FP8 rollout, disk-streamed optimizer state enabling 744B training on 32 GPUs — though some features cost throughput (true-on-policy alignment, P2P on single nodes, longer checkpoint saves with streaming). Effective: It demonstrably runs the stated workload (frontier agentic RL end to end); whether it improves model quality better than alternatives is unevaluated. Scalable: Tested at 64 GPUs end-to-end and at 1T-parameter weight transfer on 64 nodes, but the 10×–100× extrapolation (e.g., asynchronous buffer behavior, staleness discard rates, P2P scaling at hundreds of nodes) is argued from bandwidth arithmetic, not measured. The work delivers a substantial software artifact (library, launchers, recipes, CI infrastructure), not just a paper; some advertised paths (operation-driven LoRA backend, Tinker-compatible frontend, MiniMax H3 diffusion recipe) remain open pull requests rather than released features. Strengths: - Fidelity treated as a systems contract, not a loss correction: the TITO session server, R3 routing replay, and the four-stage bit-exact quantization contract together attack every identified source of train–rollout divergence (tokenization, expert routing, kernel numerics) at a different layer — a genuinely coherent architectural thesis. - Unusual, verifiable honesty: the report distinguishes claims from measurements throughout (the OPD accuracy delta declared within noise, the GLM-5.2 reward rise declared an observation, per-recipe evidence levels, explicit 'not verified' labels), which materially raises the epistemic value of the artifact. - The P2P weight-transfer design is a concrete, well-motivated contribution: transfer plans bounding RDMA sessions, a CPU-resident SGLang replica that reuses the engine's own sharding logic instead of reimplementing it, and a single registered pinned buffer keeping host memory constant as fleets grow — validated bit-exactly from 1 to 8 nodes. - A dual-backend trainer (Megatron for model parallelism, FSDP for direct Hugging Face loading) behind one interface, plus a driver that 'reads like pseudocode' with import-path extensibility, lowers the cost of research iteration — relevant to real users, not just readers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive: MXFP8 and NVFP4 are Beta and tested on few models; the GLM-5.2 case study is a single run on a single task distribution and cannot separate reward rise from run-to-run variation; P2P transfer covers only architectures with a unified Megatron–SGLang name mapping and is slower than broadcast on single nodes; disk-delta is Megatron-only and incompatible with colocation, LoRA, and prefill–decode disaggregation; the session server lacks vision/screenshot support, excluding VLMs; true-on-policy alignment covers only dense Qwen3 0.6B/4B and guarantees only per-token log-probability agreement, not full distribution agreement, and does not address stale-weight off-policyness; several day-0 recipes (Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 LoRA) live in open PRs; LoRA runs on Megatron only; some connectors and sandbox integrations are experimental. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No competitive baseline: the central implicit claim — that this design beats or matches alternative post-training stacks (verl, AReaL, OpenRLHF, slime itself) on utilization or stability — is never tested, so a reader cannot judge whether the 263s median step or the buffer metrics are good. - The flagship run disables R3, the paper's own headline fidelity mechanism for MoE models, so the system's most distinctive components are never exercised together in the one end-to-end study; the KL divergence of 0.0369 is reported without showing what TITO/R3 remove relative to a naive pipeline. - All low-precision evidence (FP8, MXFP8, NVFP4, INT4 QAT) is outsourced to self-published blog posts; the paper contains no quantitative reward-curve or log-prob-fidelity tables for these recipes, which are central to its Blackwell-native pitch. - Staleness-bounded asynchronous RL is claimed to preserve training validity, but no experiment varies the staleness limit or compares synchronous vs. fully asynchronous modes on final reward — the correctness of the asynchronous schedule is asserted through mechanism description and stability metrics, not demonstrated. - The 744B case study's memory configuration (optimizer streaming, single DP replica) is presented as necessity-driven, but no ablation of the parallel-layout choices (e.g., TP degree, PP stage boundaries) is offered, so the configuration's efficiency is unverified beyond 'it fits and runs.' Bottom Line: For practitioners building or choosing large-scale RL post-training infrastructure this is essential, unusually honest reading — the fidelity-by-construction architecture and measured weight-transfer/memory numbers stand on their own — but as a research contribution it should be scored as a strong engineering system paper, not a method advance, since it reports no comparisons against competing systems and no controlled evidence that its fidelity mechanisms improve learning outcomes.

You Know What I Mean: A Benchmark for Agentic Conversational Reference Grounding

K Fuchs, U Katz, Y Goldberg · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces REPOREF, a benchmark of 400 real developer-chat segments in which an LLM agent must resolve an indirect conversational reference to the unique GitHub issue, pull request, or commit the speaker intended, using 22 read-only GitHub API tools. - Why it's important: Collaborative workspaces are full of underspecified references ("the fix discussed yesterday"), and AI assistants deployed in software-engineering environments currently cannot reliably resolve them, blocking practical agent use in team communication contexts. - How it does it: The core construction trick is bootstrapping verifiable ground truth from Gitter messages that originally contained direct GitHub links, then LLM-rewriting the link into a natural indirect reference and filtering out examples where an LLM judge can confuse the target with retrieved look-alike candidates. - The good: The strongest evidence is the failure decomposition — when strong agents surface the gold artifact they select it correctly 87–91% of the time, and 70–92% of their failures occur before surfacing, cleanly localizing the bottleneck to exploration/search rather than disambiguation. - The missing: There is no non-agentic baseline (e.g., BM25 or dense retrieval over a locally indexed repository) to quantify how much of the task is genuinely beyond static retrieval, and all construction filters (segmentation, faithfulness, ambiguity) are LLM-assisted with audits on only 50–100 examples. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building tool-use or software-engineering agents who need a realistic multi-step search benchmark and diagnostic buckets; skippable for those seeking new methods, since the paper evaluates existing agents rather than proposing one.

Problem & Motivation: Human collaborators routinely refer to shared digital resources indirectly ("can you update the doc from yesterday?"), and human teammates resolve these references by combining conversational context with workspace knowledge. AI agents operating in collaborative workspaces lack this capability: existing conversational-retrieval work assumes an explicit information-seeking query, and existing software-agent benchmarks (SWE-bench, SWE-agent, OpenHands) start after the artifact is identified. The gap is a task where the agent must first infer which external artifact is meant from distributed conversational cues — lexical, temporal, author-based, and negation-based — before it can even begin to search, with cues that often have no lexical overlap with the target's metadata. Key Idea: The key idea is twofold. Conceptually, formalizing Conversational Reference Grounding (CoRG) as tool-mediated agentic search: the referent set is accessible only through APIs, cannot be indexed locally, and the agent must convert distributed conversational evidence into a query strategy, candidate discovery, inspection, and verification. Methodologically, the benchmark-construction trick is to mine conversations that explicitly linked GitHub artifacts (giving externally verifiable ground truth), then minimally rewrite the anchor message with an LLM to remove the identifier while preserving its pragmatic role — "I opened https://github.com/.../issues/888 for this" becomes "I opened a ticket for this" — and discard cases where strong retrieved alternatives match the conversation equally well. Methodology: The construction pipeline has five stages: (1) extract ground truth from Gitter conversations (GitterCom, 2020; Sahar et al., 2021) via regex-detected GitHub links; (2) LLM-assisted reference-centered conversation segmentation with topic-based backward/forward boundaries, validated at 96.3% agreement with human boundary judgments on 50 samples (3.8k → 2.6k segments); (3) LLM natural reference masking of the anchor message only, with a manual audit of 100 examples finding no intent changes, plus an ablation showing type-only placeholders (75%) vs. natural masks (77%) are statistically indistinguishable (McNemar, p=0.83); (4) LLM-assisted faithfulness filtering (κ=0.77 with humans) and pairwise-judge ambiguity filtering against an offline candidate pool of same-repository look-alikes (2.6k → 2.0k); (5) stratified selection of 400 instances across seven diagnostic capability buckets (cross-speaker evidence, surface mismatch, author-crowded disambiguation, competitive alternatives, no-author shortcut, sparse evidence, commit-level grounding). Evaluation uses a ReAct loop (Yao et al., 2023) at tool budget B=10 over 22 read-only GitHub tools plus submit_answer, scored by exact URL match (recall@1); a Claude Code Opus 4.7 harness variant accesses the same API via a read-only MCP server. Nine models are evaluated, plus a budget sweep (B ∈ {1,3,6,10,16,20,40,60,80}) on a 280-example subset. The pipeline is competent engineering; the decision to mask rather than collect naturally indirect references is the largest methodological bet, and the authors defend it only partially (see Gaps). Key Results: The best ReAct agent, Gemini-3-Flash, reaches 67.0% (±2.35) exact-match success; Claude Code Opus 4.7 reaches 63.25% (±2.41); DeepSeek-V4-Pro 60.25%; remaining strong models 49.0–54.0%; lightweight models collapse (Llama-3.3-70B 1.5%, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite 4.0%, the latter issuing zero tool calls on 65.5% of examples). Raising the budget for Gemini-3-Flash from B=1 to B=16 improves success from 23.21% to 73.93% on the 280-example sweep, with most gains by B=6 (63.93%). 18.5% of instances are solved by no model; manual inspection of 50 of these confirmed the gold targets remain recoverable, ruling out construction errors. Accuracy does not track price (GLM-5.1 at $0.199/example and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at $0.317 rank mid-low while Gemini-3-Flash costs $0.065). Gemini-3-Flash wins through persistent exploration (75.0% gold discovery by step 10) but is the least efficient when correct (6.27 average excess tool calls), whereas Grok-4.1 uses only 0.38 excess calls and Claude Code Opus only 0.25. Commit-level grounding is the hardest bucket for most models (8.5–46.8% across models), and 42% of instances contain distractor GitHub URLs requiring disambiguation. Baselines are current frontier models (2025–2026 vintage: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7, GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Grok-4.1), evaluated at standard benchmark scale (400–2,000 examples, 92 repositories). Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (CoRG as tool-mediated grounding of indirect conversational references) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (REPOREF, with its mask-then-verify construction pipeline and diagnostic buckets). The genuinely novel elements are the problem framing at the intersection of conversational grounding and tool-use evaluation, and the link-mining-then-masking construction recipe; the evaluation machinery (ReAct agents, exact-match scoring, budget sweeps) is a standard application of existing tool-use methodology to the new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: natural masking vs. type-only placeholders (no significant difference, p=0.83), segmenter boundary validation (96.3% on 50 human-labeled examples), and filter agreement (κ=0.77 on the faithfulness judge). Success rates are reported with binomial-style error bars (±2.35–2.50 at n=400). Code, prompts, and an extended ~2,000-instance set are released at https://github.com/karenShaked/RepoRef-Benchmark, under CC BY-NC-SA. Methodological concerns: (1) all three quality filters are LLM-assisted, with human audits on only 50–100 samples each, so systematic filter biases cannot be ruled out; (2) the pairwise ambiguity judge is itself an LLM, so "unambiguous" means LLM-judgeable-unambiguous; (3) evaluation is confined to the authors' own benchmark with no external task cross-validation; (4) the paper does not report whether extended-set results match the 400-example results; (5) no fine-grained inter-annotator statistics for the 50-case unsolvable-instance audit. No significance tests beyond the McNemar masking ablation are reported. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a constructed benchmark plus agent experiments actually run). Practical: Runs on standard API access — the environment is 22 read-only GitHub endpoints plus a Gitter chat context, reproducible by anyone with API keys. Efficient: Per-example cost ranges from $0.017 (Gemini-2.5-Lite) to $0.383 (Claude Code Opus 4.7) with 190–470k tokens per run, so full-benchmark evaluation is cheap by agent standards, though Gemini-3-Flash's 6.27 excess tool calls on correct runs is wasteful. Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark measures a real capability gap (best agent at 67.0%, 18.5% unsolved by any model), but whether solving REPOREF transfers to grounding in other workspaces (Slack, Jira, Notion) is untested — the authors scope this explicitly. Scalable: The extended ~2,000-instance set exists, but no results on it are reported, and GitHub API rate limits under larger-scale agent sweeps are not discussed. Deliverable: a software artifact (benchmark dataset, construction prompts, and evaluation code released publicly), not a trained model or reusable technique. Strengths: (1) The construction recipe — verifiable ground truth from explicit links, then targeted masking — solves the otherwise fatal problem of labeling indirect references at scale, and the masking ablation against placeholders is the right control. (2) The discovery-vs-selection failure decomposition is a genuinely informative analysis: it shows strong agents fail in search, not disambiguation, which redirects future work toward recall-oriented exploration rather than better reranking. (3) The seven diagnostic buckets with per-bucket model results (e.g., commit-level grounding collapsing to 8.5–21.3% for most models) convert a single aggregate score into actionable failure taxonomy. (4) The efficiency analysis (Average Excessive Tool Calls) surfaces a real accuracy-vs-exploration trade-off between Gemini-3-Flash and Claude Code Opus 4.7 that plain accuracy tables would hide. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront the central construction concern — conversations that originally contained links may differ systematically from naturally indirect references — and argue the task targets exactly the sparse-cue regime; this is honest but does not fully close the distribution-shift question. They also acknowledge the scope restriction to open-source GitHub artifacts (issues, PRs, commits), which may not generalize to other workspace reference patterns, and that results depend on the fixed read-only tool set, tool budget, and agent configurations. The directness of these acknowledgments is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No static-retrieval baseline: the paper builds offline candidate pools for ambiguity filtering but never evaluates BM25/dense retrieval over the same repository indexes, so the reader cannot tell how much of the 33% failure rate is agentic-search failure versus irreducible lexical mismatch — a cheap, obvious missing comparison. (2) The ambiguity filter uses an LLM judge without giving it the original URL; if that judge shares biases with the evaluated models (same family of frontier models), instances that a different disambiguation strategy would find easy may have been filtered out, biasing the benchmark toward one notion of ambiguity. (3) Potential leakage: 42% of conversations contain other GitHub URLs, and LLM rewriting may leave stylistic traces of masking that models could learn to detect across the 400 examples, especially since masking was applied by one rewrite model. (4) Only one agent harness beyond vanilla ReAct is tested; sensitivity to prompt, scaffolding, and tool-schema design is unexamined despite the authors' own claim that strategy, not model quality, drives success. (5) Single-annotator-scale human audits (50–100 items) for all validation claims; no reported inter-annotator agreement on the segmenter or audit tasks themselves. Bottom Line: Researchers building tool-using software agents should read this: REPOREF isolates a real, previously unbenchmarked capability with a clever construction recipe and a failure analysis that actually points somewhere (exploration recall, not reranking), even though the missing retrieval baseline and LLM-heavy construction leave its absolute difficulty numbers open to revision.

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ENOKI, a hallucination-detection framework that extracts text-anchored OpenIE relational triples from an LLM answer, verifies each triple against evidence with an NLI-style verifier, and projects unsupported triples back to exact answer spans — yielding claim-level verification and span-level localization from one shared representation, plus a dual-granularity dataset (ENOKIQA). - Why it's important: High-stakes LLM deployments need actionable localization of unsupported content, but unifying interpretable claim-level checking with span-level detection previously required costly multi-stage LLM pipelines with a separate claim-to-span alignment step that propagates errors. - How it does it: The core trick is text anchoring — hallucination-relevant triple arguments are constrained to stay aligned with answer spans, and incremental (coarse-to-specific) fact groups let the verifier assign unsupportedness to the newly added "delta" span, eliminating a separate alignment module. - The good: The strongest evidence is the span/entity-level sweep: ENOKI-LLM reaches 55.09 AUPRC on HalluEntity (vs. 36.63 for zero-shot GPT-5.2) and 52.07 Span Coverage F1 on MuSHROOM (vs. 44.12 for the best OpenIE baseline), while ENOKI-ENCODER/RULE retain most gains at 0.13s/0.11s per sentence — roughly two orders of magnitude faster than multi-stage LLM pipelines like Claimify (11.95s). - The missing: The headline span metric, Span Coverage F1, is defined by the authors and rewards fine-grained predictions that ENOKI structurally produces; standard boundary-sensitive metrics (exact span F1, IoU) are argued against but not reported, so cross-metric comparability is unverified. - Read it or not: Read it if you build factuality-verification or RAG-guardrail systems and need both interpretable claims and span localization under a latency budget; skip it if you only need coarse response-level factuality scoring, where decomposition-free NLI baselines remain competitive.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying LLMs in retrieval-grounded, high-stakes settings need more than a binary factuality score: they need to know which text fragments are unsupported. The field splits into claim-level methods (FActScore, SAFE, VeriScore, RefChecker) that decompose answers into verifiable units, and span-level methods (LettuceDetect, haldetect, Mu-SHROOM/RAGTruth-style detectors) that localize unsupported text. Bridging them requires a decompose-verify-align pipeline where the claim-to-span alignment step is error-prone and adds LLM calls, and where decomposition errors (omitted arguments, dropped modifiers) silently change what the verifier judges. There is also a data gap: existing fine-grained benchmarks are small (MuSHROOM en: 154 examples; HalluEntity: 157), short-answer, and single-granularity. Key Idea: Use text-anchored OpenIE triples as the single intermediate representation for hallucination detection: because hallucination-relevant arguments are constrained to remain spans of the original answer, verifying each (subject, predicate, object) triple against evidence and then marking the unsupported object (or its incremental delta within a nested fact group) directly yields both claim-level labels and span-level localization — no alignment module needed. The incremental construction (each refinement adds a small piece of information to a self-contained fact) is what enables precise delta-span projection, e.g., preserving a supported year while flagging only the unsupported birthplace. Methodology: The pipeline has two stages. (1) Fact extraction: responses are segmented with spaCy, and an OpenIE backend emits text-anchored (subject, predicate, object) triples per sentence, in nested "incremental" groups. Three backends share one interface: ENOKI-LLM (GPT-OSS-120B with the CycleOIE prompt extended with three incremental-decomposition guidelines), ENOKI-RULE (35 deterministic dependency-parse rules over spaCy en_core_web_trf, curated by a protocolized agent-assisted loop with a fixed acceptance gate S = F1 + 0.25·cov, bootstrapped on OpenIE6/LSOIE subsamples and refined on the ENOKIQA dev split with cross-seed validation), and ENOKI-ENCODER (OpenIE6's Iterative Grid Labeling architecture with ModernBERT-large, retrained on ENOKIQA-dev — 5,474 sentences, 36,865 triples — i.e., distilling the LLM extractor). (2) Verification and projection: triples become NLI hypotheses scored by ModernBERT-large-nli (hallucination probability = P(neutral) + P(contradiction)); long contexts are chunked with one-sentence overlap and the max entailment score across chunks is taken; unsupported facts project their object delta back to a hallucinated span. A notable algorithmic contribution is replacing IGL's row-wise cross-entropy with a permutation-invariant Hungarian-matching loss (DETR-style set prediction), justified because incremental extraction makes gold row order semantically meaningless. Design decisions: the text-anchoring constraint (well-justified — it is the enabling move), incremental fact construction (justified qualitatively and via the non-incremental ablation), and optional FastCoref decontextualization (presented as optional after mixed ablation results — honestly handled). Key Results: Entity-level on HalluEntity: ENOKI-LLM 79.70 AUROC / 55.09 AUPRC vs. 77.63/36.63 for zero-shot GPT-5.2 and 72.03/33.67 for the best fine-tuned baseline (LLaMA3.1-8B on RAGTruth); ENOKI-RULE reaches 76.41/46.81 and ENOKI-ENCODER 70.47/44.25. Span-level (Span Coverage F1): MuSHROOM 52.07 (ENOKI-LLM) vs. 44.12 (MinIE baseline); PsiloQA 71.15 vs. 64.06; on RAGTruth, RAGTruth-trained models remain strongest (42.20) with ENOKI-LLM at 37.32 — an honest negative transfer result. Sentence-level is mixed: on FactCheck-Bench ENOKI-LLM (59.64 F1) trails Claimify (72.71) and the decomposition-free NLI baseline (67.44); on RAGTruth-250 ENOKI-LLM leads at 76.42. Efficiency (RAGTruth): ENOKI-ENCODER achieves 69.1 F1 at 0.13s/sentence (4–10× faster than competitive baselines; ~10⁻⁴×10¹⁶ FLOPs vs. 6.21×10¹⁶ for Claimify); ENOKI-LLM reaches 76.4 F1, +9.8 over Claimify at comparable latency. Ablations: Hungarian matching improves span F1 on all three span benchmarks (e.g., MuSHROOM 41.02→46.96); a Qwen3.5-9B LLM verifier beats the encoder NLI verifier on MuSHROOM/RAGTruth; GPT-5.4 extraction adds only +1.85 AUROC over GPT-OSS-120B. ENOKIQA: 3,990 labeled + 19,594 unlabeled examples, seven generator models, avg. answer 5,682 chars and context 14,879 chars (far larger than prior fine-grained resources); automatic annotation validated on 100 human-labeled examples at sentence-F1 0.867 but span-F1 only 0.569. Baselines are current (2025-era LettuceDetect, haldetect, GPT-5.2, Qwen3-8B, LLaMA3.1). Scale is standard-benchmark, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (text-anchored OpenIE facts as a shared claim/span representation removing the alignment stage) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (ENOKIQA's dual-granularity, long-form, aligned annotations). The Hungarian-matching loss is a standard DETR technique applied to fix a real supervision-noise problem in IGL; the three-backend structure is competent systems engineering over known extractor families rather than new extraction science; Span Coverage F1 adapts existing containment-style evaluation ideas. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: non-incremental vs. incremental prompting (HalluEntity 79.70 vs. 78.11 AUROC), Hungarian matching (Table 5, consistent gains), verifier backend (encoder NLI vs. Qwen3.5-9B LLM), extractor LLM (GPT-OSS-120B vs. GPT-5.4), and decontextualization with per-dataset effects reported even when negative. No error bars or significance tests are reported for the main tables; cross-seed validation appears only inside the rule-curation gate. Code (github.com/s-nlp/Enoki), the dataset (hf.co/datasets/s-nlp/EnokiQA), and model checkpoints are released. Methodological concerns: (1) ENOKIQA's gold labels are produced by the authors' own pipeline (ENOKI-LLM extraction + Qwen3.5-9B verification), and ENOKI-ENCODER is trained on those labels — a self-distillation circularity, partially mitigated by human agreement checks and by evaluating primarily on external benchmarks; (2) the headline span metric is author-defined and described in a way that favors fine-grained systems; (3) the reported +15.3 AUPRC margin on HalluEntity in the abstract does not match the largest table gap (~18.5 vs. GPT-5.2's 36.63), suggesting a different comparison point that is not spelled out; (4) the 76–78% hallucination rate in ENOKIQA is high and unexamined. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — the paper runs and releases a working multi-backend pipeline. Practical: Yes — ENOKI-RULE and ENOKI-ENCODER (ModernBERT-large + 395M NLI model) run on commodity hardware; only ENOKI-LLM requires a 120B-parameter model (available open-weight). Efficient: Strong — 0.09–0.13s per sentence for the non-LLM variants (roughly two orders of magnitude below multi-stage LLM pipelines), with FLOPs accounting provided. Effective: Evidence supports the span- and entity-localization claims; the sentence-level setting shows genuine weaknesses against plain NLI and RefChecker, which the authors acknowledge. Scalable: Not tested beyond standard benchmark sizes; per-sentence latency extrapolates favorably, but no throughput or long-document stress experiments are reported. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (code, 35-rule library, trained encoder, dataset), not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The text-anchoring constraint is a genuinely clean formulation — it converts the claim-to-span alignment problem into a representational property, and the incremental fact-group design makes delta-span projection principled rather than heuristic. (2) The Hungarian-matching fix for IGL's row-order supervision noise is a real, ablated improvement (+5.94 F1 on MuSHROOM) that generalizes beyond this paper to incremental extraction settings. (3) The efficiency results are the paper's most practically valuable finding: a 35-rule deterministic backend retaining 46.81 AUPRC on HalluEntity (vs. 55.09 for the LLM) at ~0.11s/sentence makes explicit verification viable in latency-constrained deployment. (4) The agentic rule-curation protocol with a fixed acceptance gate and cross-seed rejection is an unusually disciplined way to build a rule library, and the limitations section is candid (extraction coverage caps recall; decontextualization gains are inconsistent). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state four: dependence on extraction coverage (recall is capped by what the extractor emits — explicitly called the main trade-off of explicit verification); imprecise incremental projection when multiple parts of a fact are unsupported or errors interact non-locally; sentence-level processing leaving coreference, ellipsis, and discourse-level attribution only partially handled (with the decontextualization module showing no consistent gain); and sensitivity to verifier calibration. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The Span Coverage F1 metric is defined by the authors, motivated by coarse gold annotations, and rewards exactly the fine-grained predictions ENOKI produces; no standard metric (exact span F1, token-level F1, IoU) is reported at span level, so the magnitude of ENOKI's span advantage against tuned encoders like LettuceDetect cannot be verified under community-standard scoring. (2) ENOKI-ENCODER is trained on ENOKIQA labels generated by ENOKI-LLM + Qwen3.5-9B, so its generalization results partly measure the distillation teacher's biases; the 0.569 human–machine span F1 agreement on 100 examples suggests the training signal is noisy at exactly the granularity the model is meant to learn. (3) The claimed +15.3 AUPRC on HalluEntity is not reconcilable with the table without knowing the intended comparison point. (4) The high hallucination rate (76–78%) in ENOKIQA is not analyzed — no-context answering from parametric memory on Wikipedia questions may create an unnatural error distribution that favors decomposition-heavy methods. (5) All evaluation is English-only despite Mu-SHROOM being a multilingual shared task. Bottom Line: For anyone engineering production hallucination guardrails that must both explain and localize errors under tight latency, this is worth reading and building on — the text-anchored formulation and the rule/encoder backends are immediately usable — but treat the span-level margins as metric-dependent until they are replicated under standard boundary-sensitive scoring.

AuK Technical Report: An Open-Source Foundational Model for Speech Generation and Editing (178 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AuK, an open-source ~1.5B-parameter flow-matching foundation model that unifies speech generation (zero-shot and instruction TTS) and instruction-guided speech editing (acoustic, paralinguistic, content, enhancement/separation) under a single instruction-plus-audio-context interface, plus a 4-step distilled variant, AuK-Flash, with a 4.5× wall-clock speedup. - Why it's important: Practical voice systems need synthesis, editing, and restoration together, but serving separate task-specific models fragments the user experience and duplicates modeling effort; a single open-weights model with broad coverage is a real deployment and research asset. - How it does it: A frozen Qwen2.5-Omni MLLM (with learnable layer-wise hidden-state aggregation) provides semantic conditioning, a jointly trained speech/music/audio VAE provides acoustic conditioning and reconstruction, and a FLUX-style hybrid backbone (dual-stream MMDiT then single-stream DiT blocks) predicts rectified-flow velocity, trained via a two-stage curriculum and split post-training: human-feedback listwise DPO for editing and Flow-GRPO with engineered rewards for generation. - The good: The evaluation is broad and benchmark-current: AuK attains 2.65% average WER and 0.795 SIM on Seed-TTS-Eval (vs. Qwen3-TTS at 3.07%/0.745), reduces Ming-Freeform-Audio-Edit Full-ZH WER from 10.46% to 3.09% over Ming-UniAudio, and the VAE beats four prior audio VAEs on all reconstruction metrics in speech, general audio, and music. - The missing: A large fraction of the editing training data is synthesized with other TTS/editing systems (Qwen3-TTS-CustomVoice, IndexTTS2, CosyVoice2, F5-TTS, OmniVoice), so no ablation isolates how much of the editing gain comes from data scale and mixture versus model design, and no error bars or significance tests accompany any reported metric. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate speech generation/editing systems and need to know the current open-source frontier and its data-recipe details; skip it if you want a validated scientific claim about why unified training works, since the transfer findings are qualitative only.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Practical Impact (85) is the cluster's best — open weights for both AuK and AuK-Flash, a reusable VAE, and SOTA results against 2025–2026 baselines — and Novelty (65) reflects a genuinely new five-family unified formulation with transcript-free zero-shot TTS. The composite is pulled down by Rigor (57): no ablation isolates the MMDiT/aggregation architectural choices, three-run means lack variance, and editing training data is synthesized with systems that are also evaluation baselines, creating circularity risk. Resilience (60) is capped because the load-bearing Prompt Enhancer is never evaluated in isolation. Weighted composite: 0.15*65 + 0.15*57 + 0.10*58 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*60 + 0.30*85 = 68.8 ≈ 69.

Problem & Motivation: Voice application users routinely issue heterogeneous requests — synthesize speech in a described style, replace a spoken span, change emotion or accent, insert a nonverbal vocalization, isolate a speaker, restore degraded audio — which today require separate, task-specific models with different conditioning interfaces (text-only vs. text+reference audio) and different supervision signals (automatic metrics for generation vs. subjective judgments for editing). Prior unified audio systems and editing benchmarks expose the problem, but a single model with broad task coverage, scalable training, and efficient inference did not exist. The intended beneficiaries are speech-product teams and open-source researchers who currently maintain model zoos of TTS, editing, enhancement, and separation systems. Key Idea: Reformulate all five task families as one supervised problem — a natural-language instruction plus optional audio context maps to a target waveform, trained with a single rectified-flow objective in a shared VAE latent space — and handle the generation/editing asymmetry in post-training rather than in the objective: human-feedback listwise preference optimization (LiPO over a Diffusion-DPO implicit score) for open-ended editing, where no reward model exists, and Flow-GRPO with automatic ASR/speaker/style rewards for generation, where they do. A secondary trick is cross-utterance in-context learning for transcript-free zero-shot TTS: enumerate distinct utterance pairs from the same speaker so the model must factor speaker identity from utterance content, removing the need for a reference transcript at deployment. Methodology: The pipeline has four phases. (1) Data construction: ~3.03B instruction–audio instances, 1.95M hours of effective supervision across five families — speech generation (transcript-free pair-enumerated zero-shot TTS; Instruct TTS captioned by Qwen3-Omni), acoustic editing (deterministic DSP transforms: 5 rate multipliers, 6 loudness offsets, 6 pitch shifts), paralinguistic editing (emotion/timbre/de-accent/nonverbal/whisper pairs synthesized with IndexTTS2, SeedVC, CosyVoice2+OmniVoice, F5-TTS masking pipelines), content editing (LLM-generated insert/delete/substitute transcripts realized by forced-alignment masked infilling, plus lyric editing on dry vocals), and enhancement/separation (randomized degradation mixtures, instruction-dependent removal targets, staged multi-speaker scenes, native-song music stems). (2) Model: frozen Qwen2.5-Omni MLLM whose 32 layers are combined by learnable unconstrained scalars after per-layer LayerNorm into the semantic condition; a frozen flow-augmented VAE (480× downsampling, 64-dim latents at 50 Hz, BigVGAN causal decoder, normalizing-flow KL regularization, trained 1.24M updates on ~3M hours with multi-scale mel + multi-period/CQT adversarial losses); a 1.5B-parameter backbone of 10 dual-stream MMDiT blocks followed by 20 single-stream DiT blocks predicting flow velocity under a masked MSE flow-matching loss with t sampled from a logistic-ish distribution biased to low t (σ of N(−0.8, 0.8)). (3) Training: 50k generation-only warm-up updates, then 600k joint updates with fixed task mixture (28.1% generation, 23.0% content editing, 23.2% enhancement/separation, 21.8% paralinguistic, 4.0% acoustic), hierarchical condition dropout for CFG, on 256 GPUs with ZeRO-2/bf16. (4) Post-training and distillation: editing preference optimization over 818 informative human-rated groups (9,080 candidates, 3-level ordinal ratings) via LiPO with label smoothing; Flow-GRPO (500 updates, G=16, MixGRPO-style 6-step stochastic window, KL-adaptive) with homophone-tolerant content rewards and constrained speaker-similarity standardization to block reward hacking; then consistency distillation initialization followed by task-routed Decoupled DMD with adaptive projected guidance (APG) replacing CFG in the CA branch, where separation examples are routed to a supervised clean-latent regression and excluded from DMD — a fix for observed distribution mismatch that otherwise regressed separation quality. Key design decisions: frozen encoder/VAE with only the backbone trained (asserted, not ablated); task-routed distillation (justified by an observed failure mode); APG substitution (justified by observed clipping in few-step students). Key Results: AuK achieves 2.65% average WER and 0.795 SIM on Seed-TTS-Eval (test-en 1.02%, test-zh 1.02%, test-zh-hard 5.91%), beating Qwen3-TTS (3.07%/0.745), Seed-TTS, and VoxCPM2; on InstructTTSEval it reaches 83.37% DSD-ZH (+2.27 pp over Qwen3-TTS-VD). On editing, MMAE-Speech gives IFR 48.23% and CR 88.11% (+4.71/+10.84 pp over Step-Audio-EditX), with AuK-Flash at the best EMR of 13.85% vs. 7.04% for Ming-UniAudio; SpeechEditBench content editing jumps to 91.83% from Ming-UniAudio's 76.46% and prosody editing to 71.33% from 26.50%; Ming-Freeform Full-ZH/Full-EN WER drops to 3.09%/3.96% from 10.46%/14.28%. On restoration it is competitive but not uniformly best: DNS Challenge dWER 2.66% (best) but DNSMOS OVRL 3.35 vs. AnyEnhance's 3.41; CHiME-4 WER 7.84% (Flash, best); Libri2Mix WER 9.12% tying specialist MossFormer2-SS on SIM (0.96); VCTK-SR Flash leads 6 of 7 metrics. AuK-VAE wins all four reconstruction metrics (e.g., speech PESQ 4.143 vs. 3.633 for MiniMax-H3-AudioVAE) across speech, AudioSet, and MUSDB18-HQ. Distillation yields 4.5× wall-clock speedup at matched hardware/batch (4 NFE, no CFG vs. 32 NFE, CFG 2.0). Baselines are current and strong (Qwen3-TTS, Ming-UniAudio, Step-Audio-EditX, RE-USE are 2025–2026 systems). Evaluation was run three times per benchmark with means reported; benchmarks are standard-scale, not stress-scale. Surprising findings: editing-supervised whisper transformation transfers to text-driven whisper generation, and Chinese-only de-accenting supervision transfers to English accented speech — both reported qualitatively only, with no quantitative benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the released unified model and AuK-Flash) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (cross-task transfer from editing to generation; cross-lingual accent transfer), with ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION components (task-routed distillation, APG substitution). The genuinely new parts are the five-family unified data recipe at 3.03B-instance scale, the transcript-free cross-utterance zero-shot TTS formulation, and the ordinal listwise DPO over flow-matching implicit scores with shared-noise candidate re-evaluation. The architecture is a competent combination of known components — Qwen2.5-Omni conditioning, FLUX-style MMDiT/DiT hybrid, rectified flow, Diffusion-DPO/LiPO, Flow-GRPO, Decoupled DMD — applied to the audio domain; the task-routing trick in distillation is the most original algorithmic piece but is a targeted patch, not a general method. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thin: the paper compares consistency vs. ODE-regression vs. MeanFlow initialization and reports the DMD-routing motivation, but provides no ablation over the MLLM layer-aggregation, the M/N block split, the task mixture ratios, or the condition-dropout schedule; the claim that cross-utterance training "improves both expressiveness and speaker similarity" is asserted without numbers. Three-run means are reported, but no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests appear anywhere. Source code and model weights are stated as released (project page/GitHub linked from the first page), supporting reproducibility. Methodological concerns: (1) much of the editing supervision is generated by systems that are also evaluation baselines or their close relatives (Qwen3-TTS-CustomVoice, CosyVoice2, IndexTTS2, F5-TTS), risking train/eval circularity on Ming-Freeform-Audio-Edit-style semantic editing; (2) perceptual gains for AuK-Flash rely heavily on DNSMOS/UTMOS, which are proxy metrics known to be gameable; (3) the human preference dataset is small (818 groups) and the RL stage is short (500 updates), so post-training effects are hard to attribute; (4) the paper reports its own benchmark harness choices (e.g., Prompt Enhancer enabled for MMAE) whose interaction with scores is not isolated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — a built and released model evaluated on external benchmarks. Practical: Yes — a 1.5B-parameter backbone at 24 kHz with bfloat16 inference runs on commodity GPU hardware, and weights are open. Efficient: AuK-Flash needs only 4 function evaluations and no CFG for a 4.5× wall-clock speedup over the 32-NFE teacher; the full model still costs 32 NFE with CFG, and the VAE encoder is non-causal (offline only). Effective: Evidence shows it solves the instruction-following generation and editing problem on benchmarks, but the authors themselves admit native free-form instruction understanding is insufficient and the Prompt Enhancer (an external LLM pipeline) is required in practice — so end-to-end effectiveness depends on an unmeasured component. Scalable: Untested beyond the demonstrated scales; nothing suggests a failure at 10×, but no long-form generation, streaming, or latency evaluation is reported, and the non-causal VAE encoder bounds real-time use. Deliverable: software artifact — released code, model weights for both AuK and AuK-Flash, plus the reusable AuK-VAE. Strengths: (1) The data engineering is the real contribution: a five-family, 3.03B-instance instruction-audio corpus with per-family quality control (WER-filtered infilling, pinyin-level lyric checks, RMS normalization), described at a reproducible level of detail rare in this genre. (2) The split post-training design — human-feedback ordinal LiPO for editing because no reward model exists, GRPO with engineered rewards for generation — is a well-reasoned answer to a real asymmetry, and the reward design (constrained speaker-similarity standardization, homophone-tolerant error rates) shows genuine attention to reward hacking. (3) Task-routed Decoupled DMD is an honest, observation-driven fix for a distillation failure mode on separation, with the failure mechanism articulated rather than hidden. (4) Breadth of evaluation: five benchmarks for editing, four for restoration, current 2025–2026 baselines, and the authors candidly report where the Flash variant wins versus the full model rather than promoting one checkpoint. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that native free-form instruction following remains incomplete: an agent-based data pipeline for free-form editing SFT did not generalize to arbitrary requests, and reaching the capability ceiling still requires the Prompt Enhancer for task identification, parameter normalization, and instruction rewriting toward the training distribution. They flag the emergent transfer observations as qualitative and "not substitutes for comprehensive benchmark evaluation." They also implicitly acknowledge the full/Flash trade-off (linguistic accuracy vs. perceptual quality) throughout the results. This is a credibility positive: the limitations section confronts the central weakness directly rather than minimizing it. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No ablation isolating the contribution of the hybrid MMDiT/DiT backbone versus a plain DiT, or of layer-wise MLLM aggregation versus last-hidden-state conditioning — the two architectural choices that most distinguish AuK from F5-TTS are unvalidated. (2) Editing-training-data circularity: several editing corpora are manufactured with baselines or their relatives, and no decontamination analysis checks overlap between synthetic training pairs and editing benchmarks (e.g., whether benchmark edit types mirror the training mixture). (3) The Prompt Enhancer is a load-bearing component (it is enabled for MMAE evaluation and required for free-form use) yet is never evaluated in isolation — its task-routing error rate and rewriting-induced failures are unmeasured. (4) Distillation is evaluated only via the downstream benchmark deltas; no study of where AuK-Flash degrades relative to the teacher across the five task families (the 4.5× speedup is claimed "under matched conditions" but per-task quality retention is not tabulated). (5) RL and DPO stages are tiny (500 updates; 818 preference groups) relative to the pre-training scale, so the marginal value of the elaborate post-training machinery over plain SFT is not established. (6) The qualitative transfer claims (whisper generation, English de-accenting) are unbenchmarked, so their robustness is unknown. Bottom Line: For anyone building speech generation or editing systems this is now a mandatory reference point — an open-weights, 1.5B-parameter model with the broadest demonstrated instruction-following editing coverage and a genuinely reusable data recipe — but readers seeking validated insights into why unification works, or a deployment-ready system without a prompt-rewriting crutch, will find the evidence here thinner than the system itself.

Virtualizing Recursion: Just-In-Time Graph Analytics in a Hyperscale Relational Warehouse

J Arnold, K Stolze · vldb.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Dataflows — an ephemeral, anonymous procedural superset of SQL executed on Ocient's MPP warehouse — plus a JIT virtualization runtime that transparently rewrites standard WITH RECURSIVE queries into imperative loops whose intermediate tables automatically transition between in-memory CTE literals and NVMe-backed storage. - Why it's important: Hyperscale warehouses on shared-nothing architectures face a dilemma for recursive/graph queries: client-side iteration suffers the N+1 problem, while a kernel-level recursive-union operator introduces cycles into the query DAG and hard-to-schedule state management; meanwhile standard SQL recursion is restricted to monotonic, (typically) linear forms, blocking algorithms like bidirectional search and stable marriage. - How it does it: A transpiler rewrites recursive CTEs into WHILE loops over scoped temp tables, and a runtime inspects exact row counts between iterations — keeping tables under 65,536 rows virtualized in Coordinator memory and injected as UNNEST constant arrays (CTE injection), materializing larger tables to NVMe, and dematerializing shrinking tables back — so each iteration is re-planned with fresh exact cardinalities. - The good: The evaluation at genuine stress scale is credible and unusually honest: WCC on a 100-billion-edge Zipfian graph completes in ~23 minutes where Spark GraphFrames fails to finish, the paper reports per-node throughput conceding Spark matches Ocient at 1B edges, and it shows single-node DuckDB/Umbra beating an 11-node Ocient cluster 25–38× at 1B edges before the advantage flips at 10B+ edges. - The missing: All experiments use synthetic Zipfian (α=1.5) graphs with no real customer workloads, no variance/error bars or repeated runs, no threshold sensitivity sweep across hardware, and the comparison against Vertica is omitted entirely (results withheld over EULA terms), so the claimed architectural superiority over MPP recursive-CTE predecessors is argued, not measured. - Read it or not: Worth reading for warehouse and graph-systems engineers designing recursion support in distributed engines — the virtualization lifecycle and the candid scale-regime analysis are instructive — but skip it if you want a peer-validated benchmark of graph analytics systems, since it is a vendor system paper with self-reported numbers on its own workloads.

Problem & Motivation: Enterprises running petabyte-scale MPP warehouses (supply-chain bills of materials, fraud networks, identity resolution) increasingly need recursive/graph queries, but supporting recursion in shared-nothing systems is architecturally awkward. Client-side iteration incurs network round-trips (N+1 problem); a native recursive-union operator introduces cycles into the execution DAG, complicating scheduling, deadlock detection, and spilling. Standard SQL recursion additionally constrains expressivity: it is monotonic (no DELETE of intermediate state, ruling out stable marriage) and effectively linear (the recursive name may appear at most once in the recursive member's FROM, ruling out bidirectional search's coupled frontiers), with no mechanism for floating-point convergence checks (PageRank). A further constraint specific to high-availability MPP: creating ephemeral physical tables requires distributed consensus (Raft) over table metadata, making per-iteration DDL cost ~4.6 s per step in their environment — prohibitive for small frontiers. The paper's audience is users of Ocient's warehouse and, more broadly, MPP vendors facing SQL:2023/GQL adoption pressure. Key Idea: The core trick is JIT table virtualization driven by exact between-iteration state: treat each loop iteration of a recursive workload as a fresh, independently planned SQL statement, and represent the small ephemeral tables (frontier/accumulator) as in-memory handles on the Coordinator whose data is injected into referencing queries as constant-column UNNEST arrays — bypassing both the storage stack and the Raft metadata round-trip that makes per-iteration DDL expensive. Because the runtime observes exact row counts each iteration, it can flip between broadcast and shuffle joins, materialize to NVMe when the frontier crosses 65,536 rows (or ~625 MiB byte budget), and dematerialize back when DELETE-driven reductions shrink tables below threshold. Making the imperative loop a first-class, user-visible language surface (rather than hiding adaptivity inside a declarative executor) is argued to buy expressivity, inspectability, and operational hooks (WLM release/acquire, cancellation, FINALLY cleanup). Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) A transpiler detects WITH RECURSIVE at parse time and rewrites the CTE into an imperative Dataflow via source-slicing against AST offsets, emitting semi-naive evaluation: a #Result accumulator, a #Queue frontier, an EXCEPT-based dedup stage for UNION (set) semantics, plus source linearization for recursive views. (2) A "Hot Swap" connection protocol (hijack → script execution → result retrieval → masquerade) runs the script server-side while presenting standard JDBC/ODBC clients with a plain result query. (3) The JIT virtualization runtime intercepts DDL/DML on #-scoped temp tables, holds sub-threshold tables in Coordinator memory, injects them into queries as UNNEST constant arrays, flushes to NVMe above 65,536 rows / 10,000 bytes-per-row, and dematerializes shrinking physical tables via SELECT→re-ingest→async DROP. (4) Operational layers add release/acquire WLM slot scheduling per statement, system/user MAX ITERATIONS limits, cancellation propagation into FINALLY cleanup, and scheduler-driven operator spilling (hash joins transition to partitioned mode under OOM pressure). Case studies (bidirectional search, stable marriage, WCC label propagation, PageRank with L1-delta convergence) exploit the imperative surface for non-monotonic and convergence-controlled algorithms. Critical design decisions: the 65,536-row default threshold is justified by measured crossover points (parsing degrades ~100K rows; I/O vs. parsing crosses ~128K) and argued to be hardware-independent because the avoided cost is a small, fixed metadata-Raft quorum — but sensitivity was not swept; the text-level transpilation with re-parse is acknowledged as trading a small re-parse cost for robustness; and the choice of a user-visible procedural layer over executor-internal adaptivity is defended via a three-point argument (expressivity, inter-iteration inspectability, operational integration) in Section 7.4. Key Results: Five experiments on Ocient clusters (2 SQL + 10 Foundation nodes, Xeon Gold, 768 GB/node; a separate 11-node AMD EPYC 9654, 2.3 TB/node cluster for hyperscale). (1) Shallow linear traversals (10–100 iterations): the client-side baseline costs ~4.6 s/step due to Raft DDL; JIT virtualization cuts this by 97%, sitting 2.3× behind a hand-unrolled SQL statement at 10 iterations (2.62 s vs. 1.16 s) and reaching near parity (1.03×) at 100. (2) Deep recursion to 600 iterations: unrolled SQL degrades super-linearly; the Dataflow is 3.2× faster at 600 iterations. (3) Throughput scaling (5-iteration loop, 1K–10M rows): a transition-zone worst case at 100K rows (49.46 s total, 98,929 ns/row), then near-flat totals at 1M/10M rows (42.5 s/48.6 s; 972 ns/row at 10M). (4) Dematerialization trace (200K→0 rows, halving): step time drops from ~20 s (physical) to ~10 s immediately after dematerialization and ~2.6–4 s in deep virtual territory. (5) WCC on Zipfian (α=1.5) graphs: at 100B edges Spark GraphFrames (5 nodes) did not finish while Ocient Dataflow completed in ~23 minutes (~17,126 s for 1T edges); per-node throughput is comparable to Spark at 100M–1B edges (0.142 vs. 0.149 M edges/node/s at 100M; 1.10 vs. 1.15 at 1B) but Ocient leads 1.2× at 10B and is the only system to complete 100B/1T. Against extrapolated single-node engines on GCP n2d-highmem-96 VMs with a disclosed 5× competitor-favorable hardware correction, DuckDB is 25× and Umbra 38× faster than 11-node Ocient at 1B edges, ~1.9× slower at 10B, and both OOM at 100B. Baselines are current (Spark GraphFrames, DuckDB, Umbra) except Vertica, which was benchmarked but withheld (EULA). All graphs are synthetic; scale is stress-scale (10⁸–10¹² edges). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION core. Genuinely novel: the bidirectional virtualization lifecycle (in-memory CTE injection ↔ NVMe materialization, triggered by row-count thresholds observed exactly between iterations) atop an ephemeral procedural execution substrate that transparently hosts standard WITH RECURSIVE. Standard components applied in a new setting: semi-naive evaluation, stored-procedure-style imperative SQL (per the authors' own related work on DB2 compound statements), adaptive query processing, Raft metadata, SPDK/NVMe-first storage, release/acquire scheduling. The closest prior architecture (Vertica's internal temp tables for iteration) is positioned against only qualitatively. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper's rigor is above average for a vendor systems paper but below academic best practice. Positive: each of Experiments 1–4 is framed as an ablation isolating one mechanism (client-side DDL cost, planner scalability, virtualization-vs-Raft trade-off, dematerialization); per-node throughput is reported to address a 2.2× hardware imbalance; the DuckDB/Umbra extrapolation methodology (5× = 4.0 core ratio × 1.15 IPC × 1.09 bandwidth, set at "competitor-favorable" ends) is fully disclosed; honest negative results are reported (single-node engines 25–38× faster at 1B edges; the 100K-row transition zone is the worst case). Negative: no error bars, seeds, or repeated-run variance anywhere; all graphs are synthetic Zipfian with no real-world workload; the virtualization threshold was never swept across hardware configurations (explicitly left as future work); WLM release/acquire and Hot Swap overhead are not isolated; the Vertica comparison is absent for EULA reasons, removing the most architecturally relevant baseline; DuckDB/Umbra numbers are extrapolations, not measurements on equivalent hardware. An artifact repository is provided (https://github.com/Ocient/vldb2026-dataflow-virtualization) including single-node harnesses, which substantially aids reproducibility. Methodological flag: the system is evaluated entirely on the authors' own platform, workloads, and harness — a peer-reviewed venue paper, but self-reported vendor numbers throughout. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, production warehouse feature evaluated by deployment). Practical: Runs on commodity hardware (NVMe/SPDK nodes, Xeon/EPYC), and is transparent to standard JDBC/ODBC clients via the Hot Swap protocol. Efficient: Avoids per-iteration Raft DDL (~4.6 s → ~0.05 s/step at 97% reduction) and delivers up to 972 ns/row in physical mode, though the 100K-row transition zone shows a real worst case; per-node throughput matches Spark in RAM-fit regimes. Effective: Evidence covers synthetic recursive and graph-analytic workloads up to 1T edges — including the honest admission that in-memory single-node engines win below ~10B edges — so the stated problem (recursion at hyperscale beyond RAM) is solved, but effectiveness on real customer graph workloads is unevaluated. Scalable: Demonstrated empirically at 10⁸–10¹² edges with stable per-iteration times (290 ± 5 s across 22 WCC iterations), though trillion-edge instrumentation and threshold auto-tuning are self-acknowledged as incomplete. Delivers a production system feature plus a public artifact repository with case-study Dataflow code and benchmark harnesses; no separate library or standalone tool. Strengths: - The virtualization lifecycle is a clean, well-motivated mechanism: identifying metadata-Raft consensus latency (not data I/O) as the dominant small-frontier cost is an empirically grounded insight (4.6 s/step measured), and CTE injection via UNNEST constant arrays is a concrete, reconstructible implementation of the fix. - Unusually candid comparative reporting for a vendor paper: conceding that Spark matches per-node throughput at 1B edges, that DuckDB/Umbra beat an 11-node cluster 25–38× in RAM-fit regimes, that the Dataflow is 2.3× slower than hand-unrolled SQL at shallow depth, and withholding per-dollar comparisons as indefensible — this honesty materially raises confidence in the favorable numbers. - The Section 7.4 argument for a user-visible procedural layer (expressivity beyond monotonic/linear recursion, inter-iteration inspectability, operational integration) is a genuine architectural position with concrete case studies (stable marriage's DELETE loop, bidirectional search's coupled frontiers, PageRank's ε-convergence) that a declarative adaptive executor cannot express, not just optimize. - Stress-scale demonstration with per-iteration stability evidence (290 ± 5 s over 22 WCC iterations on 100B edges) that directly addresses skew concerns instead of assuming round-robin placement suffices. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: the 65,536-row threshold was not swept across network-bandwidth, NVMe-IOPS, or CPU configurations and auto-tuning is future work; trillion-edge instrumentation and per-foundation-node breakdowns are future work; WLM release/acquire and Hot Swap overhead have not been isolated in controlled experiments; virtualized DELETEs are expensive (EXCEPT ALL full-column difference) and only pay off via lifecycle savings; DuckDB/Umbra comparisons are extrapolations from smaller GCP hardware; Vertica results are withheld over EULA restrictions; per-dollar comparisons are not presented. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. The synthetic-only workload restriction, however, is never acknowledged as a limitation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No real-world workloads: every graph is synthetic Zipfian (α=1.5), so claims about production behavior on bills-of-materials, fraud, or identity graphs rest on distribution assumptions; real graphs with densest substructures could stress the broadcast-join regime differently. - No variance reporting: single-run timings throughout make the 2.3× overhead figure, the 49.46 s transition-zone worst case, and per-node throughput ratios impossible to assess for noise. - The threshold-sensitivity claim ("the same threshold has worked across the two clusters this paper evaluates") generalizes from n=2 same-vendor clusters; the independence argument (metadata-Raft latency dominance) is plausible but untested on disaggregated or high-latency-network topologies. - Missing standard baselines beyond withheld Vertica: no comparison against dedicated distributed graph engines (TigerGraph, Pregel-style systems) that the paper itself positions against architecturally in Section 7.1–7.2; the Spark GraphFrames comparison is to a known under-optimized framework for whole-graph analytics. - The GQL/SQL:2023 story (Section 7.3) is entirely prospective — quantified paths, TRAIL/ACYCLIC modes, and shortest-path selectors are described as mapping designs, not implementations, yet the abstract positions the system as "well-positioned" for these standards. - The "hot-swapped" client transparency has an unexamined failure surface: a masqueraded connection presenting a rewritten result query complicates driver-side timeout, progress, and partial-result semantics; no protocol-level edge cases are discussed. Bottom Line: A systems engineer building recursion or graph support into a distributed warehouse gains real, transferable insight from the virtualization mechanism and the unusually honest scale-regime analysis, but anyone seeking an independent benchmark of hyperscale graph analytics should weigh that every number here is vendor-reported on synthetic data against architecturally withheld competitors.

ACE: Adaptive Calibration-Free Expert Skipping for MoE-based LLMs

Z Xu, Z Zhao, X Hu, J Yu, H Wen, J Li, Z Jiang, D Yang · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ACE, a training-free, calibration-free framework for token-adaptive expert-slot skipping in pretrained MoE LLMs that combines two offline, weight-derived contribution estimates (Global Spectral Proxy and Router-Conditioned Refinement) with runtime router gates to skip low-contribution expert slots at inference. - Why it's important: Fixed top-k routing executes the same number of expert slots for every token, wasting computation in memory-bandwidth-limited deployments; existing skipping methods either require calibration data, extra training, or degrade sharply when skipping more than ~40% of routed slots. - How it does it: GSP scores each expert's global transformation capacity from a norm-based bound on the coupled SwiGLU gate/up/down projections plus RMSNorm scaling, RCR scores each expert's response along a centered-router-weight direction prototype, and a slot is skipped only when the max of the two normalized scores falls below a budget-derived threshold, with the top-1 expert always retained. - The good: Across three MoE models (Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it) and 7–8 benchmarks at 10–60% skipping, ACE consistently leads all nine baselines at aggressive budgets — e.g., at 50% skipping on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it improves WikiText-2 PPL from 9.42 to 8.67 and average accuracy from 71.42% to 75.57% over the strongest competitor (MoDES) — and delivers measured 1.72–2.25× TTFT and 1.31–1.41× TPOT speedups on an A100. - The missing: All downstream results are single deterministic runs with seed 42 (the authors say sub-point differences on GPQA-Diamond should be interpreted cautiously), and the threshold for a target skipping ratio is set using one unlabeled full-model score-collection pass, which blurs the 'fully calibration-free' claim. - Read it or not: Read it if you deploy or compress MoE LLMs and need a data-free dynamic-skipping method that holds up at high skip ratios; skip it if your interest is only in mild (≤20%) skipping, where router-score baselines remain competitive and the contribution margin is small.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (70) and Resilience (68) pull the composite down: single deterministic runs at seed 42 with no error bars leave several sub-point margins within noise, the 'calibration-free' claim is softened by the unlabeled threshold-collection pass, and the evaluation stops at 3–4B-active-parameter models with no distributed/serving-scale evidence. Novelty (68) is real but bounded — new calibration-free contribution estimators and a principled fusion rule within an established problem class — and Non-Obviousness (72) benefits from the crisply argued preference-versus-contribution distinction. Completeness (75) is helped by honest reporting of where the method does not win. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*60 = 69.
