Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Operators of MoE-based LLMs (e.g., Qwen3-30B-A3B with ~3B of 35B parameters active) pay fixed top-k expert compute per token even though expert contributions vary widely per token. Existing remedies have two failure modes: static expert pruning/merging fixes a shared expert structure across all inputs and leaves fixed top-k routing intact, while dynamic skipping methods rely on router confidence (which reflects relative routing preference, not actual transformation contribution), calibration data (sensitive to calibration size, domain, and shift), or retrained routers/learned allocators. The paper targets high-ratio (40–60%) skipping, where prior methods degrade rapidly, and seeks a contribution estimator that needs no real samples, activation caching, or checkpoint modification. Key Idea: Separate expert importance from routing preference using two data-free views of contribution — a structural view (GSP: a multiplicative Frobenius-norm surrogate, derived from an upper bound ||f(x)||₂ ≤ ||x̄||²·||ΓW_gate||·||ΓW_up||·||W_down||, aggregated by a geometric mean of two branch-symmetric factorizations and normalized per layer) and a directional view (RCR: centered router weights as data-free proxies for expert-conditioned input directions, justified by translation invariance of softmax routing and a Gaussian exponential-tilting argument; each prototype is run once through its expert offline and the output/input norm ratio is stored) — then skip a slot only when both views plus the gate rank it low (intersection/max rule), always keeping the top-1 expert. The key insight is that router gates conflate preference with contribution, and a conservative dual-view intersection guards against skipping direction-specialized experts that a single view would misjudge. Methodology: Two-stage pipeline. Offline: (1) GSP computes per-expert, per-layer amplification scores a_up = ||ΓW_up||_F·||ΓW_gate·W_down||_F and a_gate = ||ΓW_gate||_F·||ΓW_up·W_down||_F, geometrically averaged and normalized by the layer mean, stored as a lookup table; (2) RCR centers router weights (invariant to shared translation, proven in Appendix A.2), RMS-normalizes them with scale ρ_l = 1, feeds each prototype q_{l,e} through its frozen SwiGLU expert once, and stores the normalized response ratio ||f(q)||₂/(||q||₂+ε). Online: for each token, slot scores s = g·A for both views are normalized within the original top-k set; the final score c = max(p_GSP, p_RCR) is compared to a threshold τ(q); skipped slots are removed (subject to top-1 retention and a minimum-active-expert constraint), surviving gates are renormalized, and only surviving experts execute. Thresholds for a requested budget are set by quantile mapping from one unlabeled score-collection pass (1.8 min, 9.2–10.5× faster than binary or frontier threshold search). Critical design decisions: (a) geometric-mean aggregation over additive (justified qualitatively by SwiGLU's multiplicative structure, ablated only implicitly); (b) max-fusion as a conservative intersection (ablated against min and mean — max wins, e.g., 79.77 vs 77.20/78.45 avg acc at 30% on Qwen3-30B); (c) ρ_l = 1 to preserve calibration-freeness (asserted, not ablated against a calibrated alternative). Key Results: Tested on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, evaluated with WikiText-2 PPL (seq len 2048) and seven zero-shot tasks (ARC-C/E, PIQA, MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench) at realized skipping ratios of 10–60%. At 50% skipping: Qwen3.6-35B — ACE reaches PPL 8.67 / 75.57% avg accuracy vs MoDES 9.42 / 71.42% (the strongest competitor); Qwen3-30B — ACE 8.85 / 74.30% vs GSP-only 8.99 / 74.10%; Gemma-4 — ACE 77.11% vs GSP 75.73%, while MoDES collapses to 38.74% and DiEP to 30.83%. At 60% skipping, ACE leads the best external baseline by 1.07 points (Qwen3-30B, 63.35% vs Top-P 61.91%) and 1.66 points (Qwen3.6, 70.70% vs MoDES 69.04%); on Gemma-4 the margin over GSP grows to 2.46 points. At ≤20% skipping, router-score baselines are competitive or better (Score beats ACE by 0.25 points at 10% on Qwen3.6), which the authors acknowledge. Efficiency: on an A100 at 60% skipping, TTFT 120.3 vs 270.9 ms and TPOT 63.0 vs 85.1 ms/token (batch 1, length 1024), i.e., 1.72–2.25× and 1.31–1.41× speedups. Baselines include nine dynamic methods (Score, NAEE, MoDES, DiEP, AIMER, Top-P, SERE, XShare, ExpertSparsity) under a controlled matched-budget BF16 protocol; DiEP, SERE, and XShare degrade severely at high ratios. A notable reported finding is that PPL and downstream accuracy diverge — competitive PPL does not guarantee preserved reasoning/coding accuracy at aggressive budgets. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (plus supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING on PPL-vs-accuracy divergence and the aggressive-skipping regime). Genuinely novel: the GSP SwiGLU-coupled spectral surrogate and the RCR centered-router direction prototype are new calibration-free contribution estimators, as is their dual-view intersection rule with formal conservativeness and output-perturbation analysis. Standard components: the overall idea of token-adaptive expert skipping, threshold-based skipping, gate renormalization, and top-1 retention are all established; the contribution is a better importance signal and a principled fusion, not a new problem or system class. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: component ablation shows GSP is the stronger single signal (at 50% on Qwen3-30B: GSP 74.10% vs RCR 67.01% vs ACE 74.30%), and fusion-strategy ablation shows max beats min and mean. Threshold-construction cost and full latency measurements are reported; complete task-level tables for all models/budgets are in Appendix B. Weaknesses the authors partially flag: single deterministic runs (seed 42, greedy decoding) with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests; no ablation of the geometric-mean vs additive aggregation or of the ρ_l choice. Code is released at https://github.com/xzktx003/moe-prune (release stated; contents not verified here). Methodological concerns: (1) the 'calibration-free' claim is softened by the unlabeled full-model score-collection pass used to map budgets to thresholds — it uses no labels or training, but it does touch evaluation-like workloads, though Appendix B.1 shows thresholds transfer across workloads (Table 8); (2) measured realized ratios rather than requested ratios are reported, which is honest but means cross-method comparisons depend on the shared threshold-search protocol; (3) evaluated only on three A3B/A4B-class instruct models — no very large (100B+ active) or base-model results. The paper is a preprint (arXiv:2609.05228) and is not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a deployed inference-speed artifact). Practical: Yes — runs in BF16 on a single NVIDIA A100 with Hugging Face tooling, no special hardware. Efficient: Offline precompute is one pass over experts (GSP is pure linear algebra; RCR is one forward per expert); online overhead is table lookups and scalar ops, with matched-budget baselines within 1% latency of ACE — the speedups (1.72–2.25× TTFT, 1.31–1.41× TPOT) come from fewer expert executions, not cheaper scoring. Effective: Strong evidence at 40–60% skipping across three models and seven tasks, but evidence at ≤20% skipping shows no advantage, and single-run results limit statistical confidence. Scalable: Not directly tested — no results on larger-active-parameter models, distributed expert dispatch (named as future work), or continuous batching beyond batch 4; the dispatch-kernel claim at high scale is asserted, not measured. Delivers: code repository plus a deployment recipe (offline lookup tables + quantile threshold mapping); no trained-model weights or library packaging is claimed. Strengths: (1) The core insight — router gates measure preference, not contribution — is crisply argued and directly operationalized into two independently motivated, data-free estimators, each with a derivation in the appendix (SwiGLU output bound for GSP; translation invariance + Gaussian tilting for RCR). (2) The conservative max-fusion rule is both theoretically grounded (equivalence to candidate-set intersection, bounded output perturbation ≤ 2αF_max) and empirically validated against min/mean fusion — a rare case where the fusion choice is ablated rather than assumed. (3) The evaluation protocol is unusually careful for this area: realized (not requested) skipping ratios, matched budgets across all baselines, complete 10–60% curves plus full task-level tables, and threshold-construction timing compared against alternative search procedures. (4) Honest reporting of the regime where the method does not win (≤20% skipping) and of single-run caveats. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that results are single deterministic runs (seed 42) so sub-point differences, especially on GPQA-Diamond, should be interpreted cautiously; that future work should examine threshold transfer, repeated-run uncertainty, and distributed expert dispatch; and that router confidence suffices in the low-sparsity regime. They also drop WikiText-2 PPL for Gemma-4 due to an anomalous baseline perplexity, reporting accuracy only. These are confronted directly rather than minimized — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No statistical uncertainty anywhere — with single greedy runs, several claimed margins (e.g., 0.28-point component-ablation gains at 10%) are within plausible run-to-run noise for some tasks. (2) The threshold-mapping pass is described as workload-agnostic, but Table 8 shows thresholds measured on the same workloads used for evaluation; a fully held-out workload transfer experiment (set τ on dataset A, evaluate on dataset B) is shown only indirectly via threshold clustering, not end-to-end accuracy. (3) Geometric-mean aggregation and the ρ_l = 1 scale choice are asserted rather than ablated. (4) All three models are small-active-parameter instruct models (3–4B active); nothing shows the offline tables remain discriminative at larger scale or with shared-attention expert variants. (5) Latency is measured at batch sizes up to 4 and length up to 1024 on one GPU; serving-relevant regimes (large batches, tensor parallelism, distributed expert placement) are named as future work but not tested, so the 2.25× prefill speedup should be read as a single-GPU measurement. (6) The claim that matched-budget baselines 'share the same dispatch path' with latency within 1% is asserted without per-method latency tables. Bottom Line: For practitioners deploying MoE LLMs who want 40–60% routed-expert savings without calibration data or retraining, ACE is currently the best-evidenced option in this comparison and worth reading — but its single-run results and untested large-scale/distributed behavior mean the speedup numbers should be validated on your own stack before committing.

TempCloze: Can Video-LLMs Identify the Missing Middle? (6 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TempCloze, a video cloze benchmark of 1,521 videos in which Video-LLMs must select the true missing middle clip from four same-source candidates, with distractors systematically constructed along Semantic, Alignment, and Progression dimensions. - Why it's important: Existing temporal-reasoning benchmarks for video are language-mediated multiple choice or captioning, letting models score well via linguistic shortcuts (prior work shows text-only LLMs beat random by 25%+), so the field lacks a clean probe of whether models actually reason over visual time. - How it does it: Each video is split into beginning/middle/ending; the middle is removed and distractors are cut from the same video — non-overlapping clips (Semantic), boundary-shifted or expanded clips (Alignment), and reversed/reordered/repeated clips (Progression) — so all candidates share scenes and objects, forcing temporal rather than appearance-based discrimination. - The good: Evaluation of 31 models (10 proprietary, 21 open-source) with a strict human baseline (97.0% vs. 48.13% proprietary mean on Alignment) pinpoints a specific, reproducible failure mode: temporal alignment — judging when an event occurs — is the bottleneck, with structured error signatures (Expanded and Reversed distractors dominate). - The missing: No non-LLM vision baselines (e.g., video encoders with temporal-matching heads) are run, so it is unverified whether low-level splice or motion artifacts could solve the task without any temporal reasoning; also, all videos are ≤90 s (mean 31.3 s), so the "temporal reasoning" claim covers only short-to-medium clips. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or benchmark Video-LLMs — it delivers a diagnostic instrument and a concrete, well-isolated capability gap — but skip it if you need long-video (minutes+) evaluation or training data, since it is purely an evaluation benchmark on short clips.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) is anchored by the same-source distractor design that jointly removes appearance shortcuts and linguistic mediation — a real methodological advance in benchmark construction, though it is a new benchmark, not a new method or formulation. Rigor (72) reflects unusually thorough sanity checks (zero boundary-frame leakage, edge baselines at chance), 31-model sweeps, and a strict dual-annotator human baseline, discounted for missing CIs on headline claims and no non-LLM vision baselines to establish construct validity. Non-Obviousness (60) comes from the specific, actionable finding that temporal Alignment — not semantics or ordering — is the bottleneck. empirical Novelty 70 Rigor 72 Non-Obv 60 Completeness 72 Resilience 68 Impact 70
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Video-LLM temporal reasoning benchmarks (TempCompass, TVBench, VideoMME, LongVideoBench) evaluate through text: models pick among textual options or generate captions. This leaves open linguistic shortcuts — option wording, answer distribution correlations, language priors — which the authors substantiate by citing evidence that text-only LLMs exceed random baselines by over 25% on such formats. Practitioners who need to know whether a Video-LLM genuinely infers temporal structure from pixels (what happens, when it occurs, how it unfolds) currently lack an evaluation format where the comparison itself is visual. The gap: a benchmark where the discriminative burden falls on comparing video segments, not reading or writing text. Key Idea: Reformulate the cloze task as video completion for evaluation (prior video-cloze work — MovieFIB, FIBER, VCP, VideoMAE — used cloze for text completion or as a training objective). The core move is same-source distractor synthesis: because all four candidates are cut from the same video, they share scenes, objects, and style, collapsing the task from "which clip looks related" to "which clip fits the temporal slot." The three-dimension taxonomy (Semantic/Alignment/Progression) turns a single accuracy number into a per-capability diagnostic. Methodology: (1) Video filtering: retain 12–90 s videos from seven public sources (LVD-2M, EgoLife, MiraData, FAVOR-Bench, CaReBench, Video-TT, Daily-Omni); screen captions with GPT-o3 for cloze suitability (temporal/causal coherence, subject consistency); remove low-quality clips (bitrate <200 kbps, sharpness <30); sample a gap from the central 50% of the timeline with length 20–40% of duration; validate gaps with Farnebäck optical flow (mean flow magnitude >1.0, up to 3 resamples). This yields 1,521 videos (mean 31.3 s, median 30.0 s). (2) Distractor generation: per dimension, three distractors with formal interval definitions — Semantic: non-overlapping same-duration clips; Alignment: Advanced/Deferred (shift by ℓ/2) and Expanded (widen by ℓ/2 per side); Progression: Reversed, Reordered (permutation of subevent partition), Repeated (duplicated subsegment, trimmed to ℓ). (3) Evaluation: 16 bin-centered frames per clip (96 frames per instance) to avoid boundary-frame leakage; models output JSON with an option letter. Auxiliary subsets: TempCloze-Mixed (300 videos, candidates mixed across dimensions) and TempCloze-Hard (150 most-misclassified instances). Behavioral analyses cover candidate-order permutation (4 permutations, temperature 0), context-direction ablation (beginning-only/ending-only/both), visible-span scaling, frame-density scaling (8–20 frames/clip), and pass@k test-time scaling. Critical design decisions: bin-centered sampling (justified by a sanity check showing zero exact boundary-frame matches across 18,252 candidate clips); edge-similarity baselines showing boundary cues give only ~25–26% (vs. 25% uniform); strict dual-annotator human baseline on 100 videos. The LLM-in-the-loop caption filtering is plausible but not independently validated against the failure modes it targets. Key Results: Alignment is the consistent bottleneck: proprietary models average 70.73% (S), 48.13% (A), 67.72% (P); open-source models 34.00%/26.54%/36.97% — versus a 97.0% human baseline. Best overall is Seed1.8 (thinking) at 88.58% mean; the best open-source model, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, reaches 68.27%. Cumulative (3/3) accuracy: proprietary average 33.24%, best 70.81% (human 92%); open-source average 7.15%. Grok4.1 is essentially at random (24.11% mean). Error patterns are structured: Seed1.8-I picks the Expanded distractor in 75% of its Alignment errors; GPT-5.4 picks Reversed in 67% of its Progression errors. In Mixed evaluation, Alignment is the most misleading dimension (error shares up to 20.3%), and accuracy drops 10–30 points versus single-dimension evaluation. Behavioral findings: clip selections flip under candidate reordering at 32.4–60.7% rates despite <4-point accuracy variance; beginning-only context often matches or beats both-context (Seed1.6: 80% vs. 82% on Progression, vs. 46% ending-only), suggesting forward-biased inference; Alignment degrades when visible span or frame density increases; pass@k gains up to ~30 points (Gemini2.5-Pro, Qwen3.5-397B) without changing the dimension ordering. Thinking is not uniformly helpful: Seed1.8 gains +5.15 mean (driven by +14.99 Alignment), but Qwen3VL-32B thinking loses −16.46 mean. The evaluation spans 31 models — current frontier systems, not outdated baselines — at standard benchmark scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK with a NEW FORMULATION component: the genuinely novel element is recasting video cloze as an evaluation task with algorithmically controlled, same-source distractors spanning three diagnostic dimensions, which removes language mediation and appearance shortcuts simultaneously. The pipeline stages (LLM filtering, optical-flow motion checks, frame sampling) are competent applications of known techniques; the contribution is the benchmark design and the resulting empirical findings, not a new method. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: boundary sanity checks (zero exact boundary-frame matches; DINOv2 edge baselines at ~25–26% vs. 25% chance), single-frame ablations (Seed1.8 drops from 83.43% to 17.31% mean with one frame per clip), thinking-pair comparisons with token costs, source-level breakdowns, and joint/video-level accuracy decomposition. Candidate-order permutation is run at temperature 0 with four permutations. However, no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported on the main headline numbers, and the human baseline covers only 100 of 1,521 videos under a strict double-judgment rule. Code is released at https://github.com/CedricPei/Temporal-Cloze; the dataset is built from public sources. Methodological concerns: (a) the filtering pipeline depends on GPT-o3 caption screening, whose false-rejection rate on the target capability is not validated beyond a small 300-rating human check (mean 4.13/5 suitability); (b) TempCloze-Hard instances are selected by cross-model errors, which risks selection bias in the behavioral analyses that use it; (c) proprietary API results are a vendor-dependent snapshot the authors themselves flag. No Goodhart-style contamination is evident since the benchmark is new, but several source datasets share authors with this paper's institutions (e.g., Meng et al. appears in both benchmark sources and this paper's citations), which is worth noting. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark with large-scale model evaluation; no new method is deployed). Practical: Yes — open-source models run on A6000 GPUs via vLLM; the benchmark itself requires only standard video decoding and any Video-LLM with multi-image input. Efficient: 96 frames per instance is moderate; the frame-density ablation suggests fewer frames often suffice, and dense sampling actively hurts. Effective: As a diagnostic for temporal alignment, the evidence is strong (large, structured human–model gaps); as a proxy for open-ended video understanding, the authors correctly scope it as measuring only fixed-candidate temporal fit. Scalable: Untested beyond 90 s clips and 4-way multiple choice; the authors claim future benchmarks should extend to longer videos but do not demonstrate it. Deliverable: a reusable benchmark artifact (dataset, construction pipeline, evaluation code, prompts) on GitHub; no trained models. Strengths: - The same-source distractor design is a real methodological advance over language-mediated temporal benchmarks: it jointly eliminates appearance shortcuts and linguistic priors, and the paper proves the residual shortcut surface is small (zero exact boundary matches, edge baselines ≈ chance) rather than asserting it. - The three-dimension decomposition converts a single score into actionable diagnosis: the finding that Alignment — not event semantics or local ordering — is the bottleneck, with Expanded and Reversed as dominant error signatures, is specific enough to drive targeted training-data or architecture work. - Behavioral sensitivity analyses (order permutation, context direction, span/density scaling, pass@k) reveal properties marginal accuracy hides — e.g., 40–60% clip flip rates under reordering despite stable accuracy, and forward-context bias — which is the kind of analysis most benchmark papers omit. - The 31-model sweep with a strict dual-annotator human baseline (97.0%, only counted correct when both annotators agree) gives the headline gap credibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section is direct and specific: the benchmark covers only missing-middle identification with fixed candidates, not open-ended generation, dialogue, audio-grounded inference, or free-form future prediction; Alignment distractors intentionally contain relevant content, so scores measure exact temporal compatibility rather than broad plausibility; results are a snapshot of changing APIs and video input limits; and the source mix (long-take, egocentric, fine-grained motion) cannot cover all domains. The authors confront limitations honestly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No non-LLM vision baselines (video encoder similarity, temporal-action-localization-style models, or simple flow/feature-matching heuristics) are run. The edge baselines rule out boundary cues, but a stronger vision-only solver (e.g., aVideoMAE-style model fine-tuned or zero-shot on clip compatibility) would establish whether the task requires LLM-level reasoning at all or merely sensitive visual matching; its absence leaves the benchmark's construct validity partially open. - The mean video length is 31.3 s with a 90 s cap, yet the paper frames the contribution around "temporal reasoning" broadly; long-horizon temporal reasoning (minutes, multi-event) is neither tested nor clearly disclaimed in the headline claims. - GPT-o3 caption screening is a single-annotator LLM with unknown precision/recall on the suitability criterion; 78% of human suitability ratings were in the top two bins, but 22% were merely "acceptable" or lower, and no inter-annotator agreement statistic is reported. - The behavioral analyses use TempCloze-Hard (150 instances selected by cross-model error counts); results like the visible-span and density-scaling trends are not shown to hold on the full benchmark, and no error bars accompany the subset plots. - Frame budget is fixed at 16 bin-centered frames per clip for all models; models with native continuous video encoders or different frame adapters may be disadvantaged in ways not disentangled from genuine capability. - Statistical rigor on headline claims (e.g., proprietary vs. open-source gaps, thinking-mode deltas) lacks significance testing or seed variance beyond the permutation study. Bottom Line: For Video-LLM builders and evaluators, TempCloze is worth adopting: it is a carefully shortcut-hardened diagnostic that isolates a specific, previously diffuse weakness (temporal alignment) with structured error evidence, and its limitations are narrower than those of the language-mediated benchmarks it replaces — though anyone needing long-video or open-ended evaluation should treat it as a complement, not a substitute.

WearableQA: A Benchmark for Health Reasoning over Real-World Wearable Data (15 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WearableQA, a benchmark of 4,084 ten-option multiple-choice questions built from the longitudinal wearable time series, blood biomarkers, and demographics of 200 real users (up to 500 days of daily measurements each), spanning 16 question types across data-vs-health and single-vs-cross-signal reasoning axes. - Why it's important: LLM-based health assistants are proliferating, but existing evaluations rely on synthetic or simulated signals, so it is unknown whether models can reason over a real user's noisy longitudinal physiological record; a reliable testbed is a prerequisite for deploying such assistants safely. - How it does it: A dual-grounding framework derives every question's ground truth deterministically from raw measurements — either from peer-reviewed literature findings (11 anchor papers, each relationship supported by ≥2 independent studies) or from cohort-mined patterns passing statistical gates for effect size (|ρ|≥0.5), robustness (bootstrap/leave-one-out stability ≥80% of resamples), and authenticity (cross-user null test with empirical FDR ≤0.20). - The good: The benchmark is genuinely discriminative (accuracy spans 19.6%–72.9% across 14 models against a 10% chance baseline, with 95% Wilson CIs) and diagnostic: ablations show withholding the wearable time series drops overall accuracy from 60.2% to 17.3%, confirming models must actually read the data. - The missing: The strongest result — agentic Python access lifting GPT-5.4 from 51.2% to 71.3% — is reported only for one model and one prompt configuration, and there is no human-expert baseline to establish headroom or question difficulty calibration. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate health/time-series LLM capabilities or wearable-data products; skip it if you only need confirmation that LLMs struggle with numeric aggregation over long contexts — the headline finding will not surprise you.

This is the most statistically careful paper in the cluster: explicit construction gates (effect size, bootstrap stability, FDR-controlled null test), 95% Wilson CIs throughout, shortcut audits with a disclosed and fixed leakage bug, and released code/data (Rigor 72). Novelty (70) rests on the dual-grounding, deterministic computation-graph labeling framework — a real methodological contribution for health benchmarks — while the model-ranking findings themselves are largely confirmatory, keeping Non-Obviousness (65) moderate. Completeness (65) and Resilience (65) are dented by the unanalyzed QC-model contamination (three evaluated frontier models also filtered the benchmark), the absence of a human-expert baseline, the permissive FDR≤0.20 threshold, and a thin limitations section. Problem & Motivation: Health-LLM developers and wearable-platform researchers need to know whether a model can compute over a real individual's longitudinal sensor history (trends, anomalies, cross-signal couplings) and interpret it clinically. Existing health benchmarks (MedQA, MedMCQA, HealthBench) are text-only; ECG-QA covers waveforms but not longitudinal multi-signal records; time-series benchmarks (TimeSeriesExam) use synthetic signals; PHIA evaluates on simulated user trajectories and mainly retrieval/aggregation. The gap: no benchmark evaluates LLM reasoning over authentic, noisy, inter-individually variable wearable records with deterministic ground truth. Key Idea: Dual grounding plus deterministic labeling — every question's answer is produced by an executable computation graph (a library of primitives like slope(), lagged_correlation(), threshold_flags()) over the user's actual measurements, where the reasoning objective itself is sourced either from verified biomedical literature or from cohort-mined patterns that survive statistical consistency gates. This makes ground truth reproducible, resistant to memorization, and anchored in physiology rather than template authorship. Methodology: Construction proceeds in phases: (1) Data — 200 real users, 16 daily wearable metrics in four domains (cardio-fitness, activity/energy, sleep, stress), 17-biomarker blood panel, demographics, and cohort-reference percentiles computed over a larger external cohort. (2) Question discovery — literature-grounded cards (11 anchor papers, DOI/PMID-verified, requiring two independent same-direction studies, explicitly excluding cohort-specific thresholds) or population-grounded patterns mined from a large cohort over 28-day windows, filtered by effect-size, robustness (bootstrap of days, leave-one-out day removal, dead-bands for near-boundary cases), and authenticity (cross-user null test yielding FDR ≤0.20). (3) Discover-then-label — a reusable primitive library instantiates the objective per user; ambiguous users are discarded, not approximated. (4) Distractors — data-reasoning distractors are verified by executing the same computation on all ten options (gold must uniquely satisfy it); health-reasoning distractors are clinically plausible but measurement-inconsistent interpretations. (5) Validation — LLM review (three frontier models) plus human verification, with explicit shortcut audits (the authors describe and fix leakage where models could answer from option priors alone). Evaluation: 14 LLMs, temperature 0, 10-option MCQ, row-wise serialization of up to 500 days, CoT default with direct-answer comparison, accuracy with 95% Wilson CIs. Critical design decisions: refusing to import study-specific clinical thresholds (well-justified — cohort-dependent cutoffs would not transfer); using 10 options to push chance to 10% (justified — improves discriminative range); discarding ambiguous users (justified for label reliability, but see gaps on selection effects). Key Results: On 4,084 questions: Gemini-3.1-Pro leads at 72.9% ±0.7; Claude-Opus-4.6 60.2%; GPT-5.4 51.2%; best open-source is Gemma-4-26B-A4B at 42.5%; weakest Llama-3.2-3B 19.6% (chance 10%). Data reasoning is harder than health reasoning for all models except Gemini-3.1-Pro (75.4% vs 67.8%); e.g., GPT-4o scores 25.3% data vs 53.5% health. Cross-signal reasoning degrades for most proprietary models (GPT-5.4: 59.1% single vs 45.7% cross). Cross-signal prediction is the hardest type (8.3% for Llama-3.1-8B to 40.5% for Claude-Opus-4.6). On definitional vs empirical signal pairs (strength-matched), Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5.4, and GPT-4o show +51.5, +48.2, and +36.0 point gaps, indicating prior-knowledge shortcuts. Agentic Python access lifts GPT-5.4 from 51.2% to 71.3% (+20.1), dwarfing all representation changes (CSV best text variant at 51.5%; image representations hurt, dropping to 34.1–36.6%). CoT gains are large for proprietary models (Claude-Opus-4.6 +19.6 overall, up to +27 on single-signal) but modest for open-weight models (+2.3 to +3.0 on signal axes). Ablations: removing longitudinal history halves history-dependent accuracy (75.9%→39.8%); removing all time series collapses overall to 17.3%. Positional bias analysis shows small models collapse onto one letter under direct answering (Llama-3.2-3B: 51.5% pick rate) while CoT restores near-uniformity. Model evaluation is on proprietary frontier APIs plus public open weights — current, strong baselines for the model-comparison axis. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the dual-grounding construction framework (literature-verified findings plus statistically gated cohort-mined patterns, instantiated as deterministic computation graphs on real users) and the first benchmark combining real longitudinal wearable data with blood biomarkers under a diagnostic 2×2 taxonomy. The evaluation machinery itself (MCQ prompting, CoT-vs-direct comparison, positional-bias analysis) is a standard combination of known techniques applied to a new setting; the agentic/tool-use finding (code execution ≫ representation tuning for numeric time-series tasks) confirms rather than establishes a trend. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a benchmark paper. Statistical gates on question construction are explicit and quantitative (|ρ|≥0.5, ≥80% bootstrap reproduction, FDR≤0.20); all 95% Wilson CIs reported; answer positions balanced; shortcut auditing is described concretely, including a bug they found and fixed (highly predictable metric pairs answerable from priors). Multi-model LLM review plus human verification is stated, though inter-annotator agreement numbers and audit sample sizes are not given in the provided text. Code and data are released (github.com/facebookresearch/WearableQA, huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/WearableQA). Concerns: (1) the three quality-control reviewer models (GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-Opus-4.6) overlap with evaluated models — frontier models helped filter the benchmark they are then scored on, and the direction of this bias is not analyzed; (2) the population-grounded pipeline selects for patterns that survive FDR gates, but the ≤0.20 FDR threshold means up to 20% of retained patterns could be artifacts; (3) no human-expert baseline; (4) 200 users is modest for a benchmark claiming population generality. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark with systematic model evaluation; no deployment). Practical: Runs on commercially available APIs and open weights; the benchmark itself is downloadable data usable by anyone with LLM API access. Efficient: Evaluation cost is dominated by long contexts (500 days serialized), which is the point, but no token/cost figures are reported. Effective: Evidence shows it discriminates and diagnoses (ablations confirm data-grounding is required), but it measures reasoning over daily aggregates — not whether a system improves real health outcomes. Scalable: Construction pipeline is programmatic and reusable, but scaling depends on cohort access; whether gates retain enough questions at 10× users or on other device ecosystems is untested and only claimed. Delivers a real software artifact: released dataset and evaluation code, not a trained model. Strengths: - The dual-grounding + deterministic-labeling pipeline is a real methodological contribution: answers are computed, not asserted, which enables reproducibility, distractor verification by execution, and resistance to memorization — most wearable/health benchmarks lack this. - The authenticity gate (cross-user null test yielding an empirical FDR) is a sophisticated and rarely-seen quality control for pattern-mined benchmarks; it directly addresses the spurious-correlation failure mode of data-mined labels. - The diagnostic analyses go beyond a leaderboard: the definitional-vs-empirical pair experiment (strength-matched, +36 to +51 point priors-reliance gaps for several frontier models) and the selective ablation (history removal hurts only history-dependent types) genuinely localize what models fail at. - Honest shortcut auditing — the authors report fixing leakage they discovered mid-construction, which is a credibility positive. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper's stated scope limits are thin in the main text: it notes that PHIA-style evaluations use simulated trajectories (positioning, not self-limitation) and that models remain far from solved, but an explicit limitations section (e.g., on cohort size, single device vendor, aggregate-only daily resolution, or the FDR threshold) is not present in the provided text. The authors do confront construction pitfalls directly via the shortcut-audit narrative, which partially compensates. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - QC-model contamination: GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Claude-Opus-4.6 both reviewed questions and were evaluated on the benchmark; no analysis of whether this inflates their scores relative to models not used in QC. - No human baseline: without expert performance on the same questions, "most models below 60%" cannot be interpreted as headroom vs. genuine ambiguity in the labels. - Ambiguous-user discarding induces selection: users whose data cleanly satisfies criteria are kept; a model deployed on the full population will face exactly the discarded ambiguity, so benchmark accuracy may overstate real-world reliability. - Single-vendor, single-granularity data: all signals appear to come from one consumer wearable ecosystem at daily aggregation; generalization to other devices, sampling rates, or missing-data regimes (beyond the '-' cells shown) is untested. - The agentic result (+20.1 points) is only run for GPT-5.4 under a fixed representation; whether the gain holds across model families and whether multi-view tool selection genuinely adds nothing (the multi-view number is lower, 69.7, unexplained) needs follow-up. - The 20% FDR allowance for population-grounded questions is permissive for a health domain; label-noise sensitivity analysis is absent. Bottom Line: This is the strongest available benchmark for LLM reasoning over real longitudinal wearable data and its construction pipeline is worth adopting wholesale, but practitioners should read it for the dataset and methodology rather than the model rankings, which are a familiar story of priors-reliance and weak numeric aggregation partially rescued by tool use.

Semantics-Guided Automatic Tensorization for Multiobjective Evolutionary Algorithms: A Multi- Agent Framework

Z Liang, B Huang, B Zheng, R Cheng · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EvoCoCo, a multi-agent LLM framework that automatically converts sequential CPU-based MOEA implementations (mostly MATLAB/PlatEMO) into GPU-tensorized EvoX/PyTorch implementations while preserving the source algorithm's optimization mechanism, and it delivers a 48-MOEA benchmark for evaluating such migrations. - Why it's important: Mature MOEA code is written for CPUs and cannot exploit GPU parallelism, and manually tensorizing dozens of structurally heterogeneous algorithms is labor-intensive; automating this closes the gap between algorithmic population-level parallelism and its program realization. - How it does it: An LLM agent pipeline reconstructs the source algorithm's semantics (states, dependencies, operators, update logic) into a shared tensorization blueprint, then parallel branches generate alternative tensor realizations under that blueprint, with execution feedback driving repair and an optimization-aware hierarchical selection. - The good: On a 48-algorithm benchmark with 240 attempts per condition, EvoCoCo with Gemini 3 Flash reaches a 78.75% convergence-pass rate versus 61.67% for the best one-shot baseline, with matched-backend gains of +17 to +52 percentage points and coverage of all 48 algorithms; tensorized code shows median speedups of 22.6× (population scaling) and 80.2× (dimension scaling) over PlatEMO on CPU. - The missing: There is no resource-normalized cost accounting for the workflow itself — EvoCoCo consumes roughly 10× more tokens per converged result than one-shot generation, and the fidelity criterion tolerates up to a 200% relative IGD increase, which is a lenient bar for claiming 'comparable optimization outcomes.' - Read it or not: Worth reading for evolutionary-computation researchers and practitioners maintaining large MOEA codebases who care about GPU migration and LLM-based program transformation; skip it if you want formal correctness guarantees or cost-efficient code translation, neither of which is provided.

Problem & Motivation Multiobjective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) solve engineering design, scheduling, and large-scale optimization problems, and their populations expose natural GPU parallelism. However, mature implementations (PlatEMO, jMetal, pymoo, etc.) encode that parallelism in CPU-oriented structures: individual-level loops, dynamic containers, conditional branches, and framework-specific state management. Prior tensorization work (EvoX, TensorRVEA, TensorNSGA-III, EvoMO) demonstrated GPU feasibility but relied on manual, algorithm-specific redesign, leaving open the automation problem: how to restructure arbitrary heterogeneous implementations into tensor form without altering the underlying optimization mechanism. The paper's stated audience is anyone needing scalable MOEA computation without rewriting each algorithm by hand. Key Idea The core insight is to separate what must be preserved (the source MOEA's algorithmic semantics — principal operators, persistent states, dependencies, update logic) from how the target computation may be restructured (tensor layout, control flow, framework idioms), encode the former in a shared 'tensorization blueprint' that constrains all generation branches, and let execution feedback — not static analysis — resolve target-side choices that cannot be determined in advance. Tensorization is thereby cast as a constrained search over alternative realizations (a generate–evaluate–refine–select loop) rather than direct code translation. Methodology EvoCoCo instantiates a four-stage pipeline: (1) a Source Analysis Agent reconstructs a structured semantic representation S of the PlatEMO source (states with lifetimes and dimensions, workflow, algorithm-specific conventions like MATLAB indexing); a rule retriever supplies target-framework (EvoX) rules matched to structures found in S; a Blueprint Agent constructs the blueprint B specifying state mappings, tensor formulations (broadcasting, Boolean masks, batched scalarization, tensor indexing), and disallowed patterns (population loops, NumPy fallbacks, host-device transfers). (2) Six parallel Tensorization Agents, each with a distinct strategy bias (broadcasting, einsum, masked operations, in-place efficiency, advanced PyTorch ops, tensorized iterative selection), generate candidate implementations under the shared B. (3) A Repair Agent uses runtime diagnostics to fix failed candidates within a refinement budget. (4) A Selection Agent hierarchically ranks validated candidates by an LLM-judged comparability of performance indicators, then execution time and a code-level tensorization assessment. The formalization frames the task as mapping source program C_S to a target in the feasible set defined by integrity, compatibility, executability, numerical validity, and mechanism-retention constraints. Notably, candidate selection uses an LLM-based qualitative judgment of indicator results rather than a fixed quantitative criterion — a design choice the authors flag as such. Fidelity is assessed by 21 paired runs per MOEA–problem combination on DTLZ/WFG/LSMOP/MaF with an IGD-based Improved/Preserved/Degraded classification under tolerances ε_abs = 0.10 and ε_rel = 2.0. Key Results - Migration reliability (240 attempts/condition, 7 conditions): EvoCoCo with Gemini 3 Flash achieves 93.33% execution-pass and 78.75% convergence-pass rates with 48/48 algorithm coverage; the best one-shot baseline (GLM-5.1) achieves 72.92%/61.67% with 45/48 coverage. Matched-backend convergence gains: +52.08 pp (Gemini 3 Flash), +38.34 pp (DeepSeek V4 Pro), +42.91 pp (DeepSeek V4 Flash). Paired sign tests with Holm correction confirm significance versus matched backends (e.g., Holm p = 1.87×10⁻⁵ for Gemini 3 Flash), but comparisons against GLM-5.1 are not significant after correction (Holm p = 0.1185 and 1.0). - Optimization fidelity: 88.2% of 1,904 valid comparisons pass (724 Improved, 956 Preserved, 224 Degraded) across DTLZ (84.0%), WFG (96.5%), LSMOP (84.8%), MaF (87.3%); 41/48 algorithms exceed the 80% algorithm-level threshold. - Scalability (DTLZ3, M = 3): median speedups of 22.6× under population scaling (N = 256 to 16,384) and 80.2× under dimension scaling (D = 1,024 to 65,536); geomeans 29.9× and 71.5×; largest measured speedup 37,339× (MOEA/D-DE at N = 16,384). EvoX OOM events (6 population, 11 dimension cases) are reported separately. - Transfer (10 external/legacy MATLAB-Octave MOEAs): 62.0% convergence vs 18.0% for one-shot; 9/10 vs 2/10 algorithms with at least one converged result. - Ablations (12 MOEAs, 60 attempts/variant): removing the Repair Agent drops execution pass from 98.3% to 60.0%; single-branch generation drops convergence from 83.3% to 40.0%; removing rule retrieval or the Blueprint Agent has smaller effects. - Cost: EvoCoCo uses ~10× more tokens per converged result than its one-shot Gemini 3 Flash counterpart (284.3k vs 28.3k). Baselines are current-generation LLMs under matched backends, though only one-shot prompting is compared — no other agentic code-translation pipelines (e.g., SWE-agent-style or KernelBench-style baselines) are evaluated. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM (automatic tensorization of MOEA implementations as a defined transformation task), NEW METHOD (the semantics-guided multi-agent pipeline with shared blueprint and diversified restructuring), and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the 48-MOEA migration benchmark with three-layer reliability metrics). The genuinely novel element is the blueprint-constrained multi-branch restructuring with execution-guided selection applied to scientific-code migration; the constituent techniques — LLM code generation, retrieval-augmented transformation, and execution-feedback repair loops — are standard, and the target-side tensorization idioms (broadcasting, masking, batched scalarization) are established in the authors' prior work (EvoX, TensorRVEA, TensorNSGA-III, EvoMO). Rigor & Reproducibility The evaluation design is unusually careful for this area: three separate validity questions (reliability, fidelity, scalability) are evaluated with distinct metrics; 240 attempts per condition across seven conditions; 21 paired runs per fidelity comparison; tolerance-sensitivity analysis; sign tests with Holm correction; per-stage failure decomposition; and explicit separate reporting of timeouts, OOM, and execution errors rather than folding them into speedup statistics. Source code is released at https://github.com/EMI-Group/evococo. Concerns: (1) the fidelity tolerances are generous — ε_rel = 2.0 permits a 200% IGD increase to count as 'Preserved' — and the 80% coverage thresholds are self-imposed; (2) the selection step uses an LLM's qualitative judgment of indicator results, which is unvalidated and subjective; (3) the method is developed and validated on PlatEMO→EvoX within the same ecosystem (the DTLZ2 validation problem is from the same suite family used for final evaluation), so some Goodhart-style adaptation of generated code to the evaluation setting cannot be excluded; (4) no comparison against alternative agentic translation pipelines beyond one-shot prompting; (5) statistical significance versus the strongest one-shot baseline (GLM-5.1) does not survive Holm correction. This is an arXiv preprint (2609.02387); it does not appear to be peer-reviewed. Deployability Profile: SYSTEMS (a built multi-agent tool evaluated by migration outcomes and deployed generated code), with a strong EMPIRICAL component. - Practical: Yes — the framework runs on consumer hardware (RTX 5060 Ti for migration experiments) with commodity LLM APIs, and generated code runs on a single RTX 4090. - Efficient: The generated code is efficient (median 22.6×–80.2× GPU speedups), but the conversion workflow itself is expensive: ~224k–430k tokens per attempt, roughly 10× the one-shot cost per converged result; the authors explicitly decline monetary cost comparison. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated goals for 41–48 of 48 algorithms under the predefined (lenient) fidelity criterion, with 7 algorithms below the 80% coverage bar and OOM limits at the largest scales. - Scalable: Tested up to N = 16,384 and D = 65,536 with speedups still growing, but EvoX GPU memory pressure becomes the binding constraint at the top scales; the authors acknowledge memory-efficient restructuring as future work rather than demonstrating it. The work delivers a released software artifact (EvoCoCo framework and the 48 tensorized implementations) plus a reusable benchmark and evaluation protocol. Strengths - The problem formulation is the real contribution: framing tensorization as semantics-guided constrained restructuring, with an explicit separation of algorithmic-retention constraints from target-side design freedom, gives the automation problem a precise statement that future work can build on or attack with non-LLM methods. - The three-layer evaluation protocol (migration reliability → optimization fidelity → computational scalability, with reference-invalid exclusions and tolerance sensitivity analysis) is methodologically more honest than the single-metric evaluations typical of LLM code-transformation papers, and the failure-stage decomposition localizes where automation actually breaks (target-side executability, not code completion). - The ablation study isolates component roles cleanly: repair dominates execution reliability (98.3% → 60.0% without it), multi-branch generation dominates convergence (83.3% → 40.0%), which supports the architecture's design rationale rather than just the aggregate result. - The benchmark of 48 structurally heterogeneous MOEAs spanning seven paradigm classes, with full taxonomy and provenance, is a reusable community asset. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations unusually directly: they state that results are specific to the PlatEMO→EvoX environments and do not establish framework-independent generality, formal program equivalence, trajectory-level equivalence, or resource-normalized superiority over direct translation; they identify optimization-level validity as the main remaining transfer limitation; they document the runtime–memory trade-off (GPU OOM at large scales from materialized broadcast intermediates); and they note that the LLM-based candidate-selection procedure is a design choice, not a methodological requirement. This explicitness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The fidelity criterion is lenient relative to the claims: a 200% relative IGD increase counts as 'Preserved,' so the 88.2% headline coverage overstates practical equivalence; no effect-size or significance testing on the IGD comparisons themselves (only mean-based classification of single-arm summaries). - The LLM-judged 'comparable optimization outcomes' grouping in candidate selection is unvalidated — no inter-rater agreement, no comparison against a quantitative grouping rule — and it is a potential source of hidden benchmark coupling. - Missing baselines beyond one-shot prompting: agentic repair-loop systems (SWE-agent, KernelBench-style refinement) are cited as related work but not run as comparisons; nor is a simpler 'single LLM call with the rule base and a repair loop' ablation that would isolate the value of the blueprint/multi-branch structure versus generic iterative refinement. - The external-transfer study (10 MOEAs) is small and still uses the DTLZ2 validation setting; generality to other target frameworks (JAX, NumPy-only) or source languages (Python sources, C++) is untested. - Statistical support versus the strongest one-shot baseline (GLM-5.1) does not survive multiple-comparison correction, which the paper reports but does not emphasize in the main-text claims. - Cost accounting stops at tokens; LLM monetary cost, human review time, and repair-loop wall-clock are not reported, which matters for the practical adoption claim. Bottom Line A practitioner maintaining a large MOEA codebase or working on LLM-based scientific-code migration gains substantial, concrete value here — the formulation, benchmark, and released tool are ahead of any comparable alternative — but readers should treat the fidelity and cost-efficiency numbers as favorable-to-the-method constructions rather than neutral measurements.

Problem & Motivation: Dropout has vanished from modern LLM pre-training recipes (GPT-3/OPT inherited it, PaLM restricted it to fine-tuning, LLaMA-style models omit it), because single-epoch training on trillion-token corpora leaves little room for classical overfitting and recent work (Liu et al., 2025) reports that activation dropout degrades accuracy. Layer dropout is a special case: it produces structured sparsity whose FLOP savings materialize in wall-clock terms (unlike activation/weight dropout), and it can induce robustness to depth-reduced inference. Prior evidence is fragmented — LayerDrop and Progressive Layer Dropping showed benefits in BERT-era multi-epoch settings, while LayerSkip reported degradations in decoder-only large-data regimes — so practitioners have no reliable answer on whether, or how, to use it at modern scale. Key Idea: The key insight is to re-derive layer dropout's scaling factor from depth-scaling principles rather than treating it as an implementation detail: because layer dropout reduces the network's effective depth, the residual-stream contribution of each block must be rescaled by the layer density (r_train = 1/ρ) to satisfy the Maximal Residual Stream Update desideratum. This single change makes optimal learning rate, weight decay, and batch size transfer across dropout rates (verified by coordinate checks and transfer tests), which in turn reveals that previously reported dropout degradations were largely artifacts of misconfigured hyperparameters — enabling the iso-FLOP search over distributions (ILD/ALD) and schedules (DTS) that identifies ILD+DTS as the Pareto-best configuration. Methodology: The paper trains decoder-only transformers (Celerity-style architecture: ALiBi, squared ReLU, Llama-3 vocabulary) under a compute-optimal 20 tokens-per-parameter budget, in stages: (1) hyperparameter optimization — tuning LR, batch size, weight decay on a base model, then transferring via µP/CompleteP/Power Lines with dropout-dependent residual scaling r_train = 1/ρ and r_eval = 1, justified by coordinate checks (Fig. 2) and transfer tests (Fig. 3); (2) granularity ablations — whole-layer vs. sub-layer (attention/FFN independently) dropout, and per-batch vs. per-sequence Bernoulli masks; (3) configuration ablations — three depth distributions (Uniform, Increasing ILD, Alternating ALD) crossed with three time schedules (Constant, Increasing ITS, Decreasing DTS), grouped by equal mean FLOP savings ¯P; (4) inference evaluations — zero-shot static early exit and intermediate layer skipping, Balcony-style frozen-backbone early-exit adapters trained with KL self-distillation, and self-speculative decoding (Draft & Verify) with layer-subset search via genetic algorithms, hill climbing, and simulated annealing; (5) scaling analysis in TPP (Fig. 8) and hero runs at 1.8B/3.9B/8.2B with p_max up to 0.99. Critical design decisions: the 1/ρ scaling (well-justified empirically and theoretically via CompleteP), whole-layer over sub-layer granularity (empirically justified, mechanistically unexplained — attributed speculatively to attention/FFN co-function), and per-sequence over per-batch masks (justified on accuracy grounds, with an acknowledged hardware caveat). The objective throughout is validation loss under matched non-embedding training FLOPs. Key Results: With ILD+DTS at matched FLOPs, 503M and 906M models at 5% savings slightly beat the dense baseline (val-loss deltas −0.06% and +0.03%), and 20% savings cost only 0.28–0.82% loss across sizes; the 1.8B model with p_max = 0.6 achieves 1.836 val loss vs. the dense baseline's 1.849 (15% FLOP savings), while the 3.9B model with p_max = 0.8 lands at 1.745 vs. 1.732 (20% savings). The 8.2B model with p_max = 0.99 reaches val loss 1.663 with 25% FLOP savings — but no dense 8.2B baseline loss is reported for comparison. Inference: dropout-trained models degrade gracefully under early exit (dense baselines blow up after skipping even one layer) and layer skipping (3.9B with dropout: 2.129 loss with alternate layers skipped vs. 6.446 for dense); self-speculative decoding gives 1.35×/1.43×/1.40× speedups at 270M/504M/906M with p_max = 0.4 (vs. 1.01×–1.06× for dense) and up to 1.55× at 8.2B, measured on XSUM. Downstream (Table A.3, 11 tasks including BBH, HellaSwag, ARC): dropout-trained models track baselines closely, e.g., 3.9B dropout model scores 0.270 BBH vs. 0.272 dense. Testing spans 2400+ runs at standard scaling-regime scale (271M–8.2B params, ≤160B tokens), all on Cerebras CS-3 systems — a credible but single-vendor platform. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW METHOD (configuration-level). Layer dropout itself, early exit, layer skipping, and self-speculative decoding are all established techniques; what is genuinely new is (a) the demonstration that properly configured layer dropout can beat dense baselines at equal FLOPs in the modern single-epoch regime, reversing the field's consensus, (b) the principled 1/ρ scaling rule enabling hyperparameter transfer across dropout rates, and (c) the first systematic ablations of granularity (layer vs. sub-layer; batch vs. sequence) and of distribution×schedule interactions at fixed FLOPs. This is a re-tuning and re-validation of known techniques, not a new algorithmic mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive and well-designed — each configuration choice (granularity, distribution, schedule, scaling factor) is isolated with controls, and the coordinate-check/transfer-test methodology for justifying r_train = 1/ρ is a model of careful practice. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; headline deltas (e.g., −0.06% val loss for 503M at 5% savings) are within plausible run-to-run noise; and the 8.2B hero run lacks its own dense baseline in Table 5. No code, data, or model weights release is mentioned. Potential methodological concerns: the recommended configuration is selected and evaluated on the same validation-loss metric across the same model family (risk of overfitting the recipe to this setting); the FLOP-savings claims are theoretical (non-embedding FLOP accounting), not measured wall-clock throughput; and all experiments run on Cerebras CS-3 hardware, whose compute-bound characteristics may not transfer to GPU clusters where memory-bandwidth and kernel-launch behavior differ. The preprint is vendor-authored (Cerebras) and, as far as stated, not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor, though no released artifact). Practical: The method requires only modifying an existing training loop — no architecture changes, extra parameters, or auxiliary losses — so it runs on any hardware, though the paper's own efficiency validation is exclusive to Cerebras CS-3. Efficient: FLOP savings are linear in the mean dropout rate (up to 25%), but wall-clock training speedup is unmeasured; per-sequence dropout forces weight loading for every layer every step, so realized speedup depends on being compute-bound, a condition the paper assumes rather than demonstrates. Effective: Evidence at 20 TPP and in the TPP scaling sweep shows validation loss is preserved or improved and depth elasticity is real (1.55× lossless spec-decode speedup, graceful skip degradation), so the training-side claim is well supported; downstream-task coverage is thin. Scalable: Tested to 8.2B/160B tokens — well beyond typical academic scale — but the paper extrapolates beyond 8.2B ("larger models will exhibit even greater robustness") without evidence, and inference-benefit scaling with TPP is explicitly not quantified. Deliverable form: paper only — no library, CLI, checkpoint release, or dataset is mentioned. Strengths: - The hyperparameter-transfer analysis is the intellectual core: deriving the 1/ρ residual scaling from the CompleteP desideratum, verifying it with coordinate checks, and showing optimal LR/WD/batch-size invariance across dropout rates (Fig. 3) converts a folkloric technique into a principled, transferable recipe — this likely explains why prior studies saw degradations. - The distribution×schedule ablation at iso-FLOPs (Tables 2–3) is a genuinely new empirical result: decreasing time schedules consistently win (ILD+DTS at 5% savings beats the dense baseline on 503M/906M), and the authors offer three testable hypotheses (noise-driven exploration, implicit model growing, curriculum) without overcommitting. - The unification of training savings and inference elasticity under one mechanism is demonstrated convincingly: average training dropout rate predicts zero-shot early-exit/skip robustness (Finding 6), and the finding that decreasing schedules do not sacrifice depth robustness (Finding 5) removes an obvious objection to the recipe. - Honest negative results are reported (ALD underperforms LayerDrop's multi-epoch claims here; the DTS spec-decode speedup is worse than constant dropout at 0.4 — 1.22× vs. 1.35× at 270M), which strengthens credibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront six limitations (a credibility positive): hyperparameter transfer degrades at very high dropout rates and was validated only for constant schedules, not the optimal decreasing ones; alternative granularities (attention-head, neuron) are unexplored; no comparison against learned depth-routing such as Mixture-of-Depths; no cross-architecture validation (MoE, non-transformers); no scaling law for choosing p_max; and no quantification of inference benefits as TPP grows. They also flag unexplored variants (dynamic early exit, router-based skipping, per-token/per-neuron dropout, dropout in mid-training/SFT) throughout as future work. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No wall-clock measurements at all: every training-efficiency claim is in FLOPs. Per-sequence dropout (their recommended granularity) requires executing layer weights for every sequence every step, so on memory-bound or small-batch regimes the promised speedup may not materialize; the paper's compute-bound argument is asserted, not tested. - No dense 8.2B baseline validation loss in Table 5, so the flagship claim that p_max = 0.99 "largely preserves baseline generalization" at 8.2B rests on interpolation from 1.8B/3.9B and downstream scores rather than a direct iso-condition comparison. - Single-run results with no variance estimates, while several headline conclusions hinge on sub-1% validation-loss differences (e.g., −0.06% at 503M) — well within typical seed variance for LLM pre-training. - Self-speculative decoding speedups are measured only on XSUM; acceptance rates are task-dependent, and no evaluation on code, chat, or longer-form generation is provided. - The early-exit and skipping evaluations are static (all tokens exit at the same layer); the practically relevant dynamic-exit setting is hypothesized but never run. - Hyperparameters were tuned on small proxy models and transferred; whether the dropout-specific transfer rules hold at 8.2B with p_max = 0.99 (where the authors admit transfer degrades) is unverified — and the authors' own Limitations section concedes transfer was validated only for constant schedules, not the DTS schedules that all hero runs use. - The 20 TPP evaluation regime is compute-optimal by construction; behavior at the sub-optimal, longer-training regimes where production models actually live is covered only by one small-model TPP sweep (Fig. 8). Bottom Line: This is the definitive reference on layer dropout for LLM pre-training — its 1/ρ scaling rule and ILD+DTS recipe are immediately actionable for any pre-training team, and its training-cost-free depth elasticity is a real (if modest) win — but readers should discount the FLOP-based efficiency claims until someone reproduces them as wall-clock speedups on commodity GPU clusters.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Q-SKEW, a membership inference attack against fine-tuned diffusion language models (DLMs) that uses the quantile-weighted skewness of per-token loss differences (target vs. reference model) as the membership indicator. - Why it's important: DLMs (LLaDA, Dream, Gemini Diffusion) are rapidly adopting a new training paradigm whose privacy properties are essentially unmeasured, and fine-tuning data (medical, personal, proprietary) is the most legally exposed stage of the pipeline. - How it does it: The core move is a theoretical observation that per-token memorization gain in masked diffusion training scales inversely with the mask ratio, so a member sample's token-level gain distribution is right-skewed (positive third central moment) while a non-member's is roughly symmetric; skewness — not mean loss — becomes the attack signal. - The good: Large, consistent gains over the strongest concurrent baseline SAMA on domain fine-tuning (e.g., ArXiv AUC 83.4 vs. 70.2; TPR@1%FPR 50.6 vs. 17.6 on LLaDA-8B-Base), plus a methodological contribution in demonstrating that the MIMIR benchmark used by prior work produces inflated MI success due to pre-existing model priors (avg. Problem & Motivation: Membership inference (MI) asks whether a specific record was in a model's training set; it serves both as an attack and as a data-auditing tool. For autoregressive LMs and continuous vision diffusion models, a mature MI toolbox exists, but diffusion language models defeat these tools for three reasons the authors identify: the any-order denoising objective acts as implicit data augmentation that reduces verbatim memorization; per-token masking randomness breaks lower-tail token-score methods (Min-K%, Min-K%++); and discrete state spaces break continuous-diffusion MI methods. Prior DLM-specific work (the concurrent SAMA, ICLR 2026) evaluated only domain fine-tuning with fixed block sizes, which the authors argue both misses the dominant real-world paradigm (instruction tuning) and can inflate apparent MI success when member/non-member sets differ in length or prior likelihood. The audience is the privacy/security community and anyone deploying fine-tuned DLMs with sensitive data. Key Idea: Token-level memorization asymmetry: under masked diffusion training, a token's single-step memorization gain is inversely proportional to the mask ratio (few masked tokens per step → concentrated gradient updates → larger per-token gain). Since the global mask ratio β ~ U(0,1), a member token's cumulative gain over K epochs is a zero-inflated mixture that is provably right-skewed (Theorem 3.2, via AM-GM/Lyapunov inequalities under Assumption 3.1 of monotonically decreasing update strength ϕ(β)), whereas a non-member's gain — stochastic generalization noise — is approximately symmetric. The attack signal is therefore the skewness of the token-level loss-difference distribution between the fine-tuned target and an unfine-tuned reference model, estimated with cyclic (full-coverage permutation) mask sampling and a Pearson's-second-skewness variant weighted at the 15th/85th ECDF percentiles for outlier robustness. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) threat model — grey-box, logits-only access to target θ_tar plus an unfine-tuned reference θ_ref ≈ θ_0 (standard for fine-tuning MI since base checkpoints are open-source); (2) score computation — for R cyclic rounds, permute token indices, partition into disjoint mask batches of size ~ρL (ρ=0.35), compute per-masked-token loss difference Δ_{i,M} = −log p_ref(w_i|x_{M^c}) + log p_tar(w_i|x_{M^c}) (Eq. 5), aggregating over 16 denoising steps for computational parity with baselines; (3) indicator — quantile-weighted skewness A′(x) = mean over tokens of W(s)·(s − median)/σ, with W(s) a sum of two Gaussian kernels anchored at ECDF positions 0.15 and 0.85 (bandwidth 0.1), thresholded at τ. The theoretical framework is a probabilistic analysis of the third central moment of a zero-inflated mixture (δ = J·V, J ~ Bernoulli(0.5), V = ϕ(β) under size-biased density f(β)=2β), extended in Appendix A.3 to the non-i.i.d. case via a mixed-moment decomposition. Critical design decisions: (a) Assumption 3.1 (inverse mask-ratio scaling) is postulated, not derived — it is validated empirically by fixing mask ratios at 0.25/0.50/0.75 and observing confidence/loss gains (Fig. 1, Fig. 3, Fig. 4 on up to 1,000 samples across three domains), a reasonable but indirect justification; (b) cyclic sampling replaces Monte Carlo mask draws to reduce variance and guarantee uniform token coverage — justified by ablation (+1.8 AUC over random sampling); (c) quantile weighting rather than raw skewness — justified by ablation (+2.1 AUC). The i.i.d.-across-epochs approximation in the proof is acknowledged and relaxed, though the relaxed argument reduces to the unproven claim that negative third-order cross-epoch dependence does not dominate. Key Results: On LLaDA-8B-Base with domain fine-tuning (6 epochs, batch 16, three runs averaged), Q-SKEW reaches AUC/TPR@10%FPR/TPR@1%FPR of 83.4/66.1/50.6 (ArXiv), 80.3/57.7/39.7 (WikiText), and 80.7/63.6/47.2 (XSUM), versus the best baseline SAMA at 70.2/34.5/17.6, 70.3/36.4/17.2, and 71.0/40.5/18.2 respectively — a >10-point average AUC margin and ~3× TPR at 1% FPR. On instruction fine-tuning with LLaDA-8B-Instruct: MedQA 72.8 AUC (vs. SAMA 65.1), Alpaca 81.4/61.4/41.6 (vs. 69.1/31.0/11.2), but Tulu-3 only 67.2/13.7/4.3 (vs. SAMA 59.7/12.1/3.7) — marginal in absolute terms. On Dream-7B models, the attack degrades to 63.4 AUC (XSUM DFT) and 59.1 AUC (Tulu-3 IFT), still best-in-table but far weaker. Misaligned reference models cost only 1.3–5.0 AUC. Ablations on WikiText DFT show each component matters but modestly (full 80.3 vs. 77.6–78.5 without components). For PII extraction on TREC (LLaDA-8B-Base, 50 phone + 50 email targets), combining CE ranking with skewness (α=0.1) yields 34% phone / 24% email top-1 ASR vs. 30%/20% for CE alone; skewness alone underperforms CE (22%/16% and 10%/8%). Baselines are current and strong (includes the concurrent SAMA under its original settings, same 16-denoising-step budget). A notable negative-adjacent finding: MIMIR — used by SAMA's evaluation — gives 0.64 average AUC for a trivial loss attack on an un-fine-tuned LLaDA, indicating prior-prior leakage rather than fine-tuning memorization. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (Q-SKEW as a distributional, skewness-based MI indicator) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the inverse mask-ratio memorization phenomenon and the DLM-vs-AR privacy distinction) and a methodological correction (MIMIR benchmark invalidity for fine-tuning MI). The genuinely novel element is shifting the MI signal from per-sample memorization magnitude to the shape (third moment) of the token-level gain distribution, grounded in a diffusion-specific mechanism. The surrounding machinery — reference-model calibration, cyclic coverage sampling, ECDF-based robust weighting, PII-extraction-as-ranking — is competent combination of known techniques adapted to the new architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and cover all three proposed components (cyclic sampling, skewness vs. mean, quantile weighting), with 2–3 AUC contributions each; epoch sweeps (Fig. 2) and reference-model-misalignment tests (Tab. 4) strengthen robustness claims. Three independent runs are averaged, but no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported anywhere — for TPR@1%FPR gaps of a few points (e.g., Tulu-3), statistical support is absent. No code, data splits, or fine-tuning checkpoints are stated as released. Methodological concerns: (1) the ρ=0.35 mask ratio is explicitly chosen to 'maximize the distinction between member and non-member sets' on the same distribution later used for evaluation — a mild Goodhart risk without held-out tuning; (2) PII experiments use only 100 targets and 50 each of two PII types on one model, with ASR differences of 4 points over the CE baseline; (3) the core Assumption 3.1 is validated empirically by its authors rather than derived; (4) evaluation covers only two DLM families (LLaDA, Dream) and six datasets, all fine-tuned by the authors themselves. The MIMIR critique is, by contrast, a rigor positive — it transparently explains why a competing evaluation inflates results. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (attack methods run against fine-tuned models; no system artifact deployed). - Practical: Yes — requires only logit queries and an open-source base model, both freely available; no training or gradient access needed. - Efficient: Query cost is bounded by 16 denoising steps per sample with cyclic mask batches (R rounds × m batches), matched to all baselines' budget, but the skew estimate needs many masked-context forward passes per candidate sample — more expensive than a single-score baseline like Loss. - Effective: For domain fine-tuning, clearly effective (AUC 80–83, TPR@1%FPR 40–50); for instruction fine-tuning on harder mixes (Tulu-3) and on Dream models, effectiveness is weak-to-marginal, so the paper solves the stated problem on a subset of the tested conditions. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 7–8B models and 6 fine-tuning epochs; behavior on 100B-scale DLMs (e.g., LLaDA-2.0), longer fine-tuning, or deduplicated/non-overlapping member sets is claimed-by-plausibility only. Deliverable form: paper only — no library, tool, dataset, or model weights are reported as released. Strengths: - The inverse mask-ratio mechanism is a genuinely diffusion-specific insight that explains why DLM MI differs from AR-LM MI, rather than just transplanting a heuristic; the theory (zero-inflated mixture, third-moment argument) and the empirical validation (fixed-ratio training runs, multiple metrics, three domains) reinforce each other. - The evaluation design fixes a real flaw in the concurrent literature: the MIMIR analysis (Tab. 7) shows a loss attack achieves 0.64–0.81 AUC on an un-fine-tuned model, exposing prior-prior leakage as a confound in SAMA's evaluation, and the authors build leakage-controlled datasets (recent RealTimeData snapshots) in response. - Coverage of both domain and instruction fine-tuning with variable-length data, plus misaligned-reference robustness tests, is a more realistic threat-model sweep than prior DLM MI work. - The PII extension is framed honestly: skewness alone underperforms CE ranking (22% vs. 30% phone ASR), and the paper positions it as a complementary signal with qualitative analysis of which PII subtypes each method recovers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section states (1) only a small set of publicly available, fine-tunable DLMs exists, so evaluation is restricted to current mainstream models, and (2) the DLM landscape is evolving rapidly, so generalization to future diffusion architectures and training mechanisms is unknown. This is direct and appropriately brief, though it omits the weaker IFT results and the small PII evaluation scale as limitations in their own right — the paper reports those numbers transparently in the tables but does not flag them as weak spots. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The instruction-fine-tuning story is uneven: Tulu-3 (67.2 AUC, 4.3 TPR@1%FPR) is close to useless as an attack, and Dream models degrade ~17 AUC below LLaDA on DFT; the paper does not explain when the inverse-mask-ratio signal survives — e.g., how instruction-tuning loss weighting or data diversity interacts with the zero-inflation mechanism. - The theoretical gap between Assumption 3.1 and practice: ϕ(β) monotonically decreasing is empirically supported but never derived from the training dynamics; additionally, the non-i.i.d. extension (Appendix A.3) reduces to assuming the mixed third-order term does not dominate — asserted, not bounded. - The ρ=0.35 mask ratio is tuned on the evaluation signal itself; no cross-dataset hyperparameter transfer is shown for MI (the α tuning for PII does use a 16-record hold-out, an inconsistency in rigor standards). - Member/non-member set construction and deduplication details (overlap between ArXiv/WikiText snapshots and LLaDA's pretraining corpus) are addressed only via recency of the data; no n-gram or embedding-based contamination audit is reported. - PII extraction uses 100 targets on one model and one dataset; the 4-point ASR gain over the CE baseline is well within plausible seed-level noise, and no variance is reported. - No defense evaluation (e.g., DP fine-tuning, early stopping) — even a single mitigation experiment would show whether the attack signal is erodible or structural. Bottom Line: For anyone studying or auditing privacy in diffusion language models, this is currently the strongest and best-motivated attack in the literature and worth reading in full; for practitioners seeking defenses or guaranteed-privacy deployment, it is an early warning signal rather than a usable tool, and the instruction-tuning results suggest its practical bite is narrower than the headline DFT numbers imply.
