GE-Act 2.0: Pretraining and Scaling a World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation (46 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GE-Act 2.0, a world–action model for robotic manipulation in which every trainable generative and action component is pretrained from scratch on manipulation data, and demonstrates systematic scaling of its zero-shot, no-fine-tuning capability across 100 real-robot tasks. - Why it's important: Existing world–action models typically bolt action heads onto inherited pretrained video generators, leaving it unknown whether the world–action pretraining itself scales; this work directly measures how manipulation capability grows with data volume, the central open question for robot foundation models. - How it does it: A control-oriented autoencoder (CoAE, 64× downsampling, 24 tokens/frame) supplies a compact latent, a single-step conditional MeanFlow visual planner (SVP) produces a fully denoised future in one differentiable pass so the planner and inverse dynamics model (IDM) can be pretrained separately on complementary data, and KASO co-training filters generated futures for action-mode compatibility with the recorded action to avoid the "validity gap." - The good: The scaling evidence is broad and consistent — suite-level zero-shot OOD success rises from 17.1% to 44.1% (G1-OP) and 13.4% to 31.1% (G2-90D) as co-training data grows from 300 to 30,000 hours, with gains in 19/20 and 18/20 skill groups, plus a strong skill-coverage/success correlation (Pearson r = 0.80, Spearman ρ = 0.85). - The missing: The data-scaling comparison is explicitly not compute-matched (each rung trains one epoch or until budget), there are no error bars or multi-seed real-robot results (10 trials per task), no head-to-head zero-shot comparison against prior WAM/VLA baselines under the identical real-robot protocol, and no public code or weights are stated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for robotics researchers working on world models, VLA pretraining, or robot data scaling — it is currently the most detailed public account of from-scratch WAM scaling — but practitioners seeking a deployable policy or reproducible artifact will find only a project page.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (75) is the highest in the cluster — the one-step MeanFlow planner enabling decoupled SVP/IDM pretraining and the falsifiable validity-gap formulation are genuine contributions, supported by a matched real-robot ablation and a toy system with disclosed seed variance. Rigor (65) is undermined by no external baseline under the zero-shot OOD real-robot protocol, 10-trial cells without variance reporting, un-ablated KASO hyperparameters, and no code/weight release (Impact 40), leaving the headline 44.1% self-referential. Completeness (70) benefits from unusually direct limitation acknowledgment, but Resilience (65) drops on the same-ecosystem simulation benchmark and untested RL-diversity claims. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*74 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*40 = 67.

Problem & Motivation: Robot labs building generalist manipulation policies face a data bottleneck: fully labeled teleoperated demonstrations are expensive, while action-free human/egocentric video and unlabeled deployment rollouts (including failures) are abundant but hard to exploit under direct imitation objectives. World–action models (WAMs) promise to use all three data types by predicting future visual states and decoding actions from them, but existing WAMs (VPP, DreamZero, GE-Act 1.0, LingBot-VA) inherit latents and generators from pretrained video foundation models (Cosmos, Wan), and their action heads are architecturally tied to multi-step generators — preventing standalone IDM pretraining on instruction-free trajectories and leaving the pretraining-and-scaling question of the WAM as a whole unaddressed. A second, evaluation-side problem motivates the paper: most WAM/VLA evaluations use task-specific supervised fine-tuning, sometimes under in-domain lighting and objects, which entangles pretrained capability with adaptation data. Key Idea: The core insight is that one-step generation is the unlock for decoupled world–action pretraining: because the SVP maps noise to a complete future in a single differentiable forward pass (conditional MeanFlow with masked conditioning tokens and a JVP-computed average-velocity identity), action gradients can flow through the generated future to update both the generator and the IDM during co-training without back-propagating through K sequential denoising steps. This makes it feasible to pretrain the generator on action-free video and the IDM on instruction-free trajectories separately, then connect them with KASO, which resolves the "validity gap" — the mismatch that arises when a sampled future depicts a different behavior mode than the recorded action it is paired with (formally, ẑ ⊥ a | (o, s, c) under independent marginals) — by best-of-N scoring candidates in action space with the active IDM at high probe noise and applying the generated-video action loss only to the most compatible candidate. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) CoAE: a framewise 2D autoencoder (initialized from 128-channel DC-AE, expanded to 512 channels, 64× spatial downsampling) trained with reconstruction (pixel + LPIPS + adversarial) plus cosine alignment to three frozen teachers (SigLIP 2, V-JEPA 2.1, DINOv3), evaluated by frozen two-layer inverse-dynamics probing (action MAE) and caption-matching accuracy. (2) SVP pretraining: a 2.51B-parameter multi-view DiT trained from random initialization with a conditional MeanFlow objective (Eq. 6–13) over masked dense (4 frames over a 52-frame horizon) and sparse (2 frames) future latents, conditioned on gated text-span states from a frozen Qwen3.5-2B VLM; 39,000 hours of instruction–video data. (3) IDM pretraining: a 0.56B-parameter flow-matching action head trained on 32,000 hours of action-labeled trajectories with recorded futures. (4) KASO co-training on 30,000 hours: per step, N=4 candidate futures are sampled gradient-free, probed at t_p = 0.95 with shared action noise, the lowest-energy candidate (Eq. 19) is replayed with gradients, and the update combines the selected E2E loss with retained SVP and IDM pretraining losses (E2E+PT backbone). A four-mode Gaussian toy system isolates the validity gap mechanism, and a controlled real-robot ablation (E2E vs. E2E+PT vs. KASO on a 300-hour alignment stage) tests the objective. Design decisions are mostly well-justified: the one-step generator rationale is argued and ablated, the action-space (vs. pixel-space) compatibility criterion is reasoned, and the toy experiment includes seed-variance disclosure. Weaker justification: k=1, N=4, and t_p=0.95 are stated without sensitivity analysis, and CoAE's "from scratch" claim is softened by DC-AE weight transfer. Key Results: On the 100-task, 20-skill-group real-robot suite (10 trials per task per embodiment per scale, OOD scenes/objects/lighting, no per-task SFT), G1-OP success rises 17.1% → 22.6% → 27.3% → 44.1% and G2-90D 13.4% → 21.0% → 23.5% → 31.1% across 300/1,200/5,000/30,000 co-training hours, with no saturation at the top scale; nonzero-SR tasks grow from 39 to 76 (G1-OP) and 24 to 72 (G2-90D). G2-90D, <2% of co-training data, gains 17.7 points, with skills having under two hours of embodiment-specific data (e.g., Flip 20.0% with 1.2 h) reaching nonzero success, suggesting cross-embodiment transfer. Skill-coverage vs. success fits 1.94 logit units per decade of data (r = 0.80, ρ = 0.85 over 19 groups, Close excluded). Grounding: Follow Score ≥90% on object/color/shape/position, but 82.5%/65.7% on size and 13.3%/26.7% on order — mirroring the 0.96%/0.67%/0.13% corpus frequencies. The controlled ablation shows KASO at 37.5% vs. 22.5% (E2E+PT) four-object pick success and 40% vs. 12% single-object. Simulation: RoboTwin Hard 60.52% vs. π0.5's 47.90%; GenieSim-Instruction average 0.770 vs. ACoT-VLA 0.757; LIBERO-Plus 80.4%, below π0.5's 84.4% with clear weaknesses on background (60.5% vs. 94.1%) and robot-state perturbations. Baselines in simulation (π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, StarVLA, ACoT-VLA, LingBot-VLA 2.0) are current and credible; the real-robot suite has no external baseline. Tested at industrial-lab scale (tens of thousands of hours, real dual-arm robots), not toy scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (native single-step robot world model from random initialization enabling decoupled SVP/IDM pretraining) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first systematic zero-shot OOD scaling curve for a from-scratch WAM, plus the skill-coverage–success relationship and sparse-embodiment transfer) + NEW FORMULATION (the validity gap as a conditional-independence mismatch between a generated future and a recorded action). The ingredients are individually known — MeanFlow is adapted from Geng et al., multi-teacher alignment from REPA/VA-VAE, best-of-K selection appears in concurrent work (Gladstone et al., 2026), and the multi-scale temporal schedule is borrowed from Act2Goal — so the genuine novelty lies in the system-level composition and the honest scaling study, not in any single component. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is unusually rigorous for an industrial report: a controlled real-robot ablation isolates KASO's contribution under matched initialization, data, and protocol; a toy system with disclosed seed spread (Appendix B.7 admits seed 0 is favorable and gives per-seed numbers for seeds 0–4) supports the validity-gap mechanism; hyperparameters, data mixtures, and per-task results for all 100 tasks × 4 scales × 2 embodiments are published in appendices. However: no confidence intervals or significance tests accompany any real-robot number (10 trials per cell makes differences of a few points noisy); the KASO ablation covers only simple pick protocols; the scaling ladder is not compute-matched (acknowledged); hyperparameters like k, N, t_p lack ablation; correlation of coverage with success is explicitly associational, not causal (acknowledged); CoAE "from scratch" involves DC-AE weight transfer; and no code, weights, or data release is stated — only a project page (https://ge-act-v2.github.io/). No Goodhart-style development-on-eval concern arises for the real-robot suite since it is held-out OOD, but the GenieSim-Instruction benchmark is from the same ecosystem (Genie Sim), which warrants mild caution. Deployability: (EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile):** - Practical: Runs on real dual-arm robots (G1-OP, G2-90D) with a 2.51B SVP + 0.56B IDM plus a frozen 2.72B VLM — feasible on high-end GPUs, though per-step inference requires a VLM forward pass plus one-step generation and 5-step IDM integration; no latency figures are reported. - Efficient: One-step generation avoids K-step denoising inside the control loop and the 64× autoencoder cuts to 24 tokens/frame, both explicitly motivated by control-loop cost; relative wall-clock cost vs. VLA baselines is not measured. - Effective: 44.1% zero-shot OOD suite-level success is far from deployment-grade for unassisted operation, but the evidence (OOD protocol, follow-vs-success decomposition, conflict stress tests) shows genuine pretrained capability rather than a fine-tuning proxy. - Scalable: Scaling to 30k hours is demonstrated and unsaturated, but the 10× further claim is extrapolation — the paper itself notes egocentric-video scaling remains untested. The work delivers no public software artifact, dataset, or weights; it stops at paper + project-page form. Strengths: - The single-step MeanFlow planner as a differentiable train–deployment interface is a genuine architectural insight: it converts "can we pretrain the IDM on unlabeled rollouts" from an intractable backprop-through-sampling problem into a solvable one, and the paper clearly traces why multi-step generators foreclose this. - The validity-gap formulation is a clean, falsifiable contribution — the observation that better generation does not fix mode mismatch between sampled futures and recorded actions (Eq. 18) — supported by both a controlled toy system with disclosed seed variance and a matched real-robot ablation. - The evaluation protocol (100 atomic tasks, zero-shot OOD, fixed across scaling checkpoints, follow-score/success decomposition) is a model for measuring pretrained capability rather than fine-tuned specialist performance, and the full per-task result grid is published. - The finding that a <2%-representation embodiment gains 17.7 points, and that skill coverage predicts success at 1.94 logits/decade, are actionable empirical results for anyone allocating robot data-collection budgets. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that egocentric video is underexploited relative to its availability; that the model is System-1 only, lacking deliberation, long-horizon planning, memory, and self-correction; that the scaling comparison is a practical end-to-end comparison, not a matched-compute isolation of data volume; that scaling trajectories are not uniformly monotonic (especially G2-90D); that the coverage–success relationship establishes association, not causation; that the toy-system figure reflects one favorable seed with nontrivial spread; and that LIBERO-Plus background and robot-state robustness remain weak. They confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No external baseline under the identical zero-shot OOD real-robot protocol — π0.5 or GE-Act 1.0 evaluated on the same 100 tasks would establish whether 44.1% is competitive or merely self-referential; simulation comparisons partially compensate but each includes an SFT stage. (2) No trial-count justification or variance reporting for 10-trial cells; several headline ablation deltas (e.g., 37.5% vs. 22.5% over 40 trials) sit within plausible binomial noise. (3) KASO hyperparameters (N=4, k=1, t_p=0.95) and the loss-coefficient triple (1, 0.1, 1) are un-ablated, so the mechanism's sensitivity is unknown. (4) The GenieSim-Instruction benchmark and its training data come from the authors' own simulator ecosystem — a mild self-evaluation concern the paper does not flag. (5) The "pretraining from scratch" framing coexists with DC-AE initialization and a frozen pretrained Qwen3.5 VLM, so not all capability originates in manipulation-data pretraining; the paper's contribution framing slightly overstates purity. (6) The claim that KASO preserves action diversity "particularly important for reinforcement learning" is asserted but never tested with any downstream RL experiment. (7) Compute cost, inference latency, and model FLOPs are absent, blocking efficiency comparison with VLAs. Bottom Line: For researchers designing world–action models or planning robot data collection, this is a must-read for its single-step-planner architecture, validity-gap analysis, and the most granular public zero-shot scaling data in manipulation; for practitioners wanting a usable policy, reproducible artifact, or head-to-head baseline comparison, stronger alternatives (π0.5, GR00T) currently offer more deployable ground truth.

CAMP: Coherent Alignment of Multimodal Prototypes for Explainable Complementary Learning

AL Pellicer, EM Kenny, S Lamba, S Sharma… · openreview.net · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CAMP, a prototype-based multimodal classifier that aligns class-wise prototype-usage distributions across modalities via entropic optimal transport, and shows a sub-1M-parameter head on frozen encoders matches or exceeds >100M-parameter AutoML ensembles on 16 multimodal benchmarks while exposing case-based explanations by design. - Why it's important: High-stakes deployments (clinical triage, fraud detection) that fuse complementary modalities (e.g., X-ray plus medical history) increasingly require auditable decision evidence (e.g., under the EU AI Act), which large black-box multimodal transformers and post-hoc explainers do not faithfully provide. - How it does it: The core trick is aligning modalities at the level of class-conditioned prototype-usage distributions (Sinkhorn OT between per-class discrete measures on the prototype bank) rather than at the instance level, so modalities agree on aggregate class definitions while retaining per-instance complementary evidence; margin, coverage, purity, and anchor regularizers keep the shared prototype support non-degenerate. - The good: The ablation evidence is unusually tight: a cumulative ladder plus leave-one-out removals show every loss block improves or degrades all 16 datasets consistently, with mechanistic diagnostics (dead-prototype rate 26.6%→2.3%, cross-modal disagreement 0.23→0.12) that match each block's intended role. - The missing: The missing-modality robustness story is selectively presented — the appendix grid contains settings where CAMP-F collapses below weak baselines (e.g., Wine tab-drop: 0.238 vs. XGBoost's 0.667 and AutoGluon's 0.774) that the main text does not surface, and no code release is mentioned. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in interpretable/prototype-based multimodal learning and practitioners needing auditable tabular+text+image classifiers under tight compute budgets; skippable for those working purely on descriptive vision–language alignment.

Problem & Motivation: Multimodal learning largely targets descriptive paired views (image–caption) where instance-level contrastive alignment is well-posed. Many deployed decision systems instead combine complementary modalities — a data-table row with structured covariates plus optional text/images — where each modality carries distinct, label-relevant evidence (positive conditional mutual information I(Y; X(m) | X(M\{m})) > 0) and inter-modality mutual information can be near zero. The authors call this setting Complementary Multimodal Classification (CMC). Stakeholders in healthcare, fraud, and content moderation need both accuracy and faithful explanations; existing CMC systems are large AutoML ensembles or transformers with post-hoc explanations (which Rudin-style arguments deem unfaithful), while prototype models — the natural interpretable-by-design alternative — fail under a single shared similarity metric because asymmetric, class-conditional modality evidence induces prototype collapse, modality dominance, dead/impure prototypes, and drift under outliers. No prior prototype framework, to the authors' knowledge, targets multimodal tasks at all. Key Idea: Align modalities at the distributional class level, not the instance level: for each class, build a discrete measure over the class's prototypes from each modality's soft assignments, and minimize pairwise Sinkhorn-regularized optimal transport between these usage measures. This makes modalities "coherent at the aggregate class level while remaining complementary at the instance level," sidestepping the alignment bias that instance-level contrastive objectives impose on low-MI modality pairs. The OT term is only meaningful because companion losses (geometry, allocation, anchors) keep the prototype support separated, utilized, class-specialized, and stable — a coupled-regularization argument the paper makes explicit. Methodology: CAMP maps each modality through an encoder f(m) and projection π(m) into a shared d-dim space, fuses observed modalities via per-instance scalar gates g(m) = softmax over observed modalities (late gated fusion, no imputation for missing modalities), L2-normalizes the fused embedding, and scores it against K prototypes per class; class logits are the mean similarity to the top-r prototypes of that class (Eq. 5). Training minimizes CE plus four blocks: (1) Lmm, class-wise entropic OT (ε=0.05, 3 Sinkhorn iterations) between modality-specific prototype-usage measures ν(m)_c; (2) Lgeo with pull/push margins plus intra-class (ρ_in) and inter-class (ρ_out) prototype–prototype separation; (3) Lalloc = KL(average usage ‖ uniform) + purity entropy to kill dead and impure prototypes; (4) Lanchor, an outlier-gated fallback to learnable class anchors tied to prototype means. Auxiliary losses are linearly ramped over ~8 epochs; frozen regime (~660K params) trains only projections, gates, prototypes, anchors; end-to-end (CAMP-E) uses a two-stage schedule with differential learning rates. Critical design decisions: gated vs. attention fusion (justified: wins 15/16 datasets and preserves per-modality channel integrity, though the median gain over concatenation is only +0.005); distributional rather than instance-level alignment (well-justified both theoretically and by the MRR gains); and theory scoped to the frozen-encoder regime (honestly acknowledged). The theory composes classical results — Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality, Pinsker's inequality, margin/Lipschitz arguments, EMA anchor stability — into CMC-specific guarantees (Theorems 4.1, B.1–B.6, Proposition C.1); the authors explicitly state no new OT theorems are proven. Key Results: On 16 public CMC datasets from the AutoGluon multimodal benchmark suite (train sizes 573–100,000; Tab+Text, Image+Text, Image+Tab, and tri-modal), with Swin-L + DeBERTa-v3 frozen embeddings for all head methods, 5 seeds, and Optuna tuning (50 trials/dataset): CAMP-F averages 0.814 vs. AutoGluon's 0.808 (matching/exceeding AG on 11/16 datasets) with ~660K vs. >100M parameters, and beats an identical-feature CE MLP by a wide MRR margin (0.448 vs. 0.174) and the strongest prototype baseline ProtoMedX (0.185). CAMP-E (end-to-end) achieves the best score on all 16 datasets, average 0.842, with the largest gains on small/imbalanced tasks: +0.068 AUC on PTech (749 samples), +0.045 on COVID (707), +0.043 on Artm (573), +0.033 on WikiArt. Across 76 missing-modality configurations, CAMP-E leads on no-drop (0.842), single-drop (0.724), and all-config (0.634) averages, though AutoGluon edges the worst-case average (0.2812 vs. 0.2802). Ablations: cumulative ladder from Proto-Classic (0.7445) to full objective (0.8139), +0.0694, with 16/16 dataset wins at every step; OT is the largest marginal contributor on 13/16 datasets; leave-one-out removal of any block degrades all 16 datasets. Inference throughput is 1,809 samples/sec vs. 50–100 for the AutoML ensemble. Baselines (AutoGluon, Tabular-Text Transformer, XGBoost, linear probe, ProtoMedX) are current and appropriate. One counter-pattern the paper understates: in the Wine tab-drop grid, CAMP-F scores 0.238 — far below XGBoost (0.667) and AutoGluon (0.774) — an unexplained failure mode for the robustness narrative. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (formalizing CMC and its prototype failure modes), NEW METHOD (CAMP, particularly class-wise entropic-OT alignment of prototype-usage distributions across modalities — the genuinely novel mechanism), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a sub-1M-parameter interpretable head rivaling >100M AutoML ensembles). The remaining machinery — prototype banks with pull/push margins, coverage/purity regularizers, gated late fusion, Sinkhorn OT, anchor stabilization — is a competent composition of existing techniques; the theory explicitly re-packages classical results, and the main novelty lies in the alignment granularity and its application to the complementary regime. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong: a fixed cumulative ladder, leave-one-out necessity checks (all 16/16 degradations), mechanistic diagnostics mapped to each loss block (dead-prototype %, purity entropy, W_ε disagreement, similarity margin), fusion-variant comparisons (Table 18), backbone sensitivity (Table 19), prototype-count stress test (mean delta within ±0.001 for K∈{1..32}), and challenge-slice analyses. Error bars are mean±std over 5 seeds; hyperparameters tuned per-dataset with Optuna (50 trials), with the authors reporting defaults land within ±1.2% of tuned configurations. No code, data, or model release is mentioned. Concerns: the explanation utility rests on a single case study (Airbnb test case 744) with the authors conceding more case studies were omitted "due to time constraints"; ProtoMedX, the closest baseline, is from overlapping authorship; the theoretical guarantees cover only the frozen-encoder regime while headline SOTA claims come from end-to-end runs; and robustness claims cherry-pick favorable drop configurations in the main text. The venue header claims ICML 2026 (PMLR 306) proceedings via OpenReview; I could not independently verify publication status. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a small THEORETICAL component). Practical: Yes — all experiments ran on a single NVIDIA V100 32GB, and the frozen-head regime needs only ~660K trainable parameters on top of standard pretrained encoders. Efficient: Training costs more than a plain MLP head (80.3s/epoch frozen, 220s end-to-end vs. 4.2s for the MLP) due to Sinkhorn alignment, but inference is cheap (1,809 samples/sec vs. 50–100 for AutoGluon) since OT is training-only. Effective: Strong benchmark evidence for accuracy and missing-modality robustness; effectiveness of the explanations is unproven — only computational faithfulness of the fixed-support probe is guaranteed, with no human evaluation. Scalable: Untested beyond ~100K training examples; the OT term scales with classes × modality pairs × Sinkhorn iterations, so very large class counts or modality universes are unexamined, and end-to-end fine-tuning cost grows with backbone size. Deliverable: currently paper-form only; the method (Algorithm E.2, G.1) and hyperparameter tables are fully specified, but no released library, checkpoint, or dataset artifact is stated. Strengths: - The instance-vs-distribution alignment distinction is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution: aligning class-conditioned prototype-usage measures rather than embeddings preserves complementarity while enforcing cross-modal coherence, and the MRR jump (0.448 vs. 0.174–0.185 for CE-MLP and prototype baselines) shows case-based ranking is what actually improves. - Ablation discipline is exemplary: every added block wins on every dataset, every removed block degrades every dataset, and mechanistic diagnostics (dead %, purity, W_ε, margin) confirm each loss does what it claims — this rules out the common "kitchen-sink regularizer" confound. - The theory is honest about its scope: authors state plainly that the proofs compose classical tools and apply only to the frozen-encoder prototype head, matching the empirical design rather than overselling. - The parameter-efficiency result is practically meaningful: ~660K trainable parameters matching a >100M-parameter AutoML ensemble on 11/16 datasets is a real capability for API-constrained or compute-limited settings. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) formal guarantees cover only the frozen-encoder regime, with end-to-end gains remaining empirical; (2) the fixed-support probe guarantees model-internal computational faithfulness, but user studies are needed to validate human-facing explanation efficacy; (3) evaluation targets discrete classification with strong pretrained encoders, leaving regression, continuous concept drift, batch-composition studies, and human-centered evaluation to future work. They also concede only one case study was provided due to time constraints. This is a direct, non-evasive limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Selective robustness reporting: the main text highlights HAM and PetFinder drop configurations where CAMP-F leads AutoGluon, but Table 23 contains Wine tab-drop where CAMP-F scores 0.238 against AutoGluon's 0.774 and XGBoost's 0.667 — a severe failure of the gating mechanism that goes unanalyzed and unacknowledged. - No code or artifact release is stated, which materially limits reproducibility given the 50-trial Optuna protocol and multi-block loss with many hyperparameters. - The interpretability claim rests on one qualitative example; no quantitative explanation-quality metrics (e.g., deletion/insertion curves vs. LIME/SHAP), no user study, and no comparison against other interpretable multimodal baselines beyond the authors' own ProtoMedX. - The CMC formalization (positive conditional MI) is never measured per dataset; whether the 16 benchmarks genuinely instantiate complementarity versus mere feature heterogeneity is asserted, not verified. - The worst-case robustness aggregate (where AutoGluon slightly leads, 0.2812 vs. 0.2802) is dominated by all-drop chance-level floors, and the paper does not dissect which single-drop regimes drive the CAMP–AG gap in either direction. Bottom Line: A practitioner building auditable multimodal classifiers on tabular-plus-text/image data should read this — the distributional OT-alignment trick and the frozen-head parameter-efficiency result are immediately actionable — but should independently probe the missing-modality edge cases and wait for a code release, as the explanation-utility claims rest on a single anecdote and the closest baseline comes from the same group.

Efficient distinctiveness maximization in datasets assemblage: from homogeneous to heterogeneous datasets

T Wang, S Huang, Z Bao, JS Culpepper, V Dedeoglu… · link.springer.com · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the distinctiveness maximization (DM) problem for datasets assemblage — selecting a budget-constrained subset of purchasable datasets that maximizes the number of distinct tuples returned under a user query set and target schema — and delivers greedy algorithms (MLG, J-MLG) that use learned distinctiveness estimation instead of exact tuple-wise computation. - Why it's important: Data marketplaces and lake-based analytics require acquiring multiple overlapping datasets under real budgets, but per-dataset relevance ranking ignores cross-dataset redundancy, so buyers routinely pay for duplicate tuples; DM directly optimizes value per dollar of purchased data. - How it does it: Each dataset is encoded offline into compact column-set embeddings (built on the IRIS summarization framework); a learned model estimates distinctiveness from query-set and query-aware dataset embeddings, and learned tuple-level/column-level merging functions compose summaries of multiple datasets (or of join results, via cross-attention over join graphs) without materializing tuples. - The good: The learned estimator achieves q-error of roughly 1.1–1.9 versus 11.6–12.7 for an adapted IRIS baseline across all percentiles on five evaluation pools, while preserving the exact-greedy distinctiveness ratio (e.g., D-ratio 0.997 vs. 0.998 for physical materialization on IMDB) at up to four orders of magnitude speedup. - The missing: The evaluation rests on synthetic candidate sets produced by controlled sampling from a handful of data pools (5 evaluation pools in Scenario 1, 2 in Scenario 2) with default repository size of only 20 candidates, and the D-ratio metric uses the authors' own exact-greedy output as ground truth — no large-scale real marketplace or third-party benchmark validation is reported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for database researchers and engineers working on data markets, dataset discovery, or learned cardinality estimation, because it defines a new, well-motivated problem and shows how learned summaries can replace exhaustive set-union computation; skippable for readers outside data preparation and lake systems.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is held back by Rigor (65) and Resilience (62): the D-ratio ground truth is the authors' own exact greedy rather than any optimality reference, candidate repositories are synthetically sampled from the same pool families used for pre-training (mild Goodhart risk and untested cross-domain generalization), no error bars are reported on D-ratio, and the hand-set joinability thresholds γ1/γ2 lack sensitivity analysis despite Scenario 2 depending entirely on them. Novelty (75) is the strongest dimension — a crisp new problem (budgeted distinctiveness maximization) with NP-hardness, an honest approximation analysis, and a new learned-relational operator (cross-attention join-summary merging) that constitutes a substantive journal extension. Completeness (65) and Impact (70) are supported by released code, a benchmark-generation protocol, and a persuasive alternative-design study (794.8× speedup at matched D-ratio), but the synthetic-repository evaluation caps real-world evidence. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*70 = 67.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations purchasing data from repositories (AWS Marketplace, Snowflake data shares, open data lakes) need a collection of datasets that jointly covers a target schema and answers a query set. Existing dataset discovery methods (table union search like SANTOS/Starmie, join search like JOSIE/DeepJoin, keyword systems like D3L) rank datasets individually by relevance to a query or exemplar, which ignores tuple overlap between retrieved datasets and assumes the user can afford everything found. Under a purchase budget, individually relevant datasets can be highly redundant (the paper's Example 1: dataset d1 adds zero new tuples after d5 is bought). The missing piece is a joint selection criterion — distinctiveness, the number of distinct tuples in the union of query results over the selected set — that quantifies each dataset's incremental value given the others. The paper distinguishes Scenario 1, where datasets matching the target schema exist in the repository, from Scenario 2 (new in this journal extension), where candidates must be constructed by joining partially matching heterogeneous datasets. Key Idea: Distinctiveness of a candidate set is a budgeted maximum coverage objective over query-result tuples, so a greedy algorithm has an approximation guarantee — but exact marginal-gain computation requires tuple-wise union checks across all candidate/query combinations, which is intractable. The core trick is to replace exact union computation with learned estimation over precomputed compact summaries: (i) a learned function estimates the fraction of tuples satisfying the query set directly from embeddings, capturing overlap among query results, and (ii) learned merging functions — operating at tuple level (embedding-level fusion of two datasets' column-set embeddings) and, for joins, column level (cross-attention over a join graph) — approximate the summary of a merged set without ever examining actual tuples. This converts an O(|d|²|D|³) combinatorial computation into a feed-forward neural network evaluation per greedy step. Methodology: The pipeline has an offline phase and an online greedy loop, formalized as DM: max D(S,Q) = |∪_{d∈S} Q(d)| subject to Σ p(d) ≤ B. Hardness: Theorem 1 proves NP-hardness via a reduction from Maximum Coverage (each MC subset becomes a dataset, elements become tuples, a single unrestricted query makes Q(d) = d; Scenario 2 reduces to Scenario 1 via singleton join collections). The baseline EXG greedily selects the dataset with best marginal-distinctiveness-per-price, using exact tuple unions, achieving a (1−1/e)/2 approximation ratio (Theorem 2, by reduction to budgeted maximum coverage of Khuller et al. and returning the better of the greedy set and the single best dataset). MLG replaces exact computation with five learned components: (1) offline data summaries via IRIS — CORDS-based correlation graphs select cliques of ≤2 columns, and a quantize/embed/ReLU row-embedding function ψ(·) is averaged over rows of each projection to produce column-set embeddings (4 KB budget, η=128 dims); (2) query-aware dataset embeddings built by iteratively merging per-query dataset embeddings through a fully connected layer φd; (3) query-set embeddings eQ via an analogous iterative layer φq over per-query embeddings of predicate bounds; (4) distinctiveness estimation D(êQ_d, eQ) = δ(φ3(δ(φ1(·)) ⊙ δ(φ2(·)))), trained with MSE loss against exact values; (5) tuple-level merging δ(φe([e_C^i, e_C^j])) ≈ e_C^{i,j}, trained with MSE against true merged embeddings. For Scenario 2, a hypergraph index (fastText name-similarity edges plus bidirectional Jaccard Set Containment content-similarity edges, requiring both thresholds) identifies joinable collections; join-result size is estimated with the classical Selinger-style formula; column-level merging uses a dataset-level encoder, bidirectional cross-attention per join edge, and a fusion layer, trained with symmetric Chamfer distance against summaries of physically materialized joins. Critical design decisions: reusing IRIS's pre-training paradigm (justified by avoiding per-dataset training, but inherits IRIS's assumptions about quantization capacity); modeling merging at the summary level rather than tuple level (justified empirically by ~2% D-ratio gain over no-TM and order-of-magnitude runtime gain); restricting Scenario 2 construction to connected subgraphs of a pre-built graph index with pruning of non-joinable column pairs (complexity O(|C| + |C|·(|D_J| + |E_DJ|)), reasonable but sensitive to threshold choices γ1=0.7, γ2=0.1, which are hand-set without ablation). Key Results: On Scenario 1 (24 real pools from IRIS plus RealEstate; 19 pre-training / 5 evaluation; candidate sets of 20 datasets by default, up to 160; up to 36M rows per pool, e.g., CastInfo): DE's q-error spans 1.139–1.876 across all percentiles versus 11.629–12.658 for adapted IRIS — more than an order of magnitude better. MLG matches EXG's distinctiveness closely on several pools and exceeds MLGIRIS by up to 13 percentage points in D-ratio (tuple-level merging adds ~2% over MLGnoTM). Runtime: MLG is at least two orders of magnitude faster than EXG and other baselines across all swept parameters, reaching up to four orders of magnitude; DE alone is up to three orders of magnitude faster than EXG and 2–4× faster than IRIS. Scenario 2 (PRICE pools; IMDB with 62M rows and NewRealEstate; repositories up to 200 datasets, τ joins up to 5): J-MLG attains up to 20% higher D-ratio than J-MLGPRICE as |Q| grows and up to 80% higher as τ grows, with up to two orders of magnitude speedup. The alternative-design study is the most convincing table: on IMDB, J-MLG achieves D-ratio 0.997 at 3.66 s versus J-MLGMat's 0.998 at 2909 s (794.8× faster), J-MLGPRICE's 0.935 at 304 s, and J-MLGPessEst's 0.940 at 414 s. The downstream case study (two tasks from prior work, HR classification and House price regression): assemblage with MLG/EXG yields AUC 63.5% vs. 60.3% for D3L discovery on HR (5,325 vs. 3,196 distinct tuples) and RMSE 0.569 vs. 0.601 on House (110,404 vs. 52,472 distinct tuples), with MLG selecting exactly the same datasets as EXG in both tasks. Hardware: one Xeon server, 512 GB RAM, two Tesla P100 GPUs. Baselines are current and appropriate for the estimation component (IRIS, PRICE, PessEst, D3L), though no competing subset-selection optimizers (e.g., submodular maximization under knapsack variants, or the (1−1/e) enumeration algorithm of Khuller et al., whose exclusion is argued on cost grounds) are compared. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (budgeted distinctiveness maximization in datasets assemblage, with an explicit price model), NEW METHOD (learned distinctiveness estimation with tuple-level and column-level summary merging, including cross-attention-based join-summary composition), and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (systematic generation protocol controlling tuple overlap across datasets and query-result overlap, released as a benchmark). Genuinely novel is the reformulation of dataset value as set-union cardinality across queries and datasets and the learned merging of summaries to avoid materialization; the greedy selection loop, the coverage-reduction proofs, the Selinger join-size formula, the graph-index joinability discovery, and the IRIS summarization backbone are standard machinery competently recombined. This is a journal extension of a WWW 2025 paper; the Scenario 2 machinery (graph index, J-EXG/J-MLG, column-level merging, new experiments) is the new content. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: MLGnoTM isolates tuple-level merging, MLGIRIS isolates the estimator, J-MLGMat isolates column-level merging against physical materialization, and J-MLGPessEst/J-MLGPRICE isolate the estimation approach. Parameter sweeps cover |Q|, budget B-ratio, |D|, sampling rate, overlap ratio, and number of joins across two scenarios. The NP-hardness proof and the (1−1/e)/2 approximation proof are correct modulo standard reduction to budgeted maximum coverage. Source code is publicly released (github.com/DataAutonomyLab/DM) and the underlying data pools are from public sources (IRIS, PRICE repos). Methodological concerns: (1) runtime is averaged over five runs, but no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for D-ratio; (2) the D-ratio ground truth is the authors' own EXG, so the accuracy metric measures fidelity to their own exact algorithm, not to true optimality — no optimal or stronger-approximation reference on small instances is provided; (3) candidate repositories are synthetically sampled from single pools with controlled overlap, so real-market overlap distributions are untested; (4) Scenario 1 evaluation uses only 5 pools and Scenario 2 only 2 pools (IMDB, NewRealEstate), all adjacent to the pre-training corpora, leaving cross-domain generalization unquantified; (5) the model is trained on the same pool families it is evaluated on in several cases (per-pool evaluation), raising mild Goodhart risk. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (learned methods run end-to-end on real data pools with a released system). Practical: Runs on a single CPU server with two 16 GB GPUs (P100-era); column-set summary budget of 4 KB per dataset makes offline summarization cheap. Efficient: Orders-of-magnitude cheaper than exact greedy at selection time (e.g., 3.66 s vs. 2909 s on IMDB); offline cost includes IRIS-style pre-training plus per-pool fine-tuning data generation, whose total cost is not separately reported. Effective: Evidence shows the selected sets match the exact greedy's distinctiveness and improve downstream ML metrics versus a discovery baseline, but only on synthetic repositories and two downstream tasks — a proxy for real marketplace value. Scalable: Sweeps reach 160–200 candidate datasets and 5 joins; the claimed O(|D|²) online complexity and two-orders-of-magnitude constant-factor gap suggest headroom, but 10⁵-dataset marketplaces are untested, and the D-ratio degradation as |D| and τ grow is itself reported. The work delivers a software artifact (public code repository) plus a benchmark-generation protocol; no trained model weights or packaged tool are mentioned beyond the code link. Strengths: - A crisp, well-motivated new problem: pricing-aware joint dataset selection where value is set-union cardinality, with a clean formal definition, NP-hardness, and an honest (1−1/e)/2 approximation analysis for the exact baseline — including a candid explanation of why the stronger (1−1/e) enumeration algorithm is not adopted. - The identification that existing cardinality estimators fundamentally cannot handle UNION-style overlap across queries and datasets, plus a learned solution whose q-error improvement over the direct IRIS adaptation (≈1.2–1.9 vs. ≈12) is large and unambiguous. - The alternative-design study (Table 5) is the paper's most persuasive evidence: replacing column-level merging with materialization costs 794.8× runtime at identical D-ratio, directly attributing the gain to the learned component rather than confounds. - The Scenario 2 extension is a substantive contribution over the WWW'25 conference version, not a padding exercise: join-summary composition via cross-attention over a join graph, trained with Chamfer distance, is a genuinely interesting learned-relational operator. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that data cleaning and schema alignment are assumed as preprocessing, that the target schema alignment is delegated to external schema-matching techniques, that data pricing is out of scope (tuple-based pricing adopted for simplicity), and that a default unrestricted query is used when the user provides no query set. They also explicitly note that J-MLG's runtime advantage narrows when the number of joinable collections and connected subgraphs becomes extremely large, and that joinable-collection identification cost is excluded from Scenario 2 runtime comparisons. These limitations are stated directly rather than minimized — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No optimality reference: on small instances (e.g., |D| = 10), an exact or integer-programming solver could verify how far even EXG is from optimal; the paper only measures fidelity to its own greedy, so both the baseline and the learned method could be jointly far from optimal. - Synthetic repositories: all candidate sets are sampled from single data pools with a controlled overlap parameter; real data markets exhibit heterogeneous pricing, duplicate provenance, and skewed overlap that the smin/smax/ol generation may not capture. The price model also assigns a single unit price per dataset with random w_d, decoupling price from information content. - Generalization is under-tested: 5 evaluation pools in Scenario 1 and 2 in Scenario 2, all drawn from the same corpus families used for pre-training; there is no held-out-domain experiment demonstrating the estimator transfers to unseen schemas or vocabularies. - The graph-index thresholds γ1 and γ2 are fixed by hand with no sensitivity analysis, even though Scenario 2 correctness (which joinable collections are discovered) depends entirely on them; the number of false joinable collections and its effect on D-ratio is never measured. - No variance reporting on D-ratio across the (implicitly random) candidate-set and query-pool generations; with 20-dataset repositories, run-to-run variation could be comparable to the reported 2–6% differences between MLG variants. Bottom Line: For anyone building data-market acquisition, lake exploration, or budget-aware data preparation systems, this is the reference treatment of a problem that was previously only implicit, with strong engineering and credible evidence — read it; but treat the learned estimator's cross-domain generalization and the synthetic-repository evaluation as open questions rather than settled results.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Gander, a 9B end-to-end omni interaction agent that unifies streaming full-duplex audio-visual conversation with delegated long-horizon agentic task execution in a single deployed system. - Why it's important: Human-AI interaction is still dominated by turn-based, text-shaped exchanges, and no existing single model handles interruption, proactive feedback, noise robustness, and multi-step tool-driven workflows simultaneously. - How it does it: It decouples the system into a realtime "Cerebellum" (a Thinker-Talker model that serializes audio, video, and its own text into 1-second chunks and predicts a discrete listen/speak/interrupt/tool control token per chunk) plus a training-free, plug-and-play "Brain" (Codex/Claude Code) invoked through a tool-call runtime. - The good: The interaction-timing evidence is credible: on Full-Duplex-Bench v3 Gander takes the floor in 100% of scenarios with only an 8.0% premature-interruption rate (vs. 13.5% for GPT-Realtime and 47.9% for Ultravox), and the back-brain-only ablation (ToolSel 0.934, above GPT-Realtime's 0.876) cleanly shows the execution tier is not the bottleneck. - The missing: The paper reports internal human evaluations as a claim but gives no protocol, numbers, or judge details, and it includes no ablation isolating which training-data families drive the interaction behavior versus the retained conversational ability. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building full-duplex or voice-agent systems — the chunk-flattening formulation, duplex data synthesis pipeline, and honest interaction-metric analysis are directly reusable — but skippable if you only care about raw multimodal understanding benchmarks, where it trails its own base model.

Problem & Motivation: Builders of voice assistants and omni models face a paradigm gap: current systems either use external VAD/ASR pipelines that decide turn boundaries acoustically (failing on hesitation, overlap, barge-in, and noise) or full-duplex speech models that remain audio-only and conversational. Meanwhile, agentic execution (code, files, multi-step workflows) is bolted on as a separate interface. The paper targets practitioners who need one system that continuously perceives speech/video, regulates its own participation in a conversation, and coordinates asynchronous task execution — and it explicitly asks whether interactivity must be intrinsic to the model rather than an orchestration layer, and whether responsiveness and long-horizon reasoning trade off irreconcilably in one model. Key Idea: The core trick is the streaming chunk-flattening formulation: all modalities and both input and output are serialized into one causal token stream of 1-second chunks, each chunk containing time-aligned audio+video tokens, a predicted control token (listen / speak / interrupt / tool), and up to N text tokens — so "whether to speak" is decoupled from "what to say" within a single autoregressive forward process, and proactive behavior and interruption emerge without any external VAD. The second enabling decision is the Brain-Cerebellum split: the Cerebellum keeps a bounded 128-chunk (~2 minute) sliding context for latency, and delegates long-horizon work to a training-free, swappable Brain via task_start/task_send/task_resolve tool calls, so reasoning capability upgrades require no retraining of the interaction model. Methodology: The front Cerebellum runs concurrent streaming encoders: a SigLIP visual path with any-resolution partitioning and a query-based resampler yielding ~16× token compression at ≤448×448 resolution, and a Whisper-style chunk-wise speech encoder at ~50 fps downsampled 5× to ~10 tokens/second. The 9B Thinker backbone (initialized from MiniCPM-o 4.5) consumes flattened chunks and emits a control token plus text; a small autoregressive speech-token decoder conditioned on the backbone's final hidden states, followed by a streaming causal flow-matching decoder conditioned on reference audio, produces the waveform chunk-by-chunk (zero-shot voice cloning). The agent orchestration runtime binds tool calls to confirmed user turns, manages Project/Task/Run/WorkerEvent/Delivery entities, and offers lean vs. coordinator control modes; the default Brain is a Codex app-server worker (driven by GPT-5.6) exposing context_fetch, memory_search, and share. Training data total 2.7M examples: ~20% general spoken dialogue, 9.67% InteractionSpeech (260.8K synthesized full-duplex dialogues with annotated competitive interruptions and supportive backchannels, voice-cloned user audio and textual assistant turns with explicit timeline supervision), 40.66% audio-visual interaction (1.1M pairs from JoyAI-VL, LiveCC, Streamo with temporal alignment corrected by Qwen3.5-297B-A17B), 13.33% agentic interaction (seed-driven trajectory synthesis with DeepSeek-V4-Pro over user/Cerebellum/Brain interactions, plus 36K GUI-grounded examples), and ~8.5% robustness/negative data (irrelevant video, no-command silence, anti-interference, multi-party). Critical design decisions: (1) control-token-first prediction per chunk — justified only by the ablation-free assertion that it yields "more stable full-duplex behavior"; (2) the Brain staying training-free — well-justified by the back-brain-only ablation showing the execution tier outperforms all baselines; (3) 16× visual compression at 448×448 — motivated by latency but unexamined as a cause of the WorldSense regression. Key Results: On Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (100 tool-augmented scenarios, GPT-4o judge, unmodified released scoring scripts, end-to-end audio path including TTS/ASR error), Gander scores ToolSel 0.759 / ArgAcc 0.503 / RespQual 0.490 / Pass@1 0.400 — trailing GPT-Realtime (0.876/0.680/0.792/0.600) and even slightly behind Ultravox v0.7 on task metrics — but leads all six baselines on interaction timing: Take-turn 100% (matched only by the cascaded pipeline), Interrupt 8.0% (best; GPT-Realtime 13.5%), Filler 51.6% (worst but argued to reflect delegation-holding-floor behavior). The back-brain-only condition (text-mediated) reaches ToolSel 0.934, Pass@1 0.520, RespQual 0.740, showing the execution tier exceeds every baseline once the audio path is removed. On SpokenQA/VoiceBench (2,052 utterances), Gander leads the full-duplex group with 75.60 (Llama Questions) and 59.30 (Web Questions) — second overall even against turn-based models (2.90 and 3.50 points behind Baichuan-Omni-1.5 and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B respectively) — but places 5th-6th on AlpacaEval (3.96) and SD-QA (46.84). On omni understanding, Gander reaches 49.62 on WorldSense (a 6.08-point regression from its MiniCPM-o 4.5 base's 55.70) and 78.53 on Daily-Omni (−1.67 from base, ahead of Qwen3-Omni's 70.70); a modality ablation over 13,107 inferences shows genuine fusion gains of +5.01 (WorldSense) and +19.13 (Daily-Omni) over the best single stream. Baselines include current commercial systems (GPT-Realtime, Gemini Live 3.1, Grok), but several baseline rows come from the benchmark release rather than the authors' own runs. Internal human evaluations are claimed, not detailed. Claims of robustness in noise, multi-party, and backchannel settings are illustrated with scenarios but not measured against baselines on any reported benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the integration of native full-duplex chunk-level interaction control with training-free agentic delegation under one harness, plus the InteractionSpeech duplex-data synthesis pipeline with explicit interruption/backchannel timeline supervision and information-leakage verification. Not novel in themselves: Thinker-Talker speech generation, flow-matching waveform synthesis, SigLIP+resampler vision, Brain-Cerebellum style decoupling (explicitly credited to prior work), and the flattened interaction formulation (credited to Thinking Machines Lab) — the paper is a competent, well-instrumented combination of existing techniques pointed at a new unified setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial but meaningful: a back-brain-only condition separates the two tiers, and a three-condition (AV/Video/Audio) modality ablation demonstrates genuine cross-modal fusion rather than single-modality reliance. Decoding is greedy on the omni benchmarks (deterministic), but no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and the LLM-judged metrics (RespQual, AlpacaEval, and much of Full-Duplex-Bench) carry unquantified judge variance. The paper is commendably transparent about negative results (task-accuracy losses, WorldSense regression, worst filler rate) and about a benchmark-prompt asymmetry they had to correct via a contract file. Model weights, code, and data are stated for release (github.com/Omni-Interaction-Gander/Omni-Interaction-Agent), which supports reproducibility — though the default Brain runs on GPT-5.6/Codex, a closed, versioned dependency that undermines full-stack replication. Concerns: several baseline rows on Full-Duplex-Bench are taken from the benchmark release rather than re-run; the duplex training data is fully synthetic, so interaction behavior is learned from a distribution the authors themselves constructed; the Filler-rate explanation (delegation rather than defect) is plausible but untested; and robustness/multi-party claims have no quantitative evaluation in the paper. This is a non-peer-reviewed technical report. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL + SYSTEMS (a built, evaluated system with a deployed industrial sibling, Hy-Realtime). - Practical: Yes — a 9B backbone with compact SigLIP/Whisper encoders and small decoders is plausible on a single commodity GPU, and the runtime's prefix caching and token compression target that; exact hardware is not stated. - Efficient: The 128-chunk sliding window keeps per-step inference cost bounded over long sessions, and 16× visual + 5× audio compression keep the token budget small; the Filler metric (51.6%) implies users often wait through delegated-task intervals, an efficiency cost in interaction terms. - Effective: Partially — interaction timing and spoken QA are demonstrably solved relative to full-duplex peers, but task-execution accuracy through the full audio path (Pass@1 0.400 vs 0.600 for GPT-Realtime) is the weakest in the comparison, so the stated goal of unifying interaction and agency is only half-evidenced. - Scalable: Not tested — the authors acknowledge that agent invocation is sensitive to training-data distribution and defer systematic scaling to the industrial Hy-Realtime model; no experiment probes 10× data or larger models. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: released model weights, code, data, plus a reusable agent orchestration runtime and duplex-data synthesis pipeline. Strengths: - The chunk-flattening formulation with a first-token control decision per second is a clean, implementable mechanism that measurably wins the metric a full-duplex architecture exists to win (100% take-turn, 8.0% interruption), and the paper's joint reading of the take-turn/interrupt trade-off (showing why competitors trade one for the other) is genuinely insightful analysis. - The evaluation design is unusually honest for a technical report: it reports losing task metrics alongside winning interaction metrics, runs a diagnostic back-brain-only ablation that localizes the accuracy gap to the front end and speech channel, and names its WorldSense regression as "the present trade-off rather than" something explained away. - The InteractionSpeech pipeline is a substantive data contribution: 260.8K dialogues with enforced event semantics (backchannels bounded by length/lexicon/intent criteria, hidden-continuation leakage checks, interruption onsets spread across turns rather than clustered at utterance ends), addressing a real deficit in duplex training data. - The training-free, plug-and-play Brain is validated empirically (ToolSel 0.934 exceeds every baseline including GPT-Realtime), giving the architecture a credible scaling path for reasoning capability without retraining. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion candidly lists: (1) sensitivity of agent invocation and conversational behavior to training-data distribution, with scaling deferred to Hy-Realtime; (2) absence of on-policy distillation or RL post-training for long-horizon omni interaction; (3) Brain-Cerebellum communication currently limited to ASR-derived signals, with richer bidirectional structure left as future work; (4) unmanaged memory/long-context needs beyond the 2-minute window; and (5) the absence of any unified benchmark for omni interaction agents or for Brain-Cerebellum coordination. In the results sections they also concede the task-accuracy deficit on Full-Duplex-Bench, the weak AlpacaEval/SD-QA scores (attributed to missing long-form supervision and narrow accent coverage), and the WorldSense regression. This directness is a credibility positive; the paper does not minimize its losses. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The claimed robustness to background noise, multi-party interaction, and backchanneling — a headline capability in the abstract and Figure 1 — is never quantified against any baseline; the corresponding 8.5% of training data is validated only anecdotally. - No ablation removes or varies the control-token mechanism, the chunk size, the context-window length, or the 16× visual compression, so the central architectural claim (control-token-first prediction yields more stable duplex behavior) rests on a single aggregate benchmark result rather than component-level evidence. - Several duplex baselines (GPT-Realtime, Gemini Live 3.1, Grok) are quoted from the benchmark release rather than re-run, and re-run conditions (decoding, audio paths) may differ; the single LLM-judge (GPT-4o) with no inter-judge or seed variance limits confidence in close comparisons (e.g., Pass@1 0.400 vs 0.410). - Synthetic-only duplex training data risks a distribution gap: the model may learn the synthesizer's interruption statistics rather than human barge-in behavior, and no real recorded duplex conversations are used for training or evaluation. - The Brain's reasoning ability is conflated with GPT-5.6 specifically; no experiment swaps in a weaker/open Brain, so the "plug-and-play" claim is untested across backends. - The stated Filler-rate defense (holding the floor during delegation is appropriate) is asserted, not measured — no analysis links filler occurrences to actual back-brain invocations. Bottom Line: For anyone building full-duplex voice or omni agents, this is worth reading for its chunk-flattening formulation, duplex data recipe, and unusually honest evaluation of the interaction-vs-accuracy trade-off — but its task-execution accuracy still trails closed commercial systems, so it is a strong open starting point rather than the current performance frontier.

Parallel SAT Sweeping on CNFs

N Rigi-Luperti, A Biere, D Schreiber · repositum.tuwien.at · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MALLOBSWEEP, a distributed parallelization of clausal SAT sweeping that operates purely on CNF, and couples it with the MALLOBSAT CDCL solver into a combined setup (MALLOBSNS) for combinational equivalence checking. - Why it's important: Combinational equivalence checking (CEC) of optimized circuits against golden models is a bottleneck in the EDA flow, and prior parallel CEC techniques all require structural AIG information — this work removes that constraint and shows scalable preprocessing on the CNF level. - How it does it: The key move is recognizing that per-root-variable sweep calls in KISSAT's sequential sweeping are independent, so they can be distributed across hundreds of processes via randomized work-stealing, with periodic binary-tree all-to-all exchange of discovered units and equivalences. - The good: Sweeping shows genuinely near-linear scaling — for instances needing ≥2000s sequentially, MALLOBSWEEP achieves a ~910x inprocessing speedup at 1536 cores on HWMCC'12 (59% parallel efficiency), far above the <30% efficiency typical of distributed SAT solving at that scale. - The missing: End-to-end scaling is benchmark-dependent and not uniformly demonstrated: on HWMCC'12 the full MALLOBSNS setup achieves only a 12x speedup at 768 cores (1.5% efficiency), and evaluation is confined to unsatisfiable optimized miter instances — no general CNFs, no satisfiable (buggy) miters, and no proof generation. - Read it or not: Worth reading for SAT/EDA researchers working on parallel inprocessing or CEC at scale; practitioners needing a production CEC flow today should note it is a short paper whose coupled solver only beats ABC on the harder HWMCC'20 instances and at larger core counts.

Problem & Motivation: CEC verifies that a synthesized, optimized candidate netlist is functionally equivalent to a reference golden model (a miter). State-of-the-art hybrid CEC tools use SAT sweeping to find equivalent variables, but these approaches rely on full structural circuit information (AIGER format). A monolithic CNF-level alternative — where clausal congruence closure (CCC) handles easy syntactic equivalences and clausal SAT sweeping (CSS, from KISSAT/FMCAD 2024) handles harder semantic ones — lacked any parallelization. The authors target the gap: scale CNF-level sweeping to hundreds of cores so it can serve as preprocessing/inprocessing for CEC inputs without structural access. Key Idea: The core insight is that KISSAT's SWEEP(v) calls around different root variables are mutually independent, so the sweep workload (a shuffled list of root variables) can be partitioned across solver processes using randomized work-stealing (steal every second element of a random victim's worklist), with correctness preserved by a periodic, communication-lean binary-tree all-to-all aggregation and broadcast of discovered equivalences and units. Everything stays at the CNF level — no gate extraction beyond the single sequential CCC pre-pass. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) each solver runs CCC once to cheaply remove syntactic equivalences; (2) a sweep iteration distributes all variables in random order to worklists, each solver expanding breadth-first clausal environments around root variables (bounded by depth k, variable limit Nv, clause limit Nc, starting at k=2, Nv=256, Nc=1024, doubled and k incremented each iteration) and answering equivalence queries with the small internal solver KITTEN, capped at 10^6 propagations per call; (3) equivalences/units are shared every 20 ms via tree-aggregated all-to-all exchange and applied by unit propagation. Notably, the authors depart from KISSAT's hard limit k=3 by allowing unbounded environment growth — most instances terminate by k=7–9. MALLOBSNS then runs MALLOBSWEEP and MALLOBSAT concurrently as two MALLOB tasks with cross-task clause sharing, KISSAT backends stripped of all pre/inprocessing ("pure" CDCL), default 50:50 resource split. Critical design decisions: synchronized iteration structure (chosen for clean speedup measurement and faithful generalization of sequential sweeping — justified); 20 ms sharing cadence (empirically motivated but admittedly at MALLOB's technical floor); unbounded environment growth with propagation caps (well-motivated by the observation that default limits are exhausted in seconds, though the cap interacts with completeness of individual sweep calls). Key Results: Evaluated on SuperMUC-NG (up to 32 nodes / 1536 cores) on HWMCC'12 (341 instances) and HWMCC'20 (324 instances) optimized miters, all unsatisfiable, with 300s distributed / 5000s sequential timeouts. Isolated sweeping: 1-core solves 137 (HW'12) / 155 (HW'20) instances vs. 284 / 285 at 1536 cores; weak-scaling speedup ~910 (HW'12) and ~720 (HW'20) at 1536 cores for instances needing ≥2000s sequentially, with near-100% efficiency up to 384 cores on HW'12. Full solving at 192 cores (PAR-2): MALLOBSNS 4:4 scores 33.4 (HW'12) and 17.6 (HW'20), beating ABC &fraig -y (43.4 / 31.3), KISSAT (60.0 / 68.6), X-SAT (172.1 / 159.9), and standalone MALLOBSAT (36.1 / 61.1). At 768 cores MALLOBSNS solves 332 / 322 instances with PAR-2 22.5 / 9.6; end-to-end speedup over KISSAT reaches ~220 at 768 cores on HW'20 (36% efficiency) but only ~12 at 768 cores on HW'12 (1.5% efficiency) — the authors attribute this to KISSAT's own inprocessing being exceptionally strong on HW'12. A resource-split study shows balanced 4:4 allocation is best and that CDCL deserves more resources than sweeping (1:7 beats 7:1). Baselines (KISSAT, ABC, X-SAT 2025) are current and strong, though ABC's parallel &cec -P -S implementation was reportedly unavailable publicly. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (parallel CNF-level SAT sweeping) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (MALLOBSWEEP/MALLOBSNS integrated into MALLOB). The genuinely novel element is the distributed work-stealing parallelization of clausal sweeping with periodic equivalence sharing — prior parallel CEC work all assumed AIGER structure. The individual ingredients (work-stealing, tree-based clause aggregation, MALLOB clause sharing, KISSAT sweeping, CCC) are established techniques; the contribution is their careful combination at the CNF level and the empirical scaling evidence, which is an honest but incremental-architectural advance rather than an algorithmic breakthrough. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation is careful for a short paper: ablation-style parameter studies cover resource splits (1:7 / 4:4 / 7:1), environment-limit variants were explored, and a fair 1-core baseline was implemented inside KISSAT itself to inherit its sequential optimizations. Weak-scaling speedups are computed on commonly solved instances with geometric means and instance-count cutoffs. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported (typical for SAT benchmarking but notable given claims of near-linear speedup), and results rest on exactly two benchmark suites that are also the venue's own competition sets — the same CNF encodings from the authors' prior CSS paper. The artifact is reviewed and archived at Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/21740976), which is a strong reproducibility positive. A methodological caveat: X-SAT crashed (assertion failure) on 28/341 HW'12 instances, so its curve is acknowledged as not fully representative. The headline 900x speedup is an inprocessing-only metric; end-to-end claims are the ~220x figure, and the authors commendably report the unfavorable 1.5%-efficiency HW'12 scaling rather than hiding it. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL — a built distributed tool, evaluated by benchmark deployment on an HPC cluster. - Practical: Requires an MPI-style distributed cluster (SuperMUC-NG); it runs on commodity multi-node CPU infrastructure but is not a laptop-scale tool, and single-core use of MALLOBSWEEP solves fewer instances than KISSAT. - Efficient: Resource efficiency of 36–59% on hard instances is unusually high for distributed SAT tooling, though the coupled setup halves the effective core count for CDCL by design (50:50 split). - Effective: It demonstrably solves the stated problem (UNSAT miter proving) faster than ABC and KISSAT on HWMCC'20 and at scale, but only on unsatisfiable optimized miters; usefulness for buggy miters and general CNFs is untested. - Scalable: Tested honestly to 1536 cores; the authors show scaling degrades sharply on HW'12, and extrapolation beyond miter inputs is explicitly left to future work (preliminary tests on SAT competition instances required adaptive sweeping limits they did not implement). The work delivers a real software artifact (reviewed, Zenodo-archived), not just a paper. Strengths: - Removing the structural-information requirement: this is the first parallel SAT sweeping approach that works purely on CNF, making scalable inprocessing applicable where AIGER structure is absent or expensive to recover. - The scaling evidence is genuinely strong and well-instrumented: ~910x inprocessing speedup at 1536 cores with 59% efficiency, and near-linear scaling to 384 cores, exceeding what distributed CDCL clause sharing typically achieves. - Honest negative reporting: the 1.5% end-to-end efficiency on HWMCC'12 is presented and analyzed (KISSAT's inprocessing dominance, sequential-only CCC) rather than buried — this is a credibility asset. - The coupled design is validated as more than the sum of parts: MALLOBSNS beats both MALLOBSAT alone and MALLOBSWEEP alone, with a 1.9x geometric-mean speedup of the coupling over MALLOBSAT on non-trivial inputs, and the resource-split ablation gives actionable tuning guidance. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: no unsatisfiability proof generation (left to future work); evaluation restricted to unsatisfiable optimized miters, with satisfiable miters excluded because they were trivially easy; no evaluation on general CNFs (preliminary tests showed adaptive sweeping-time limits would be needed); KITTEN is pushed to its limits and may need replacement by distributed low-latency SAT calls; the sequential-variable-scheduling inherited from KISSAT is likely suboptimal for the parallel case; and end-to-end scaling is input-dependent (HW'12 vs HW'20 divergence). They confront limitations directly, which strengthens the paper's credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limitations: (1) the comparison to ABC's parallel CEC is against &fraig -y and &splitprove, while the dedicated parallel &cec -P -S algorithm was unavailable — so the "outperforms the state-of-the-art parallel CEC" framing rests on a baseline that may not be ABC's best parallel offering; (2) the 20 ms sharing interval and the 10^6-propagation KITTEN cap are tuned on the same benchmarks used for evaluation, risking overfitting of constants; (3) no comparison against PARAHYBRIDCEC, PDP-CEC, or FASTLEC despite citing them as recent parallel CEC work — the field's strongest parallel competitors are not in the tables; (4) all instances are UNSAT and encode post-optimization equivalence, so the method's value for the bug-finding (SAT) half of CEC workflows is unmeasured; (5) the CNF encodings come from the authors' own prior work, so encoding choices could favor CNF-level sweeping over structure-aware baselines. None of these undermine the core scaling result, but they bound how far the "beats ABC" claim generalizes. Bottom Line: For researchers building parallel SAT/CEC infrastructure this is a worthwhile, honestly-reported systems contribution with a reviewed artifact and unusually good scaling evidence, but a practitioner needing a deployable CEC solution today should treat it as a promising direction whose advantage over ABC is demonstrated mainly on one benchmark family and at large core counts.

Iris: Climbing to the Search Frontier

Z Liu, H Liu, Z Wang, Y Qin, J Liang, X Chu, S Chen… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Iris-mini and Iris-pro, two open-weight-announced search agents (35B-A3B and 397B-A17B MoE) trained with a full data-construction, SFT, RL, and evaluation recipe that scores 82.2/84.8/86.9/52.3 (mini) and 88.6/85.1/92.9/56.4 (pro) on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, DeepSearchQA, and HLE-text with context management enabled. - Why it's important: Benchmark scores for search agents conflate the trained policy with inference-time context-management harnesses, and this work is one of the first to report every benchmark both with and without context management under a fixed harness, making the policy's intrinsic capability measurable. - How it does it: Multi-hop questions are reverse-constructed from a web hyperlink graph, stripped of searchable anchors by rewriting every non-answer entity into a descriptive reference, verified by a dual criterion (reference model fails closed-book but succeeds with evidence supplied), then distilled into filtered trajectories and optimized by RL against live search, with SFT–RL rounds alternated ('climbing'). - The good: The with/without-CM decomposition shows the gains are not harness artifacts: without any CM, Iris-mini scores 64.7 on BrowseComp versus 55.9 (FORT-Searcher), 46.0 (OpenSeeker-v2), and 42.1 (REDSearcher), and Iris-pro reaches 72.6. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or variance analysis are reported; all headline numbers come from a single pass@1 rollout judged by an LLM, and models are only compared on four benchmarks where the training data construction (multi-hop entity-path questions) plausibly overlaps the test distribution. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or benchmarking search agents — the data pipeline and the with/without-CM evaluation protocol are directly reusable, even though the individual techniques are largely known combinations.
