Problem & Motivation: Search agents must decide what to search, how to interpret evidence, and when to stop, but two practical obstacles dominate. First, naturally occurring web questions are too easy for training — they are either answerable from parametric memory or solvable by a single string-matching lookup — so prior work synthesizes hard tasks by masking entities along hyperlink or knowledge-graph paths. Second, long-horizon search exhausts the context window before the agent resolves all constraints, so reported benchmark differences may come from the inference-time harness (trajectory summarization, history pruning, context reset) rather than the trained policy. The authors argue this conflation makes it impossible to compare systems fairly, since many teams report only context-managed results while others report raw results. Key Idea: The core technical move is anchor abstraction with dual-criteria verification: every non-answer entity in a synthesized multi-hop question is rewritten into a unique descriptive reference (so no clue can be resolved by string matching), and a question is admitted only if a reference model fails it closed-book yet answers it correctly when the distilled entity graph is supplied as context — filtering jointly for difficulty and verifiability without human labels. A secondary key idea is treating context management as part of the measured system: every benchmark is reported with and without it, holding tools, context budget, and judge fixed. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Data pipeline: sample an answer-anchored seed page, expand its out-links into a local subgraph (recovering links from RDF triples merged with rendered markup), distill pages into a compact entity graph, author a question whose reasoning path contains at least N coupled relations to the answer entity, then apply the abstraction operator to rewrite all non-answer entities descriptively; verify with the closed-book-fail/evidence-supplied-succeed criterion using a semantic-matching judge. (2) Training: a strong teacher produces ReAct trajectories (SEARCH/SCRAPE tools, on-the-fly per-page summaries as observations); coarse filtering removes incorrect, degenerate (detected via a sliding-window zlib compression ratio plus auxiliary detectors for periodic lines and byte-identical repeated tool calls), and shallow (<K tool turns) trajectories, with exact deduplication; fine filtering uses an LLM judge whose rubric is induced from free-form critiques of sampled trajectories rather than hand-written, outputting KEEP/MASK per assistant turn (≤10% masked, masked turns excluded from loss but kept in context); the SFT loss is per-turn cross-entropy on reasoning and tool calls only. RL uses group-relative policy gradient against live search, with a request-level partial-rollout scheme (over-long sessions aborted and resumed from committed prefixes across weight versions, corrected by truncated importance sampling, organized as a message-state forest, ~2× over-sampling headroom) and an in-cluster FP8 Qwen3.5-397B serving both as binary-verdict GenRM reward and observation summarizer. (3) SFT–RL climbing: after each RL round, queries with pass rate in (0, 1/2] are selected, the shortest valid rollout with ≥K tool turns is distilled back via SFT, giving a self-paced curriculum. Training runs on the Relax RL engine; base models are Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with 256K context. Key Results: On BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, DeepSearchQA (F1), and HLE-text with the discard-all CM strategy: Iris-mini scores 82.2/84.8/86.9/52.3 (best-in-class among 30–35B open models on three of four; behind XYZ-Aquila-mini's 89.5 on DeepSearchQA) and Iris-pro scores 88.6/85.1/92.9/56.4, leading or tying the ~400B open cohort on all four (vs. XYZ-Aquila-pro at 84.8/85.1/92.5/53.3). Without CM, Iris-mini scores 64.7/72.3/81.0/43.2 and Iris-pro 72.6/76.8/86.4/50.8. CM adds up to +21.2 (BrowseComp, discard-all + retry) for Iris-mini but only +5.6–8.3 for Iris-pro; the gain correlates with how often sessions exhaust context, not with baseline headroom. Iris-pro without CM approaches heavy-compute configurations of MiroThinker-H1 and Apodex-1.0-H. Baselines are contemporaneous 2026 open systems, several results marked as reproduced by an independent team (r), but frontier proprietary numbers (GPT-5.6 Sol 90.4 BrowseComp, Claude Fable 5 64.5 HLE) still exceed Iris-pro. On BrowseComp-ZH (289 questions), three configurations converge to exactly 246 correct answers, which the authors read as a benchmark ceiling. A transfer observation (not tabulated) claims positive transfer to BFCL, τ-bench, OfficeQA, and APEX. All results are single-rollout pass@1 with LLM-judge scoring. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely novel elements are the rigorous with/without-CM dual reporting protocol (with the finding that CM gains track context-exhaustion frequency, not task headroom), the data-induced turn-level judging rubric, and the request-level partial-rollout scheme with prefix-splicing across weight versions. The rest — graph-walk question synthesis, entity masking, trajectory filtering, live-search RL, iterative SFT–RL distillation — is a competent combination of established ideas from WebSailor/WebShaper/WebDancer, Search-R1/DeepResearcher, and recent self-distillation pipelines applied at scale. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations isolate which data-pipeline components (abstraction, dual-criteria filter, turn masking, climbing) contribute to the final scores — the recipe is presented holistically. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; every headline number is a single pass@1 sample scored by an LLM judge, so differences of 3–4 points (e.g., the 82.2 vs. 78.8 BrowseComp margin) are within plausible single-run variance. Benchmark-contamination controls are concrete and unusually explicit: HF datasets/spaces pages are blocked at three enforcement points. Comparisons are strengthened by third-party reproductions (r marks) of some competitor numbers, but competitor CM configurations are not always matched (Table 2 shows only three competitors with no-CM results, and no competitor is evaluated under discard-all by the authors themselves). Weights and pipeline components are only planned for release; no URL is live in the paper. Methodological concern: training questions are reverse-constructed from the same kind of web multi-hop structure that BrowseComp and DeepSearchQA test, so distributional train–test proximity cannot be ruled out, and the LLM judge scoring both training rewards and evaluation creates a judge-consistency coupling. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (systems trained and evaluated, though as a technical report the artifact is not yet deployed). Practical: Both models are MoE (35B-A3B, 397B-A17B); the mini model's 3B active parameters make it deployable on commodity multi-GPU setups, the pro model requires serious infrastructure. Efficient: The authors explicitly refuse to claim the retry-augmented numbers as headline results because each retry costs a full search pass, and they note discard-all is the cheaper default — a creditable cost-aware stance. Effective: Evidence covers exactly the four benchmarks tested; the claim that search is an 'atomic capability' transferring to general agentic domains is asserted but not evidenced with numbers. Scalable: Not tested beyond 397B; the self-paced climbing curriculum has a natural stopping signal, but behavior at larger scale or longer horizons is unexamined. Deliverable: planned model weights and pipeline code (GitHub/HuggingFace links present in the header but contents not verifiable from the paper); currently paper-form only. Strengths: - The dual with/without-CM evaluation is the paper's most valuable contribution: it quantifies that CM is worth up to +21.2 points on BrowseComp (more than most reported inter-system gaps) and provides the cleanest available separation of policy capability from harness effects in this literature. - The anchor-abstraction + dual-criteria verification filter is a well-motivated, formally stated (Eqs. 6–9) solution to the twin failure modes of synthetic data: string-match shortcuts and unverifiable answers. - The data-induced judging rubric — sampling trajectories, having a judge critique them freely, consolidating failure modes into an explicit rubric — is a sensible answer to the real problem that a seemingly wasteful turn may be legitimate exploration. - The engineering of request-level partial rollout with prefix reuse and truncated importance sampling addresses a genuine throughput pathology (heavy-tailed long-horizon rollouts stalling synchronous RL steps) without full asynchrony. - Willingness to report unflattering numbers (no-CM results, the DeepSearchQA loss to XYZ-Aquila-mini, the BrowseComp-ZH annotation-error case study) raises credibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge: (1) a remaining gap to frontier closed models ('Closing this gap remains an important direction for future work'); (2) that retry inflates scores at substantial inference cost and should not be the default reporting configuration; (3) that benchmark performance captures only part of agent capability and broader realistic search scenarios are needed; (4) a concrete BrowseComp-ZH annotation error (Question 85, 'Bolton' vs. official 'Lannister') where their correct answer went unscored, motivating better benchmarks; and (5) that the transfer observation to general tool use is an interpretation, not a demonstrated result. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Single pass@1 with no variance reporting makes all inter-model margins of 3–5 points statistically unevaluated — the paper's core ranking claims rest on noise-unquantified single samples. (2) Zero component ablations: the reader cannot tell whether anchor abstraction, the dual-criteria filter, turn-level masking, or SFT–RL climbing drives the gains. (3) Potential train–test distributional overlap between graph-constructed multi-hop training questions and BrowseComp-style tasks is never probed (no held-out natural-question evaluation). (4) The GenRM judge (Qwen3.5-397B) is the same base family and scale as Iris-pro's initialization, so reward-model and actor biases may correlate. (5) The cross-domain transfer claim ('search as an atomic capability') is presented in the conclusion with no numbers, no baselines, and no table. (6) CM comparison is asymmetric: competitors' no-CM numbers are quoted from their papers under different harnesses, not re-run under the authors' fixed setup. Bottom Line: A practitioner building search agents gains real value from the data-construction recipe, the CM quantification, and the evaluation-protocol discipline — this is currently the most transparent OpenSearch-agent report on harness-vs-policy attribution — but the absence of variance reporting, ablations, and released artifacts means the ranking claims should be treated as provisional until weights and code actually ship.

Problem & Motivation: The thesis targets two decision problems in financial services. First, credit card issuers — traditional banks and fintech 'super-apps' — must periodically decide whether to raise a customer's credit limit and by how much. Prior approaches either ignore the provisioning cost of expected default losses, rely on strong distributional assumptions, or treat the decision statically, even though limit changes alter portfolio-level provisions sequentially and thus future decisions. The motivating institution is a Latin American super-app (Rappi) pursuing a low-limit/high-volume strategy whose ad-hoc limit policy the thesis aims to beat. Second, motor third-party liability (MTPL) insurers need zone-level claim frequency models; the open question is whether non-traditional geographic information (road structure, land use, imagery) adds predictive signal beyond standard actuarial rating factors, motivated by evidence that crashes cluster near home beyond what driving exposure explains. Key Idea: The core move in the credit studies is encoding the financial economics of revolving credit directly into the learning objective: the RL reward is the incremental expected profit (three months of interest revenue on predicted balance, net of PD·LGD·EAD provisions using the credit conversion factor), and the state carries the cumulative ΔProvisions from prior decisions in the episode, making a per-customer batch decision a proper sequential MDP. The companion insight in Chapter 3 is that point estimates of potential outcomes are not sufficient for policy selection — bootstrap-estimated uncertainty should enter the decision rule via VaR/CVaR over the dose–response curve. Chapter 4's idea is constructing multi-radius (0.5–5 km) environmental features from masked OSM layers and CORINE plus pretrained image embeddings as drop-in predictors in an interpretable actuarial GLM framework. Methodology: Chapter 2 (published, EJOR 315(2):802–817, 2024) formulates an episodic MDP over N eligible customers; the state is per-customer financial features (utilization, payment and consumption rates, non-payments, limit, interest) plus portfolio ΔProvisions; actions are {maintain, increase by fixed factor β}; the reward (Eq. 2.11) is the one-step expected-profit advantage over maintaining. Because online experimentation is infeasible and rewards realize three months out, a two-stage simulator is fit on Rappi data (12,258 customers for the simulator, 11,101 for RL training): an XGBoost three-class balance-type classifier (using SMOTENC for class imbalance; CV weighted F1 0.77 with alternative+financial vs 0.76 financial-only) followed by class-conditional regressors (XGBoost for class 0, random forest for class 1). Tabular Double Q-learning (γ=1, ε=0.1, α=10⁻², states discretized on uniform 5% grids) is trained offline in this simulator, with row order permuted per episode and hyperparameters grid-searched. Chapter 3 reframes the problem as counterfactual learning with a mixed treatment: no-dose control (maintain) plus a continuous dose (percentage increase), adapting single-model and two-part dose–response estimators, constructing an overlap region, and building a semisynthetic evaluation where oracle dose–response curves are known; policies from point estimates are compared against VaR- and CVaR-based criteria computed on bootstrap distributions of the potential-outcome estimates, scored by √PE and oracle matching rate. Chapter 4 builds postcode-level predictors — OSM/CORINE environmental counts at four radii, raw orthoimage tiles (apothems 0.5/1/3 km), and ResNet18/Nomic embeddings — and evaluates GLM, regularized GLM, XGBoost, MLP, and CNN variants on BeMTPL97 under an extended six-fold cross-validation scheme plus a five-seed robustness analysis, testing held-out postcode generalization. Key Results: Chapter 2: alternative data gave only ~1% weighted F1 gain (0.77 vs 0.76 CV) and sometimes worse regression RMSE (class 1: 209.32 vs 192.30 USD), so financial-only features were kept; the ensemble simulator reached test RMSE 132.32 USD (95% CI [115.27, 149.37]) versus 268.32 USD for a mean predictor. The Double Q-learning agent dominated random, all-increase, no-arrears, current-policy (propensity-modeled), and bureau-score-percentile (P85/P95) baselines in synthetic trials; the extracted greedy policy recommends increases for 19% of customers and yields a net incremental expected profit of ~USD 3,847 (USD 6,802 favorable profit against USD 2,956 regret), with ~USD 33,327 in avoided losses from maintained customers — all simulator-mediated. Appendix B checks that gains persist at matched intervention rates, addressing the 'more increases = more profit' confound. Chapter 3: reported qualitatively in the available text — risk-aware VaR/CVaR criteria achieve lower policy error (√PE) than point-estimate recommendations, with dose–response recovery errors tabulated for single-model vs two-part strategies; exact numbers appear in tables 3.3–3.5 but values are not fully legible in the provided text. Chapter 4: geographic features improve test RMSE, most strongly when environmental features at 5 km radius are combined with coordinates; pretrained image embeddings help when structured environmental features are absent; results are stable across six folds and five seeds (per Tables 4.5–4.15, values not printed in the provided excerpt). Baselines are reasonable within-domain (logistic/GLM, gradient boosting, the institution's policy) but no external deep-RL methods (e.g., FQI, batch-constrained RL) are compared. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (credit limit adjustment as an MDP whose reward explicitly prices revolving-credit provisions via CCF — prior limit-setting work ignored this) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (app-based alternative data do not help balance prediction) in Chapter 2; NEW METHOD in Chapter 3 is modest — risk-aware (VaR/CVaR) policy selection over dose–response estimates is a sensible transplant of financial risk measures into counterfactual decision-making, with the mixed no-dose/continuous-dose design the most original element; Chapter 4 is a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING / ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION study of feature value. All algorithms are standard; novelty lies in domain formulation and honest empirical evaluation, not in learning-theoretic contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and meaningful: alternative-vs-financial feature sets (Chapter 2), single-model vs two-part dose–response strategies (Chapter 3), and a systematic predictor-set, radius, and embedding ablation with a five-seed robustness study (Chapter 4). Chapter 2 reports 95% confidence intervals throughout, 10-seed RL training with mean±std learning curves, and a post-hoc matched-intervention-rate comparison — above-average rigor for applied banking analytics. Concerns: (1) the Rappi dataset is proprietary and not releasable, so full reproduction is impossible (BeMTPL97 is public); (2) the RL policy is judged by rewards generated inside the simulator the simulator-selection stage built — the authors mitigate this by selecting simulator models on validation prediction error only, not on reward, but residual Goodhart risk remains; (3) Chapter 3's ground truth is synthetic by construction, so policy-error results measure estimator recovery under the authors' own data-generating assumptions; (4) no uncertainty quantification for Chapter 3 policy comparisons is visible in the provided text. Code release is not mentioned. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (three studies with experiments on real and semisynthetic data; a deployment workflow is designed but not executed). - Practical: Yes — tabular Double Q-learning, XGBoost/GLM, and ResNet18 inference run on commodity hardware; the pipeline is explicitly packaged as a 6-month retraining deployment workflow (Fig. 2.7). - Efficient: Low cost — tabular RL with discretized states and gradient-boosted simulators are cheap; no GPU-scale training reported beyond standard model fits. - Effective: Only proxy evidence — profit gains are measured inside a learned simulator and semisynthetic oracles, not against realized portfolio outcomes; the thesis is candid about this. - Scalable: Untested — the tabular/discretized formulation will strain with large state spaces or continuous multi-action treatment, and the authors concede the fixed-β action space is a data limitation, not a design choice. The thesis delivers methods and a deployment blueprint but no released software artifact, dataset, or trained model. Strengths: - The provisions-aware reward function with explicit CCF/EAD treatment is a genuine domain formulation contribution that distinguishes this from prior limit-setting literature, and the authors show the CCF term was a major determinant of learned behavior. - The negative result on alternative data is a valuable, well-quantified correction to the fintech data-advantage narrative, and publishing it (in EJOR, with 18 citations) rather than burying it is credible. - The matched-intervention-rate and post-hoc policy comparisons (Appendix B) directly address the most obvious confound in policy evaluation — that the RL agent simply grants fewer increases. - Chapter 4's design — multiple radii, multiple data sources, held-out postcodes, multi-seed robustness, and interpretability via regularized GLM coefficients — is a careful empirical answer to a question (does open geographic data help MTPL frequency?) that insurers actually face. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) only a fixed β increase factor was observable, preventing a richer multi-action or continuous-action RL treatment; (2) results are simulator-mediated synthetic experiments, valuable as a trigger for real-world testing but not real-world proof; (3) limit decreases carry reputational/commercial risk outside scope; (4) evaluation windows are fixed at three months and longer horizons await a more mature portfolio; (5) a human analyst should retain final judgment. Chapter 5 lists limitations and future-work directions (individualized increase factors via counterfactuals). The thesis confronts limitations directly — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged items: (1) the simulator's own error (ensemble WAPE 0.54, RMSE 132 USD, ~49% of target SD) propagates unmodeled into RL policy quality — no sensitivity analysis of policy quality to simulator misspecification is reported; (2) no comparison against off-policy evaluation or batch RL baselines (FQI, BCQ, CQL), so it is unknown whether Double Q-learning specifically matters or any reasonable policy learner suffices; (3) Chapter 3's semisynthetic outcome generation embeds author-chosen dose–response shapes, and no real-data downstream validation (even backtesting on realized outcomes) is shown; (4) Chapter 4's BeMTPL97 zone-level aggregation limits individual-level ratemaking claims, and the abstract's mention of 'vision-transformer embeddings' conflicts with the ResNet18/Nomic embeddings detailed in the tables — a consistency issue; (5) fairness and regulatory-acceptability of the RL policy (disparate impact of the learned 19% intervention rule) are raised only in passing despite the thesis's own framing around access to credit. Bottom Line: A practitioner in credit risk or actuarial analytics gains concrete, honestly evaluated decision frameworks and two deployable findings — provisions-aware RL for limit setting and open geographic features for MTPL frequency — while a methods researcher will find standard algorithms competently applied and should look elsewhere for novelty.

J Liu, C Rizzi, P Jaipuriyar, U Schorr, S Richter, A Sood… · dynamo.ethz.ch · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GLOW, an open-source mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation of register retiming that simultaneously meets a target clock period and minimizes dynamic power by preventing the formation and propagation of glitches. - Why it's important: Retiming is a standard logic-synthesis optimization in every commercial flow, but existing retiming either ignores power entirely or uses iterative hotspot heuristics that miss global glitch-elimination opportunities, so dynamic power is left on the table at zero architectural cost. - How it does it: The key trick is treating switch propagation like delay propagation — both travel through combinational nodes and are blocked by registers — enabling a step-wise probabilistic switch model embedded in a single MILP alongside timing, load-capacitance, and register-count constraints. - The good: Across 9 benchmarks under identical timing constraints, GLOW reduces total dynamic power by 8.01% vs. classic retiming and 20.37% vs. power-oriented retiming (Monteiro et al., ICCAD'93), and its power estimate correlates with Cadence Joules post-synthesis measurements at Pearson R = 0.98. - The missing: MILP solve times reach the 1-hour timeout on 3 of 9 benchmarks, evaluation uses randomly generated input vectors rather than realistic workloads, the power-model correlation study covers only one small benchmark (b03, 137 gates), and code is promised open-source but not yet released. - Read it or not: Worth reading for logic-synthesis and EDA engineers working on power optimization, and for anyone retiming circuits in an academic or industrial flow; skip it if you need leakage/thermal optimization or work at scales where an exact MILP cannot be applied even with partitioning.

Problem & Motivation Dynamic power remains the dominant component of total power in digital CMOS, and logic synthesis is an increasingly important stage for attacking it. Retiming (Leiserson–Saxe), one of the most widely deployed logic optimizations, repositions registers to meet a target clock period but classically ignores power; register placement, however, directly affects both load capacitances and glitch-induced switching activity. Prior power-aware retiming work (Monteiro et al. 1993 and successors) is either scenario-specific, un-automated, or based on iterative heuristics that eliminate power hotspots — the nodes with the largest glitch power reduction potential — rather than the glitches themselves. Because hotspot elimination removes the consequence of glitching but not its root cause (unbalanced input arrival times at reconvergent paths), the glitch source continues to dissipate power and can even create new hotspots in later iterations. The authors motivate this with a worked six-node example where hotspot elimination (Monteiro) achieves external dynamic power of 36 while a root-cause retiming achieves 21 with fewer registers. The problem affects any digital design flow where retiming runs under a fixed timing constraint, i.e., essentially every ASIC and FPGA synthesis flow. Key Idea The core insight is that glitch (switch) propagation through combinational logic is structurally analogous to delay propagation — both are regulated by register placement — so a retiming MILP can include a discrete-time, probability-based switch propagation model (adapted from HLS scheduling delay models) that tracks, per time step within the clock period, the probability of a switch at every node output. Registers are then placed to balance arrival times on reconvergent paths, eliminating the multi-step switching that constitutes glitches, while the same MILP accounts for load-capacitance changes, timing feasibility, and register count. Methodology GLOW models the circuit as a DAG with retiming variables r(n) and standard legality constraints; binary variables R_{x,y} indicate register presence on each edge (linearized against the retimed edge weight). Timing regulation uses an HLS-style delay propagation model (Equations 9–11): combinational delays propagate from fanins to fanouts unless a register blocks propagation, with all path delays bounded by T_clk. The switch propagation model (Equations 12–15) is the novel part: per-node, per-time-step switching probabilities φ^i_x propagate across edges unless a register is present, and through nodes scaled by pre-computed sensitivities s_{x,y} (probability that a switch at x causes a switch at y, from Ghosh et al.'s probabilistic switching estimation). Multiple input switches arriving in the same step contribute the maximum sensitivity-weighted probability; the node delay determines the step offset. Load capacitances are computed per-edge depending on register presence (Equation 16), and external/internal dynamic power follow the standard V²DD·f·C·switching formulation. The objective (Equation 20) minimizes α·(combinational + sequential dynamic power) + β·(total register count), with α=1, β=10⁻⁵ in experiments; setting α=0 recovers classic register-minimizing retiming. Critical design decisions: (1) the step-granularity τ, which trades model fidelity against MILP size — justified by an explicit ablation (AES runtime drops from ~315 s at τ=10 ps to ~15 s at τ=350 ps while external power rises ~7%); (2) sensitivity-based probabilistic switching rather than simulation-based glitch counts, which makes the model compatible with MILP but rests on the accuracy of pre-computed sensitivities; (3) solving the problem exactly rather than iteratively — well motivated by the demonstration that Monteiro's iterations can increase power (Figure 2). The max-instead-of-sum combination rule for same-step switches is a conservative approximation that is stated but not deeply justified. Key Results Experiments use a subset of ITC'99 benchmarks plus AES (137–7,406 gates), synthesized with Cadence Genus v25.11 in Nangate45, solved with Gurobi v10.0.1 (1-hour limit), and measured post-synthesis with Cadence Joules; functional equivalence is verified with Conformal. Against classic retiming, GLOW reduces total dynamic power by an average of 8.01% (per-benchmark range roughly −0.58% on b03 to −22.41% on b20) with register count within 1.61% of the classic minimum; against Monteiro's power-oriented retiming, it reduces total dynamic power by an average of 20.37% (up to −42.49% on b22) while Monteiro inflates register counts by up to 57% and often lands worse than classic retiming (e.g.

AI Research Preference Models

arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AI Research Preference Models (RPMs), frozen-weight LLM judges that rank unexecuted candidate solutions in an AI research agent's search tree so the agent spends its GPU-hours only on the most promising ones. - Why it's important: Frontier ML experiments cost hours-to-days of GPU time to evaluate, so an agent's progress is capped by which candidates it chooses to run, not which it can generate; better allocation directly buys more research progress per compute dollar. - How it does it: Reformulate experimental allocation as pairwise preference ranking — an inference-only variant reasons over candidate plans/code plus search-tree history, and an agentic variant runs 5-minute sandboxed pilot experiments before judging — plugged into AIRA-dojo's child-creation step. - The good: End-to-end evaluation on 20 AIRS-Bench tasks with 10 seeds shows statistically significant gains (0.684 → 0.711 / 0.729 against validation/test-oracle ceilings of 0.748/0.759), plus a strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.55, p = 0.0007) between per-step selection quality and final score that validates the mechanism. - The missing: All end-to-end evidence comes from one scaffold (AIRA-dojo), one backbone (Qwen3.6-27B), and one benchmark family (AIRS-Bench), despite the scaffold-agnostic claim; and the Agentic RPM's per-decision compute overhead means its net compute-efficiency win is not actually demonstrated (both variants converge to ~15 hours of wall-clock benefit regardless of pilot-experiment cost accounting). - Read it or not: Read it if you build AI research agents or long-horizon search scaffolds and care about compute allocation; skip it if you want the preference-modeling idea generalized beyond one scaffold — the limitations section confirms transfer is untested.

Rigor (~72) is otherwise above the subfield norm — 10 seeds, rliable bootstrap testing, oracle ceilings, and mechanism-level correlation (r=0.55) between selection quality and final score — with unusually honest cost accounting in the limitations. Problem & Motivation: AI research agents (AIRAs) that autonomously propose, implement, and evaluate ML experiments face an asymmetry of verification: generating a candidate is cheap (minutes), but executing it — training a model — costs hours to days of GPU time. Benchmarks like SWE-bench and MLE-bench progress quickly because verification is cheap; frontier research lacks cheap feedback, so an agent that proposes far more candidates than it can afford to run needs a good policy for deciding which ones deserve execution. Prior AIRA scaffolds (AIRA-dojo, MLGym, AIDE, MARS) either execute every candidate they generate or rely on greedy validation-score heuristics over already-executed nodes; none address the pre-execution allocation decision, which the authors identify as the dominant cost lever. The gap the paper closes: predicting, before paying for training, which candidate will yield the best long-term return on the execution budget. Key Idea: Reframe "which experiment should I run?" as a pairwise preference-ranking problem over unexecuted candidates rather than absolute outcome prediction — the authors report LLMs forecast absolute metrics unreliably but rank relative promise usefully. The second key move is grounding each judgment in the live search tree: candidate comparisons are conditioned on BFS-sampled previously executed solutions and their validation scores, plus (in the agentic variant) cheap pilot-experiment evidence, instead of judging code in isolation. Methodology: The pipeline modifies AIRA-dojo's child-creation step: (1) select a parent node greedily by validation score; (2) apply a mutation operator N=15 times in parallel to produce N unexecuted candidate children; (3) an RPM runs a knockout tournament of pairwise comparisons — each comparison shows the task description, up to K non-buggy context nodes from the tree (with their validation scores), and the two candidates' plans/code — and the winner is the only candidate executed and added to the tree. Two RPM variants: Inference-only (pure LLM-as-a-judge reasoning; prompt optimized via MIPROv2/DSPy with Thompson sampling over Beta posteriors; no weight updates) and Agentic (a pilot-experiment agent with python/bash/submit_solution tools runs scaled-down experiments in a sandbox clone of the environment — single split validation, data subsampling, reduced epochs — within a real 300-second budget that is deliberately overstated as 2,700 seconds, with a separate feedback model proposing the next most informative experiment; final selection uses the collected findings). Both variants share the agent's Qwen3.6-27B backbone, standardizing selection and generation model so improvements are attributable to the framework. Design decisions with varying justification: the overstated time budget (justified by ablation — removing it reduces accuracy and causes premature stopping), restricting Agentic RPM to Draft/Improve operators only (motivated by compute balance, but not ablated end-to-end), and the tournament structure for >2 candidates (standard, not compared against listwise ranking). Key Results: End-to-end on 20 AIRS-Bench text/tabular tasks (24 H200-hours per task, 10 seeds): No-RPM baseline 0.684, Inference-only RPM 0.711, Agentic RPM 0.729, versus validation-oracle 0.748 and test-oracle 0.759 ceilings. Improvement probabilities vs. baseline are 0.5923 (Inference-only) and 0.5913 (Agentic) with 95% CI lower bounds of 0.5066 and 0.5018, excluding the 0.5 no-difference point — statistically significant but modest margins. Both RPM variants match the baseline's 24-hour score of 0.684 in 14.88 and 15.50 hours respectively (~1.6× speedup). Claimed new SOTA on two tasks: WinoGrande 94.1% (prior agentic SOTA 90.4%) and SVAMP 95.7% (prior human SOTA 94.2%). Offline evaluation on 1,000 sibling pairs from 40 held-out AIRS-Bench tasks (image/video/audio modalities, avoiding contamination): individual frontier judges reach 64.66–67.44% selection accuracy vs. a 50% random floor; ensembling three models via LLM-arbiter reaches 69.35%. Agentic offline accuracy scales with time budget: 78.52% (5 min), 82.78% (30 min), 84.02% (4 hours). Selection advantage correlates with final score (Pearson r = 0.55, p = 0.0007). Baselines are current and the oracle ceilings are a thoughtful addition, but there is no comparison against any alternative selection heuristic other than random and oracles (e.g., a cheap non-LLM heuristic such as code-length or static-analysis-based filtering). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is inserting a pre-execution preference judge into an AIRA's search loop, grounded in live tree context, and the demonstration that this allocation decision is a tractable and productive target for test-time compute; the agentic variant's pilot-experiment approach to ranking is a new application. The components themselves — LLM-as-a-judge, prompt optimization via MIPROv2, evolutionary tree search, ReAct-style tool use — are all standard; the closest prior work (Zheng et al. 2026 on predicting ML solution preference, and Goldie et al. 2026's unimplemented judge proposal) differs mainly in conditioning on search-tree history and in implementing pilot experiments, so the novelty is a well-executed synthesis in a new position within the pipeline rather than a new learning technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is above average for this subfield: 10 seeds per end-to-end configuration, 95% confidence intervals, task-stratified bootstrap significance testing via rliable, oracle ceiling baselines, an offline development protocol explicitly split by modality from the end-to-end tasks to prevent contamination, and a mechanism-validation analysis (selection advantage vs. final score). Ablations are present and informative: Agentic RPM variants (no overstating, no feedback, no GPU) each degrade accuracy, and offline scaling studies cover context size, suggestion count, reasoning budget, and time budget. However: the margin over baseline is small (improvement probability ~0.59 vs. coin-flip), no code, prompts, or logs release is mentioned anywhere in the paper, and the offline labels inherit a documented bias from greedy search (subtree-max labels favor early-scoring nodes). The offline tuning data uses different backbones (GPT-5) than the end-to-end system (Qwen3.6-27B), which weakens the transfer claim from offline findings to online configuration choices. One methodological concern: development iterations on the offline set plus end-to-end evaluation on a sibling benchmark from the same suite creates mild Goodhart risk, though the modality split mitigates it. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (built and run system with end-to-end experiments). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single H200 per task plus a self-hosted 27B open-weights model, though the Agentic RPM additionally requires a sandboxed GPU clone of the execution environment for every decision. - Efficient: The Inference-only RPM is cheap (0.660 hours of inference latency per 24-hour run, scoring 0.708 when adjusted); the Agentic RPM consumes 5 minutes of GPU time per pairwise selection inside a 15-candidate tournament, a substantial overhead the paper manages but never fully accounts for in its efficiency claims. - Effective: The evidence supports the stated allocation problem on AIRS-Bench — both final performance and time-to-threshold improve, and the mechanism (selection advantage → final score) is validated — but only on one benchmark family. - Scalable: Untested beyond N=15 candidates per step and 20 tasks; the paper claims scaffold-agnostic transfer but provides no experiment on a second scaffold, backbone, or benchmark, and the Agentic RPM's per-decision cost may not amortize at larger candidate pools. The work delivers methods and results in paper form; no software artifact, model weights, or dataset release is mentioned. Strengths: - Targets the correct bottleneck. Most AIRA work optimizes candidate generation; this paper identifies pre-execution allocation as the dominant cost lever and builds directly for it, with oracle ceilings (0.748/0.759) that show how much headroom selection quality controls. - The reformulation from absolute prediction to relative preference is a real, defensible insight, backed by the observation that LLMs fail at forecasting scores but rank candidates above the 50% random floor. - Mechanism-level validation: the Pearson/Spearman correlation between step-wise selection advantage and final score (r = 0.55, p = 0.0007) connects the intervention to the outcome, rather than relying only on end-to-end deltas. - Honest cost accounting in the limitations — the authors recompute their headline number under inference latency (0.711 → 0.708) and disclose the off-policy bias and subtree-max label bias in their offline data. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) LLM inference latency is nonzero and they quantify its effect; (2) offline data is off-policy and biased (greedy-search subtree-max labels), so main claims rest on end-to-end results; (3) RPM integration covers only child creation — final-node selection showed no significant improvement over validation-based selection (Appendix D), and parent selection is left to future work; (4) scaffold-agnosticism is claimed but demonstrated only on AIRA-dojo with one backbone (Qwen3.6-27B) on one benchmark, and the Agentic variant needs a sandboxed environment clone. They confront limitations directly, including publishing the negative final-node-selection result — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The Agentic RPM's wall-clock/compute accounting is opaque: pilot experiments run on the shared H200 during the same 24-hour budget, yet the 15.50-hour time-to-baseline claim does not itemize how much of that budget went to pilot experiments versus actual search; a fully compute-matched comparison (same total GPU-hours for search + selection) is missing. - No non-trivial selection baseline: the only non-oracle comparison is uniform random selection; cheap heuristics (judge on plan only, shorter code, static analysis) or a learned lightweight ranker would establish whether 27B-scale reasoning is necessary. - Offline tuning and prompt optimization were done with GPT-5 while end-to-end results use Qwen3.6-27B; the paper does not validate that offline-derived design choices (N=15 suggestions, max context, high reasoning) transfer to the backbone actually deployed. - Only text/tabular AIRS-Bench tasks get end-to-end evaluation, while the offline development tasks are image/video/audio — neither modality is evaluated end-to-end, so the paper's own modality split leaves half the benchmark untested online. - The two SOTA claims (WinoGrande, SVAMP) rest on single-agent runs with ad-hoc tricks (shuffled-label logit averaging, temperature-sampled majority voting); no seeds, error bars, or cost accounting are given for these headline results. - No release of code, prompts-as-config, or the offline evaluation dataset (1,000 pairs from 40 unreleased tasks) is mentioned, limiting independent reproduction. Bottom Line: Practitioners building AI research agents or expensive-search systems should read this — it is the first credible end-to-end demonstration that pre-execution candidate selection is a high-leverage, measurable control point in research-agent scaffolds, and its oracle-ceiling and mechanism-correlation analyses are reusable methodology — but the narrow single-scaffold, single-benchmark evidence means its transfer claims remain, for now, a hypothesis rather than a result.

READY or Not: Reliable Enterprise Agent Deployment

V Chatrath, B Zhu, J Fan, G Pu, SD Tiwari, S Dan… · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces READY, a deployment-qualification framework that converts agent-benchmark evidence into a statistically qualified oversight policy, selecting the minimum-cost human-review rule that meets a target reliability and certifying it on held-out cases. - Why it's important: Enterprises cannot deploy agents based on autonomous benchmark accuracy alone; they need to know how much human review, at what cost, is required to hit a workflow-specific reliability bar, and current capability benchmarks do not answer that question. - How it does it: It casts oversight-policy selection as constrained optimization over a policy class (minimize cost subject to reliability ≥ Y), exploits trajectory invariance to replay saved runs under many candidate policies, and separates policy selection on development data from one-sided lower-confidence-bound (Clopper–Pearson) qualification on held-out data. - The good: On 16 agent systems and 750 CliniCARE-Bench clinical-audit cases, two systems with near-identical autonomous accuracy (72.8% vs. 72.5%) require very different review burdens to qualify at the same 76% reliability target (39.2% vs. 29.6% of cases routed to review), cleanly demonstrating that benchmark ties hide deployment differences. - The missing: Human-review effectiveness is never measured — it is assumed (a_h = 0.90) — and the empirical validation covers only the authors' own terminal accept-or-escalate setting on a single benchmark (CliniCARE-Bench, from a companion paper by overlapping authors); trajectory-dependent oversight is formulated but untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building agent-evaluation infrastructure or making enterprise deployment decisions, because it names and operationalizes a real gap (capability ≠ deployability); ML researchers seeking technical novelty in the selective-prediction machinery itself will find it familiar.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (72) is solid — the deployment-qualification formulation with evidence/assumption separation and held-out Clopper–Pearson certification is a genuinely new framing, even if the machinery (selective prediction, learning-to-defer) is standard. Rigor (65) and Completeness (68) are dragged down by the self-referential CliniCARE-Bench evaluation, the never-measured a_h=0.90 that the entire quantitative structure leans on, and a single trivial policy class. Resilience (65) is moderate — the qualification claims are honestly bounded, but generality beyond one owned benchmark is untested. Problem & Motivation: Organizations evaluating AI agents for professional workflows face a decision gap: benchmarks like Agents' Last Exam, GDPval, and τ-bench measure whether an agent can complete work autonomously, but deployment questions are different — can the human–AI system reach a required reliability level, with how much oversight, at what cost? An agent that is right 80% of the time is deployable if the failing 20% can be cheaply identified and routed to humans, and undeployable otherwise. Prior work partially covers pieces of this (selective prediction and learning-to-defer, cost-aware cascades that route to stronger models, scalable-oversight literature, assurance frameworks like model cards), but none combine executable task evidence, measured reliability against a target, operating cost, human-oversight modeling, and statistical qualification into a single deployment claim (Table 4 makes this six-axis comparison). The intended audience is enterprise evaluators and agent vendors deciding whether and under what oversight to deploy. Key Idea: The core insight is that deployment value is a property of the human–AI system under an oversight policy, not of the agent alone — and for terminal (post-hoc) oversight, the policy can be optimized by replaying saved execution evidence, since routing a completed result does not change the trajectory. Concretely: record each run's outcome u_i, a routing signal s_i (here, the agent's self-stated confidence), and costs; then find the threshold τ minimizing cost C(τ) = k_m + k_h(1 − c(τ)) subject to R(τ) = c(τ)a(τ) + (1 − c(τ))a_h ≥ Y; then freeze the policy and require a one-sided lower confidence bound on held-out reliability to clear Y. The second enabling move is the strict separation of measured evidence (u_i, s_i, costs) from declared deployment assumptions (target Y, assumed review success a_h, cost model), so the same evidence can be re-qualified under different requirements. Methodology: READY defines a formal evaluation stack: a workflow w with environment E_w, task instances x_i ~ D_w, a trajectory Z_i produced by agent m, a workflow evaluator g_w mapping trajectories to measurement vectors q_i, and a success predicate φ_w mapping q_i to binary success u_i. Deployment reliability is R(π) = E[u^π] and cost is C(π) = E[K_w(Z^π)]; policy selection solves argmin C(π) s.t. R(π) ≥ Y (optionally with a CVaR-style risk constraint). Three phases: (1) execution and evaluation produce per-instance evidence; (2) oversight-policy optimization estimates R and C per candidate policy — trivially by replay for trajectory-invariant policies, or via policy-in-the-loop execution/simulation for trajectory-dependent ones (formulated, not empirically evaluated); (3) statistical qualification freezes the selected policy and grants qualification only if the 1−α lower confidence bound on held-out reliability clears Y. For the case study, the policy class is a single confidence-threshold accept-or-escalate rule; thresholds are fit on a development half against a margin-adjusted target Y + δ (δ = 0.05) to absorb selection bias, and the confidence bound attaches exactly (Clopper–Pearson) to the observed accepted-case component while attaching no confidence to the assumed a_h. Critical design decisions: (a) the margin δ — justified by data: without it only 46% of policies qualify across the frontier sweep vs. 95% with it; (b) treating routing-signal granularity as deployment-relevant (Gemini-3.1-Pro emits only 5 distinct confidence values, limiting reachable operating points) — well-observed; (c) the break-even review assumption a_h^min, an auditable statement of the weakest review path under which the policy still qualifies — a genuinely useful reporting device. Key Results: Evaluated on 750 CliniCARE-Bench retrospective clinical-audit cases (four-way verdicts: Yes 46.9%, No 33.1%, Indeterminate-Lack-of-Data 16.4%, Indeterminate-Medically-Ambiguous 3.6%), 16 agent systems, 12,000 system–case runs, one fixed 375/375 case split. At reliability target Y = 0.76 and assumed review success a_h = 0.90, 15 of 16 systems qualify; review burdens range from 10.9% (GLM-5.2, which fails qualification — point estimate 0.762 clears by only 0.002 with the widest interval, LCB 0.725) to 100% (Gemini-3.1-Pro qualifies only by routing everything to review, attaining exactly a_h without deploying). Headline finding: GPT-5.4 (a_0 = 72.8%) and Sonnet 5 (a_0 = 72.5%) are 0.3 points apart on autonomous accuracy but require 39.2% vs. 29.6% human review to qualify at Y = 0.76 — a third more human work for the same reliability — because Sonnet 5's confidence ranks its own failures better (AUROC 0.681 vs. 0.601). Base accuracy and routing-signal AUROC are essentially uncorrelated across systems (Pearson ρ = −0.12), while AURC tracks accuracy (ρ = −0.80). A reported negative case: Qwen-3.7-Plus has better routing metrics than MiniMax-M3 at identical accuracy yet needs 61.9% vs. 33.9% review at Y = 0.76 due to threshold-grid overshoot, so single-target review burden is a noisy cross-system summary. The a_h = 0.90 assumption imposes a structural reliability ceiling of 0.90 regardless of agent quality. Baselines are effectively the leading frontier coding/agent systems of the paper's vintage (Opus 5, GPT-5.5/5.6, Gemini-3.x, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.2, Kimi-K2.7), though evaluated on the authors' own benchmark. Scale is modest (750 cases) but appropriate for the statistical method. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the framing and integration: deployment qualification of a human–AI system as constrained optimization plus held-out statistical certification, with measured evidence deliberately separated from declared deployment assumptions, and the replay-based evaluation of trajectory-invariant policies. The mathematical machinery is standard: threshold-based selective prediction (Chow 1970, risk–coverage curves, AURC), learning-to-defer, one-sided binomial bounds, and confidence-based cascades (FrugalGPT) — the paper is candid that it repackages these at the workflow level; the deferral target being a human rather than a stronger model, and the qualification bar being a statistical LCB rather than an average operating point, are the substantive deltas. Rigor & Reproducibility: Reasonably strong for the terminal setting: the development/qualification split is enforced (policy frozen before held-out inspection), the qualification statistic is exact (Clopper–Pearson on accepted cases), repeated runs and clustered cases are explicitly handled at the correct sampling unit, and the pair comparison in Section 5.6 was pre-committed on development data. The margin ablation is reported (46% → 95% qualification rate), and sensitivity analyses to a_h, the process-aware success definition, and a conflation control are in Appendix B. Concerns: (1) evaluation is entirely on CliniCARE-Bench, the authors' own benchmark from a companion paper (arXiv:2608.07796) with heavy author overlap — a self-referential loop for both the framework and the model comparisons; (2) a_h = 0.90 is assumed, never measured, and all qualification claims are conditional on it; (3) the paper says the testbed is open and built on Inspect AI, but no repository URL or release is given in the provided text; (4) qualification claims are pointwise, acknowledged by the authors; (5) confidence (verbalized, sometimes coarse) is the only routing signal studied — richer signals or trained routers are untested. Preprint (arXiv:2609.02095), not stated as peer-reviewed; vendor-affiliated (Scale AI) self-evaluation on proprietary-adjacent infrastructure warrants moderate confidence. Deployability: (profile: EMPIRICAL with a SYSTEMS component):** - Practical: Runs on Inspect AI and standard hosted LLM APIs; replay-based policy evaluation requires only saved evaluation logs, so it is cheap to adopt wherever Inspect-style evaluation already exists. - Efficient: Trajectory-invariant policy evaluation is essentially free per candidate policy (replay of 12,000 saved runs); the trajectory-dependent setting would require policy-in-the-loop re-execution, whose cost the paper does not quantify. - Effective: Evidence shows the framework distinguishes systems that capability benchmarks tie, but the qualified operating point is conditional on an unmeasured a_h, so real-world effectiveness of the review path remains a proxy-level claim. - Scalable: Tested on 750 cases / 16 systems; nothing suggests statistical breakage at 10–100× cases, but multi-workflow generalization, drift monitoring, and requalification triggers are untested and explicitly deferred to future work. The work delivers a framework specification, a formal qualification methodology, and an open testbed layered on Inspect AI (the paper claims extensibility and contribution interfaces, but no public repo is cited in the provided text). Strengths: - The central empirical result is crisp and well-isolated: near-tied autonomous accuracy (0.3 points) maps to a 9.6-point difference in required review burden, with the mechanism (routing-signal quality, AUROC 0.601 vs. 0.681) identified rather than merely asserted. - The evidence/assumption separation is a real methodological contribution: deployment profiles are explicitly conditional statements ("qualified at Y under review assumption a_h"), with versioned lineage, which is the correct shape for auditable enterprise claims and contrasts favorably with model-card-style reporting. - The break-even review assumption (a_h^min) converts an assumption into an auditable requirement on the human process — a practical device missing from the selective-prediction literature. - Honest negative reporting: the Qwen/MiniMax overshoot case and the GLM-5.2 point-estimate-vs-qualification failure are presented as findings, not suppressed, and they justify the margin design. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state clearly (Section 7): the empirical validation covers only the trajectory-invariant terminal setting on one benchmark, with trajectory-dependent oversight left to future work; human-review effectiveness, latency, and cost are assumed rather than measured; qualification claims hold only for the represented population and versioned configuration, with no guarantee under distribution shift (monitoring and requalification triggers out of scope); binary success plus optional risk constraints do not capture all deployment considerations (security, privacy, regulation remain external). They confront these directly and do not minimize them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-workflow validation on the authors' own benchmark, from a companion paper with overlapping authors: the framework's generality across "enterprise workflows" is asserted via the interface, not demonstrated; no second workflow is instantiated. - The review path is never executed: even a small measured subset of escalated cases (e.g., clinician review of 30–50 routed audits) would substantially strengthen the a_h = 0.90 assumption; the paper's entire quantitative structure leans on this unvalidated number. - Only one trivial policy class (a single global confidence threshold) is optimized; the paper's claim to be a general oversight-policy optimization framework is not stress-tested even within the terminal setting (e.g., per-verdict thresholds, multi-signal routers, learned deferral). - Confidence-signal quality drives everything, but no attempt is made to improve signals (calibration tuning, self-consistency, semantic entropy are cited but untested), leaving open whether the Sonnet-vs-GPT gap is an artifact of elicitation rather than a durable system property. - Statistical power at N_qual = 375 with ~70–90% acceptance means LCBs sit ~0.03 below point estimates; several frontier targets are effectively unresolvable at this sample size, which the paper shows but does not discuss as a design constraint on benchmark size. - No multiple-comparison handling across the 16 systems × sweep of targets (the paper flags pointwise vs. simultaneous claims but reports no corrected procedure). Bottom Line: Practitioners building enterprise agent-evaluation programs should read this: the evidence/assumption separation, held-out qualification discipline, and the accuracy-vs-deployability demonstration are immediately actionable, even though the technical machinery is standard and the framework's generalization beyond one self-owned clinical benchmark and one assumed review-success rate remains unproven.

One Symptom, Three Levers: A Critical Review of On-Policy Self-Distillation (10 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper delivers a critical, no-new-experiments review of On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), organizing the field's ~200 papers around one symptom (collapse of reasoning diversity) and three control levers (token-level signal weighting, the nature of the teacher's privileged information, and the temporal dynamics of the self-teacher). - Why it's important: OPSD promises RL-comparable reasoning gains at a fraction of generated tokens and without a larger teacher model, but its dominant failure mode — collapse — is named inconsistently across papers and poorly measured, so practitioners currently cannot tell which safeguards matter. - How it does it: The core move is a re-framing: collapse is split into a generic RL/self-training cause and an OPSD-specific cause (conditioning the teacher on the answer turns it into an oracle that, via pointwise mutual information, suppresses deliberation tokens), which naturally induces the three levers and a safety criterion imported from robotics (privileged information helps only if the student can reconstruct it at test time). - The good: The synthesis is genuinely clarifying and evidence-anchored: e.g., it shows entropy is not a valid proxy for diversity (a self-distilled Qwen3-8B can have higher entropy than an RL-trained one while pass@16 drops from 83.6 to 78.5), and it re-connects the LLM literature to Vapnik's learning-using-privileged-information theory and to robotics results (Learning by Cheating, RMA, imitation gap) that the field rediscovered without inheriting. - The missing: The framework itself is never tested — the PMI-based prediction grid and the conjectured forgetting ordering (raw SFT > dense self-distillation > sparse RL) are presented as conjectures, and the entire evidence base is preprints under six months old, mostly Qwen-family models at ≤8B, on the fragile benchmarks the authors themselves flag. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM post-training, distillation, or RLVR and need a map of OPSD failure modes and open problems; skip it if you want primary experiments or an exhaustive survey of on-policy distillation with external teachers (the authors point to Song & Zheng and Zhang for that).

Problem & Motivation: Since DeepSeek-R1, RLVR has been the dominant route to reasoning in LLMs, but it is sparse (one terminal reward for hundreds of tokens), expensive (many long rollouts), and tends to concentrate probability mass on existing behaviors. On-policy distillation restores dense token-level supervision but requires a larger teacher. OPSD (Zhao et al., 2026) and SDPO (Hübotter et al., 2026) remove that dependency by making the teacher the model itself, conditioned on privileged information (a reference solution, or environment feedback). The informational asymmetry that produces the dense signal also biases it, and one failure mode — collapse, the progressive narrowing of producible reasoning paths — now dominates the literature. Researchers and practitioners training small reasoning models lack a shared vocabulary, a trustworthy reading of the evidence (which is riddled with benchmark-variance, contamination, and Qwen-family artifacts), and a demarcation of settled results from open disputes. The paper closes that gap for mathematical reasoning, where the method originated and failure modes are best documented; it explicitly excludes the multimodal and agentic branches. Key Idea: The single organizing insight is that collapse is a symptom, not a method-specific defect, and that the OPSD-specific portion of it is driven by pointwise mutual information between the teacher's tokens and the privileged context: a teacher shown the solution stops needing deliberation tokens ("wait", "maybe"), so the distillation signal inflates solution-entailed tokens (connectives, verifiable content) and penalizes the exploration tokens the student needs at test time. This yields the "one symptom, three levers" framework — (A) where the signal is applied (divergence direction and token weighting), (B) what the teacher is shown (privileged information type, ranked by how much it presupposes the solution), and (C) when the signal changes (teacher-weight dynamics and decay of privileged information) — plus the safety criterion that privileged information helps only if the student can reconstruct it from its own test-time observations. Methodology: This is a structured literature review; the "method" is a synthesis protocol, not an algorithm. The paper first reconstructs the OPSD mechanism in pedagogical depth (student rollout generation, capped at 1,024 tokens; a double forward pass producing two ~1,024×150,000 probability matrices; per-token clipped forward KL with per-vocabulary-item cap τ; rollout-averaged, batch-averaged loss; backpropagation into the student only, teacher frozen at the initial policy), and contrasts it with SDPO (environment feedback as privileged information, EMA or interpolated teacher). It then applies a stated evaluation grid to all subsequent evidence: avg@k with confidence intervals over multiple seeds, pass@k and G-Pass@k to expose diversity loss, and four protocol controls (null/random privileged information, compute-equalized comparison, old-vs-new benchmark contamination contrast, replication outside the Qwen family). Each lever section follows a fixed pattern — state of the art at the founding paper, developments since (e.g., entropy-aware forward-KL on high-entropy tokens; DPH-RL's problem-level divergence scheduling; AR-OPD's anchored-residual target q_λ = p_anchor + λ(p_oracle − p_anchor), λ = 0.6; Purified OPSD's shortcut probe; rubric conditioning; DemoPSD's disagreement-modulated following; CGTR's gated teacher refresh; ATESD's adaptive teacher exposure), then explicit open problems. Critical design decisions of the review itself — restricting scope to mathematical reasoning, insisting on pass@k over mean scores, and importing the robotics reconstructibility criterion — are all explicitly justified, though the risk-ordered taxonomy of privileged information is honestly labeled "only partially supported by the literature." Key Results: As a review, the paper reports no new measurements; its headline content is curated results from cited work, filtered through its evaluation grid. Founding-paper claims (best-over-checkpoints, which the review explicitly flags as inflated): Qwen3-1.7B OPSD reaches 57.2% AIME24, 43.9% AIME25, 29.2% HMMT25, using one rollout of ≤1,024 tokens versus GRPO's 8 rollouts of up to 16k; forward KL raises AIME25 from 36.7 to 43.9 by step 50. Cost is reframed: an OPSD step costs ~20.6 s vs 11.2 s for GRPO on Qwen3-8B (8×H100) due to the double forward pass, so the advantage is faster convergence in steps, not lower unit cost. Documented harms: up to −17% (avg@16) on thinking models from privileged information (Kaur et al.); pass@1 71.9→73.4 while pass@16 83.6→78.5 on Qwen3-8B with token entropy paradoxically higher than GRPO's (Nicolicioiu et al.); student retaining 6.8% high-entropy tokens vs the teacher's 18.5% under reverse KL. Remedy results: error-aligned critique beats solution-conditioned OPSD by +5.27 and GRPO by +16.11 (avg@12); step-wise hints without execution reach 71.3 on C-Eval vs 63.0 with no privileged information, while the final answer alone scores 59.5 (below the no-PI baseline); AR-OPD cuts shortcut events by >20%; SDPO reaches 48.8% vs 41.2% for GRPO on LiveCodeBench v6; ATESD gains +0.95 to +2.33 avg@12 across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B. An oracle result is highlighted as undemonstrated promise: distilling only on positively aligned tokens is estimated to improve the signal 10–15×, but no method has converted this into an effective gain. Baseline strength varies across the cited works and is not systematically current; the review itself benchmarks nothing. Novelty Classification: This is a survey/position contribution — best classified as NEW FORMULATION (a taxonomy and predictive framing) rather than NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET, or NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the collapse-cause split (generic RL/self-training vs OPSD-specific PMI mechanism), the three-lever mapping onto the training loop, the reconstruction-based risk ranking of privileged information inherited from robotics, the imported stop-gradient/EMA/asymmetry rules from vision self-supervision (SimSiam, BYOL, Mean Teacher), and the proposed forgetting ordering SFT > dense self-distillation > sparse RL as a reconciliation of conflicting results. Everything else — the underlying methods, mechanisms, and measurements — is a competent synthesis of existing preprints, which the authors state plainly ("We report no new experiments. The contribution is structural."). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations, error bars, seeds, and significance tests are not applicable to the review itself — it runs no experiments — so its rigor rests on the credibility of its curation, which is unusually high: it defines and applies an explicit evaluation grid (multi-seed avg@k, pass@k/G-Pass@k, contamination tests, Qwen-family controls) and flags its own cited founding numbers as best-over-checkpoints figures that checkpoint selection inflates. No code or artifact is released by this paper; it points to the OPSD repository (github.com/siyan-zhao/OPSD) for the founding method. Methodological concerns a reviewer should hold: (1) the entire evidence base is preprints under six months old, un-peer-reviewed, predominantly on one model family at ≤8B — the authors acknowledge this but the conclusions still inherit it; (2) several load-bearing results (PMI mechanism, alignment score, shortcut leakage) come from single papers without independent replication; (3) the review's own conjectures (forgetting ordering; PMI as a predictor of collapse severity) are stated as untested, which is honest but means the framework's predictive value is unverified; (4) the paper is developed on the same fragile benchmarks (AIME/HMMT) whose weaknesses it documents, though it turns that fragility into part of its analytical grid. Deployability: Profile: this is neither EMPIRAL nor SYSTEMS; closest to THEORETICAL in that its claims are analytical/synthetic rather than experimental — the 4-property check is applied in that spirit. Sound: The argument structure is careful, claims are traceable to cited measurements, and competing readings (e.g., SDFT vs Denser≠Better on forgetting) are presented as unresolved rather than forced. General: Deliberately restrictive — mathematical reasoning only, Qwen-dominant evidence, ≤8B parameters; the authors state the conclusions "should be read with that reservation." Tight: Not applicable (no bounds); the framework makes one falsifiable prediction — collapse severity tracks how directly the privileged information entails the solution — that remains untested. Implementable: Yes in practice — the evaluation grid and lever checklist are directly actionable by any team running OPSD, and the review's verdict ("not naively for production; a post-SFT fine-tuning method at research stage") is a usable deployment guideline. The deliverable is paper form only: a reusable analytical framework and vocabulary, no library, dataset, or model. Strengths: - The entropy-vs-diversity finding is a real analytical contribution: showing that a self-distilled model can have higher token entropy than an RL-trained one while pass@16 falls (71.9/83.6 → 73.4/78.5 on Qwen3-8B) invalidates a common proxy and motivates the pass@k-first evaluation grid the review applies consistently. - Reconnecting OPSD to Vapnik–Vashist's learning-using-privileged-information and to the robotics literature (Learning by Cheating, RMA, the Weihs et al. imitation gap) is more than citation decoration: it imports a tested design rule — reconstructibility of privileged information — that the LLM field had rediscovered in vocabulary only, and it yields the paper's most actionable result, the risk ranking of privileged-information types. - The honest, skeptical treatment of evidence (benchmark variance of ±3+ points on 30-question AIME, contamination, Qwen-family spurious-reward effects, best-checkpoint inflation of the founding numbers) models the kind of review the subfield needs and materially changes how the cited gains should be read. - Each axis ends with concrete, well-scoped open problems (e.g., an online weighting criterion correlated with token usefulness; a single-protocol comparison of five privileged-information types under strict self-distillation; EMA momentum calibration on LLM teachers), which are genuine research directions rather than filler. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which strengthens credibility. They state: scope is restricted to mathematical reasoning, excluding the multimodal and agentic branches; nearly all cited work consists of preprints less than six months old, mostly on a single model family (Qwen) at sizes up to a few billion parameters, a ceiling the founding paper itself attributes to compute constraints; the risk-ordered taxonomy of privileged information is "only partially supported by the literature and may therefore contain errors"; the founding paper's best scores are checkpoint-selection-inflated; and the production recommendation is deliberately qualified — "not naively," a research-stage technique, not a turnkey training method. They also flag that collapse dynamics manifest over hundreds of steps, so short runs cannot see them, and that two of the three collapse-remedy families address the generic cause rather than the OPSD-specific PMI mechanism. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The framework's central claims are self-referentially untested: the PMI-based prediction grid ("the more the privileged information entails the solution, the worse the collapse") and the forgetting ordering are conjectures, and no experiment in the review — because there are none — validates that the three levers are the right factorization rather than one of several possible cuts of the same literature. - The evidence base is heterogeneous preprints with incompatible protocols (self-distillation vs strong-to-weak regimes, single-task vs continual settings), and several key numbers (the +5.27/+16.11 critique gains, the 10–15× oracle alignment estimate) come from single unreplicated sources; the review flags protocol mismatches but the synthesis still aggregates across them. - Conflict-of-interest and independence are unstated: the review comes from an industry LLM group (OVHai LLM) with a plausible interest in frugal small-model training, and while no specific bias is evident, the paper does not discuss whether its favorable framing of OPSD's production prospects is independent. - The review dismisses entropy as a diversity proxy based on one model and one measurement; whether that generalizes beyond Qwen3-8B is not established, even under the review's own out-of-family replication criterion. - Existing competing surveys (Song & Zheng 2026; Zhang 2026; the brief OPSD overview) are cited and differentiated, but the paper offers no systematic comparison showing its failure-mode framing covers ground they miss beyond assertion — the differentiation rests on the reader's trust. Bottom Line: Anyone training or evaluating small reasoning models should read this: it is the sharpest available synthesis of why OPSD collapses, how to measure that collapse honestly (pass@k, not entropy or mean score), and which safeguards (intermediate-abstraction privileged information, selective token weighting, controlled teacher dynamics) currently have evidence behind them — with the standing caveat that its framework is a well-argued conjecture built on six-month-old preprints, not a validated recipe.

Show-Harness: Just a VLM Agent Can Play Robots (126 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Show-Harness, an agentic harness that lets frozen frontier VLMs (e.g., Gemini-3.1 Pro) or lightly fine-tuned 2B-scale VLMs control real robot arms through a compact discrete semantic action space (MV_FWD/BACK/LEFT/RIGHT/UP/DOWN, ROTATE_CW/CCW, GRASP, RELEASE, DONE) that a per-embodiment interpreter deterministically grounds into Cartesian setpoint updates. - Why it's important: Current VLA models collapse pretrained VLM semantics into opaque, embodiment-specific sensorimotor regressions requiring fresh robot data per task family, while hierarchical systems delegate the "how" to opaque controllers; a semantic-but-fine-grained interface could inherit frontier-model progress without embodiment-specific pretraining. - How it does it: The key move is splitting control into a model-facing discrete vocabulary of small, visually-referenced movement units plus a deterministic interpreter that converts each unit into a bounded 6-DoF Cartesian pose update (Eq. 4), so the VLM makes every fine-grained physical decision in a symbol space it natively understands while embodiment specifics live outside the model. - The good: Zero-shot Gemini-3.1 Pro reaches 89% average success across 10 real pick-and-place tasks (vs. 57% for the strongest baseline, RATS), 100% under cross-environment shifts, and the same interface transfers across Franka and AgileX arms and achieves 13/20 real-robot success from simulation-only training data, where π0.5 and GR00T both score 0/20. - The missing: The fine-tuned cross-embodiment result evaluates arms the policy was co-trained on rather than a held-out embodiment, error bars and significance tests are absent from 10-trials-per-task comparisons, and sim-to-real is only tested for the FT mode (ZS shows "–" in that row). - Read it or not: Read it if you work on robot learning interfaces, agentic control, or VLA alternatives — the action-space representation ablation (arbitrary symbols with conventions nearly match semantic names; unconstrained symbols collapse to 1/20) is a genuinely useful empirical finding; skip it if you only need another demonstration that closed-source VLMs can drive arms, since the headline relies on a proprietary API model and pick-and-place-centric tasks.
