Problem & Motivation: Robotists need foundation VLM intelligence translated into physical manipulation without either (a) fine-tuning the whole model to regress embodiment-specific continuous actions (VLA route), which collapses semantics into opaque sensorimotor mappings and demands new trajectory data per task/embodiment, or (b) delegating execution to hand-engineered controllers (hierarchical/code-as-policy route), where the VLM states intent but never sees how it is realized. The gap is an interface that is semantically meaningful to the model yet fine-grained enough that the model itself remains responsible for the physical execution decisions — analogous to how navigation has discrete directional primitives but real manipulation does not. Practitioners without teleoperation rigs or large robot datasets are the implied users. Key Idea: Expose to the VLM a small vocabulary of incremental, visually grounded, embodiment-agnostic semantic action units (view-relative translations, incremental axis rotations, gripper open/close), each deterministically grounded by an embodiment-specific interpreter into a small, workspace-projected Cartesian setpoint update — so semantic intent and physical granularity meet in one interface, while safety limits and control mode (impedance control on Franka, streamed IK joint targets on AgileX, operational-space commands in sim) stay behind the interpreter boundary. Methodology: The system is a closed perceive–reason–act loop: (1) Perception plugins assemble multi-view images (global + wrist), textualized proprioception (gripper height, per-step displacement, contact state), and interaction history into a context c_t = Φ_P(ℓ, o_t, h_t); (2) a configurable reasoning layer runs subtask planning (VLM decomposes the instruction into stages with visually checkable completion criteria), situated planning (defers conditional branches until evidence appears), action chunking (open-loop bursts when the target is far), adaptive step size (2 cm fine vs. 4 cm coarse based on wrist-view visibility), visual prompting (highlights ambiguous affordances), action history with anti-oscillation rules, and failure recovery (empty-grasp detection → re-approach); (3) the VLM selects one semantic unit a_t ∈ A, and the interpreter g_E maps it to a pose setpoint via s_{t+1} = Π_E(x_t + σ_t R_E d_a, exp(θ_t [R_E r_a]_×) Q_t), with workspace and per-step limits enforced by projection. For deployment mode, a small VLM (Qwen3.5-2B default, rank-64 LoRA on ~3% of parameters, vision tower frozen) is trained with token-level cross-entropy on semantic action tokens (Eq. 5) using the model's native vocabulary — no action heads or special tokens. GUMI reuses the same action space as a keyboard/GUI teleoperation front-end that records (observation, semantic action) pairs, optionally with low-level commands, enabling human, agent, and mixed data collection plus cross-embodiment reuse without teleop hardware. Design decisions — incremental unit granularity, view-relative direction definitions, and conventions-as-grounding — are each individually ablated, which is uncommon for harness papers. Key Results: On 10 real object→receptacle pick-and-place tasks (Franka 7-DoF and bimanual AgileX, 10 randomized trials each, 50-step cap), zero-shot Gemini-3.1 Pro averages 89% and fine-tuned Qwen3.5-2B 86%, versus π0.5 (39%), GR00T (35%), H-VLA (50%), G-VLA (13%), CaP-X (44%), and RATS (57%) — a current, reasonably strong baseline set fine-tuned on the same demonstration data for the trainable comparisons. Under environment shifts (background, lighting, viewpoint, distractors) ZS scores 100% and FT 88–95% per condition vs. 65% for RATS. Sim-to-real with simulation-only training: FT achieves 13/20 while both trainable VLAs achieve 0/20. Capability probes: reducing interpreter step from 2 cm to 1 cm (no retraining) lifts ZS from 60%→82% and FT 40%→65% on stacking/peg insertion; rotation composition reaches 70% on an unseen 90° carrot orientation from 0°/45° training data (π0.5: 20%); joint dual-arm prediction eliminates collisions on handover tasks; in-context learning from video gives 20/20 for ZS on ordered tidying. Ablations show every default plugin contributes (e.g., removing proprioception drops success 96→68, removing failure recovery 96→72), thinking effort mainly cuts redundant steps rather than raising success, fine-tuned performance is already near-saturated at 2B (1B over-corrects locally), and the action-representation 2×2 shows conventions carry most of the grounding (arbitrary symbols + conventions: 95%; no semantics and no conventions: 1/20, 23.3% correct inferred mappings). ~30 model calls per episode for the zero-shot agent. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the physically grounded semantic action interface plus harness) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (GUMI data collection GUI), with a supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the action-representation ablation showing conventions, not names, provide the grounding). Discretized action tokens exist in VLAs (RT-2, OpenVLA) and discrete primitives in navigation/game agents are standard; the genuinely novel piece is the placement of the interface at a semantic-yet-single-step granularity with deterministic per-embodiment grounding — i.e., a new operating point between skill-level primitives and motor tokens — rather than a fundamentally new learning or control technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough: leave-one-out for nine plugins on dedicated probe tasks, backbone scaling (0.8B–9B across Qwen and InternVL), thinking-effort sweeps across three frontier families, and a clean 2×2 action-representation study with an inferred-mapping analysis. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; comparisons rest on 10–20 trials per condition, and several headline gaps (e.g., ZS 89% vs. RATS 57%) involve only 100 total episodes per condition. Code, models, and the demonstration dataset (164 real / 230 sim episodes, 21K steps) are stated to be released via the project site and Hugging Face (showlab/Show-Harness-Data). The paper is an arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed, and zero-shot results depend on a proprietary Gemini API whose behavior may drift. One methodological caution: the harness, action space, and evaluation tasks were designed by the same authors on the same task family, so the tuning of prompts, plugins, and step sizes against these tasks is a potential Goodhart channel, though the OOD (teddy bear, chess piece held out from fine-tuning) and sim-to-real results partially mitigate this. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (real-robot experiments) with a SYSTEMS component (GUMI harness, released dataset). Practical: Fine-tuned mode runs on a single RTX 5090 for inference and trains on 24 GB-class GPUs (<2 hours on one H200 for the 2B model); zero-shot mode requires access to a proprietary frontier API. Efficient: Fine-tuning is cheap (few GPU-hours, ~3% parameters via LoRA), but the zero-shot agent needs ~30 VLM calls per episode and higher thinking effort inflates wall-clock cost up to 3.4× for one backbone; episode-level wall-clock versus fast VLA inference is not directly reported. Effective: Evidence is on real robots with randomized placements, held-out objects, environment shifts, and sim-to-real — not just proxies — though tasks remain pick-and-place-centric with parallel-jaw grippers. Scalable: Only two embodiments and one dexterity regime are tested; claims about extending to humanoids or dexterous hands, and about the interface inheriting future frontier-model gains, are untested. Deliverable: a software artifact (harness, GUMI GUI, prompts, dataset, LoRA checkpoints) stated as released, not merely a paper. Strengths: - The interpreter split — semantic decisions model-facing, metric execution deterministically grounded — is architecturally clean and yields measurable payoffs that pure learning cannot match: precision adaptation by changing step size (60%→82%) and rotation-angle extrapolation via unit composition, both without retraining. - The action-space representation ablation is a genuine intellectual contribution: it isolates that written conventions, not semantic naming, carry the grounding (95% vs. 5% for unconstrained symbols), which directly informs interface design for future agentic systems. - Zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer by swapping only the interpreter (93% average) and the 13/20 sim-to-real result for the fine-tuned model (vs. 0/20 for identically-trained VLAs) provide the strongest evidence that the interface, not the data, drives generalization. - GUMI is a competent, practical data pipeline: the same discrete action space serves humans, computer-use agents, and policy training, and one demonstration trains both semantic-action and continuous-control policies. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that evaluation covers only single- and dual-arm manipulation with parallel-jaw grippers, that extension to humanoids or dexterous hands is open, and that perceptual modalities such as tactile and force feedback are needed for contact-rich, fine-grained interaction. This is a frank, non-defensive limitations section, though it addresses scope rather than evaluation weaknesses. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical treatment: 10 trials per task with no confidence intervals or seed variation means several baseline comparisons (e.g., 89% vs. 86% ZS-vs-FT on overlapping conditions) are within plausible noise. - Sim-to-real is only demonstrated for FT mode; the ZS row is blank ("–"), so the paper's flagship zero-shot claim is untested under the distribution shift it highlights. - FT cross-embodiment evaluation is on arms included in the co-training corpus, which is not a transfer test; no unseen third embodiment is evaluated for either mode. - Wall-clock latency and per-episode runtime against VLA inference are not reported — a deployment-critical omission when the agent makes ~30–50 sequential API calls. - The zero-shot comparisons use one default frontier model (Gemini-3.1 Pro) at medium thinking effort for the headline table; backbone sweeps appear only in ablations on subsets, so the headline number may be the best-of-family rather than a typical outcome. - Data collection throughput for GUMI (episodes/hour, operator burden, demo quality variance) is not quantified against teleoperation baselines, leaving the "no specialized hardware" advantage unmeasured. - Safety is limited to interpreter-side workspace blocking; no quantitative safety evaluation or failure taxonomy beyond grasp recovery is provided. Bottom Line: A practitioner building VLM-driven manipulation systems gains concrete, reusable lessons here — especially the conventions-over-names action-space finding and the interpreter/step-size precision lever — making this worth reading, but the headline zero-shot numbers rest on a proprietary model, small trial counts without error bars, and pick-and-place-centric tasks, so treat the 89% as a strong existence proof rather than a deployment-ready benchmark.

Who Judges the Judges? A Chinese Safety QA Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Responses and Safety Judges

R Yang, S Huang, J Liu, Z Zhao, Q Yan, Y Sun, C Liu… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces C-SafeQA, a policy-grounded Chinese benchmark of 9,415 queries (538 base + 8,877 adversarially transformed from 269 internal policy risk points via 21 mechanism-labeled transformations) and 37,660 query–response records from four target LLMs, used to jointly measure target-model safety behavior and audit seven automated safety judges against three-way (safe/unsafe/disputed) reference labels. - Why it's important: Safety evaluation pipelines chain an imperfect target model to an imperfect automated judge, and this paper shows that judge blind spots — not just model weaknesses — can silently corrupt Chinese harmful-content measurement, where homophones, acrostics, and mixed-script obfuscation are cheap to deploy. - How it does it: The core move is response-level labeling of query–response pairs under a fixed internal policy, with reference labels built by agreement-aware routing (three frontier LLM judges, with Opus-4.8 tie-breaking) plus stratified blind review by three safety experts at 20/40/80% sampling rates by agreement tier. - The good: The mechanism-conditioned judge audit is the strongest evidence: both acrostic transformations drive unsafe-response recall down to 0.67–26.43% across all seven judges while target-model unsafe rates for those mechanisms reach 69.71–91.05%, demonstrating a systematic, shared judge failure mode on the benchmark's most effective attack class. - The missing: Reference labels are model-assisted with only stratified (not exhaustive) human auditing, so the reliability of the reference set against which the seven judges are scored is itself unverified — the paper audits judges against labels whose own accuracy is estimated, not measured. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or selecting safety guardrails for Chinese-language deployment, or benchmarking judges in any language (the recall/FPR trade-off and acrostic blind-spot findings generalize); skippable if you only work on English-only safety and already know HarmBench/JAILBENCH-style results.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The dual-audit design (policy-linked response-level labeling plus mechanism-conditioned judge auditing) is a genuinely novel conjunction (Novelty 70), and the universal acrostic blind-spot finding is specific and actionable. Rigor (60) is pulled down by unverified reference labels — most labels are LLM-generated with only 20/40/80% stratified human inspection and no reported agreement statistics — single generations with no uncertainty quantification, and preprint status. Completeness (70) benefits from unusually candid self-limitation, while Resilience (65) is capped by the circularity risk that the routing judges share the failure modes under audit. Practical Impact (65) reflects a real released dataset plus judge runners, though construction tooling is withheld. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*65 = 66.

Problem & Motivation Deployers of Chinese-language QA systems need to know whether an LLM response actually violates a safety policy, but existing Chinese safety benchmarks (SafetyPrompts, CValues, CHiSafetyBench, ChineseSafe, JailBench) mostly measure prompt-level risk recognition, safety knowledge, or refusal behavior. The paper's motivating observation is that query risk and response violation are different objects: a clearly harmful query can receive a safe refusal, and an innocuous-looking transformed query (acrostic, encoding, translation) can elicit an unsafe answer. A second, less common motivation is evaluator reliability: automated judges and guardrail models are themselves error-prone, and prior judge-audit work (JAILJUDGE, HarmMetric Eval, Know Thy Judge, A Coin Flip for Safety) does not cover the conjunction of policy-linked Chinese query–response pairs, mechanism-labeled adversarial transformations, and multi-judge auditing. The unstated practical driver is regulatory/compliance pressure in China, where an internal policy must map traceably to test cases. Key Idea The key idea is a dual-audit design grounded in response-level, policy-linked labeling: (1) decompose an internal safety policy into 269 risk points and instantiate each as one question-form and one declarative-form query, so every seed is traceable to the policy boundary it tests; (2) apply 21 transformation methods tagged by attack mechanism (not just template), so failures can be conditioned on capability being probed; and (3) use the same three-way reference labels to evaluate both target LLMs and seven automated judges, treating judge reliability as a first-class measurement object. The three-way label (safe/unsafe/disputed) with explicit disputed handling and per-judge normalization status is the methodological device that prevents binary-metric gaming. Methodology Pipeline: (1) Policy-grounded query construction — internal policy decomposed into 269 risk points, each instantiated as question-form and declarative-form seeds (538 total), mostly manually authored, none sourced from user logs. (2) Adversarial transformation — 21 methods across three generation channels (template-based, LLM-rewrite, programmatic), constrained by semantic-preservation, attack-mechanism, and diagnostic constraints; nine methods apply only to declarative seeds (9×269 + 12×538 = 8,877). (3) Response collection — unquantized full-model deployments of Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Kimi-K2.5, DeepSeek-V3.2, MiniMax-M2.5, thinking disabled, external guardrails disabled, one generation per query, fixed per-model sampling parameters, yielding 37,660 records. (4) Reference labeling — three independent LLM judges (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Gemini-3.1-Pro, GPT-5.5) vote; unanimous cases accepted with 20% human spot-check, 2:1 splits routed to Opus-4.8 with 40% human inspection, full disagreement with 80% inspection; three blind safety experts adjudicate inspected cases and supersede model labels. (5) Evaluation — unsafe-response rate for target models; unsafe recall, safe-response FPR, precision, accuracy, F1, and conflict rate for seven judges (Llama Guard 4, MD-Judge, NeMo Guard, PolyGuard, Qwen3Guard, WildGuard, YuFeng-XGuard), with disputed references excluded from binary denominators and D→Safe/D→Unsafe reported separately. Critical design decisions: response-centered rubric (transformation of harmful content remains unsafe unless safety-preserving context bounds it — well-justified with a worked translation example); agreement-tiered human sampling (a cost/quality compromise the authors openly flag as non-exhaustive); withholding transformation generators and the internal policy from release (justified as misuse mitigation, but it blocks independent regeneration). No explicit loss function — this is a benchmark/dataset paper, not a modeling paper. Key Results Target LLMs: overall unsafe-response rates span 11.06% (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) to 28.43% (Kimi-K2.5) over 9,415 queries each; on base queries unsafe rates are 0.93–3.35% versus 11.68–30.05% on adversarial queries (rate ratios 7.43×–16.17×, though the pools differ in query-form composition and the comparison is explicitly descriptive, not causal). Mechanism-level: acrostic answer extraction averages 91.05% unsafe across models, acrostic generation 69.71%, text concatenation 56.74% — representation-level attacks dominate persona-based jailbreaks for several models. Category-level: Kimi-K2.5 is the most vulnerable model in six of seven categories; Illegal and Non-compliant Activities has the lowest mean unsafe rate (18.27%) but the highest high-actionability violation rate (13.28%). Judge audit on the 35,508-record transformed subset: YuFeng-XGuard leads recall (63.52%) and F1 (59.65%); WildGuard has the lowest safe-response FPR (3.13%) but recall of only 23.12%; PolyGuard collapses (68.88% safe-response FPR, precision 13.70%); Qwen3Guard's D→Unsafe mapping lifts recall from 45.40% to 60.17% at the cost of FPR rising from 6.81% to 14.93%; acrostic-generation unsafe recall is 0.67–13.81% across all judges. Conflict rates rise in 45 of 49 judge–category cells after transformation. Baselines are current judge models (2024–2026 releases), and the comparison is between judges rather than against a stronger alternative — no judge dominates, which is itself the headline. Tested at standard benchmark scale (~37K records), not stress scale. The paper carefully labels the base-vs-adversarial comparison as descriptive, not a paired causal estimate — a counter-intuitive level of honesty for this genre. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the specific conjunction in the paper's Table 1 — policy-linked Chinese query–response pairs with 21 mechanism-labeled transformations, seven heterogeneous judges, three-way reference labels, and category- and mechanism-conditioned error analysis. Not novel taken separately: response-level safety labeling (HarmBench), judge auditing (JAILJUDGE, Know Thy Judge, A Coin Flip for Safety — the authors explicitly disclaim a first-work claim), Chinese adversarial patterns (ChineseSafe, JailBench), and the transformation catalog itself is a competent adaptation of known jailbreak techniques (AIM, DAN, cipher, acrostic) to Chinese QA. The engineering contribution is the pipeline and the disciplined labeling protocol, not a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations in the benchmark sense: yes — mechanism-conditioned and category-conditioned breakdowns, per-judge normalization coverage, and both disputed-mapping policies are reported, and the analysis isolates which components drive conclusions (e.g., acrostic blind spots hold for all seven judges). Error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests: none; each target model produces exactly one generation per query and no confidence intervals are reported anywhere, so rate differences (e.g., 11.06% vs 12.91%) carry no uncertainty quantification. Artifacts: publicly released at Hugging Face (SparkShieldLab/C-SafeQA; 37,660 JSONL records, schema, manifest) and GitHub (integrity verifier plus runners for all seven judges with checkpoint IDs, prompts, deterministic decoding). Reproducibility is deliberately partial: released-field analyses and the judge audit are recomputable, but benchmark construction, target-response generation, reference-label regeneration, and the internal policy are outside the release boundary — so no third party can regenerate the dataset or verify the reference labels independently. Methodological concerns: (a) reference labels are partially self-certified by LLM judges whose own failure modes are the paper's subject — the authors note the four routing judges are distinct from the seven evaluated judges, but this is circularity mitigation, not elimination; (b) human auditing covers only 20/40/80% of agreement tiers, so ~most labels are machine-generated; (c) the benchmark is built and evaluated within the same internal policy (an acknowledged Goodhart-adjacent risk); (d) this is an arXiv-style preprint from an industry team (iFLYTEK-affiliated SparkShield), not peer-reviewed, and one evaluated guard (YuFeng-XGuard) is from a different industry group, so no direct vendor self-promotion is apparent in the judge rankings. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and measurement study with executed experiments; the artifact is a dataset plus evaluation scripts, not a deployed system). - Practical: Yes — all seven judges run from public checkpoints via released scripts, and the benchmark is plain-text JSONL consumable on commodity hardware; the four target models require large-GPU hosting, but only for replication of response generation, not for judge evaluation. - Efficient: Judge evaluation over 35,508 records with 7–12B-parameter guards is cheap relative to frontier-LLM judging; the expensive parts (four full-model deployments, three frontier reference judges plus Opus-4.8 routing, three human experts) are one-time construction costs borne by the authors. - Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark discriminates between models and exposes real judge failure modes; but it does not measure over-refusal on benign traffic (no benign-query set), so safe-response FPR here is risk-conditioned FPR — a proxy for operational moderation cost, not a substitute for it. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 37,660 records; scaling would require re-running the agreement-routing and expert-audit machinery whose cost is not reported, and label quality at higher volume is unexamined. The work delivers a durable software/data artifact (Hugging Face dataset + GitHub verifier and judge runners) but stops at paper form regarding any reusable construction tooling. Strengths - The mechanism-conditioned judge analysis is the paper's real contribution: showing that all seven judges miss 73–99% of unsafe responses under two acrostic mechanisms that simultaneously produce the highest target-model unsafe rates (69.71–91.05%) is a specific, actionable, and non-obvious finding that aggregate metrics would average away. - The three-way label schema with explicit disputed handling, dual binary-mapping policies, and per-judge normalization status is unusually careful measurement hygiene; refusing to merge disputed references into either binary class and reporting non-normalizable outputs per judge (e.g., NeMo Guard's 625) prevents several common benchmark-gaming routes. - Constructing queries from 269 policy risk points with traceable seed-to-policy linkage gives the benchmark diagnostic structure (category, mechanism, actionability) that hazard-taxonomy benchmarks lack, and the separate tracking of unsafe frequency versus high-actionability severity (Illegal Activities: 18.27% vs 13.28%) is a genuinely useful distinction for compliance triage. - Unusually candid self-limitation: the paper repeatedly and explicitly downgrades its own claims (base-vs-adversarial comparison is 'descriptive, not a matched causal estimate'; reference labels are 'model-assisted and stratified by expert auditing rather than fully human-annotated'; reproducibility claim 'concerns evaluation reproducibility rather than independent reconstruction'). Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state: single-turn Chinese harmful-content QA under one internal policy, with no coverage of other languages, multi-turn dialogue, agent traces, or other policy regimes; the internal risk-point hierarchy cannot be independently reconstructed; references are model-assisted and expert-audited, not exhaustively human-labeled, with the caveat that stratified review can miss systematic errors shared by the provisional judges; nine mechanisms apply only to declarative seeds, making base-versus-transformed and cross-method comparisons descriptive rather than matched; one response per checkpoint under one decoding configuration; no dedicated benign-query set, so real-world over-refusal cannot be estimated; and non-normalizable judge outputs are excluded from binary metrics as a coverage limitation. They also recommend that benchmark maintainers avoid using the same models to create and validate references — while their own pipeline uses four frontier LLM judges in reference routing (distinct from, but structurally the same practice as, the evaluated judges). This is direct confrontation of limitations rather than minimization, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central unverified assumption is reference-label accuracy: with only 20% human inspection of unanimous LLM-judge labels (the majority of the 37,660 records), the paper cannot estimate the reference set's own error rate, yet every judge metric is computed against it. If the routing judges share the acrostic blind spot, the headline finding that all seven evaluated judges miss acrostic unsafe responses could be partially an artifact of reference labels missing them too — a dogs-not-barking omission given the paper audits a 20% sample but never reports inter-expert or expert-vs-model agreement statistics on the audited subsets. - No benign-query control set means the safe-response FPR comparisons between judges (e.g., WildGuard 3.13% vs PolyGuard 68.88%) are computed only on risky/adversarial queries, which is the easier direction for FPR; benign-set FPR would likely reorder the judges and is the operationally relevant number for deployers. - Single generation per query with temperature up to 1.0 means target-model unsafe rates conflate model policy with sampling variance; even a small repeated-sampling subset would have grounded this. - The 'cue dispersion' explanation for the acrostic judge failure is offered as plausible and explicitly not causally isolated — no intervention (e.g., flattened acrostics) is run. - Release boundary: withholding transformation templates, the internal policy, and target-response generation code is defensible for misuse, but it makes the benchmark unauditable for policy bias (whether the 269 risk points themselves encode a contestable corporate compliance standard is unknowable from outside iFLYTEK). - No statistical testing or multiple-comparison handling for the 49-cell conflict analysis. Bottom Line A practitioner deploying or selecting Chinese-language safety guardrails should read this for the judge-audit findings — especially the universal acrostic blind spot and the recall/FPR operating-trade-off framing — but should treat the reference labels as unverified approximations and pair it with an independently human-audited benchmark before drawing fine-grained conclusions; no existing alternative covers the same Chinese policy-grounded response-level conjunction, though A Coin Flip for Safety and GuardBench cover parts of the judge-audit ground in English. }

WorldSculpt: Generating Compositional Worlds from Grounded Videos (21 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WorldSculpt, a framework that converts posed multi-view images of a cluttered scene into a compositional set of individual object meshes in a shared world frame, by adapting the Pixal3D single-object generative prior with a multi-view conditioning pathway, plus a new benchmark (UE-MeshyScene) of six Unreal Engine scenes with 93–701 objects each. - Why it's important: Downstream consumers of 3D content — game engines, simulators, robotics pipelines — need scenes as selectable, movable object meshes, but current world models (e.g., Marble, HY-World 2.0) and reconstruction methods produce fused geometry that leaves occluded regions incomplete and cannot be edited per object. - How it does it: Each object's observations are mapped into an anchor-aligned canonical cube via a closed-form similarity transform; per-view DINOv3 features are lifted into this shared voxel volume, fused with an IBR-style permutation-invariant aggregator, and injected through zero-initialized projections plus LoRA into a frozen flow-matching object prior — all trained only on single objects. - The good: The prior, finetuned entirely on isolated objects in canonical space, generalizes without any scene-level training to scenes with hundreds of heavily occluded objects, and on UE-MeshyScene it roughly halves Chamfer distance versus the strongest multi-view baseline (CD-ℓ2 2.48 vs. ShapeR's 7.42, ×10⁻³). - The missing: The pipeline assumes oracle-quality camera poses, instance masks, and 3D localization boxes, and the end-to-end demonstration on real generated worlds (Marble 3DGS) is qualitative only, so robustness under realistic upstream errors is not quantified. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on 3D scene generation, amodal reconstruction, or world-model post-processing; skip it if you need textured/appearance synthesis, dynamic scenes, or a full deployable system — the paper is geometry-only and a preprint with self-built benchmarks.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (68) and Practical Impact (68) lead: the finding that a single-object prior finetuned only in canonical space transfers zero-shot to 701-object cluttered scenes is a genuinely non-obvious result, backed by released code and a new benchmark. Rigor (65) is hurt by missing ablations on the load-bearing augmentation curriculum, no seeds or error bars, a single baseline on the authors' own UE-MeshyScene, and unexamined train/eval data hygiene. Completeness (68) is helped by direct limitation acknowledgment, but Resilience (62) suffers because the heavy upstream assumptions (oracle poses, masks, 3D boxes) are validated only by one qualitative demo. empirical Novelty 65 Rigor 65 Non-Obv 68 Completeness 68 Resilience 62 Impact 68
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Robotics, simulation, AR/VR, and game content pipelines require scenes decomposed into individually addressable object meshes placed in a common world frame. Existing options fail on this: geometry-centric reconstruction (per-scene optimization, Gaussian/pointmap regressors like DUSt3R/VGGT) recovers accurate visible geometry but leaves holes under occlusion and outputs a fused representation; scene-level generators like Marble synthesize unseen regions but emit a monolithic result; object-level generative priors (TRELLIS, Hunyuan3D, Pixal3D) model complete single objects but only from one pose-free image with no scene-frame grounding; recent compositional methods (MIDI, SceneGen, SceneMaker, PartCrafter) have been shown mainly on simple tabletop or sparse indoor scenes. The gap is compositional, complete 3D generation for genuinely cluttered scenes — hundreds of mutually occluding objects where each view reveals only fragments. The paper is a preprint (arXiv 2609.05416, dated September 2026) and not peer-reviewed. Key Idea: The core trick is decoupling — treat per-object amodal completion as a single-object generation problem, and make a pretrained single-image object prior multi-view-aware by geometrically aligning all observations into one anchor-aligned canonical cube before they reach the network. Because every view's DINOv3 features are projected into the same canonical voxel coordinates (via exact crop-aware camera projection), cross-view fusion reduces to a well-posed voxel-wise aggregation problem, and scene composition reduces to applying the closed-form canonical-to-world similarity transform. No scene-level supervision or joint optimization is ever needed. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Anchor-aligned canonicalization: for each object, the most-fully-observed view defines a canonical front-facing frame; a normalized cube [−½,½]³ is fit around the coarse localization box (isotropic scaling, grown until projections cover all masks), yielding a similarity transform T_ow; per-view crops come with adjusted intrinsics Ḱ = A·K, and each canonical voxel is projected into every crop by Eq. (7). (2) Multi-view conditioned generation: each masked crop is encoded with frozen DINOv3; per-view features are sampled at projected voxel locations, then fused per voxel by an IBRNet-style module (cross-view mean/variance, two small MLPs, softmax-weighted residual with zero-initialized feature MLP so training starts as exact mean fusion). The aggregated 3D grid is injected additively into both Pixal3D geometry stages (sparse-structure flow matching on a 64³ occupancy grid, then a sparse structured-latent shape stage on TRELLIS.2 backbone); the prior is frozen, LoRA (r=32) adapts attention/projections, anchor-view global tokens preserve the original cross-attention interface. (3) Placement: each decoded canonical mesh is transformed to world coordinates — no cross-object fusion. Training uses 15k iterations per stage on TexVerse with 1–20 randomly sampled views, plus a conditioning-view augmentation curriculum (2D/3D-consistent occluders, non-anchor pose perturbation, mask-boundary corruption, resolution downsampling) whose strength ramps from zero over the first 3k iterations. Critical design decisions: isotropic similarity canonicalization to match the prior's normalized domain (justified by the prior's cubic training convention); anchor-token retention to preserve pretrained behavior (supported by matching single-view Pixal3D on clean single-view inputs); and the degradation curriculum, which is plausible but its individual components are not ablated separately. Key Results: (1) Single-object, Toys4k (500 objects): with clean inputs and 16 views, CD-ℓ2 = 1.19×10⁻³ and F@.05 = 0.967, versus TRELLIS's best multi-view 8.29×10⁻³ and single-view Pixal3D at 2.17×10⁻³; under 75% per-view occlusion with 16 views, CD-ℓ2 = 2.25×10⁻³ versus 33.81–39.15×10⁻³ for TRELLIS — an order-of-magnitude advantage. Performance improves monotonically with view count. (2) Multi-object scenes: on real HouseCat6D, CD-ℓ2 = 0.28×10⁻³ and F-Score = 0.995 versus ShapeR's 1.26×10⁻³/0.973, RecGen's 7.22×10⁻³, and SceneMaker/SAM3D/SceneGen all ≥16.3×10⁻³; on synthetic Toys4k-Scene, CD-ℓ2 = 0.61×10⁻³ vs. ShapeR's 8.38×10⁻³. (3) UE-MeshyScene (6 scenes, 2,299 objects, 5,964 views at 2560×1440): CD-ℓ2 = 2.48×10⁻³ (median 0.25) and F-Score = 0.951 versus ShapeR's 7.42×10⁻³ and 0.813; the median gap is larger than the mean gap, indicating consistent per-object improvement. (4) Fusion ablation: the learned IBR aggregator beats arithmetic mean fusion mostly in high-view/high-occlusion regimes (e.g., 2 views/75% occlusion: CD-ℓ2 10.03 vs. 12.91) and its margin grows with scene clutter (UE-MeshyScene CD-ℓ2 −12%). (5) Application: a qualitative, unquantified demonstration converting a Marble-generated 3DGS world into a compositional mesh scene using SAM3 + rendered depth for upstream inputs. Baselines on the multi-object benchmarks are current and reasonably strong (ShapeR, RecGen, SceneGen are 2025–2026 works), though UE-MeshyScene is compared against only ShapeR. Evaluation scale is genuinely stress-scale for the benchmark; runtime and memory per scene are not reported. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the demonstration that a single-object prior finetuned only on isolated canonical objects transfers, with zero scene-level training, to hundred-object cluttered scenes via canonical multi-view conditioning, and (b) UE-MeshyScene's per-object mesh ground truth at 93–701 objects/scene, which nothing prior offers. The components themselves — IBRNet aggregation, LoRA adaptation, zero-init injection, flow-matching 3D priors, DINOv3 features — are standard; Amodal3R already adapted a native-3D prior to occluded single images, so the contribution is a well-engineered extension of a known idea to a new, harder setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: fusion module (learned IBR vs. mean) across view counts and occlusion levels on both canonical and scene benchmarks, and view-count/occlusion sweeps on single-object generation. Missing component ablations include the augmentation curriculum (no per-degradation ablation), the anchor-alignment scheme, and the cube-growth heuristic. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; results appear to be single-run. Code and project page are released (github.com/AlayaLab/WorldSculpt); UE-MeshyScene release is promised on the project page, but dataset weights/availability are not confirmed in the text. Methodological concerns: the headline benchmark is the authors' own dataset, where only one baseline (ShapeR) is compared; per-instance ICP alignment is used for canonical-space comparison, which partially normalizes away frame errors but differs from the no-ICP world-frame protocol used elsewhere; training data (TexVerse) overlap with the Toys4k evaluation set is not discussed. Metrics are self-computed; the strong HouseCat6D result on real data partially mitigates the synthetic-benchmark concern. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method with experiments and a system demonstration; no theoretical claims). - Practical: Runs from released checkpoints on standard GPUs (bf16, 512px/1024px inputs, gradient checkpointing); no indication of exotic hardware needs. - Efficient: Per-object cost is that of a two-stage flow-matching generator plus per-object feature lifting; with hundreds of objects this is inherently expensive, and no wall-clock, GPU-hour, or memory figures are reported — so cost relative to baselines is unknown. - Effective: Evidence strongly supports the stated problem on benchmarks with exact ground truth (F-Score 0.951 on UE-MeshyScene), but the end-to-end path from real raw video (segmentation, pose estimation, 3D detection) is assumed, not validated quantitatively. - Scalable: Tested to 701 objects/scene, the largest reported scale for compositional generation; behavior at 10× scale (and total compute for thousands of generations) is untested and unclaimed. Deliverables: code repository, planned benchmark, and (implicitly) finetuned checkpoints — a reusable artifact beyond the paper, though geometry-only. Strengths: - The central empirical finding — canonical-space-only finetuning of an object prior generalizing to hundreds of densely occluded objects with no scene-level training — is a real, non-obvious result that reframes how compositional generation can be approached. - The conditioning-view augmentation curriculum (3D-consistent occluders, pose perturbation, mask corruption, downsampling) directly targets the train/test gap of cluttered scenes and demonstrably yields robustness (stable metrics up to 50% occlusion with 16 views). - UE-MeshyScene fills a genuine evaluation gap: exact per-object meshes, poses, and 3D boxes at photorealistic scale (2,299 objects, 5,964 views), which neither HouseCat6D nor Toys4k-Scene provides. - Honest metric design: world-frame, no-ICP evaluation jointly scores geometry and placement, and the median metrics rule out gains driven by a few easy objects. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) dependence on upstream camera poses, instance masks, and 3D boxes, with robustness only to moderate errors; (2) geometry-only output — no texture or material generation (though the backbone supports PBR stages); (3) a static-scene assumption, excluding moving or deforming objects. They confront these directly and name concrete remedies (integrated detection/localization/generation, texture-stage extension, optical flow and articulated models), which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The upstream assumptions are heavy: posed cameras, per-view instance masks, and 3D boxes are treated as given, yet the qualitative Marble demo is the only test of the full pipeline, with no quantitative sensitivity study to realistic mask/box/pose error levels. - UE-MeshyScene is compared against a single baseline (ShapeR); scene-level methods like SceneGen or SAM3D, and amodal baselines like Amodal3R composed per object, are absent from the large-scale table. - The augmentation curriculum — arguably the load-bearing component for robustness — has no ablation isolating its contribution or its individual degradations. - No runtime, memory, or total-compute figures for generating a 701-object scene, despite per-object generation being the method's central cost driver. - Training-data hygiene is not addressed: whether TexVerse overlaps Toys4k or UE-MeshyScene assets is unstated, leaving possible train/eval contamination unexamined. - The benchmark has only six scenes from one renderer with one orbiting camera style, raising mild overfitting/Goodhart risk for a benchmark the authors also win. Bottom Line: For researchers in 3D scene generation, amodal reconstruction, or world-model post-processing, this is worth reading — it delivers both a credible method for object-complete compositional generation at unprecedented clutter scale and the first benchmark that can measure it — but practitioners needing end-to-end robustness, textured output, or verified compute costs should treat the results as a strong but unreplicated preprint claim.

Act More, Decide Less: Skill-Guided Adaptive Action Chunking for Long - Horizon LLM Agents

Y Yang, C Jin, J Zhao, J Wu, Y Zhou, Z Wang, Z Wang… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SPACE, a training framework that teaches LLM agents to emit variable-length action chunks (multiple primitive actions per LLM decision) by distilling chunk-boundary supervision from programmatic skills induced off successful trajectories. - Why it's important: ReAct-style agents spend one costly LLM round per primitive action, wasting inference compute on routine sequences in long-horizon tasks; amortizing rounds across chunks cuts decision cost by up to 78.9% while raising success rates. - How it does it: Successful trajectories are segmented by an LLM into two-level programmatic skills whose subskill boundaries define chunk divisions; these are distilled into a flat chunk policy via hybrid on-policy RL (clipped PPO-style loss) and off-policy self-imitation on expanded skill trajectories, with two-level (trajectory + anchor-state) chunk-aware advantages. - The good: The paper demonstrates and diagnoses two concrete failure modes of naive multi-action GRPO — single-action collapse (Qwen3-4B) and over-commitment (Llama-3.1-8B) — and shows SPACE avoids both, sustaining ~3–4 actions per round at 94.5–99.2% success on ALFWorld. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, no public code release is mentioned, and ALFWorld results near ceiling (99.2%) plus exclusion of ScienceWorld tasks exceeding 100 steps leave generalization and statistical reliability unverified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on LLM agent RL, temporal abstraction, or inference-cost reduction, since the chunk-boundary-learning diagnosis is a genuinely useful insight; practitioners seeking deployable agent frameworks can skim for the experimental tables only.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) is solid — the skill-boundary-distillation insight and the documented failure modes of multi-action GRPO are genuinely new, though built from known components (GiGPO, self-imitation, ACT-style chunking). Non-Obviousness (72) is the paper's strength — the diagnosis that boundary supervision, not multi-action output, is the bottleneck reframes the problem usefully. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: LLM agents on long-horizon interactive tasks (text games, scientific simulations) typically follow the ReAct protocol: one LLM round per primitive action. This granularity is wasteful — many rounds execute routine sub-sequences rather than make decisions — and prior work links step-by-step interaction to short-sightedness, compounding errors, and repetitive loops. The natural fix, letting the policy emit variable-length action chunks, fails under standard RL: the authors show empirically that multi-action GRPO either collapses to single actions per round (Qwen3-4B) or over-commits to 5–6-action chunks with no success gain (Llama-3.1-8B). Both failures stem from a common root: sparse terminal rewards carry no signal about where chunk boundaries should fall. Who has this problem: anyone training LLM agents under inference-cost or rollout-budget constraints on multi-step interactive tasks. Key Idea: The core insight is that successful trajectories already contain chunk-boundary supervision: if you induce two-level programmatic skills from them — composite skills decomposing into ordered subskill calls, where each subskill is one locally executable routine — the subskill boundaries mark exactly where one chunk should end and the next begin. These boundaries are then distilled into a flat primitive-chunk policy (which never sees skills at deployment) through skill-to-chunk expansion: skill calls in training rollouts are unrolled into chunk-level supervision targets, optimized jointly with on-policy chunk RL and off-policy advantage-weighted self-imitation. Methodology: SPACE treats the environment as a POMDP and reformulates acting as a semi-MDP over variable-length LLM rounds, with chunks u_i ∈ U_K (max chunk length K=6) executed open-loop until completion or an invalid action. The pipeline has four stages. (1) Skill induction: an LLM segments successful trajectories into subtask phases and emits one composite skill plus subskills as executable Python, filtered by syntax/compilability checks and deduplicated via AST canonicalization; the library is seeded with 3–5 hand-written cold-start skills and capped at 20 composite skills per task category. (2) Hybrid rollouts: per task, a fraction ρ_prim of rollouts use the deployment-time primitive-chunk action space (on-policy data), the rest use a skill-augmented mode where the policy may call retrieved skills (chosen via UCB-style scoring or similarity retrieval). (3) Skill-to-chunk expansion: composite-skill calls are unrolled along their subskill-call sequence into chunk-level (history, chunk) pairs forming an off-policy dataset. (4) Chunk-aware optimization: a GiGPO-style combined advantage A = A_traj + λ_step·A_step, where A_traj is group-normalized terminal reward and A_step normalizes discounted returns G_τ,i = γ_c^(M−i)·r(τ) within anchor-state groups; the on-policy loss is a clipped PPO-style surrogate over Don, the off-policy loss is advantage-clipped self-imitation (Oh et al., 2018) over Doff, combined as L = Lon + λ_off·Loff. Critical design decisions: two-level skill structure as the boundary source (justified by the failure-mode analysis of Fig. 1, though the segmentation quality of the induction LLM is not independently validated); skills as training-only scaffolds (validated by the deployment interface using only primitive chunks); the ρ_prim mixing ratio (ablated, 0.75 best on ScienceWorld). Built on GRPO/GiGPO and self-imitation — known machinery — with the skill-boundary distillation being the new move. Key Results: On ALFWorld (seen/unseen, Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) SPACE reaches 99.2/96.9% and 96.1/94.5% success at 3.7–5.2 LLM rounds per episode, versus GiGPO at 85.2/72.7% (Qwen3-4B, 15.9/21.7 rounds) and GRPO at 71.9/54.7% — improvements of 7.0–15.6 points over the strongest baseline per setting with up to 12.2 fewer rounds. On ScienceWorld (Llama-3.1-8B) SPACE reaches 67.2/61.7% at 5.2/5.8 rounds versus GiGPO's 35.9/34.4% at ~10 rounds (+27–31.3 points, roughly halving rounds); Multi-action GRPO there reaches only 17.2/11.7%, confirming chunk learning — not merely multi-action output — drives the gains. SPACE reaches GRPO's final ALFWorld performance using 43.60K rollout rounds (26.6% of training steps to match multi-action GRPO's final level by step 40 of 150). Ablations (ALFWorld, Llama-3.1-8B): removing skills drops success to 86.7/88.3%, removing chunk-aware advantage to 90.6/89.1% (from 96.1/94.5%). Test-time Best-of-N (N=8) on a hard ScienceWorld subset: SPACE+BoN hits 60.4% SR at 48.3 LLM calls versus GRPO+BoN at 37.5% and 74.9 calls — chunk policies gain nearly twice as much from BoN (+8.3 vs +4.2 points). Scale: 7B-parameter backbones, 4×H200 or 4×GH200 GPUs, single node. Baselines are current (GiGPO, GRPO, RLOO, Reflexion) and reasonably strong, though the prompting baselines are weak. Notably, per-task ALFWorld results show gains concentrated on longer task types (heat, cool, pick-two). ScienceWorld results at ~62–67% (not saturated) are more informative than the near-ceiling ALFWorld numbers. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (skill-distilled variable-length action chunking for LLM agents) with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (documented failure modes of naive multi-action GRPO and the diagnosis that chunk-boundary learning, not multi-action output, is the bottleneck). The genuinely novel element is using subskill boundaries from induced programmatic skills as free chunk-boundary supervision, decoupled from the skill library at test time. The components — GRPO-style RL, GiGPO's two-level advantages, self-imitation distillation, ACT/Q-chunking lineage, ASI-style programmatic skill induction — are each existing ideas; the contribution is their specific combination and the training-only-scaffolds framing, applied to a setting (discrete textual actions, context-dependent chunk length) where fixed-length chunking from robotics does not transfer. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover the two core components (skills, chunk-aware advantage) and the rollout mixing ratio, and the training-dynamics analysis (entropy, actions-per-round, rollout efficiency) is more diagnostic than typical for this area — the two failure-mode characterizations across backbones are convincing. However: no error bars, seed counts, or significance tests are reported anywhere; single-run results near 99% on ALFWorld make differences hard to interpret; the hard ScienceWorld BoN subset is small (implied ~48–96 tasks given SR jumps of 4–8 points). No code, data, or model release is mentioned in the paper. Methodological concerns: (1) ScienceWorld tasks with oracle solutions over 100 steps are excluded for compute reasons, capping tested horizon length; (2) skill induction and evaluation both depend on the same backbone LLM family, so skill quality is not independently verified; (3) the TTS comparison uses a 3-step lookahead scorer for primitive candidates versus full-chunk rollout scoring for chunk candidates — a scoring asymmetry that partially advantages the chunk policy; (4) off-policy distillation data comes from skill-augmented rollouts whose high success rate (Fig. 5c) means the distillation signal is self-generated and could propagate induction-LLM biases. This is a preprint (arXiv 2609.02042), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trains and evaluates policies in simulated environments). - Practical: Runs on a single node of 4×H200 (8B) or 4×GH200 (4B) GPUs — within reach of academic labs, though not consumer hardware. - Efficient: The whole point: 78.9% fewer LLM decision rounds at test time and ~2.3× less rollout data to match GRPO, so inference cost per task drops substantially; training itself requires the usual multi-GPU RL budget. - Effective: Strong evidence in the two tested simulators, including on unseen splits, but effectiveness in stochastic or safety-critical settings is untested (and the authors concede chunked execution reduces replanning frequency). - Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B models, ~100-step horizons (ScienceWorld >100-step tasks excluded), and two text simulators; behavior at 10× horizon length or with larger backbones is claimed only implicitly. Deliverable: stops at paper form — no library, CLI, checkpoints, or released skill libraries are mentioned. Strengths: - The failure-mode analysis of naive multi-action GRPO (collapse vs. over-commitment, with opposite signs on different backbones) is a real empirical contribution that reframes the problem from "enable chunking" to "supervise boundaries" — this diagnosis, not the algorithm, is the paper's most transferable insight. - The skill-to-chunk expansion trick cleanly solves the train/deploy mismatch: skills supply structure during training, the final policy is a flat chunk generator with no library dependency, which sidesteps the usual brittleness of skill-retrieval deployments. - Demonstrated sample efficiency is concrete: matching GRPO's final performance with 26.6% of training steps and 43.60K rollout rounds, plus higher training entropy with graceful decay — evidence the method changes exploration dynamics, not just the output interface. - The chunk-policy/test-time-search complementarity finding (BoN gains of +8.3 points on chunks vs +4.2 on primitives, at structurally lower call counts) is a non-obvious bonus result relevant to the inference-scaling community. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) evaluation is limited to text-based environments, leaving broader interactive scenarios unvalidated; (2) skill induction depends on successful trajectories, so other domains may need stronger exploration, retrieval, or validation mechanisms; (3) chunked execution reduces observation and replanning frequency, which is risky in highly stochastic or safety-critical environments. They confront these directly and without minimizing — the third limitation in particular honestly qualifies the method's headline efficiency gain as a robustness trade-off. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical rigor: single-run results, no seeds, no variance estimates — the 7-point margins on ALFWorld unseen are probably robust, but the smaller differences (e.g., GRPO vs. RLOO on ScienceWorld) are unverifiable. - ALFWorld saturation: 99.2% seen success leaves almost no headroom, so the headline +14.0 is measured against a baseline that itself has little room; ScienceWorld is the only non-saturated test, and it is the one with tasks excluded and a lower absolute gap-closure (67.2% still leaves a third of tasks unsolved). - The skill-induction stage is validated only end-to-end: no measurement of induced-skill correctness, boundary-alignment accuracy, or how induction quality degrades when the backbone model is weaker — yet this stage is the paper's load-bearing assumption. - Missing baselines from adjacent work: Q-chunking (fixed-length RL chunking), ASI (the programmatic-skill induction method the paper builds on, used only as prompting guidance), and fixed-length chunk ablations (K=1,2,3 fixed) that would isolate whether variable-length boundaries matter or any chunking suffices. - The BoN comparison's asymmetric scoring (3-step lookahead for primitives vs. full-chunk rollout for chunks) means the "chunks are better for TTS" claim is confounded by the scorer choice. - No analysis of failure cases where chunked execution commits to a wrong multi-action sequence that per-step ReAct would have caught — the cost side of the replanning trade-off is illustrated anecdotally (Fig. 6) but never quantified. Bottom Line: A practitioner training RL-based LLM agents should read this for the chunk-boundary diagnosis and the hybrid on-/off-policy distillation recipe — the empirical gains on ScienceWorld are large enough to take seriously — but should wait for a code release and multi-seed replication before adopting it, as the near-ceiling ALFWorld results and missing statistical controls flatter the method more than the evidence strictly supports.

NeuroSTAR: Automata-guided Neuro-symbolic Specification Formalization

J Saha, T Woodlief, S Elbaum, MB Dwyer · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces NEUROSTAR, a training-free framework that translates natural-language requirements into LTLf formulas by generating multiple candidate formulas with LLMs, compiling them to DFAs, extracting concrete witness traces where the candidates' behaviors disagree, and using LLM judges over those traces to drive iterative refinement until convergence. - Why it's important: NL-to-temporal-logic translation is the bottleneck for applying formal verification, monitoring, and synthesis to cyber-physical systems, and current LLM methods produce syntactically valid formulas that are often semantically wrong because nothing checks actual formula behavior. - How it does it: The core trick is automata-theoretic differencing — building difference automata (D_i \ ∪D_j and ∪D_j \ D_i) between candidate formulas, sampling finite witness traces from them, and having LLM judges vote on whether those traces match the NL's intent, converting per-trace verdicts into structured refinement feedback and a stability/medoid-based convergence test. - The good: The authors first audit the four standard benchmarks, removing up to 48.43% of entries for train-test contamination, trivial formulas, LTL→LTLf incompatibility, and ambiguity; on the cleaned (and harder strict) versions, NEUROSTAR reaches 96.4% on CONFONLst and 100% on SYNTHNLst, beating ADARULE by 8.3–18.4 pp. - The missing: The real-world evaluation on 108 Virginia driving laws uses only a necessary-condition metric (VWV: one human-adjudicated shortest violating trace per law, rated by the authors themselves), so the 83.9% figure cannot establish semantic correctness, and there are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in specification formalization, LLM+formal-methods hybrids, and autonomous-vehicle requirements engineering; practitioners wanting a mature, costed, deployable NL-to-LTL tool or a careful statistical comparison should wait for follow-up.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building verified, monitored, or synthesized cyber-physical systems (robotics, automotive, aerospace) rarely have formal temporal specifications; behavior is described in natural language. LLM-based NL-to-LTL(f) translators have emerged but, as the paper cites (Danso et al., "Syntax is easy, semantics is hard"), often get syntax right while missing semantic constraints — and no prior method exploits the fact that the target logic has decidable, automata-encodable semantics. A second, adjacent problem is that the benchmarks used to claim progress are compromised: the authors, while replicating ADARULE (the prior SoTA), found train-test duplication (76 of 100 LANGNL test pairs exactly duplicated), trivial true/false labels, incorrect ground truth, LTL↔LTLf mismatches, and systematically ambiguous temporal phrasing that a training-based method can exploit without understanding the NL. Anyone evaluating NL-to-LTL translation — and anyone deploying it on real requirements like legal driving code — currently has both a weak technique and a broken yardstick. Key Idea: Treat NL-to-LTLf translation as multi-generator consensus grounded in symbolic semantics: generate several candidate formulas with diverse LLMs, make their disagreements concrete by compiling each to a DFA and extracting witness traces from pairwise difference automata, then shift the LLM's job from the hard task of synthesizing a complete formula to the easier task of judging whether specific finite traces match the NL intent. The judges' per-trace verdicts become removal/insertion feedback per generator, and iteration stops when a candidate is both locally stable (few judge corrections) and semantically close to another independently generated stable candidate (medoid Jaccard distance below threshold θ). This is the paper's one reconstructible insight: use the automaton, not the text, as the inter-model communication channel. Methodology: NEUROSTAR takes an NL requirement plus an atomic-proposition (AP) library and runs three modules iteratively. (1) Candidate Generation and Validation: four generators (Gemini 3.5 Flash and Kimi K2.5, each at temperatures 0.1 and 0.9, with 5 few-shot examples from the ADARULE train split) each produce an LTLf formula; candidates must pass a syntax check and an AP-consistency check (AP(φ) ⊆ L_AP), with bounded repair retries. (2) Automata-Based Differencing: each valid candidate is compiled to a DFA via Spot; two difference automata per candidate (U_i = D_i \ ∪_{j≠i} D_j; V_i = ∪_{j≠i} D_j \ D_i) yield sets K_i (uniquely accepted traces) and A_i (traces missed relative to others). Witness traces are selected by a globally optimal MILP (HiGHS) maximizing edge coverage of the difference DFAs, with trace length bound l_C = 5 and budget b = 5 on benchmarks (10/10 for VALAW). (3) Judging and Feedback: two panels of Kimi K2.5 judges (Judge_keep, Judge_add) each describe a trace and vote on whether it matches the NL, decided by majority; votes yield stability scores J_K = (|K_i|−|R_i|)/|K_i| and J_A = (|A_i|−|I_i|)/|A_i|. Convergence requires ≥3 candidates with J_K ≥ m and J_A ≥ n, then picks the medoid of the stable set under bounded-trace Jaccard distance and returns it if within θ of another stable candidate. Notable design decisions: (a) targeting LTLf (DFA-compilable) rather than LTL (Büchi), justified by finite-horizon CPS missions — reasonable but it forces removal of benchmark pairs not LTLf-equivalent; (b) converging even when all generators agree on the same formula, explicitly accepting the correlated-failure risk with the claim that joint error is empirically rarer; (c) full-edge-coverage MILP trace selection rather than greedy — justified but the l_C bound means traces longer than 5 (10) steps are invisible. Key Results: Evaluation is on cleaned variants of four prior benchmarks — CONFONLf (87.8%), SYNTHNLf (75.8%), SPECNLf (92.9%), LANGNLf (94.1%) — versus ADARULE (77.6 / 78.9 / 92.9 / 94.1), LfF (68.4 / 43.2 / 85.7 / 76.5), and an n-shot prompting baseline (86.2 / 76.5 / 87.5 / 89.7); and on strict versions — CONFONLst 96.4% vs ADARULE 88.1% and n-shot 93.4%; SYNTHNLst 100% vs 81.6% and 97.4%. Accuracy is semantic equivalence checked with Spot. NEUROSTAR loses to ADARULE on SYNTHNLf by 3.1 pp, attributed to ADARULE memorizing the eight synthetic patterns. Baselines are recent and reasonably strong (ADARULE is ICSE 2026, LfF 2024), though all rely on textual patterns rather than semantics. The abstract's "8–18 pp" claim holds only against ADARULE on the strict datasets and subset of filtered datasets; on LANGNlf and SPECNlf it is joint-best (0 pp gain). The benchmark audit is itself a headline result: 76 LANGNL test pairs (76%) duplicated in train, 18 pairs (5.7%) removed as incorrect/trivial/LTLf-incompatible, 60 pairs (31.08%) removed for strict/non-strict temporal ambiguity, 7 edits (8.3%) for anaphora. RQ2 quantifies the realism gap: CONFONLf entries average 9 words vs 273 for VALAW; cross-generator mean syntactic (AST edit) distance is 4.5× and semantic (Jaccard) distance 11× higher on VALAW. On VALAW (108 laws, no ground truth), 107 converge within 8 iterations, 1 is trivially true, and human raters find the generated formula's shortest violating trace to be a true violation in 89/106 (83.9%) cases. Scale tested is standard-benchmark plus one small real-world corpus (108 sections); no stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (VALAW) and a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the benchmark audit). The genuinely novel element is automata-guided, trace-level differencing of multi-generator candidates as a training-free refinement signal — no prior NL-to-LTL work uses the target logic's automata semantics to arbitrate between LLM outputs. The components are individually standard: LLM ensembling/self-refinement, majority-vote LLM judges, DFA compilation with Spot, difference automata (classic automata theory), and medoid-based consensus. The paper's own audit showing 76% train-test duplication in a published benchmark is a notable empirical contribution in its own right. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are weak: there is no component ablation isolating how much the automata-guided loop contributes versus simply running four generators and voting (the n-shot baseline partially serves this, but only for a single generator average). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for any RQ3 number, and dataset sizes after filtering are small (≈98–176 entries). The paper claims cleaned datasets and judge annotations are released ("see § VIII"), but § VIII provides no URL or artifact link — as presented, the artifact release is asserted, not verifiable. Methodological concerns: (1) the authors modified the evaluation sets themselves (including removing 31% of pairs for a strict/non-strict ambiguity dispute where they argue from Grice's maxim), which benefits their training-free method relative to ADARULE, whose training data was the original split — a confound partially addressed by also reporting n-shot results but never fully disentangled; (2) the judge model (Kimi K2.5) is also one of the generators, an unacknowledged self-judging bias; (3) the VALAW metric is author-rated (two authors per section, third on disagreement) with a conservative-instruction protocol and released judgments — a real but partially mitigated conflict of interest. The threat-to-validity section is unusually candid about parameter sensitivity (m, n, θ, l_C, b), Jaccard trace-bound saturation, and author bias. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — it needs only commercial LLM APIs, the open-source Spot library, and HiGHS via SciPy; no training. Efficient: Cost is not quantified, but each iteration involves 4 generator calls plus 2×b judge calls per candidate plus DFA compilation and an MILP solve; versus a single prompt for n-shot, this is roughly an order-of-magnitude more LLM calls per input, and the paper gives no token/dollar/latency figures. Effective: On benchmarks with ground truth, yes (100% semantic-equivalence accuracy on SYNTHNLst); on the realistic VALAW corpus, only a necessary condition is checked — a valid violating witness supports the formula, but formula correctness is not established. Scalable: Untested — trace enumeration up to length l_C over difference DFAs and 273-word legal texts with 352 APs is the current frontier; laws needing deeper traces or a richer AP vocabulary fail, and the authors do not test longer traces or larger AP libraries. The work stops at paper form plus asserted datasets/annotations; no library, CLI, or trained model artifact is concretely delivered. Strengths: (1) The core mechanism — difference automata as the medium for inter-candidate disagreement and as structured feedback for LLM refinement — is a real conceptual advance for neuro-symbolic specification, converting an unobservable semantic gap into concrete, judgeable traces. (2) The benchmark audit is genuinely valuable to the community: documenting 76% train-test duplication in LANGNL, incorrect/trivial labels, and a systematic strict/non-strict labeling convention that training-based methods exploit changes how all prior results on these datasets should be read. (3) The VALAW construction and RQ2 distance analysis (9 vs 273 words; 4.5×/11× syntactic/semantic candidate divergence) provides the first quantified evidence that existing benchmarks underrepresent real-world formalization difficulty. (4) The qualitative VALAW analysis (7 recurring strengths, e.g., correct negated-antecedent "unless" handling in 22.6% of sections, weak-until obligations, operative-core isolation in § 46.2-873) shows specific, checkable formalization capabilities rather than aggregate scores alone. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: implementation-bug risk in parsing, automata construction, and trace generation; sensitivity to hyperparameters (θ, m, n, trace bound, budget) chosen by pilot runs; residual dataset-cleaning errors; author bias in VWV rating (mitigated by conservative rating, a third reviewer, and released judgments); the VWV metric being only a necessary condition that does not verify full accepted/rejected trace language; Jaccard distance on bounded traces potentially causing spurious convergence (mitigated by empirically choosing k at saturation); model-choice sensitivity of external validity; the AP vocabulary gap as the dominant limitation (e.g., § 46.2-868.1 collapsing distinct aggressive-driving scenarios into one AP); and that benchmark datasets are simpler than real specifications. This is direct and unusually thorough confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits: (1) the judge generator and judge are the same model family (Kimi K2.5), so judge blind spots are correlated with one generator's blind spots — never discussed; (2) no ablation with diverse judges or more/fewer generators, so the necessity of multi-generator diversity is asserted via intuition, not measured; (3) dataset modification confounds: removing ambiguous pairs by the authors' own Gricean reading then declaring victory on the "strict" versions is evaluated on data shaped by the method's design philosophy, and ADARULE's training data was not regenerated for the new splits; (4) no comparison against any symbolic-verifier or user-in-the-loop reference baseline (e.g., nl2spec's interactive refinement) on semantics-grounded refinement; (5) convergence guarantee is purely empirical — there is no analysis of non-convergence, oscillation, or judge-noise effects on termination, and 1 of 108 laws is reported as non-converging (107/108) without explanation; (6) the claimed cost profile is absent — no token counts or wall-clock, which matters because the method multiplies LLM calls; (7) the LLMs and citations are 2026-era models with no static versioning of outputs, so exact replication is fragile; (8) the "8–18 pp" headline in the abstract is achievable only against ADARULE, not against n-shot prompting (gaps of 0–3 pp on three of six dataset variants). Bottom Line: This is the most credible semantics-grounded advance in NL-to-LTLf formalization I have seen, and its benchmark audit alone justifies attention, but the unquantified cost, missing ablations and error bars, and author-scored real-world evaluation mean a practitioner should adopt the idea (automata-guided multi-generator refinement) while treating the headline numbers as promising rather than settled.

NCP-ArchPreview Technical Report: Moving towards Latent Space Language Models through Next Concept Prediction (177 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds and trains NCP-ArchPreview, an 8.9B-parameter autoregressive language model that augments next-token prediction with next-concept prediction over a learned product-quantized discrete latent vocabulary, pretrained on 5.73T tokens of the Dolma-3 corpus. - Why it's important: It demonstrates, at the largest scale to date (roughly 6× the 1.5B scale of the foundational ConceptLM work), that explicit latent-space prediction objectives can cut pretraining compute rather than just add parameters — a potential lever against the rising cost of foundation-model training. - How it does it: A 16-layer token encoder feeds mean-pooled 4-token chunks into an 8-layer Concept Module that predicts the next concept as a differentiable weighted combination of product-quantized codebook entries; the causally shifted prediction is injected back into the 16-layer token decoder, trained end-to-end with a joint loss L_NTP + α·L_NCP + β·L_VQ plus MUDDFormer-style hierarchical residual routing. - The good: The headline evidence is a same-data, same-recipe comparison against OLMo-3-7B in which NCP-ArchPreview reaches the baseline's final Stage-1 loss using 51.3% of the tokens (1.95× token efficiency, 0.091 lower final loss) and adds +2.45 points on the 26-benchmark downstream macro-average (+5.99 on GSM8K). - The missing: The ablation that attributes gains to components runs only over the first 200B tokens (~3.5% of the full run), there are no seeds, error bars, or significance tests on any downstream number, and the Stage-2 downstream advantage shrinks to +0.59 points with code benchmarks actually regressing (Code AVG −0.65). - Read it or not: Read it if you design pretraining architectures or objectives and want the current largest-scale evidence on latent/concept-level prediction; skip it if you need long-context behavior, inference-time latency numbers for the main model, or results beyond the single OLMo-3 baseline family.
Why this rank

The composite is pulled down by Rigor (65) — no seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere, component attribution resting on a 200B-token ablation that is under 4% of the full run, and evaluation against a single baseline family — and by Resilience (60), since the headline 1.74× efficiency factor is extrapolated from IsoFLOP fits well below the flagship scale and the Stage-2 downstream gain (+0.59 with code regression) may sit within run-to-run noise.
