Problem & Motivation: Studios and 3D-asset creators can now obtain rigged meshes at scale (via tools like UniRig, MagicArticulate, Puppeteer), but no learned animator can drive those rigs: template-based motion models (built on SMPL/SMAL) cannot handle skeletons that depart from the template; per-skeleton methods (GANimator, SinMDM) train one model per rig; retargeting methods require a source motion; mesh-based methods either need costly per-asset optimization or regress kinematically unconstrained vertex deformations. The closest prior work, AnyTop, trains one diffusion model over heterogeneous animal skeletons but is unconditional, needs a reference motion of the target skeleton at inference to estimate normalization statistics, and covers a small animal-only corpus. The field lacks a single feed-forward model that animates any rig from a high-level description. Key Idea: Treat skeletal topology as an explicit, per-sample input to a shared transformer rather than baking it into architecture weights: encode the kinematic tree through (1) a Graphormer-style attention bias from relation-type and graph-distance embeddings, (2) Spec-RoPE — replacing arbitrary BFS joint indices with rotary angles computed from the leading non-trivial Laplacian eigenvectors (via SignNet to resolve eigenvector sign ambiguity), which is provably translation-invariant in spectral coordinates, permutation-equivariant, and reduces to standard RoPE on path graphs, and (3) a joint-count-invariant global conditioner pooled from skeleton tokens and injected through AdaLN-Zero. Joint training over thousands of heterogeneous rigs then lets motion priors transfer across topologies. Methodology: UniMate is a conditional flow-matching model (rectified-flow style, learning a velocity field from Gaussian noise to motion, integrated with 50-step Euler and classifier-free guidance at scale 3.0). Motion is represented as per-joint position (root-relative, facing-canonical), 6D rotation (rest-pose relative), and world-frame velocity (D=12). Skeleton tokens (from rest-pose joint/parent positions) are prepended to per-frame motion tokens; 8 transformer blocks with hidden dim 512 use factorized joint-branch and temporal-branch attention, with topology signals entering only the joint branch. The loss is a masked flow-matching MSE plus a geodesic SO(3) rotation loss on one-step denoised rotations (λ=0.5) plus a velocity-acceleration smoothness regularizer (λ=0.1). UniML3D (13,006 sequences, 2,140,232 frames, 3,584 prompts, from Truebones/Mixamo/Objaverse-XL) is built via a five-stage filtering pipeline (single-tree pruning, root realignment, phantom-joint removal, static-clip and implausibility filtering), LLM-based joint-name standardization and captioning (DeepSeek-V4-Flash / Qwen3.5-9B with human QC), BFS serialization, topology-diameter normalization, and four kinematics-preserving online augmentations (joint removal/addition, skeleton pooling, bone-length perturbation) with square-root-balanced sampling. Critical design decisions: deriving position from the graph spectrum rather than indices (justified by three propositions in Appendix C, with honest discussion of degenerate-eigenspace caveats); applying topology only to the joint branch for tractability (reasonable but not ablated against full joint-temporal injection); and LLM-generated text supervision (mitigated by manual quality control, though the QC pass rate is not quantified). Key Results: On 7 held-out Truebones skeleton types (58 sequences, 5,861 frames), UniMate achieves FID 0.757 and diversity 9.200 versus 2.711/8.139 for a text-augmented AnyTop — a 3.6× FID reduction on unseen topologies. On a mesh-animation benchmark of 18 meshes, UniMate scores OC 0.186, DD 0.833, AQ 0.544 versus AnimateAnyMesh (0.151/0.352/0.498) and V2M4 (0.167/0.667/0.506), at 1.214 s per animation versus 15.542 s and 1.641 h; AnimateAnyMesh's higher motion smoothness (0.995 vs 0.993) is attributed to near-static outputs with 0.352 dynamic degree. The 32-participant anonymized user study rates UniMate best on all four criteria (text agreement 4.617, plausibility 4.568, expressiveness 4.646, shape preservation 4.630 vs overall averages of 2.808 and 2.413). Ablations show each component contributes: removing the conditioner raises FID to 0.825 (largest drop, with jitter), removing Spec-RoPE to 0.798 (worst generalization), removing the graph bias to 0.773. Foot-locking post-processing reduces the skating ratio from 0.107 to 0.023 on 20 held-out legged skeletons. Training is modest: 8 H100 GPUs for ~1 day (100k steps, batch 256); inference runs at 50 FPS (~1.2 s per 60-frame clip on one H100). Note that the AnyTop comparison is on Truebones, where AnyTop was originally trained, while UniMate trains on a much larger mixed corpus — favorable to UniMate. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (Spec-RoPE, a principled generalization of RoPE to arbitrary kinematic trees with formal properties) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (UniML3D, the largest cross-topology text-paired motion corpus claimed to date). The overall recipe — flow matching, AdaLN-Zero conditioning, factorized spatio-temporal attention, Graphormer-style biases, SignNet — is a competent assembly of known techniques applied to a new setting; the genuinely novel pieces are Spec-RoPE and the demonstration that a single model can span bipedal through articulated-object topologies with text control, which no prior system does. Rigor & Reproducibility: Component-wise ablations exist for all three architectural mechanisms and for two dataset-curation stages (rest-pose rotation rebasing: FID 0.757→1.179 without; augmentations: diversity 9.200→8.265 without), which is a strength. However, the headline FID is computed over 58 held-out sequences with a single fixed seed (seed 10), no confidence intervals, no significance tests, and no multi-seed variance — small-sample FID at this size is notoriously noisy. The user study (32 participants, 12 cases) does report error bars. Evaluation mixes paradigms: skeleton-space FID against one adapted baseline, VBench video metrics and a user study against two mesh-animation baselines on the authors' own 18-mesh benchmark. Two relevant baselines (How to Move Your Dragon, AnimaX) are excluded because code/models are unreleased — acknowledged and defensible, but it weakens the SOTA claim. The GitHub repository is stated (github.com/Friedrich-M/UniMate) but currently serves only as a project entry point; training code, checkpoints, and the dataset are promised "upon publication." This is an arXiv preprint (2609.05415); the SIGGRAPH-style venue formatting suggests submission to a peer-reviewed graphics venue, but no acceptance is stated. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained generative model evaluated on benchmarks and qualitative tasks; not a deployed SYSTEMS artifact). - Practical: Yes — 8 transformer blocks at d=512 with a frozen FLAN-T5 encoder are small by modern standards; inference needs a single (high-end) GPU, though timings are reported only on H100. - Efficient: Favorable — 1.214 s per mesh animation versus 15.5 s (AnimateAnyMesh) and 1.64 h (V2M4); training cost (~8 H100-days) is modest for a foundation-model claim. - Effective: The evidence supports the core claim on seen-like and held-out rigs via FID, user study, and four zero-shot applications, but the stated problem is production animation, and the authors show contact-rich motions still exhibit foot sliding (skate ratio 0.107) and rare topologies fail (e.g., a lamp that never tips over) — so it solves the proxy (plausible skeleton motion) more than the full deployment problem. - Scalable: Not tested — no experiments at 10× data or model scale, and the paper itself identifies long-tail data scarcity as the binding constraint, so cross-topology coverage at larger scale is a claim, not a measurement. Deliverable: a paper plus a promised software artifact (code, checkpoints, UniML3D dataset at the stated GitHub URL, currently pending) and a live interactive demo; reusable contributions include the curation pipeline and the Spec-RoPE proof technique. Strengths: - Spec-RoPE is a real, formally grounded contribution: the paper proves translation invariance in spectral coordinates, permutation equivariance (with explicit SignNet handling of sign ambiguity), reduction to standard RoPE on path graphs, and an effective-resistance interpretation — and it honestly flags the degenerate-eigenspace caveats rather than overclaiming. - UniML3D fills a genuine resource gap: 13,006 sequences over thousands of rigs across seven morphology classes with unified canonicalization, LLM-standardized joint semantics, and human-audited captions; the data-pipeline ablations (rest-pose rebasing, augmentation, filtering) show each stage measurably matters. - The generalization result is the right one to measure: evaluation on 7 skeleton types never seen in training, with the qualitative failure mode of the baseline (near-static outputs that ignore the prompt) clearly diagnosed rather than buried. - The zero-shot applications (text-mediated cross-topology transfer, in-betweening, expansion, editing) follow from the architecture rather than from task-specific modules — a meaningful test of whether the model learned transferable motion priors. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and in detail, which is a credibility positive: (1) foot sliding, drifting, hovering, and ground penetration in contact-rich motions, because no unified contact model exists across morphologies (quantified in Appendix E.5 with an IK foot-locking remedy); (2) degraded reliability on rare topologies and out-of-distribution motions, attributed to long-tailed 4D data (bipeds are 84.1% of UniML3D; serpentine 0.3%); (3) text-only conditioning with no fine-grained spatial control channel; (4) supervision bounded by 4D data, orders of magnitude smaller than image/video corpora. They also acknowledge in Appendix D that AnyTop required adaptation for text conditioning and that two baselines were excluded for lack of released code. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Statistical robustness: FID over 58 sequences from one seed, with no variance estimate — the 0.757 vs 0.773 margin over the graph-bias ablation (~2%) is within plausible noise, making the per-component attribution weaker than presented. (2) Train/test asymmetry in the flagship comparison: AnyTop is evaluated on Truebones (its native domain) while UniMate is trained on a 13k-sequence corpus that includes large amounts of Mixamo human data — the comparison conflates architecture with data scale; a data-matched control (UniMate trained only on Truebones) is absent. (3) No cross-topology quantitative evaluation of the zero-shot transfer/editing applications — these are shown only qualitatively. (4) LLM-generated captions with unquantified human-QC coverage could inject text–motion noise that the paper cannot rule out. (5) Inference cost is reported only on H100; no consumer-GPU latency, and the 50-step Euler solver's cost/quality trade-off is not swept. (6) Eigenvector computation at inference for novel skeletons with near-degenerate spectra could be unstable — the paper proves properties for simple eigenvalues but does not measure failure frequency in practice. Bottom Line: A practitioner in motion synthesis or 3D animation tooling gains concrete value from this paper — both for the UniML3D resource and the Spec-RoPE design pattern — but should treat the headline SOTA numbers as an early, small-sample signal rather than a validated production result, and should watch for the promised code release before adopting it.

Scaling Domain Data Repetition in LLM Pretraining

J Li, X Gu, R Dai, X Hao, C Xu, Y Wu, S Zheng, J Zhang · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper experimentally and theoretically characterizes how many times high-quality domain data (code, math, Wikipedia, medical) can be repeated during LLM pretraining before overfitting, under the practical regime where the training-token budget scales proportionally with model size (fixed tokens-per-parameter, TPP). - Why it's important: High-quality domain data cannot scale as fast as web data, so its fraction in the training mixture shrinks as models grow; knowing how safely to repeat it determines whether scarce domain data can be stretched without hurting the model. - How it does it: It sweeps unique-data fractions (α ∈ {1/40, 1/20, 1/10}) and repetition counts (e ∈ {1..7}) at fixed total token budgets across model sizes, fits a quadratic to validation loss vs. repetition count to estimate the optimum, and explains the observed trends with an exact risk decomposition in a one-hot linear regression model with power-law knowledge frequencies. - The good: The optimal repetition count correlates strongly and negatively with the domain's minimum validation loss (Pearson −0.944), giving a simple, actionable rule: sweep repetition on a smaller proxy model at the same TPP and the choice transfers conservatively to larger models. - The missing: All experiments repeat only one domain per run, evaluate only validation loss (no downstream task benchmarks), and the supporting theory is confined to linear regression — so the headline transfer rule is validated only within the tested scale range, not at production scale. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners designing pretraining data mixtures for data-constrained domains, since it delivers a concrete, cheap recipe for setting repetition counts; skip if you only need general data-repetition scaling laws already covered by Muennighoff et al. or repetition-aware mixture-law work.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (62) and Completeness (60) pull the composite down: no seeds or error bars anywhere, no downstream task evaluation (validation loss only), the headline proxy-to-large-model transfer rule is never actually executed as a transfer experiment, and reproducibility is impaired by unstated model sizes and unquantified quadratic-fit estimation — compounded by unreviewed preprint status and no released artifact. Problem & Motivation: Teams pretraining LLMs face an asymmetric data-scaling problem: compute-optimal training requires the token budget to grow with model size (maintaining a roughly constant TPP = D/N), but high-quality domain corpora (math, code, medical, encyclopedic) are finite and cannot grow at the same rate. As the total budget expands, the domain's mixing fraction falls — and prior work suggests knowledge-dense domains are only learned once their mixing ratio exceeds a critical threshold. Repeating the finite domain data counters this dilution, but prior cross-scale studies (holding D fixed) concluded that larger models overfit repeated data earlier, recommending minimal repetition. The paper identifies that this conclusion is an artifact of holding D fixed rather than preserving TPP, leaving open what the correct repetition policy is under realistic scaling. Key Idea: The core insight is a regime switch: under fixed-TPP scaling, the optimal repetition count increases with model size (opposite to the fixed-data-budget regime), and the optimal count is governed primarily by the domain's final validation loss — lower-loss domains tolerate more repetition — rather than by the amount of unique data. Theoretically, this is captured by decomposing population risk into a knowledge-acquisition error (decreasing with more optimization steps) and a noise-fitting error (increasing with more steps); the optimal stopping time (repetition count) is where the noise term starts to dominate, and under linear data–model scaling the signal term dominates for r = Θ(D^(α/β)) more steps. Methodology: Empirical pipeline: for each model size N, fix total tokens D_N = TPP·N (TPP > 100); for each domain d ∈ {Code, Math, Wiki, Medical}, select U_{N,α} = αD_N unique domain tokens, repeat them e times, and fill the remaining (1 − eα)D_N tokens with unique web data — the total budget is held fixed, only its composition changes. The grid spans 4 domains × multiple model sizes × 3 unique-data fractions × 7 repetition counts; models use the Muon optimizer with power-law-scaled learning rate and batch size, 200-step warmup, 0.1 attention dropout, and (unless stated) a WSD-style schedule. The optimum is estimated by fitting a quadratic L̂(e) = ae² + be + c to final validation loss vs. repetition count and taking −b/2a. Theoretical framework: one-hot linear regression in R^∞ with power-law input distribution p_k ∝ k^(−α), source condition E[(θ_k)²p_k] = k^(−β), capacity-limited projection to R^N, full-batch gradient descent; three theorems bound the optimal stopping time r(D, N): (4.2) monotonicity in noise σ² with r ≈ log(1/σ²)/(−log(1 − η/D)), (4.3) under fixed D, r decreases once N exceeds a crossover N₀(D, σ²) = Θ((D/σ²)^(1/(β−α))), and (4.4) under D/N → C₀, r* = Θ(D^(α/β)) — jointly explaining all three empirical trends. Critical design decisions: (i) fixing TPP rather than D across scales — well-justified as matching practice and explicitly contrasted against the fixed-D regime; (ii) quadratic-fit estimation of the discrete optimum — reasonable but unvalidated against the true argmin; (iii) one-domain-per-run isolation — clean but admittedly unrealistic relative to production mixtures. Key Results: The estimated optimal repetition count correlates with minimum domain validation loss at Pearson r = −0.944, with model size at r = 0.400, and with unique-data fraction at r = 0.018. Per-domain optima (from Appendix B): Math ~5–6 repetitions, Code ~4–5, Wiki ~3–4, Medical ~3–4, each mildly increasing with model size and flat across α ∈ {1/40, 1/20, 1/10}. Under fixed total high-quality fraction, Math degrades only slightly from 1→4 repetitions (repeated data largely substitutes for unique data), while Wiki, Code, and Medical degrade sharply beyond ~2 repetitions — contradicting a universal ~4-repetition threshold from prior single-dataset work. Replacing unique with repeated tokens at fixed domain and web fractions barely changes OOD validation loss on ArXiv and News. Learning-rate schedule matters: earlier WSD decay lowers the tolerable repetition count, and a constant learning rate tolerates the most. Model sizes tested are not stated numerically in the provided text; baselines are prior repetition studies (Hernandez et al., Muennighoff et al., Xue et al.) re-analyzed under the fixed-D regime rather than head-to-head model comparisons. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with supporting NEW FORMULATION (fixed-TPP repetition analysis) — the genuinely novel element is the demonstration that the fixed-D prior conclusion (bigger models need less repetition) inverts under fixed-TPP scaling, plus the strong loss–optimum correlation and its theoretical explanation via exact risk decomposition in linear regression; the experimental machinery (repetition sweeps, quadratic fitting) and the theory (extending Yan et al.'s multi-epoch linear-regression analysis to capacity-limited projection and scaling regimes) are competent extensions of existing ideas. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive within the claimed scope: all four domains, three α values, multiple model sizes, OOD splits (ArXiv, News), and five learning-rate schedules are reported, with full per-domain curves in Appendix B and complete proofs in Appendix D. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; conclusions rest on single runs per configuration. No code, data, or model release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (i) the estimated optimum comes from a quadratic fit to a coarse 7-point grid, and no validation that the fit's argmin matches the empirical argmin; (ii) the key transfer claim (proxy-model estimates are safe for larger models) is extrapolated from the observed trend rather than tested by an actual proxy-to-target transfer experiment; (iii) evaluation is entirely validation loss on the authors' own corpora — no perplexity on standard benchmarks or downstream tasks; (iv) the theory assumes β > α for the scaling theorems, and the mapping from real transformer training to one-hot linear regression is heuristic. This is a preprint (arXiv 2608.14071, Aug 2026), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (training sweeps with an accompanying theoretical model). Practical: The procedure runs on standard pretraining infrastructure (Muon optimizer, WSD schedules); the recommended workflow — sweep repetition on a small proxy model — is cheap for any lab already training small proxies. Efficient: No compute overhead beyond the proxy-model sweeps already common in mixture tuning; the delivered rule adds negligible cost. Effective: Evidence shows the rule controls in-domain validation loss and preserves OOD loss at tested scales, but the paper never demonstrates it on a downstream task or at production model scale — effectiveness is shown on a proxy metric. Scalable: The fixed-TPP trend is measured only over the tested size range; whether the increase in optimal repetition continues, plateaus, or reverses at 10–100× the tested scale is claimed by extrapolation (Theorem 4.4 in the linear model), not measured in LLMs. The deliverable is a paper with a recipe; no software artifact, dataset, or model weights are released. Strengths: - Identifies and empirically demonstrates a genuine regime artifact: prior cross-scale repetition conclusions were derived under fixed token budgets, and the paper shows the recommendation inverts under fixed TPP — a correction with direct practical consequence. - The loss–optimum correlation (Pearson −0.944 across 4 domains, multiple sizes, and 3 α values) is a simple, predictive, and immediately usable heuristic that reduces repetition tuning to reading off a validation loss. - The theory is unusually well-matched to the experiments: the exact three-term risk decomposition (unrepresented / knowledge-acquisition / noise-fitting) yields theorems whose qualitative predictions (noise monotonicity, fixed-D crossover, Θ(D^(α/β)) scaling) correspond one-to-one with the three empirical findings. - The domain-resolved analysis (Math robust to repetition, Wiki/Code/Medical not) overturns the implicit universality of prior single-dataset repetition results, and the OOD-stability finding (Section 5.2) carefully controls web-data fraction to isolate the repetition effect — a confound many papers in this area miss. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that each run repeats only one high-quality domain, so interactions among simultaneously repeated domains are unexplored, and that they lack a quantitative scaling rule predicting a large model's optimal repetition count from small-model results (offering only the conservative-transfer heuristic). They do not otherwise dwell on limitations; the acknowledgment is direct but brief, and they do not address the absence of downstream evaluation, single-run variance, or the linear-model gap. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline practical claim — sweep on a small proxy, transfer to the large model — is never executed as an actual transfer experiment; it is inferred from the monotone size trend, which itself is mild (r = 0.400) and could flatten or reverse outside the tested range. - No downstream task evaluation (e.g., GSM8K, HumanEval, MMLU) — validation loss on the repeated domain may not track capability gains where they matter, and repetition-induced memorization risks (deduplication, contamination) are not measured despite being cited in related work. - Model sizes, exact token budgets, and dataset identities/sizes are never stated numerically in the main text, hindering reproducibility and making the "practical scaling" framing hard to verify. - The quadratic-fit estimator is used for all correlations but is never validated against the discrete argmin or given uncertainty estimates; with only 7 repetition points and no seeds, correlation coefficients like −0.944 carry unquantified uncertainty. - The theory requires β > α (target signal spectrum decays slower than the input frequency law) and no statement of the actual (α, β) values for real domains, so the Θ(D^(α/β)) prediction cannot be checked against the LLM experiments even qualitatively in rate. - Absence of comparison against repetition-aware mixture scaling laws (e.g., InfoLaw, Sedova et al.) on shared settings — the paper cites them as concurrent approaches but does not test whether its heuristic agrees with or outperforms them. Bottom Line: For anyone allocating a pretraining data budget across scarce high-quality domains, this paper offers a cheap, evidence-backed rule (tune repetition by domain validation loss on a fixed-TPP proxy model, and repeat more of your lowest-loss domains) that corrects a misleading prior recommendation — but it is a preprint validated only by loss curves at moderate scale, so treat the large-model transfer guarantee as a well-motivated hypothesis rather than a settled result.

The Attention Triangle in Audio-Video Models (25 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a training-free, inference-time attention-steering framework that mitigates cross-modal semantic leakage (wrong sound-source attribution and appearance bleed) in joint text-to-audio-video diffusion models, instantiated on LTX-2. - Why it's important: Joint audio-video generators systematically override explicit prompt instructions — e.g., routing speech to a human character instead of the prompt-designated talking parrot — because learned priors in cross-modal attention beat user intent, a failure that undermines controllability of an emerging commercial model class. - How it does it: It models the text/audio/video token streams as an "attention triangle" of pairwise cross-attention edges and adds pre-softmax logit biases on all three edges (built from SAM3 visual masks, attention-derived audio masks, and annotated text-token spans) to reinforce intended and suppress conflicting source-sound pairings. - The good: The edge-wise ablation is clean and decisive — steering text edges only fixes appearance but not attribution, steering audio-video only fixes attribution but not appearance, and only joint steering (Ours-Full) fixes both, confirmed by a 30-participant user study preferring Ours-Full in 79.2% (attribution) and 82.9% (leakage) of decided votes (p < 10^-28, Bonferroni-corrected). - The missing: All experiments are on a single model family (LTX-2), prompts require manual annotation of source/action/competing phrases, and the 100-prompt evaluation set was adversarially curated by the authors, so generality and automatic applicability remain untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone working on audio-video generation, attention analysis, or training-free diffusion steering — the diagnostic Markov-rollout analysis of the audio-video edge is genuinely instructive — but practitioners wanting a turnkey tool should note the per-prompt annotation burden and single-model scope.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) diffusion models such as LTX-2 couple video and audio streams through cross-attention, and this coupling introduces a failure mode absent from silent text-to-video: semantic leakage across modalities. Concretely, when a prompt assigns a sound to an entity that conflicts with the model's learned priors (a parrot that speaks, a teddy bear that growls), the model routes the sound to the visually canonical source (the human pirate, the monster) and can even leak appearance (the pirate grows parrot-like features). The affected parties are users of open T2AV generators needing prompt-faithful source binding; prior work on attention steering and leakage mitigation addresses only image-domain, entity-to-entity leakage, and prior T2AV research redesigns architectures or accelerates inference rather than repairing entity-level source attribution in a frozen pretrained generator. The paper closes this gap with an analysis of how semantics are routed across the three cross-attention edges and a training-free intervention. Key Idea: The core insight is that leakage in T2AV models is driven substantially by the audio↔video cross-attention edge — a bidirectional, bias-encoded pathway not directly specified by the prompt — and that this second-order routing can be exposed by composing attention matrices as a Markov-chain rollout (P_eff_VV = P_VA · P_AV, showing mass migrating from intended to canonical source via the audio bridge) and then corrected by adding fixed pre-softmax logit biases simultaneously on all three triangle edges. The hypothesized root cause is a dimensional asymmetry: audio tokens carry temporal but not spatial positional information, leaving sound-source localization underconstrained and forced to rely on learned semantic compatibility. Methodology: The pipeline has two phases. (1) Anchor extraction: one unsteered baseline denoising pass produces (a) text-token index sets for the user-annotated intended-source, sound/action, and optional competing-source phrases; (b) hard visual masks from SAM3 prompted on decoded baseline frames; (c) a soft audio sound-mask from audio-query/text-key attention aggregated across steps, thresholded at θ_A = 0.3. (2) Steering: a second full denoising pass adds three additive pre-softmax biases at every transformer block and step: an audio↔video agreement bias B_A→V = −λ(1 − G_VA), where G_VA is an outer-product agreement matrix between visual source masks and audio sound masks (λ = 10, applied transposed in the reverse direction); and three-class intended/conflicting masks on both text-conditioned surfaces, B_T→V = βM_int − γM_conf and B_T→A = βM_int − γM_conf (β = 0.5, γ = 2.0), with the asymmetry deliberately weighting suppression of conflicting cells over reinforcement of intended ones. Hyperparameters are fixed across all prompts and not tuned per prompt. Three variants isolate edge families: Ours-Text (text edges only), Ours-AV (audio-video edge only), Ours-Full (all three). Critical design decisions: the fixed-hyperparameter policy (justified by reporting in the appendix, though no sweep sensitivity analysis is shown in the main text); hard external masks for video (where SAM3 exists) vs. soft model-derived masks for audio (where no segmenter exists — reasonable but introduces asymmetry in anchor reliability); and the two-pass anchor-then-steer scheme, whose cost is acknowledged (~2.5× unsteered generation). Key Results: Evaluation uses a 100-prompt "leakage challenge set" (curated via human-in-the-loop evolutionary prompt search to be failure-enriched), 4 seeds per prompt, 400 videos per method, 2,400 videos total, all on LTX-2 at 960×544, 97 frames, 20 steps. Headline numbers: Qwen3-Omni source-attribution score (1 − conditional leakage from a counterbalanced five-option judge) of 0.1349 for Ours-Full vs. 0.1216 native LTX-2, 0.1207 Ovi, 0.0925 adapted Bounded Attention, 0.1140 Ours-Text, 0.1302 Ours-AV. CLAP audio-text alignment is essentially unchanged (0.383 vs. 0.384 best baseline). VBench: subject consistency 0.990, background consistency 0.986, aesthetic quality 0.604 — best or tied-best across methods. VA-Judger pairwise preference for Ours-Full ranges 57.6%–73.3% against all alternatives with all bootstrap 95% CIs above 50%. Human study (30 participants, 480 trials): 79.2% attribution, 82.9% leakage, 80.1% overall preference among decided votes, significant at p < 10^-28 after Bonferroni correction. Second-order routing quantification: intended-source attention mass rises from 46.1% to 90.3% and 21.2% to 88.6% in two rollout case studies. The only baseline beyond LTX-2 variants is Ovi (a twin-DiT open model) and an adapted Bounded Attention — reasonable but thin; no training-based or learned-routing competitor (e.g., CCL-style) is compared. Absolute attribution scores are low even for the best method (~0.13), indicating the metric is harsh and the task far from solved. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (cross-modal source-attribution and appearance leakage in joint T2AV generation, as distinct from image-domain entity leakage) plus NEW METHOD (joint three-edge attention-bias steering) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the audio↔video edge as a dominant, bidirectional leakage pathway, exposed via Markov-chain attention rollouts). The individual techniques — pre-softmax attention biases, SAM3-derived masks, attention-map visualization, inference-time steering — are standard tools from text-to-image attention control (Chefer et al., Dahary et al., Rassin et al.); the genuine novelty is extending the routing-failure lens to the trimodal triangle and the demonstration that no single edge suffices, not any new steering primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: The ablation structure is the paper's strongest rigor point: the two partial variants (Ours-Text, Ours-AV) are well-designed controls that directly support the central claim that joint steering is necessary, and the shared-backbone T2V/T2AV comparison in LTX-2 isolates the audio branch cleanly. Evaluation protocols are unusually well documented: exact judge prompts, counterbalancing, logit extraction, deterministic decoding settings, bootstrap CIs, an audit of parsing failures, and per-dimension breakdowns are all in the supplement. However, no error bars or seeds are reported for the headline Qwen attribution score (only CLAP gets ±std), hyperparameters are fixed without reported sensitivity sweeps, the challenge set was constructed by the authors specifically to exhibit the failure being repaired (adverse selection by design, acknowledged by the authors as unsuitable for estimating real-world leakage prevalence), and no code or data release is mentioned in the provided text. The evaluation is confined to one model family (LTX-2), with Ovi comparisons limited to qualitative figures; the Qwen3-Omni judge itself is a generative model whose own cross-modal biases are not validated against human ground truth on this task, though the 30-participant human study partially mitigates this concern. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (analysis plus inference-time intervention, actually run). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB), ~29 GB peak memory. - Efficient: Moderate cost — roughly 2.5× unsteered generation (~13–14 min/clip vs. ~5.5 min baseline) due to the anchor-extraction pass plus SAM3; ~1,300 A6000 GPU-hours for the full project. - Effective: The evidence (Qwen attribution, VA-Judger, human study) shows it substantially improves source attribution and appearance preservation on the targeted failure modes, but only with manual prompt annotation and on deliberately leakage-prone prompts; effectiveness on ordinary generations is not measured. - Scalable: Untested beyond 960×544/97-frame clips and a single model; the method's dependence on SAM3 masks and a clean baseline pass gives no evidence about behavior at higher resolution, longer clips, many-entity scenes, or other architectures (single-stream models are explicitly flagged as open). The paper delivers a method and evaluation protocol but no released software artifact, dataset, or model weights mentioned in the text. Strengths: - The trimodal "attention triangle" framing is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution that reframes T2AV leakage as structured cross-edge routing rather than generic attention diffusion, and the bidirectionality finding (audio shapes video and video shapes audio) is non-obvious. - The second-order diagnostic — composing P_VA and P_AV into an audio-mediated video-to-video rollout and showing probability mass migrating from intended to canonical source — is a concrete, reusable analysis technique (built on the attention-as-Markov-chain view) that makes an invisible failure mechanism observable and quantifiable (46.1%→90.3% intended-source mass after steering). - The ablation design (text-only vs. AV-only vs. full steering, plus a shared-backbone T2V vs. T2AV comparison) cleanly attributes the failure to the audio-video pathway rather than assuming it. - Evaluation discipline is above average for this area: counterbalanced LLM-judge protocols with logit-level extraction, order-randomization, exact-binomial significance tests with Bonferroni correction, and a genuine (if small) human study rather than judge-only claims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Supp. F and Discussion): (1) steering can only redirect associations the model already represents and cannot create out-of-distribution bindings; (2) anchors come from an unsteered pass, so fully ungrounded audio or visually static intended sources provide too little signal; (3) SAM3-based visual anchors are sensitive to segmentation errors on small, occluded, or ambiguous entities; (4) the extra pass increases inference cost; (5) experiments cover only LTX-2-style cross-attention architectures, and transfer to single-stream self-attention models is open. They also candidly state their evidence establishes the audio-video pathway's contribution but not a unique mechanism, and that the temporal-only audio positional encoding hypothesis is unverified. This is a direct, non-defensive limitations treatment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Manual prompt annotation is load-bearing: the user must tag the intended source, sound, and competing phrases for every prompt; the paper does not report any automatic pipeline for extracting these, so "training-free" understates the per-prompt human cost, and performance without annotation is unknown. - Curated adversarial evaluation: the 100-prompt set was selected precisely because it produces interpretable failures; the authors note it cannot estimate prevalence but still use it as the sole quantitative benchmark, so real-world leakage rates and method performance on natural prompts are unknown. - No unsupervised baseline: a comparison against prompt-engineering mitigations (e.g., rephrasing, negative prompts, stage-aware prompting as in Huberman et al.) is absent; only an attention-intervention baseline (Bounded Attention) is adapted. - Judge circularity risk: the Qwen3-Omni attribution judge and the VA-Judger reward model are themselves multimodal models that may share the very prior-biases under study; no human-labeled ground-truth subset validates the automatic metric, though the 30-participant study partially covers this. - Missing error quantification on the headline metric: the Qwen score (0.1216 → 0.1349) is a small absolute improvement, and no per-prompt variance, confidence interval, or per-seed breakdown is reported for it; the practical significance of a +0.013 gain rests largely on the human study. - No code release stated in the provided text, limiting reproducibility of the anchor-extraction and bias-injection implementation details. - Single-model evidence for a general claim: the "Attention Lesson" (more cross-modal coupling amplifies bias-driven routing) is generalized in the Discussion from one architecture, one resolution, and 100 curated prompts. Bottom Line: A practitioner in audio-video generation or attention-based steering gains real value from the diagnostic rollout analysis and the well-controlled demonstration that the audio-video edge drives source-attribution leakage, but the method's manual annotation requirement, single-model scope, and curated evaluation mean it is best read as an insightful analysis paper with a promising prototype rather than a deployable solution.

checkpoint selection uses development subsets capped at 25 utterances per benchmark, so small margins (including the 16-layer model's −0.34 pp improvement over baseline) cannot be distinguished from noise. - Read it or not: Read it if you are deploying speech LLMs on edge hardware or studying encoder pruning/distillation — it is an unusually honest industrial report with useful negative results (on-policy distillation does not beat a matched off-policy control) — but skip it if you need generalizable pruning theory, since it covers one model family and one data recipe.

Problem & Motivation: Speech LLMs couple a deep audio encoder with a pretrained autoregressive text decoder, and the encoder processes every input frame, making its depth a direct contributor to first-token latency in streaming, mobile, and in-vehicle systems (XPeng's own deployment context). Removing whole Transformer blocks is attractive because it yields a regular, deployment-friendly architecture, but it perturbs the conditioning embeddings the decoder consumes, triggering premature end-of-sequence (EOS) predictions and large deletion errors. Two practical questions for already-pretrained speech LLMs remained open: which layer combinations can be removed and recovered under a fixed training budget, and how recovery should address both hidden-state mismatch and errors induced by the student's own decoding history. Prior work (Distil-Whisper, LiteASR, LayerDrop, supernet methods, and Kolluri et al.'s Whisper encoder-layer pruning with LoRA) either compresses during training, prunes single layers, or uses static importance scores — none of which predict whether a multi-layer candidate can be recovered on a short budget. Key Idea: The core insight is that layer recoverability is a property of a layer combination, not an additive per-layer score, so selection and recovery must be evaluated jointly: short behavioral probes run each candidate under matched initialization, data, and budget after the previous hop's recovery, and the winner is then restored through a three-stage schedule that first aligns hidden states (fixing the embedding shift that causes EOS errors) and only later supervises token distributions under both teacher-forced and student-generated contexts. A secondary finding with real practical weight is that cross-scale supervision from a larger model (1.7B teacher distilling into a 0.6B student) is what makes recovery work at all — self-distillation from the unpruned 0.6B model fails badly. Methodology: The pipeline has four phases. (1) Transcript-consistency filtering: each reference-bearing utterance is decoded offline by Qwen3-ASR-1.7B and Qwen3.5-Omni; the maximum pairwise edit rate (CER for Mandarin, WER for English) among the transcript–hypothesis triplet assigns one of nine consistency tiers; only the exact-agreement class 1 tier is used for training (~299k records per epoch for hop 1, ~292k for hop 2, from a >280k-hour pool including public corpora plus proprietary cockpit-domain speech). (2) Behavioral probes: single-layer removals and a fixed set of layer pairs are each warmed up for 0.3 epochs from the same recovered 16-layer checkpoint, ranked by macro TER on a five-benchmark development suite; {5,6} is selected for the 16→14 hop. (3) Three-stage recovery per hop: Stage 0 (first 5% of the distillation epoch) combines intermediate-layer, bridge, logit (temperature-scaled KL under gold prefixes), and CE losses, with uniform grouped teacher–student layer matching and a learned two-layer MLP with 256-d bottleneck bridging the 2048→1024 width gap; Stage 1 (remaining 95%) drops the layer loss, and after 20% of the stage every fifth step switches to student-policy supervision (student greedy prefix, teacher and student compared over union top-512 support, with rollout filters for degenerate generations); Stage 2 is one epoch of pure gold-CE finetuning at 5×10⁻⁶ with corpus reweighting toward target-domain sources. (4) Parameter protocol: decoder base weights stay frozen throughout; rank-32 LoRA adapters on decoder q/k/v/o projections train during Stages 0–1, and the tied output embedding trains during Stages 0–1 and freezes in Stage 2. Critical design decisions: (a) behavioral probes over static importance scores — justified by the measured non-additive interaction ({6,8}, the two best single removals, underperforms {5,6} by 0.85 pp after matched recovery); (b) cross-scale teacher — justified by the 8.45%→5.55% control, though the authors correctly note this conflates pruning recovery with gains the recipe might give an unpruned student; (c) scheduled on-policy batches — the weakest link, since their own ablation shows hybrid on-policy (6.41%) does not beat a matched off-policy control (6.23%), and the authors retain it anyway. Key Results: On ten public Chinese–English benchmarks (AISHELL-1, Fleurs zh/en, LibriSpeech test-clean/other, THCHS-30, Tedlium, CommonVoice v15 zh/en, WenetSpeech-meeting), macro-averaging equally: the 16-layer model reaches 5.27% vs. 5.61% for the 18-layer baseline (−6.1% relative), improving four benchmarks — largest gains on CommonVoice zh (−1.83 pp), CommonVoice en (−1.85 pp), and WenetSpeech-meeting (−1.30 pp), worst degradation 0.44 pp on Tedlium. The 14-layer model reaches 5.75% (+0.14 pp vs. baseline) with 147.8M vs. 186.4M audio-tower parameters (−20.7%), with most additional loss on CommonVoice en (+1.99 pp) and WenetSpeech-meeting (+1.72 pp) relative to the 16-layer model. Controls: the 1.7B teacher beats self-distillation 5.55% vs. 8.45% (better on all ten benchmarks, e.g., Tedlium 3.92% vs. 11.28%); progressive 18→16→14 beats direct 18→14 pruning 5.75% vs. 6.73% (better on all ten). Efficiency: encoder latency −21.4% on an in-vehicle PPU and −11.4% on H800, but end-to-end only −4.7%/−2.6% because autoregressive decoding dominates; RTF improves ~4–5%. Scale is modest (a 0.6B model, ~292–299k training records/epoch, 32 accelerators). A notable honest negative result: in the on-policy strategy comparison, hybrid on-policy training (best 6.41%) does not outperform a matched off-policy control (6.23%). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely novel elements are the demonstration that multi-layer recoverability is non-additive (pair probes necessary; {6,8} vs. {5,6} inversion) and the quantified superiority of cross-scale over self-distillation for encoder-layer recovery in speech LLMs. The recipe itself — progressive pruning, hidden-state/logit distillation, scheduled on-policy batches, LoRA finetuning, confidence-based data filtering — is a competent combination of existing techniques (LayerDrop, Distil-Whisper, on-policy distillation à la Ark-ASR, LoRA) assembled for a new setting (post-hoc depth reduction of a pretrained speech-LLM audio tower with a frozen decoder backbone), extending Kolluri et al.'s single-layer Whisper pruning to multi-hop, multi-layer selection. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a strength: teacher-scale (matched recipe), pair-probe layer selection with an explicit interaction-penalty definition, progressive-vs-direct pruning, a 2×2 premature-EOS mitigation ablation, an on-policy strategy comparison, and hyperparameter tables in Appendix A.1. However, the paper is candid that all main results are single runs with seed 42, with no repeated seeds, no bootstrap confidence intervals, and no significance tests — boldface explicitly denotes best-observed, not significant, values. Checkpoint selection uses a five-benchmark dev suite capped at 25 utterances per benchmark, introducing selection noise on the same distribution of margins (0.14–0.34 pp) the headline claims rest on. A methodological concern: behavioral probes and checkpoint selection use a proprietary cockpit subset (SC) alongside public dev sets; it is excluded from main-result tables but is inside the selection loop for the pair choice. Efficiency numbers are descriptive averages from one retained benchmark output with no variance retained. No code, data, or model weights release is stated; only a project website (https://xpeng-ai.github.io/x-aut) is mentioned. The pipeline depends on proprietary data (cockpit speech) and proprietary teacher systems (Qwen3.5-Omni), limiting full reproduction. There is no direct Goodhart risk since selection and final evaluation suites are disjoint, but the 25-utterance selection probes are thin. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor given in-vehicle deployment motivation; no artifact release stated). - Practical: Yes — the student is a 0.6B model trainable on 32 accelerators with bf16 and runnable on an in-vehicle PPU and a single H800, and the teacher is discarded at inference. - Efficient: Audio-tower parameters drop 20.7% at 14 layers and encoder latency drops 21.4% (PPU), but end-to-end latency improves only 2.6–4.7% and peak memory only ~4%, so the efficiency claim is real but localized. - Effective: The 16-layer point is arguably effective (improves macro error over baseline, though within noise), while the 14-layer point preserves accuracy at a small cost; both conclusions rest on single runs, so effectiveness evidence is suggestive rather than established. - Scalable: Not tested beyond one 0.6B model family and one teacher; the authors say so explicitly, and behavior on Whisper-style encoder–decoder or Qwen2-Audio architectures is unknown. The work delivers a recipe and two operating points in paper form; no library, checkpoint, or tool is reported as released. Strengths: - The layer-interaction finding is a real empirical contribution: the two best single-layer removals (L6 at 6.29%, L8 at 6.52% TER) form a pair that loses to {5,6} by 0.85 pp after matched recovery, directly demonstrating that static importance scoring is insufficient for multi-layer pruning. - The teacher-scale control is well designed — matched schedule, data, LoRA configuration, and optimization, with the 8.45% vs. 5.55% gap spanning all ten benchmarks — and gives the cross-scale distillation claim unusually strong (if single-run) support. - Reporting hygiene is above the norm for industrial papers: exact parameter counts (186.376M, 9.645M per block) instead of rounded labels, explicit tier definitions for data filtering, full hyperparameters, and the appendix honestly reports that the hybrid on-policy ablation fails to beat the matched off-policy control. - The premature-EOS analysis (2×2 ablation of tied-head training and min-token gating, with empty-rollout and rejection counts) attacks the actual failure mode of layer pruning in embedding-conditioned speech LLMs rather than only reporting aggregate CER. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive: they state that results are single runs (seed 42) without repeated seeds, paired utterance-level confidence intervals, or significance tests; that 25-utterance selection subsets introduce noise making the 0.14-pp 14-layer gap descriptive only; that the study covers one model family and a limited candidate set (Whisper, Qwen2-Audio, and other architectures may behave differently); that only class 1 of nine consistency tiers was used; that the teacher-scale comparison cannot separate pruning recovery from gains the recipe gives an unpruned student; that only the audio tower is compressed so autoregressive decoding caps end-to-end latency reduction; and that efficiency measurements lack run-to-run uncertainty and a fixed software stack. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline 16-layer improvement (−0.34 pp) plausibly stems from the extra training (cross-scale distillation plus finetuning) rather than from pruning itself, and the authors note this conflation for the teacher comparison but do not run the obvious control: applying the same recipe to the unpruned 18-layer model. If the unpruned student also improves to ~5.27%, the pruning claim weakens substantially. - Layer selection was evaluated on only a handful of the 15 remaining layers (five singles, six pairs); the paper's own untested contiguous-vs-dispersed discontinuity hypothesis is never validated with activation analysis, so the selection rule's generality is unknown. - The pair-probe selection suite includes the proprietary SC subset, so the {5,6}-vs-{6,8} decision (0.85 pp margin, single run) is partially driven by non-reproducible data. - Reported results depend on proprietary cockpit-domain data and the unreleased Qwen3.5-Omni system for filtering; academic replication is impossible, and no code or weights are released despite the project page. - No comparison against cheaper alternatives at equal parameter/latency budgets — e.g., low-rank factorization (LiteASR) or structured sparsity applied to the same audio tower — so the reader cannot tell whether layer removal is the right compression axis, only that it works when done this way. - The on-policy machinery is retained in the main recipe despite the authors' own ablation showing it underperforms a matched off-policy control, an inconsistency between the reported recipe and the evidence supporting it. Bottom Line: Practitioners deploying speech LLMs on latency-constrained hardware gain a concrete, well-controlled recipe and two validated operating points (16-layer: better accuracy; 14-layer: −20.7% encoder parameters at +0.14 pp cost), plus a genuinely useful lesson that layer recoverability is non-additive and that a larger teacher is essential for recovery — but researchers seeking generalizable pruning methodology should treat all margins as unverified noise until repeated runs and an unpruned-student control exist.

OutageDiT: A Generative Foundation Model for Power Outage Forecasting and Scenario Simulation

Y Zhu, F Qiu, Y Xie · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OutageDiT, a 183.46M-parameter conditional flow-matching transformer pre-trained on U.S. county-level outage and weather records that generates complete seven-day power-outage trajectories at quarter-hour resolution for point forecasting, uncertainty quantification, and scenario simulation. - Why it's important: Utilities must stage crews and allocate resources before an outage event's magnitude and duration are known, but severe trajectories are too rare in any single region's data to train a regional generative model that preserves temporal dependence and calibration. - How it does it: A condition encoder maps 14 days of outage history plus known future weather/calendar covariates into 168 horizon-aligned conditioning states once per forecast, and a shallow two-block flow decoder with cached key–values generates trajectories via conditional flow matching over a carry-aware reflected-digit encoding of nonnegative integer counts. - The good: OutageDiT beats every tested baseline on every national metric — e.g., MSE 0.857 vs. 1.041 for fine-tuned Chronos-2 and event-split MSE 1.552 vs. 1.892 — and wins all five reported zero-shot metrics on Michigan, a state excluded from training (Avg RMSE 164.21 vs. 175.59 for the IISE challenge winner). - The missing: The 90% prediction interval covers only 0.839 against a 0.90 target, with the authors attributing undercoverage on extreme events to the primary limitation, and the model conditions on weather actually observed through the forecast horizon rather than forecasts available at decision time. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in probabilistic time-series foundation models and power-system operations planning; skippable for readers seeking decision-theoretic validation, which the paper explicitly leaves to future work.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (80) is the top dimension: a new problem framing (conditional generative scenario simulation for outage planning as a foundation-model task) plus a genuinely new carry-aware reflected-digit encoding with analytic decoding, validated by ablation on both forecast error and joint MMD. Resilience (60) and Completeness (60) are held back by the perfect-weather-forecast assumption — the ablation shows future conditioning is the single largest accuracy contributor, so real-world skill is unquantified — and by the 90% prediction interval covering only 0.839, which undercuts the headline scenario-generation claim despite the honest acknowledgment. Rigor (60) reflects good ablations and strong current baselines (fine-tuned Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, CSDI) but is reduced for the arXiv-preprint status, no released code or weights, only 60 test windows from 10 distinct events with no seed variance, and a cross-protocol Michigan comparison. Impact (45) is limited by the absence of any released artifact — notable for a paper framed as a foundation model. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*45 = 64.

Problem & Motivation: Outage-response decisions (crew staging, resource allocation) must be made before an event's magnitude and duration are known, and scenario-based planning requires full trajectories that preserve temporal dependence through escalation, peak, and restoration. Who has this problem: utilities, emergency managers, and researchers building outage decision-support tools. The specific gap: existing regional outage models (Guikema et al., He et al., Taylor et al., Watson et al.) train on data from one region and see few severe events, so they cannot represent the rare, heterogeneous extreme trajectories that planning under uncertainty most needs. The authors argue that cross-region pre-training broadens exposure to severe-event patterns while conditioning on local history, weather, and calendar preserves regional context, enabling transfer to data-poor regions. This framing positions conditional scenario generation — not just point forecasting — as the deliverable. Key Idea: The core trick is a two-part conditioning/generation factorization: encode all observed and known-future information once into horizon-aligned states, then use a lightweight flow-matching decoder that reuses those states (with cached key–value projections) to generate the full noisy trajectory — combined with a carry-aware "reflected digit" encoding that maps each integer outage count to 8 coordinates (reflected decimal digits plus normalized log magnitude) so that consecutive counts remain adjacent across carry boundaries and decoding back to valid nonnegative integers is analytic and parameter-free. The digit representation plus uniform dequantization noise (U(−0.05, 0.05) per digit coordinate) is what makes a continuous flow model well-suited to discrete counts spanning 10^7 in dynamic range. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) count representation — each quarter-hour outage/customer count is transformed via Eq. (2) into 8 continuous coordinates (reflected decimal digits in [0,1]-scaled bins plus a log-magnitude coordinate); (2) condition encoder — 336 hourly history tokens (4 quarter-hour observations patched per token), a 24-token overlapping recent-outage stream, and 168 future weather/calendar tokens, all sharing a signed time axis via RoPE, processed by 4 transformer blocks (width 1024, 16 heads); history is a read-only key–value bank, and the final block returns 168 horizon-aligned states Q; (3) flow decoder — 2 transformer blocks with adaLN flow-time modulation; training uses conditional flow matching (Lipman et al.) along Y_τ = (1−τ)Y + τZ with velocity target Z−Y, plus an auxiliary head predicting log10(1+y) from Q at quarter-hour resolution; the total loss is the flow MSE plus 10^-3 times the auxiliary log-count MSE (Eq. 3); (4) inference — the encoder runs once, its KV cache is reused across 64 scrambled-Sobol-Gaussian Monte Carlo samples and 20 Euler ODE steps; only the noisy future tokens update; hourly velocities unfold to quarter-hour and g^-1 maps coordinates to integer counts. Critical design decisions: (a) the reflected-digit encoding — justified by the ablation (removing it raises MSE from 0.857 to 0.903 and joint MMD from 0.1368 to 0.2125); (b) future-covariate conditioning including weather observed over the full horizon — the largest-ablation contributor (MSE 1.346 without future), but it assumes weather is known at forecast time, a strong assumption the paper defers to future work; (c) a small decoder (2 blocks) with KV caching for sampling efficiency — reasonable but justified only by cost accounting, not by an efficiency benchmark against alternatives. Training uses Muon + AdamW, bfloat16, batch 512, 25,000 updates, EMA decay 0.999. Key Results: National seven-day forecasting (test March–May 2025, 30 normal + 30 event windows from 10 distinct events; metrics in log10(1+y) space): OutageDiT MSE 0.857 (All), 0.162 (Normal), 1.552 (Event) vs. fine-tuned Chronos-2 at 1.041/0.190/1.892, TimesFM 2.5 at 1.233/0.209/2.257, CSDI at 1.445/0.358/2.533, TFT at 1.853, DeepAR at 2.356; WQL 0.328 vs. 0.361 (Chronos-2). Scenario quality: variogram score 0.151 vs. Sundial 0.207, CSDI 0.234, DeepAR 0.354; 90% interval coverage 0.839 (target 0.90) with width 1.483 — coverage below all baselines' deficit is the acknowledged weakness, and event-window coverage is lower still. Zero-shot Michigan transfer (state excluded from training): Avg RMSE 164.21 vs. 175.59 (RSFM, the IISE challenge winner) and 177.24 (SARIMAX, the DMDA challenge best); tail RMSE 257.58 vs. 286.61; nonzero F1 0.715 vs. 0.649; Winkler 2479 vs. 2615. Ablations show every conditioning branch matters, with future weather conditioning the largest single contributor. The baselines are current and strong (2024–2025 foundation models, fine-tuned) — not straw men. Tested at national scale (all U.S. counties outside Michigan, 2018–2024 outage data, HRRR weather from 2022 onward); no multi-seed error bars are reported. Caveat: the Michigan comparison reuses official scores from third-party competitions whose entries followed different input protocols, as the authors disclose. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (first generative foundation model for conditional power-outage trajectory simulation) plus NEW PROBLEM framing (conditional scenario generation for outage planning as a foundation-model task, rather than regional point forecasting). The genuinely novel elements are the domain formulation and the carry-aware reflected-digit count representation with analytic decoding; the architecture itself (DiT-style encoder/decoder, conditional flow matching, adaLN, RoPE, patching, KV caching) is a competent, well-adapted combination of existing techniques from image diffusion and time-series foundation models applied to a new domain. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: the paper isolates the contribution of each conditioning stream (history/recent/future), the digit representation, dequantization noise, and the auxiliary loss, all under the same training budget — this is above the norm for domain papers. Metrics are formally defined (MSE, WQL, variogram score, coverage/width, Michigan RMSE variants, Winkler score). Concerns: (1) no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported, and the national evaluation uses only 60 test windows (30 event from 10 events), so headline gaps could be sensitive to window selection; (2) no public code, data, or model weights are mentioned — reproducibility depends on the detailed appendix alone; (3) the Michigan evaluation compares against external competition scores produced under different input protocols, a cross-protocol comparison the authors acknowledge; (4) the model conditions on weather observed through the forecast horizon (perfect-forecast assumption), which inflates effective forecast skill relative to operational deployment; (5) event windows are defined by a fixed threshold (800 outages AND 4% of tracked customers for 6 hours), a reasonable but idiosyncratic selection rule. The work is an arXiv preprint (2609.01896) and does not appear peer-reviewed. Deployability: (profile: EMPIRICAL):* Practical: Yes — at 183.46M parameters with bfloat16 inference and a single encoder pass, the model runs on commodity accelerators; no special hardware is implied. Efficient: Favorable relative to naive diffusion sampling — the condition encoder runs once and its KV cache is reused, so each of 64 Monte Carlo samples requires only decoder evaluations over 20 Euler steps; no direct FLOP/latency comparison against Chronos-2 or CSDI sampling cost is reported. Effective: The evidence supports improved point and probabilistic forecasting and better temporal dependence in scenarios, but the stated goal of planning-grade uncertainty representation is only partially met — 0.839 coverage against a 0.90 target and degraded event-window calibration mean the generated scenarios understate extreme-event uncertainty. Scalable:* Training already spans the contiguous U.S. at county level, so 10× data scale is partially exercised, but no test examines more regions, longer horizons, or higher resolution; scaling behavior is claimed implicitly, not measured. The paper stops at paper form — no software artifact, dataset release, or trained weights are stated as available. Strengths: (1) The carry-aware reflected-digit count representation with analytic inverse is a genuinely new, parameter-free solution to encoding wide-range integer counts for continuous generative models, validated by both forecast-error and distributional (joint MMD) ablations. (2) The encoder-once/KV-cached decoder design makes Monte Carlo scenario sampling from a flow model computationally tractable, directly serving the scenario-simulation use case rather than only point forecasts. (3) The zero-shot geographic transfer result on Michigan — beating the official winners of two independent competitions on all five reported metrics without any Michigan training data — is a credible out-of-distribution test that most domain papers lack. (4) The ablation table cleanly attributes gains to specific components under a fixed budget, which strengthens the causal story behind the headline numbers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that extreme-event undercoverage is the primary limitation (visible in the 0.839 national coverage and lower event-window coverage). In the conclusion they further note the model has not been evaluated within actual crew-staging and resource-allocation decisions, does not account for weather-forecast error (inputs use weather observed through the horizon), and covers nominal rather than worst-case planning under distribution shift. This is a direct, non-defensive confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The perfect-weather-forecast assumption is more consequential than "future work" framing suggests: the ablation shows future conditioning is the single largest contributor to accuracy, so an evaluation with degraded or operational forecast weather is needed to quantify real-world skill. (2) The 60-window national test set (10 distinct events) is small relative to the breadth of the claims, and no seed variance is reported — the 0.86 log-space MSE gap to Chronos-2 may not be robust. (3) The Michigan cross-protocol comparison (OutageDiT uses horizon weather per its national protocol while competition entries followed their own input rules) is not apples-to-apples, despite disclosure. (4) No release of code, data pipeline, or weights is mentioned, limiting verification of the HRRR-derived feature engineering, which involves 84 weather variables that could be a major hidden contributor. (5) The paper does not report the Sundial baseline's configuration or compare against any dedicated spatio-temporal generative model beyond CSDI, and no calibration post-processing (e.g., conformal correction) is attempted despite the known undercoverage. (6) Training-window sampling details (e.g., half of examples retaining full 14-day history) and weather-masking augmentation choices are stated but not ablated. Bottom Line: For researchers building probabilistic forecast foundation models or outage decision-support systems, this is the strongest published demonstration of generative, transferable outage trajectory simulation and worth reading for its count-encoding trick and transfer evidence; practitioners seeking deployment-ready uncertainty calibration or peer-reviewed validation should treat it as a promising preprint whose headline scenario-quality claim is undermined by its own coverage numbers.

AgentGrad: Intervention-guided Prompt Optimization for Multi Agent Systems (59 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AgentGrad, a textual-gradient prompt optimization framework for LLM multi-agent systems that uses sequential intervention to identify the agent whose correction resolves each failure and semantic clustering to aggregate gradients into coherent update directions. - Why it's important: Prompt optimization for multi-agent systems is bottlenecked by credit assignment — knowing which agent's prompt to update and with what supervision — and current textual-gradient methods waste rollouts on uninformative updates, making optimization slow and prone to prompts that don't generalize. - How it does it: The core move is to inject ground-truth-derived hints into one agent at a time (in reverse execution order), treat the hint-corrected output as an agent-level pseudo-label against the failed output, then have an LLM cluster the resulting sample-level gradients by shared corrective pattern and abstract each cluster into one generalized gradient. - The good: Across five benchmarks and two backbones (GPT-5-mini, Qwen3-8B) with 3 seeds each, AgentGrad beats MIPROv2, TextGrad, and GEPA on every benchmark while being 2.5× faster in wall-clock time than the next-fastest baseline, with component-level ablations and a mechanism analysis (minibatch/validation improvement ratios) explaining where the gains come from. - The missing: The entire intervention mechanism hinges on a hand-designed hint H successfully repairing the target agent's behavior; the paper does not report intervention success rates, how sensitive results are to hint construction, or how often the single-responsible-agent assumption breaks (multi-agent failures become 'hard cases' and are dropped from the round). - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building automatic prompt optimization for compound LLM pipelines, since it converts failure-attribution research into a practical optimization signal; skippable if you only work on single-prompt optimization or already use trajectory-level methods like GEPA and don't care about multi-agent credit assignment.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (68) are the drivers — recasting intervention-based failure attribution as a supervision generator (hint-corrected output as agent-level pseudo-label) is a genuinely new connection, and semantic gradient clustering is a sensible fix to an identified defect. Rigor (68) is respectable — three seeds, current strong baselines (GEPA, TextGrad, MIPROv2), component ablations, and transfer tests — but no significance tests, no released code, and the unmeasured intervention success rate (the load-bearing assumption) hold it back. Completeness (58) and Resilience (58) are the weakest links: a thin limitations section, hard multi-agent failures silently excluded, the cyclic cluster schedule un-ablated, and 'multi-agent systems' claims extrapolated from ≤5-agent static pipelines. Impact (50) reflects no released artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*70 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*58 + 0.10*50 = 64.
