Problem & Motivation: Reconstructing a depicted 3D world as an executable scene program from one image is attractive because code exposes geometry, materials, and spatial relationships for inspection, editing, reuse, and simulation — unlike pixels. Prior agentic approaches (VIGA, SEIG/Thinking in Blender, img2threejs) reconstruct scenes through interleaved program generation, execution, and render-based visual feedback, but they organize construction as either a single editing trajectory or a fixed scene→object→factor pipeline. The gap: when a world contains structure at many scales (a town containing buildings containing facades containing signs), a single global trajectory cannot resolve fine detail, while independent local reconstruction breaks spatial relationships that only become visible when parts are reassembled. The motivating audience is anyone building code-based world models for simulation, editing, or game asset creation. Key Idea: The core insight is that subworld construction should be recursive, not merely hierarchical: each part is treated as a subworld that receives the same complete solve as the root — establish the whole, recurse on unresolved parts, revisit and refine the composition after children return — rather than being generated as an asset and inserted. Two supporting mechanisms make this work in practice: (1) reference-aligned views, where a child's camera is the parent camera with its intrinsic matrix composed with a crop/magnification homography (Eq. 10–11), so local inspection shares the parent's pose and coordinate frame; and (2) parent revisitation, where the parent re-renders the assembled whole after children return and repairs cross-part boundaries, overlaps, and shared errors at the ancestor that owns their cause. Methodology: The output is a Recursive Scene Program (RSP): nested Three.js subworld modules connected by parent "children" references, with editable parameters and shared code dependencies, executed as S = Exec(P), Ĩ = R(S; κ). Construction is a recursive solver F driven by a frozen VLM coding agent; each call F(q(k)_i, C(k)_i; A) maintains a state (component code, reference view, matched camera, remaining budget) and loops through three stages: (1) Establish the whole — render the component inside its inherited context C(k)_i (built by recursively composing the candidate into parent snapshots, Eq. 7) and compare against the reference to fix layout, shared structures, and interfaces; (2) Prepare and recurse — select unresolved children, cut matched reference crops and camera viewports with overlapping windows, allocate budgets, and call F on each; (3) Compose, refine, and return — integrate returned child programs via Compose, render the assembled whole, repair relationships, and CONTINUE or RETURN based on whether any actionable discrepancy remains, with budget exhaustion forcing return. The framework is a form of agentic program search with render-and-compare visual feedback; there is no learned objective — the stopping and decomposition decisions are made by the model's visual judgment, with a fixed total inference budget b. Critical design decisions: (a) the crop-homography camera inheritance, well-justified because it keeps local comparisons in a globally consistent frame; (b) trusting model visual judgment over metric gates for stopping — stated as a philosophy but not empirically defended against metric-gated alternatives; (c) the fixed solver instruction applied verbatim at every node (Appendix A.1), which is the system's real control logic and includes sensible anti-flatness heuristics (rotated-view checks for paper-thin geometry). Key Results: On 10 references (4 whole scenes + 5 crops from a CC0 "Isometric city" sprite pack; 1 whole scene + 1 crop from WorldClaw demonstration renders), with all methods driven by the same gpt-6-astra base model: RCWM achieves the best PSNR and LPIPS on every reference, e.g., city-full 18.2 PSNR / 0.158 LPIPS vs. img2threejs 15.5/0.243, SEIG 14.5/0.339, VIGA 9.5/0.670; japan-island 19.3 PSNR; park-lake 23.3 PSNR / 0.075 LPIPS. It leads SSIM on 9 of 10 references (VIGA edges it on valley-village, 0.41 vs. 0.38, where all methods are weak: PSNR ≤ 14.1, LPIPS ≥ 0.583). Ablations on two scenes with five workflows show the recursive free-depth variant best on medieval-village (19.0 PSNR, 0.73 SSIM, 0.60 local SSIM vs. 16.8/0.67/0.52 for fixed 2-level, and 16.4/0.66/0.50 for Flat+zoom), but on school-block free depth used only two levels and matched fixed 2-level within noise (16.5 vs. 16.8 PSNR). Baselines are recent (2026) and the shared-base-model protocol is a genuine strength, but SEIG is the authors' reproduction from the paper, all results are single runs with no variance, and the reference images are stylized isometric illustrations rather than photographs. Recorded call trees reach depth 4 with up to 63 nodes and 169 sessions (japan-island), showing the recursion is actually exercised. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD (with an engineering component): the genuinely novel element is formulating image-to-scene-program construction as self-recursive solving — the same whole/parts/whole cycle at every scale, with parent revisitation — rather than a fixed scene–object pipeline or repeated flat editing. The ingredients (VLM coding agents, render-compare refinement, scene decomposition, camera-projected inspection) are all established; the contribution is the recursive control structure plus the crop-homography view inheritance that makes recursion concrete. Compared to concurrent FuncRoom-Agent (a recursive DSL distilled for indoor rooms), RCWM's claim of a domain-general recursion without a prescribed semantic hierarchy is a real differentiator, though the distinction is partly one of generality of prompting versus a learned specialist. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and are well-designed: five construction workflows (Flat+zoom, Local→global, Global→local, Recursive fixed 2-level, Recursive free depth) sharing base model, representation, tools, reference resolution, and crop access — this is the paper's most rigorous element and credibly isolates the recursive organization. However: one run per variant per scene, no seeds, no error bars, no significance tests; ablations cover only 2 of 10 scenes, and the one case where free-depth recursion beat fixed 2-level was also the one where it actually descended to depth 3 — a confound the authors acknowledge only implicitly. The verbatim solver instruction is reproduced in Appendix A.1, and call trees "are released with the code," but no repository URL is printed in the text. Methodological concerns: the benchmark consists of 10 images, several of which are renders of a baseline-adjacent system (WorldClaw), and none are real photographs; SEIG is a self-reproduction; the solver receives magnified crops while metrics are computed against the native-resolution reference, potentially advantaging multi-scale methods on edge F1; there is no 3D geometric ground truth, so 3D quality is only qualitatively inspected (rotated/orbit renders); and compute cost per method is never reported despite recursion multiplying session counts (169 sessions for one scene). Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (a framework run end-to-end on a commercial agent; the artifact is the released prompt, runner, and generated scene programs). - Practical: Yes — needs only API access to a coding agent and Three.js; no training or GPUs for the method itself. - Efficient: No evidence — the paper reports session counts (up to 169 sessions, 92 calls for one scene) and admits "substantial computation" but provides no token/time/cost measurements or comparison against baseline cost. - Effective: The evidence shows faithful reconstruction of stylized isometric references under image-similarity metrics and qualitative multi-view inspection; it does not establish effectiveness on real photos, absolute scale, or hidden-geometry plausibility beyond self-checks. - Scalable: Only claimed implicitly — the runner caps depth at 5, one scene used depth 4 with 63 nodes, and behavior at 10× scene complexity or under budget pressure is untested; convergence is explicitly not guaranteed. The work delivers a reusable artifact (solver prompt, runner, call trees, generated programs, stated code release without a printed URL). Strengths: - A clean, well-motivated conceptual contribution: recasting hierarchical scene construction as self-recursion with parent revisitation, articulated with unusual formal care (states, contexts, Compose/Observe operators) for an agentic systems paper. - The matched crop-homography camera scheme (Eq. 10–11) is a concrete, transferable trick for giving child solves globally consistent local evidence. - The controlled comparison — same frozen base model and reasoning effort across all four methods — plus the five-variant ablation sharing runner and tools, makes the procedure-level claims about recursion the best-supported part of the paper. - Transparency of mechanism: the full solver prompt is printed verbatim, and logged call trees with per-node session counts are shown, which is more operational disclosure than typical agent papers provide. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: single-view input leaves hidden geometry and absolute scale ambiguous; visual inspection can overlook errors; repeated refinement is computationally substantial and convergence is not guaranteed; and evaluation covers a limited scene set with single runs on one base model and ablations on two scenes, calling for larger benchmarks, repeated runs, and human evaluation. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section and a credibility positive; the authors correctly identify the statistical fragility of their own evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No real photographic references: all 10 references are CC0 isometric sprite art or renders of another generation system, so generalization to the domain where image-to-3D actually matters (photos, captures) is untested and arguably unfavorable to a low-poly Three.js pipeline — an omission that materially bounds the claims. - No compute accounting: given the recursion multiplies sessions (e.g., 169 sessions vs. presumably one trajectory for Flat+zoom), a cost-matched or cost-reported comparison is needed to know whether the fidelity gains come from recursion or simply from spending more inference compute; the ablation variants may not be budget-matched. - Only image-space metrics: no geometric evaluation (depth, mesh, or multi-view consistency) despite the contribution being a 3D program; the rotated-view renders are illustrative, not measured. - One baseline (SEIG) is a paper-based reproduction, introducing implementation-fairness risk; and single runs on 10 images with best-per-scene bolding invites selection concerns, especially given the authors report the medieval-village depth-3 result where free depth happens to help. - The stopping rule and decomposition quality rest entirely on the model's visual judgment and the engineered prompt; no analysis of failure modes of the recursion itself (e.g., bad decompositions, cascading parent errors, child–parent camera drift) is provided beyond one weak scene (valley-village). Bottom Line: A conceptually tidy and unusually well-instrumented agentic-systems paper whose recursive whole–parts–whole construction is a genuinely reusable design pattern worth stealing, but whose evidence — 10 stylized images, single runs, no cost accounting, no real photos — supports it as a promising principle rather than a validated method, so read it for the formulation and prompt design, not for proof that it beats alternatives where it counts.

CAGE: Coherence-Aware Graph Encoding for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

T Qi, J Wu, Y Yin, S Hong, D Liu, E Babinsky · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CAGE, a post-retrieval reranking framework that scores each retrieved passage by its structural coherence with the rest of the retrieved set—via per-passage entity graphs encoded by a Relational GCN—fused with query relevance, and shows it improves multi-hop QA recall and Exact Match over relevance-only reranking. - Why it's important: Standard retrievers and rerankers score each chunk independently, so assembled contexts can be individually relevant yet collectively contradictory or disconnected, which caps answer quality no matter how capable the generator is. - How it does it: Each passage becomes a directed heterogeneous entity graph (spaCy dependency parsing with coreference), low-out-degree "factual anchor" nodes are amplified, a single-layer R-GCN plus global sum pooling produces a 128-dim graph embedding, and passages are reranked by f_i = α·sim(q,C_i) + (1−α)/(k−1)·Σ_j cos(Z_i,Z_j) with α=0.7. - The good: A component-wise ablation cleanly isolates the contribution: replacing a vanilla GCN with an R-GCN lifts Recall@5 by up to +10.5 points on MuSiQue, and the coherence term adds +4.4 EM on HotpotQA (81% bridge questions) where semantically distant gold bridge passages get rescued. - The missing: No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple seeds for margins that are often under 1 point, and the closest related method (G-RAG) is discussed but never compared empirically; code is not stated as released. - Read it or not: Worth reading for RAG reranking researchers who want a concrete instantiation of set-level coherence scoring and its honest failure analysis on adversarial misinformation; practitioners seeking a drop-in production reranker can skip it until gains are validated at scale and against G-RAG.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (68) is solid — the between-chunk coherence formulation is a genuine NEW FORMULATION — but Rigor (50) pulls the composite down hard: no seeds, error bars, or significance tests for sub-point margins, the closest prior method G-RAG is never compared empirically, no code release, and evaluation uses 10-20 candidate pools with a weak 2019-era retriever. Completeness (65) is helped by candid limitations and an exemplary RAMDocs failure analysis, but Resilience (58) suffers because headline claims rest on unvalidated proxy labels and margins within noise. Problem & Motivation: RAG pipelines rank passages by per-chunk query similarity in both the retrieval and reranking stages, so the final top-k context is a bag of independently high-scoring fragments. The authors document a failure mode where gold supporting chunks in multi-hop benchmarks are displaced by hard distractors that outscore them on individual relevance metrics—for example, a query about current Type 2 diabetes treatment retrieving a 2010 passage, a 2023 passage, an off-topic Type 1 diabetes passage, and a contradictory opinion piece. Existing evaluation frameworks (RAGAS, TruLens) measure generation-side faithfulness, and graph-based RAG systems (GraphRAG, HippoRAG, GNN-RAG, HyperGraphRAG, G-RAG) use graphs for navigation or pairwise affinity, not as validators of set-level evidence integrity. The gap is that between-chunk coherence—whether the retrieved set forms a logically integrable, traversable evidence base—has never been formalized as an optimization objective. Key Idea: Formalize between-chunk coherence as a four-dimensional property of the retrieved set (Intra-Domain Relevance, Noise Resistance, Informational Bonding, Factual Consistency) and operationalize it as mean pairwise cosine similarity between per-passage graph embeddings from an R-GCN, on the argument that structurally compatible passages (shared entities, compatible relations, bridge connectivity) embed closer together while isolated distractors and relational contradictions embed apart. The four-dimension taxonomy and the coherence-as-graph-similarity scoring function are the core ideas; the individual components (dependency-parse graphs, R-GCN, cosine fusion with a retriever score) are standard. Methodology: Four-stage pipeline. (1) Graph construction: each passage is parsed with spaCy en_core_web_lg plus coreference resolution into a directed heterogeneous graph whose nodes are lemmatized content words (300-dim contextual embedding, one-hot POS, one-hot entity type, scalar weight) and whose edges carry relation types from dependency structure (verb-labeled subject–object links with negation, modifiers, prepositional relations, NER co-occurrence). (2) Reweighting: nodes with minimum out-degree (assumed to be specific entities, numbers, and factual endpoints) have features and adjacent edge weights scaled by β=2. (3) Encoding: a single-layer R-GCN with ReLU and global sum pooling yields a 128-dim graph embedding, trained per query for 30–60 epochs (<0.5 s on the k passage graphs) with a diversity objective minimizing mean pairwise cosine similarity within the batch to prevent representation collapse. (4) Scoring: coherence s_i = Σ_j cos(Z_i,Z_j) is fused with the original query–passage cosine at α=0.7 (grid-searched over 0.1–1.0 and fixed across datasets). A theoretical section proves R-GCN/Relational-WL equivalence (Proposition 1), a Coherence Separability theorem, and four lemmas mapping each coherence dimension to a structural property. Critical design decisions: the min-out-degree prior is intuitively motivated but only post-hoc validated by ablation; the diversity objective substitutes for the injectivity the degree-normalized implementation loses (acknowledged in Appendix B.1); and L=1 layers is justified by bridge entities appearing within 1-hop neighborhoods of compact passage graphs. Key Results: Evaluated on 1,000-sample subsets each of MuSiQue, HotpotQA (distractor), and 2WikiMultihopQA, and 500 samples of RAMDocs, with candidate pools of 10–20 passages (3–12 for RAMDocs), against BM25, GTR, ColBERTv2, RAPTOR, HyperGraphRAG, mxbai-rerank, monoT5, and Vanilla RAG (same first-stage all-MiniLM-L6-v2 retriever). Recall@5: CAGE 64.0 (MuSiQue), 85.4 (2Wiki), 84.2 (HotpotQA), 87.0 (RAMDocs)—best on MuSiQue (vs. 63.5 mxbai-rerank, 62.8 monoT5), best on 2Wiki (+5.0 over Vanilla RAG, +17.2 over ColBERTv2), tied with monoT5 on HotpotQA (84.2), and slightly worst on RAMDocs (87.0 vs. 87.6 ColBERTv2). Downstream generation with Gemma 4 26B A4B and Llama 3.3 70B: CAGE takes the highest EM in 5 of 8 dataset–model combinations (e.g., Llama on HotpotQA 55.0 EM vs. 50.6 Vanilla RAG and 54.2 monoT5) with more modest F1 movement. Ablations attribute +10.5 Recall@5 on MuSiQue to the relational (vs. vanilla GCN) encoder and +3.9/+1.8 on 2Wiki/HotpotQA to reweighting. The most instructive negative result: on RAMDocs, adversarial passages that alter one assertion while preserving entity structure produce near-isomorphic graphs that CAGE cannot distinguish, costing −1.0 EM versus relevance-only ranking—an honest, mechanistically explained failure (the paper ties it to a boundary condition of its own Lemma 4). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (between-chunk coherence as an explicit set-level reranking objective with a four-dimension decomposition) plus NEW METHOD; genuinely new is the framing and the coherence-similarity scoring, while the machinery—dependency-parse entity graphs, R-GCN encoding, min-degree heuristics, linear fusion with retriever scores—is a competent combination of existing techniques applied to this new objective. The theory section repackages known results (Xu et al. 2018 WL-equivalence; Schlichtkrull et al. 2018 R-GCN) into a coherence framing rather than proving new machinery. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed: GCN vs. R-GCN, with/without reweighting, and fused score vs. text-only relevance (Figure 4), covering both retrieval and generation metrics across two generators. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for margins that are frequently 0.3–1.0 points (e.g., 64.0 vs. 63.6 on MuSiQue), which is thin given 500–1,000-sample evaluation subsets. The fusion weight α was grid-searched (Figure 6 shows per-dataset sensitivity) and fixed at 0.7; the paper states it was fixed across datasets, but the selection procedure's relationship to the test sets is not fully specified. No code or model release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (a) evaluation relies on multi-hop supporting-fact annotations as a proxy for coherence labels—acknowledged by the authors, but it means the four-dimension theory is never directly validated; (b) the closest related method, G-RAG, is analyzed in related work but absent from the baseline table; (c) the first-stage retriever is all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a weak 2019-era encoder, and pools contain only 10–20 candidates, so gains over stronger modern pipelines in realistic large-corpus settings are untested. The injectivity gap between the proved unnormalized R-GCN and the implemented normalized variant is candidly disclosed in Appendix B.1. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: Yes—~210K parameters, spaCy parsing on CPU, per-query R-GCN training under 0.5 s on a single GPU, and open-weight generators run locally. - Efficient: Graph construction is the bottleneck at roughly 2 seconds per passage on CPU (6 hours for 10,000 passages), and the per-query training loop adds latency that a production system would need to amortize or distill; baselines like monoT5 require no such per-query fitting. - Effective: The evidence supports the claim on bridge-dominated multi-hop sets (2Wiki, HotpotQA) but shows the method does not solve the stated factual-consistency goal on adversarial misinformation, where it underperforms a plain reranker. - Scalable: Untested—evaluation covers candidate pools of at most 20 passages from curated benchmark sets; behavior with hundreds of candidates, longer documents, or corpora-scale retrieval is only claimed via the L-layer theory, not measured. The work stops at paper form: no library, CLI, dataset, or trained model artifact is stated as released. Strengths: - The four-dimension decomposition of between-chunk coherence is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution that names and separates failure modes (referent disambiguation, cross-domain keyword traps, missing bridges, assertion conflicts) that per-chunk relevance scoring conflates. - The ablation program is unusually clean for a RAG paper: it isolates the encoder architecture, the reweighting prior, and the coherence term itself across four datasets and two generators, so the reader can see exactly where the gains come from. - The RAMDocs failure analysis is exemplary: instead of burying the −1.0 EM result, the authors trace it to near-isomorphic adversarial graphs, connect it to an explicit boundary condition of their own Lemma 4 (assertion-level substitution is invisible to non-commutativity arguments), and name NLI verification as the necessary complement. - The per-dimension case studies (Figures 7–10) map each benchmark to a specific coherence dimension, making the empirical proxy assumption inspectable rather than implicit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three constraints directly: (1) rule-based spaCy parsing caps relation-extraction quality and propagates parser errors into graph topology; (2) no benchmark provides per-dimension coherence annotations, so evaluation uses multi-hop supporting facts as a proxy—their proposed dedicated benchmark is future work; (3) α is set by grid search and an adaptive per-query mechanism could improve robustness on adversarial benchmarks. They also explicitly identify claim-level NLI verification as required for adversarial settings. This is a credibility positive: the limitations section confronts the proxy-evaluation problem and the RAMDocs failure head-on rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical rigor around small margins: several headline comparisons (MuSiQue 64.0 vs. 63.5/63.6; RAMDocs 87.0 vs. 87.2) are within noise for 500–1,000 samples, yet no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. - G-RAG is the closest prior method (graph-based reranking of retrieved passages) and is discussed at length in related work as insufficient, but it never appears in the baseline table—an obvious missing comparison that would directly test the claimed delta over pairwise graph reranking. - The R-GCN is trained per query with only a diversity objective and no supervision; the paper's claim that the encoder learns coherence-relevant representations is essentially a structural prior plus regularization, and the theory/implementation gap (normalized aggregation breaks injectivity) means Theorem 1's guarantees hold only approximately, in a sense never quantified. - Evaluation pools of 10–20 candidates with a 2019-era MiniLM first-stage retriever inflate the reranker's room to help; no experiment tests CAGE on top of a strong modern retriever or at production-scale candidate counts. - The four-dimension taxonomy is never directly measured—the datasets are mapped to dimensions by construction (e.g., "HotpotQA is 81% bridge") rather than by annotating coherence dimensions, so the theory-to-empirics link rests entirely on the proxy assumption. - The arXiv version is a preprint (2609.04647) and appears not to have undergone peer review; results should be weighted accordingly. Bottom Line: A researcher working on RAG reranking gains real value from the between-chunk coherence formulation, the honest adversarial-failure analysis, and the clean ablations, but the sub-point margins without significance testing, the missing G-RAG comparison, and the small-pool evaluation mean this is a promising research direction rather than a validated replacement for strong cross-encoder rerankers.

Theory of Agent : The Science of Internalization and Externalization for LLM-Based Agents

Z Cheng, Y Li, S Yue, Y Lu, Y Qiu, Y Tian, H Zhang… · preprints.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the "Theory of Agent" (ToA), a ~100-page survey and position framework that recasts LLM-agent design as a single decision problem — where competence should live across the model–harness boundary — and organizes the field's literature around internalization (compiling competence into parameters) versus externalization (offloading it to memory, tools, and orchestration). - Why it's important: Agent builders currently make internalize-vs-externalize choices (RAG vs long context, tool-integrated vs tool-internalized reasoning, learned vs scaffolded orchestration) community by community without a shared vocabulary, and misallocation produces the field's most common failures: wasted compute, hallucination from under-acting, and latency/cost/safety exposure from over-acting. - How it does it: The core move is a reinterpretation of a standard POMDP: partition the action space into internal operators (reasoning, generated by the model's own map) and external operators (acting on the world), define a latent knowledge boundary between the internal and world task sets, and treat all four classic failure modes (over/under-thinking, over/under-acting) as one defect — a miscalibrated estimate of internal solvability against a cost-ratio-dependent threshold. - The good: The unification is genuinely clarifying: it collapses the efficient-reasoning and efficient-tool-use literatures into a single calibration target, and its proposal to evaluate agents by epistemic effort allocation (a utility-gain-per-cost ratio η) rather than task success alone is a sharp, testable critique of success-rate scoring. - The missing: The framework's central quantitative object — the epistemic intelligence ratio η and the boundary estimate p_int — is never operationalized or validated on any benchmark within the paper; all normative claims remain programmatic, with zero experiments, measurements, or worked case studies. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building or evaluating LLM agents who want a coherent organizing lens and a massive curated literature map (the taxonomy alone, with a companion GitHub resource list, is valuable); practitioners seeking concrete algorithms or evaluated metrics will find only a research agenda.
Why this rank
Scored using Theoretical profile. Rigor (40) is the primary drag — no theorem is proven (the effort-conservation claim is definitional, the monotonicity claim has an escape clause), and the central quantitative objects (p_int, η) are never instantiated on even one benchmark despite the paper claiming they make epistemic intelligence 'measurable.' Novelty (72) and Non-Obviousness (70) rescue the score: the internalization–externalization boundary framing and the four-failure-modes-as-one-miscalibration argument genuinely unify the efficient-reasoning and efficient-tool-use literatures, which is a real conceptual contribution. Completeness (50) is reduced by the absence of any empirical instantiation of the paper's own metrics and unstated survey methodology; Resilience (50) reflects that the framework survives as a hypothesis but its strongest claims collapse under demands for evidence; Impact (45) is limited to a curated repository with no algorithm or reference implementation. Weighted composite: 0.25*72 + 0.20*40 + 0.25*70 + 0.10*50 + 0.15*50 + 0.05*45 = 58.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: LLM agents couple a model (parametric weights holding knowledge and reasoning) to a harness (context, memory, tools, retrieval, orchestration). Nearly every advance in the field improves one side or the other, but the governing design decision — which knowledge, skills, and control to internalize into weights versus keep external in the harness — is made implicitly and inconsistently. The authors argue this placement is probabilistic (agents can only estimate what they know), context-dependent (it shifts with model strength, task, and within-trajectory evidence), and asymmetrically costly (external actions buy grounding at the price of latency, money, irreversibility, and permission exposure). Existing surveys, they claim, catalog harness components engineering-style rather than organizing the field around this trade-off; the paper targets researchers deciding what to train into models versus what to scaffold around them. Key Idea: The single core insight: reasoning and acting are not different kinds of activity but two implementations of one primitive — a belief-update operator b_t → b_{t+1} — differing only in where the reducing information originates (parameters vs. world). Once this is accepted, the agent's job at each step becomes estimating internal solvability p_int(q, m; W) and applying a threshold rule (Eq. 7) that encodes the cost ratio c_int/c_ext; over-thinking, under-acting, over-acting, and under-thinking are then one defect (boundary miscalibration) seen from two error directions and two operator types, and efficient-reasoning and efficient-tool-calling research become two repairs of the same calibration target. Methodology: This is a survey/position paper; its "method" is a formal reframing plus a five-chapter literature synthesis. Formally, the paper adopts an unchanged POMDP ⟨S, A, O, T, Z, b_0, c⟩, augments the transition kernel with an epistemic annotation (internal actions produce observations via the model's generative map f_m without touching state; external actions query or alter the environment), and defines: internal task set Q_int ⊆ world task set Q_world; the knowledge boundary B as their separation; a decision threshold α over the estimated solvability p_int; additive epistemic effort E = E_int + E_ext with a conserved minimum E*(q,m) (an infimum over successful policies); a deployed cost E_total = c_int·E_int + c_ext·E_ext; and an epistemic intelligence ratio η = ΔU_useful/(E_int + E_ext) measured against ground-truth belief change rather than agent-reported confidence. The synthesis chapters map Learning (internalization of memory, planning, tool-use policy, and world models via SFT/distillation/RL; externalization via memory stores, skill libraries, harness/protocols), Aligning (calibration against cognitive boundaries, efficiency budgets, human preferences, environment constraints, and other agents), Evolving (model-side, harness-side, and agent–environment co-evolution), and Evaluation (reinterpreting ~30 named benchmarks through the epistemic-effort lens). Critical design decisions: (1) the reframing is deliberately a "conservative addition" to POMDPs rather than new math — well-justified for accessibility, but it caps formal depth; (2) the claim that all four failure modes share one calibration target — the most load-bearing unifying claim, argued but not experimentally demonstrated; (3) the choice to define utility against ground-truth answer distributions — sensible, but pushes the hard measurement problem into ΔU, which is left unspecified. Key Results: No empirical results — the paper reports no experiments, measurements, accuracy figures, or runtime comparisons of its own. Its outputs are conceptual: the ToA formalism, a taxonomy figure mapping roughly 200+ cited systems into Learning/Aligning/Evolving/Evaluation categories, structured comparison tables (e.g., Table 1 cataloguing internalization routes by source/method/carrier/adaptive-use; Table 2 for externalization; Tables 3–5 for knowledge-boundary, ability-boundary, and efficiency-alignment methods along multi-dimensional axes), and a set of benchmark-reinterpretation principles (controllable information conditions, counterfactual tool access, trajectory-level observation, multi-axis reporting, longitudinal measurement). The normative headline is the argument that success-rate scoring is structurally blind to over- and under-internalization, and that η would rank an agent improving from 0.40 to 0.92 above one going from 0.90 to 0.92 on the same effort. Benchmark and system names cited (ToolLLM's 16,464 APIs, API-Bank's 2,138 APIs, SWE-bench, WebArena, etc.) are prior work, not results of this paper. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (a unifying reframing of agent design as boundary placement, with the four-failure-modes-as-one-miscalibration argument) plus a substantive survey synthesis. What is genuinely novel: the internalization–externalization axis as an explicit, named, cross-community design principle and the effort-allocation/η vocabulary for evaluation. What is standard: the underlying formalism is textbook POMDP with a definitional action-space partition; ReAct, Toolformer, MemGPT, Voyager, and the hundreds of other systems surveyed are reclassified, not extended; the "know when you don't know" calibration literature is imported wholesale. The paper is honest about this lineage, explicitly crediting a prior ToA work [19] for the core formalism. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a survey, there are no ablations, seeds, error bars, or significance tests to assess. The formal claims are definitions or trivialities: Eq. 10's effort conservation holds by construction (E* is defined as an infimum), Eq. 8's monotonicity is asserted for "relevant and non-degrading" context — an escape clause that admits counterexamples without analyzing them — and Eq. 12's η is never instantiated against real trajectories. A companion GitHub repository (https://github.com/BUAA-IRIP-LLM/Awesome-LLM-Powered-Agent) provides the curated resource list, which is the only reproducible artifact. Methodological concerns: the paper is a non-peer-reviewed preprint (explicitly marked "NOT PEER-REVIEWED", posted 3 September 2026 on Preprints.org); its evaluation chapter proposes benchmark principles it does not implement, instantiate, or test on even one benchmark; and its central empirical claims (e.g., that miscalibrated p_int produces all four failure modes, that misallocation stunts long-run competence growth) cite scattered prior evidence rather than any direct demonstration. The 20-author, multi-institution authorship (Beihang, SUSTech, Fudan, BIT, Edinburgh, CAS, Baidu) without a stated systematic literature-review methodology raises selection-bias questions about coverage. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL — the paper offers formal definitions and conceptual claims with no primary experimental result; it is a framework/survey, not a system. Applying the theoretical check: Sound — the definitions are internally consistent but no theorem is proven; the one formal claim (effort conservation) is definitional, and the monotonicity claim (Eq. 8) is qualified away from generality. General — the framing is broadly realistic by design (it deliberately covers MDPs, POMDPs, single and multi-agent settings), but its key quantities (p_int, ΔU, η) are acknowledged to be latent or hard to measure, which limits operational generality. Tight — not applicable in the bound sense; there are no bounds, and the framework offers no approximation or learnability guarantees for estimating the boundary. Implementable — partially: the threshold rule (Eq. 7) and η are directly implementable as diagnostics, and the paper points to proxies (self-consistency, rollout agreement, hidden-state probes), but no algorithm, pseudocode, or reference implementation is given, and no follow-up operationalization is demonstrated within the paper. The work delivers a paper plus a curated resource repository; no library, trained model, dataset, or CLI. Strengths: - The unifying diagnosis is a real intellectual contribution: collapsing over-thinking, under-acting, over-acting, and under-thinking into a single miscalibrated boundary estimate, with the cost ratio c_int/c_ext as the implicit threshold, makes the efficient-reasoning and efficient-tool-use literatures commensurable for the first time in a way that suggests concrete joint training objectives. - The epistemic-effort accounting and the η ratio give evaluation researchers a specific, falsifiable alternative to success-rate scoring, including the correct observation that ΔU measured against ground-truth priors neutralizes the accuracy artifact where easy gains are undervalued relative to hard ones. - The multi-dimensional comparison tables (Tables 1–5) organize a very large and fragmented literature along genuinely decision-relevant axes (signal, localization, control mechanism, access requirements, failure addressed) — this is competent, reusable synthesis beyond a reading list. - The three-timescales observation (boundary drift within a trajectory, across training, across a deployment lifetime) connects intra-episode context effects to lifelong-learning questions under one object. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly acknowledges that the knowledge boundary is latent and unobservable (agents act on estimates, not the true boundary); that boundary placement is model-, task-, and environment-relative with no universally correct policy; that η can be gamed on fixed task distributions ("an agent that refuses to act and gets lucky"); that η is an observable signature of epistemic intelligence, not the capacity itself; that prompted self-reflection is prompt-sensitive and prone to rationalization; and that uncertainty scores can be adversarially manipulated or collapsed by ambiguity. The authors confront the framework's measurement gaps reasonably directly in §2.4 and §4, which is a credibility positive; however, they do not acknowledge the absence of any empirical instantiation of their own metrics as a limitation of the paper itself. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The framework's central quantities are never measured: no benchmark, even a toy one, is analyzed through η or p_int, despite the paper's own claim that η "makes epistemic intelligence measurable" — the strongest claim in the paper is left entirely untested. - The evaluation chapter proposes five benchmark principles (controllable information conditions, counterfactual tool access, etc.) without constructing even a minimal prototype task, so the paper's most actionable contribution exists only as prose. - The claimed learning consequence — that over-externalization stunts long-run internal competence growth — is a strong developmental claim cited to indirect evidence, not demonstrated in any trajectory. - Coverage methodology is unstated: with ~300 citations across five chapters written by ~20 authors, there is no stated inclusion criterion, so the taxonomy's completeness and the fairness of its reclassifications cannot be assessed. - The formalism's added value over plain POMDPs is asserted rather than shown: no worked example demonstrates that a decision made with the A_int/A_ext annotation would differ from, or beat, one made without it. - The survey necessarily predates or omits rapid-moving adjacent debates (e.g., post-training-era tool-internalization results) and, as a preprint with a Baidu co-author and no peer review, its framing claims should be weighted accordingly. Bottom Line: For agent researchers and evaluation-focused practitioners, this is a genuinely useful organizing lens and the best single map of the internalize-vs-externalize design space I have seen — but it is a research agenda, not a validated method, and anyone needing evaluated metrics or algorithms should treat its formalism as a hypothesis to test rather than a result to cite.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LevelSyn, a physical-aware logic synthesis framework that uses a level-asynchronous GNN (LA-GNN) to predict gate coordinates and orientations from an And-Inverter Graph, then feeds these spatial priors into an augmented technology-mapping cost function inside Berkeley ABC. - Why it's important: Traditional synthesis uses non-physical wire load models while GNN-based placement predictors ignore circuit hierarchy and signal direction, so netlists reach physical design poorly matched to layout and design closure cycles stay long; Problem & Motivation: At nanometer technology nodes, interconnect delay dominates gate delay, yet logic synthesis traditionally evaluates netlists with logical abstractions like wire load models, causing PPA degradation and long design-closure iterations. Existing GNN-based predictors (Net2, wirelength estimators) are tied to fixed netlist structures that synthesis constantly reshapes, and placement-guided mappers like PigMap rely on fast analytical placement (GiFt) whose spatial estimates are noisy. Spectral placement predictors scale poorly (cubic-cost Laplacian eigendecomposition) and ignore hierarchical logic depth and directional signal flow. The gap LevelSyn targets: obtaining high-fidelity, layout-consistent spatial estimates for arbitrary logic structures during synthesis, at industrial scale. Key Idea: Encode the fixed floorplan positions of primary inputs and outputs as spatial anchors in node features, then propagate information level-asynchronously (forward along signal flow, backward from POs) through the AIG's topological levels so each internal gate's coordinates are interpolated from both directions' constraints; derive cell orientation deterministically from the predicted y-coordinate's standard-cell row index (VDD-VSS rail structure), and inject a Normalized Level Index (Level(v)/L) so partitioned subgraphs share a global coordinate frame. Methodology: Three phases. (1) Hierarchical pre-processing: parse the AIG, encode PI/PO floorplan coordinates as normalized spatial anchors, initialize internal gates at (0.5, 0.5), and partition the graph into N level-aligned windows (V_k = nodes with (k−1)·w ≤ Level(v) < k·w, w = ⌈L/N⌉), processing subgraphs in parallel GPU batches. (2) Spatial prediction: LA-GNN with bidirectional message passing — forward AGGREGATE over fan-ins at lower levels, backward over fan-outs at higher levels, states fused by concatenation — trained with L = L_MSE(x̂,ŷ) + L_BCE(Ô) using AdamW (lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4), hidden dim 128, 6 layers; pre-trained on 500–10,000 randomly generated AIGs then fine-tuned per target circuit. (3) Physical-aware mapping: predicted (x̂, ŷ, Ô) back-annotated into ABC node structures; the mapping cost adds Predicted Wirelength (sum of Manhattan distances to adjacent pins for power mode pwmap; max distance for delay mode pfmap) plus a local gate-swapping/sizing refinement. Key design decisions: level-asynchronous (single-round, topologically ordered) message passing — justified by convergence loss 0.61 vs 0.75 for a 5-layer GCN; level-aligned rather than min-cut partitioning — justified by preserving local logic slices; deterministic orientation from row parity — physically motivated but no independent evaluation of orientation accuracy is reported. Key Results: Evaluated on the 20 EPFL combinational benchmarks (181 to 214,591 nodes) with SkyWater PDK and DREAMPlace for ground truth. Versus PigMap-power: LevelSyn-pwmap averages 6.52% area, 6.89% power, and 27.48% delay improvement; LevelSyn-pfmap averages 22.44% delay improvement versus PigMap-performance but −2.89% (worse) area. The 27.48% delay figure is driven largely by outliers (e.g., multiplier −56.5%, mem_ctrl 22.2%, hyp 27.5%); several circuits show regressions (i2c −24.8% for pwmap, adder −10.3% power for pfmap). Post-routing on bar only: LevelSyn-pwmap achieves 254,439 µm wirelength, 24,330 vias, and 4 DRC violations vs PigMap-power's 320,689 µm, 33,963 vias, 966 violations (99.59% DRC reduction). Memory ablation on hyp: LA-GNN with LASP uses 4,709 MB allocated vs 8,956 MB for standard GCN (−47.4%), though LA-GNN uses more memory than GCN on small/medium circuits. Runtime is competitive with PigMap on most circuits but degrades on the largest (hyp: ~1,647 s vs 969 s for PigMap; sqrt: 58 s vs 33 s). Baselines are recent and relevant (PigMap, ICCAD '25), but only two baselines are used. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (level-asynchronous bidirectional message passing for coordinate regression on AIGs) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (level-aligned subgraph partitioning for memory-bounded GNN training; ABC integration). The physical-informed mapping cost function is explicitly adapted from PigMap's differentiated-cost paradigm, and the GNN architecture builds on DeepGate2; the genuinely new elements are the PI/PO spatial-anchor conditioning with bi-directional level-asynchronous propagation, the row-parity orientation derivation, and the NLI-based global positional prior for parallel subgraph processing. Rigor & Reproducibility: Training hyperparameters, loss functions, hardware (A100), and window size are disclosed, and code is released at https://github.com/zhoujy22/PhysicalAwareSynthesis. Ablations cover memory scaling (LA-GNN vs GCN) and training convergence, but there is no ablation isolating the contribution of orientation prediction, NLI, or bidirectional vs unidirectional propagation to final PPA. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, despite mixed per-circuit results that make the averages sensitive to a few large circuits. A methodological concern: DREAMPlace supplies both the GNN's ground-truth coordinates and the evaluation flow, so the model is optimized against the same placer used to judge it; the wirelength/delay PPA in Table 1 appears to be estimated/placement-level rather than routed, and routed evidence exists only for bar. The 27.48% headline delay number comes from the power-optimized variant outperforming the delay-optimized one — a result the paper explains post hoc via 'global structural alignment' without direct measurement. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (an end-to-end synthesis framework built into ABC, evaluated through physical design). Practical: Runs on a single A100 GPU plus a Linux workstation with open-source tools (ABC, DREAMPlace, OpenROAD, SkyWater PDK), so it is deployable in academic and open-flow settings. Efficient: Fine-tuning adds 0.05–743 s depending on circuit size, and total runtime is comparable to PigMap on most circuits but roughly 1.7× PigMap on hyp (1,647 s vs 969 s). Effective: The evidence shows improved estimated PPA across EPFL and near-eliminated DRC violations on one circuit, but the effectiveness claim is supported by placement-level metrics plus a single-circuit routed case study rather than full-flow validation across the suite. Scalable: Memory is demonstrably capped at industrial scale (214k nodes in 4.7 GB), which is the paper's strongest scaling evidence, but 10×–100× beyond that, and multi-corner or larger floorplans, are untested. Deliverable: open-source code integrated into ABC, forming a reusable tool; no trained model weights are explicitly mentioned as released. Strengths: - The level-asynchronous message-passing formulation is a real architectural idea for DAG-structured circuits: it respects topological order, gives a principled way to inject fixed PI/PO boundary constraints from both ends, and converges to lower loss (0.61 vs 0.75) than a synchronous GCN. - The LASP partitioning result is well-executed and honestly reported: the paper shows LA-GNN alone uses more memory than a GCN on small circuits and only wins at scale, and quantifies the crossover (47.4% memory reduction on hyp) rather than claiming unconditional superiority. - The end-to-end integration into ABC with per-objective cost functions (sum-of-distances for power, max-distance for delay) is a clean, reusable engineering contribution, and the runtime table transparently discloses where the method is slower. - Validating through actual place-and-route (OpenROAD flow, 20 fixed routing iterations) on bar, rather than stopping at estimated PPA, is the right kind of evidence for this problem area. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states the framework currently handles only combinational circuits (sequential extension with flip-flop positioning is future work) and lists congestion and thermal distribution as unaddressed multi-objective targets. The runtime discussion acknowledges that mapping time increases for large circuits (sqrt, hyp), framed as negligible relative to hours-long physical design. The paper acknowledges that PigMap-style fast placement yields low-fidelity spatial data — its own motivating weakness for GiFt. It does not discuss the mixed per-circuit PPA results, the single-circuit scope of the routed study, or the DREAMPlace ground-truth circularity. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline 27.48% delay improvement comes from LevelSyn-pwmap, the power-oriented variant, beating PigMap's delay-oriented variant; LevelSyn-pfmap's own delay gain is 22.44% and its average area is worse than the baseline. The paper explains this via an unmeasured 'global structural alignment' hypothesis. A reviewer should treat the headline number cautiously. - The DRC claim (99.59%) generalizes from exactly one circuit (bar), chosen because it is PigMap's case-study circuit; no other circuit receives routed validation. - Per-circuit variance is large and unexplained (e.g., −56.5% delay on multiplier vs −24.8% regression on i2c for pwmap), and with no seeds or significance testing the averages may not be robust. - Ground-truth coordinates come from DREAMPlace, and DREAMPlace is also the physical-design backend — a Goodhart risk where the GNN learns to match the placer's own bias rather than truly optimal layouts. - The GNN is fine-tuned per benchmark circuit; generalization to unseen designs (the industrial 'shift-left' use case) is asserted via transfer-learning language but never tested with a held-out-circuit evaluation. - Only two baselines (ABC map and PigMap) are compared; WLM-based flows, CPA-Remap, or placement-aware resynthesis baselines are absent, and the paper reports 'PhySyn' as the framework name in the conclusion — an internal inconsistency suggesting a draft not fully reconciled. - Orientation prediction (Eq. 7–8) is never evaluated for accuracy against actual placement orientations; its contribution to the PPA gains is unknown. Bottom Line: For researchers in ML-for-EDA and physical-aware synthesis, this is worth reading for the level-asynchronous GNN and memory-bounded partitioning techniques, which are genuinely useful and open-sourced; but the headline PPA and DRC numbers rest on mixed per-circuit evidence, a single routed test case, and a circular ground-truth setup, so practitioners should verify the gains on their own designs before adoption.

Xiaomi-TabLDM: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report

T Team, P Wang, W Liu, H Wang, C Huang, Y Sun… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Xiaomi-TabLDM, a ~71M-parameter tabular foundation model that performs classification and regression via in-context learning, pretrained entirely on synthetic data from structural causal models (SCMs), and evaluates it across four public benchmark suites. - Why it's important: Tabular prediction still requires dataset-specific training/tuning of gradient-boosted trees or per-dataset neural models; a single zero-fine-tuning predictor that rivals tuned ensembles would cut deployment cost substantially for the many practitioners working with structured data. - How it does it: The core move is an in-context-learning transformer that consumes a target dataset's labeled training rows as context, built from a dual-stream circular-shift feature grouping, learned attention-residual depth aggregation, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts layers, trained with a three-stage curriculum over an expanded SCM-based synthetic prior. - The good: The regression evidence is broad and consistent: 1st average rank (3.03) on OpenML-CTR23 over 33 datasets, 2nd on TALENT regression (4.03 vs TabFM's 3.72), and 2nd Elo (1900) on TabArena regression with 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than the leader TabFM. - The missing: There is no component-wise ablation on real data isolating how much each architectural contribution (dual-stream grouping, AttnRes, sparse MoE, test-time scaling) actually contributes to the results, and the TabArena regression subset contains only 13 datasets with overlapping bootstrap confidence intervals. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners building or selecting tabular foundation models — it is a credible, well-benchmarked competitor to TabPFN-3/TabICLv2 with an unusually strong efficiency profile — but skippable for readers outside tabular ML since it introduces no transferable methodological insight beyond assembling known components.
Why this rank

Problem & Motivation: Tabular data prediction has been dominated for decades by per-dataset pipelines — gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) and AutoML ensembles like AutoGluon — which require training and tuning a separate model for every dataset. Deep tabular architectures (TabNet, TabTransformer, TabR, etc.) largely retain this paradigm. Tabular foundation models (TabPFN lineage, TabICL, TabDPT, LimiX, TabFM, EXAONE-Tabular) instead pretrain once on synthetic tabular tasks and predict on unseen datasets in a single forward pass using labeled examples as context. The open problem is that current tabular foundation models still trail the best tuned pipelines in some regimes and face a performance–cost trade-off: stronger models (e.g., TabFM) cost substantially more at train and predict time. The authors target practitioners who need strong out-of-the-box prediction on structured data in healthcare, finance, logistics, and manufacturing without per-dataset fine-tuning. Key Idea: The central technical move is to combine flexible context utilization with capacity scaling inside an in-context-learning transformer: dual-stream feature grouping breaks column symmetry by encoding each column with two circular-shift-selected neighbor columns (one fixed dyadic stream, one width-adaptive stream spanning up to the table width), lightweight Attention Residual connections let deeper layers retrieve earlier block representations via learned softmax-weighted aggregation, and sparse MoE layers (top-1 of 2 routed experts plus 1 shared expert, in the last 8 of 24 ICL blocks) expand parameters without proportional compute. None of these is individually novel — they adapt known techniques (Set Transformer inducing points, Block AttnRes from Kimi, DeepSeekMoE/ST-MoE routing, TabICLv2's Cauchy-DAG prior and QASSMax softmax, TabFM's NNLS ensemble combination) to the tabular ICL setting. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) column-wise feature embedding via dual-stream circular-shift grouping (each group of 3 columns through a shared Linear(3→d), two streams with offsets (1,2,4) and (1,⌊√s⌋,s), s = min(32, m−1), summed), each group encoded by a Set Transformer with 128 inducing points; (2) row-wise aggregation with 4 CLS tokens through 3 self-attention blocks with AttnRes connections (learnable pseudo-query scoring RMSNorm'd block outputs, applied at stride 4); (3) dataset-level ICL prediction with 24 transformer blocks where test rows attend only to training rows, MoE in the final 8 blocks, and query-aware scalable softmax attention for length generalization. Classification is trained with cross-entropy (max 10 classes; many-class tasks handled by TabICLv2-style mixed-radix ensembling) and regression with pinball loss over 999 quantiles. Pretraining uses an SCM prior: sample dataset properties, sample a Cauchy DAG, propagate latent representations in topological order through 12 random-function classes, observe selected dimensions, then filter tasks where ExtraTrees cannot beat a constant predictor. A three-stage curriculum scales dataset size from 1,024 samples (500K steps cls / 300K reg) to 60,000 samples (10K steps), trained with Muon on 8 A100-80GB GPUs (~11–14 days total). Test-time scaling combines predictions from shuffled feature orders, diverse preprocessing views (quantile transforms, SVD, feature interactions, target transforms), and NNLS-weighted combination fit on holdout or K-fold out-of-fold predictions, followed by probability calibration. Critical design decisions: the AttnRes mechanism is justified by a claimed training-collapse failure without it (past ~1,200 samples in Stage 1), MoE experts are initialized from the frozen dense FFN, and the shared-expert design offloads common computation — the last two are stated but not experimentally justified. Key Results: Evaluation covers TALENT (300 datasets), TabArena (51 datasets, 816 tasks), BCCO (156 datasets), and OpenML-CTR23 (33 regression datasets), against current strong baselines including TabFM, EXAONE-Tabular, TabPFN-3, TabICLv2, LimiX, RealTabPFN-2.5, AutoGluon 1.5, and tuned GBDTs. Headline numbers: OpenML-CTR23 — 1st with average rank 3.03 (TabPFN-3: 3.71); TALENT regression — 2nd at 4.03 behind TabFM's 3.72; TALENT overall — 2nd at 4.82 (TabFM 4.23); TALENT binary classification — tied 1st with TabFM at 5.72; TabArena regression — Elo 1900 (2nd) behind TabFM (2019), beating EXAONE-Tabular (1885), TabPFN-3 (1800), and AutoGluon 1.5 extreme (1776), with 82% less training time (6.99s vs 38.85s per 1K) and 68% less prediction time (3.12s vs 9.67s) than TabFM; TabArena overall — 4th at Elo 1659, statistically near-tied with AutoGluon 1.5 (1662) and TabPFN-3 (1650); BCCO — 2nd on regression (mean rank 2.940), 3rd overall. An appendix sensitivity study over 2,240 synthetic datasets (factorial: 2 graph densities × 4 SNR levels × 14 noise conditions) reports 70.3% first-place R² share versus LimiX (16.0%) and TabICLv2 (13.7%). Notable caveats to these numbers: Elo bootstrap CIs are wide and overlapping (Xiaomi-TabLDM 1900−148/+278 vs TabFM 2019−127/+181), the TabArena regression subset is only 13 datasets, and the sensitivity study is on the authors' own synthetic generator, not real data. The claimed test-time scaling benefit over the base model is described but not quantified in a dedicated ablation table. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. Genuinely novel is the specific integration — particularly the width-adaptive second feature-grouping stream and the demonstrated regression-efficiency Pareto position relative to TabFM — but the components (SCM pretraining, inducing-point column encoding, ICL transformers, MoE, residual aggregation, NNLS ensembling) are all existing ideas assembled per the TabICLv2/TabFM lineage. This is a competent engineering synthesis, not a new formulation or method. Rigor & Reproducibility: Evaluation is extensive and follows established third-party protocols (official TabArena evaluation code; TALENT with TabICLv2's imputation protocol; 95% bootstrap CIs for Elo over 200 rounds and for TALENT ranks). Ablations are essentially absent: no component-wise ablation table on real benchmarks isolates dual-stream grouping, AttnRes, MoE, or test-time scaling contributions; the only ablation-like evidence is the informal claim that removing AttnRes caused training collapse in Stage 1. Seeds are not reported for the main benchmarks (bootstrap CIs partially compensate). Code and checkpoints are released (GitHub: github.com/xiaomi-research/xiaomi-tabldm; Hugging Face: occams/Xiaomi-TabLDM), with full architectural hyperparameters in the appendix — a reproducibility positive. Concerns: (1) the appendix sensitivity analysis evaluates on synthetic data generated by the authors' own SCM prior, which plausibly favors models trained on that prior (Goodhart-style self-evaluation); (2) the closest competitor, TabFM, is cited only as a Google Research blog post, so its numbers rest on a non-peer-reviewed source; (3) Xiaomi-TabLDM is compared only in default configuration while several baselines appear in tuned and tuned+ensembled variants; (4) the arXiv report is a vendor technical report (dated September 2026), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built model with benchmark evaluation). Practical: Yes — pretrained on 8 A100-80GB GPUs and inference is a single forward pass plus optional ensemble, well within commercially available hardware; the released checkpoints are ~71M total parameters (61.7–62.7M active). Efficient: Strong — 6.99s train / 3.12s predict per 1K samples on TabArena regression, roughly an order of magnitude cheaper than tuned+ensembled baselines like RealMLP (3,995s train) and TabDPT (4,787s train), though slower per-sample than TabPFN-3 (0.42s predict). Effective: The evidence shows it solves the zero-shot prediction problem on the tested benchmark distribution (mostly <10K training rows), with regression its strongest regime; effectiveness beyond 50K–100K rows is claimed via the Stage-3 long-context adaptation but not directly demonstrated on large real datasets. Scalable: Only partially tested — the paper's own benchmark caps (BCCO excludes >50K samples), and behavior at 10–100× context length is extrapolated from the training curriculum rather than measured. Deliverable: a software artifact — released code, model checkpoints, and an inference pipeline with test-time scaling. Strengths: - Genuinely strong regression results relative to the current frontier: 1st on OpenML-CTR23, 2nd on TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO regression, against contemporaneous foundation models (TabFM, TabPFN-3, EXAONE-Tabular) — regression is where tabular foundation models have historically been weakest, so this is a substantive empirical advance. - The efficiency result is concrete and well-measured: second-best TabArena regression Elo at 6.99s/3.12s train/predict per 1K versus 38.85s/9.67s for TabFM, establishing a credible Pareto point rather than a vague efficiency claim. - Transparency of the training recipe: full hyperparameter tables (including MoE auxiliary-loss coefficients and parameter counts: 70.08M/71.08M total, 61.67M/62.68M active) plus public code and checkpoints make this one of the more reproducible entries in this model family. - The factorial sensitivity analysis (2,240 datasets, 14 noise conditions, A/A exponential–Weibull control used as an honest repeatability yardstick) shows methodological sophistication, even though its synthetic setting limits external validity. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper states that regression is the model's strongest regime while overall/classification performance is competitive but not leading (4th overall on TabArena). It acknowledges via benchmark descriptions that most evaluated datasets are small (<10K training rows) and that BCCO excludes datasets above 50K samples/10K features/10 classes. The classifier is limited to 10 pretraining classes, handled at inference via mixed-radix ensembling. The authors do not include a dedicated limitations section; the constraints above are implicit in the evaluation design rather than confronted directly, and failure modes (e.g., where the model loses badly) are not analyzed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No component ablation: the paper claims AttnRes "stabilizes convergence" and that MoE and dual-stream grouping "enrich feature interactions," but never measures the marginal contribution of any component on a real benchmark, so the reader cannot tell which parts of the architecture matter or whether the design is over-engineered. - The headline TabArena regression result rests on 13 datasets with overlapping 95% bootstrap CIs between 1st (TabFM, 2019) and 2nd (1900, CI as low as 1752) — the gap may not be statistically meaningful, yet the abstract frames "2nd on regression" as a fixed achievement. - The appendix robustness study is run on the authors' own SCM generator — the same distribution family the model was pretrained on — so the 70.3% first-place share plausibly measures prior-matching rather than real-world robustness; no real-data noise-perturbation experiment is provided. - The test-time scaling section (Section 3) claims inference-time compute "consistently improves predictive performance over the base model" but no table quantifies the base-model-versus-scaled gap, leaving the third headline claim ("Test-time scaling") unevidenced in isolation. - Missing analysis of the default-vs-tuned asymmetry: Xiaomi-TabLDM appears only as (D) while key competitors include (T+E) configurations, and there is no experiment showing whether the model itself benefits from tuning. - The regression advantage could partly reflect the 999-quantile pinball-loss output design; no comparison against a variant with a simpler regression head is reported (dogs-not-barking: no architectural design exploration at all). Bottom Line: For teams selecting or building tabular foundation models, this is a worthwhile read — it documents a credible, open, efficiency-focused regression contender with a fully specified recipe — but it is an incremental assembly of known components with unverifiable individual contributions, and readers seeking a principled methodological advance should look to the TabICLv2 and TabPFN line it builds on.

From Language Models to World-Acting Systems: Progress and Limits of Agentic AI across Digital, Social, Virtual, and Physical Environments

L Zhu, M Cai · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a critical review that reorganizes the agentic-AI literature (cutoff 31 August 2026) around a configured-system formalism S = (M, H, E, U) and three dimensions — delegated authority, temporal persistence, and environmental coupling — and argues that evidence for expanded action interfaces has grown faster than evidence for verifiable, recoverable autonomy. - Why it's important: Adoption decisions and research roadmaps currently conflate model competence, harness integration, persistence, and safe authority, so grant/evaluation effort flows toward measurable capability rather than toward the assurance layer that determines real-world risk. - How it does it: It imposes a source-taxonomy with explicit claim boundaries (what a benchmark, a protocol spec, a preprint, or a vendor preview can and cannot establish) and uses representative contrasts — e.g., WebArena/OSWorld success rates, τ-bench pass^k reliability decay, equal-budget multi-agent comparisons — to test conceptual claims rather than pooling scores. - The good: The evidential discipline is unusually explicit: each cited artifact is tagged by category (e.g., Genie 3 and Project Eden as first-party previews, MCP/A2A as specifications not performance evidence), and the paper consistently refuses to convert capability demonstrations into autonomy claims. - The missing: The central "asymmetry" claim — that interface growth outpaces assurance evidence — is asserted from selective reading rather than operationalized, measured, or validated against a reproducible corpus or a counterfactual case where assurance evidence kept pace. - Read it or not: Yes for researchers building agent benchmarks, harnesses, or governance frameworks who need a defensible vocabulary separating model/harness/environment/delegator; skippable for practitioners seeking a quantitative survey of agent performance, since it deliberately reports no pooled results.
Why this rank

Novelty (62) is the top dimension — the S=(M,H,E,U) decomposition, six-object persistence split, and source-typing/claim-boundary rules are transferable methodological contributions that resolve real confusion in the agentic-AI literature. Non-Obviousness (60) is supported by sharp insights (durable authority vs. durable memory, the RentAHuman escalation path). However, Rigor (52) is capped because the central action/assurance 'asymmetry' thesis is never operationalized — no metric, no corpus, no contrast case — and the judgment-sampled corpus is biased toward sources that make the thesis easier. Completeness (60) and Resilience (58) are buoyed by exceptional candor about limitations and evidence categories, but the six-object reporting standard is prescribed, not audited. Impact (40) is limited to vocabulary and an agenda. Weighted composite: 0.25*62 + 0.20*52 + 0.25*60 + 0.10*60 + 0.15*58 + 0.05*40 = 58.
