Problem & Motivation: The paper targets a conceptual failure in how agentic AI progress is described. "More agentic" is used interchangeably for at least four distinct changes: a stronger base model, a richer software harness, longer-lived tasks, and access to more consequential environments — and these do not imply one another. Practitioners deciding whether to delegate consequential work (database writes, live-account operation, lab instrument control) inherit a literature where capability numbers (e.g., GPT-4 completing 14.41% of WebArena tasks vs. 78.24% for humans; OSWorld's best agent under 12.2% vs. 72.4% human) coexist with vendor previews and protocol specifications, with no shared standard for what each kind of evidence licenses. The gap prior surveys leave, per the authors, is that component- or benchmark-centric reviews keep model, harness, environment, delegator, and affected parties collapsed, hiding where verification, recovery, and governance evidence stops. Key Idea: The core move is the decomposition of an agent into a configured system S = (M, H, E, U) — model, harness, environment, delegator, with affected parties explicitly outside the boundary — analyzed on three orthogonal axes (delegated authority, temporal persistence, environmental coupling), plus a source-typing rule that binds evidence quality to a specific claim rather than to a system. From this follows the prescriptive heuristic of "justified delegation": expand action scope only where evidence supports provenance, bounded authority, failure detection, safe recovery, and calibrated human control — explicitly offered as a decision criterion, not a score or law. Methodology: This is a critical, question-driven review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis; the authors state this design supports no prevalence claims and no pooled effect sizes. The method has three stages: (1) an evidence taxonomy (Table 1) with five source categories — peer-reviewed benchmark/systems paper, peer-reviewed controlled physical experiment, preprint/technical report, open specification, first-party preview/system card — each annotated with its strongest defensible use and typical blind spot; (2) claim-boundary rules (capability ≠ reliable frequency; persistence decomposed object-by-object across conversation, task, memory, skill, environment, authority; openness of environment ≠ visual richness); (3) domain-by-domain synthesis across digital (APIs vs. computer use, coding agents), delegation/persistence/multi-agent, virtual worlds/world models, and physical/robotics/laboratory settings, culminating in a seven-item research agenda and a six-object minimum reporting standard for agent evaluations. Critical design decisions: privileging primary evidence over surveys (justified); retaining first-party previews like Genie 3, Project Eden, and the Model Hardware Standard while segregating their evidential status (justified, though it imports vendor positioning into the corpus); using representative contrasts instead of exhaustive coverage (acknowledged as a limitation of the design). Key Results: As a review, its headline outputs are synthesis claims, anchored by numbers drawn from primary sources: original WebArena GPT-4 baseline 14.41% vs. 78.24% human; original OSWorld <12.2% vs. 72.4% human (369 tasks); OpenAI CUA preview at 38.1% OSWorld / 58.1% WebArena, with the vendor itself deeming 38.1% unreliable for OS automation; SWE-agent's 12.5% pass@1 on SWE-bench demonstrating harness-as-causal-factor; τ-bench's pass^k result that consistency across repeated trials falls well below one-shot success; a 2026 preprint showing single agents match multi-agent systems under equal thinking-token budgets; V-JEPA 2 post-trained on <62 hours of robot video after 1M+ hours of video pretraining with zero-shot planning on Franka arms; Genie 3 at 24 fps/720p with ~1 minute of visual memory; RentAHuman marketplace measurement of 303 bounties with 32.7% arriving via API/MCP channels, including credential fraud and impersonation tasks; and the AILA/AFMBench finding that domain question-answering skill did not translate into laboratory competence ("sleepwalking" failures). Baselines cited are the original benchmark papers — the review explicitly marks them as historical configurations, not current leaderboards, which is honest but means the empirical picture is partly dated by construction. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (qualitative). Genuinely novel: the S = (M, H, E, U) unit of analysis with affected parties outside the system boundary, the three-axis decomposition of persistence into six distinct objects, the claim-boundary rules mapping source types to defensible claims, and the "justified delegation" reframing that inverts the default of benchmark score unlocking action scope. Standard combination: the individual domain syntheses (tool use, computer use, multi-agent, world models, robotics) reassemble well-known results; the value is the cross-domain evidential comparison, not new technical content. Rigor & Reproducibility: For a critical review, rigor is above the genre's norm: an explicit cutoff date, a published evidence taxonomy with per-claim category assignments, explicit disclaimers that the design cannot support bibliometric or prevalence claims, and careful marking of which citations are preprints versus peer-reviewed (e.g., A-Lab treated via its 2026 author correction). There are no ablations, seeds, or significance tests by design — not applicable to this genre, but also no reproducible inclusion/exclusion procedure: no search strings, no database, no inter-rater reliability, so the corpus is judgment-sampled and the "asymmetry" finding is not falsifiable within the paper. No code or artifact is released, and the six-object reporting standard is proposed but not applied to the cited papers as a scored audit, which would have been the natural validation of the framework. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL — a conceptual formalism and normative framework with no primary experimental claim. Sound: Assumptions and claim boundaries are unusually explicit; the formalism is definitional rather than derived, so there is nothing to falsify internally. General: The framework applies across all four environment types by construction, though its evidence base is concentrated in software engineering, web tasks, games, robotics labs, and English-language interfaces (acknowledged). Tight: Not a bound — the authors correctly frame justified delegation as a heuristic, not a certified score, so no tightness question arises. Implementable: The six-object reporting standard and seven research priorities are directly operationalizable as checklist and agenda; no follow-up operationalization exists within the paper itself. Deliverable: paper form only — no library, dataset, benchmark, or tool ships with it. Strengths: (1) The source-typing discipline — attaching evidence quality to claims rather than systems, and refusing to let a protocol specification stand in for reliability or a preview stand in for a result — is a transferable methodological contribution other reviews should copy. (2) The decomposition of persistence into six non-interchangeable objects (conversation, task, episodic memory, skill, environment, authority) resolves real confusion in the literature, and the observation that durable authority is a categorically different risk than durable memory is a genuine insight. (3) The §5.2 analysis of agent-to-human escalation, including the RentAHuman marketplace data showing agents purchasing physical presence and identity-dependent access, identifies a capability-escalation path that bypasses the agent's own runtime boundary — an under-discussed threat model. (4) The inversion that a narrow, well-verified agent may deserve broader authority than a stronger, hard-to-verify one is a sharp, actionable reordering of the usual autonomy narrative. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (§9.8): the review is selective and supports no prevalence claims; the 31 August 2026 cutoff dates quickly; Genie 3, Project Eden, and MHS are first-party previews without archival papers or independent replication; coverage is asymmetric toward software, games, robotics labs, and English-language settings; absence of public failure evidence is not evidence of rarity; and the digital/social/virtual/physical taxonomy is overlapping, not developmental. The paper also self-identifies that generative AI assisted literature discovery and drafting, with author verification. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Three gaps the authors do not fully confront. First, the central thesis — the action/assurance asymmetry — is never operationalized: no metric, no corpus over which it is computed, no contrast case where assurance evidence matched interface growth; a skeptical reader can accept every individual claim-boundary rule while doubting the aggregate characterization. Second, the corpus itself is weighted toward sources that make the thesis easier: vendor previews are included because they "expose architectural directions," which guarantees a large volume of under-verified action interfaces in the sample; a corpus restricted to independently evaluated systems might show a different ratio. Third, the six-object reporting standard is prescribed but not audited — applying it to even the 15–20 most-cited works, scoring each object present/absent, would have converted the paper's most useful proposal from exhortation into evidence, and its absence is the difference between a framework and a measurement program. Bottom Line: For anyone designing agent benchmarks, harnesses, delegation protocols, or governance mechanisms, this is a worth-reading reframing whose vocabulary (S = (M,H,E,U), justified delegation, claim-boundary rules) will outlast its literature cutoff — but readers wanting a measured account of how agentic capability actually compares to assurance, or a reproducible survey, will need to build both from the agenda this paper sets rather than find them in it.

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ENEAS, a text-promptable segmentation pipeline that unifies instance tracking and open-concept semantic discovery by adding a text-driven initialization to the SeC tracker and routing ambiguous detection candidates to a conditional VLM judge. - Why it's important: Text-promptable models like SAM 3 hallucinate targets when objects disappear and segment statues, paintings, and reflections as real people — an unacceptable failure in 3D reconstruction pipelines where one false positive destroys the asset. - How it does it: A cascade of escalating-cost verifiers — Florence-2 proposals, SigLIP 2 sigmoid embedding scoring with prompt ensembles, and a Qwen3-VL judge invoked only inside an uncertainty interval between two thresholds (τ_rej < τ_acc) — decouples geometric proposal from semantic verification. - The good: On the authors' Church Statues capture, ENEAS raises F1 from 19.5% (SAM 3, precision 11.1%) to 82.8% (2B judge) and 87.6% (4B judge) with precision above 94%, and the ablations credibly show the conditional-VLM design beats both embedding-only and VLM-only configurations. - The missing: All quantitative ontological-robustness evidence comes from a single self-annotated 3D-reconstruction capture of one church interior; there is no public benchmark measuring statue/painting rejection, no error bars or seeds, and no end-to-end 3D reconstruction result demonstrating the motivating claim. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners building text-promptable tracking/segmentation pipelines or distractor removal for NeRF/Gaussian Splatting captures; skippable for those expecting generalizable semantic-segmentation science, since the evaluation is narrow and the components are off-the-shelf.

Problem & Motivation: The paper targets a reliability gap in text-guided segmentation that persists in foundation models like SAM 3 on uncurated video: (1) detection-driven trackers lack identity — when the target leaves the field of view they re-detect the prompt on whatever looks similar, and under extreme close-ups they fragment the object into parts; (2) semantic discovery relies on visual priors alone, so hyper-realistic statues, pop-art portraits, and mannequins are segmented as persons. The authors frame this as 'strong perception coupled with weak verification.' The motivating domain is 3D reconstruction (NeRF / Gaussian Splatting) of cultural-heritage captures, where unordered, low-frame-rate views must be cleaned of visitors while sparing sculptures, and where the error costs are asymmetric: a false positive masks and destroys part of the asset, a false negative leaves a visible artifact. The gap ENEAS closes: existing detect-then-segment systems (Grounded SAM, Florence-2 chains) have no temporal memory, and memory trackers (SAM 2, SeC) accept only point/spatial prompts — neither verifies the ontology of a candidate against a linguistic prompt. Key Idea: The core insight is to decouple geometric proposal from semantic verification via a certainty-gated cascade: score every candidate crop independently with a sigmoid-based vision-language embedding (SigLIP 2, avoiding the softmax mutual-exclusivity that suppresses the target when distractor objects co-occur in the crop), accept or discard on thresholds, and invoke a small VLM judge only for candidates in the uncertainty interval — with neighbor pixels black-masked to isolate the candidate and a constrained no-free-reasoning prompt keeping each verdict cheap. The second, smaller idea is text-driven initialization of the SeC concept-memory tracker: ground the prompt once on a reference frame with Florence-2 and let SeC's concept-level memory propagate identity, so absence yields an empty mask rather than drift. Methodology: ENEAS takes frames {I_t} and a prompt p and exposes a grounding operator G (Florence-2-Large) and segmentation operator S (SAM 2/2.1). Instance tracking: on reference frame I_t0, r0 = G(I_t0, p); all other masks come from propagation M_t = T(I_t | r0, H_t) where T is the SeC tracker (SAM 2 plus a VLM-built concept-level memory injected at scene changes) — the paper's contribution here is the adapter making SeC text-promptable, since SeC originally supports only point interaction. Semantic discovery runs per frame as a cascade: (1) Florence-2 proposes candidate regions R_t, deliberately permissive, with duplicate merging; (2) each candidate is scored s(r) ∈ [0,1] against the category by SigLIP 2 using a prompt ensemble (averaged phrasings) to bridge the full-image-pretraining / crop-inference domain shift, with the NaFlex native-aspect-ratio encoder; two thresholds split candidates into accept (s ≥ τ_acc), discard (s < τ_rej), verify (in between); (3) ambiguous candidates go to a Qwen3-VL judge (2B default, 4B option) that answers a fixed binary verdict with neighbor-masked crops and no deep-reasoning token generation; (4) accepted candidates are segmented by SAM 2. No training is described — the system is assembled from pretrained components; the objective is implicit (precision-first filtering for 3D reconstruction), not an explicit loss. Three critical design decisions: (a) sigmoid over softmax scoring — well justified by the Phase-2 failure analysis (score suppression when a person holds a microphone); (b) conditional VLM invocation — justified by the ablation showing VLM-only is both slower (5.05 s vs 3.29 s/frame) and less accurate (F1 79.1% vs 82.8%), an 'over-reasoning' effect; (c) neighbor masking and constrained decoding for the judge — plausible but justified only qualitatively. Key Results: The headline comparison is on Church Statues, the authors' own capture with manually produced ground truth, under the prompt 'person': SAM 3 gets 11.1% precision / 83.7% recall / 19.5% F1 (roughly eight hallucinated artifacts per correct detection); ENEAS-2B gets 94.7% / 73.5% / 82.8%; ENEAS-4B gets 97.5% / 79.6% / 87.6%. The component ablation (Table 4) shows RPN-only at 18.6% F1, RPN+flexible embeddings at 65.5%, RPN+strict embeddings at 78.6% (precision 94.3% but recall drops to 67.4%), and the conditional VLM at 82.8–87.6%. Threshold analysis (Table 5): Aggressive (0.40–0.60) → 74.3% F1 at 1.04 s/frame with 16.2% VLM activation; Robust (0.10–0.90) → 82.8% F1 at 3.29 s/frame with 78.1% activation; VLM-only → 79.1% F1 at 5.05 s. On Moving Boxes with a fast configuration, ENEAS reaches 98.0% F1 with zero false positives at 1.14 s/frame (VLM activation 27.0%). On a SA-Co/VEval (SA-V test subsample) evaluation with the official SAM 3 evaluator, differences versus SAM 3 are marginal: instance tracking HOTA 26.70 vs 26.51, semantic discovery HOTA 9.23 vs 9.19, with ENEAS ahead on AssA/TETA and behind on LocA. Qualitative results (Grounded SAM, SAM 3 baselines) show Grounded SAM segmenting curtains and hair as the target painting and boxes/tables as chairs, while ENEAS reports empty masks on absence. Latency was measured end-to-end on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU (24 GB) — a deliberately modest, production-realistic setup. All results are from a small industrial lab (SperidLabs) as a preprint with no external peer review; the strongest numbers come from the authors' own benchmark. Baseline selection is current (SAM 3, Grounded SAM) but the SA-Co/VEval margins are within noise given no variance reporting. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the conditional VLM-verification cascade for ontologically robust text-promptable segmentation) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (text-adapter for SeC; latency-accuracy tuning of the uncertainty interval). Genuinely novel is the framing of 'ontological robustness' — rejecting look-alikes (statues, paintings) that visual-only models cannot distinguish — and the demonstration that selective VLM adjudication beats both embedding-only and VLM-everywhere filtering. The ingredients are all standard, existing components (Florence-2, SigLIP 2, Qwen3-VL, SAM 2.1, SeC) combined without training; the cascade/certainty-gated-judge pattern is a known LLM-systems idea (FrugalGPT-style frugal cascades, selective classification) applied to a new setting. The Church Statues benchmark is a new but private dataset. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and genuinely informative: the component-necessity table isolates each stage, the threshold-sensitivity table quantifies the latency/accuracy Pareto, and the VLM-size table (2B → 4B: 3.29 → 5.02 s/frame, 82.8 → 87.6 F1) shows where capacity helps. The design-evolution narrative (Phases 1–4, including failed dense-captioning and softmax-filtering designs with reported failure modes) is an unusual transparency positive. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; the headline benchmark is the authors' own capture with author-annotated ground truth, developed and evaluated on the same data (a Goodhart risk the authors partly acknowledge by arguing standard benchmarks 'lack the semantic complexity'); the SA-Co/VEval subsample and prompt-based split are non-standard and differences there are ~0.2 HOTA points; no inter-annotator agreement or dataset size (frame/instance counts) for Church Statues is reported; and the 3D-reconstruction motivation is never validated end-to-end — no reconstructed scene is shown with and without ENEAS cleaning. Code and models are stated to be available at github.com/speridlabs/eneas. The iterative design phases were tuned on the same Church Statues data used for final evaluation. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built pipeline evaluated on real captures; no training, assembly of pretrained models). Practical: Yes — runs on a single 24 GB NVIDIA L4 GPU plus a modest Xeon, explicitly chosen to simulate cost-effective production. Efficient: ~3.29 s/frame in Robust mode (not real-time, acknowledged), 1.04–1.14 s/frame in fast mode; latency adapts to scene ambiguity (VLM activation 16–78%), and the 4B judge costs 1.5× more latency for +4.8 F1. Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated precision-first filtering problem on the target distribution (Church Statues, Moving Boxes), but only via the authors' own benchmarks; on the external SA-Co/VEval benchmark it is essentially at parity with SAM 3. Scalable: Not tested — the authors state dense scenes (crowded streets) fall outside the design regime because per-candidate verification cost grows with candidate count; per-frame discovery without temporal identity linking implies cost scales linearly with frames, which is only viable for the offline reconstruction use case they target. The work delivers a software artifact (code and models, per the abstract) rather than stopping at paper form. Strengths: (1) The certainty-gated VLM judge is a well-reasoned architectural contribution: the ablation demonstrates a non-obvious, quantified result — invoking the VLM on every candidate is both ~54% slower and 3.7 F1 points worse (79.1 vs 82.8), the 'over-reasoning' phenomenon — which turns a cost heuristic into an accuracy argument. (2) The sigmoid-vs-softmax analysis is a concrete, transferable insight: softmax normalization over target plus dynamic distractor labels suppresses the target score when accessories co-occur (person + microphone), and pairwise sigmoid scoring fixes it. (3) The four-phase design-evolution section honestly documents failed architectures with specific failure modes (open-set hallucinated proper nouns, spatial aggregation of chair+table, 15+ s/frame latency), which is more credible than presenting only the final system. (4) The problem framing — asymmetric error costs in heritage 3D reconstruction — is real and gives the precision-first design a principled rationale, and the text-adapter for the point-only SeC tracker is a useful, reusable contribution. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a credibility positive): recall is bounded by Florence-2's proposal stage (small, distant, occluded instances are never recovered); the VLM judge fails on context-free extreme close-ups and low-resolution crops, where it can accept the same artifacts as visual-only models; verification cost grows with candidate density, excluding crowded scenes; semantic discovery assigns no persistent identities across frames; no confidence scores are produced, limiting compatibility with score-based evaluation; and ~3 s/frame on an L4 is not real time. They also note in the results that both ENEAS and SAM 3 leak on extreme close-ups. These acknowledgments are candid and specific rather than minimizing. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The headline evaluation is a single self-built, self-annotated capture of one church interior, used both to develop the method (Phases 1–4 iterate against presumably similar data) and to report the headline numbers — no external benchmark measures ontological rejection, so generalization beyond this distribution is unverified. (2) The paper claims applicability to 'broad libraries' and unordered collections but reports no experiment on unordered image collections beyond the church capture. (3) The motivating 3D-reconstruction pipeline is never demonstrated — no NeRF/GS reconstruction quality with versus without ENEAS cleaning, so the end-to-end value proposition rests on proxy metrics (precision of person masks). (4) No comparison against a cheaper obvious alternative: asking the VLM judge (or a stronger embedding model) directly on Grounded-SAM proposals without the embedding stage, or SAM 3 + a post-hoc VLM filter on its outputs, which would isolate how much of the gain is the cascade versus merely adding any VLM anywhere. (5) Ground-truth annotation was done by the authors with no inter-annotator agreement, dataset statistics (frames, instances), or release of Church Statues mentioned. (6) The SA-Co/VEval gains (e.g., HOTA 26.70 vs 26.51) are presented as wins but are within plausible seed variance given no variance reporting. (7) The 'doppelganger' failure space is only tested for two artifact types (statues, paintings); reflections, mannequins, and costumed performers — mentioned in the abstract — are not evaluated. Bottom Line: A practitioner building distractor-removal or identity-stable tracking for capture pipelines gains concrete, transferable design lessons (sigmoid scoring over softmax for crop verification, certainty-gated VLM judges, the over-reasoning effect) from a transparent engineering report, but the scientific evidence is thin — one self-annotated benchmark, no variance, no external ontological evaluation — so it should be read as a credible systems report, not as validated general-purpose segmentation research.

Are LLM-Enhanced GNNs Privacy-Safe?

L He, Z Wen, C Li, S Su · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a systematic empirical evaluation of privacy risks (link, label, and membership inference) in LLM-enhanced GNNs, showing that semantic enrichment from LLM/LM feature enhancers consistently increases attack vulnerability relative to shallow text baselines, and that differential privacy only partially mitigates this at a large utility cost. - Why it's important: LLM-enhanced GNNs are being adopted for text-attributed graphs containing sensitive social, medical, and e-commerce data, and practitioners currently lack evidence on whether the accuracy gains from LLM features come at a privacy cost. - How it does it: It runs a five-stage evaluation pipeline (dataset preparation, victim training, attack, risk assessment, defense) over 42 victim configurations built by crossing six LLM/LM-based feature enhancers with seven GNN backbones, attacked by six established black-box inference attacks. - The good: The finding is consistent across 6 datasets, 3 attack types, and 42 configurations with 5-seed error bars, and the in-depth CDF analyses give a concrete geometric mechanism (sharper connected/unconnected, intra-class/inter-class, and member/non-member separability) for why enrichment amplifies leakage. - The missing: The defense analysis is thin and internally inconsistent (one sentence says Cora, the figures say Tape-Arxiv23), covers only local DP mechanisms on one backbone/enhancer pair, and no code or artifacts are reported as released. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on graph privacy or LLM-graph integration who need the first quantitative baseline for this trade-off; practitioners seeking deployable defenses will find only a confirmation that off-the-shelf local DP is inadequate.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (65) is moderate: the first systematic measurement of the enrichment-amplifies-leakage effect is a genuine empirical finding, but it is a benchmark study with no new algorithm, and the direction of the effect is plausibly predictable from the 'more information in, more information out' intuition. Non-Obviousness (55) is the weakest dimension — a competent practitioner would likely hypothesize that richer embeddings increase attack surface; the CDF mechanism analysis helps but does not surprise. Rigor (62) benefits from 42 configurations and 5-seed error bars but is undercut by no code release, internal dataset-name inconsistencies (Cora vs Tape-Arxiv23, Pubmed vs CiteSeer), a defense analysis confined to one backbone/enhancer/dataset, and non-adaptive attacks. Completeness (55) drops for the internal inconsistency and a defense conclusion generalized from a single defense family. Resilience (55) is limited because the causal claim rests on correlation plus one geometric observation with no controlled information-matching intervention. Impact (50) — useful cautionary finding for practitioners, but paper-only with no artifact and no working defense. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*50 = 58.

Problem & Motivation: LLM-enhanced GNNs — GNNs whose node features are produced or augmented by LLMs or pretrained LMs (e.g., TAPE, KEA, SimTeG) — deliver large node-classification gains on text-attributed graphs, but prior privacy-attack literature studied only conventional GNNs with shallow features (BoW, Word2Vec). Operators exposing such models via MLaaS query interfaces (the paper's motivating threat), and the individuals whose social ties, labels, or training participation those models encode, have no evidence on whether richer semantic embeddings also leak more. The paper closes the gap that no prior work has measured whether LLM-based semantic enrichment changes attack vulnerability. Key Idea: The core hypothesis is that LLM-induced semantic enrichment increases the information content and geometric separability of node embeddings — pushing apart connected vs. unconnected, same-label vs. different-label, and member vs. non-member distributions — so that the same representation quality that raises utility simultaneously raises attack AUC/accuracy. There is no new algorithm; the contribution is the hypothesis plus a controlled empirical test of it. Methodology: The framework has five stages. (1) Six TAG datasets are curated spanning citation, social, and e-commerce domains (2,708–33,434 nodes). (2) 42 victim models are trained by combining six feature enhancers (explanation-based: TAPE, KEA via GPT-3.5 Turbo + DeBERTa/E5 encoders; embedding-based: LLaMA-2-7b, Linq-Embed-Mistral, fine-tuned SimTeG, E5-Large) with seven GNN backbones (GCN, SAGE, GAT, GIN, APPNP, SGC, SSGC), two layers, hidden dim 256, 10/10/80 train/val/test split. (3) Six black-box attacks are run against node posteriors: link inference via Manhattan/Euclidean posterior distance (MLA, ELA); label inference via homophily guessing (HGA) and node infiltration with an injected probe node (NIA); membership inference via shadow-model attack (MIA) and a 0-hop/2-hop top-2 posterior fusion attack (NMA). (4) Risk assessment uses attack AUC/accuracy vs. node-classification accuracy, plus CDF analyses of embedding distances and prediction confidence. (5) Defense analysis applies six local DP mechanisms for embedding perturbation (1B, LP, AG, SW, MB, PM), randomized response for link structure, and k-RR for labels, sweeping privacy budgets ε ∈ {0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0, 10.0}. The key design decisions — restricting to black-box query access consistent with prior attack literature, using shallow embeddings as the sole control condition, and choosing widely adopted rather than cutting-edge enhancer/backbone combinations for reproducibility — are stated but the single-control design and the shallow baseline choice are only lightly justified. Key Results: Utility: with a GCN backbone, LLM enhancement raises node classification accuracy substantially, e.g., Ogbn-Products from 65.6% (Shallow) to 83.1% (TAPE) and Tape-Arxiv23 from 55.4% to 72.3% (TAPE), while gains on the two social datasets are small (Instagram 63.7% → 67.7%, Reddit 60.0% → 62.8%). Link inference: attack AUC rises with enrichment, e.g., on Ogbn-Products ELA goes from 92.3% (Shallow) to 95.7–96.1% for enhancers; on Instagram MLA from 55.5% to 73.4% (E5-Large). Label inference: on Ogbn-Products, HGA accuracy jumps from 49.7% (Shallow) to 85.3% (TAPE); on Cora, NIA rises from 58.2% to 77.6% (LLaMA). Membership inference: increases are real but modest, e.g., Cora MIA AUC 67.4% → 73.3% (KEA), Tape-Arxiv23 MIA 51.3% → 66.3% (E5-Large). Defense: at ε_e = 5.0, embedding perturbation reduces all three attacks to varying degrees but causes a large utility drop; tighter budgets (ε = 0.1) collapse both attack performance and utility toward uninformative levels. Experiments ran on a single A800 80GB GPU; every result is averaged over 5 seeds with standard deviations. Baselines are appropriate for the causal question asked (shallow encoders as the control) but are not current SOTA graph encoders, and the datasets are small-to-moderate scale (≤33K nodes) — standard, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the first systematic measurement that LLM-based semantic enrichment monotonically amplifies link, label, and membership leakage in GNNs, plus the geometric explanation via embedding-distance and confidence CDFs. Everything else — the attacks, the DP mechanisms, the enhancers, the backbones — is a standard combination of existing techniques applied to a new setting, and the five-stage framework itself is a study design rather than a reusable technical artifact. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style coverage is decent: 7 backbones × 6 enhancers × 6 datasets isolates the enrichment effect from any particular model, and results are reported as 5-seed means with standard deviations; no significance tests are given, but the headline gaps (e.g., 49.7% → 85.3% HGA) far exceed the reported ±1–2% variance. The in-depth CDF analyses on Tape-Arxiv23 with GCN/Linq serve as a mechanism ablation. No code, data splits, or model weights are reported as publicly released — a reproducibility gap for a paper whose value is its benchmark numbers. Methodological concerns: (a) the defense analysis is confined to one dataset, one backbone (GCN), and one enhancer (Linq) despite being a headline contribution; (b) the text contains an internal inconsistency, stating defenses are evaluated "on the Cora dataset" while all defense figures and captions specify Tape-Arxiv23; (c) Sec. 4.1 lists the citation datasets as Cora, Pubmed, Tape-Arxiv23 while Table 1 contains CiteSeer instead of Pubmed; (d) the membership and label attacks are pre-existing and non-adaptive, so the measured vulnerability is a lower bound on real risk. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement/benchmark study, no new system). - Practical: Yes — all experiments fit on a single 80GB A800 GPU and the models (GCN-class GNNs, 7B-max LLM encoders) run on commercially available hardware. - Efficient: Not evaluated as a cost study; the paper does not report the encoding cost of LLM-based enhancers (e.g., GPT-3.5 calls, LLaMA-2-7b embedding inference) relative to BoW/Word2Vec, which is a material omission for the deployment decision the paper informs. - Effective: The evidence shows the diagnostic claim convincingly (enrichment amplifies leakage against these six attacks), but the defense side only demonstrates that local DP is a poor fix, not that any deployable protection works. - Scalable: Untested — datasets max out at 33,434 nodes; behavior at production graph scale (10^6–10^8 nodes) and against attackers with graph-level auxiliary data is only assumed, not measured. The paper delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model release; its output is paper-form findings. Strengths: - A genuinely underexplored and timely question answered with a controlled experimental design: the shallow-baseline control cleanly isolates the effect of semantic enrichment, and the conclusion holds uniformly across 42 configurations rather than on cherry-picked models. - The in-depth CDF analyses elevate the paper above a benchmark table by providing a concrete, inspectable mechanism — larger connected/unconnected and member/non-member distribution gaps — that plausibly explains the observed attack gains. - Coverage of three distinct privacy threat surfaces with attacks of graded adversarial strength (label-aware HGA vs. fully black-box NIA) makes the threat picture more informative than single-attack studies. - Honest reporting of the defense outcome: rather than promoting a mitigation, the paper shows existing local DP mechanisms fail the trade-off, which is a more useful negative result than a fragile positive one. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the defense results "highlight a fundamental privacy-utility trade-off" and that no effective protection currently exists for this setting. They also explicitly acknowledge, in choosing well-established model combinations, that they deliberately avoid advanced architectures for reproducibility. They do not otherwise enumerate scope limits (e.g., small datasets, single-backbone defense evaluation, black-box-only attacks) as limitations; the limitations are implicit in the experimental design rather than confronted in a dedicated discussion, which is a mild credibility deduction. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The defense evaluation covers only local DP, ignoring the broader defense landscape for graph models (e.g., DP-SGD with formal ε guarantees, embedding truncation/noise baselines, adversarial representation regularization), so the conclusion that defenses fail is really the conclusion that this one defense family fails. - The measured risk is defined by the six chosen attacks; no stronger or adaptive attacker (e.g., model extraction followed by attack, attackers with partial graph knowledge, label-only or gradient-based threats) is considered, so the "vulnerability gap" could be understated — or, conversely, a stronger attacker might achieve near-ceiling success on both shallow and enriched models, shrinking the relative difference. - No code or artifact release is stated, and the dataset inventory inconsistency (Pubmed vs. CiteSeer) plus the Cora/Tape-Arxiv23 inconsistency in the defense section undercut confidence in experimental bookkeeping. - The causal claim — enrichment amplifies leakage — is supported by correlation plus a geometric observation on one dataset/one model pair; no intervention (e.g., controlled dimensionality or information-content matching between shallow and LLM embeddings) rules out the alternative that higher raw embedding informativeness of any kind, not LLM semantics specifically, drives the effect. - Only node classification is studied, though LLM-enhanced graphs are also used for link prediction and recommendation, where the privacy profile may differ. Bottom Line: For anyone building or auditing LLM-enhanced graph systems, this is the first quantitative evidence that the semantic-enrichment accuracy gains come bundled with measurably higher inference-attack exposure (and that local DP cannot buy it back cheaply), so it is worth reading despite small-scale evaluation, no artifact release, and a defense analysis too narrow to be the last word.

What Else Needs Fixing? Exploring Cost-Effective Test-Time Compute for Revision Propagation in Artifacts Generated Through Conversation (3 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RevPropBench, a 150-sample human-annotated benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can propagate a local revision across dependent elements of JSON artifacts generated through multi-turn conversation, and reports a controlled cost-effectiveness study of nine revision methods across six LLMs. - Why it's important: In practical LLM-assisted artifact creation (plans, invoices, configs), users specify only local edits, and missed cascading updates break artifact consistency in settings where — unlike code or knowledge graphs — no pre-existing dependency structure exists to exploit. - How it does it: The benchmark seeds scenario templates that force deterministic dependency cascades established through synthetic conversation history, then evaluates single-pass baselines (artifact-only, history-only, both) against sequential reflection, rule-based parallel merging (OR/AND/MAJORITY), medoid selection (minimum Bayes-risk style), and LLM-based selection, all scored by exact-match completion rate over RFC 6902 JSON patches. - The good: Single-pass baselines already reach 68.3–93.0% completion, and the most cost-effective method — selecting from three parallel samples via LLM-based or medoid selection — gains +2.2–9.7% over the J+H baseline; the finding that conversation history matters (J < H < J+H on every model) directly validates the benchmark's premise. - The missing: All data is synthetic (GPT-5.5 conversations, Claude-Opus-4.8 tentative gold patches) with a single annotator, no inter-annotator agreement statistics, and no real human–LLM interaction data, leaving open whether the measured propagation gaps reflect real usage. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building conversational artifact-editing systems or agentic state management who need a concrete evaluation target and cost-per-gain guidance; skip it if you want a new algorithm — the methods evaluated are all standard test-time compute techniques.

Problem & Motivation When users ask an LLM to revise an artifact it generated through conversation (a travel plan, invoice, deployment config), they typically specify only a local change; the LLM must infer which other elements depend on the edited element and update them to preserve consistency. Prior revision-propagation work targets settings with explicit or statically analyzable dependencies: repository-level coding (call graphs, imports), knowledge editing (knowledge graphs, ripple effects), and document editing (sections, references). In conversationally generated artifacts like plans and records, dependencies are often implicit and established through the conversation itself — outside the artifact — making this setting unexplored. The authors also argue that since JSON is the de facto structured-output format for LLM systems, this setting has direct practical relevance. Key Idea The core insight is that dependency information for propagation lives in the conversation history rather than in the artifact, so the benchmark must deliberately construct conversations where a dependency is only resolvable from history (e.g., "three days after the trip begins" ties a date to an anchor date stated several turns earlier). Once this design principle is fixed, the rest is a careful empirical study: the key open question becomes not "can we build a better method" but "which existing test-time compute strategy buys the most accuracy per dollar in this setting." Methodology RevPropBench construction has three phases: (1) scenario design — 50 human-created scenarios (with LLM assistance) spanning 9 domains and 6 propagation patterns (arithmetic recompute, reference substitution, structural add/remove, threshold gating, temporal shift, status flip); (2) synthetic sampling — GPT-5.5 generates multi-turn conversations turn-by-turn under strict prompts (natural user phrasing, uniquely determined gold values, aggregate values added only after their dependencies), with artifact size controlled by a leaf-value budget to yield 10/50/100-element JSON artifacts; (3) LLM-assisted human annotation — Claude Opus 4.8 produces tentative gold patches, a single human annotator reviews/corrects them in a custom GUI (>32 hours over 10 days; 15% of samples revised), with support for regex matchers, reference equality, and an "optional" flag for contextually valid edits. Evaluation compares generated patches against gold patches by completion rate (exact match of the resulting artifact), plus miss/over-edit/wrong-value failure breakdowns. Nine methods are tested: single-pass baselines with artifact (J), history (H), or both (J+H); REFLECT (4 reflection iterations); rule-based parallel merges OR/AND/MAJ over 5 samples comparing candidate artifacts at leaf level; MED (medoid by mean leaf-level disagreement, inspired by minimum Bayes-risk decoding); and SELECT (LLM picks one of 4 candidates). Six LLMs are used (gpt-oss-20b/120b, gpt-5.4-mini, qwen3.5-9b/27b/122b), 5 seeds per sample, temperature 0.6, local models served via vLLM on A100s, with per-token API cost and latency measured in appendices. Critical design decisions: scenario-level train/test splitting (30 dev / 120 test, seed 42) is sensible; the deterministic-dependency constraint enables exact automatic scoring but excludes ambiguous real-world cases; the "optional" flag mechanism is a reasonable but annotator-subjective device. Key Results On the 120-sample test split (5 seeds, error bars reported): single-pass J+H baselines achieve 83.8% (gpt-oss-20b), 86.7% (gpt-oss-120b), 93.0% (gpt-5.4-mini), 68.3% (qwen3.5-9b), 90.0% (qwen3.5-27b), 90.3% (qwen3.5-122b). Context ordering J < H < J+H holds for every model (e.g., 81.7% < 86.7% < 90.3% for qwen3.5-122b), showing history carries dependency information not recoverable from the artifact. SELECT gives the most consistent test-time compute gain (+3.3–12.5% over J+H, top on 4 of 6 models); MED is second (+1.8–7.7%); REFLECT gives small consistent gains (+0.5–8.2%); AND is consistently harmful (−13.2 to −21.3%) because unanimity discards correct edits; OR and MAJ are inconsistent. Failure analysis shows miss dominates over-edit and wrong-value for most methods — models under-propagate rather than over-propagate. Cost analysis: at 5 LLM calls, SELECT costs 5.7–7.5× J+H for Qwen models (extra reasoning tokens) but is comparable for GPT models; cost alignment does not change method rankings; performance saturates at 4–5 calls. The recommended operating points are SELECT with 4 calls (best cost-effectiveness) or MED with 3 calls (competitive accuracy, latency only ~1.2–1.4× J+H since sampling parallelizes). MED with k=3 is the most latency-efficient method on average. These are preprint results and the cost figures derive from published token price tables (OpenRouter/OpenAI, June 2026), not billing data. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the problem setting (propagation where dependencies are implicit and established conversationally, outside the artifact) and the systematic cost-effectiveness comparison of test-time compute in it. The methods themselves (self-consistency, best-of-N selection, Self-Refine-style reflection, MBR-style medoid) are standard techniques applied unchanged; the benchmark construction pipeline (scenario-driven synthetic sampling with LLM-assisted annotation) follows known synthetic-data practices. Rigor & Reproducibility The evaluation design is solid for a benchmark paper: 5 evaluation seeds with reported standard deviations, scenario-level data splitting balanced by domain/propagation-size/pattern, cost alignment experiments to rule out "SELECT wins because it costs more," a latency analysis, and element-level failure decomposition. Code, dataset, and the full annotation/generation tool are released at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-revision-propagation, and all system prompts are included in the paper. Concerns: single annotator with no inter-annotator agreement statistic and only 15% of patches revised (actual annotation error rate unknown); 120 test samples is small, so per-cell differences of 1–3 points may not be meaningful despite error bars; gold patches for the dev split were used for prompt tuning; the deterministic-dependency constraint means the benchmark measures propagation only in unambiguous cases; cost figures rely on third-party pricing tables as of a fixed date. There is no Goodhart-style train-on-test issue (split is scenario-disjoint), and evaluated models are not the judge. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus evaluation study; no new method or system is deployed). - Practical: Yes — all six models run on commodity APIs or up to four A100 80GB GPUs via vLLM; nothing exotic. - Efficient: The recommended configurations are cheap — SELECT at 4 calls or MED at 3 calls adds roughly 2–7× the single-inference API cost, with MED keeping latency under ~1.4× via parallel sampling. - Effective: The evidence shows LLMs solve propagation reasonably well on this benchmark (68.3–93% single-pass, up to 96.3% with SELECT) and that test-time compute reliably helps, but the benchmark is synthetic and deterministic, so it is a proxy for real conversational revision. - Scalable: Not tested — artifacts cap at 100 JSON elements and one local edit per sample; behavior at 1,000+ elements, multi-edit requests, or chained revisions is unknown. Deliverable: a released benchmark dataset, generation/annotation tool, and evaluation code; no trained model or standalone library. Strengths - The benchmark design principle — making dependencies recoverable only from conversation history — cleanly separates this setting from code/knowledge/document editing and is validated empirically by the consistent J < H < J+H ordering across all six models. - The cost-effectiveness analysis goes beyond headline accuracy: cost alignment, performance-convergence curves, latency multipliers, and explicit deployment recommendations (SELECT-4 vs MED-3 as a latency trade-off) are the kind of analysis most test-time compute papers omit. - Honest, detailed failure analysis showing the dominant error mode is under-propagation (miss), which is actionable for system designers (it argues for candidate-selection over conservative single-pass inference). - Releasing the full pipeline tool (not just the static dataset) directly addresses the acknowledged benchmark-saturation problem, and the annotation methodology (LLM-drafted gold patches with human correction) is documented with unusual transparency including per-batch revision counts. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly and at length: the setting does not transfer to code/knowledge/document editing where dependency structures pre-exist; conversations are synthetic (GPT-5.5) with no real human–LLM interaction data and dependencies forced to be deterministic, excluding ambiguous cases; coverage is 150 samples across 9 domains and does not exhaust all propagation patterns; GPT-family models generated the data, which may favor GPT models (partially mitigated by human-designed scenarios and meta-level generation instructions); and gpt-5.4-mini already at 93% completion raises saturation concerns, motivating the released re-generation tool. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No inter-annotator agreement or second-annotator validation: with one annotator and LLM-drafted gold patches, systematic annotation biases (especially in the "optional" flag and regex matchers) cannot be quantified. - The revision request always targets exactly one element; real users issue compound or vague edits, and the benchmark says nothing about multi-edit propagation. - Baseline prompting is fixed and shared across models; no prompt-tuning per model beyond the dev split, and no comparison against stronger propagation-specific strategies from adjacent settings (e.g., explicitly asking the model to first enumerate dependencies before patching), which is the obvious next baseline. - Sample size (120 test samples spread over 9 domains × 3 sizes) makes per-domain conclusions statistically fragile; no significance tests are reported, only standard deviations. - The claim that SELECT's reasoning "targets the most complete candidate, reducing misses" is an interpretation of failure counts, not a verified mechanism. - The cost-effectiveness ranking depends on June 2026 token prices and reasoning-token behavior that will change with model versions; the practical guidance is time-bound. Bottom Line A practitioner building conversational artifact-editing agents gains a usable evaluation target and concrete, money-quantified guidance on test-time compute, but the field lacks no stronger alternative benchmark for this exact setting — read it for the benchmark and the cost methodology, not for algorithmic novelty.

Problem & Motivation: Automated issue resolution — given an issue description and repository snapshot, produce a patch validated by fail-to-pass tests — has become the representative benchmark task for LLM-based coding agents since SWE-bench. The core challenge distinguishing it from isolated code generation is that agents must operate over large, evolving, heterogeneous contexts (code structures, dependency configurations, tests, commit history, project conventions) where the model's parametric knowledge is incomplete or stale. Existing surveys (the paper cites two, refs [32, 38]) organize the field by benchmarks, workflow phases, agent architectures, and training paradigms, but none explains what knowledge systems rely on, where it originates, how it is extracted and represented, how it is operationalized, and at which workflow stages it applies. Researchers therefore lack a unified vocabulary for comparing multi-source knowledge strategies and for identifying underexplored knowledge types. Key Idea: Recast automated issue resolution as a knowledge-management problem and classify it through a three-layer taxonomy grounded inductively in the literature: L1 Background Knowledge (project-independent: Programming Language, Domain-Specific, Technology Stack), L2 Repository Knowledge (project-specific: Existing Code, Design Architecture, Repository Evolution), and L3 Procedural Knowledge (execution-oriented: Development Tool, Experiential). This knowledge-system layer is embedded in a five-layer cognitive framework adding a Grounding Layer (5 sources × 3 extraction methods), an Externalization Layer (Unstructured Text / Structured Text / Graph), an Operationalization Layer (Passive Retrieval / Active Retrieval / Feedback-Based Usage / Parametric Injection), and an Issue-Resolution Process Layer (7 stages from Environment Building to Patch Validation). The trick is coding each paper along all six dimensions with multi-label annotation, enabling cross-dimensional frequency and trend analysis rather than a flat list of systems. Methodology: The review protocol proceeds in five phases: (1) citation querying — all Google Scholar papers citing SWE-bench (849 studies); (2) filtering by explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria (repository-level issue resolution tasks, sufficient methodological detail, full-length articles or detailed preprints) yielding 82 papers; (3) backward and forward snowballing plus expert review, expanding to 133 studies spanning March 2024–April 2026; (4) iterative qualitative coding — open coding of knowledge-use phenomena, axial coding into the three-layer hierarchy, selective coding aligning categories with the six analytical dimensions, then full-corpus multi-label coding; (5) synthesis via frequency analysis, cross-dimensional comparison, representative-work analysis, and temporal trend analysis. The framework explicitly defines category boundaries (e.g., Repository Evolution Knowledge = repository-derived temporal evidence vs. Experiential Knowledge = process-level trajectories/memories) to reduce coding overlap. Critical design decisions: inductive rather than imposed taxonomy (well-justified via the grounded-theory staging); SWE-bench citation as sole seed for retrieval (convenient but a single-point anchoring risk); treatment of the Coding Agent Runtime as a descriptive context rather than a coded dimension (defensible, keeps the schema manageable). No explicit mathematical formalism is used — this is a qualitative coding study, and no objective function applies. Key Results: The headline outcome is the knowledge-type distribution across 133 studies: Existing Code Knowledge 128 papers (96.2%), Development Tool Knowledge 103 (77.4%), Experiential Knowledge 68 (51.1%), Repository Evolution Knowledge 42 (31.6%), Design Architecture Knowledge 13 (9.8%), Technology Stack Knowledge 4 (3.0%), Programming Language Knowledge 3 (2.3%), Domain-Specific Knowledge 1 (0.8%). Venue distribution: 73.7% arXiv preprints, with ACL (7.5%), ICLR (5.3%), NeurIPS (3.8%), ICML/FSE (3.0% each), and TSE/ASE/ISSTA/ICSE under 1% each. Temporal analysis shows cumulative publication accelerating sharply after mid-2024 (from ~14 papers by mid-2024 to 133 by April 2026). Qualitatively, the survey finds a field built on a code-and-tool foundation shifting toward history-informed and experience-oriented methods (trajectory memory banks like EXPEREPAIR, SWE-Exp, ReasoningBank, Agent KB; training-trajectory distillation like SWE-Gym, Devstral, SWE-Master), while architectural intent and L1 background knowledge remain underexplored. Baselines are not applicable; the corpus itself and its frequencies are the results. No benchmark accuracy numbers are reported by the survey itself — it analyzes methods, not their measured performance. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (a knowledge-centric taxonomy and cognitive framework) plus a synthesis of the field. What is genuinely novel is the three-layer knowledge hierarchy with six coded lifecycle dimensions — no prior survey of this area uses knowledge type/source/representation/usage/stage/evolution as the organizing axes. The underlying literature (RAG for localization, execution feedback, experience banks, RL post-training) consists of known techniques; the contribution is the unifying lens and the quantified gap map, not new technical mechanisms. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria, a documented snowballing protocol with consolidation and expert-verification steps, a four-stage inductive coding process, multi-label coding with published boundary definitions, and a maintained public repository (https://github.com/SYSUSELab/Awesome-Knowledge-for-AIR) supporting the survey's claims. Concerns: (1) no inter-rater reliability (e.g., Cohen's kappa) or independent-coder protocol is reported in the provided text for the 133-paper annotation, so coding subjectivity is unquantified; (2) the corpus is seeded exclusively on SWE-bench-citing papers from Google Scholar — systems addressing issue resolution without citing SWE-bench are invisible; (3) 73.7% of the corpus is arXiv preprints, so many included works carry unreviewed claims that the survey inherits; (4) being a survey, it reports no ablations, error bars, or significance tests — none apply. The paper is an arXiv preprint (July 2026, ACM manuscript submitted), not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a systematic literature study — the 'experiment' is the corpus analysis; no theorem proofs and no deployed software system). Applied to the survey artifact itself: Practical: Yes — the taxonomy and coding schema are paper-level artifacts usable by any researcher without hardware. Efficient: The coding effort (133 papers × 6 dimensions, multi-label) is substantial but done once and released. Effective: The evidence (frequency distributions, trend curves) supports the descriptive claims about the field, but the prescriptive claim — that background/architectural knowledge investment will improve agents — is argued, not measured. Scalable: Coverage decays by construction; a corpus frozen in April 2026 in a field publishing >10 papers/month will age within a year, and the authors implicitly acknowledge this via the maintained GitHub list. The work delivers a reusable artifact (curated paper list + taxonomy + coding schema on GitHub), not a tool, dataset, or trained model. Strengths: - The taxonomy is derived inductively (open → axial → selective coding) from the corpus rather than imposed a priori, and the paper publishes explicit boundary definitions for confusable categories (Repository Evolution vs. Experiential; Existing Code vs. Development Tool) — this is more disciplined than most SE surveys. - The quantified distribution results are actionable: knowing that Domain-Specific Knowledge appears in 0.8% of 133 studies while Existing Code Knowledge appears in 96.2% gives a researcher a defensible, evidence-backed case for where open problems lie. - The six-dimensional coding (type × source × extraction × representation × usage × stage) enables cross-cutting analyses (e.g., which sources feed which knowledge types via which extraction methods) that flat method-survey taxonomies cannot produce. - The boundary clarifications between paradigms (workflow-oriented vs. agent-oriented) and the treatment of the Coding Agent Runtime as context rather than a coded dimension show conceptual care. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Not stated in the provided text. The excerpt (Sections 1–5.2 of a 91-page manuscript) contains no explicit threats-to-validity or limitations section; whether one appears later in the paper cannot be confirmed from the provided material. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No inter-rater reliability or independent-coder agreement statistics for the multi-label coding of 133 papers — for a survey whose central contribution is a classification, this is the single most important missing rigor check. - Single-seed retrieval (SWE-bench citers via Google Scholar only) means arXiv/DBLP keyword searches and non-citing work (e.g., industrial systems not published as papers) are structurally excluded; the paper does not discuss this coverage bias. - With 73.7% preprints and a field moving this fast, the frequency 'findings' (e.g., the rise of Experiential Knowledge) may partly reflect publication-wave timing rather than settled field structure; no sensitivity analysis of the cutoff date is reported. - The survey categorizes but does not evaluate: it provides no synthesis of how knowledge strategies correlate with measured SWE-bench performance, so a reader cannot tell from this survey whether, e.g., experience-bank methods actually outperform strong retrieval baselines. (The abstract mentions analysis of 'high-performing SWE-bench Verified systems,' but the provided text contains no quantitative outcome data.)* - The taxonomy's practical utility for building systems (does the L1/L2/L3 decomposition predict which additions improve resolution rates?) is asserted as a future direction, not demonstrated. Bottom Line: For anyone designing SWE-bench-style agents or surveying the automated issue-resolution space, this is currently the most systematic knowledge-centric map available and worth reading for its taxonomy and gap analysis — but treat it as a well-executed categorization with unquantified coding reliability, not as evidence about which knowledge strategies actually improve patch resolution rates. *Note: The provided PDF text is truncated mid-Section 5.2.2; later sections (RQ3–RQ6, discussion, threats to validity, if any) could not be assessed, and statements about the paper's full 91-page contents beyond this point are based only on the abstract and front matter.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a framework that decouples world-state evolution from visual generation by maintaining an explicit, programmable world state in a lightweight engine and using a pretrained video model purely as a generative renderer conditioned on state-augmented 3D oriented bounding boxes (OBBs). - Why it's important: Interactive video world models cannot reliably remember world facts (who is alive, what is off-screen, inventory, rules) across occlusion and long horizons, which blocks their use as actual playable games or world engines. - How it does it: A VLM coding agent compiles natural-language rules into executable programs; an engine deterministically updates a persistent entity state; a state compiler projects state-augmented 3D OBBs into pixel-aligned identity/semantic/motion-direction control maps that steer a frozen video backbone via a trained ControlNet. - The good: On the authors' CombatStateBench, the system reaches 94% Count Accuracy and 98% State Accuracy versus 40.75%/8% (LingBot-World-V2) and 32%/58% (YUME), while also leading on all four VBench quality metrics. - The missing: All quantitative evaluation is on a self-introduced 50-clip benchmark with VLM-judged, deliberately permissive metrics, against baselines forced to communicate state via prompt switching, and with no component ablations, error bars, or human evaluation. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building interactive world models or generative rendering systems who need to think about explicit state interfaces; skippable for those seeking rigorously validated general video-generation improvements.

Problem & Motivation: Video world models (Genie 3, LingBot-World, YUME, Matrix-Game, AlayaWorld) generate plausible action-conditioned video but lack three capabilities needed for true interactive world engines: (1) direct manipulation of individual entities, (2) a persistent global state that includes off-screen entities and non-visual attributes (health, inventory, faction), and (3) user-programmable rules governing world evolution — prompting an outcome does not create an executable rule. Prior explicit-state work is acknowledged as insufficient: StatePlay predicts state with the model itself (errors accumulate), and MASS advances state via a learned Logic Engine (transition errors corrupt the authoritative state). The target users are creators of interactive/game-like generative worlds. Key Idea: Separate what is true from what is seen: keep an executable, rule-driven canonical world state outside the generative model, and connect it to video generation through a deliberately intermediate representation — state-augmented 3D OBBs — that is compact enough to be authored and evolved by programs, yet geometric enough to be deterministically projected into pixel-aligned control maps. The paper's Section 2 articulates this as a train/inference asymmetry argument: training extracts structure from already-realized dynamics, while inference must synthesize structure from high-level state transitions, so the representation should specify only entity-level structure and leave articulation, texture, and secondary dynamics to the generative prior. Methodology: The pipeline is (1) World programming: a 3D detector recovers initial entity OBBs from the first frame; a VLM-based coding agent (off-the-shelf) assigns attributes, relations, and writes executable rules (e.g., on_hit: hp -= damage) to instantiate state s = (E, A, Q; R). (2) Engine execution: a lightweight engine applies player actions, validates them against rules, resolves events, and updates the canonical state — deterministic, not learned. (3) Control compilation: a deterministic compiler projects OBBs under the target camera and rasterizes three channel-concatenated maps — identity (from a bank of K learnable, per-sequence-randomized instance embeddings), semantic (text-encoder embeddings of category labels), and direction (world-space velocity rotated into camera frame and quantized into 7 states). (4) Generative rendering: a Structured Spatial ControlNet is attached to a frozen LingBot-World-v1 camera-controlled video backbone, injecting layer-wise features additively; only the control branch and cross-chunk conditioning are trained. Long horizons use chunk-autoregressive generation with multi-scale temporal history (stochastically degraded during training) plus a geometry-aligned spatial memory (depth-lifted, reprojected past frames, adopted from AlayaWorld). Training data come from an automatic pipeline: ViPE for camera/depth, Qwen3-VL for category discovery, SAM3 for instance segmentation/tracking, WildDet3D for 3D OBBs, applied to HUD-free gameplay footage from Cyberpunk 2077, Forza Horizon 6, and GTA V. Critical design decisions: the OBB abstraction level (argued via the trade-off analysis, but validated only empirically, not against intermediate alternatives like meshes or 2D controls), the 7-way direction quantization (coarse; justification is brevity), and frozen-backbone ControlNet adaptation (standard practice, reasonable). Key Results: On the authors' CombatStateBench (50 clips, synthesized combat scenarios with diverse camera/entity motion), the method achieves 94.00 Count Accuracy (400 VLM-judged frames) and 98.00 State Accuracy (50 death events), versus Count/State of 40.75/8.00 for LingBot-World-V2 and 32.00/58.00 for YUME — gains of 53.25–62.00 and 40.00–90.00 percentage points respectively. On four VBench metrics it edges out both baselines (Imaging 67.62, Subject Consistency 94.74, Background Consistency 96.98, Temporal Stability 99.00). Baselines were run with their native conditioning and state transitions communicated only via prompt switching, since neither exposes an instance-level state interface — a significant asymmetry. Qualitative results cover a minotaur scene (synthetic GPT Image 2 first frame), a large-angle camera rotation revealing off-screen characters, a racing scenario, heterogeneous humans+vehicles, and an 897-frame autoregressive rollout with accumulating NPCs. Baselines are recent and relevant, but the comparison protocol favors the proposed method; the quality-margin on VBench metrics is small (e.g., Imaging 67.62 vs 67.46). Tested scale: 50 benchmark clips and curated gameplay footage from three games; no dataset size, model size, or training compute is reported. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD + NEW BENCHMARK (+ partial NEW SYSTEM/TOOL). The genuinely novel element is the combination of a deterministic, externally programmed state engine with a generative renderer through OBB-compiled control maps — prior explicit-state world models (StatePlay, MASS) still learn the state transition, whereas here transitions are executable rules. Individual components (agent-generated game code, ControlNet conditioning, chunk-autoregressive video generation, depth-lifted spatial memory from AlayaWorld, SAM3/ViPE/WildDet3D annotation) are established techniques competently integrated; the representation trade-off analysis (Section 2) is a thoughtful articulation but an argument, not a new formal result. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are absent — no experiment isolates the contribution of the identity, semantic, or direction maps, the spatial memory, or the OBB representation against weaker/stronger alternatives (e.g., 2D boxes, text-only state), despite the paper's own representation trade-off analysis motivating exactly such a comparison. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; VLM-judge metrics on 50 clips / 50 death events are small samples with no judge-validation against human labels. Code is released (github.com/AlayaLab/pwm) with a project page, which aids reproducibility. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation is entirely on the authors' own CombatStateBench, designed around the method's strengths (count and death-state consistency); (2) baselines are handicapped by the prompt-switching protocol, making the 90-point State Accuracy gap partly an artifact of interface mismatch rather than a like-for-like comparison; (3) the judge ("Qwen3.6-27B") sees only RGB frames and the metrics are explicitly permissive and global, which could be gamed; (4) no human evaluation. The preprint is not peer-reviewed, so results warrant moderate confidence. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built framework with an empirical evaluation; released code). Practical: Builds on the open LingBot-World-v1 backbone plus a trainable ControlNet, so it runs on hardware that supports that video model, though specific GPU requirements are not stated. Efficient: Cost relative to the base video model is the ControlNet plus compiler overhead; real-time performance is not measured — the authors cite a separate flash renderer for that, so interactivity latency is unevaluated. Effective: The evidence shows the system solves its stated problem (state-consistent rendering) on its own benchmark, but through coarse proxy metrics judged by a VLM rather than instance-level or human verification. Scalable: An 897-frame rollout and multi-entity scenes are demonstrated, but behavior at 10–100× more entities, longer horizons, or open-domain (non-game) video is only claimed, not tested; training data are limited to three games. Delivers a software artifact (code, benchmark construction procedure) plus a reusable design pattern (deterministic state engine + compiled OBB controls); no trained model weights release is mentioned. Strengths: - The architectural separation of executable state from generative rendering is a clean, well-motivated answer to a real failure mode of observation-centric world models, and the Section 2 train/inference asymmetry analysis is a genuinely useful framing for representation selection in generative rendering. - The OBB-plus-controls interface is well chosen: compact, program-editable, view-independent, and compatible with rasterized conditioning that a video diffusion model can consume — avoiding both brittle text-only state and heavyweight G-buffer supervision. - The automatic data engine (ViPE → Qwen3-VL → SAM3 → WildDet3D → conditioning maps) is a practical, reusable path to scaling structured supervision from unlabeled video, addressing the annotation bottleneck of this representation. - The reported absolute numbers (94/98 on the state metrics) and qualitative off-screen-entity persistence under large camera rotations are the most convincing evidence that the engine-maintained state actually transmits through generation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion is brief and does not contain an explicit limitations section. The paper implicitly concedes scope boundaries: CombatStateBench covers only combat-style state consistency (counts and death states); the benchmark description notes only verified-consistent sequences are retained; and the qualitative sections acknowledge that some first frames are synthetic and that state metrics are deliberately coarse/permissive. The authors do not confront training-domain narrowness, VLM-judge reliability, or missing ablations directly. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablations: the reader cannot tell whether the identity map, semantic map, direction map, or spatial memory individually matter, nor how OBBs compare to the weaker/stronger representations the paper's own trade-off analysis enumerates — the central design argument is never tested. - The baseline protocol (prompt switching for systems lacking a state interface) makes the headline gaps partly tautological: a system given ground-truth entity controls should beat systems given only text prompts; a fairer comparison would include an oracle-control variant or at least a stronger prompt-engineering effort. - VLM-judge metrics are unvalidated (no agreement study against human raters or automated detectors) and the judge's identity ("Qwen3.6-27B") is unusual; 50 clips and 50 death events give wide confidence intervals that are unreported. - Open-domain generalization is shown only via a handful of synthetic-image-initialized qualitative examples; all quantitative training and evaluation is on three commercial games, and state-relevant attributes like physics, occlusion of partially visible entities, or continuous (non-combat) mechanics are untested. - No latency, memory, or throughput numbers, so real-time playability — the stated application — is unevaluated. - Error accumulation across the chunk-autoregressive loop (drift between compiled controls and generated content feeding back through spatial memory) is not quantified. Bottom Line: A practitioner building interactive world models gains a concrete, code-released blueprint for combining deterministic state engines with generative renderers, but should treat the headline numbers as a demonstration on the authors' own benchmark rather than proof of general superiority, and should look to ablation-free follow-up work before adopting the specific OBB design over alternatives.
