Problem & Motivation The paper addresses the selection problem created by the transition from information-centric AI services to task-oriented executable systems. Users browsing model hubs (Hugging Face), agent marketplaces (agent.ai), and tool platforms (RapidAPI) face large candidate pools whose capability descriptions are incomplete, inconsistent, and verifiable only through execution; system-side, orchestrators in modular agentic workflows must dynamically pick executors for subtasks under latency, cost, and reliability constraints. The authors argue this differs from classical IR because relevance is grounded in competence, reliability, and downstream task success rather than topical similarity; it differs from orchestration work (e.g., MetaGPT-style coordination) because orchestration assumes the candidate pool is given, whereas agent search addresses the upstream identification problem. Existing surveys cover tool learning, agent architectures, planning, and evaluation separately, leaving the integrated selection problem fragmented across communities — the gap this survey claims to close. Key Idea The core move is a reframing rather than a technique: treat agents and tools uniformly as 'executable capability-bearing systems' and cast selection as a retrieval and decision-making problem whose relevance signal is expected task execution outcome, organized as a two-stage pipeline (offline capability preparation; online task-conditioned selection) parameterized by what is knowable about candidates (description-level, behavioral-evidence, trajectory-level, or full white-box access). This is a NEW PROBLEM formulation with a taxonomy, not an algorithmic trick; the paper does not pretend otherwise. Methodology Methodologically this is a synthesis: a systematic literature organization rather than an experimental pipeline. The framework defines agent search over task specification, candidate agent space, and search outcome, then instantiates it across six substantive sections: (1) task understanding — sequential vs. structured (tree/DAG) vs. global vs. iterative planning, planning augmentation via agentic post-training (SFT → DPO-style preference learning → GRPO-style RL, with process reward modeling flagged as unsolved), multi-agent frameworks, planning offloading to PDDL-style symbolic planners, agentic harnesses, and closed-ended attribute-based vs. open-ended LLM-based intent clarification; (2) representation and indexing — with useful field-level tables (name/description/schema/signature/examples/environment metadata/code/learned tool tokens) and a methods table classifying ~35 systems by sparse, dense, rerank, query-expansion, hierarchical, graph, cache, active, and in-model-token retrieval mechanisms; (3) retrieval and selection — similarity matching, LLM-based selection (training-free vs. parametric tool internalization), task-agnostic vs. task-specific structural retrieval, ReAct-style iterative retrieval, and preference-aware agent recommendation borrowed from CRS and LLM-based recommenders (CLLM4Rec, AgentCF, PTool, PRefine); (4) evaluation — intrinsic (Recall/MRR/NDCG, ToolRet's 7,600 tasks over 43,000 tools, COMP@K for completeness, BFCL AST matching, τ-bench pass^k, StableToolBench virtualization) vs. extrinsic (LLM-as-a-judge, Agent-as-a-judge). Critical design decisions — the four-level capability-access axis and the execution-grounded notion of relevance — are argued qualitatively but not empirically justified. Key Results Not applicable in the experimental sense; the paper reports no new measurements. The quantitative content it relays includes: ToolRet shows strong general-purpose IR models degrade substantially on tool retrieval due to low lexical overlap between queries and tool documentation; τ-bench's pass^k shows success consistency drops sharply across repeated trials even for strong models; AnyTool's hierarchical agent structure enables retrieval over 16,000+ APIs within context limits; Qu et al.'s COMP@K metric exposes that semantic matching retrieves redundant rather than complete tool sets. The paper's headline claim — that existing benchmarks are tool-centric and agent-level intrinsic evaluation is underdeveloped — is an assertion synthesized from the literature, not a measured finding. Baseline quality and scale questions do not apply. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM (formalization and naming of agent/tool search as a distinct retrieval-over-executable-systems problem) plus a survey synthesis; the underlying components — dense/sparse retrieval, hierarchical routing, ReAct loops, LLM-as-judge, DAI mechanisms like Contract Net — are all existing ideas, and the survey's value is the integrated framing, dimension taxonomy, and capability-access axis rather than any new method, dataset, or empirical result. Rigor & Reproducibility As a survey, there are no ablations, seeds, or significance tests to assess; internal rigor rests on taxonomy coverage and citation breadth (the document spans 72 pages with a hierarchical section-to-papers mapping in Figure 3). The authors maintain a public GitHub repo ('Awesome-Agent-Search') as an artifact. Methodological concerns: the framework is self-defined and never operationalized into a metric, benchmark, or experiment, so its usefulness is unfalsifiable as presented; the field-coverage claim ('systematic overview') is not accompanied by a stated search methodology (databases queried, inclusion criteria, date range), which a systematic survey would normally report. Specific cited numbers (ToolRet scale, AnyTool's 16,000 APIs) are second-hand and appear plausible, but were not independently verified here. Note the paper is explicitly a non-peer-reviewed Preprints.org posting (September 2026). Deployability Profile: THEORETICAL (a formalization/survey with no primary experimental claim and no proofs in the strict sense; the four properties are applied in adapted form). - Sound: The problem definition and dimensions are internally consistent and clearly stated, but they are informal conceptual commitments, not assumptions with proofs, so there is nothing to verify or falsify. - General: The framework is deliberately abstract — it spans tools, agents, and multi-agent systems across open ecosystems — which is its strength and its weakness: no setting is excluded, so no prediction is made. - Tight: Vacuous-tightness language does not apply; the closest analogue is that the taxonomy classifies but does not discriminate — nothing in the paper shows which pipeline stage or access level matters most. - Implementable: The framework directly suggests artifacts (an agent-search benchmark spanning the identified dimensions, capability-drift-aware indexes, delegation-experience preference profiles) but builds none of them; the deliverable is the paper plus a literature repo, not a tool, dataset, or model. Strengths - The Section 3 formalization and the orthogonal pipeline-stage × capability-access-level grid give the fragmented literature a shared vocabulary; the distinction between orchestration (downstream coordination) and search (upstream selection) is drawn cleanly and is useful. - The historical grounding — connecting modern agent registries to distributed IR resource selection, expert finding, and 1980s DAI (blackboard architecture, Contract Net Protocol) — is more than decoration; it correctly identifies which machinery (query routing, capability advertisement, bidding) transfers and which (offline-assessable relevance) does not. - The representation/indexing tables (Tables 1–2) are concrete, field-level comparisons across ~35 systems that a practitioner could use as a design checklist. - The evaluation section diagnoses real pathologies with named evidence: IR metrics masking incompleteness (COMP@K), single-trial overestimation (pass^k), live-API reproducibility drift (StableToolBench), and judge biases (verbosity, self-preference) that would systematically favor verbose agent descriptions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors are explicit that the literature is fragmented and that key pieces are immature: agent representations are 'markedly less standardized' than tool representations; index maintenance is treated by prior work as an engineering afterthought rather than a continuous representation problem; no unified metric captures capability, safety, reliability, and user-specific utility jointly; Agent-as-a-judge application to agent search is 'nascent'; process reward modeling remains unsolved; agentic-harness evidence is 'dominated by software-engineering settings' with transfer, cost, and selection bias underexplored. The provided text ends mid-Section 8.3, so the dedicated open-challenges section (Section 10) could not be assessed, but the per-section takeaway boxes confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No stated systematic-review methodology (search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, cutoff date), so 'systematic overview' is a claim about organization, not about reproducible coverage; the citations (through 2026) suggest a living survey, but coverage bias toward the authors' own communities is possible. - The framework is never stress-tested: even a small worked example instantiating the dimensions on two real ecosystems and showing where the taxonomy changes a design decision would materially strengthen it; none is provided in the visible text. - The 2026-dated citations (e.g., Wu et al. 2026a,b,c; Kim et al. 2026b) are heavily relied on to motivate the problem; several appear to be the authors' own closely related work, and the survey does not flag this self-citation concentration. - The paper claims agent search differs from tool retrieval in requiring execution-grounded competence estimation, but does not evaluate whether existing tool-retrieval methods already fail on agent-selection tasks in a way the taxonomy would predict — the motivating gap is asserted, not demonstrated. - The provided document truncates mid-security discussion, so the completeness of Sections 8.3–10 (and hence the fairness of judging the synthesis as a whole) cannot be confirmed. Bottom Line For researchers and platform builders entering agent/tool discovery, this is currently the best available map of the area and worth reading for its framework and bibliography alone; specialists in tool learning, recommendation, or agentic evaluation will find their own corner already familiar and should read it for the cross-connections rather than for new methods or evidence.

High Level Synthesis and Verification of Solidity Smart Contracts

Y Cai, K Nelaturu, A Veneris · eecg.utoronto.ca · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a two-tier synthesis framework in which programmers author domain-specific languages (DSLs) and non-programmer domain experts specify smart contracts as verifiable finite-state-machine models that are automatically compiled into Solidity. - Why it's important: Smart-contract development currently requires specialized programming skills that domain experts lack, and deployed contracts are immutable, so small errors (e.g., the DAO and Parity hacks) cause large irreversible financial losses; the framework separates domain knowledge from contract engineering and checks properties before deployment rather than post-hoc. - How it does it: The programmer publishes a DSL of typed variables and domain operations; the expert builds an FSM lifecycle model; safety/liveness properties written in natural-language templates are translated to CTL and model-checked with VeriSolid/nuXmv; only accepted models are lowered to a single self-contained Solidity contract with an enum-based control-flow skeleton. - The good: Across 10 case studies (5 card games, 5 NFT marketplace patterns), generated contracts achieve ~53% lower deployment gas (994k vs. 2122k average) and ~51% smaller bytecode (4264 B vs. 8764 B) than hand-written references, with 90.5% average AST construct similarity and verified safety/liveness properties on every model. - The missing: Verification is performed on the expert's high-level model, not on the emitted Solidity, leaving a soundness gap between what is checked and what is deployed; evaluation is limited to 10 toy-domain contracts with author-selected references and no usability study with real non-programmers. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in smart-contract synthesis, DSL design, or correct-by-construction generation who want a template for model-then-verify-then-codegen pipelines; practitioners seeking production-grade verified Solidity should look elsewhere.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (a prototype with evaluation, not a deployed system). Novelty (62) reflects a real framework-pattern contribution (two-role DSL/model separation), but Rigor (50) is undermined by hand-picked references, a weak AST-similarity metric, an internal inconsistency about whether verification runs on the model or the generated code, and the unresolved model-to-Solidity soundness gap. Non-Obviousness (55) is moderate — the pipeline pattern is sensible but largely assembles VeriSolid-style ideas — and Resilience (55) drops because the gas/bytecode advantage is confounded by admitted feature disparity and no security or usability evidence exists for a security-motivated paper. Impact (60) benefits from a public repository with ten working contracts. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*50 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*60 = 57.

Problem & Motivation: Non-programmer domain experts (game designers, legal professionals, NFT market operators) can articulate contractual intent but cannot produce correct, vulnerability-free Solidity, and errors in immutable deployed contracts are costly or impossible to fix. Prior DSL approaches (ADICO-based institutional contracts, CML for legal contracts, Psamathe for asset flows, Nomos, Peyton Jones-style financial contracts) are each fixed to one modeling concern with disjoint notations, forcing users who span domains to learn new syntaxes and toolchains. Post-hoc verifiers (VeriSolid, Celestial, ESBMC-Solidity) assume developer-level Solidity authorship plus formal annotations that non-specialists cannot produce, and none let non-programmers author contracts and properties directly from domain concepts. Key Idea: Split contract development into two roles with a verified intermediate representation: the programmer encodes domain vocabulary (renamable primitive types, composite types, built-in and domain operations) into a DSL, and the domain expert assembles a lifecycle FSM from those building blocks; because every expert construct maps deterministically to Solidity and to VeriSolid transition-system atoms, the same model serves both property checking (CTL via templates) and code generation, with a branch atom t→s (a transition execution reaching state s) bridging multi-successor states to VeriSolid's statement-level atoms. Methodology: The pipeline has four layers. (1) DSL Definition: the programmer declares persistent variables from three primitives (integer, user, bytes), composes them into structs/mappings, and supplies domain operations (e.g., dealCard, transferToken, computeProfitWithFee) on top of platform built-ins (Ether transfer, encoding, randomness). (2) Contract Specification: the expert builds an FSM whose states are contract lifecycle phases (state 0 = constructor, optional absorbing terminal state), with transitions guarded by conditions expressible via local variables, conditionals, arithmetic, and calls to built-in/programmer/expert-defined functions, plus persistent-variable updates. (3) Verification: following VeriSolid, the model is compiled to a transition system and expert-stated properties in four natural-language templates (forbidden ordering, constrained ordering, required ordering, eventual occurrence) are translated to CTL and discharged with VeriSolid/nuXmv; failures return counterexample traces. (4) Code Generation: verified models are lowered to a single Solidity ≥0.8.20 file where each state becomes a function (require state, enforce guards, execute actions, try outgoing transitions in declaration order, revert if none qualifies), with automatic-continuation states emitted as internal functions. Implemented as a web-based prototype. Critical design decisions: template-based property authoring (justified by the non-programmer audience, but expressiveness is limited to the four templates); verification on the model rather than generated code (convenient but not formally justified as sound with respect to the emitted Solidity); declaration-order transition resolution (a concrete semantic choice that constrains what contracts experts can express, not empirically evaluated for expressiveness). Key Results: On 10 generated-vs-reference pairs (references from GitHub/Etherscan, selected by the authors as best matching the generated design, compiled with optimizer at 200 runs and deployed on a local EVM): average deployment gas 994k (generated) vs. 2122k (reference), a ~53% reduction; average bytecode 4264 B vs. 8764 B; average public API signature overlap 10.6%; average AST node-type frequency cosine similarity 90.5%. Manually authored scenario tests (~16 per pair, 182 total) matched stated rules in 162/182 cases (~89%), with the Paired bilateral-pass metric averaging 46.3% — attributed by the authors to the generated contracts intentionally exposing only the compact FSM interface while references include multiplayer coordination, commit–reveal flows, and operator controls. All ten safety and liveness properties (one or more per contract, e.g., "dealCard(player) will not happen after calculateScoreBc(hand)==8 or ==9") passed verification. Scale is toy-to-standard: small game and NFT-pattern contracts; no complex DeFi contracts, no adversarial/security testing (reentrancy, oracle manipulation), and Goldfish is the one case where the generated contract is larger than its reference. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. Genuinely novel: the two-role programmer-defines-DSL / expert-authors-model separation with a shared model serving both verification and synthesis, decoupling expert skills from any fixed notation. Standard combinations: the FSM-as-contract representation and template-based CTL checking are taken directly from VeriSolid; the codegen lowering (enum + currentState dispatch) is conventional; the DSL building blocks are ordinary Solidity constructs. Compared to prior single-purpose DSLs, the contribution is the framework pattern rather than any new verification or compilation technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are absent — no experiment isolates which framework components (DSL vocabulary design, branch atoms, automatic continuation) matter. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests (arguably inapplicable to the deterministic gas/bytecode measurements, but scenario-test selection is unquantified). The project repository is public (https://github.com/cai-yuntao/High-level-synthesis-and-verification-of-smart-contracts), with reference sources and full property lists claimed to be included. Methodological concerns: references were hand-picked by the authors rather than sampled; the AST similarity metric (node-type frequency cosine) is a weak structural proxy that large auto-generated boilerplate could inflate; the Paired metric (46.3%) is defined post-hoc and its interpretation is contested in the paper itself; verification is claimed to be discharged "on the generated contract" in one sentence while the methodology clearly checks the pre-generation model, an internal inconsistency. The venue/peer-review status is not stated; the paper reads as a conference submission/preprint, so results should be treated as not yet independently reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built prototype with an evaluation, not a deployed system). Practical: Yes — targets standard Solidity ≥0.8.20 and a local EVM; generated contracts are plain deployable Solidity. Efficient: Generated contracts use ~47% of reference deployment gas and ~49% of bytecode on average, so runtime deployment cost compares favorably, though runtime execution gas is not reported. Effective: The evidence shows the pipeline produces deployable contracts matching an expert-specified lifecycle on toy domains (10 contracts, ~89% scenario rule agreement, all properties verified) — it does not show real-world contracts, security against exploits, or equivalence to references (explicitly disclaimed). Scalable: Not tested beyond 10 small contracts across 2 domains; behavior on complex contracts with external calls, adversarial users, or the full expressiveness needed beyond card games and simple NFT patterns is only claimed via future work. Deliverable: a web-based prototype plus public repository with generated contracts and properties; no trained models, no formal soundness proof of the model-to-Solidity lowering. Strengths: - The two-role separation (programmer-authored DSL vs. expert-authored model) is a genuine conceptual contribution that addresses the fragmentation problem of prior fixed single-purpose DSLs, and the branch atom t→s is a concrete, reusable trick for reconciling FSM states with VeriSolid's statement-level property atoms. - Verification is positioned before code generation with counterexample feedback to the expert, inverting the usual post-hoc audit workflow and making properties authorable via natural-language templates. - Honest, self-undermining reporting: the paper explicitly states that low API overlap and mid-range Paired scores reflect a deliberate design gap rather than spinning them as wins, and disclaims formal equivalence with references. - End-to-end working prototype with a public repository, ten compiling contracts, and consistent ~50% deployment-cost reductions backed by concrete measurements rather than claims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that (i) their metrics do not establish semantic or formal equivalence with reference contracts, only operational agreement on a fixed behavioral checklist; (ii) generated contracts expose only the compact FSM interface and lack reference features (multiplayer coordination, commit–reveal, operator controls, native ETH payments), which explains the gas/bytecode advantage rather than codegen leanness on identical feature sets; (iii) the Paired share is bounded by this design gap; (iv) property automation and additional application domains are deferred to future work. They confront these limitations directly, which is a credibility positive, though they do not discuss security of generated code or model-vs-code verification soundness. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Model-code soundness gap: properties are checked on the expert FSM, but the paper never proves or tests that the emitted Solidity faithfully implements the verified transition system; the sentence claiming CTL is discharged "on the generated contract" contradicts the model-level methodology and is unresolved. - No security evaluation: for a paper motivated by the DAO and Parity hacks, there is no analysis of generated contracts against common vulnerability classes (reentrancy, access-control flaws, integer issues), and no comparison to audited reference patterns beyond surface similarity. - No usability study: the central claim — that non-programmer domain experts can author models and properties — is never tested with actual non-programmers; all models were presumably built by the authors. - Reference selection and metric weakness: references were chosen by the authors to match generated designs; AST frequency-cosine similarity can be high for structurally different contracts sharing a construct mix; the gas/bytecode advantage is confounded by the admitted feature disparity (the authors acknowledge this, but then no like-for-like cost comparison exists). - DSL-authoring cost unquantified: the burden on the programmer to define a domain DSL — the framework's prerequisite — is never measured, so the two-role economics are untested. - Missing baselines: no quantitative comparison against VeriSolid-authored contracts, other DSL-to-Solidity generators, or LLM-based contract generation, leaving the framework's advantage over alternatives anecdotal. Bottom Line: A credible early prototype of a verify-then-generate contract pipeline with an appealing role-separation idea and honest reporting, but with model-level-only verification, toy-scale evaluation, and no security or usability evidence — read it for the framework pattern, not as evidence the approach is production-ready or clearly superior to existing DSL and verification alternatives.

SP Kizhakel, SD Pande · link.springer.com · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CIPHER-A, a closed-loop agentic incident-response pipeline that validates each LLM-proposed response action against predicted counterfactual outcomes before execution and re-validates remaining plan steps after every action using an adversarial state predictor grounded in MITRE ATT&CK. - Why it's important: Current LLM-augmented SOAR platforms execute response plans blindly against adaptive attackers, so unsafe actions (host shutdowns, collateral IP blocks) hit production systems with no consequence check, and plans generated once become stale mid-incident during multi-stage APT attacks. - How it does it: A Claude-3-based Counterfactual Validation Engine generates K=3 outcome scenarios per action and routes via a Composite Validation Score to EXECUTE/MODIFY/ESCALATE, while a Mistral-7B Attacker Simulation Agent predicts the adversary's ATT&CK-constrained next state after each executed action, feeding updated threat state back into the validation loop. - The good: The headline metric — Response Plan Degradation Rate (RPDR) — is independently cross-validated against DARPA OPTC red-team ground-truth logs, with 97.2% of RPDR-flagged degradations confirmed by actual attacker pivots, plus a Wilcoxon-tested ablation (p<0.001, n=143) showing CVE and ASA contribute roughly equally. - The missing: The comparative figures for the two adaptive baselines (Liu [10], Babar et al. [23]) were not run by the authors — they were back-derived by applying CIPHER-A's own scoring framework to those papers' published indicators, so the 55–67% improvement margins over adaptive baselines are estimates, not head-to-head experiments; additionally, calibration splits overlap the evaluation scenarios and no code is released. - Read it or not: Worth reading for SOC/SOAR automation researchers and security-agent builders who need a concrete template for action-level safety gating and a reusable degradation metric; skippable for general ML readers, since the core mechanism is prompt-based LLM scoring orchestrated in LangGraph rather than a new learning method.

Problem & Motivation: Security Operations Centers running SOAR platforms (Palo Alto Cortex XSOAR, Splunk SOAR, IBM QRadar) automate incident response via static playbooks, and recent LLM-augmented tools (Security Copilot, Chronicle AI) generate response plans once at alert ingestion and execute them sequentially. Two failure modes result: (1) no pre-execution check of what a proposed action (e.g., host isolation, account suspension) will do to the live environment, and (2) no re-evaluation of remaining plan steps as the adversary adapts — critical for multi-stage APT attacks where, e.g., the attacker switches C2 channels within seconds of a block. The authors identify three gaps across a 25-paper survey (2022–2026): no pre-execution counterfactual consequence assessment, no post-execution loop closure, and no dynamic attacker modeling during active response. Key Idea: Treat each response action as a bet against predicted futures: before executing, ask an LLM "what happens if I do this?" (counterfactual scenarios scored for severity/scope/reversibility); after executing, ask "where is the attacker now?" (ATT&CK-constrained state transition), and re-validate everything downstream against that updated state. The Response Plan Degradation Rate — the fraction of initially-safe actions that become high-risk under attacker adaptation — operationalizes why static validation fails. Methodology: The pipeline is a LangGraph v0.2 directed state graph of five components: (1) AISNA normalizes Wazuh 4.7 SIEM alerts into an incident state tuple s=(A, N, U, T, Ψ) covering affected assets, a 1–2-hop topology subgraph from PostgreSQL, active AD sessions, CVSS-derived threat severity, and the latest attacker-state estimate; (2) the CVE (Claude 3 Sonnet, ~480 input/220 output tokens per action) generates K=3 outcome scenarios and computes a Risk Score as a weighted sum of CVSS-based severity (w₁=0.50), blast-radius scope (w₂=0.30), and reversibility (w₃=0.20), extended into a Composite Validation Score with asset criticality (α=0.6) and urgency (γ=0.15) factors; (3) routing via piecewise thresholds τ_low=0.35, τ_high=0.65 to EXECUTE/MODIFY/ESCALATE; (4) the ASA (Mistral-7B-Instruct, ~310/180 tokens) predicts the attacker's next state constrained to ATT&CK v14.1 (14 tactics, 190+ techniques), outputting a JSON object with technique ID, next target, and confidence (gating updates at confidence ≥0.7); (5) the ARC persists to a PostgreSQL 16 audit schema and triggers replanning when running RPDR exceeds 0.30. Weights and thresholds were calibrated by grid search on a validation split (n=92 OPTC cases, scenarios A/C) minimizing false safety rate under a 15% escalation cap. Critical design decisions: the JSON-schema-constrained probability output (plausibly justified as hallucination mitigation, though calibration is only indirectly evidenced via FSR/EA); the 3-scenario cap on K (acknowledged as a computation/variation compromise, not ablated); and first-hop-only subgraph fallback for high-degree hosts like domain controllers (a stated accuracy risk, untested). Key Results: On 143 incidents from three DARPA OPTC APT scenarios (A: lateral movement, n=43; B: privilege escalation/exfiltration, n=51; C: C2/ransomware, n=49) plus 847 CTU-13 blocking tests: CIPHER-A achieves mean RPDR 15.6% ± 3.1 vs CIPHER-static 38.2% ± 6.6, LLM-SOAR 55.7% ± 8.9, Baseline SOAR 64.4% ± 9.8 (a 59.2% relative reduction vs its own static variant); FSR 3.2% ± 1.1 vs Baseline SOAR 22.7%; escalation accuracy 91.7% ± 3.2; MTTC 8.9 min vs 14.3 min (37.8% reduction). CTU-13 collateral-damage prediction accuracy is 94.3% (95% CI [92.5, 95.6]) vs 61.2% for CIPHER-static. ASA prediction accuracy is 81.3% on Scenario C (correctly predicting the 4.7-second C2 failover in 81.3% of cases), 84.1%/78.6%/81.3% across scenarios with wide CIs (e.g., [65.6, 87.7%] for Scenario B). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests report p<0.001 against all five baselines on RPDR and the three internal baselines on MTTC. Per-action latency is 2.45 s (~8,330 tokens per 7.2-action incident). The ablation attributes 43.6% of the RPDR reduction to CVE and 56.4% to ASA, with the authors appropriately cautioning this is incremental attribution, not an interaction-free causal estimate. Notably, the RPDR figures for the two adaptive external baselines (Liu: 47.3%, Babar: 34.7%) were computed by the authors from those papers' published indicators, not measured in a shared environment — the authors flag these as "indicative." Scale is standard research-scale (replayed datasets, ~500-host simulated enterprise), not production stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (pre-execution counterfactual action validation plus post-execution adversarial lookahead in one closed loop), NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the end-to-end pipeline with live CrowdStrike/AWS/AD dispatch), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING/METRIC (RPDR with ground-truth validation). The genuinely novel element is the combination and the RPDR metric — the underlying techniques (LLM scenario generation, heuristic weighted risk scoring, knowledge-base-constrained state prediction, LangGraph orchestration) are standard components; the claim of no prior system combining pre-execution validation with adversarial re-validation is supported by the authors' 25-paper table, though "first" claims are hedged and one concurrent work (AgentSOC, ICAIC 2026) applies counterfactual reasoning to the attacker-side question instead. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed — the LLM-SOAR → CIPHER-static → CIPHER-A sequence isolates CVE and ASA contributions with per-component attribution. Sensitivity analyses over both thresholds and weights (Figs. 8–9) show Pareto-optimal calibration with a broad ±0.10 minimum. Wilcoxon tests with n=143 and CIs (including Wilson intervals for CTU-13) are reported. However: no multiple seeds or repeated LLM runs are mentioned despite non-deterministic Claude API inference; no code or model weights are released (only links to the three public datasets); calibration used scenarios A/C (n=92) which also appear in the 143-incident evaluation set, so thresholds were tuned partly on test scenarios — a Goodhart risk the paper does not discuss; FSR and EA ground truth comes from the system's own PostgreSQL audit logs and analyst determinations within the replay environment; and the external-baseline numbers are author-derived approximations, transparently labeled but not independently verified. The RPDR circularity concern is genuinely addressed via the 97.2% red-team-log agreement — the strongest single rigor element. The PDF's displayed equations appear corrupted in the source text, which limits independent verification of the formal formulations. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS with an EMPIRICAL evaluation (built pipeline, replayed-dataset experiments). Practical: Runs on one A100-80GB server plus a Claude API subscription and commercial security APIs (CrowdStrike Falcon, AWS, Active Directory) — accessible to any mid-size SOC, though the local Mistral-7B inference requires an 80GB-class GPU. Efficient: 2.45 s per action and ~8,330 tokens per incident is cheap relative to analyst time (8.9 vs 14.3 min MTTC), so compute cost is not a barrier. Effective: The evidence shows effectiveness against replayed OPTC/CTU-13 incidents — a faithful but still proxy setting; "live execution API connectivity" is built but no production deployment or live-red-team exercise is reported. Scalable: Not tested — the paper honestly states concurrency was not stress-tested, that MTTC figures should not be extrapolated beyond ~500 hosts, and that domain-controller fallback may degrade collateral-damage accuracy; only qualitative scaling recommendations are given. Delivers a described prototype architecture and audit schema but no released software artifact; the reusable outputs are the RPDR metric definition and the validation/lookahead pipeline pattern. Strengths: - The RPDR metric with independent validation against DARPA OPTC red-team ground-truth logs (97.2% agreement across 143 cases) is a real methodological contribution — it converts "adaptive re-validation seems useful" into a measurable, externally anchored quantity. - Clean ablation design (CVE-only vs CVE+ASA) with explicit per-component attribution percentages and honest framing of it as sequential incremental attribution rather than causal decomposition. - Thorough sensitivity analysis (τ_low, τ_high, w₁–w₃, α) showing Pareto-optimal thresholds under an operational escalation-rate ceiling, which demonstrates the calibration was constrained by deployment realities (≤15% analyst escalation), not just metric maximization. - Unusually candid treatment of the derived external baselines (Sect. 5.4 explicitly warns the Liu/Babar numbers are indicative, not independently replicable) and of the metric-circularity objection before rebutting it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: - External baseline RPDR/FSR/EA/MTTC values were derived by the authors, not measured in a shared environment, and "should be regarded as indicative." - Concurrent-incident processing and >500-host scale were not experimentally stress-tested; reported MTTC "should not be extrapolated." - Domain-controller fallback (first-hop-only subgraph) may omit second-hop dependencies and reduce collateral-damage accuracy; GPT-4 was used for manuscript language editing (declared). - The authors confront limitations directly and in detail — a credibility positive; nothing material is minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Calibration/evaluation leakage: thresholds and weights were tuned on scenarios A/C (n=92) while the 143-incident evaluation includes those same scenarios; a strictly held-out scenario split is absent, inflating confidence in the FSR/EA numbers. - FSR ground truth is defined by rollbacks logged in the system's own audit trail within a replayed environment — the "unsafe action" criterion is internal, and no independent safety adjudicator (e.g., red-team assessment of executed actions) is applied. - No variance across repeated LLM inference runs or seeds for the Claude-based CVE; single-run results on a stochastic API are reported with per-incident SD only. - No comparison against a stronger, obvious baseline: a fine-tuned or prompted LLM asked directly to rate action risk in one shot (no scenario generation), or a learned risk model trained on the audit logs — the gap to CIPHER-static could partly be prompting overhead rather than the counterfactual structure. - The claim of "live action execution via CrowdStrike, AWS, and Active Directory APIs" is architecture, not evidence: no experiment in the paper executes actions on a live environment; all results come from dataset replay. - The 97.2% RPDR ground-truth agreement is computed with a margin threshold (>0.05 RS increase) chosen by the authors, with no sensitivity analysis of that threshold. Bottom Line: A practitioner building LLM-driven SOAR automation gains a genuinely useful blueprint — a grounded degradation metric, a routing-threshold calibration recipe, and a rare ground-truth-validated argument that static plans degrade — but should treat the headline margins over adaptive baselines as estimates, discount the leakage-prone calibration, and expect to reimplement everything from scratch given the absence of released code.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a two-tier LLM multi-agent architecture — with natural-language-specification 'Agent Reasoning Tools' (ARTs) and an immutable Shared Memory Bus — that detects its own systemic failures, generates evidence-grounded diagnoses and recovery plans, and proposes new tool specifications for human-approved system evolution. - Why it's important: Agentic AI systems fail opaquely in ways that post-hoc XAI cannot repair, and regulated deployments need auditable, human-in-the-loop recovery rather than just explanations after the fact. - How it does it: It splits processing into a fast 'System 1' executor-critic refinement loop and a deliberative 'System 2' escalation workflow whose diagnostic claims must cite immutable log entries, culminating in a human-readable proposal for a new ART that a human implements. - The good: The tiered workflow reaches a median weighted F1 of 0.93 on SemEval-2014 Task 4 restaurant ATE (vs. 0.81 single-pass ART, 0.74 direct prompting), and escalated batches are measurably harder (mean F1 0.68 vs. 0.89, p<.01), showing the escalation triggers target real failures. - The missing: The closed-loop co-evolution validation — the paper's headline 'actionability' claim — was implemented by the paper's own authors rather than independent developers, the human expert study has only N=8 raters over 8 cases, and no code is released. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building human-in-the-loop agentic systems or HC-XAI evaluation methodologies; ML practitioners seeking a drop-on engineable component or a benchmark-topping ATE method can skip it.

Problem & Motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems in high-stakes, human-supervised domains fail in ways that current infrastructure handles poorly. Prevailing agentic frameworks (ReAct-style tool calling) treat internal reasoning as transient and non-programmable, while prevailing XAI produces passive, post-hoc artifacts that neither reflect agentic compositional reasoning nor tell a human collaborator what to do next. The authors target three named gaps: an architectural gap (no programmable reasoning substrate), an adaptability/performance gap (blackboard architectures bottleneck at LLM latency), and an actionability gap (explanations that do not support 'what to do next'). The audience is the information systems and HC-XAI community, particularly for deployments under compliance scrutiny (healthcare, finance, autonomous systems). Key Idea: The core insight is to make the agent's reasoning capabilities themselves inspectable, structured artifacts: an ART is a function signature plus a natural-language docstring, 'executed' by the LLM interpreting that specification rather than by calling external code. Wrapping a black-box LLM in these glass-box capability definitions yields (a) justifications generated before actions and written to an immutable ledger, (b) domain-agnostic modular architecture (swap the ART library, keep the cognitive workflow), and (c) a concrete mechanism for self-identified capability limits — when no ART fits, the system proposes a new one for human approval ('explainability-driven evolution'). Tiering follows Kahneman's dual-process theory: routine work stays in Tier 1; failures escalate to Tier 2. Methodology: Design science research with four architectural artifacts: (1) the two-tier structure, (2) ARTs, (3) a Shared Memory Bus (SQLite-based, natural-language logs rather than vector embeddings, with role-based access control so the Decision Agent never sees ground-truth labels), and (4) a stateful, event-driven lifecycle with named phases (PENDING_DIAGNOSIS, PLANNING, AWAITING_VALIDATION). Tier 1 is an asynchronous executor-critic loop: a Decision Agent (extract/revise modes) and a Review Agent (review/validate modes) exchange structured natural-language critiques on the Bus, stopping at an F1 threshold (0.85) or two iterations. Tier 2, gated by an Escalation Analyzer with pre-defined triggers (batch-level: F1 below calibrated θ<0.80, ΔF1<0 during refinement; cohort-level: sustained per-aspect F1 deficit, high variance over N=5 rolling batches), performs evidence-cited diagnosis, a recovery plan, and an ART proposal. Underlying model is gemma-3-27b-it at temperature 1.0, top-p 0.7 — a deliberate robustness stress test. Evaluation: 40 bootstrapped batches of 50 instances from the SemEval-2014 Task 4 restaurant test split; escalation thresholds calibrated on a separate 250-instance holdout; three baselines (literature-reported fine-tuned transformers, zero-shot direct prompting, single-pass ART); a human expert study (10 recruited, 8 retained after ICC-based exclusion; 8 escalated cases; seven Likert measures plus an actionability vote) and a 20-member LLM persona committee (5 personas × 4 frontier reasoning LLMs, all distinct from the system's own model); a closed-loop implementation of proposed ARTs; and cross-domain tests on ADE Corpus V2 and the AWARE Productivity dataset. Critical design decisions — high-temperature operation, text-based instead of vector memory, holdout-calibrated triggers — are each explicitly justified, though the justification for high temperature (stress test) means headline numbers may understate or, conversely, may not transfer to deterministic deployments. Key Results: Tier 1 achieves median weighted F1 0.93 (IQR narrowest of all systems) versus 0.81 for single-pass SP-ART, 0.74 for direct prompting (IQR 0.63–0.79), and literature-reported fine-tuned transformer baselines; all pairwise differences significant at p<.001 with Bonferroni correction. Eight of 40 batches escalated; escalated batches average F1 0.68 (SD 0.12) vs. 0.89 (SD 0.06) for non-escalated (p<.01), and one cross-batch trigger isolated 'anecdotes/miscellaneous' at cohort F1 0.41 vs. 0.79 elsewhere. Human experts rated Tier 2 diagnoses 3.54–4.36 across six measures (all above the neutral midpoint; p<.05 to p<.001); actionability votes: 5/8 approved, 1 clarification, 1 tie, 1 reject. The LLM committee aligned with humans (no significant mean differences; case-level correlations 0.656–0.935, but the coherence CI includes zero). Closed-loop co-evolution: overall Macro F1 0.68→0.86 on escalated batches; 'ambience' F1 0.67→1.00; recall 0.61→0.98 at a precision cost of 0.03; one of five control batches regressed 7.15% via over-extraction at category boundaries (an honestly reported recall-precision trade-off). Ablation of integration strategies showed single-tier prompt-patching collapsed Food F1 from 0.91 to 0.36 (instruction conflict), evidencing that the tiering is necessary rather than overhead. Generalizability: ADE Corpus V2 achieved macro F1 0.915 (precision 0.952) with no escalation; AWARE triggered escalation with 12/12 and 11/11 trigger accuracy across two model families, with diagnoses converging cross-model on domain-specific confusion patterns — though Tier 1 macro F1 on AWARE was only 0.418–0.454 and small (4B) models showed 18–92% empty extraction rates. Cost: ~202s and 230k tokens per batch vs. 98s and 100k for direct prompting, ~$0.20/batch. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW METHOD, with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the single-tier prompt-patching ablation showing instruction-conflict collapse). Genuinely novel: the ART construct (natural-language docstrings as the executable capability substrate) and the 'planning-as-explanation' / 'explainability-driven evolution' loop coupling diagnosis to a human-implementable tool specification, plus the LLM-persona 'HC-XAI Evaluation Committee' evaluation methodology. Standard components reused competently: executor-critic pattern, blackboard architecture, dual-process tiering, and LLM self-diagnosis are all known ideas recombined into a new architecture — the contribution is the integration and the human-in-the-loop governance design, not any single underlying algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above-average methodological hygiene for this venue tier: holdout-calibrated escalation thresholds, 40 bootstrap batches with variance estimation, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests, explicit power analysis acknowledging N=8 detects only very large effects (d≥1.16), ICC-based inter-rater reliability reporting (0.827 human, 0.930 committee), a lexical-overlap check (Jaccard 0.33%) to rule out memorization in transfer, and a control-batch analysis quantifying post-evolution regression (mean −0.15%, SD 4.47pp). Ablations exist for integration strategy but not for individual ART components or trigger designs. No code repository is released; supplementary materials and data are 'available upon request,' which limits reproducibility of a system paper whose artifact is the code. Baselines are mixed: Baseline-DP and SP-ART are self-run and appropriate, but Baseline-LB is literature-reported numbers rather than a controlled comparison, and no agentic baseline (ReAct, Reflexion-style self-correction, or an off-the-shelf MAS framework) is tested — the strongest known alternatives for the same problem are absent. Concern: the 'Structural Test' philosophy explicitly prioritizes architectural validity over task generalization, so the evaluation design is partially self-justifying. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built architecture, empirically evaluated). Practical: Yes — runs on an open-weight 27B model on a single GPU, with a 4B variant tested for GPU-poor settings, at ~$0.20 per 50-instance batch. Efficient: Roughly 2× latency (202s vs. 98s) and 2.3× token cost versus direct prompting, justified by a 26%→7% error-rate reduction; Tier 2 cost is unquantified but escalation-limited. Effective: Evidence supports failure diagnosis and recovery quality on ATE and diagnosis transfer to AWARE, but 'actionability' is validated only through ratings and an author-executed implementation — a proxy for real co-evolution. Scalable: Only claimed; nothing tests 10–100× batch volume, larger cohorts, or concurrent-agent load on the Shared Memory Bus, and the 4B-model failures show the ART scaffold is scale-sensitive. Deliverable is a paper plus on-request supplementary materials; no library, CLI, dataset, or trained model is publicly released, so the artifact is currently non-replicable in practice. Strengths: - The ART abstraction is a genuinely interesting design move: making capability definitions the unit of audit, modularity, and evolution simultaneously, which gives the HC-XAI principles (explanation, meaningfulness, accuracy, knowledge limits) concrete architectural instantiations rather than rhetoric. - The escalation-trigger validation is unusually careful: thresholds calibrated on a separate holdout, and demonstrated trigger specificity (escalated batches at F1 0.68 vs. 0.89; per-aspect F1 0.41 vs. 0.79) rather than assumed. - The single-tier vs. modular vs. holistic integration ablation provides real evidence for the central architectural claim — prompt-patching caused Food F1 to drop from 0.91 to 0.36 — turning a design philosophy into a measured result. - Honest, quantified reporting of failure modes, including the 7.15% control-batch regression from recall-optimized evolution and the empty-extraction pathology of 4B models with built-in chain-of-thought. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and in detail — a credibility positive. They acknowledge: evaluation bounded to text-classification domains (ATE primary; biomedical and app-review secondary); reliance on LLM-simulated personas rather than real user studies for preference modeling; the closed-loop co-evolution experiment was executed by the authors themselves (inherent expert bias), so it is 'an illustrative case study... rather than evidence of general implementability'; the N=8 expert sample with upward-biased effect-size estimates and a recommendation to reach N≥34 cases; wide CIs on the committee-human correlation (coherence CI includes −0.09); scale-dependent ART-format compliance (empty schemas from Qwen3.6, name-only proposals from Gemma); and low AWARE Tier 1 macro F1 (0.418–0.454) as a deliberate stress-test property. They also note the missing paired comparison against evidence-stripped diagnoses. This level of self-critique is above the norm. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No agentic baseline: the system is never compared against ReAct-style self-correction, Reflexion, or any published LLM-MAS framework on the same task, so it is impossible to know how much of the gain comes from the tiering/ART design versus generic iterative refinement with any critic loop. The SP-ART baseline isolates iteration, not architecture. - Baseline-LB is literature-reported fine-tuned transformer performance, i.e., a cross-paper comparison with different splits/protocols; a controlled fine-tuned baseline on identical data is missing. - The escalation threshold (F1<0.80) and the Tier 1 stopping rule (F1≥0.85) are the same quantity the system optimizes; trigger calibration and evaluation occur on bootstrap samples of the same test split, a mild Goodhart risk for the escalation-accuracy figure (12/12, 11/11), which is really 'the trigger fires when F1 is low' — near-tautological without false-positive analysis on hard-but-recoverable batches. - The 'propose its own tool' loop terminates in a human writing code; the paper does not test whether the proposed ART specifications are implementable by anyone else (acknowledged only as future work), and the relationship between the two proposed-ART examples shown (ContextualAspectIdentifier vs. ExtractAspectFromAnalogy) and the three capability gaps is loosely traced. - The human study's eight cases are all from the primary ATE benchmark and were selected by the authors to 'represent a diverse set of triggering conditions'; rater exclusion details and the actionability tie-handling leave room for analyst discretion. - The Shared Memory Bus is claimed to avoid blackboard bottlenecks, but no latency/throughput measurement under concurrency is reported — the performance-gap motivation is asserted, not measured. Bottom Line: A thoughtful and unusually self-critical design-science paper that delivers a credible architectural pattern (inspectable capability specs + tiered escalation + human-gated evolution) and a reusable evaluation methodology, but the absence of agentic baselines, no code release, and an author-executed co-evolution validation mean a practitioner should read it for design ideas rather than adopt it as a validated framework.

What Happens When the Model Eats the Stack? Rethinking the Research Agenda for Data Agents to Withstand the Bitter Lesson

TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents an empirical study showing that general coding agents (Codex harness with o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.6 Sol) overtake purpose-built data agents on TAG-Bench and DAB, and proposes a research agenda for database systems centered on serving "persistent semantic context" — offline-authored, language-based knowledge about a data environment — as a first-class abstraction. - Why it's important: The data systems community is investing in agent scaffolding layers that frontier models may absorb (Sutton's bitter lesson), so researchers need to know which system problems will endure rather than be internalized by models. - How it does it: It measures capability evolution across three model generations on two data-agent benchmarks, root-causes failures with a five-cluster taxonomy, and runs controlled experiments with offline-generated contexts (Self-Curated variants and GEPA) to isolate what agents still cannot get from the model alone. - The good: The failure analysis showing >60% of remaining GPT-5.6 Sol failures stem from environmental knowledge (semantic misinterpretation, wrong sources/schema, entity mismatches) — not reasoning — directly motivates the proposed context layer, and the context experiments show a +19 percentage-point accuracy gain on held-out DAB tasks. - The missing: The context experiments are run on a tiny scale (12 development trajectories, 12 datasets, 42 held-out queries) with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, and the human-designed baselines are approximations (Agentar-Scale-SQL's inference code is not public), so both halves of the empirical case are weaker than they appear. - Read it or not: Worth reading for database and agentic-systems researchers deciding what to work on next — the empirical trend and the semantic-consistency framing are agenda-setting — but skippable for practitioners seeking a deployable system, since no artifact is released.

Problem & Motivation: Data systems researchers and builders of data agents face an existential question: as frontier LLMs internalize planning, code generation, tool use, debugging, and validation, which engineered system layers will survive? Prior work (Liu et al., "Supporting Our AI Overlords", CIDR 2026) argues future data systems must be redesigned around high-volume, speculative, inefficient agent-issued queries. The authors observe this premise may be wrong: newer models issue fewer, more efficient queries per task, and hand-designed agent scaffolds that compensate for model weaknesses are being displaced. The gap they target is identifying what remains for the data systems community to build — specifically, knowledge about a particular data environment that is external to the model, changes with the data, and is wastefully re-derived by every query. Key Idea: Separate what models will internalize (reasoning, planning, code synthesis — doomed scaffolding) from what they cannot (environment-specific semantic knowledge — enduring), and argue the enduring layer is persistent semantic context: an explicit, language-based knowledge state about schemas, metric definitions, join paths, authoritative sources, and organizational conventions, built offline once and amortized across many queries. The paper's key empirical insight is that as models improve, per-task reasoning turns collapse (~4× fewer turns from o3 to GPT-5.6 Sol on DAB) while the relative share of schema exploration and environmental grounding grows, so the bottleneck migrates from reasoning to context acquisition. Methodology: The paper has three parts. (1) A longitudinal capability study: a Codex coding-agent harness versus human-designed data agents (an Agentar-Scale-SQL-inspired SQL pipeline with execution-guided refinement on 60 non-aggregation TAG-Bench queries; DeepEye on DAB) across o3, GPT-5, and GPT-5.6 Sol, measuring accuracy, average output tokens, and turns per query decomposed into schema exploration, analytical/semantic queries, and verification/recovery. (2) A failure analysis: GPT-5.6 Sol classifies each failed coding-agent trace into a five-cluster taxonomy (semantic mistakes, source/schema misgrounding, entity resolution, analytical logic, execution errors). (3) A context experiment: offline context generation with GPT-5.6 Sol given 12 development trajectories per objective (Accuracy, Latency, Schema) plus GEPA prompt optimization; the frozen context is appended to held-out DAB prompts, and accuracy, turns, latency, build time, build cost, and context size are measured against a No Context baseline. Design decisions: using an approximation of Agentar-Scale-SQL (justified by unavailable code, but acknowledged incompleteness), and using GPT-5.6 Sol itself as the failure labeler (not independently validated). Sweeps across reasoning levels are mentioned; only low reasoning is reported. Key Results: (1) With GPT-5.6 Sol, the general coding agent beats the human-designed data agent on both benchmarks in accuracy and token efficiency; with o3 on TAG-Bench the ordering is reversed, showing the crossover across generations. (2) The GPT-5.6 Sol coding agent reaches accuracy comparable to the Oracle pipeline (expert-written queries run with LOTUS) on TAG-Bench. (3) On DAB, the GPT-5.6 Sol coding agent gains over 35 percentage points of accuracy over the o3 coding agent with over 2× better token efficiency; turns per query drop ~4× (from 23.2 with o3 to 6.0 with GPT-5.6 Sol). (4) Over 60% of remaining failures on TAG+DAB (n=40, 52, 73 failures per model) are environmental-knowledge failures (clusters C1–C3) for GPT-5.6 Sol, versus execution errors dominating for o3. (5) Self-Curated (Accuracy) context yields +19 percentage points over No Context on held-out DAB; Self-Curated (Schema) cuts schema-exploration share but modestly reduces accuracy (possible overfitting to the 12-trajectory sample); even the Latency-targeted context increases latency over No Context. (6) Context build overheads are substantial even at toy scale: Self-Curated (Schema) takes 3,413.6 s, costs $9.60, and produces 162 KB of context. Baselines are current and the scale is deliberately small (single-agent harness, 42–60 test queries per benchmark). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the crossover where general coding agents beat specialized data agents, and the shift of failure mass from execution errors to environmental-knowledge errors) plus a position/vision paper (NEW PROBLEM framing for "semantic consistency" and persistent-context physical design). The individual techniques — coding-agent harnesses, GEPA prompt optimization, agent-authored context files — are standard existing tools; the contribution is the measurement and the reframing of data-system research directions around them, which is genuinely useful but not a new method or system. Rigor & Reproducibility: No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; every headline claim rests on single runs. Ablations exist in a limited sense — context objectives (Accuracy/Latency/Schema/GEPA) are varied against a No Context baseline — but no ablation isolates why contexts help (e.g., which context sections matter). Code and generated contexts are not stated as released; prompts are usefully included in appendices. Methodological concerns: (a) the Agentar-Scale-SQL baseline is a re-implementation from a published prompt, not the actual leaderboard system, so the "general agents beat human-designed agents" claim is against a degraded proxy; (b) failure traces are labeled by GPT-5.6 Sol itself — the same model whose capability is being celebrated — with no human validation of cluster assignments; (c) the core context experiments run on 12 dev queries and 42 held-out queries, a scale the authors admit, yet the research agenda generalizes to terabyte-scale enterprise environments; (d) the DeepEye baseline required new connectors added by the authors, an unvalidated adaptation. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (measurements and small experiments in service of a vision paper; no system is built or deployed). - Practical: The experiments run on commercially available models via a Codex harness, so reproduction is feasible for anyone with API access. - Efficient: The paper's own numbers show the proposed context layer is currently expensive — thousands of seconds and ~$10 to build a single context at toy scale — and the paper argues, rather than demonstrates, that amortization across queries justifies this. - Effective: Contexts demonstrably improve held-out accuracy on one benchmark (+19 pp), but latency-targeted contexts fail to beat No Context on latency, so the claimed benefit is real but partial and only shown on DAB. - Scalable: Not tested — the authors explicitly note their setting has 12 datasets and 12 traces versus real environments with thousands of tables and terabytes, and all scalability claims about the agenda are extrapolation. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model; it stops at paper form, with prompt templates in an appendix as the closest thing to a reusable technique. Strengths: (1) The capability-evolution measurement is the paper's real evidence: the o3→GPT-5→GPT-5.6 Sol crossover, where the same human-designed scaffold flips from winning to losing against a generic coding agent, is a concrete, falsifiable demonstration of the bitter lesson applied to data agents. (2) The turn-decomposition analysis (schema exploration rising from 22% to 25% of turns even as total turns drop from 23.2 to 6.0) is a non-obvious finding that directly refutes the agentic-speculation workload premise of CIDR 2026 work. (3) The semantic consistency framing — consistency scope, consistency models, and consistency methods for natural-language context artifacts — is a genuinely new problem formulation that maps classical database concepts onto an underexplored layer. (4) Reporting context build costs ($1.09–$12.16, 2.25–162 KB, 155–3,414 s) alongside benefits is honest accounting most context-engineering papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that their context experiments are small-scale (12 historical traces, 12 datasets) versus realistic terabyte, thousands-of-table environments; that the Schema-targeted context may cause over-reliance and overfitting to the small sample (accuracy drops modestly); that even at this scale context construction takes hundreds to thousands of seconds; and, in the appendix, that the Agentar-Scale-SQL baseline is only an approximation because its full inference pipeline is not public. They confront the scale limitation directly, which is a credibility positive, but they do not dwell on the single-run/no-variance nature of their results. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No variance reporting at all — with test sets of 42–60 queries, a 19-point accuracy swing is plausibly within run-to-run noise for agentic systems, so the headline context result may not replicate. (2) The failure taxonomy is machine-labeled by the strongest model under study, and a model biased toward "environmental knowledge" failures would manufacture support for the paper's thesis; no human audit is reported. (3) The claim that the agentic-speculation premise (Liu et al.) is "countered" rests on one vendor's model family (OpenAI-only) on two benchmarks; scaling behavior could differ for other model lines or cheaper deployment regimes where token inefficiency persists economically. (4) The context experiments never test context staleness — the very problem the proposed semantic-consistency agenda targets — so the paper's central system challenge is motivated but entirely unmeasured. (5) Vendor-model numbers (o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.6 Sol) are self-reported capabilities from OpenAI pages used as ground truth for release timing and capability ordering. (6) The +19 pp result is on DAB only; TAG-Bench is not included in the context experiments, limiting generality. Bottom Line: For database and agent-systems researchers, this is a agenda-shaping read that usefully redirects effort from agent scaffolding toward persistent semantic context and its unmeasured system challenges; for anyone wanting validated techniques or deployable systems, the empirical base — single runs, ~100 total test queries, approximated baselines — is too thin, and the stronger alternative is to treat this as a position paper and wait for the follow-up systems work it calls for.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations running S&OP struggle with three interacting pressures: (1) cross-functional integration is hard to achieve because functions hold conflicting goals, and the prevailing integration framework (Tuomikangas and Kaipia, 2014) treats S&OP as a monolith with uniform integration requirements; (2) the 2020–2023 cascade of disruptions (COVID-19, semiconductor shortages, Suez blockage, Ukraine invasion, trade wars) exposed that S&OP's formalized, monthly cadence cannot absorb unknown-unknown disruptions, and systematic reviews conclude disruption management in S&OP is under-specified; (3) generative AI has raised expectations that planning can be automated, yet almost no empirical evidence exists on AI embedded in S&OP specifically, as opposed to adjacent areas like procurement or transportation. The thesis targets operations management researchers and S&OP process owners who need to know how the process should be (re)designed under these conditions. Key Idea: Decompose S&OP into its constituent sub-processes and treat integration, resilience, and AI adoption as context-contingent per sub-process rather than as uniform process-level properties. Concretely: integration = coordination (formal information flow) + collaboration (joint solution creation) + alignment (shared strategic goals), with the mix differing across demand planning, supply planning, pre-S&OP, and executive S&OP; resilience arises from the interaction of routine processes (S&OP/S&OE) with temporary, disruption-specific planning configurations rather than from S&OP alone; and AI adoption is explained via CIMO logic where mechanisms (human oversight, organizational flexibility, data readiness) mediate between interventions and outcomes. Methodology: Qualitative, exploratory multiple-case design across three studies: Study 1 (integration, 5 cases, 10 interviews averaging 1h15), Study 2 (resilience, 4 cases of manufacturers affected by COVID-19, 18 + 29 interviews for the two papers), Study 3 (AI, 3 cases, 4 + 9 interviews). Seven case companies spanning telecom equipment (263b SEK), automotive (552b SEK), healthcare equipment, confectionery, mining equipment, industrial equipment, and pharmaceuticals, selected by theoretical sampling with the criterion of an established S&OP process at ≥ Stage 3 maturity (Danese et al. 2018 model). Data collection used semi-structured interviews (≥2 rounds per study, third verification round where possible), process documents, group interviews, and five workshops under the VINNOVA-funded REAL project. Analysis followed a priori coding (Paper I), open coding (Papers II–III), pattern matching of AI applications onto S&OP steps (Paper IV, conceptual), and Gioia methodology in NVivo 15 (Paper V), with within-case then cross-case comparison matrices per Eisenhardt (1989); the author coded, with co-author discussion to check interpretations, and case companies verified case descriptions. Key Results: This is theory-building, so results are frameworks and propositions, not effect sizes. Paper I: coordination is present in demand planning across all five cases but is missing in one case's supply planning sub-process; an unexpected finding is that collaboration can substitute for coordination in small, informal setups; active alignment (direct finance/product-development participation) versus passive alignment (post-hoc executive feedback) distinguishes integration maturity, formalized in a four-stage maturity model culminating in strategic alignment. Paper II: S&OP's formalization reduces responsiveness during major disruptions; organizations create temporary, disruption-specific SCP processes — executive-led decision meetings, operational monitoring teams, tactical continuity planning — coordinated mainly through intra-process formalization rather than inter-process ties. Paper III: during disruptions, organizations prioritize IT maintenance over advancement and rely on basic communication channels over advanced planning systems — a counter-intuitive result given maturity-model assumptions that IT drives risk management. Paper IV (conceptual): AI is mapped onto each S&OP sub-process — strongest in demand planning (forecasting from structured and unstructured external data), weaker in supply planning (optimization algorithms dominate), supportive-but-not-replacing human judgement in pre-S&OP and executive S&OP. Paper V: analysis of 8 AI implementations across 3 organizations identifies human motivation/skill/capacity, organizational flexibility and investment, long-term AI strategy, data quality, awareness of AI limits, human validation, and avoidance of black-box syndrome and deskilling as conditions for success. No quantitative performance outcomes (e.g., forecast accuracy improvement, service-level change) are measured for any framework. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (reframing S&OP integration at sub-process granularity via the coordination-collaboration-alignment triad) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (routine-vs-temporary planning process interaction during disruptions; the diminished role of advanced IT during crisis). The individual ingredients — contingency theory, CIMO, Gioia coding, Danese maturity staging — are all standard; the novelty lies in the granularity of the decomposition and the application of CIMO to AI-in-S&OP, a setting where empirical evidence is genuinely scarce. Paper IV is a conceptual mapping exercise and its applications are largely foreseeable from the AI-in-SCM literature. Rigor & Reproducibility: Within the norms of exploratory case research: interview guides and analysis appendices are provided, at least two interview rounds per study, member verification of case descriptions, triangulation across multiple respondents and documents in Papers II–III, and conference presentations (NOFOMA, EUROMA, EDSI) that provided external critique. Weaker points acknowledged by the author: Paper I interviewed only S&OP managers (no cross-functional corroboration); Paper V lacked process documentation; no direct observations were possible because S&OP is commercially sensitive. Statistical generalization is explicitly disclaimed in favor of analytical generalization. No code/data release is stated (unsurprising for interview-based research under confidentiality). Methodological concerns a reviewer should note: (1) none of the five papers was peer-reviewed in journal form at thesis submission, so claims have not survived external review; (2) the resilience studies rely on retrospective interview accounts of COVID-19, which risks recall bias and survivor bias (all selected cases 'managed to overcome' the disruption — failed adaptations are unobserved); (3) Paper IV's AI-application mapping is not validated against implemented systems, only two illustrative cases; (4) the four-stage integration maturity model is derived from the same five cases that motivated it, with no out-of-sample testing. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (qualitative case research with conceptual outputs; no algorithm or system is built). - Practical: The outputs are frameworks, maturity models, and design guidelines usable by S&OP process owners without special hardware; nothing requires implementation effort beyond process redesign. - Efficient: Not applicable in a compute sense; the 'cost' is organizational — the thesis itself argues integration and AI demand sustained investment in people, data infrastructure, and management attention rather than quick tooling fixes. - Effective: The evidence shows descriptive and explanatory insight into how integration, resilience behaviors, and AI adoption occurred in 7 firms; it does not demonstrate that applying the frameworks improves performance outcomes, which are asserted, not measured. - Scalable: Not tested — the cases are large multinationals, so behavior in small/mid-sized firms or non-manufacturing contexts is unexamined, and the frameworks' transferability is claimed analytically, not demonstrated. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or tool; it stops at paper form with conceptual frameworks and propositions. Strengths: - The sub-process decomposition of S&OP is a real conceptual advance over Tuomikangas and Kaipia's (2014) process-level treatment: it shows integration requirements differ across demand planning, supply planning, pre-S&OP, and executive S&OP, directly supporting the contingency claim that one-size-fits-all S&OP design fails. - The routine-versus-temporary planning process finding (Paper II) reframes resilience as an emergent property of interacting planning configurations rather than an S&OP feature, which is a non-obvious and practice-relevant empirical insight. - The counter-intuitive Paper III result — advanced IT mattered less than in-house IT teams and basic communication during disruption — directly challenges IT-centric maturity models and is grounded in longitudinal data collected during the disruption itself. - Methodological transparency improves across the five papers (culminating in a structured Gioia analysis in Paper V), and the author honestly documents how case boundaries and research focus shifted as data emerged. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author states: no direct observations (companies treat S&OP as sensitive); lack of access to executive teams, leaving the executive S&OP sub-process under-studied across all papers; Paper I's informant base restricted to S&OP managers, limiting construct validity; Paper V's missing process documentation; Paper III's weaker coverage of the post-disruption stage because the empirical material favored the pre-disruption phase; software-vendor perspectives dropped from Study 3 due to shallow data; generalization limited to the S&OP domain and to settings with similar planning characteristics; and qualitative studies cannot achieve full reproducibility. These are confronted directly and candidly — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Survivorship and recall bias in the resilience studies: all four disruption cases are firms that overcame COVID-19, so the frameworks cannot speak to failure modes, and retrospective interviews conducted years after the events may reconstruct rather than report decision processes. - Geographical and national-context homogeneity is not discussed: all seven cases appear to be Swedish or Swedish-connected manufacturers, yet the thesis draws on claims that national context does not matter (citing prior cross-country studies) without testing this in its own sample. - No longitudinal performance measurement: the four-stage integration maturity model and the CIMO mechanisms are never linked to quantified outcomes (service level, forecast accuracy, inventory), so the 'Outcome' leg of CIMO rests on informants' perceptions. - The AI findings rest on 8 implementations, several of which appear to be pilots or ML forecasting tools rather than genuinely AI-enabled S&OP; the boundary of what counts as 'AI' is acknowledged as fuzzy but not resolved, risking inflated generality of Paper V's conclusions. - Paper IV's mapping of AI to S&OP sub-processes is not validated with executives (the very decision-makers whose judgment the paper says AI cannot replace), repeating the executive-access gap in the one paper where it matters most. Bottom Line: For an S&OP researcher or practitioner designing or maturing a planning process, this thesis offers genuinely useful, context-contingent frameworks — especially the sub-process integration model and the routine/temporary process insight — but because none of the constituent work is yet peer-reviewed and no performance outcomes are measured, it should be treated as promising exploratory theory-building rather than validated guidance, and readers wanting quantified AI-in-S&OP evidence must look elsewhere.

World in World: Explore the World with World Models (5 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces World in World (WiW), a training-free inference-time interface that converts heterogeneous visual evidence (source observations, target-view depth projections, rendered geometry, retrieved generated history) into camera- and time-labelled clean visual states that a frozen causal video world model reads through its native self-attention, enabling camera-controlled rerendering, long-horizon revisiting, and human-motion transfer without any retraining. - Why it's important: Existing video world models require control-specific conditioning modules or additional training for each new evidence type, so extending controllability of a large pretrained world model is expensive; a shared, frozen-backbone interface makes the same model reusable across controls at inference time. - How it does it: The core trick is expressing every control as clean visual states (cached K/V from a t=0 forward pass with RoPE time/camera labels) injected into native attention, with correspondence-guided attention routing (CGAR) deciding where queries read evidence and evidence-wise attention CFG (EWA) deciding how strongly each channel contributes, computed from responses of the same denoising pass at zero extra NFE. - The good: On DAVIS and OpenVid-1M camera rerendering, WiW achieves the best Overall VBench score (85.192 vs. 84.295 for the strongest baseline UniWorld-View) and the lowest camera trajectory errors (RotError 2.83°, TransError 0.0686) against six baselines, and the warping ablation cleanly shows the spatial reference is the dominant component. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; evaluation relies on pose errors estimated by monocular estimators (Depth Anything 3, ViPE) themselves; and no code release is stated, so the numbers are single-run, self-evaluated, and hard to verify. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on controllable video generation or world models and care about training-free conditioning via native attention; skip it if you need rigorous benchmarking or a released artifact, since the evaluation protocol and reproducibility story are thin.
