Practical Impact (40) is the lowest contributor: an inference-time method with no released artifact and no efficiency measurements despite a zero-extra-NFE claim. The clean-state interface abstraction (Novelty 68) and the unusually honest ablation showing CGAR/EWA contribute only marginally keep Completeness (55) and Resilience (55) from collapsing further. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*50 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*50 + 0.10*40 = 56.

Problem & Motivation: Users of autoregressive video world models want to explore the world depicted in a source video along arbitrary camera trajectories — rerendering a recorded event from new viewpoints while preserving its dynamics, plausibly completing newly exposed surfaces, and recovering earlier appearance on revisits. Practitioners building interactive content creation, virtual production, game generation, and embodied-agent simulation tools face this. Prior systems address each requirement with dedicated conditioning pathways (camera rays, rendered proxies, source-video adapter modules, explicit geometric memory), so combining or adding evidence types demands redesign and retraining. The gap is a shared interface through which one frozen world model can consume heterogeneous current and historical visual evidence without task-specific adaptation. Key Idea: Recast world-model control as visual-evidence construction rather than model adaptation: any evidence source can be converted into the exact representation the causal backbone already consumes — clean visual states with camera pose, event-time index, spatial-support weights, and a per-denoising-step activation schedule — and injected through native self-attention. Two refinements make this usable: CGAR adds a log correspondence weight to attention logits to route queries to geometrically matched source-video tokens when appearance matching is ambiguous, and EWA amplifies only the component of each evidence channel's attention response orthogonal to the native response (scaled by max(0, cos(o_e, o_0))), regulating per-channel guidance without extra network evaluations. Methodology: The pipeline is inference-time only, instantiated on the frozen causal-fast checkpoint of LingBot-World 2.0. (1) Shared interface: each evidence channel b is mapped by a converter Ψb to visual content Xb, per-frame camera/time metadata Pb, token-level support ωb, and a step-dependent activation γb(s); content is encoded by a t=0 forward pass of the frozen backbone to cache clean K/V per layer, injected either into the backbone's native 18 latent slots (6 source anchors, 8 rolling history, 4 current chunk) or as temporary auxiliary attention blocks removed after the chunk. (2) Target-view scene evidence: source RGB is depth-estimated with DepthCrafter, back-projected, and reprojected from source to target camera; visibility plus geometric reliability set support weights. (3) Rendered geometry evidence: for humans, an LHM++-reconstructed avatar driven by per-frame SMPL-X parameters is rendered from the target camera at the aligned event time, providing shape/appearance proposals for surfaces absent from the source; rendered depth also prunes unreliable background projections near subject boundaries. (4) Retrieved generated evidence: per-layer clean K/V of evicted finalized states are archived with pose/time tags; a top-K retrieval ranks by target-view surface coverage and viewing-direction compatibility for revisits. (5) CGAR routes current queries to tracked, depth- and camera-matched source tokens via ℓ = qᵀk/√dh + log βij with joint normalization; EWA applies Equation (5) per evidence channel per layer, bounding output magnitude by the native response norm. Critical design decisions: target-view warping as the primary spatial reference (well justified — removing it raises RotError from 1.78° to 6.12° and TransError from 0.053 to 0.582, ~3.4× and ~10.9×); separate where-to-read vs. how-strong regulation (supported by ablations, though individual gains of CGAR/EWA are small); and reliance on external perception models (DepthCrafter, LHM++, point tracking) whose failure modes propagate silently into evidence quality. Key Results: On DAVIS and OpenVid-1M camera-controlled rerendering against ReCamMaster, TrajectoryCrafter, WorldForge, InSpatio-World, UniWorld-View, and CameraAnything (official checkpoints and configs, matched source videos and camera paths), WiW reports Overall VBench 85.192 (best baseline UniWorld-View 84.295), Dynamic Degree 98.750 (tied best), RotError 2.83° (best baseline CameraAnything 3.19°), TransError 0.0686 (tied best), PSNR 23.15, SSIM 0.787, and LPIPS 0.1217 (statistically tied with UniWorld-View's 0.1217/0.121668 vs. 0.121664). Baselines are current (2025–2026 methods including concurrent work), so the comparison is credible, though frame counts differ per method (81/49) before alignment. Ablations on DAVIS show target-view warping is the load-bearing component; removing CGAR or EWA individually changes RotError by only ~0.2° (1.99°→1.78° for EWA, 1.78°→1.78° for CGAR removal), indicating their contribution is modest relative to warping. Applications (bullet-time, stabilization, editing, cross-instance K/V sharing, human motion transfer) are demonstrated qualitatively only. Tested scale: standard short-video benchmarks (DAVIS, OpenVid-1M subsets), not stress-scale rollouts. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel element is the unified clean-state interface that reuses the pretrained backbone's native self-attention (with its existing slot layout and Q/K/V projections) as the sole channel for all evidence types, plus EWA's response-space, projection-removed guidance computed within a single forward pass. Individual ingredients — warped-depth conditioning, 3D-proxy rendering, memory retrieval, CFG-style guidance, attention biasing — are established; Warp-as-History in particular already feeds warped observations as pseudo-history, so WiW's advance is the generalization and orchestration, not the primitives. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover the main components (EWA/CGAR, warping, source Plücker, 3D body, history retrieval), and the warping ablation is decisive. However: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests anywhere; ablations are on DAVIS only; Section 4.2 contains no discussion of Table 1 beyond a pointer, and qualitative claims are not backed by user studies. Camera errors are measured by estimating poses from generated videos with Depth Anything 3 and ViPE and averaging — a proxy metric whose estimator bias is not analyzed. A potential Goodhart risk: evidence construction uses depth estimation from the same family of tools used for evaluation. LPIPS for the top two methods differs by 4×10⁻⁶, effectively a tie presented as a win. No code or data release is stated; only a project page (chenxi-song.github.io/worldinworld) is given, so reproducibility currently depends on author goodwill. This is an arXiv preprint (2609.11548), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (inference-time method run on a real frozen checkpoint). Practical: Runs on a single publicly released world-model checkpoint plus commodity perception models (DepthCrafter, LHM++, point tracker), so it should run wherever the backbone runs — no fine-tuning infrastructure needed. Efficient: EWA and CGAR add no NFEs by construction, but the pipeline requires extra forward passes to cache K/V for each evidence channel, depth/avatar/track preprocessing, and maintenance of a rollout-wide K/V archive; no latency, memory, or FLOP numbers are reported. Effective: Evidence supports the claim for camera-following fidelity on short clips; long-horizon revisiting and motion transfer are shown qualitatively, not measured, so effectiveness at the stated exploration task is only partially evidenced. Scalable: Not tested — all quantitative results are short single-video rerenderings; behavior over hundreds of chunks with an ever-growing history bank and accumulating depth/projection error is untested and plausibly degraded. Delivers a method demonstrated in paper form; no software artifact release is stated. Strengths: - The clean-state interface is a genuinely useful abstraction: treating every control (including cross-instance K/V communication between two model instances) as camera/time-labelled states in native attention is a reframing that others can adopt for any frozen causal DiT. - EWA's design is technically sharp: removing the projection onto the native response before amplification, gated by non-negative cosine similarity, regulates evidence strength without extra denoising passes — a concrete improvement over naive CFG-style scaling of auxiliary conditions. - Honest component attribution in the ablations: the paper's own Table 2 shows CGAR/EWA contribute marginally (~0.2° RotError) while warping dominates, which is more informative than typical all-positive ablation tables. - Baseline selection is current and includes concurrent 2026 systems (UniWorld-View, CameraAnything, WorldForge, InSpatio-World) evaluated with official checkpoints, avoiding strawman comparisons. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper does not include an explicit limitations section. Implicitly acknowledged through ablations: warping is indispensable (its removal is catastrophic), evidence reliability varies across regions and stages (motivating ω and γ schedules), and appearance-based attention is ambiguous under large viewpoint change (motivating CGAR). The authors do not confront evaluation-noise, proxy-metric, or scalability limitations directly. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical rigor: single-run results, no seeds or variance, on benchmarks (DAVIS in particular) small enough that several Table 1 margins are within plausible noise (LPIPS ties to 4 decimal places). - Camera-error evaluation depends on monocular pose estimators applied to generated videos — the method's own evidence pipeline uses depth estimation, creating a possible shared-bias loop; no human-verified pose accuracy is reported. - No efficiency measurements despite claiming a zero-extra-NFE advantage; the cost of per-channel K/V caching, preprocessing, and the growing history bank is never quantified. - Long-horizon revisiting — a headline capability — is evaluated only with qualitative figures, not the quantitative protocol used for rerendering. - Dependence on LHM++/SMPL-X limits the rendered-geometry evidence channel to humans; generalization to other subject categories is unaddressed. - No code or checkpoint release stated, so the training-free claim and numbers cannot be independently verified. Bottom Line: A practitioner in controllable video generation gains real value from the clean-state interface idea and the projection-removed attention guidance, but the evidence for superiority over UniWorld-View is thin, single-run, and proxy-measured — read it for the formulation, not for the leaderboard.

Toward Latent Language Model Skills Steering and Optimization: An Empirical Study

X Jiang, J Wu, Y Xiong, S Yu, T Yu, D Arbour, R Sinha… · arxiv.org · Julian McAuley - new articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents an empirical study showing that procedural LLM skills (atomic math operations, algorithmic strategies like DFS vs. BFS) can be represented as directions in activation space that are steerable, composable, personalizable, and evolve non-monotonically under gradient optimization. - Why it's important: It shifts skill control from surface-level prompting to representation-level intervention, which would allow inference-time activation, recombination, and adaptation of procedural capabilities without retraining — relevant to model control, personalization, and interpretability communities. - How it does it: The core move is extracting skill-conditioned layerwise vectors (single-class PCA for math skills, contrastive mean-difference for paired algorithmic strategies) and adding them to hidden states of the last 50% of layers at inference time, plus gradient-based optimization of parameterized directions via RePS. - The good: The composition result is the most credible finding — vector composition of independently extracted atomic directions beats text-based chain-of-thought composition on 13 of 18 composite skills (77.1% vs. 74.2% average on Qwen3-0.6B) with no composite-skill supervision, and reproduces across model families (Llama-2-7B-chat in the appendix). - The missing: There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, and the headline composition margin over the strongest text baseline is only +1.4 points on average — small enough that per-skill variance could plausibly explain the 13/18 count; the personalization result on Qwen3-1.7B is also mixed (steering hurts in 2 of 3 categories). - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in activation steering and LLM interpretability who want a first map of how procedural (rather than stylistic) skills organize in activation space; practitioners seeking deployable skill-control techniques can skip it until the margins and evaluation rigor improve.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (68) is the bright spot — the first systematic map of *procedural* skill steering is a real empirical gap filled, with commendable cross-family replication. Non-Obviousness (55) is moderate since extending activation steering to a new behavior class is a natural next question for the field. Completeness (60) is helped by unusually candid disclosure (answer-in-prompt confound, α grid selection) but hurt by presenting a mixed personalization result as uniform. Problem & Motivation: Prior work treats LLM skills as explicit, surface-level constructs — composable textual operators, executable Python modules, or prompt-specified reasoning chains (SKiC, SkillWeaver, Learning Composable CoT). In parallel, activation steering has controlled stylistic and attribute-level behaviors (tone, persona, refusal, factual associations) but not procedural capabilities with verifiable execution. The open question is whether procedural skills — multi-step behaviors like multi-digit addition or DFS-vs-BFS algorithm selection — are encoded as manipulable structured objects inside the model, or only exist as prompt-level descriptions. Whoever wants fine-grained, training-free control over how a model executes a task (not just what style it answers in) currently lacks such a mechanism. Key Idea: Treat a procedural skill as a layerwise vector v = {vℓ} in activation space, additively injected into hidden states (h̃ℓ = hℓ + αvℓ) on the last 50% of layers, and characterize it through four operational properties: steerability (∃α improving task objective), composition (joint intervention of independently extracted atomic directions, assessed via an empirical proxy Γ̃ = Acc(vector-composed) − Acc(text-CoT)), personalization (preference-conditioned directions from contrastive mean-differences), and evolution (non-monotonic optimization trajectories over the direction parameterization). The conceptual reframing — from skill-as-prompt to skill-as-latent-vector — is the trick; the extraction methods themselves are standard. Methodology: Two extraction schemes matched to skill structure: (1) single-class PCA — for each of 34 SKILLSET-MATH skills, collect up to 500 examples, record last-token hidden states per layer, center activations, and take the top-1 principal component, ℓ2-normalized, applied at α = 2.0; (2) contrastive mean-difference — for each of 9 SKILLSET-CODE approach pairs, v = μ+ − μ− over 200 positive and 200 negative GPT-4o-generated and execution-verified solutions, ℓ2-normalized, applied at α = 1.0. Composition concatenates atomic directions with equal weights αi = 1/k and renormalizes. Evolution optimizes a parameterized direction with RePS for T = 200 steps and evaluates approach match rate (GPT-4o-mini judge) at checkpoints. The formal definitions of validity (∂J/∂α ≠ 0 at α = 0) and steerability are clean, but the paper explicitly does not estimate the interaction gain Γ; it substitutes a performance proxy against text baselines. Critical design decisions: (a) extracting PCA directions from prompts that include the correct answer — disclosed and honestly flagged, but it materially changes interpretation (the direction reflects problem-and-answer conditioning, not autonomous generation); (b) no sign correction for PCA direction indeterminacy, with a fixed α sign across skills — weakly justified; (c) equal-weight additive composition — justified only as a first pass, with richer arithmetic explicitly deferred. Key Results: On SKILLSET-MATH with Qwen3-0.6B, PCA directions improve accuracy on 29 of 34 skills with an average gain of 19.1 percentage points (largest: algebraic_simplification +86, solve_linear_equation +58). Vector composition beats text-CoT composition on 13 of 18 composite skills (Vec 77.1% vs. Txt-CoT 74.2%, Txt-C 75.7%, Base 51.9%). On real benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500) across Qwen3 0.6B–14B, steering matches or exceeds zero-shot in 8 of 10 (model, dataset) cells (e.g., Qwen3-0.6B GSM8K 75.66% vs. 74.00% zero-shot) but offers only modest gains on 4B–14B models where baselines are already 89–97%, and the steered configuration does not beat the strongest few-shot baseline on larger models. Personalization: approach match rate improves on Qwen3-0.6B (e.g., Data Structures/String 16.7% → 45.8%) but degrades on Qwen3-1.7B Graph Search (25.0% → 16.7%); absolute match rates are low (peak 24% for DFS vs. BFS at 0.6B). Evolution: 14 of 18 (pair, model) settings peak strictly before the final optimization step (e.g., Stack vs. Recursion: 4% → 16% at step 8, falling to 10%). Cross-family (Llama-2-7B-chat, appendix): composition reproduces at 13/18, transfer gives +3.26 (GSM8K from 25.25) and +2.80 (MATH500 from 6.00). Baselines are reasonable for the controlled setting (text-concise, text-CoT prompting), but no comparison against modern steering extraction baselines (CAA, SAE-based CorrSteer) is run on the skill tasks. Scale is standard-small: 100 test samples per math skill, 72 code evaluation records, models up to 14B. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. The genuinely novel element is the empirical demonstration that procedural (verifiably-executed) skills — as opposed to the stylistic/attribute behaviors studied in prior steering work — admit direction-based control, composition, and personalization, plus the two controlled skill benchmarks. The extraction methods (top-1 PCA, mean-difference vectors), additive intervention, and RePS optimization are all standard; the contribution is applying them to a new target and characterizing four properties of the result. Rigor & Reproducibility: No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; given composition margins of +1.4 points over the text baseline and code evaluation sets of 72 records, statistical support is thin. The authors are unusually transparent about two confounds: extraction prompts contain the correct answer, and the α = 1.0 for RQ3 was selected from a configured grid {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4} based on tracker runs — a mild cherry-picking risk they disclose. The LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o-mini) protocol for personalization/evolution measures procedural controllability, not functional correctness, and no human validation of judge agreement is reported. Evaluation is primarily on the authors' own controlled benchmarks; the real-benchmark transfer (GSM8K/MATH500) mitigates this but shows shrinking gains with model capability. No code, data, or model release is mentioned. The cross-family Llama-2 appendix is a credibility positive, confirming the composition finding is not Qwen3-specific. The datasets are synthetic/programmatic by design, which the authors defend explicitly as necessary for isolable skills. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (methods run and evaluated in the paper, no deployed system). - Practical: Yes — activation addition requires only forward-pass hooks on open-weight models (Qwen3, Llama-2), all runnable on commodity hardware. - Efficient: Near-zero overhead relative to the base model — one vector addition per layer at inference — and direction extraction is cheap ($63 total API cost for SKILLSET-CODE generation, PCA over ≤500 examples per skill). - Effective: Partially — the evidence supports behavior-shifting on controlled tasks (+19.1pp average) and small real-benchmark gains on small models, but large-model gains are within noise of prompting baselines and code-controllability match rates top out at 24% on the smallest model. - Scalable: Untested beyond 14B; the paper itself shows the intervention's headroom shrinks with model capability, so extrapolation to frontier-scale models is a claim, not a measurement. The work delivers two constructed benchmarks (SKILLSET-MATH, SKILLSET-CODE) and extraction/evaluation procedures but stops at paper form — no released library, tool, or trained artifact is mentioned. Strengths: - First systematic empirical map of procedural skill steering — a genuine gap, since prior steering work targeted style, persona, refusal, and facts; the four-property framing (steerability, composition, personalization, evolution) is a clean, reusable evaluation template. - The composition experiment is well-designed: composed vectors are built only from atomic directions with no composite supervision, so the 13/18 win over text-CoT is evidence of emergent vector-space recombination, not leakage. - Disclosure quality is above average: the authors explicitly flag the answer-in-prompt extraction confound, the PCA sign indeterminacy, the α selection procedure, and that they do not estimate the interaction gain Γ directly — rare candor for this area. - Cross-family replication (Llama-2-7B-chat, different tokenizer/training recipe) with matched 13/18 composition results strengthens the finding beyond a single model family. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper states its claims are bounded by the controlled SKILLSET benchmarks and Qwen3 models, that the controlled datasets do not exhaust real-world procedural skill complexity, and that composition is limited to equal-weighted additive combination — richer vector arithmetic testing whether the geometry encodes procedural relationships is left open. Section C explicitly discusses the answer-in-prompt extraction confound and its interpretive consequences. The authors confront limitations directly rather than minimize them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical treatment anywhere: no seeds, confidence intervals, or tests; the composition margin (+1.4pp over Txt-C, 13/18 skills) and the 14/18 non-monotonicity count could plausibly arise from sampling noise given 100-sample skill test sets and 72-record code evaluations. - Missing steering-method baselines: the paper compares vector composition only against text prompting, never against alternative extraction methods (CAA, SAE features, task vectors) on the same skills, so it is unclear whether PCA extraction is doing anything beyond generic activation perturbation. - The personalization result is fragile: steered performance degrades in 2 of 3 categories on Qwen3-1.7B, yet the abstract and conclusion present personalization as a uniform finding without conditioning on model scale. - Judge-based evaluation without human verification: GPT-4o-mini approach match rates (peaking at 24% at 0.6B) are never validated against human or execution-based agreement, and the judge prompt for the evolution study truncates outputs to 1,500 characters, which could distort code-structure judgments. - The real-benchmark transfer uses a single skill direction (not skill-specific directions), leaving the transfer mechanism unexplained — the paper does not analyze which procedural content the transferred direction encodes. - No ablation over layer scope (why the last 50%?) or over the equal-weight composition scheme. Bottom Line: A useful and unusually honest first empirical map for interpretability researchers specifically interested in whether procedural capabilities live as manipulable directions in activation space — but the thin statistics, missing steering baselines, and near-zero gains on capable models mean practitioners looking for a deployable skill-control technique should wait for a follow-up with proper significance testing and stronger-model evidence.

Analysis of ZigBee implementations using protocol state fuzzing

E Papadopoulou · dspace.lib.ntua.gr · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper (an NTUA diploma thesis) applies protocol state fuzzing — active automata learning of Mealy machines — to the Zigbee protocol for the first time, building a Zigbee-specific mapper and learning alphabet that infer behavioral state-machine models of Zigbee stack implementations. - Why it's important: Zigbee secures billions of deployed smart-home and industrial IoT devices, and its security-critical joining/key-establishment logic is stateful and mostly implemented in closed firmware that conventional testing tools cannot systematically explore. - How it does it: The TTT learning algorithm (via the ProtocolState-Fuzzer/LearnLib stack) sends abstract message symbols through a Python/Scapy mapper that synthesizes concrete IEEE 802.15.4/Zigbee frames, injected either into a virtual radio co-processor interface for a software stack or over-the-air via custom nRF52840 injector/sniffer firmware. - The good: The software-only experiment fully converged to a 7-state Mealy machine (1,228 test sequences, 13,944 input symbols, ~30.5 hours) and surfaced three concrete spec deviations in zigbee-on-host, including authentication bypassing the unique Trust Center Link Key exchange. - The missing: The over-the-air experiment on real hardware (TI CC2652P/Z-Stack) never converged due to timing non-determinism, so the headline claim that PSF works for wireless Zigbee is demonstrated on only one software stack, with the hardware result being a manually constructed exploratory diagram, not a learned model. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you work on model learning of IoT/industrial protocols or want a practical account of the mapper/non-determinism engineering required to port PSF from wired protocols to a wireless stack; skip it if you want new learning algorithms, formal guarantees, or broadly generalizable vulnerability findings.
Why this rank

The composite is pulled down by Rigor (55) — a single converged software stack, non-converged hardware runs, an unreviewed thesis, and no released mapper/firmware — and by Practical Impact (40), since the reusable artifacts are not stated as public. Novelty (62) is genuine but incremental: first PSF application to Zigbee is a new empirical finding, not a new formulation. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Zigbee stack implementations are stateful programs whose security-critical procedures (association, network-key transport, Trust Center Link Key exchange, rejoin) can harbor invalid state transitions that enable security bypasses — a bug class previously exposed by protocol state fuzzing in TLS, DTLS, SSH, EDHOC, QUIC, and BLE. Most Zigbee implementations are closed-source and embedded, so source-level analysis is unavailable, and manual testing cannot exhaust the state space of invalid message orderings. Prior Zigbee security work (SecBee, KillerBee-based attacks, Touchlink/rejoin attacks) and coverage-guided fuzzers (Z-Fuzzer, TaintBFuzz) either require manual test design or target crash/coverage-based vulnerability discovery rather than inferring an implementation's state machine. The gap this work closes: no prior study applies black-box state-machine learning to Zigbee, and it is non-trivial to do so because a wireless stack emits asynchronous MAC ACKs, beacons, and periodic link-status traffic that violate the determinism assumption of active learning. Key Idea: The core move is to treat Zigbee message types as the input alphabet of a Mealy-machine learning problem and to absorb all wireless/timing non-determinism into a carefully engineered mapper — defaulting packet fields to keep the alphabet combinatorially small, filtering periodic frames (NWK_LINK_STATUS), polling with MAC_DATA_REQUEST to flush queued responses, matching late beacons to their triggering requests, and using dual min/max response timeouts — so that the standard TTT active-learning loop converges against a wireless protocol stack. This is an adaptation of an existing technique to a new protocol, with the intellectual weight in the abstraction/filtering design rather than in a new algorithm. Methodology: The pipeline uses the open-source ProtocolState-Fuzzer framework with LearnLib's TTT algorithm, alternating hypothesis construction and approximated equivalence checking. A Zigbee-specific mapper (Python, Scapy) translates between 10 abstract input symbols (MAC_BEACON_REQUEST, MAC_ASSOCIATION_REQUEST, MAC_DATA_REQUEST, MAC_DISASSOCIATION_NOTIFY, NWK_REJOIN_REQUEST_TC/SECURE, APS_TCLK_REQUEST, APS_NWK_KEY_REQUEST, APS_VERIFY_TCLK, ZDO_NODE_DESCRIPTOR_REQUEST) and concrete frames; output symbols are deduplicated, alphabetically sorted concatenations of response types, with EMPTYRESPONSE for silence. Two setups are compared: (1) software-only — the zigbee-on-host stack runs on the host, its Radio Co-Processor emulated via a virtual Spinel/HDLC endpoint on localhost:6000, with SUT reset by killing the process, deleting zoh.save, and restarting after a 2-second delay; (2) over-the-air — a Sonoff Zigbee 3.0 dongle (TI CC2652P running Z-Stack/ZNP) as coordinator, driven by custom injector/sniffer firmware written for nRF52840 on Zephyr, with SUT reset by reloading a saved ZNP JSON state file. The final ZOH experiment used an 8-frame alphabet. Critical design decisions: (a) collapsing packet parameters into mapper defaults rather than into symbol names (justified — the alternative causes combinatorial alphabet explosion); (b) ignoring periodic messages and polling for queued responses (well-justified, with evidence that polling otherwise nearly doubles model size); (c) resetting the OTA coordinator via ZNP state-file restore rather than hardware reset (sensible, but insufficient to achieve convergence, as the non-determinism turned out to be response timing, not state contamination). An embedded CPython interpreter inside the Java PSF process bridges the learner to the Python mapper. Key Results: For zigbee-on-host (commit d086975, pinned for reproducibility), the learned Mealy machine has 7 states, obtained after 6 hypotheses and 5 counterexamples; 1,228 test sequences comprising 13,944 input symbols ran in ~30.5 hours, with the final hypothesis produced after 2.82 hours (225 sequences, 1,084 input symbols); the equivalence-testing budget was cut from 3,000 to ~1,000 sequences after results stabilized. The model exposes three specification deviations: (1) an authenticated state is reachable by verifying the global TCLK (ZigBeeAlliance09) immediately after receiving the Network Key, skipping the unique-TCLK exchange — because ZOH reuses the same key for both roles; (2) the NWK Key can be requested and received before any MAC association; (3) MAC association is accepted from multiple partially-progressed states rather than only the pre-join state. For the over-the-air TI CC2652P/Z-Stack target, the learning algorithm did not converge in any run due to timing non-determinism; exploratory runs confirmed association, NWK Key transport, and a coordinator-initiated "ZDO Interview" sequence (node/active-endpoint/simple-descriptor requests plus ZCL attribute read), summarized in a manually constructed, essentially linear 7-state diagram that the authors explicitly distinguish from a formally learned model. Baselines: there are no competing tools benchmarked — Z-Fuzzer and TaintBFuzz are discussed as related but with different objectives; the only implementation with a converged model is one open-source stack. Scale is modest: one software stack plus one hardware dongle, an 8-symbol alphabet, single-digit state counts. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (with a weak claim to a new-application setting). Genuinely novel: the first protocol-state-fuzzing models of Zigbee stacks and the specific ZOH deviations (pre-association key acquisition, dual-use of the global TCLK). Standard combination of existing ideas: L*/TTT active learning, the PSF framework, LearnLib, Scapy, and the mapper pattern are all established — the contribution is porting them to Zigbee and the non-determinism engineering, mirroring how the same group previously ported the framework to BLE. No new learning algorithm or formulation is introduced. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist implicitly — multiple alphabets were tried, and the paper reports that including ZDO_NODE_DESCRIPTOR_REQUEST and MAC_DISASSOCIATION in exploratory runs added noise, motivating the trimmed final alphabet; the polling-vs-no-polling effect on model size is quantified qualitatively ("almost doubling the number of states"). No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported — inevitable for a single-run learning experiment, but the equivalence check is approximated and the budget reduction from 3,000 to ~1,000 sequences is an experimenter decision that weakens confidence guarantees. Reproducibility is helped by pinning zigbee-on-host to commit d086975 (full SHA-1 given); no URL for the thesis's own mapper, firmware, or models is provided — the custom nRF52840 firmware and Zigbee mapper are described but not stated as publicly released. Methodological concerns: the central security finding is derived from a single open-source implementation (ZOH), and the hardware result is non-converged, so "PSF works for wireless Zigbee" rests on one success case; the operational definition of "authenticated state" is honestly flagged as behavioral, not specification-faithful, but no exploit or impact analysis backs the security relevance of the deviations. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — custom firmware and mapper were built and run). - Practical: Yes — the software setup runs on a single host machine with a virtual RCP endpoint, and the hardware setup needs only commodity dongles (Sonoff CC2652P, nRF52840), all commercially available. - Efficient: Not efficient in absolute terms — 30.5 hours of learning for a 7-state model on a fast local interface; over-the-air runs are slower still, and the per-query reset cost (process restart or JSON state restore) dominates. - Effective: Effective for the software target (a converged model with real spec deviations was produced), but only partially effective for the stated hardware goal, where the evidence is exploratory observation rather than a learned model. - Scalable: Untested beyond one target per setup; the authors themselves propose, but do not evaluate, adaptive timeouts, per-input delay profiles, and statistical equivalence checking as prerequisites for scaling to more stacks and larger alphabets. The work delivers a partially reusable artifact (Zigbee mapper, virtual RCP endpoint, nRF52840 injector/sniffer firmware) whose release is not stated; as published it primarily exists in paper form. Strengths: - First successful application of protocol state fuzzing to Zigbee, with a genuinely converged Mealy model on a real stack and concrete, spec-referenced deviations — the pre-association NWK-key path and the global/unique TCLK reuse are specific, verifiable findings, not generic fuzzing noise. - The non-determinism treatment (Section 5.5) is the most transferable contribution: dual timeouts with a response-adequacy heuristic, periodic-frame filtering, forced polling, beacon-to-request matching, and conditional ZDO-response filtering form a practical playbook for anyone learning models of asynchronous wireless stacks. - Honest reporting of negative results: the thesis explicitly states the over-the-air learning did not converge, clearly separates the manually constructed exploratory diagram from formally learned models, and defines "authenticated" operationally rather than overclaiming specification conformance semantics. - Dual-setup comparison (virtual RCP vs. over-the-air) is a well-designed controlled contrast that isolates exactly which difficulties come from the wireless medium — timing non-determinism — versus the stack itself. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: the over-the-air experiment failed to converge due to timing-induced non-determinism and produced no stable model; the exploratory OTA model is manually constructed, not learned; TCLK acquisition/verification on the hardware target could not be established (and is presumed unsupported in that build); consumer Zigbee devices requiring manual button presses to enter pairing mode make broad OTA testing impractical; the alphabet covers only joining/rejoin-related frames, excluding ZDO commands, application-layer frames, and ZCL sequences; and the fuzzer acted only as an end device, leaving coordinator/router-role behavior untested. They confront limitations directly and propose concrete remedies (adaptive timeout calibration, per-input delay profiles, statistical equivalence tolerating bounded non-determinism, role impersonation, additional stacks) — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Several issues a critical reviewer would flag that the authors do not fully address: (1) The security significance of the ZOH deviations is asserted but not demonstrated — the pre-association NWK key is protected under the publicly known ZigBeeAlliance09 global key, so the paper does not show any attacker-advantage scenario, exploit, or model-checked security property violation; "deviation from spec" and "vulnerability" are conflated at points. (2) Only one implementation yielded a learned model, so the claim that PSF "scales to a realistic IoT protocol" generalizes from n=1 success; the hardware failure is described but no solution is attempted (e.g., the adaptive-timeout approaches are left as future work despite being the crux). (3) No comparison of learning cost or bug-finding yield against coverage-guided alternatives (Z-Fuzzer, TaintBFuzz) on the same target, making it impossible to judge whether state fuzzing is the right tool for Zigbee versus merely a feasible one. (4) The mapper's filtering rules (ignoring periodic frames, conditional ZDO-response handling) could in principle mask real non-deterministic or security-relevant behaviors; the paper does not analyze what was filtered away. (5) No release of the mapper, firmware, or learned models (dot/沟 files) is stated, limiting reproducibility despite the pinned commit. (6) As a diploma thesis dated June 2026, it has not undergone external peer review. Bottom Line: For researchers extending automata-learning-based protocol analysis to new wireless or embedded protocols, this thesis is a worthwhile, practically instructive case study — the mapper design and honest non-determinism accounting are directly reusable — but its empirical findings are narrow (one software stack, unverified security impact, non-converged hardware run), and no stronger published alternative currently covers protocol state fuzzing of Zigbee.

CORAL

arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CORAL, an LLM-agent harness that runs a continual closed loop around a live production recommender, autonomously reallocating constrained resources (retrieval budgets, serving-capacity treatments) and learning from the A/B-measured consequences of its own prior decisions. - Why it's important: Production recommender tuning is bounded by engineer-weeks per lever while the optimal operating point drifts continuously; an autonomous loop compresses a tuning cycle from several engineer-weeks to a few autonomous days at negligible inference cost (order of tens of USD per deployment). - How it does it: An LLM reasons over per-unit operating statistics plus a three-store memory of its past configurations and attributed outcomes, and delegates budget feasibility to a constrained optimizer that projects each proposal onto the budget-feasible set, so every deployed configuration provably satisfies the cost cap. - The good: Two A/B experiments on large-scale production platforms at Meta — one improving watch time by +0.15% and sessions by +0.16% at no added serving cost (and +0.23% sessions for new low-signal users), the other saving millions of USD in annualized capacity with engagement statistically unchanged — with the same harness reused across both decision types. - The missing: There is no baseline comparison against non-LLM alternatives (Bayesian optimization, bandits, or the constrained optimizer driven without the LLM), no ablations isolating which harness components matter, and no offline or simulated evaluation; all evidence is two self-reported deployments on the authors' own platforms. - Read it or not: Worth reading for RecSys and agentic-systems practitioners interested in productionizing LLM agents on live infrastructure; skippable for readers seeking methodological novelty in optimization or agent learning, since the technical machinery is standard.

Problem & Motivation: A modern industrial recommender is a multi-stage system (retrieval, ranking, serving) governed by many hand-set parameters — retrieval-source budget shares, per-segment serving treatments, caching policies — that engineers revise slowly through online experiments. Because each experiment probes a small region of the design space and each cycle is expensive, parts of the system are revisited infrequently and drift as content, user behavior, and upstream models shift; the paper argues low-signal and new users are systematically underserved under aggregate-metric-driven manual tuning. Prior LLM-agent work acts on models, user representations, or offline development pipelines; comparatively few place an agent in a continual loop acting on a live deployed system and adapting from measured consequences. The gap CORAL targets is autonomous, continual reconfiguration of a live recommender's control surface under hard operating constraints. Key Idea: The core move is a division of labor: the LLM contributes only bounded, per-unit adjustment proposals informed by memory of its own past decisions and their measured effects, while deterministic tools — most critically a constrained optimizer that projects any proposal onto the budget-feasible set {s : c(s) ≤ B} — supply hard guarantees the model cannot. Wrapped in a fixed-cadence loop where each deployed configuration persists for one cycle so its effect can be attributed to the agent's most recent decision, this lets a frozen (no parameter updates) LLM policy improve in context over successive cycles. The budget-projection tool is the load-bearing trick: it converts an unreliable free-form proposer into a provably budget-feasible controller. Methodology: The paper formulates the task as a partially observed, non-stationary, constrained optimization problem: at cycle t the agent selects configuration s_t = (s_t,1,…,s_t,N) over N control units to minimize cumulative shortfall Σ_t [J_t(s_t) − J_t(s_t)] subject to c_t(s_t) ≤ B, where the oracle optimum s_t moves as the operating context drifts. The policy is an LLM mapping observation o_t and memory M_t (window of m = 3 cycles) to a configuration. The harness has three parts: (1) a persistent memory with observation, assessment (the model's own natural-language diagnoses), and decision-plus-attributed-outcome stores; (2) deterministic tools — analysis, memory retrieval, effect attribution, the constrained optimizer (projection onto the feasible set, identity when already feasible), and a deployment tool; (3) a closed loop on a k = 3-day cadence with fixed control flow (the model does not choose the workflow), where each configuration's A/B-measured effect is written back to memory. Design decisions worth flagging: k and m are explicitly chosen as "sensible defaults" rather than tuned (acknowledged); fixed control flow rather than agentic planning is justified only informally; and the attribution of outcome deltas to the agent's last decision is confounded by non-stationarity, addressed only by the 3-day window logic, not rigorously. Key Results: Case study 1 (retrieval-budget allocation on a large-scale video service, A/B over millions of users): across three successive loop rounds, watch time went +0.13% (R1, zero-shot), neutral (R2, agent overcorrected), then the deployed R3 configuration achieved +0.15% watch time, +0.16% sessions overall, and +0.77% sessions in the largest market, at no additional serving cost. Per-segment allocation raised video-viewing sessions for new low-signal users by +0.23%. Case study 2 (serving-capacity treatment per user segment, different service): round one saved "millions of USD in annualized capacity expenditure" (no exact figure given); round two extended the same change to additional segments, increasing savings by 44% with engagement statistically unchanged. LLM compute cost is per-cycle, not per-request: roughly 8–10 calls of ~1,500–2,500 output tokens per cycle, total ~10^6 tokens per deployment, on the order of tens of USD. Baselines are absent — there is no comparison against manual engineering baselines, Bayesian optimization, bandits, or an LLM-free optimizer pipeline; "improvement over cycles" is shown by comparing the agent's own successive rounds. Scale is production-grade (millions of users), which is the paper's strongest evidentiary asset. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. What is genuinely novel is the deployment pattern: an LLM agent in a continual closed loop acting directly on a live production recommender's control surface and adapting from its own A/B-measured outcomes — a setting the related work (AgentX, NOVA, agentic recommenders) largely does not cover. The formulation (constrained resource allocation), the components (LLM + memory + tools + projection onto a feasible set), and the evaluation method (A/B testing) are all standard; the contribution is their competent integration and the rare production evidence, not a new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are effectively absent: the memory horizon (m = 3), cadence (k = 3 days), and the contribution of each tool/memory store are not ablated — the authors state these were chosen as defaults. No error bars, seeds, or confidence intervals beyond the A/B significance statements are reported; effect sizes are small (+0.13% to +0.77%) and only assertively labeled statistically significant. No code, prompts beyond one abstracted template, data, or model identity are released, and the underlying systems are Meta-internal, so reproduction is impossible for outsiders. Two methodological concerns stand out: (1) all evidence is self-reported on the authors' own platforms with no external baseline, and (2) the attribution mechanism (before/after comparison over a single cycle in a non-stationary system) risks crediting or blaming the agent for context drift. The non-monotonic R2 result (neutral) is honestly reported, which is a credibility positive. This is a preprint (arXiv 2609.02730, September 2026) and appears not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL / SYSTEMS (a built harness run on two live production services). - Practical: Yes — it runs on commodity LLM APIs at tens of USD per deployment and requires only read access to telemetry and write access to an existing control surface, though that control surface itself exists only inside Meta. - Efficient: Highly — cost is per decision cycle (a handful of ~10^3-token calls), independent of traffic and user count, which the paper correctly identifies as the decisive economic property versus per-request LLM inference. - Effective: The A/B evidence supports the specific claimed outcomes (engagement gains at flat cost; savings at flat engagement), but only for one decision class — constrained allocation — and with attribution confounded by non-stationarity. - Scalable: Cost is argued (correctly) to be traffic-independent, but scaling to 10–100× more control units or finer cadences is untested; the prompt packs all per-unit signals into a few thousand input tokens, which may not survive many more units. The work delivers no public software artifact — the harness, code, and platforms are internal, so it stops at paper form plus an abstracted prompt template. Strengths: - Real production evidence: two A/B-tested deployments on large-scale live platforms spanning both the engagement objective (+0.15% watch time, +0.16% sessions, +0.23% for new low-signal users) and the efficiency objective (millions of USD annualized savings, +44% in round two) — a level of evidence most agentic-RecSys papers lack. - The constrained-optimizer-as-projection design cleanly separates LLM judgment from numerical feasibility, giving provable budget compliance — a concrete answer to the reliability objection against LLM controllers. - Honest reporting of the non-monotonic learning trajectory (R1 positive, R2 neutral, R3 best), which is more persuasive evidence of genuine in-context adaptation than a uniformly improving curve would be. - The cost analysis (per-cycle, traffic-independent inference cost, ~10^6 tokens per deployment) is a correct and often-missed insight distinguishing control-surface agents from per-request LLM serving. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) the loop still requires human supervision, with automated guardrails (feasibility checks, bounded-change limits, safety constraints) only partially replacing oversight; (2) both deployments instantiate a single decision class — constrained allocation of resources across components — leaving other levers (retrieval and ranking logic itself) untested; (3) evaluation relies on costly, setting-specific A/B experiments with no standardized pre-deployment evaluation method for agent-driven optimization. They also flag that k and m are untuned defaults. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No baselines of any kind: the central unstated comparison is whether an LLM agent beats Bayesian optimization, contextual bandits, or even the constrained optimizer driven by simple heuristic signals — all cheaper and more reproducible candidates for constrained allocation. Without this, the LLM's marginal value over classical methods is unquantified. - Ablations are missing: no experiment isolates whether the memory of past decisions (versus current statistics alone) drives the improvement, whether the assessment store matters, or whether a smaller/cheaper model suffices. - Effect attribution over a single 3-day window in a non-stationary system is confounded (seasonality, upstream model pushes, content mix shifts); the paper's learning-in-context claim rests on this fragile attribution. - The LLM backbone, its version, and prompting variants are unspecified beyond an abstracted template, blocking reproduction and making the results uninterpretable across model generations. - The claimed "order-of-magnitude faster turnaround than engineer-weeks" is asserted, not measured — no human-engineer control arm was run. - Small effect sizes (+0.13–0.23% on most metrics) are individually modest; only the efficiency case has a headline number, and it is reported as "millions of USD" without a figure. Bottom Line: This is a valuable field report on an underexplored deployment pattern — LLM agents as continual optimizers of live recommender control surfaces — and practitioners building agentic infrastructure should read it for the harness design and cost analysis, but as a scientific claim about LLM agents' optimization ability it is unproven until tested against classical constrained-optimization baselines.

TL;DR - What it does: This master's thesis builds and evaluates an integrated pipeline — assumed symbolic planner → templated language module → frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 → contrastive goal-conditioned policy — and shows that CLIP-encoded text and symbolic goals can drive the same contrastive policy that image goals do on five simulated Sawyer manipulation tasks. - Why it's important: Goal images are impractical at deployment and entangle goals with irrelevant visual detail, while symbolic/language goals are compositional and planner-friendly; skip it if you need real-robot evidence or end-to-end perception-to-planning systems.

Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires both deciding which subtasks to achieve and in what order (high-level) and continuous control to achieve each (low-level). Pure RL struggles to discover long-horizon structure from raw pixels under sparse rewards; symbolic planners reason about structure but their abstractions are hard to ground in perception. The natural middle ground — planner supplies structure, learned policy supplies control — needs an interface between them. Contrastive goal-conditioned RL offers a reward-free controller but typically conditions on goal images, which are impractical to obtain at deployment and over-specify the goal. The open question is whether a cheaper, abstract goal (a sentence or predicate set) encoded by CLIP carries enough information to condition the same contrastive policy, and whether any residual gap is due to the encoding or to missing information. The thesis also isolates a second axis: how sub-goal granularity interacts with goal type. Key Idea: Treat a frozen vision-language embedding space (CLIP) as the entire goal interface between a symbolic planner and a contrastive continuous controller — and then disentangle two confounds via level-matched ablations: (a) encoding vs. information, by making a raw predicate vector and a rendered sentence express exactly the same facts through the same frozen state-action encoder, and (b) granularity vs. goal type, by evaluating coarse/medium/fine decompositions for all four representations. The planner itself is deliberately assumed (predicates read from ground-truth simulator state) so the goal interface is studied in isolation. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages: (1) an assumed high-level planner emits a sequence of symbolic sub-goal states from a 12-predicate vocabulary (nine skill-level configuration predicates, three contact predicates, arity ≤1, closed-world); (2) a language module renders active predicates into text via fixed templates in three styles (pddl-tuples, short phrases, long narratives), selected from 324 phrasing variants by a policy-free template study on discriminability, image–text alignment, and text distinctness; (3) a frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 embeds both the 224×224 observation and the goal (image, text, or — for ablations — identity-encoded 9–12-d predicate vector or 700-d voxel multi-hot); (4) a contrastive actor-critic (factored critic φ(s,a)·ψ(g) trained with a binary NCE objective whose optimum is Q-proportional per Eysenbach et al., plus a Gaussian actor and behavior-cloning term) acts on the embeddings. Training uses a 48-run stage-1 sweep (trajectory granularity, width, batch, LR, augmentation) on scripted-expert offline data (20 scene variants × 200 rollouts, 75-step skills), then a two-stage image-then-text curriculum warm-starting stage 2 from the two best stage-1 checkpoints with the state-action encoder frozen. Critical design decisions: freezing the state-action encoder for clean ablation attribution (well-justified, but acknowledged to run on a conservative substrate since from-scratch does better); skill-divider detection by first object motion rather than noisy contact predicates (well-justified with 90%+ consistency checks); augmentation applied only to the behavior-cloning term, not the critic targets (reasoned and consistent with the baseline). Symbolic predicates are computed directly from simulator state — no PDDL planner is actually run. Key Results: On the five fixed tasks from the baseline paper (drawer, pnp, pnp+drawer, push+drawer, drawer+push): (RQ1) the best single deployable CLIP-text configuration reaches ≈58% cross-task mean success vs ≈76% for the raw-image baseline of Zheng et al., tying/beating on drawer (100/100 vs 100) and drawer+push (80/80 vs 60) but trailing on pnp (30/40 vs 60), pnp+drawer (70/50 vs 100), and push+drawer (10/20 vs 60); manual failure analysis attributes roughly half the push+drawer shortfall to a strict geometric success criterion rejecting goal-reaching rollouts (5 of 9 "failures" are measurement artifacts). (RQ2) With information level-matched, CLIP-text > pddl-direct > voxel on composite goals (e.g., coarse: 43 vs 15 vs 10 on push+drawer), but the encodings converge on isolated single skills (iso-fine: 86/86 vs 83/81); the gap is one of composing goals, not reaching them. (RQ3) Granularity inverts with goal type: the oracle CLIP-image goal is best coarse (73% vs 54/52%), while all three abstract goals peak at medium (CLIP-text 57%, exceeding the oracle's 54% at that granularity); sequence penalty mostly matches the independence prediction (r=0.87, MAE 0.12), with one genuine broken hand-off (push+drawer at medium: 15% despite 86% product prediction). (RQ4) LoRA adaptation lifts held-out image-to-text retrieval ~10× (0.01–0.02 → 0.14) but hurts end-to-end control (42% vs 58% best config); the from-scratch policy matches or beats the two-stage curriculum at every granularity (coarse 56 vs 45, iso-medium 100 vs 81). Zero-shot text transfer on the stage-1 policy drops success from 76/70% to 25/34%. Baselines are current (the direct 2024-era contrastive-RL baseline paper) but the study is at toy scale: one simulated domain, five tasks, two carried checkpoints. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the granularity effect inverting between image and abstract goals; encoding mattering only for goal composition) plus a modest NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the planner→language→CLIP→contrastive-policy integration with symbolic-conditioned variants of stable contrastive RL). The core components — contrastive RL, CLIP, LoRA, STRIPS-style sub-goaling, template rendering — are all standard; the genuinely novel part is the controlled encoding-vs-information ablation design and the systematic granularity×goal-representation grid, not any single algorithmic mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are the thesis's strength: four goal representations share one frozen state-action encoder, symbolic and language goals are level-matched to identical facts, and the evaluation scheme separates selection-time from reporting-time metrics with an explicit peak convention, held-out diagnostics never used for selection, 95% CIs over per-(model, task) rates for the granularity analysis, and a quantitative failure taxonomy over all 50 rollouts. Deterministic seeds and fixed tasks are stated. Concerns: a single training seed per sweep cell (training instability is itself documented — per-task success is strongly non-monotonic, MASD ≈0.15–0.18 between checkpoints), only two carried stage-1 checkpoints, very small n (10 cells behind the headline CIs, which are wide — e.g., coarse oracle 73 ± 18.5), the peak convention inflates best-cell numbers, and no code release URL is stated in the provided text. The symbolic side is an oracle (predicates read from ground-truth state), so the system is never evaluated under its own stated motivation of grounding planner abstractions in perception. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a simulated system with experiments actually run; no theoretical claims). Practical: Yes — PyBullet simulation, CLIP ViT-B/32, and small MLP heads run on commodity hardware. Effective: Partially — the evidence shows abstract goals can drive the policy at all (never collapsing to zero) but does not show it matching the baseline at a single deployable configuration on composite tasks. Scalable: Untested — nothing beyond the single 7-DOF Sawyer tabletop domain; the authors claim no scaling, and the frozen-encoder, oracle-planner assumptions would each need re-examination at scale. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model to the community per the provided text (reproducibility is stated via determinism, not release); it stops at thesis form. Strengths: - The encoding-vs-information ablation is a genuinely careful experimental design: level-matching predicate vectors and rendered sentences to identical facts, with a shared frozen state-action encoder, makes the RQ2 conclusion (the gap is compositional, not informational) well-earned rather than asserted. - The granularity-inversion finding — coarser is better for image goals (73 vs 54/52), medium is best for all abstract goals, with CLIP-text exceeding the oracle image at medium (57 vs 54) — is a non-obvious, actionable result for anyone designing hierarchical goal interfaces. - The honest treatment of its own negative results (LoRA and the curriculum both fail to help; the headline method trails its own baseline) plus a quantitative error-composition analysis (sequence success ≈ product of isolated sub-goal successes, r=0.87) that localizes the one genuinely broken skill hand-off. - The skill-divider methodology (first-object-motion ground truth for validating contact predicates, with 90%+ step-function consistency checks) is a competent, verifiable data-engineering contribution. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The abstract and Section 7.2 state directly: confinement to a single simulated domain with no real-robot transfer; a frozen CLIP backbone; symbolic sub-goals computed directly from environment state in place of a PDDL planner; weak off-the-shelf CLIP grounding of rendered scenes; and the reproducible five-task protocol inherited from the baseline. The thesis also confronts the frozen-encoder conservatism (from-scratch beats the curriculum, so ablations run on a substrate below what end-to-end training achieves), the strict success-criterion measurement artifact inflating push+drawer failures, and that RQ4 is "largely a negative result." This is direct, non-minimizing limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No perception component at all: predicates are read from ground-truth simulator state, so the system never tests the perception-grounding problem that motivates the entire symbolic-to-embedding bridge — the hardest part of the claimed application is assumed away twice (planner and predicate detection). - Single training seed throughout a sweep whose own diagnostics show severe non-monotonicity and overfitting (held-out GCBC loss rising while training loss falls); the peak convention applied on top of one seed makes the ≈58% vs ≈76% headline comparison fragile. - Only two carried stage-1 checkpoints seed all stage-2 conclusions; checkpoint-selection variance is unquantified. - The template study's image-to-text retrieval sits at chance for every style and its ordering is unstable — the intrinsic metrics used to select the training templates are admitted weak proxies, an unquantified selection risk for the downstream results. - The voxel ablation's failure is partly by construction (height bins of ≈7 cm against a 1 cm placement tolerance), which the authors note but which means the "CLIP-text > voxel" ordering partially measures bin resolution, not representation quality. - No comparison to the natural alternatives in its own related-work section — e.g., LIV's jointly trained vision-language value function, or a language-conditioned behavior-cloning baseline — so "CLIP embeddings as interface" is only compared against image goals, not against other language-conditioning mechanisms. Bottom Line: A rigorously controlled but deliberately narrow simulation study that earns its two real findings — granularity inverting with goal type, and the abstract-goal gap being compositional rather than informational — and is worth reading for anyone designing goal-representation interfaces, though practitioners needing a working symbolic-to-control system will find the oracle-planner and ground-truth-predicate assumptions leave the hard problems unaddressed.

#142 — Moderately Innovative (54)

EmbodiedSkills: A Unified Framework for Orchestrating, Training, and Deploying VLA Agents (11 ▲ )

arxiv.org · Daily papers of 8 Sep 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EmbodiedSkills, a framework that turns a VLA action policy into a closed-loop robot agent by wrapping low-level action generation in a six-phase skill loop (Observe, Plan, Preflight, Execute, Verify, Recover) where a guarded runtime validates every skill decision before execution and verifies outcomes after. - Why it's important: End-to-end VLA policies can make it impossible to localize why a long-horizon manipulation failed (grounding, planning, execution, or verification), and no runtime mechanism currently enforces that a model's proposed skill call is valid against the live physical state. - How it does it: The core move is policy–runtime separation: the high-level VLM only proposes structured skill calls against typed contracts with explicit prerequisites, while a deterministic guarded runtime enforces artifact freshness, action validity, and legal state transitions — so a textual proposal can never be silently executed as a physical action. - The good: The controlled AgentLoop ablation on 5,000 RoboTwin 2.0 episodes is the strongest evidence: removing verification drops success from 86.20% to 48.2%, removing subtask conditioning to 34.4%, and forcing one 32-step chunk per subtask to 19.5%, isolating exactly which loop mechanisms matter. - The missing: The headline 86.20% comes from 50 per-task fine-tuned π0.5 specialists, not from the framework itself, and the paper never evaluates the full AgentLoop against a strong agentic baseline (e.g., Inner Monologue-style replanning or RoboClaw), so the loop's net benefit over simpler closed-loop orchestration is not quantified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for robotics researchers building agent layers on top of VLA policies — the contract/guard design and ablation numbers are concrete and reusable — but skip it if you want a validated generalist agent or real-robot deployment results.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. The paper's central weakness is that Novelty (55) and Rigor (58) are both middling: the guarded skill-contract runtime is a well-formalized but largely behavioral-tree-adjacent orchestration layer, and the headline 86.20% comes from 50 per-task π0.5 specialists rather than the framework, which is never compared against any agentic baseline (Inner Monologue-style replanning, SayCan-style systems). Resilience (50) collapses under the observation that the loop's net contribution over the underlying policies is unquantified, and no verifier error rates, seeds, or artifact release (Impact 30) are provided. The honest limitations section and the genuinely diagnostic three-way ablation keep Completeness (62) respectable. Weighted composite: 0.20*55 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*50 + 0.10*30 = 54.

Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires more than next-action prediction: an agent must coordinate perception, subgoal planning, execution, progress verification, and recovery under partial observability. End-to-end VLA policies leave these intermediate decisions implicit, so failures are hard to attribute; LLM-based robotic agents make decisions explicit, but a model-generated decision can be stale, schema-invalid, or physically unexecutable, and prompting alone cannot enforce execution constraints or verify physical outcomes. The intended users are robotics and embodied-AI teams who need a diagnosable, trainable agent layer around VLA backends such as π0.5. Key Idea: Treat every skill decision as an execution proposal checked by a guarded runtime: each skill is a typed contract (inputs, outputs, prerequisites, execution, post-state update, failure mapping), artifacts carry provenance and freshness so stale observations cannot authorize new actions, and the runtime — not the prompt — owns validity, giving a closed loop that is diagnosable by construction. This is a formalization of the policy–environment separation familiar from behavior trees and hierarchical RL, expressed as a finite-state guard system over a VLM planner and a VLA executor. Methodology: The method formalizes an episode state st = (zt, Mt, Ht) — phase, typed artifacts, ordered trace — over six phases (Observe, Plan, Preflight, Execute, Verify, Recover), which the paper stresses is a semantic structure, not a one-pass pipeline. The high-level policy emits one of three controls (RunSkill, AdvanceStage, FinishRun); guards (Eqs. 7–9) validate stage compatibility, prerequisites, freshness, action schema, horizon bounds (0 < H ≤ Hmax), and legality, with blocked decisions recorded as evidence rather than executed (Eq. 10, Algorithm 1). Execute runs bounded action chunks from a subgoal-conditioned π0.5 policy; Verify judges the active subgoal from fresh post-action observations and picks one of six routes (Advance/Continue/Reobserve/Replan/Recover/Finish); terminal success remains the benchmark evaluator's, not the verifier's. Training is component-level SFT on deployment-consistent traces (planner, scheduler on Qwen3-VL with the VLA frozen, optional verifier), plus an optional GRPO-style group-relative online objective (Eqs. 17–18) that the authors explicitly demote to refinement. Critical design decisions: (1) freezing the low-level VLA during high-level SFT — justified as isolating continuous control learning, but untested against joint tuning; (2) bounded chunking with adaptive continuation — strongly justified by the ablation; (3) per-task VLA specialization — acknowledged as costly but used anyway. Key Results: On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (100 episodes each), the task-adapted per-task π0.5 policies reach 86.20% macro-average versus 82.74% for the π0.5 reference reported by LingBot-VA (+3.46 pp; better on 39 tasks, worse on 10), against baselines ACT (29.7%), DP (28.0%), RDT (34.5%), DP3 (55.2%), π0 (65.9%), and X-VLA (72.8%). On LIBERO the instantiation averages 97.40% versus the official OpenPI 96.85% (+0.55 pp; LIBERO-Long +1.2 pp) — a margin within plausible seed noise given near-saturated suites. On four memory-dependent RMBench M(n) tasks, the same approach reaches 12.5% versus 7.3% for X-VLA and 5.5% for π0.5 — low absolute performance, honestly reported. The AgentLoop ablations (Full 86.20 → w/o Verify 48.2 → w/o Subtask 34.4 → one-chunk 19.5) are the most informative quantitative finding: intermediate verification and adaptive multi-chunk continuation each contribute roughly 38–67 points. All evaluation is in simulation; baselines are current for VLA comparisons but the framework itself is never compared against an alternative agentic orchestration method. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely new element is the guarded skill-contract runtime that separates policy proposals from enforced execution semantics and doubles as a trajectory schema for training and diagnosis; the constituent ideas (LLM planners with affordance grounding à la SayCan/Inner Monologue, options/HRL phase structure, subgoal-conditioned VLA execution, GRPO-style agent RL) are all established and here combined into a new, well-specified orchestration layer. No new algorithm, theorem, or dataset is contributed. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports a well-designed controlled ablation (5,000 episodes, fixed planner, policy, initial states, and evaluator; only one mechanism varied at a time), which is above the norm for systems papers in this area. However, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for any comparison; the +0.55 pp LIBERO and +3.46 pp RoboTwin margins are single-run point estimates. The RoboTwin comparison mixes the authors' full 50-task evaluation with reference numbers imported from the LingBot-VA preprint rather than re-run under identical conditions. No code, weights, or trajectory data release is mentioned anywhere in the paper. A mild Goodhart concern: the ablation and headline numbers are both on RoboTwin 2.0, and the RMBench evaluation is limited to four tasks. Methodologically the strongest point is that terminal success is always the benchmark's evaluator, not the agent's own verifier. Deployability: - Practical: (EMPIRICAL profile) Runs on standard simulation benchmarks with Qwen3-VL and open-source OpenPI/π0.5, so components are commercially available; no real-robot results are shown. - Efficient: The authors concede added VLM calls and post-action observation introduce latency relative to single-pass policies, but no latency or FLOP numbers are reported; per-task π0.5 specialists multiply training, storage, and deployment cost by 50. - Effective: The ablations show the loop mechanisms solve the stated closed-loop problem in simulation, but the framework's benefit over a simple replanning baseline is not isolated, and the 12.5% RMBench result shows it does not yet handle history-dependent tasks well. - Scalable: Not tested — all results are 50-task tabletop manipulation in sim; behavior on real hardware, contact-rich failure, or 10× task diversity is unexamined. The paper's deliverable is a described framework and instantiation; no library, CLI, dataset, or model artifact is stated as released, so it currently stops at paper form. Strengths: - The policy–runtime separation is a crisp, well-formalized design (guards Eqs. 7–10, artifact freshness/invalidation semantics) that concretely addresses a real failure mode: model proposals being treated as physical state transitions. - The three-way ablation is genuinely diagnostic — it separates the contributions of verification (+38.0 pp), subtask conditioning (+13.8 pp), and adaptive multi-chunk continuation (+14.9 pp) under a fixed budget and fixed evaluator, rather than ablating into a mush. - Honest reporting: the near-saturation of LIBERO suites is acknowledged, the low 12.5% RMBench result is included rather than hidden, and the RMBench baselines are labeled as published numbers not re-estimated. - The deployment-consistent training-data construction (same history compaction at train and test time) is a specific, transferable engineering discipline that many agent papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that performance is bounded by both layers; that maintaining 50 per-task VLA specialists is costly relative to a generalist policy; that extra VLM calls add latency; that valid-schema decisions can still be semantically wrong (an incorrect grounding passes the contract); that verification fails under occlusion or visually ambiguous progress; that modular adapters must remain compatible at interfaces; and that long episodes accumulate errors and increase model-call counts. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive — covering most of what a reviewer would raise about the runtime itself. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline results conflate the framework with the underlying policies: 86.20% is produced by per-task specialists and would likely be nearly identical without the AgentLoop; the framework's incremental value over naive closed-loop baselines (e.g., Inner Monologue-style re-prompt on failure, or a behavior tree with the same π0.5 backend) is never measured. - No comparison against any LLM/VLM-based agentic orchestration system (SayCan, RoboClaw, HiVLA are cited but not compared), so the "unified framework" claim rests on design argument plus internal ablations only. - The optional online RL path (Eqs. 17–18) is presented but never run — no experiment exercises it, and the episode-level credit-assignment weakness the authors note is unquantified. - Verifier accuracy is never reported (verifier error rate vs. ground truth, false-advance/false-retry rates), even though the ablation shows verification is the single most important mechanism. - No seeds/error bars anywhere; the LIBERO +0.55 pp improvement is presented as a gain despite being well within run-to-run variance. - Simulation-only evaluation on tabletop benchmarks despite the paper's deployment framing; the DEEP Robotics industrial affiliation suggests real-robot access, making its absence conspicuous. - No code or artifact release mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a framework paper whose value is largely its interfaces. Bottom Line: A practitioner building an agent layer over VLA policies gains a concrete, well-ablated reference design for guarded skill orchestration that is worth reading, but the paper does not demonstrate that this framework outperforms simpler closed-loop alternatives — its headline numbers belong to per-task π0.5 fine-tuning, so treat it as a solid systems blueprint rather than a validated win.

DeepAffinity: Long-Term Aspect Preference Prediction in eCommerce using Small Language Models

Y Eshel, G Hadad, G Feigenblat, YM Brovman… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Aspect Affinity task — predicting a user's future aspect values (brand, size, color, etc.) for purchases in a given category — and builds DeepAffinity, a 135M-parameter SLM with per-aspect linear prediction heads fine-tuned on stringified user activity sequences. - Why it's important: Fine-grained, long-horizon preference prediction (e.g., a child's shoe size drifting over months) directly powers personalization in search ranking, recommendations, and marketing, and the paper targets industrial deployment where full-size LLMs are too expensive for real-time inference. - How it does it: It serializes each user event into a structured string with special tokens, appends a BERT-style [CLS] token per event, trains causally over whole sequences with cross-entropy at every [CLS] position (prediction horizon ≥24 hours ahead), and concatenates the resulting Affinity Embedding with a category embedding before per-aspect classification heads. - The good: DeepAffinity (135M) reaches mean micro-F1 0.34 on Fashion and 0.35 on All-Categories, beating a QLoRA-fine-tuned 3B generative model (0.30) and zero-shot Gemini 1.5 Flash (0.26) — an order-of-magnitude parameter advantage. - The missing: All evaluation is on proprietary eBay data with no public benchmark, no significance tests or error bars, and the production ranker gains are modest (Recall@1 +0.6%) without reported confidence intervals. - Read it or not: Worth reading for practitioners building industrial recommender/user-modeling systems with LLM backbones under latency constraints; skippable for academic researchers seeking methodological novelty or reproducible benchmarks.

Practical Impact (45) is limited by the absence of any public artifact, with only a modest +0.6% Recall@1 production lift reported without variance. Novelty (58) benefits from a genuinely new task formulation (long-horizon aspect-value prediction), but the method is standard machinery and Non-Obviousness (55) is modest.
