Problem & Motivation: Developers, security teams, and educators face a rapidly expanding attack surface as AI assistants evolve from suggesting single functions to planning multi-step work, editing multiple files, running terminal commands, installing packages, and persisting project rules across sessions. Prior reviews covered LLM code-generation security (the authors identify at least nine 2024 systematic reviews) but stop short of agentic environments — Cursor-style editors, coding CLI agents, and MCP tool ecosystems — where the peer-reviewed record is immature and the failure mode shifts from an insecure snippet to an orchestration-level compromise. The gap this review closes is a unified account connecting model-level vulnerabilities, human trust factors, and the new orchestration attack surface, with evidence-grounded mitigations rather than vendor advice. Key Idea: The organizing insight is a capability-based separation of four assistant classes (completion, conversational, repository-aware, agentic) and a two-layer vulnerability model: code-layer failures map to existing CWE classes (AI changes production and propagation dynamics, not the weakness classes), while orchestration-layer failures — indirect prompt injection, context/RAG poisoning, persistent rule poisoning, tool and MCP supply-chain attacks, approval spoofing, cross-file propagation — have no direct CWE counterpart and require controls (provenance labeling, sandboxing, capability tokens, informed human authorization) beyond standard secure-coding practice. A secondary methodological idea is the refusal to pool insecurity rates across incompatible study designs, instead synthesizing mechanisms. Methodology: The review follows Kitchenham/Charters and Petersen guidance with PRISMA concepts and Wohlin-style snowballing. Search strings covered AI code generation, Copilot, Cursor, coding agents, code LLMs, CWE, prompt injection, MCP, and supply-chain terms across eight databases (IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, USENIX, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, arXiv, Google Scholar, standards/disclosure portals), cutoff 12 July 2026; the verified corpus after deduplication is 216 records spanning peer-reviewed studies, preprints, benchmarks, standards, and technical disclosures, with preprints weighted lower than replicated findings and disclosures used only for concrete attack paths. Six research questions (RQ1–RQ6) structure the synthesis, answered by narrative/taxonomic synthesis rather than meta-analysis, with explicit justification that heterogeneous prompts, models, languages, and oracles make pooled percentages misleading. Critical design decisions: (1) evidence stratification by study type (Table 3's matrix of CWE suites, static-analysis studies, dynamic/exploit studies, developer experiments, repository studies, agent red-teaming, disclosures) — well justified and one of the review's best artifacts; (2) retaining preprints for fast-moving agentic topics — pragmatic but weakens evidentiary weight; (3) a three-criteria test for claiming a "new vulnerability class" (not covered by CWE, exploitation depends on orchestration, mitigation exceeds standard practice) — a clean, defensible rule. Quality appraisal criteria are named (reproducibility of prompts/model versions, oracle validity, contamination control) but scoring or agreement statistics are not reported. Key Results: As a synthesis, the paper reports qualitative findings rather than new measurements. Headline syntheses: (1) plausible, compilable AI-generated code repeatedly contains established CWE classes — injection, memory/resource safety, missing authorization, cryptographic misuse, insecure deserialization, hallucinated/typosquatted dependencies — with rates varying strongly by task, language, prompt, and model version, so no stable model ranking is supported; (2) LLM detection/repair is useful for triage, explanation, and candidate patches but degrades on repository-scale and semantically complex defects, and no reviewed method produces dependable patches without external validation; (3) human factors (expertise, task familiarity, automation bias, review capacity) mediate realized risk at least as much as model output; (4) iterative refinement can degrade security (Shukla et al. found "improvement" prompts increased critical findings); (5) agentic settings convert model errors into system actions — prompt-to-agent injection through issues/PRs is the dominant vector, auto-approving agents are significantly more vulnerable, and preliminary evidence (Kozak et al.) suggests agents exhibit more unsafe behavior than one-shot completion evaluations show. Baselines here are the primary studies themselves; the review explicitly declines a headline number. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (two-layer code/orchestration vulnerability model with a CWE-extension proposal and a three-criteria test for new classes) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK-adjacent contributions in the form of a minimum reporting checklist (Table 7) and risk-tiered assurance profiles (Table 9); no new empirical data. Genuinely novel: the agentic threat taxonomy, the exploit-chain decomposition with per-stage controls, and the explicit evidence-interpretation discipline. Standard combination: the Copilot/CWE code-layer material is a competent re-synthesis of at least nine existing 2024 surveys, and the defense-in-depth architecture (inventory, least privilege, sandboxing, SAST/SCA, provenance, human authorization) maps directly onto NIST SSDF, OWASP LLM Top 10, and SLSA — the review itself concedes the taxonomy is "organizational." Rigor & Reproducibility: Methodological strengths: explicit search strategy, cutoff date, database list, inclusion/exclusion criteria, snowballing, and a stated evidence-weighting hierarchy (peer-reviewed > preprint > disclosure). Weaknesses: no PRISMA flow diagram or exclusion counts; no protocol registration mentioned; quality appraisal described qualitatively with no inter-rater agreement or scoring instrument; no public artifact (data extraction forms, coded corpus, or search strings verbatim). The review is self-aware about Goodhart-style pitfalls in the underlying literature (contamination, synthetic tasks, oracle mismatch) and handles conflicting results well, but the synthesis's own reliability rests on unreported analyst judgment. The venue (JSSSEE, Vol. 1 No. 2, 2026 — an early-stage open-access journal) and four self-citations from the first author's malware-classification work ([217]–[220], two of which are to the same journal) warrant moderate confidence; much of the agentic-security evidence base is 2025–2026 preprints. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS-adjacent survey (EMPIRICAL synthesis of others' systems; the deliverable is a reference architecture and checklists, not software). - Practical: The proposed controls (tool inventories, provenance labels, sandboxing, capability tokens, SAST/SCA integration, approval design) run on conventional infrastructure; nothing requires exotic hardware. - Efficient: Not evaluated — the review offers no measurement of overhead (e.g., review-time or latency cost of provenance labeling, two-person approval, or sandboxing); the economics question is explicitly deferred to the research agenda. - Effective: The architecture is evidence-informed by construction, but no control in the architecture has been independently validated end-to-end; the review itself notes the field offers "risk correlates but few controlled tests demonstrating that a given mitigation actually works." - Scalable: Not tested; the risk-tiered assurance profiles are a plausible scaling argument but only a claim, not an experiment. Deliverable form: paper only — taxonomy, threat model, architecture diagrams, checklist tables, and research agenda; no library, dataset release, or tool accompanies it. Strengths: - The evidence-interpretation matrix (Table 3) mapping seven evidence types to their appropriate claims and typical limitations is the review's most reusable artifact and directly improves how practitioners read this contested literature. - Explicit epistemic discipline: refusing pooled insecurity percentages, separating preliminary/disputed findings from stable conclusions, and treating hosted-model evaluations as time-bound snapshots rather than durable brand properties. - The orchestration-layer threat taxonomy (Table 6) and exploit-chain decomposition (ingestion → interpretation → tool-call → execution, with a distinct control at each transition) give the immature agentic-security area its first coherent structure within a review. - The three-criteria test for "new vulnerability class" and the argument for a lightweight CWE extension rather than a competing taxonomy is a concrete, falsifiable contribution to vulnerability classification. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The threats-to-validity section names four: publication/novelty bias favoring successful attacks and prominent tools; no completeness guarantee in a fast-moving field; subjective quality appraisal; and a synthesis bounded by the 12 July 2026 cutoff. The authors also flag incomplete bibliographic metadata for very recent preprints, note that MCP-in-production evidence is absent ([223] is explicitly an analogy from other domains), and repeatedly caution that Kozak et al.'s agentic findings are small-sample and single-environment. This is direct, non-defensive limitation reporting — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No PRISMA flow accounting (records identified, screened, excluded per reason), no registered protocol, and no inter-rater reliability — the reader cannot audit the 216-record corpus construction. - The continuous-assurance architecture is presented as a contribution but borrows almost wholesale from NIST SSDF/AI RMF/OWASP/SLSA; the review never identifies which specific controls are newly justified by AI-specific evidence versus rebranded practice. - Several load-bearing empirical claims in the synthesis come from preprints dated 2025–2026 that a top-tier reviewer cannot verify (e.g., arXiv:2603.21642, 2606.09935), and the review's own evidence-weighting rule should arguably demote some of its agentic conclusions further than it does. - No discussion of whether the proposed controls (provenance labels, capability tokens, typed tool schemas) are implementable in current commercial products (Cursor, Copilot agent mode, Claude Code) — the practical-guidance section assumes vendor cooperation the market may not provide. - The human-factors chapter relies on small controlled studies with acknowledged disagreements about effect direction, yet the derived "review debt" metrics (generated/reviewed lines, review depth, generation-to-check interval) are proposed without validation. - Self-citations to the authors' malware-classification work ([219]–[220]) are tangential to the review's scope. Bottom Line: For security and platform teams adopting agentic coding tools, and for researchers needing a structured entry point into the 2024–2026 agentic-security preprint stream, this is a genuinely useful map whose taxonomy and reporting checklist justify reading it despite a weak reproducibility trail; for experts already tracking the Copilot-insecurity and prompt-injection literatures, the code-layer half re-covers familiar ground and the architecture chapter adds assembly rather than new evidence.

Environment Evolution for Terminal Agents

Z Fan, T Yu, Y Cai, J Zhou, J Guan, J Liu, Y Yang, D Hu… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces environment evolution, an off-policy method that incrementally increases the difficulty of existing terminal-agent RL environments generation by generation, and an Evolution-Lineage scheduler that orders these generations during training, improving Terminal-Bench 2.1 performance by 14.4 and 18.0 percentage points on Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B respectively. - Why it's important: Synthetic terminal environments are frequently solved by frontier models and thus yield zero-advantage rollout groups that waste construction cost and starve RL of learning signal; a difficulty-scaling mechanism that does not depend on the training model addresses this directly. - How it does it: It derives a model-agnostic difficulty decomposition from the multi-turn learning objective — trajectory length, scenario novelty, and skill rarity — and uses a loop-engineered multi-agent harness (proposer → plan reviewer → modifier → three parallel verifiers) to edit one of these three factors per generation, then schedules lineages from easiest to hardest gated by an 8-rollout pass-rate threshold of 6/8. - The good: Difficulty increases are validated off-policy across three independent frontier models (Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol), so the hardness gains are not an artifact of the training model's own weaknesses. - The missing: The core difficulty metric, p_T over scenarios and skills, is operationalized only vaguely as a 'deep-research agent' web-search estimate; no code, data, or environments are released, and the version note concedes full details and RSI experiments are deferred to future versions. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building RL environment pipelines for coding/terminal agents — the difficulty decomposition and lineage scheduler are directly reusable — but skip if you need reproducible specifics, which the paper does not yet provide.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (42) is the decisive weakness: the load-bearing p_T reference distribution is never operationally specified or validated ('a deep-research agent estimates it via web search'), no code, data, or environments are released, no error bars or significance tests accompany best-of-20-checkpoint headline numbers, and the appendix concedes the manuscript is incomplete. Novelty (68) and Non-Obviousness (65) are respectable — the off-policy difficulty decomposition that decouples environment hardness from the training model's idiosyncratic weaknesses is a useful conceptual contribution descending from POET/UED. Completeness (50) and Resilience (50) suffer from the single-benchmark evaluation, author-implemented baselines, and unquantified human-in-the-loop curation; Impact (30) is minimal with no artifact of any kind. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*42 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*50 + 0.15*50 + 0.10*30 = 52.

Problem & Motivation: Teams training terminal agents with verifiable RL face an environment bottleneck: from-scratch synthesized environments (Endless Terminals, CLI-Universe, etc.) are frequently solved by current frontier models across repeated rollouts, so they produce all-success rollout groups with zero within-group advantage and are discarded, wasting construction cost and shrinking the training distribution. Existing co-evolution methods (GenEnv, CoEvolve, SPADE-style) couple synthesis to on-policy rollouts — failures of the current model seed new environments — but this ties the synthesized distribution to the rollout model's weaknesses and the initial environment distribution, and the signal dries up as failures become sparse. The paper targets a way to keep environments near the learnable frontier without requiring rollouts from the training model. Key Idea: Derive environment difficulty off-policy by decomposing the negative log-likelihood of a high-level trajectory into three model-dependent contributors — number of solver turns L, scenario novelty −log p(σ|g), and skill rarity −log p(κ|σ,g) — then replace the model-dependent probabilities with probabilities under a reference distribution p_T grounded in broad world knowledge, yielding a policy-independent difficulty triple (L, −log p_T(σ|g), −log p_T(κ|σ,g)). Evolution then increments difficulty by editing exactly one component of this triple per generation (insert scenario-skill pairs for length, substitute a scenario, or substitute a skill), which also cleanly explains why on-policy co-evolution only targets skill-selection errors under seed-distribution scenarios. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Seed curation: 47,678 non-benchmark terminal environments from Hugging Face and GitHub are filtered by rubric-based quality checks, executable oracle solutions, and a difficulty floor (Claude Opus 5 pass rate ≤ 4/8, average turns ≥ 30), supplemented by SkillSynth, yielding a 500-environment seed pool. (2) Evolution harness: each generation, a Proposer extracts the expected execution sequence ξ_E = (σ1,κ1),...,(σL,κL), applies the selected direction's edit, and writes an evolution plan; a rubric-based Reviewer gates the plan; a Modifier applies the residual edit; three parallel verifiers enforce oracle-solvability, no-op-failure (invalid-test), and quality rubrics, with human-in-the-loop review during development feeding discovered issues back into the rubrics. An 'evolution effort' parameter (low/high/max) controls edit scope from a single (σ,κ) pair to an unrestricted span; directions are randomly ordered per generation with cross-mode fallback. (3) RL: GRPO with partial rollouts, asynchronous GPU placement, and staleness bound 5, run 200 steps from an RFT checkpoint using the Claude Code harness (256K context, auto-compaction); the EL Scheduler advances through lineage generations in order, moving on when mean pass rate over B=8 rollouts exceeds τ=6/8. Critical design decisions: off-policy (reference-distribution) difficulty rather than on-policy pass rate — justified by the derivation but the estimation of p_T is only sketched; verifier-gated solvability — well motivated by observed reward-signal corruption in open-source environments; the τ=6/8 threshold for scheduling — reasonable but not ablated. Key Results: Rollout difficulty: under high/max effort, pass rate falls monotonically toward zero over 15 generations while average turns rise (e.g., max effort reaches zero pass rate earliest), consistent across Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Sol; low effort produces non-monotonic pass rates. Direction ablation: length gives the largest single-step pass-rate drop (−7.1 pp), scenario/skill give larger turn increases (+13.5/+12.5); 1-step and 15-step effects agree, suggesting stable per-direction profiles. RL: peaks of 71.5% (Qwen3.6-27B) and 64.9% (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) on Terminal-Bench 2.1 Verified versus 62.9%/55.1% for agent-environment co-evolution and 60.0%/52.8% for environment ensemble, all with Claude Opus 5 as the fixed synthesis model and equal environment counts; gains of 14.4 and 18.0 pp over the RFT step-0 checkpoint. The EL Scheduler beats random scheduling on partial-solved rate over the first 50 steps. Trajectory length grows during training (to 190/174 turns and 192k/232k tokens). Scale is moderate: two open models of 27B and 35B-A3B parameters, 500 seed environments, 15-generation lineages, 200 RL steps. Baselines are reasonable but implemented by the authors under a fixed synthesis model; no external strong results are cited for comparison. Notably, evolved environments provided usable RL signal even when seed environments had already been used for SFT — a somewhat surprising persistence of signal. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (off-policy environment evolution along a derived difficulty decomposition, plus the EL lineage scheduler) with a NEW FORMULATION component (the model-agnostic difficulty triple and weakness-as-excess-difficulty decomposition). The conceptual move — mutating environments along a difficulty gradient — descends directly from POET and Unsupervised Environment Design; the genuinely new element is the off-policy, reference-distribution difficulty formulation that removes dependence on target-model rollouts, and the demonstration that this transfers to LLM terminal agents at RL training scale. The multi-agent harness itself is competent engineering of known synthesis/verification patterns. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: three evolution efforts, three directions with 1-step vs 15-step consistency checks, scheduler vs random, and three scaling paradigms under a fixed synthesis model and matched environment count. Benchmark evaluation averages over five runs, but no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the headline Terminal-Bench numbers, and peak accuracies are selected post hoc from 20 offline checkpoints (a multiple-comparison concern). No code, data, or evolved environments are released (no URL given). The theoretical derivation is informal — p_T is 'estimated by a deep-research agent through broad web search' with no validation that these estimates track actual difficulty. Human-in-the-loop review during harness development introduces an unquantified human curation component. Methodological flags: the comparison baselines (co-evolution, ensemble) are author-implemented and may be under-tuned; the difficulty metric and the difficulty outcomes are partially validated on the same rollout infrastructure; and the appendix states more details and RSI results will appear in future versions, signaling an incomplete manuscript. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (trains and evaluates real models; the formalism is motivation, not a theorem-proving contribution). - Practical: Yes for well-resourced labs — RL runs on 27B/35B open-weight models with a 256K-context harness and standard GRPO infrastructure, but environment evolution consumes frontier-model API rollouts (Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, 1M context) for difficulty verification. - Efficient: Off-policy evolution avoids the target-model rollout cost of co-evolution, but each lineage requires 15 generations of frontier-model synthesis plus 8-rollout difficulty gating per environment; the paper reports no wall-clock or API cost figures. - Effective: The evidence shows large Terminal-Bench 2.1 gains over author-implemented baselines on two models — a real held-out benchmark — though peak values are best-of-20 checkpoints and no significance testing is reported. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — the paper does not run multiple lineages at larger seed-pool scale, longer training, or larger models; whether the 15-generation cap (limited by zero-pass resolution) generalizes is unexamined. The work delivers a method and training recipe in paper form only; no software artifact, dataset, or model release is stated. Strengths: - The off-policy difficulty decomposition is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution: separating environment difficulty from model-specific weakness gives a clean theoretical explanation for why on-policy co-evolution saturates (it only targets skill-selection errors under seed-distribution scenarios) and motivates a method that does not. - Difficulty gains are validated against three independent frontier models rather than only the training model, which credibly rules out the most obvious confound (hardness that is merely one model's idiosyncratic weakness). - The verifier triple (oracle solvability, invalid-test, quality rubrics) with issues fed back into rubrics addresses the documented reward-corruption problem in open-source terminal environments, and the direction ablation's 1-step vs 15-step agreement is a careful consistency check few papers in this area perform. - The empirical comparison controls the synthesis model and environment count across all three scaling paradigms, making the +8.6/+9.8 pp margins over co-evolution meaningful within the paper's own setup. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: - Pass rate provides no resolution once a lineage enters the zero-pass regime, capping measurable evolution at 15 generations — a candid and correct acknowledgment. - The appendix (Version Note) states that full details are forthcoming and future versions will report RSI results in which the same model constructs and learns from the environments — an admission that the current manuscript is incomplete. - The paper notes open-source environments suffer from low-quality reward signals and insufficiency for frontier models, implicitly acknowledging that its seed filtering and human-in-the-loop development were necessary; beyond these, the authors do not dwell on limitations, and several (below) go unmentioned. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The p_T reference distribution — the load-bearing component of the off-policy difficulty metric — is never concretely specified or validated; 'a deep-research agent estimates both distributions through broad web search' is not an operational definition, so the theoretical contribution cannot be reproduced or falsified from the paper. - No error bars, seed variance, or significance tests on the Terminal-Bench 2.1 comparisons, and peak accuracy is reported at the best of 20 evaluated checkpoints, which inflates apparent margins between methods whose curves visually track within a few points. - The co-evolution and ensemble baselines are author-implemented with a fixed external synthesis model (Claude Opus 5); a co-evolution variant that updates the synthesizer with the training model, or prior published co-evolution numbers, is absent, so the claim of 'longer-lasting learning signals' rests on one configuration. - Human-in-the-loop review during harness development means the released-style environments passed through human curation; the paper does not quantify how much of the quality derives from this unscalable step. - Evaluation is exclusively Terminal-Bench 2.1; no second held-out benchmark (e.g., SWE-bench-style tasks) tests whether gains transfer beyond the terminal domain or whether the method overfits the benchmark's task distribution. - All difficulty and mutation measurements use frontier models (Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Hy4) for both evolution and verification, but training uses Qwen models — the paper does not test whether difficulty calibrated against frontier models is optimally matched to weaker students, though the positive results suggest it is at least not harmful. Bottom Line: A practitioner building RL environment pipelines for terminal or coding agents should read this for the difficulty decomposition and lineage scheduler, which are concrete and immediately reusable, but should treat the formalism as unvalidated and the comparison numbers as provisional until the promised complete version and released artifacts arrive.

P Tassis · dione.lib.unipi.gr · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This MSc thesis builds and evaluates an automated, reproducible cyber range on a single workstation — a Ludus/Proxmox-deployed enterprise topology (Windows Server 2022 Domain Controller, Windows 11 workstation, Kali attacker node, OpenEMR clinical server) — and validates detection of a full-chain attack against it via Wazuh/Sysmon telemetry. - Why it's important: Organizations, especially healthcare providers now bound by the EU NIS2 Directive, need affordable, repeatable environments to train defenders and verify that their detection stack actually fires on realistic intrusions; commercial ranges are expensive and static. - How it does it: The core move is infrastructure-as-code reproducibility — YAML-defined Ludus ranges on Proxmox with Ansible provisioning — combined with BadBlood-generated Active Directory content and a deliberately vulnerable OpenEMR 5.0.1 instance (CVE-2018-17179) to exercise identity attacks and application-layer exploitation end-to-end. - The good: The resource-footprint analysis is genuinely measured, not asserted: a 5-VM range consumes ~17.6 GB RAM (67.8% of a 26 GB host), 8 vCPU over 6 physical cores (1.33:1 over-commit), and ~160 GB of 200 GB storage, yielding a concrete projection that 4–8 concurrent training instances fit on one mid-tier server. - The missing: Multi-instance scaling is a first-order projection from a single validated deployment, not an experiment; the provided text also shows no quantified detection-coverage results (no rates, thresholds, or true/false-positive counts), and the thesis claims a "container-based" architecture while the implementation is VM-based. - Read it or not: Read it if you are a SOC engineer, educator, or NIS2-compliance team deciding how to stand up a low-cost, repeatable attack-and-detection lab; skip it if you seek new research methods, since it is a competent integration study of existing tools (Ludus, BadBlood, BloodHound, Wazuh).

Problem & Motivation: Cybersecurity teams and educators lack training and detection-validation environments that are realistic, current, and affordable. Existing cyber ranges are described as static, expensive, weakly scalable, and poorly integrated with organizational IT — they cannot keep pace with new threats or support many concurrent users (Sections 1.8–1.9). The thesis grounds the problem in the healthcare sector: ENISA's sectoral threat landscape (215 reported incidents) found ransomware in 54% of cases, healthcare providers as 53% of affected entities, and 80% of surveyed health organizations attributing over 61% of security incidents to exploitable vulnerabilities; the 2021 Conti ransomware attack on Ireland's HSE encrypted ~80% of its IT estate. Regulatory pressure comes from Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2), which lists healthcare in Annex I, imposes fines up to EUR 10M or 2% of turnover, and was transposed in Greece by Law 5160/2024. The intended users are defenders, trainers, and compliance-driven organizations in the public and private sectors. Key Idea: The core insight is that a credible, full-lifecycle attack-and-detection range does not require bespoke infrastructure: it can be assembled from an automation-first open-source stack (Ludus on Proxmox, Ansible-provisioned templates, YAML range definitions) plus freely available adversary tooling (BadBlood for AD population, SharpHound/BloodHound for path discovery, Kerberoasting/AS-REP roasting, an intentionally vulnerable OpenEMR 5.0.1 for initial access), with Wazuh agents plus Sysmon closing the loop as the detection-validation substrate. Reproducibility — identical exercise outcomes across repeated executions — is treated as the defining design requirement, achieved through build-from-ISO templates and IaC configuration rather than stale pre-customized VM images. Methodology: The work follows six phases (Section 1.11): (1) define objectives around a repeatable full-chain attack lifecycle and detection validation; (2) design the core topology from Ludus's Basic AD Network template — Windows Server 2022 DC (ludus.domain), a Windows 11 Enterprise workstation, a Kali attacker node, and an OpenEMR server; (3) populate Active Directory with BadBlood (users, groups, computers, ACLs, LAPS) to create realistic enumeration surface without extra VMs; (4) plant misconfigurations and vulnerabilities, including OpenEMR 5.0.1 with CVE-2018-17179; (5) execute a structured kill chain — initial access via the exposed OpenEMR service, privilege escalation with a reverse shell, internal AD reconnaissance (SharpHound), credential attacks (Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting), lateral movement, and impact/exfiltration simulation; (6) validate detection by shipping endpoint telemetry (Wazuh agents, Sysmon on the DC) to a centralized Wazuh SIEM and checking that each attack step generates detectable events. There is no formal objective function; the framework is adversary emulation mapped to the MITRE-style kill chain rather than an optimization. Critical design decisions: (a) VLAN segmentation (VLAN 10 Windows, VLAN 99 Kali) with asymmetric firewall rules — Kali has full reachability, Windows hosts can reach Kali only on TCP 80/443/8080 — is justified as mimicking real DMZ constraints; (b) build-from-ISO templates instead of maintained customized images is well-justified for reproducibility; (c) deploying on a 26 GB RAM VM host (below Ludus's 32 GB recommendation, nested virtualized) is acknowledged as a constraint under which the environment still deployed successfully. Key Results: The validated headline result is a measured resource footprint for one range instance (Table 3.1/3.2): five VMs consuming ~67.8% of 26 GB host RAM (~17.6 GB, ~3.5 GB/VM average; DC and workstation each ~28% of host RAM), 8 vCPU against 6 physical cores (1.33:1 over-commit, viable because workloads are idle between exercises), and 80.1% storage utilization (~160/200 GB) — storage is identified as the first resource to saturate. From this single validated instance the authors project (not test) requirements for concurrent instances: 2 instances ≈ 35 GB RAM/260 GB storage, 4 instances ≈ 70 GB/460 GB, 8 instances ≈ 140 GB/860 GB, concluding that a small class of trainees fits on one mid-tier server. The testing chapters (per TOC and intro text) demonstrate AD population via BadBlood, attack-path identification via BloodHound, execution of Kerberoasting and AS-REP roasting, exploitation of OpenEMR CVE-2018-17179 with a persistent reverse shell, Sysmon telemetry integration into Wazuh, and a qualitative detection-coverage assessment across the attack lifecycle (Section 4.15). Note: the provided document text is truncated partway through Section 3.13, so quantitative detection results from Chapters 4–5 cannot be independently verified from the visible pages. No accuracy/F1-style metrics, baselines against other ranges, or significance tests are visible. All findings are at single-workstation scale (5 VMs); nothing is demonstrated at multi-instance or datacenter scale. Novelty Classification: ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION and, at most, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL at thesis scale; not a NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel element for this audience is the end-to-end recipe combining Ludus range automation with a healthcare-specific hybrid topology (Windows AD + Linux clinical application) and a closed attack-to-Wazuh validation loop; every individual ingredient (Ludus, Proxmox, Ansible, BadBlood, BloodHound, Sysmon, Wazuh, OpenEMR exploitation) is an existing, public tool. The claim in Section 1.10 of a "novel, lightweight, container-based CR architecture" is not supported by the implementation, which is hypervisor/VM-based — the standard combination of known ideas applied to a healthcare-flavored setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Reproducibility is the thesis's strongest methodological commitment: ISO-built templates, YAML range configs, IaC provisioning, and snapshot-based restoration are all documented with command-level detail, and the resource tables trace measurements to specific figures (Figure 21). The authors explicitly flag that the multi-instance projection is "a first-order derived from a single measured instance, not an empirically validated multi-instance benchmark" — a credibility positive. However: no ablations show which components matter (e.g., BadBlood density vs. attack-path richness); no error bars, seeds, or repeated runs are reported for the attack/detection experiments; no code or range-definition artifact release is mentioned beyond pointers to existing public repos (ludus.gitlab.com/badsectorlabs); detection coverage is assessed qualitatively in the visible text with no true/false-positive quantification; and there is no controlled comparison against alternative approaches (e.g., Attack Range, GOAD) on equal footing — only a feature checklist (Table 2). The related-work comparison uses self-described characteristics of competing projects, which risks unfair characterization. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact). Practical: Yes — the entire range runs on one workstation-class machine (26 GB RAM, 6 cores, 200 GB NVMe) using open-source software with no licensing costs. Efficient: ~3.5 GB RAM and ~1.6 vCPU per VM average, with storage (~160 GB for one instance) as the binding constraint; cheaper than commercial ranges and cloud-hosted alternatives, though the paper does not benchmark against them. Effective: The evidence shows the range supports a full attack chain and that attack steps generate Wazuh/Sysmon telemetry, but effective detection (coverage rates, alert quality, analyst workload) is only demonstrated at the level of individual validation checks, not measured comprehensively. Scalable: Only claimed via projection — 4–8 concurrent instances on a mid-tier server is an extrapolation from one deployment, with the authors themselves noting storage I/O contention during simultaneous boot of dozens of VMs as the likely bottleneck; no multi-instance experiment was run. The work delivers a documented, reconstructable environment (deployment scripts, templates, configuration files described in the text) but no packaged software release of its own is stated. Strengths: - The measured resource-footprint analysis (Tables 3.1–3.2) converts a usually hand-waved scalability claim into concrete numbers — RAM share per VM, CPU over-commit ratio, storage saturation point — and honestly separates measurement from projection. - The healthcare-domain grounding is unusually rigorous for a thesis of this type: the sector choice is justified with ENISA incident statistics (54% ransomware share, 53% provider share), NIS2 obligations, and Greek transposition law (5160/2024), and the vulnerable OpenEMR deployment is argued to reproduce the empirically dominant initial-access vector rather than an artificial one. - The deliberate exploitation of CVE-2018-17179 for reproducibility — a documented, stably repeatable vulnerability so exercises yield identical outcomes — is a sound methodological decision for training environments. - The closed loop from adversary emulation (BadBlood, BloodHound, Kerberoasting, OpenEMR exploitation) through Sysmon/Wazuh telemetry to detection validation is competently executed and fully documented at command level. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (a) the multi-instance scaling figures are a first-order projection from one measured instance, not a validated benchmark; (b) storage I/O contention is the most probable practical bottleneck at scale, motivating NVMe in every tier; (c) the range models only the IT layer of a healthcare provider — no medical devices, clinical engineering networks, or OT, which are deferred to future work under a distinct regulatory regime (Regulation (EU) 2017/745, IEC 80001); (d) the host ran below Ludus's 32 GB RAM recommendation and as a nested VM with added overhead. These are confronted directly rather than minimized, which strengthens confidence in the reported measurements. The conclusion chapter (per the introduction) also revisits the scalability/flexibility/integration gaps and lists cluster/cloud deployment, SIEM/detection-engineering expansion, automated threat emulation, and ML integration as future work. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The contribution statement overclaims: Section 1.10 describes a "container-based" architecture, but the implementation is VM/hypervisor-based (Proxmox/KVM with Docker only as a Ludus dependency); no container-based design is evaluated. - No quantified detection results are visible: Section 4.15 promises a detection-coverage assessment across the attack lifecycle, but the provided text contains no coverage percentages, alert-fidelity metrics, or false-positive analysis — without these, "detection validation" remains a checklist of events observed, not a measured capability. - The comparative Table 2 judges competing projects (GOAD, Attack Range, CyTrONE, Ludus) on features but never runs a head-to-head deployment, so the choice of Ludus is justified qualitatively, not empirically. - The motivating challenges (Section 1.8) include integration with LMS/organizational systems and AI/ML-driven adaptivity, but neither is implemented or tested — the LMS integration gap is silently dropped rather than addressed or re-scoped. - Security of the range itself is not evaluated: no assessment of escape risk from the nested-virtualization design, Kali's unrestricted outbound internet access during testing, or isolation guarantees between concurrent user ranges. - The evaluation uses one attack chain against one deliberately vulnerable application version; generalization to other sectors, APT-style multi-stage scenarios, or defender-variant exercises is untested. Bottom Line: A practitioner standing up a low-cost, repeatable NIS2-oriented attack-and-detection lab will get real operational value from this thesis's measured footprint data and command-level recipe, but researchers should look elsewhere — it integrates existing open-source tools competently without contributing a new method, and its scalability and detection-coverage claims remain projections rather than experiments.

DK Shukla, F Neha, D Bhati · preprints.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SAI-V, a conceptual framework that characterizes self-improving AI systems along six dimensions (target, trigger, mechanism, evaluator, persistence, autonomy) and couples this with a Variation–Assessment–Verification–Integration lifecycle and a six-criteria evaluation model for deciding when a modification counts as genuine improvement. - Why it's important: The term "self-improvement" is currently applied indiscriminately to everything from transient inference-time revision to recursive code modification, making claims across the literature incomparable and frequently overstated; a shared validation vocabulary addresses that. - How it does it: It factorizes any improvement process into a tuple P = (T, Tr, M, E, P, A), defines a target taxonomy ordered by structural depth (output → context → memory → workflow → data → parameters → architecture/code), a seven-level autonomy scale, and treats retention of a change as acceptance of a six-dimensional evaluation profile within a constrained admissible region. - The good: The central conceptual distinction — that modification is not improvement and that retention requires demonstrated net benefit against a baseline under generalization, stability, and safety constraints — is argued crisply and applied consistently throughout. - The missing: The paper offers no empirical instantiation: no case study scores a single real system (e.g., a self-refining LLM agent or an evolutionary scaffold) on the SAI-V dimensions or the evaluation profile, so the framework's usability, discriminative power, and inter-rater reliability are untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers organizing the self-improving/evolving-agents literature or designing evaluation protocols for adaptive agents; practitioners seeking a working method or empirical evidence for building self-improving systems will find nothing operational here.

Problem & Motivation: Researchers and practitioners working on agentic and continually learning AI systems face a definitional and evaluative morass: reflection, memory adaptation, synthetic-data training, workflow optimization, parameter updates, and code modification are all labeled "self-improvement," despite differing in what is modified, what initiates change, how modifications are validated, and how much control the system exercises. Prior surveys (which the authors cite, e.g., arXiv:2507.21046, arXiv:2508.07407) organize these directions but, per the authors, conflate the locus of modification, the generation mechanism, autonomy, and the evidence needed to establish genuine improvement. The paper's motivating stake is that unvalidated or overstated improvement claims — driven by self-preference, benchmark exploitation, reward hacking, and inference-time compute masquerading as durable change — undermine both scientific progress and safety governance. Key Idea: The core move is the separation of characterization from validation: decompose any self-improvement process into six orthogonal-ish dimensions (target, trigger, mechanism, evaluator, persistence, autonomy) for description, and independently require that a candidate modification pass a four-stage lifecycle (Variation → Assessment → Verification → Integration, plus monitoring and rollback) before it counts as improvement. The slogan "Modification ≠ Improvement, Performance Gain ≠ System-Level Benefit, Greater Autonomy ≠ Greater Self-Improvement" is the conceptual payload; the formal apparatus (an evaluation profile E = (ΔC, E_imp, G, Σ, A, Q) with acceptance iff E ∈ A, an admissible region) formalizes this as constrained multi-objective validation. This is a framing insight, not an algorithmic trick. Methodology: This is a conceptual/position paper; the "method" is the framework itself. The components are: (1) a definition of self-improvement requiring self-identification, self-modification, self-evaluation, persistence, and autonomy, with boundary tables separating it from self-correction, adaptation, continual learning, self-training, self-evolution, and recursive self-improvement; (2) the six-dimension characterization tuple, with each dimension enumerated (e.g., seven mechanism families: reflection/critique, experience learning, synthetic-data self-training, self-play/self-challenge, multi-agent improvement, tool-mediated improvement, meta-optimization); (3) a seven-level target taxonomy ordered by structural depth; (4) a seven-level autonomy scale A = f(I, P, D) built from initiative, persistence, and modification depth, with the claim that current systems cluster at Levels 1–4; (5) an evaluation profile of capability gain (Eq. 1), improvement efficiency as ΔC/R with an explicit resource vector (Eq. 2), generalization, stability (capability trajectory across cycles), autonomy (measured intervention), and safety preservation treated as a validation constraint (Eq. 3). Critical design decisions: decoupling target from mechanism (justified by showing one target admits many mechanisms); ordering targets by structural depth rather than capability (explicitly argued, and sensibly so); treating safety as a hard constraint rather than an objective (stated, not derived). No loss functions, no optimization procedure — the equations are definitional notation, not derived results. Key Results: Not applicable — the paper reports no experiments, measurements, or quantitative results of any kind. There are no baselines, datasets, benchmarks, or compute figures. The closest thing to empirical content is the qualitative claim that current systems operate between autonomy Levels 1 and 4, with Level 5 constrained and Level 6 unsupported by evidence, and qualitative syntheses of cited systems (e.g., SAGE for memory adaptation, multi-agent fine-tuning for sustained improvement rounds). All "results" are analytical assertions about how improvement should be classified and validated, not measured findings. Not evaluated. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (a characterization vocabulary and validation-criteria framework), positioned within an already crowded survey/taxonomy space — the paper itself cites at least four 2025–2026 surveys on self-improving/self-evolving agents. What is genuinely contributed is the specific six-dimension decomposition plus the insistence on a formal acceptance region and lifecycle separation of candidate from validated change; the underlying ingredients (targets, mechanisms, autonomy levels, evaluation criteria) are standard combinations of ideas already present in the cited literature (Omohundro 2007; metacognitive-loop work 2005; recent agent surveys; Darwin Gödel machine). The autonomy scale resembles existing capability-level taxonomies (e.g., autonomous-driving-style level scales applied to agents); the evaluation profile generalizes standard continual-learning evaluation (forgetting, transfer) to the agent setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a non-empirical framework paper, standard rigor signals do not apply: no ablations, no error bars, no seeds, no code, data, or artifacts (nothing is released). Methodological concerns: (1) the framework is never applied end-to-end to even one concrete system, so its practical discriminative power is self-reported rather than demonstrated; (2) the claim that prior surveys "conflate" dimensions is asserted without a systematic comparison table against those surveys' actual schemes; (3) the framework was developed on the same literature it evaluates, with no external validation such as having independent annotators classify systems and measure agreement; (4) several equations (Eqs. 1–3) are notation, not formal results — nothing is proved or bounded. The conceptual argumentation itself is internally consistent and carefully hedged, which is the appropriate rigor bar for this genre, but it is a low bar relative to what the framing implies. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a conceptual formalism with no primary experimental claim). - Sound: The definitions are explicit and the conceptual boundaries are argued carefully, but nothing is proved, and key constructs ("appropriate baseline," "admissible region A," resource aggregation) are left as context-dependent choices, which is where the hard problems actually live. - General: The framework is domain-independent by construction and its scope conditions (persistence, system participation, validation) are stated, though the boundary-of-the-self problem it itself flags partially undermines the generality of its own classifications. - Tight: Not applicable — no bounds are derived; the framework's "tightness" would be its ability to distinguish real systems, which is untested. - Implementable: It suggests a checklist-style protocol (evaluation profile + lifecycle gates) that a team could adopt for agent-release governance, but no operational procedure, thresholds, or tooling is provided, and no follow-up work exists given the posting date. The work delivers paper form only — no software artifact, dataset, or reusable proof technique. Strengths: - The persistent discipline of separating modification from validated improvement, and of requiring baseline-relative, multi-dimensional (generalization, stability, safety) evidence for retention, is a genuinely useful corrective to inflated claims in this subfield, and the paper applies it consistently rather than paying it lip service. - The target taxonomy's ordering principle — structural depth, explicitly not capability or quality — avoids a common conflation and enables the sensible observation that shallow (context/memory) changes can outperform deep (parameter/code) changes. - The autonomy scale's Level 5→6 transition criterion (meta-level control over the improvement process itself, requiring validated gains across subsequent cycles) gives a concrete, falsifiable test that would deflate most current "recursive self-improvement" claims. - The treatment of evaluator independence — including correlated failure modes among multi-agent critics that share architectures or training distributions — is a substantive and often-overlooked point, well-grounded in cited evidence (self-preference effects). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually forthright in Section 9 and 10: they identify error propagation across cycles, catastrophic forgetting, reward hacking and benchmark exploitation, evaluator contamination, limited transfer, reproducibility difficulties under stochastic operation, compute costs that can exceed gains, the unresolved boundary-of-the-self problem, ambiguity around external feedback and human involvement, inference-time scaling masquerading as improvement, goal drift, safeguard erosion, oversight infeasibility at scale, and the near-total lack of evidence for recursive (Level 6) improvement. This direct confrontation with limitations is a credibility positive. They do not, however, acknowledge the framework's own untested status — that SAI-V has never been applied to classify or evaluate an actual system. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No worked example: the single largest omission. Applying SAI-V to even three or four known systems (Self-Refine, Darwin Gödel Machine, SAGE, multi-agent fine-tuning) and showing the framework yields non-obvious or contested classifications would transform it from taxonomy to instrument. - No comparison against existing taxonomies: the paper cites competing surveys but never tabulates where SAI-V agrees, disagrees, or adds coverage, so the marginal contribution over, e.g., the self-evolving-agents surveys it references is asserted, not shown. - The evaluation profile's dimensions are named but not operationalized: no metric definitions, no guidance on thresholds for A, no handling of the measurement problems (confounded A/B comparisons, non-stationary baselines) that make longitudinal agent evaluation hard in practice. - The framework's dimensions are claimed to be jointly interpretable but their potential dependencies (e.g., autonomy level plausibly constrains feasible evaluator independence; persistence constrains testable stability) are not analyzed, which matters if profiles are meant to be compared cell by cell. - Related work coverage has visible gaps for a survey-adjacent contribution (no discussion of Voyager-style skill libraries, prompt-propagation systems, or RLHF/RLAIF governance literature beyond a handful of citations), and several references are 2026 preprints whose status a reader cannot verify — the paper itself is a non-peer-reviewed preprint and all quantitative claims about cited systems inherit that uncertainty. Bottom Line: A carefully argued and honest conceptual taxonomy that articulates the right validation questions for self-improving AI, but with zero empirical grounding and stiff competition from existing surveys — read it as a well-organized checklist for designing agent-improvement evaluations, not as a contribution that establishes anything a rigorous reader could falsify or build on quantitatively.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces QUEST, a parameter-free drop-in extension of the ssCDL uncertain knowledge graph completion framework that initializes entity embeddings from the confidence-weighted graph Laplacian and applies a scheduled Dirichlet energy regularizer. - Why it's important: UKG completion methods ignore the global community and hub topology of the confidence-weighted graph, causing gradient conflict between pseudo-label self-training and structural smoothness that manifests as large training-instability spikes on dense graphs and unreliable checkpoints. - How it does it: Entity embeddings are seeded with the k smallest non-trivial eigenvectors of the confidence-weighted Laplacian (spectral coordinates), and a mini-batch Dirichlet energy regularizer is active only before the PCDG meta-learning stage starts (epoch 30), then deactivated to avoid conflicting gradients. - The good: Ablations plus training-dynamics curves on NL27k and CN15k show both components matter, with the scheduling rule removing the epoch-30 instability spike (ablations spike to ~0.27 MAE / 0.18 MSE on CN15k) and standard deviations across runs reported for all headline numbers. - The missing: Evaluation covers only the two small standard UKG benchmarks (≤27k entities), the scheduling cutoff is hard-coded to ssCDL's fixed PCDG epoch rather than principled, and the paper does not test whether the spectral initialization cost is tractable beyond these graphs despite admitting this concern. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on UKG completion or graph-regularized semi-supervised learning and want a cheap, well-ablated structural prior for embedding pipelines; skip it if you need relation-type- or direction-aware structure or large-graph scalability, since neither is addressed.

Problem & Motivation: Uncertain knowledge graphs (UKGs) annotate each triple with a continuous confidence score, and most possible triples lack observed confidences, so completion is cast as semi-supervised learning with pseudo-labeling (the ssCDL framework). Who has this problem: anyone building reasoning systems over noisy, confidence-annotated knowledge bases (e.g., NELL-style extractions, ConceptNet-style commonsense), where uncalibrated embeddings degrade downstream reliability. The specific gap: existing UKG methods (UKGE, BEUrRE, PASSLEAF, UPGAT, ssCDL) randomly initialize entity embeddings and treat triples locally, discarding the community and hub structure encoded in the confidence-weighted graph; on dense graphs this produces a gradient conflict between meta-learned pseudo-labels and any structural smoothness objective, causing sharp error spikes at the point self-training activates. Key Idea: Encode global topology before training by using the k smallest non-trivial eigenvectors of the confidence-weighted graph Laplacian as the entity embedding initialization, and resolve the gradient conflict between graph smoothness and uniform entity-corruption pseudo-labeling by scheduling: run a mini-batch Dirichlet energy regularizer only during the pre-PCDG phase and switch it off exactly when meta-learned self-training begins. Methodology: QUEST extends ssCDL, which maps feature vectors φ(h,r,t) = [e_h ∥ e_r ∥ e_t] to a 101-bin confidence distribution trained against a truncated Gaussian target, combined with a confidence-weighted margin-ranking loss via Kendall uncertainty weighting. QUEST adds two parameter-free components: (1) Spectral initialization — build a symmetric confidence-weighted adjacency A (summing confidence over triples in either direction), form the unnormalized Laplacian L = D − A, Tikhonov-regularize with εI (ε = 10⁻⁵), extract the d smallest non-trivial eigenvectors via ARPACK shift-invert, rescale to standard deviation τ = √2/(n+d), and set E⁽⁰⁾ = U; relation embeddings keep Xavier initialization. Complexity is O(|E|) to build A and roughly O(d·|E|) one-time for sparse graphs. (2) Scheduled smoothness — an unbiased Monte Carlo mini-batch estimate L_smooth = (1/m)Σ s_i‖e_{h_i} − e_{t_i}‖² (m = min(2048, |E|)) of the full Dirichlet energy, added with λ = 0.01 for t < 30 epochs and set to 0 afterward (the cutoff follows ssCDL's fixed PCDG schedule, not test-set tuning). Critical design decisions: aggregating directed relations into an undirected Laplacian (standard in structural KGE, but discards direction/type — acknowledged); hard-deactivating the regularizer at the fixed PCDG epoch rather than adaptively detecting conflict (justified empirically by the density-correlated spike analysis, but brittle); mini-batch sampling as an unbiased estimator of full Dirichlet energy (well-justified, keeps per-step overhead at O(m·d)). Key Results: On NL27k (27,221 entities, 175,412 quadruples) and CN15k (15,000 entities, 241,158 quadruples), QUESTFull reports the best result on six of eight metric–dataset pairs and ties ssCDL on the other two (CN15k MSE 0.031 vs. ssCDL 0.034, MAE 0.118 vs. 0.116). Headline gains vs. ssCDL: CN15k MSE improves from 0.034 to 0.031 (−11.8% claimed as +2.4%/+11.8% relative across metrics; CN15k Hits@1 0.133 → 0.141, +6.0%; NL27k MAE 0.042 → 0.041, +2.4%; NL27k WMRR 0.727 → 0.736). Baselines span UKGE, BEUrRE, PASSLEAF (DistMult/ComplEx/RotatE), UKGsE, UPGAT, and ssCDL; ssCDL is the current state of the art, so the comparison set is strong. The 0.094 → 0.031 CN15k MSE improvement over PASSLEAF-RotatE (67% reduction) without changing the scoring function supports the claim that initialization geometry, not scorer expressiveness, is the bottleneck. The most interesting finding is the density-dependent instability: ablations spike to ~0.27 MAE / 0.18 MSE at epoch 30 on the denser CN15k (2.5× more edges per entity) and need 30–50 epochs to recover, while NL27k is unaffected and QUESTFull shows no discontinuity. Scale is standard (small academic benchmarks), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a modest one) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the density-dependent gradient conflict between Dirichlet regularization and uniform pseudo-label corruption). The genuinely novel part is the scheduled deactivation tied to the PCDG boundary and the mechanistic analysis of the conflict; the spectral initialization itself is a standard application of Laplacian eigenvector embeddings / spectral clustering (Ng et al. 2001) and Laplacian eigenvector pre-training applied to UKG entity tables, and the Dirichlet regularizer is classical — the contribution is their configuration and interaction analysis within ssCDL, not new mathematics. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative — the two single-component variants isolate which component drives which metric (spectral init drives regression quality on the sparse graph, e.g., removing it causes a 4.5% MAE regression on NL27k), and the authors honestly report that QUEST w/o graph-reg achieves the best CN15k MSE (0.030) but through an unstable trajectory sensitive to checkpoint selection. Standard deviations across runs are reported for all QUEST rows (e.g., 0.009±0.0001 MSE on NL27k), though the number of seeds and significance tests are not stated. Evaluation follows the unKR benchmark protocol with the filtered setting. No code, data, or model release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation is confined to the two datasets on which the method and its backbone were developed, so benchmark gaming risk is low but generalization is untested; (2) the epoch-30 scheduling rule is derived from observations on these same two datasets, so the gradient-conflict mechanism is fitted to the observed instability rather than validated prospectively; (3) hyperparameters (λ = 0.01, ε = 10⁻⁵) have no sensitivity analysis. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent flavor since it modifies a training pipeline, but there is no released artifact, so EMPIRICAL). Practical: Yes — it runs on standard hardware as a drop-in modification of ssCDL with no added trainable parameters; the one-time eigendecomposition is the only extra cost. Efficient: Per-epoch training and inference cost are unchanged; the ARPACK shift-invert eigendecomposition is a one-time O(d·|E|)-ish cost for sparse graphs, but this becomes the bottleneck at 10⁶+ entities, and the paper concedes this without measuring it. Effective: Evidence shows modest improvements on the standard UKG benchmarks (six of eight metric–dataset pairs best or tied) and, more compellingly, elimination of the checkpoint-selection instability on dense graphs — the practical benefit may be reliability more than final accuracy, since ablations recover to within a few percent of full QUEST. Scalable: Not tested; the paper only claims the one-time spectral step "may become expensive on very large graphs,

Problem & Motivation: Coding agents blur the division of labor between probabilistic models (good at interpretation, analogy, decomposition) and deterministic infrastructure (compilers, transactions, build systems that must be reproducible, inspectable, and bounded). Today's agents ask the model to regenerate thousands of tokens of implementation syntax, then use the same model to judge or repair it — expensive, hard to audit, and prone to repeating errors on already-solved work. The paper targets anyone building autonomous software-engineering agents: it argues the gap is that validated knowledge remains trapped in transient conversations instead of becoming persistent, reusable deterministic mechanism. Key Idea: Put probability at the decision boundary, determinism inside the execution boundary, and evidence at the promotion boundary — the model picks from a closed set of typed strategies; registered versioned tools do everything they already know how to do; independent validators, not model self-assessment, decide state transitions; and a recurring failure is converted into a new versioned capability (learning lives in the registry, not in weights or prompts). Methodology: This is a position paper with one preliminary empirical study. Architecturally: (1) a Task Envelope binds user intent to repository snapshot, scopes, budgets, and authority; (2) the planner samples a typed Plan IR, z_t ~ p_θ(z | u_t, x_t, C_t, e_{t<}), conforming to a closed machine-checkable schema; (3) a capability registry of versioned skills with declared contracts executes the plan (Equation 2: y_t = E(C_t, x_t, z_t)); (4) an evidence kernel runs a ladder of gates — strict compiler diagnostics, exact differential tests, ABI probes, performance/tail-latency, memory limits, provenance, policy — producing e_t = V(y_t; s_t, q_t, h_t); (5) promotion is an atomic transactional state transition (Equation 4), not a conversational conclusion. The proposed continuous-learning loop localizes a failure, classifies it as a bad plan vs. a missing capability, generates k materially distinct strategies, expands them via deterministic mutation into thousands of variants, ranks on a Pareto frontier, and promotes the winner as a versioned skill (Equation 5), with search tests separated from held-out admission tests and new capabilities entering in shadow mode. Critical design decisions: only registered strategy identifiers may alter emitted code (well-justified and demonstrated by the failure case in §6.3); free-form prose retained as evidence only (same); and the honest fail-closed boundary for unsupported language features (justified in principle, but the eligibility boundary is not yet machine-measured). Key Results: In the single reported experiment, five Python module sizes (20, 40, 80, 160, 320 nonblank lines) of one workload family were driven by two supervisors: GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek V4 Flash both passed 5/5 sizes first shot under strict gates (MSVC C++20 warnings-as-errors, exact agreement on 20,050 differential cases per size-combination, 100,250 total; throughput above Python; MHC generation <1s; clean build+test <15s). Mean native throughput was 35.26 and 35.64 MiB/s, i.e., 4.047x and 4.050x the Python reference. Plan leverage grew with size: GPT plans stayed at 271 tokens while generated project text grew from 6,457 to 18,141 tokens (23.8x to 66.9x leverage; DeepSeek 12.9x–49.0x), so ~98% of generated syntax was not model-authored. MHC generation scaled from ~5.8–6.3 ms (20 lines) to ~74.3–79.8 ms (320 lines) while validation took ~12–13 s — proof, not emission, dominates wall clock. A notable finding: DeepSeek's plan prose contained multiple errors (wrong backend language, misread speed threshold, invented ABI details) that had no effect on the executable because prose carried no authority. There are no baseline comparisons against direct LLM code generation or other agent frameworks; the only comparison is Python vs. generated C++ within the system. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the planner-prose-error neutralization demonstration). The genuinely novel move is reframing where learning accumulates — persistent versioned tool capability rather than weights, prompts, or episodic memory — plus the strict typed plan/prose authority separation. The components are standard: CEGIS, proof-carrying code, STOKE-style search, DreamCoder-style abstraction growth, PAL-style program delegation, DSPy, AlphaDev/FunSearch; the paper itself provides an honest related-work table conceding it "combines these motifs but assigns them different system roles." Rigor & Reproducibility: The experiment is carefully instrumented for what it covers: pre-registered gates, exact differential case counts, per-provider token accounting with explicit caveats about cross-provider comparability, and a candid §6.4 enumerating what the results do not show (no general Python translation, 20,050 tests ≠ formal equivalence, no workload generalization, learning loop not operational). No error bars, seeds, or variance analysis are reported despite the paper itself calling for repeated measurements and noise bounds elsewhere (§8.2) — an internal inconsistency. The reproducibility note says artifacts are "stored in the Sif research workspace" as sealed contracts and logs, but no public repository or URL is given, so nothing is independently verifiable. Methodological concerns: the benchmark is the authors' own workload family developed on their own system; there is no external baseline; both model names (GPT-5.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash) and results are self-reported from a single machine/toolchain (MSVC); and the document is a self-published working draft v0.1, not peer-reviewed, dated August 4, 2026. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a large position/vision component). Practical: The described stack is ordinary workstation hardware (MSVC, CUDA, CPython FFI), so yes in principle, though only the authors have run it. Efficient: Generation is milliseconds and plans are hundreds of tokens, but the paper's own measurements show validation costs ~200x generation time, and the one-time cost of authoring each new deterministic capability is unquantified. Effective: The evidence shows the system works on one engineered workload family; it does not show it solves general coding-agent problems, and the continuous-learning loop — the core claim — is untested end to end. Scalable: Untested beyond 320 lines and one operation family; scaling claims (§7) are arguments, not experiments, and the paper's own research agenda (§9) acknowledges this. Deliverable status: no public software artifact, dataset, or model is released; the work currently exists as an unpublished prototype plus a paper. Strengths: (1) The clearest articulation in this reviewer's reading of a coherent alternative to end-to-end model code generation, with the authority boundary between plan, prose, and implementation made precise and machine-checkable rather than rhetorical. (2) The §6.3 failure case is a genuinely convincing micro-demonstration: model prose errors (wrong language, wrong threshold, invented ABI) were architecturally incapable of corrupting the build — the kind of claim most agent papers assert but never exhibit. (3) Unusual intellectual honesty: §6.4 pre-emptively states what the experiment does not show, §7.6 concedes "deterministic does not mean safe," and §8 systematically enumerates failure modes (oracle problem, Goodhart, capability poisoning) that this paradigm is vulnerable to. (4) The identification of verification throughput as the emerging bottleneck (ms-scale generation vs. seconds-scale proof) is a non-obvious, falsifiable prediction worth pursuing. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: the experiment covers an in-family supported subset, not arbitrary Python; 320 lines is not an upper bound claim; 20,050 tests are not formal equivalence; speedup does not generalize to other workloads or machines; the continuously self-expanding registry is not operational end to end (§9.6 calls gap-to-skill packaging "the missing bridge"); token accounting across providers is not a reliable price comparison; determinism does not imply safety; and the oracle problem, test overfitting, capability poisoning, registry bloat, performance portability, dual-use risk, and human accountability are all named with mitigations. The paper confronts limitations directly and repeatedly — a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No baseline: the paper never compares MHC against a straightforward LLM agent writing the same C++ directly, or against existing frameworks (e.g., a ReAct/PAL loop with a compiler in the loop), so the core claim that compact plans are cheaper and end-to-end accepted work is lower is unmeasured against the obvious alternative. (2) The headline 4.05x speedup is the trivially expected result of compiling Python to C++; it is presented as evidence but tests the compiler, not the architecture. (3) Single workload family, single machine, single toolchain, single author, no released artifacts — the entire empirical base is one controlled in-house run, and "sealed workspace" is not reproducibility. (4) No variance/noise analysis despite performance gates being part of acceptance, on a paper that itself lectures the field about noise bounds and hardware provenance. (5) The continuous-learning loop — the paper's defining contribution — is entirely prospective; nothing in the experiment exercises failure localization, strategy search, packaging, or registry promotion. (6) The workload family (text fingerprinting, transport encoding) is small, deterministic, and string-shaped — a domain chosen where differential oracles are easy; behavior on numerical code, concurrency, or I/O-heavy workloads is unknown. (7) The paper's dated 2026 models and self-referential framing cannot be independently verified from the document. Bottom Line: A well-written, unusually self-aware position paper with one narrow supporting experiment and no released artifact — read it for the sharpest available articulation of the "learn in the tools, not the weights" thesis and its failure-mode analysis, but expect no evidence yet that the full vision (or even the continuous-learning loop) works, and look elsewhere for validated alternatives like PAL/ReAct-plus-compilers or verified-synthesis pipelines that cover adjacent ground with published results.

H $^{2} $ MT: Semantic Hierarchy-Aware Context-Time Memory for Beyond-Window Language Modeling

M Haghifam, Z He, J Cong, Y Sun · openreview.net · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces H2MT, a framework that represents a long document as a semantic tree of cached latent memory embeddings (one per node, built bottom-up) and answers questions by coarse-to-fine routing over these memories with a frozen backbone, instead of prefilling long raw context. - Why it's important: Practitioners serving QA over long structured documents (manuals, papers, narratives) pay large prefill latency and GPU memory for context mostly irrelevant to the query; the paper targets the quality-latency-memory trade-off of beyond-window conditioning. - How it does it: Each node gets a single memory embedding produced by a learnable read-slot readout over its text plus aggregated child memories; at inference a top-down, per-parent top-k routing over cached memories prunes subtrees, and only the small selected memory set is prefilled with the question. - The good: Large, consistently reproduced time-to-first-token reductions versus HMT (up to 23× on Qwen2.5-7B: 276.89 ms vs 6,398.96 ms) while averaging higher ROUGE-L across four QA datasets on most backbones (e.g., 35.86 vs 33.32 on Qwen2.5-14B). - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; the strongest quality baseline (SBERT+RAPTOR, 56.39 vs 46.64 ROUGE-L on HotpotQA) is confined to an appendix, and the headline LVS evaluation is a private, self-generated QA set. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on context compression, memory tokens, or structure-aware retrieval who want a concrete latent-memory alternative to raw-text RAG; skip if you need a deployment-ready recipe, since no code release is stated and gains are hierarchy-dependent.
