Problem & Motivation: Organizations adopting digital twins face a gap between technology deployment and benefits realization. The author identifies two gaps in the existing DT literature: (1) prior work emphasizes positive outcomes of DT implementation while paying little attention to the factors and challenges that affect the implementation process, leaving practitioners without guidance on effective implementation; and (2) most existing reviews examine technologies and industry-specific applications, but few examine implementation and benefits realisation from an organizational perspective. The intended audience is management researchers and practitioners deciding how to implement DTs and realize returns on what the paper describes as substantial capital investment. Key Idea: The key move is not a technical insight but a methodological one: use text mining (term-frequency/TF-IDF analysis and cluster extraction in WordStat) on a Scopus corpus to let the thematic structure of the DT literature emerge empirically, then organize the resulting 15 clusters into an implementation-and-benefits group (real time, scenario/architecture, decision making, optimization, related technologies) and an applications group (BIM, supply chain, manufacturing, healthcare, services, smart cities, urbanization/transportation, energy). This is a competent but standard application of established review-plus-text-mining technique; the paper states no reconceptualization or framework of its own beyond the grouping. Methodology: The review follows the Tranfield et al. (2003) three-stage protocol (planning, conducting, reporting), referencing PRISMA 2020 in the process diagram. The conducting stage searched Scopus with keywords "digital" and "twins" (7,353 initial hits), restricted to full-text, English-language, business-subject-area papers, yielding 296 articles with abstract screening for quality and relevance. Preprocessing included term normalization (e.g., "Digital Twin"/"Digital Twins" → "DigitalTwin") before importing into WordStat (QDA Miner add-on) for frequency, TF-IDF, and cluster analysis. Critical design decisions: (1) limiting the subject area to "business," which explains the corpus composition but excludes large portions of the engineering DT literature — justified by the organizational framing but a consequential scoping choice; (2) no publication-year limit, appropriate for a young field; (3) cluster-to-group mapping into two groups (the abstract says two groups; the introduction says three dimensions — implementation, benefits realization, practical application — a minor internal inconsistency). No formal quality-appraisal step (e.g., per-study scoring) and no duplicate-coding or reliability check on cluster assignment are reported. Key Results: As a review, the paper reports synthesized literature rather than measured outcomes. Headline outputs: 296 articles analyzed; 15 clusters extracted with reported frequencies (GREEN; TRANSITION 490; REAL TIME 427; TECHNOLOGIES 346; BIM; BUILDING 309; CREATION; SERVICE 231; CDC DAMPER; HYBRID 198; COVID-19 PANDEMIC 207; SUPPLY CHAIN 57; TRAFFIC; SCENARIOS 10); term-frequency table (DIGITALTWIN in 80.34% of cases, TF-IDF 74.8; SUPPLY TF-IDF 127.3). The synthesis catalogs claimed benefits per domain — real-time monitoring reducing machine breakdown time, DT-based warehouse optimization, supply chain resilience during COVID-19 disruption (Burgos and Ivanov, 2021), smart-city resource allocation — but presents these as claims from the reviewed literature without assessing the strength or consistency of the underlying evidence. Baseline comparison to prior DT reviews is qualitative and limited to the introduction's gap claims. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING at best, weakly: the genuinely novel element is the text-mining-derived cluster map of the business-facing DT literature with an explicit implementation/benefits lens; everything else — the Tranfield protocol, WordStat clustering, the domain-by-domain applications survey — is a standard combination of existing review techniques applied to a corpus defined by a business-subject filter. The paper itself claims no new method, dataset, or theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: The review protocol is documented at a level that supports coarse replication (database, keywords, filters, software, cluster counts), but several rigor elements are absent: no per-study quality appraisal, no inter-rater reliability or second coder for cluster assignment, no reporting of clustering parameters or how cluster labels were validated, and no PRISMA flow counts beyond the initial 7,353 → 296 funnel. No public release of the corpus, the WordStat project, or extracted data is mentioned. A methodological concern: benefits claims are aggregated from the reviewed papers' own (often qualitative, single-case) reports without critical weighting, so the review inherits rather than tests its evidence base; the author acknowledges this in the limitations section. The narrow "business" subject-area filter risks systematically excluding relevant implementation studies published in engineering venues. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a systematic review with text-mining analysis; no system is built and no primary experiments are run). - Practical: The text-mining pipeline uses commercially available, widely licensed software (WordStat/QDA Miner) and a standard database, so the method is reproducible by any researcher. - Efficient: The corpus (296 documents) is small for text mining; cost is negligible relative to alternatives. - Effective: It delivers a thematic map and research agenda, which addresses the stated gap at the level of literature organization, but it does not — and does not claim to — produce validated guidance that improves implementation success rates. - Scalable: Not applicable to deployment; the review's coverage itself is bounded by the single-database, business-subject filter, and the paper does not test sensitivity of the clusters to those choices. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset release, or reusable instrument — it stops at paper form (a citation-dense narrative map plus a research agenda in Table 5). Strengths: - The explicit implementation-and-benefits framing is a real positioning contribution: most prior DT reviews target technical architectures or single industries, and this review deliberately centers organizational factors (organizational, technological, economic, socio-political determinants; post-implementation benefit monitoring). - The text mining is used to ground the thematic structure rather than as decoration — cluster frequencies (e.g., only 10 hits for TRAFFIC; SCENARIOS versus 427 for REAL TIME) give readers a quantified sense of where the literature is thin, which directly informs the research agenda. - The future research agenda (Table 5) is specific and answerable — individual-level adoption factors, training/resource support, post-implementation benefit monitoring, DT security and privacy in critical sectors — rather than the generic "more research is needed" typical of reviews. - Honest self-assessment of evidence limitations: the author directly flags that the reviewed empirical base is dominated by qualitative case studies and cross-sectional designs. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author states that (1) the majority of reviewed empirical papers used qualitative methods (case studies), limiting generalizability; (2) most quantitative work is cross-sectional; and (3) the review focuses on dominant contexts and may not capture scaling challenges across organizational types, specifically the SME-versus-large-corporation difference. These limitations are stated plainly and without minimizing, which is a credibility positive. The author does not, however, acknowledge limitations of the review method itself (single database, business-subject filter, no quality appraisal). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No study-quality appraisal or evidence weighting: benefits are cataloged by citation count and narrative repetition, so a widely repeated but weakly supported claim is indistinguishable from a well-validated one. - Single-database (Scopus-only) search with a business subject-area filter likely excludes implementation-relevant work in engineering and computer-science venues; no sensitivity check or cross-database validation is reported. - The cluster extraction is unvalidated: no inter-coder reliability, no description of clustering algorithm parameters, and no check that the 15 clusters are stable or exhaustive; the abstract's "two groups" versus the introduction's "three groups" suggests the grouping taxonomy was not finalized. - No comparison against existing DT reviews (e.g., engineering-focused surveys the paper cites, such as Fuller et al. 2020 or Rathore et al. 2021) to demonstrate what the organizational lens adds beyond those syntheses. - The COVID-19 cluster and the GREEN; TRANSITION cluster (the largest, at 490 frequency) are listed but the narrative synthesis underweights them relative to the implementation themes, leaving the reader without an account of what the twin/green-transition literature actually concludes. Bottom Line: A competently executed, honestly limitation-stated mapping of the business-facing DT literature that is useful as an entry-point bibliography and research-agenda source, but scholars seeking a critical, quality-weighted synthesis of DT implementation evidence — or practitioners seeking actionable implementation frameworks — will find stronger, more analytically demanding alternatives in the engineering-focused DT surveys it cites.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations running ERP systems face a fragmented evidence base on how AI (ML, DL, RL, NLP, computer vision, LLMs, GenAI) is actually being integrated across ERP modules. Prior reviews, the authors argue, focus on a single AI technology, one ERP module, or one industry, and no comprehensive review combines bibliometric trends, thematic synthesis of all AI technologies and ERP functions, and a future research agenda in one framework. The intended audience is ERP researchers, vendors (SAP, Oracle, Microsoft), CIOs, and policymakers. Key Idea: There is no single technical insight — the contribution is a PRISMA-structured synthesis whose organizing device is a five-period evolution taxonomy of ERP (Traditional ERP 1989–1999 → ERP II → Cloud ERP → Intelligent ERP → AI-driven/GenAI ERP 2023–2026) mapped against eleven AI technologies and eleven ERP functional modules. This is a competent but standard review structure. Methodology: The pipeline follows PRISMA 2020: identification via Boolean keyword searches in Scopus across three concept blocks (AI terms including LLM-specific names like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini; ERP terms; business-application terms), then sequential filtering — 3,278 records → 1,069 journal articles → 1,018 English-language → 485 after title/abstract/keyword screening → 443 after full-text screening. Conference papers, reviews, book chapters, and editorials were excluded by design. Analysis proceeds in two stages: bibliometric (VOSviewer: annual trends, sources, authors, institutions, countries, keyword co-occurrence networks) and manual thematic classification into four themes (evolution, AI technologies, ERP modules, enabling digital technologies). Critical design decisions: single-database sourcing (justified by Scopus coverage and VOSviewer compatibility), exclusion of non-journal literature (justified as quality control but acknowledged as a bias source), and a subjective thematic coding process with no reported inter-coder reliability. No formal quality-appraisal instrument (e.g., exclusion scoring) is described. Key Results: This is a survey, so "results" are descriptive statistics: publications grew from <15/year (1998–2017) to 20 (2021), 21 (2022), 20 (2023), 39 (2024), and 118 (2025) — a 3× jump in 2024–2025 attributed to GenAI/LLMs. Top sources: Expert Systems with Applications (17 papers, 866 citations), IEEE Access (15), Applied Sciences (10); Decision Support Systems has the highest citations per journal (920 from 7 papers). Top authors: Sarferaz (5 papers), Lin and Michel (4 each); Rouhani has the highest author citations (155 from 3 papers). Top countries: China (87 papers), USA (78; 3,842 citations), India (36), UK (32), Germany (28). Top keywords: Artificial Intelligence (99 occurrences), ERP (40+35), ML (34), Decision Support Systems (22). Thematic findings identify finance, SCM, manufacturing, HR, CRM, and BI as primary application domains, and data governance, cybersecurity, interoperability, explainability, and human-AI collaboration as dominant challenges. There are no baselines in the comparative sense; the only implicit comparison is against prior narrower reviews, and the marginal differentiation from Hurbean et al. [10] is not empirically demonstrated. Internal inconsistencies appear: Section 4.1 duplicates an entire paragraph with conflicting details (<15 vs. <10 publications/year pre-2018), and Figure 8 is mislabeled as a country collaboration network when it shows keyword co-occurrence. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the 443-article curated corpus) and a modest synthesis contribution; the PRISMA methodology, VOSviewer workflow, and thematic categorization are standard combinations of existing techniques. The genuinely new element is the inclusion window extending into 2026 and coverage of GenAI/LLM-era ERP literature — but the closest competing review [10] covers substantially the same ground, so the incremental novelty over existing reviews is limited. Rigor & Reproducibility: The PRISMA flow diagram and full numeric screening trail support reproducibility of the search, and the Boolean keyword lists are published. However: no inter-rater reliability for the manual screening and thematic coding; no quality-appraisal scoring of included studies; no error bars or uncertainty quantification for bibliometric counts (though these are census-like within the chosen database); no released dataset, code, or search-string artifact beyond what is in the text. Methodological concerns: single-database coverage (Scopus only) and journal-only inclusion systematically exclude the conference and preprint literature where LLM/GenAI-ERP work most likely appears — meaning the claimed 2025 surge (118 papers) may undercount or skew the field. Several self-citations to the authors' own review papers appear in the reference list. The duplicated paragraph and figure-caption errors in the bibliometric section undermine confidence in editorial care. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL/SURVEY (no system is built or experiment run; the deliverable is a synthesis). Sound: The PRISMA protocol is explicit and the selection arithmetic is internally checkable, though coding reliability is unreported. General: Findings are constrained to English-language Scopus-indexed journal articles, 1989–2026. Tight: Not applicable (no bounds); the closest analogue — completeness of coverage — is admittedly loose per the authors' own limitations. Implementable: The conceptual framework (Fig. 9) and ten-item research agenda are actionable as a research-roadmap artifact for reviewers and PhD students, not as software. Deliverable is paper-form only; no library, dataset export, or tool is released. Strengths: - Fully documented PRISMA screening trail with explicit numeric transitions (3,278 → 443), which many competing narrative reviews in this space lack. - The five-generation ERP evolution table (Table 1) mapping periods to AI capability is a genuinely useful didactic artifact that others can cite and extend. - Coverage extends into 2026, capturing the earliest GenAI/LLM-copilot-in-ERP literature that older reviews miss. - The gap analysis (explainable AI for ERP, AI governance frameworks, human-AI collaboration, Digital-Twin-ERP linkage, federated learning) is specific enough to seed concrete research projects rather than generic calls for "more work." Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: Scopus-only sourcing, English-only and journal-only inclusion (language, publication, and outlet bias), exclusion of conference/book/chapter literature that may contain the fastest-moving AI-ERP developments, dependence on Scopus metadata quality for bibliometric validity, and rapid obsolescence risk given the pace of GenAI change. They confront these directly and recommend periodic review updates — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No critical quality assessment of the 443 included studies; the synthesis treats all sources as equally credible, and the source list includes low-tier venues, so thematic "findings" may rest on weak primary evidence. - No differentiation from the nearly contemporaneous Hurbean et al. [10] review beyond a one-paragraph summary — the paper does not demonstrate what its synthesis adds over that work. - The thematic analysis method is never specified (no coding scheme, no coders, no reliability measure), making the four-theme classification unreproducible. - Several bibliometric claims are internally inconsistent (Section 4.1 states both "<15" and "<10" annual publications pre-2018 in duplicated text) and one figure is mislabeled, suggesting limited verification of the quantitative analysis. - The institutional analysis is nearly vacuous — the text reports the top institutions each published one paper, meaning the institutional network figure carries little signal, yet it is presented as a finding. - The "opportunities" and "challenges" sections are generic narrative (predictive analytics good, data quality hard) that could have been written without the 443-paper corpus, weakening the link between the bibliometric evidence and the synthesized conclusions. - The venue (International Scientific Spectrum, ISSN 3104-3305, Vol. 2, Issue 1, 2026) is a very new, low-visibility outlet; peer-review depth is uncertain and this is effectively an unvalidated preprint-quality publication. Bottom Line: A methodologically transparent but low-differentiation bibliometric review whose 443-article corpus and research-gap list are useful as a citation seed for newcomers to AI-ERP research, while specialists will get more critical value from the overlapping 2026 reviews it cites — and should treat its quantitative claims cautiously given the internal inconsistencies and the unestablished venue.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes ESOA, an enhanced Seagull Optimization Algorithm that augments the seagull metaheuristic with collaborative subgrouping, simulated offspring generation, and random population rearrangement, and applies it to multi-objective routing optimization (energy, delay, congestion, packet loss) in heterogeneous, mobile IoT networks. - Why it's important: Routing in large, mobile, battery-constrained IoT deployments directly determines network lifetime and quality of service, and prior metaheuristic routing optimizers reportedly suffer premature convergence and poor mobility handling, so a better-balanced search could extend device lifetime and delivery reliability. - How it does it: It retains the original SOA's migration (exploration) and spiral-attack (exploitation) phases, then partitions the population into fitness-selected subgroups whose leaders are updated via differential-style trial vectors and a bimodal crossover-rate schedule, with stochastic offspring creation and periodic re-partitioning to maintain diversity. - The good: On 10 CEC'2020 functions across 30 runs, ESOA ranks first in the Friedman test (average rank 1.5 vs. 2.6 for PSO, 4.3 for baseline SOA) and wins 9 of 10 functions with lower variance, and in NS-3 simulations with 1000 nodes it reaches 96.7–98.8% packet delivery ratio versus 78.1–85.9% for six baselines across six mobility regimes. - The missing: There is no component-wise ablation isolating which of the three added mechanisms (subgrouping, offspring generation, rearrangement) drives the gains, and all IoT results come from simulation with a single fixed deployment configuration — no hardware, no testbed, no code release. - Read it or not: Read it only if you work specifically on bio-inspired metaheuristics for IoT/WSN routing and need a recent data point in that literature; practitioners designing real routing systems will find little actionable or reproducible material here.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses routing and parameter optimization in large-scale heterogeneous IoT networks — smart cities, industrial automation — where devices differ in energy reserves and mobility, topologies change dynamically, and battery replacement is impractical. The authors argue that classical metaheuristics (GA, PSO, ACO) and the original Seagull Optimization Algorithm suffer premature convergence, poor exploration–exploitation balance at high dimensionality, and instability under mobility, and that prior IoT routing methods (MFO clustering, SDN-assisted cat swarm, fuzzy-grasshopper, IMOGWO, BWOA-fuzzy, etc.) each fail on at least one of scalability, convergence speed, mobility adaptation, or simultaneous optimization of energy, latency, congestion, and packet loss. The gap claimed is a lightweight, distributed-friendly optimizer that handles all four objectives jointly under heterogeneity and mobility. Key Idea: The core move is to restructure the SOA population into cooperating subgroups that evolve semi-autonomously — subgroup leaders are updated through a differential-evolution-style trial vector (leader coordinate, pull toward global best, and inter-peer differential perturbation) gated by a bimodally scheduled crossover rate, while offspring are synthesized from random parent pairs and the population is periodically reshuffled. This is intended to parallelize exploration across basins and prevent the premature convergence of the original SOA, while the standard migration/spiral phases supply global search and local refinement. Methodology: ESOA alternates two inherited phases with three added mechanisms. (1) Migration (exploration): collision avoidance via a linearly decaying control variable A, movement toward the best-performing neighbor with a random scaling factor β ∈ [0,1], and a Euclidean-like distance computation. (2) Spiral attack (exploitation): agents spiral around the best solution with radius decaying exponentially (µ initial size, ν decay rate), position updated by multiplying spiral coordinates by the migration distance. (3) Collaborative subgrouping: the population is split into small groups, leaders chosen by fitness, each leader's coordinates blended via a trial vector and crossover rate CR following a bimodal schedule that shifts mass from high to low CR over iterations. (4) Simulated generation: two offspring per pair of stochastically chosen parents via convex combination with random factor ρ. (5) Random rearrangement: periodic re-partitioning of agents. The IoT network model assigns nodes to heterogeneous energy classes with per-class multipliers and fractions summing to one; energy per node sums transmission, reception, and idle terms; congestion is a function of buffer occupancy and interference; latency combines transmission, processing, queuing, and propagation delays. A composite multi-objective fitness (energy, congestion, delay, packet loss) drives route selection, though the explicit weighting/selection formulation is not legible from the provided text. Complexity analysis gives O(N²D) per iteration (fitness evaluation is O(N²)), unchanged asymptotically from SOA. Design decisions worth flagging: the bimodal CR schedule is plausible but not justified empirically; the heterogeneous energy-class model is standard; the choice of waypoint mobility and 802.11 DCF is conventional for NS-3 IoT studies. Key Results: CEC'2020 (30 runs, 10 functions): ESOA wins 9/10 functions on mean fitness with the lowest Friedman average rank (1.5) versus SOA (4.3), WCA (5.7), PSO (2.6), GWO (4.6), EFO (6.1), BBO (4.5), and a harmony-search variant (7.2); e.g., F1 mean 1.16E+02 ± 4.33E+01 vs. 1.07E+04 for SOA; F5 1.96E+03 vs. 6.50E+03 for SOA. IoT simulation (NS-3, 1000 nodes, 5000×5000 m, 802.11/UDP/CBR at 1 pkt/s, 512 B packets, 3000 J initial energy, 100 min, 30 runs, six mobility scenarios from fully static to 50% mobile): PDR 96.71–98.75% vs. 78.05–85.94% for GA/ACO/PSO/GWO/WOA/SOA; end-to-end delay 6.13–8.13 (units as tabulated) vs. 10.01–14.89 for baselines; bandwidth utilization 81.6–88.9% vs. 58.0–67.4%; residual energy ~1417–1598 vs. 308–998 for baselines; routing cost 1580–1860 vs. 1790–2482; alive nodes 858–930 vs. 649–789; energy usage 1410–1595 vs. 2018–2672. Baselines are standard metaheuristics but not state-of-the-art routing protocols from the last several years (e.g., no deep-RL or recent 2024–2025 routing baselines from the paper's own literature review are simulated). One suspicious claim: the text reports ESOA "can reduce delays by up to 102.7% in high-mobility scenarios" — a reduction exceeding 100% is not meaningful and suggests a reporting or percentage-basis error. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (an incremental variant) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the specific combination of subgrouping, offspring synthesis, and rearrangement layered onto SOA with a bimodal CR schedule; however, each ingredient is a known metaheuristic operator (island models, differential-evolution trial vectors, generational recombination, random re-initialization) applied to a known base algorithm in a new application setting, which is the dominant pattern in this literature. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are absent: no experiment isolates the contribution of subgrouping, simulated generation, or rearrangement individually, so attribution of gains to any specific mechanism is unsupported. The benchmark study reports mean ± standard deviation over 30 runs and a Friedman rank test, which is appropriate; no post-hoc pairwise significance tests (e.g., Wilcoxon) are reported. The NS-3 study lists 30 independent runs and a "fixed simulation seed for repeatability" (contradictory on its face), and the tables report means only without error bars. No code, model, or simulation scripts are released; data are "available from the corresponding author on reasonable request." The network model is developed and evaluated in the authors' own simulation configuration only; no external benchmark scenario is used. Several equations are garbled in the text, hindering independent reimplementation. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation-based evaluation only). - Practical: The algorithm itself is lightweight and hardware-agnostic, but it was never run on physical or constrained devices — only MATLAB analysis on top of NS-3 simulation. - Efficient: The authors claim unchanged O(N²D) asymptotic complexity versus SOA, but concede constant-factor overhead from subgrouping, offspring generation, and rearrangement; no wall-clock runtimes are reported. - Effective: Evidence shows proxy gains in a simulator (PDR, delay, energy) under one deployment configuration; effectiveness on real radios, real interference, and real hardware energy profiles is untested. - Scalable: Tested at 1000 nodes in a 25 km² field; claims of scalability to larger networks are asserted via asymptotic complexity, not measured at 10×–100× scale. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model — it stops at paper form. Strengths: (1) The evaluation is broader than typical for this genre: 10 CEC'2020 functions with 30-run statistics and a Friedman test, plus eight network metrics across six mobility regimes, with full simulation-parameter disclosure (Table 4). (2) The paper honestly acknowledges that all results are simulation-based and that the added mechanisms cost extra computation — a more candid limitations section than is common in metaheuristic-routing papers. (3) The heterogeneous energy-class model and multi-objective fitness tying energy, congestion, delay, and packet loss into route evaluation is a reasonable, if standard, problem formalization. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (a) results rely on benchmarks and simulation, so communication and hardware constraints and edge-device differences may alter real performance; (b) subgrouping, offspring generation, and dynamic rearrangement add computational overhead; and (c) the system addresses optimization only, omitting security, trust management, and resource allocation. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive, and they commit to adaptive parameter tuning, hybrid light-optimization, edge/fog integration, and practical testing as future work. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No component-wise ablation — the central claim that subgrouping + offspring + rearrangement cause the improvement is never tested against an SOA with only one or two of the mechanisms. (2) The routing baselines simulated (GA, ACO, PSO, GWO, WOA, SOA) are generic optimizers, not the strongest recent IoT routing protocols the paper itself reviews (e.g., IMOGWO, BWOA-fuzzy, QEMR), so the headline gains may partly reflect baseline weakness. (3) The "102.7% delay reduction" figure is internally inconsistent and undermines confidence in the percentage accounting. (4) Six mobility scenarios are described but only five are enumerated in the text, and the multi-objective fitness weighting is never made explicit, blocking reproduction. (5) Mobility is modeled exclusively as random waypoint; no trace-driven or realistic mobility (e.g., real vehicular or pedestrian traces) is evaluated. (6) Standard deviations are reported for benchmarks but not for the network simulation tables, and the fixed-seed vs. 30-run statement is contradictory. Bottom Line: A competent but conventional metaheuristic-variant paper that will mainly interest researchers tracking the bio-inspired IoT-routing literature; anyone seeking deployable, reproducible, or rigorously ablated routing optimization should look to stronger recent baselines and testbed-validated methods instead.

GO4RES: Goal-based Modeling for Reward Function Engineering and Shaping

KH Chan, S Zilberman, BHC Cheng · modre.ece.mcgill.ca · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GO4RES, a framework that uses KAOS-style goal models with weighted AND/OR decompositions and leaf-level utility functions to systematically construct and fine-tune reward functions for search-based techniques such as reinforcement learning and evolutionary search. - Why it's important: Reward functions are typically written by ad-hoc, trial-and-error developer effort, producing nested, hard-to-interpret mathematical expressions whose failure modes (reward hacking, mis-specified objectives) are a documented pain point in RL and evolutionary computing. - How it does it: The core move is compiling a reward function automatically from a goal tree via post-order traversal: leaf goals carry normalized [0,1] utility functions bound to system components, AND-nodes aggregate as linear weighted sums, OR-nodes aggregate via min/max, and edge weights on the model let developers reshape priorities without editing code. - The good: The reverse-engineering of Hornby et al.'s NASA ST5 evolved-antenna reward function into a GO4RES goal model — and recovering the exact original Expression (3) from the model — concretely demonstrates that the representation can faithfully capture a real, historically significant reward function. - The missing: No experiment actually runs the generated reward functions: the rover-parking RL example is a paper exercise with a shown model and function but no training curves, no comparison against the ad-hoc alternative, and no evidence that GO4RES-produced rewards yield equal or better search outcomes. - Read it or not: Worth reading for requirements-engineering (GORE) researchers and SBSE practitioners exploring structured reward specification, but ML-for-RL researchers seeking evidence of improved reward design will find only a position/proof-of-concept paper with the formalization deferred to future work.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Developers using search-based techniques (RL, evolutionary algorithms, game theory, search-based testing) must transcribe abstract, natural-language objectives into mathematical reward functions. Current practice is ad-hoc — driven by domain expertise, simulation-specific constraints, and trial-and-error — and produces long, nested, error-prone expressions that lose traceability to the original objectives, resist extension, and make reward shaping (weight fine-tuning) a low-level code-editing exercise. The authors argue this gap is underexplored relative to algorithmic improvements to the search methods themselves, and that the problem matters for software assurance because the reward function is the only feedback channel to otherwise uninterpretable learned models. The intended audience is SBSE and requirements-engineering researchers; the paper is a workshop-level vision/proof-of-concept contribution (MoDRE 2026 proceedings). Key Idea: Reward engineering is structurally analogous to goal-oriented requirements engineering: a high-level objective can be hierarchically AND/OR-decomposed until leaf goals are concretely measurable, at which point utility functions (u = f(v), normalized to [0,1]) attached to leaves and weights attached to decomposition edges allow the reward function to be compiled from the model by tree traversal rather than hand-written. The mapping is: AND-decomposition → normalized linear weighted sum of child aggregates; OR-decomposition → weighted min/max over children; maximization terms in a minimization problem → complement (1 − u). Methodology: GO4RES proceeds in four phases. (1) Goal decomposition: the root objective (e.g., 'G1: Rover parks autonomously') is refined via KAOS-style AND/OR decomposition into measurable leaf goals, explicitly separating functional subgoals (e.g., avoid collisions) from non-functional ones (e.g., complete the maneuver quickly). (2) Utility functions: each leaf goal is bound to a system component (GPS, LiDAR, radar, bumper sensor, clock) whose observable properties are converted to a scalar in [0,1]; normalization prevents large-unit measurements from dominating the reward. (3) Weights: default edge weight 1.0; developers raise weights on safety-critical subtrees (e.g., collision avoidance at 3.0 in the running example) or lower them to express sensor distrust (LiDAR down-weighted to 0.3 in fog). (4) Construction: a post-order traversal aggregates leaf utility terms upward — weighted sums at AND nodes with weights normalized to sum to 1.0 across siblings, min/max at OR nodes — producing the final expression. The framework defaults to minimization problems. Two design decisions stand out: linear weighted-sum aggregation (standard, but means interaction effects between subgoals cannot be expressed except via the ^5 penalty exponent admitted ad hoc in the antenna case), and model-level weight editing as the reward-shaping interface (well-motivated for traceability but untested empirically). The paper explicitly defers the formalization of the language and aggregation semantics, plus the graphical front end, to a forthcoming paper. Key Results: No empirical results are reported. The two demonstrations are: (1) a running example building the goal model for an autonomous rover parking task with RL, yielding the reward function in Figure 2b — but no training run, learning curve, or success metric for the rover is given; (2) a reverse-engineering exercise reconstructing Hornby et al.'s NASA ST5 evolved-antenna objective (Σ_f [rms(3, v_f)^5 + rms(1.5, v_f) + rms(1.0, v_f)] + min(0, 15.25 − g_f0) + min(0, 10.25 − g_f20)) from a goal model, recovering the identical expression. There are no baselines, no datasets/benchmarks, no quantitative outcomes, and no evaluation at any scale. The claim that GO4RES-produced rewards match ad-hoc rewards is asserted by construction, not measured. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (arguably NEW FORMULATION): the genuinely new element is the automatic compilation of a reward function from a weighted goal model with utility-function leaves — prior work either decomposes rewards into per-subtask controllers (Marthi, Juozapaitis et al.), uses goal models only for run-time monitoring (Langford et al.) or simulation generation (Liaskos et al.), or engineers rewards via FSM/verification artifacts (MoVEMo). The underlying ingredients — KAOS decomposition, utility functions from prior work by the same group (Langford et al., MODAS/Anunnaki), weighted linear aggregation — are standard; the contribution is their composition into a design-time reward-compiler pipeline, which is competent but incremental from an ML standpoint. Rigor & Reproducibility: There are no ablations, no error bars, no seeds, no significance tests, and no quantitative evaluation of any kind — the paper is a position/proof-of-concept contribution. No code, tool, or model artifact is released or linked; the graphical front end is 'currently under development.' Methodological concerns: the framework is evaluated only through the authors' own illustrative models and a single reverse-engineering exercise; the central claim (systematic goal-based engineering yields better/more maintainable rewards than ad-hoc authoring) is never tested on the same benchmark it is argued for; the reward-shaping workflow (adjust weights, recompile, rerun) is described but never demonstrated end-to-end on a real training problem. The formal semantics being deferred makes independent reimplementation currently impossible. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS-aspirational but currently EMPIRICAL-in-name-only — no artifact is delivered; classify as a vision paper with paper-form only. Practical: Not evaluable; the generated reward functions are ordinary scalar expressions runnable on commodity hardware, but no tool exists yet. Efficient: Compilation cost is trivial (tree traversal), but training cost relative to alternatives is unstudied. Effective: No evidence the approach solves the stated problem — the rover example produces a reward function that is never used to train anything. Scalable: Not tested; whether weighted-sum aggregation with a handful of goals scales to reward functions with dozens of interacting terms (common in deep RL fine-tuning) is only claimed. Deliverable: stops at paper form; the language formalization, aggregation semantics, and tooling are future work. Strengths: - The core analogy — reward engineering as goal-oriented requirements engineering with a concrete, mechanical compilation semantics (post-order traversal, weighted sums, min/max OR nodes) — is crisp and genuinely maps a mature RE formalism onto a need in SBSE that the literature has under-served. - The ST5 antenna reverse-engineering is a smart validation strategy for a paper without experiments: it shows the representation is expressive enough to exactly reproduce a real, historically significant reward function, and demonstrates the model-introduction abstraction level as a migration path for legacy reward functions. - The functional/non-functional separation with per-edge weights gives a defensible, traceable interface for reward shaping that avoids error-prone code edits, and the sensor-confidence weighting use case (fog-degraded LiDAR) is a concrete, credible application. - Honest scoping in the Discussion: the authors state plainly that domain expertise is still required for decomposition and weight assignment and that GO4RES does not address long-standing goal-modeling challenges. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge that (1) a domain expert is still needed to identify top-level goals, decompose, and weigh tradeoffs — GO4RES does not automate the hard judgment calls; (2) the inherent challenges of goal-based modeling and abstraction engineering are out of scope; (3) the formalization of the GO4RES language and aggregation semantics is omitted (deferred to a forthcoming paper along with the graphical front end); and (4) utility functions require developer-written measurement code. This is a credibility positive — they confront the human-in-the-loop nature of the approach directly rather than implying automation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The title promises 'reward shaping,' but no shaping experiment exists — not even a single RL episode or evolutionary generation is run with a GO4RES-constructed reward; the entire empirical claim rests on the visual plausibility of the compiled expressions. - Linear weighted-sum aggregation cannot express known reward-design phenomena (reward hacking from additive terms, non-monotone interactions, temporal credit assignment); the antenna case sidesteps this by admitting an ad hoc exponent-5 penalty notation, revealing the semantics are not yet principled. - No comparison against the closest competing abstractions (MoVEMo's FSM-based approach, iStar-based simulation generation) even at the qualitative level of what each can express. - Interpretability and maintainability benefits — the paper's central selling points — are asserted without any user study, maintainability metric, or even a worked failure case of the ad-hoc alternative they criticize. - Min/max OR aggregation over weighted children has subtle semantics (weighting inside a min can invert the intended preference) that go unanalyzed. - The related-work positioning against the fast-moving LLM-as-reward-model literature (RL-VLM-F, goal-guided LLM RL) is dismissive in one sentence; given that line of work directly targets the same specification bottleneck, a comparison of tradeoffs is warranted. Bottom Line: A readable and well-motivated RE-side vision paper that usefully reframes reward engineering as goal modeling, but with zero experimental validation, no artifact, and deferred formalization it offers practitioners a promising sketch rather than a usable alternative — read it for the framing, not for evidence.

Problem & Motivation: Conventional CNN-based vision models detect and classify objects from pixel patterns but cannot interpret scenes semantically — they cannot infer that a detected cat looks scared, that a pedestrian at a crosswalk intends to cross, or that a segmented tumor has clinical significance. The paper argues this gap between perception and world knowledge limits deployment in autonomous driving, medical imaging, robotics, and human-AI interaction. Prior surveys have treated individual facets in isolation (VQA, neuro-symbolic integration, scene graph generation), and the authors claim no prior survey unifies the full spectrum of commonsense integration approaches in vision. The problem the survey addresses is fragmentation: practitioners lack a cross-paradigm framework for comparing how systems represent, retrieve, and fuse commonsense knowledge. Key Idea: The paper has no algorithmic key idea; it is a survey. Its closest analogue to a core insight is the unified pipeline abstraction — every commonsense-enhanced vision system can be decomposed into Perception → Knowledge Retrieval → Fusion → Reasoning (plus constraint validation and explanation stages) — combined with the temporal thesis that the field has moved through three eras: static knowledge bases (ConceptNet, ATOMIC, scene graphs), dynamic retrieval-augmented pipelines (KRISP, REVIVE), and implicit parametric knowledge in foundation models (BEiT-3, Flamingo, GPT-4V). The eras thesis is the paper's most reusable framing, though it is a synthesis of known history rather than a new discovery. Methodology: The authors run a PRISMA-style selection: 1,050 records from IEEE Xplore, arXiv, CVPR/ICCV/ECCV proceedings, and other sources; 450 duplicates removed; title/abstract screening excludes 400; full-text assessment of 160 with 117 excluded (pre-2018, insufficient evaluation, theoretical-only, low significance); 44 studies included (categorized as 10 foundation models, 25 vision-language integration, 9 surveys/meta-analyses). Included papers are organized into three methodological categories — knowledge graphs/scene graphs, neuro-symbolic models, and commonsense-enhanced vision transformers — and evaluated along four qualitative criteria: accuracy (mAP/IoU/Top-1), depth of commonsense integration (dynamic vs. pre-encoded), scalability, and generalization. The comparative analysis (Section 6) assigns subjective High/Medium/Low ratings to five representative models (SENet, NSCL, LXMERT, ViLT, Graph R-CNN), explicitly disclaimed as non-reproducible relative indicators. Sections 7–9 cover 2022–2025 trends (REVIVE, OmniVL, BEiT-3, OSCAR++, Flamingo), failure modes, and future directions. Critical design decisions: the PRISMA protocol is a strength for transparency, but the rating methodology for Table 5 is unstated, and the 44-study corpus is small relative to the 1,050-record candidate pool without a stated reason for the final category counts. Key Results: As a survey, the paper reports no new experimental results. Its substantive outputs are: (1) the four-stage pipeline taxonomy (Table 4) mapping subtasks, techniques, tools (ConceptNet, ATOMIC, FAISS, DETR, Mask2Former, BLIP-2, LLaVA), and metrics (mAP, Rel-mAP, mIoU, PQ, CIDEr, SPICE) across five task families; (2) a comparative table (Table 5) rating five models on accuracy, commonsense integration, scalability, and real-world applicability — e.g., NSCL rated "Very High" integration but "Low" scalability due to symbolic-execution overhead, while ViLT is rated "Very High" on both accuracy and applicability but expensive for edge deployment; (3) a failure-mode taxonomy (Table 7) covering prior–evidence conflict, incomplete/outdated knowledge, and cascading errors, with worked examples (misinterpreted Yield signs in driving, missed lung nodules from population-level priors, 15–20% accuracy drops on counter-stereotypical images attributed to Zhao et al. 2017, and up to 12% accuracy loss from anatomical priors on rare variants such as dextrocardia per Oakden-Rayner et al. 2020). No benchmark numbers are newly measured; all quantitative claims are inherited from cited work, and several (the bias percentages) are cited to papers whose original scope may differ. Baselines are not applicable; the surveyed systems span 2018–2025 so coverage of the newest foundation-model era is partial. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the four-stage pipeline abstraction and three-era paradigm taxonomy) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING in the weak survey sense (synthesized failure-mode taxonomy). Nothing here is a new method, dataset, or system: the pipeline abstraction is a sensible relabeling of stages that retrieval-augmented and neuro-symbolic papers already describe piecemeal, the era taxonomy is a retrospective reading of a well-known trend (symbolic KBs → RAG → implicit pretraining), and the failure analysis assembles known results from the hallucination, bias, and safety literatures. The genuine contribution is organizational: giving practitioners a shared vocabulary for cross-paradigm comparison. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a survey, there are no ablations, seeds, or significance tests to report, and none are claimed — the reproducibility checklist explicitly states the paper includes no computational experiments and introduces no datasets. Methodological concerns a reviewer should flag: (1) Table 5's ratings have no documented derivation procedure — the paper admits they are "qualitative and relative indicators rather than absolute or directly reproducible measurements," which undermines its comparative analysis section; (2) the SENet entry cites "(senet2020)" and describes a "Semantic Enrichment Network," which risks confusion with the well-known squeeze-excitation SENet and lacks a verifiable primary reference; (3) the "DeepLogic" attribution to DeepMind has a broken citation (rendered as "(deepLogic)") and appears unverifiable, raising contamination concerns; (4) quantitative claims in Section 8 (15–20% bias amplification, 12% prior-induced degradation) are cited to works (Zhao et al. 2017; Oakden-Rayner et al. 2020) that studied related but different settings, so the numbers should be treated as illustrative rather than established; (5) inclusion/exclusion reasons for the PRISMA funnel are coarse ("less significant contributions": n=28) and the tie between the 44 included studies and the papers actually discussed in Sections 4–7 is not traceable. No code, data, or artifact release is applicable or provided. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: THEORETICAL-adjacent SURVEY — no primary experimental claim, no built artifact; the four-property check for deployed systems does not literally apply, so it is assessed in the survey's own terms. - Sound: The synthesis is internally coherent and the PRISMA protocol is explicit, but the subjective comparative ratings and at least one suspect citation (DeepLogic, SENet) are soundness blemishes. - General: The pipeline abstraction is claimed to apply across all paradigms; the paper does not test it against any system that resists the decomposition, so its generality is asserted, not demonstrated. - Tight: Not applicable (no bounds); the closest analogue — whether the taxonomy discriminates cleanly between paradigms — is loose, since hybrid systems (e.g., retrieval-augmented foundation models) straddle the era boundaries the paper itself acknowledges. - Implementable: The survey delivers a reusable design checklist (Table 4's task → technique → tool → metric mapping) that a practitioner could act on; there is no software artifact, dataset, or trained model, and the work stops at paper form. Strengths: - The unified four-stage pipeline abstraction is the paper's real contribution: it lets a reader locate any commonsense-in-vision system by pipeline stage and identify which stage (retrieval latency, fusion alignment) is the bottleneck, which is genuinely actionable for composing hybrid systems. - The static → dynamic-retrieval → implicit-knowledge periodization (2019–2025) is a sharp, teachable framing that connects Symbolic-AI-era work to foundation models and correctly foregrounds the transparency/efficiency trade-off the field has made. - The failure-mode treatment (Section 8) is unusually concrete for a survey: it names mechanisms (confirmation bias in query generation, lack of source verification, multi-hop bias compounding, missing uncertainty propagation and backtracking) rather than listing generic concerns, and pairs each failure with a needed solution in Table 7. - The PRISMA-style selection funnel with explicit exclusion counts is more transparent than most vision surveys, which typically omit methodology entirely. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: dataset bias and knowledge-base incompleteness (ConceptNet/ATOMIC gaps, encoded stereotypes like <doctor, male>); the opacity of implicit knowledge in foundation models versus auditable symbolic systems (Table 6 contrasts "traceable" retrieval failures with "silent, high-confidence" parametric failures); scalability of symbolic execution and scene-graph generation in real-time settings; hallucination amplification in retrieval-augmented systems; the brittleness of current pipelines for safety-critical, tail-risk applications; and that most work addresses static images rather than video. They also explicitly flag that Table 5's ratings are qualitative and not directly reproducible — a direct confrontation of their weakest section, which is a credibility positive. Overall the limitations section is candid rather than minimizing. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The comparative analysis covers only five models, all from 2018–2021; the 2022–2025 systems the paper itself identifies as the current paradigm (BEiT-3, Flamingo, OmniVL, GPT-4V) are described qualitatively in Section 7 but excluded from Table 5, so the comparative analysis is dated relative to the paper's own thesis. - No quantitative meta-analysis: the survey never aggregates benchmark numbers (VQA accuracy, CIDEr, mAP) across the 44 included studies, so claims like "recent methods improve performance" remain anecdotal. - The evaluation criteria (accuracy, integration depth, scalability, generalization) are announced in Section 3 but the per-paper application of these criteria is never shown — the reader cannot see how any individual study scored. - The link between the PRISMA-included 44 studies and the systems actually reviewed (REVIVE, OmniVL, BEiT-3, OSCAR++, Flamingo, etc.) is not demonstrated; several discussed systems' provenance through the funnel is untraceable. - Internal inconsistencies that survived review: Figure 4's caption describes a striped horse while the body text describes an occluded zebra; the 15–20% bias figure is attributed to a 2017 captioning-bias paper whose experimental setting differs; a broken citation ("(deepLogic)") suggests unverified sourcing. - The "What this survey adds" claims are self-assessed; no search of prior surveys (e.g., existing neuro-symbolic or VQA surveys with pipeline framings) is performed to substantiate the "no prior survey provides this" assertion. Bottom Line: A serviceable, honestly-constructed entry-point survey whose pipeline taxonomy and era framing are worth adopting as shared vocabulary, but whose dated comparative table, thin methodological transparency, and citation hygiene issues mean an experienced researcher will get more from reading the primary papers (KRISP, NSCL, REVIVE, Flamingo) directly — read it if you are entering the field, skip it if you are not.

Enhanced Multi-Agent Framework for Predictive Process Mining with Object-Centric Analysis and Vision-Based Task Mining

SS Baidya, A Baidya · avestia.com · business process mining or process mining - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a 21-agent CrewAI-based open-source framework for enterprise process mining that adds three capabilities to the authors' prior five-agent system: object-centric process mining with OCEL 2.0 support, a persistent "Living Process Intelligence Graph" with drift detection, and desktop task mining via a local vision LLM (llava:13b). - Why it's important: Commercial process mining platforms (Celonis, UiPath, IBM) are expensive licensed SaaS with closed architectures, so a zero-inference-cost open-source alternative with comparable feature coverage would lower the barrier for enterprises without platform budgets. - How it does it: The core move is architectural composition: orchestrating 21 specialized LLM-driven agents across six layers through nine formally characterized communication channels, wrapping PM4Py's OCEL 2.0 primitives, a NetworkX-SQLite graph store with Welford online statistics, and Ollama-hosted llava:13b for screenshot classification. - The good: The paper's most credible evidence is convergent, cross-agent validation on a live Workday HCM production tenant (39,986 events) — e.g., two independent agents both flag "Calculate Pay" as the top automation target (81% automation potential), and the OCEL export shows 33,696 event-to-object relations with zero object-to-object relations, an honest structural characterization of how Workday encodes process state. - The missing: There is no controlled baseline comparison whatsoever — the "competitive parity on 9 of 10 dimensions" claim is a self-scored feature checklist against commercial products, not a head-to-head benchmark, and no ablations isolate which of the 21 agents or 9 channels materially contribute. - Read it or not: Worth skimming for process-mining practitioners or BPM tooling builders evaluating open-source multi-agent architectures against commercial platforms; skip it if you want algorithmic novelty, statistical rigor, or reproducible benchmarks, since it offers none of those.

Problem & Motivation: Enterprises need data-driven visibility into executed business processes, but the authors' prior multi-agent process mining framework (5 agents, then 18) had three gaps relative to commercial platforms: it handled only case-centric event logs (missing many-to-many object relationships that cause known convergence/divergence distortions), produced a one-shot static digital twin with no persistence or drift awareness, and had no visibility into desktop-level user activity, where industry estimates claim 40–60% of knowledge-worker time is spent on invisible microtasks. The intended users are process mining / BPM teams in enterprises, particularly those already running Workday HCM, who lack commercial platform budgets. The paper aims to close these three gaps while preserving prior baseline metrics (98.7% preprocessing accuracy, 0.94 fitness, 23.7% cycle-time reduction). Key Idea: There is no single algorithmic insight; the core idea is an integration architecture — a six-layer, nine-channel multi-agent topology in which (a) object-centric event logs replace case-centric ones, (b) a write-through NetworkX-SQLite graph with Welford incremental statistics and seven-category statistical drift detection replaces a static simulation snapshot, and (c) a local vision LLM classifies desktop screenshots to correlate UI activity with system events. Each ingredient (OCEL 2.0, PM4Py, NetworkX, SQLite, CrewAI, llava:13b, Welford's algorithm) is off-the-shelf; the contribution is their composition under an agent coordination contract. Methodology: The pipeline has six layers. (1) Data Ingestion (4 agents) extracts from a Workday HCM tenant via OAuth 2.0/SOAP/REST/RaaS and emits a validated OCEL 2.0 or CSV event log as a sole data contract. (2) A Core Pipeline of 5 sequential CrewAI agents (inherited from prior work) performs preprocessing, DFG/process-tree discovery, conformance checking, bottleneck detection (false-positive target <5%), and Monte Carlo ROI-based optimization, with guardrails including a minimum 0.80 fitness threshold and per-agent tool-access control. (3) An Orchestration Layer (5 agents) brokers LLM inference through a single LLM Manager with 2s failover and runs predictive intervention: bottleneck prediction at a 1.5σ threshold over a 2.5-hour horizon, resource reallocation (<40% underutilized to >85% overloaded), and Monte Carlo evaluation of four intervention scenarios across 1,000 runs. (4) An OCPM Layer (4 agents) discovers OC-DFGs with per-type perspective switching, builds an N×N object interaction matrix with cardinality detection, and tracks object lifecycles (72-hour stuck-object threshold). (5) The Process Intelligence Graph (4 agents) maintains a NetworkX DiGraph with SQLite write-through persistence (claimed sub-5ms latency), O(1) Welford incremental statistics, drift detection across seven categories via z-tests and chi-squared tests with CRITICAL/WARNING/INFO classification, and disk-based version control with branching/rollback. (6) A Task Mining side channel (4 agents) records desktop events in three privacy modes, classifies screenshots into a nine-category taxonomy via llava:13b, correlates desktop-to-system events via four matching strategies, and auto-generates RPA bot specifications. Critical design decisions: sequential (rather than parallel) core-agent execution — justified by the prior work's context-chain design but not ablated here; local-only LLM inference (zero API cost but likely explains the modest 78–85% classification accuracy); and task mining as a read-only side channel, well-justified for isolation but meaning the correlation engine cannot write back corrections. The Monte Carlo intervention ROI assumes $100 per prevented delay-hour — an assumption, not a measured value. Key Results: Validation ran on a live Workday HCM production tenant producing 39,986 events; the OCEL 2.0 export contained 1,378 objects across 3 object types, 11,232 events across 18 event types, and 33,696 event-to-object relations with zero object-to-object relations. The HR Process module yielded 356 cases / 34,986 events / 47 variants with four HIGH-IMPACT bottlenecks and 30 active cases averaging 274 days in-flight; Payroll showed a 31-day average cycle time (8% period-on-period improvement), 95% completion, and a fifth-ranked variant averaging 882 days. The Violation Tagger flagged 39% of cases on one 24-hour rule ($34,953 value at risk, 100% per-resource violation rate), while the aggregate compliance score was 97.2% with 68 active violations including a HIGH-severity SOX segregation-of-duties breach. HCM Recruiting showed 624 cases at 26.8-day cycle time with 0% SLA compliance. The Digital Twin detected 0% live SLA compliance across 246 active cases concurrent with 100% resource utilization — a real-time finding batch analysis cannot surface. Task mining achieved 78–85% screenshot classification accuracy (sub-3s latency) and a 72% desktop-to-system match rate, identifying copy-paste operations consuming 22% of user time as the top RPA candidate. The Automation Simulator projected $3,038/year for Calculate Pay alone, within $57,000 in claimed realized savings at 1.2× ROI. The claim of "full parity or superiority on 9 of 10 capability dimensions" against Celonis/UiPath/IBM is a self-assessed feature matrix, not a benchmark; no competing tool was run on the same data. All headline quantitative claims are single-tenant, single-run, with no baselines, seeds, or significance testing. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. Genuinely novel is the claim of being the most complete open-source OCEL 2.0 implementation demonstrated on enterprise HCM data with an integrated live-twin-plus-task-mining stack; however, every underlying technique (OCEL 2.0, OC-DFG discovery, Welford statistics, z/chi-squared drift tests, vision-LLM screenshot classification, CrewAI agent orchestration) is a standard existing component, and the paper is best read as a competent systems-integration report rather than a new method. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak. There are no ablations showing which of the 21 agents or 9 channels matter, no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, and no code repository URL despite the paper repeatedly calling the framework "open-source." The paper was developed and evaluated on a single production tenant (the authors' own Workday deployment), so all metrics are self-reported on the authors' own deployment with no external ground truth; the "competitive benchmarking" is a self-scored capability checklist rather than an experiment; the 78–85% llava classification accuracy is stated without describing the labeled evaluation set or annotation protocol; and the sub-5ms write-through latency claim lacks measurement methodology. The 98.7% preprocessing accuracy, 0.94 fitness, and 23.7% cycle-time reduction are inherited from prior self-published work and are not re-validated here. The conference venue (EECSS/ICAIIS, Avestia) is a low-barrier congress, so these results should be treated as pre-peer-scrutiny systems reporting, not peer-reviewed benchmark evidence. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool evaluated on a live production tenant, though largely via self-report). Practical: Yes — it runs entirely on local infrastructure (Ollama-hosted llava:13b, SQLite, NetworkX) with no cloud dependency, so commodity hardware suffices. Efficient: Zero inference cost versus commercial SaaS is the headline advantage, and O(1) Welford statistics are cheap, but llava:13b's sub-3s-per-screenshot latency implies limited task-mining throughput on desktop-scale capture volumes. Effective: The evidence shows it surfaces plausible findings (bottlenecks, compliance violations, automation candidates) on one tenant, but effectiveness versus commercial tools is only asserted via the self-scored feature matrix, and the 23.7% cycle-time reduction claim from prior work is not re-demonstrated here. Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — 39,986 events and 356–624 cases per module is small by commercial standards (platforms process billions of records), and no evidence shows the NetworkX in-memory graph, SQLite write-through, or sequential CrewAI chain survives 10–100× event volumes. The work claims an open-source framework artifact, but no repository, release, or download is cited in the paper, so as published it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The live-tenant validation is unusually concrete for a systems paper: 0% live SLA compliance concurrent with 100% resource utilization, with five bottleneck instances localized to onboarding, is a genuinely real-time finding that retrospective batch analysis cannot produce, and the paper correctly frames the gap between the lagging 97.2% aggregate compliance score and point-in-time SOX/GDPR exposure. - The convergent-evidence design — two architecturally independent agents (Core Pipeline and Automation Simulator) both designating "Calculate Pay" as the top automation target — is a small but credible internal-consistency check rarely seen in agent-framework papers. - The structural finding that Workday HCM emits 33,696 E2O relations with zero O2O relations (i.e., encodes state via event sequences, not object graphs) is an honest, useful empirical characterization for anyone attempting OCPM on Workday data. - The nine-channel communication architecture is specified at an unusually formal level (direction, protocol, and guarantee per channel, Tables 2), which aids reconstruction of the coordination design even without code. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that the framework was validated on a single Workday HCM tenant with limited module coverage (HR Process and Payroll, with full hire-to-retire coverage deferred to future work), that the digital twin remains passive (intervention via the Workday REST API is listed as future work rather than implemented), and that most optimization opportunity remains unrealized (Efficiency Score 34/100). They do not confront the absence of quantitative baselines, ablations, or reproducibility artifacts, and the "competitive parity" framing minimizes rather than addresses the fact that no head-to-head comparison was run — a credibility negative. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Inconsistent provenance of the headline OCPM finding: "18% of orders blocked by invoice-approval delays" appears repeatedly, but the validation tenant is a Workday HCM system (workers, payroll, recruiting) — orders and invoice approvals are procure-to-pay objects, suggesting this figure may be carried over from a different dataset or template rather than measured on the tenant, which undermines the paper's flagship "invisible to case-centric analysis" claim. - Zero O2O relations arguably defeats the OCPM motivation on this dataset: with no object-to-object relationships, the object-centric layer reduces to per-type event logs, so the claimed OCPM advantage on this validation data is thinner than presented. - The 65–75% bottleneck-prevention rate (cited as the framework's "most distinctive differentiator" absent from commercial tools) comes from prior work and Monte Carlo simulation of assumed scenarios (e.g., $100/delay-hour, ±6–12% bands), not from any measured intervention — the paper presents simulated counterfactuals as if they were prevention evidence. - No human-in-the-loop or ground-truth evaluation of task mining: the 72% correlation rate and 78–85% classification accuracy are unverifiable without the labeled set, annotation protocol, and inter-annotator agreement, and the "22% of user time on copy-paste" ROI claim rests entirely on this unvalidated classifier. - Single-tenant, single-domain, self-deployed evaluation with no external dataset (e.g., public OCEL logs used by the OCPM community) means no result can be independently checked; the compliance findings ($34,953 at risk, SOX breach) are produced by the tool's own rule engine and never audited. - Scale claims vs. evidence: the architecture is pitched against platforms processing "billions of records" via 200+ connectors, but is validated on ~40K events on one connector; no stress test of the graph store or drift detector is reported. Bottom Line: A practitioner considering open-source process mining stacks will find a useful, detailed integration blueprint and a few honest field findings from a live Workday tenant, but anyone seeking validated performance claims, reproducible artifacts, or evidence of parity with Celonis-class platforms should look elsewhere — nothing here is measured against an external baseline, and the flagship numbers do not fully withstand provenance scrutiny.

Problem & Motivation: Industrial IoT deployments (sensors, controllers, gateways, manufacturing lines) generate security-relevant telemetry that is commercially sensitive, so centralized ML-based intrusion detection creates data-governance risk. Federated learning addresses raw-data locality but produces opaque models, and industrial security operators need to know why an event was flagged to distinguish attacks from legitimate process changes. The paper targets researchers and practitioners in industrial cybersecurity who need a design that jointly satisfies privacy, low latency, interpretability, and heterogeneous client conditions — a gap the author argues no single prior work covers, since the literature treats feature selection, dimensionality reduction, FL, and explainability separately. Key Idea: The core move is architectural integration: treat privacy (federated aggregation), representation management (mutual-information feature selection plus empirically-gated dimensionality reduction), and explainability (feature-attribution over the selected features) as interdependent design objectives rather than independent pipeline stages. This is a framing insight, not a new algorithm — no component is technically new, and the paper says so. Methodology: The paper describes, but does not run, a five-layer pipeline: (1) local data acquisition keeps raw observations on-site; (2) local preprocessing performs missing-value handling, normalization, encoding, then mutual-information-based feature selection (citing Vergara & Estevez 2014; Beraha et al. 2019); (3) an optional dimensionality-reduction stage transforms features only if discriminative information for anomaly detection is preserved; (4) clients train local models (logistic regression as an interpretable baseline, more complex models optional) and communicate only model updates to a global aggregation step; (5) an explanation layer reports the dominant contributing features per decision, explicitly framed as decision-support evidence, not causal explanation. Heterogeneity is handled by retaining client-specific preprocessing and evaluation alongside the global model, with a call for a common feature schema. The proposed evaluation protocol specifies three levels (predictive metrics such as precision/recall/F-score, operational efficiency, explanation quality) and a four-configuration comparison plus before/after feature-reduction ablations and per-client versus global performance reporting. Critical design decisions — gating dimensionality reduction on empirical evidence, per-client evaluation to catch global-metric masking, non-causal interpretation of explanations — are reasonable and literature-justified but remain design recommendations only. Key Results: No empirical results are reported. The Results section is a literature synthesis restating six qualitative findings (e.g., "privacy benefit should be interpreted as a reduction in raw-data exposure rather than a complete privacy guarantee"; precision/recall trade-offs matter more than accuracy under class imbalance). The paper states outright: "the literature... does not provide sufficient evidence to claim a specific numerical performance improvement for the proposed XFL system." The CIC-DDoS 2019 dataset is named as a possible future experimental baseline, along with client-partition experiments to simulate heterogeneous factories. No accuracy, F1, communication-cost, or timing figures exist anywhere in the paper. Novelty Classification: At most a weak NEW FORMULATION / position paper: the genuinely novel element is the argument that the four requirements (privacy, heterogeneity handling, dimensionality management, explainability) must be co-designed and co-evaluated in IIoT security; every technical ingredient (FL aggregation, MI-based feature selection, PCA-style reduction, feature-importance explanations, precision/recall evaluation) is standard and cited from prior work. No new method, dataset, tool, or empirical finding is contributed. Rigor & Reproducibility: There is nothing to reproduce: no code, no weights, no experiments, no error bars, no seeds, no significance tests. The proposed evaluation protocol is well-specified (four configurations, per-client reporting, explanation-quality assessment) and would constitute a solid experimental design if executed, but it exists only as a plan. The referenced evaluation metrics (Hicks et al. 2022; scikit-learn documentation) are generic rather than security-specific. Positive note: the paper does not fabricate results or imply empirical support — it explicitly labels itself "a research framework rather than a claim of experimentally proven superiority." Concerns: the citation list is thin (~16 entries, including textbooks and two apparently peripheral self-referential items on evolutionary software engineering and project-risk prediction), and the closest related framework (SecureRiskNet) is discussed only conceptually, with no comparison table to actual XFL or federated-intrusion-detection systems in the literature. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a design framework with no implementation; no primary experimental claim). - Sound: The design arguments are internally consistent and the stated limitations are honest, but there are no formal results or proofs; soundness rests on plausibility. - General: The framework is stated broadly (any client type, model, or reduction technique), which makes it unfalsifiable until specific instantiations are chosen. - Tight: Not applicable — no bounds or quantitative claims are made; the only quasi-quantitative claim (communication reduction via feature selection) is asserted without measurement. - Implementable: Yes in principle — the components are all standard and could be assembled with off-the-shelf tools, but the paper provides no pseudocode, system specification, or artifact. Deliverable: paper form only; no library, dataset, trained model, or reusable technique beyond the framing argument. Strengths: - The most honest aspect is the explicit refusal to overclaim: the Results and Discussion sections state that all findings are methodological and that no numerical improvement is demonstrated, which is rarer than it should be in framework papers. - The proposed four-configuration experimental design (centralized vs. local-only vs. FL vs. XFL) cleanly decouples the contribution of collaboration from that of explanation, and the before/after feature-reduction ablation directly tests the paper's central trade-off — a genuinely useful blueprint for follow-on empirical work. - The paper correctly identifies and articulates several real design tensions specific to this setting: dimensionality reduction as an empirically-gated choice rather than default (grounded in Altin & Cakir 2024), global metrics masking per-client failure under heterogeneity, and the non-causal status of feature-importance explanations. - Positioning privacy as a system-level objective (local retention, controlled communication, secure aggregation) rather than an automatic property of FL is a correct and useful correction to common overclaims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge: (1) no empirical validation in a deployed smart factory; (2) CIC-DDoS 2019 cannot represent the diversity of industrial cyber-physical processes; (3) communication and synchronization overhead of FL is unquantified; (4) client heterogeneity may impede convergence and cause uneven performance; (5) explanation fidelity/consistency is hard to measure and misleading explanations can create false confidence; (6) FL alone does not guarantee privacy (model updates can leak); (7) stronger privacy mechanisms may further affect performance. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations and is the paper's strongest credibility feature. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The related-work coverage is too thin to support the claimed research gap: the paper cites no concrete federated intrusion-detection or explainable-FL systems (e.g., FedDefend-style or SHAP/LIME-based industrial IDS literature), so the assertion that prior work has not integrated these four requirements is asserted rather than established by comparison. - The explanation layer is specified only as "identify which features contributed most strongly" — no concrete attribution technique (SHAP, LIME, gradient-based, or even logistic-regression coefficients) is chosen, yet explanation quality is listed as a headline evaluation dimension. This leaves the paper's differentiating component unoperationalized. - The privacy story stops at "FL is not a complete guarantee"; no threat model (gradient inversion, membership inference, poisoning by malicious factories) is analyzed, and secure aggregation is invoked without any mechanism — for a security venue this is a significant omission. - The proposal to handle heterogeneity via a "common feature schema" contradicts the stated reality that features differ across sites; how a shared schema is negotiated across organizations is unresolved. - The two 2026 citations (EvoGraphCoder, AI-driven project risk prediction) are tangential to the paper's subject and suggest citation-padding rather than substantive engagement; future-dated publication (submitted May 2026, published August 2026) means the work has undergone limited post-publication scrutiny. - Even as a conceptual paper, it offers no complexity or communication-cost analysis that would let a reader assess whether the proposed pipeline is feasible on realistic industrial edge hardware. Bottom Line: A practitioner will gain little from this paper — it is a competent but unexecuted design proposal assembling well-known components, with no experiments, no artifact, and a thin literature base; readers seeking federated or explainable industrial intrusion detection should look to empirical XFL/FL-IDS work, or use this paper only as a checklist of evaluation-design considerations.
