Problem & Motivation: VANETs (vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure communication for intelligent transportation systems) are exposed to DoS, DDoS, Sybil, blackhole, wormhole, spoofing, and false-data-injection attacks due to open wireless channels and decentralized, highly dynamic topology. The paper argues that signature-based IDS cannot catch zero-day attacks, that standalone ML detectors suffer from class imbalance, high false alarms, and poor adaptability, and — the specific gap it claims to close — that existing work treats threat detection and network performance optimization (packet delivery ratio, delay, routing overhead, throughput) separately rather than in one integrated framework. The intended audience is ITS and vehicular network security researchers and practitioners. Key Idea: No identifiable single key idea. The paper is a combination of textbook techniques: supervised multi-class classification with softmax and cross-entropy, z-score anomaly detection with adaptive thresholds, and a weighted linear route-cost function. The claimed integration of detection and routing optimization into one framework is the closest thing to a thesis, but no novel mechanism links the two modules — the optimization module is described only at the level of generic metric definitions and an argmax response decision. Methodology: The pipeline has five stages: (1) data acquisition from OBUs/RSUs/edge nodes (described narratively; experiments actually use the public CICIDS2017 dataset), (2) preprocessing — statistical imputation, deduplication, min-max normalization, label/one-hot encoding, feature selection, (3) hybrid detection via deep feature extraction feeding ensemble classifiers (Decision Tree with entropy/information gain, Random Forest with bootstrap majority voting, SVM with RBF kernel, XGBoost with regularized objective Obj = L + Ω where Ω(f) = γT + ½λΣw²), (4) anomaly classification via z-score AS = |X−μ|/σ with adaptive thresholds, and (5) a decision/response layer performing node isolation and route selection via RC = αD + βL + γO, with a gradient-descent feedback update W(t+1) = W(t) − η∇L(W(t)) for online retraining. Critical design decisions: (a) choice of CICIDS2017 — a generic wired-network IDS benchmark, not VANET traffic, and not justified as a proxy for vehicular communication (unjustified); (b) the hybrid 'deep feature extraction + ensemble' architecture — the deep feature extractor is never specified (no architecture, layers, or parameters given) and Table 2 evaluates only the four classical classifiers, so the 'deep' component appears to be cosmetic (unjustified); (c) the weighted route-cost function — weights α, β, γ are never defined, tuned, or ablated (unjustified). Key Results: On CICIDS2017 (70/15/15 split, 5-fold cross-validation claimed), XGBoost leads with 96.3% accuracy, 95.8% precision, 95.4% recall, 95.6% F1, and 96.8% AUC, versus Decision Tree at 91.1%/90.1% F1, SVM at 93.1%/92.4% F1, and Random Forest at 94.5%/93.9% F1. Per-attack-class results report precision 97.1–98.4%, F1 ≥96.8%, false positive rates 1.3–2.2%, with DoS and Spoofing best (98.4% and 98.2% precision) and Wormhole worst (97.1% precision). Network results compare 'ML-Based Routing' (95.8% PDR, 7.24 Mbps throughput, 31.7 ms delay, 13.1% routing overhead, 96.2% availability) against AODV (90.8% PDR, 42.6 ms), DSR (91.9%, 39.4 ms), and OLSR (93.5%, 35.8 ms) — but the simulator, mobility model, node count, and scenario parameters are never stated, so these numbers cannot be situated. The baselines are classical and neither current nor strong; no deep-learning baseline (CNN-LSTM, autoencoder, attention) that the related-work section itself surveys is actually run. The attack-class results are surprising not for their values but for their provenance: CICIDS2017 contains no Sybil, Blackhole, or Wormhole attacks, making Table 3 impossible to have produced from the stated dataset. Novelty Classification: ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION at best, and a weak instance of it — the genuinely existing contribution is running four off-the-shelf classifiers on a public benchmark and reporting per-class metrics; the claimed NEW FORMULATION (joint threat detection + performance optimization in one framework) is asserted in prose but not instantiated in any algorithm, architecture, or experiment that differs from prior hybrid-IDS papers the authors themselves cite (e.g., their own Table 1 rows). Rigor & Reproducibility: Not rigorous. There are no ablations isolating any component (preprocessing, deep features, ensemble combination, adaptive thresholds, the route-cost function); the hybrid model's constituents and hyperparameters are unspecified; no code, data splits, model weights, or repository is released; the VANET simulation environment for Table 4 is unnamed, making those results unverifiable. The paper claims 5-fold cross-validation and 'statistical significance analysis' but reports neither variance across folds, standard deviations, nor significance tests anywhere. Most seriously, there is a Goodhart-style mismatch: the framework is developed and evaluated on CICIDS2017 (a static wired-network dataset from 2017) while all framing, threat modeling, and conclusions target dynamic VANET environments, and Table 3 reports attack categories absent from the evaluation dataset — suggesting either an undeclared second data source or fabricated/inherited numbers. Confidence should be low; this reads as a venue with minimal review (SvedbergOpen, 2026 volume) rather than a peer-reviewed top-tier result. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs classifiers on a benchmark dataset and reports simulation-style network metrics). - Practical: Yes trivially — Decision Tree/RF/SVM/XGBoost on tabular flows run on commodity CPUs (the authors used a GPU workstation with TensorFlow/Scikit-learn, which is unnecessary overhead for the models actually evaluated). - Efficient: The classical models are cheap, but the claimed 'deep feature extraction' layer's cost is unreported; the routing module's computational overhead in a real vehicle or RSU is unmeasured. - Effective: The evidence shows the classifiers separate CICIDS2017 flow classes — a standard proxy — not that they detect attacks in real vehicular traffic, and the optimization module's effectiveness rests on an unrepeatable simulation. - Scalable: Untested; scalability to high-density VANETs is claimed repeatedly but no experiment varies node count, traffic density, or mobility, and online retraining cost at fleet scale is unaddressed. Deliverable: paper only — no software artifact, dataset, trained model, or reusable technique is released. Strengths: - The per-attack-class evaluation (Table 3) includes false positive rate and detection rate alongside precision/recall/F1, a fuller metric set than many hybrid-IDS papers report. - The related-work table (Table 1) honestly enumerates specific limitations of prior approaches per method, dataset, and technique, which frames the contribution more precisely than the surrounding prose. - The dual-metric framing (security metrics + network performance metrics: PDR, delay, routing overhead, availability) is the right evaluation lens for the joint problem, even though the paper fails to execute it credibly. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: - None stated. The paper acknowledges no scope boundaries, dataset-transfer concerns, or failure modes; the limitations section of the discussion is absent, and the conclusion asserts the framework is 'viable and strong' without qualification. This non-confrontation is a credibility negative. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central inconsistency: Sybil, Blackhole, and Wormhole detection results (Table 3) cannot come from CICIDS2017, which contains none of these attacks; the actual data source for these rows is never disclosed. - The 'deep feature extraction' component is never specified or evaluated — no architecture, no comparison against raw features — so the 'hybrid' label is unsupported. - The network-performance experiments lack a simulator name, topology, node counts, mobility traces, or attack-traffic interaction with routing, so Table 4 is unreproducible and could plausibly be illustrative rather than measured. - The route-cost weights (α, β, γ) are never set, tuned, or sensitivity-tested, leaving the optimization module effectively undefined. - No deep-learning or 2018+ baselines are run despite the related work citing CNN-LSTM, autoencoder, federated, and attention-based detectors with published numbers on the same dataset. - Real-time claims (real-time detection, online adaptation via W(t+1) = W(t) − η∇L) are made with zero latency, throughput, or drift measurements. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains almost nothing here — the only verifiable content is a commodity CICIDS2017 classifier comparison that any stronger alternative (e.g., the very CNN-LSTM, ensemble, or federated VANET-IDS papers the authors cite) covers with better methodology, and the VANET-specific and optimization claims should be treated as unsupported.

Problem & Motivation: Pharmacies are attractive cybercrime targets because they hold electronic health records, insurance details, and payment information, and the healthcare sector's shift to EHRs and IoT has enlarged the attack surface; the SingHealth breach (1.5 million patient records, 2018) and WannaCry attacks on Indonesian hospitals are cited as motivating incidents. The authors argue the "human factor" is the weakest link and that pharmacists, technicians, and support personnel must serve as the first line of defense, so organizations need evidence that awareness/training programs actually change behavior. The gap claimed is that the effectiveness of such training specifically for pharmacy staff is under-examined, especially for remote pharmacy workers. Key Idea: There is no distinct technical insight. The core move is applying a standard binary SVM classifier to staff survey features to label a training program "effective" or "ineffective," then reading feature importance as guidance for where training falls short. This is a known technique (SVM classification with RBF/linear kernels, grid-search hyperparameter tuning, standard metrics) applied to a new domain, not a new formulation. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) collect labeled cybersecurity data via surveys/performance metrics from pharmacy staff; (2) preprocess (encode categorical variables, normalize numerical data, handle missing values); (3) split data — the algorithm listing uses a 70/30 train/test split while the results section states 80/20, an internal inconsistency; (4) train an SVM (kernel and regularization unspecified in the results) to separate "trained/untrained" or "effective/ineffective" classes via maximum-margin hyperplane; (5) evaluate with accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and a confusion matrix. A conceptual input–process–output model of training effectiveness (user characteristics → program design/delivery → behavior change) is described narratively but not formalized. Critical design decisions: choosing SVM over baselines is unargued; the binary effectiveness label construction is undefined; feature selection ("demographics, knowledge scores, behavior assessments") is asserted without justification. None of the three is well-justified. Key Results: Reported metrics on an undisclosed dataset: accuracy 86.67%, precision 92.1%, recall 87.5%, F1-score 89.7%. No sample size, no dataset description beyond hypothetical categories, no baseline comparison of any kind (no decision tree, logistic regression, or even a majority-class baseline), no confusion matrix values shown despite the figure reference, and no statistical significance testing. No baselines are compared at all, so "strong" vs. "weak" is inapplicable. The tested scale is at best toy-scale; there is no evidence any real pharmacy data was collected. The claim that "awareness campaigns get people talking but don't change behavior, while skill-based training improves confidence and performance but costs more" is presented as a narrative finding, not a measured one. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (claimed, not demonstrated) at best; realistically this is a standard combination of existing ideas — a textbook SVM classifier plus an off-the-shelf training-effectiveness conceptual model — applied to the pharmacy-staff setting. Nothing in the method, data, or findings is technically novel; the domain framing (pharmacy personnel) is the only differentiator. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, no multiple seeds, no error bars, no significance tests, no code or data release. The dataset's existence, size, and provenance are unverifiable — it is described in conditional language ("would normally include"), strongly suggesting no real data collection occurred. The confusion matrix and Figure 2 are referenced but the matrix values are missing from the provided text. The algorithm pseudocode is boilerplate scikit-learn (train_test_split, StandardScaler, SVM, accuracy_score) with a random_state of 42 and no tuning results. Methodological red flags: evaluation on what appears to be a synthetic or hypothetical dataset, no external baselines, inconsistent train/test ratios between sections, and no demographic description of any actual cohort. Not reproducible in any meaningful sense. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile (the paper claims to run a classifier). Practical: The method runs on any commodity laptop via scikit-learn, so compute feasibility is trivial — but only if a labeled dataset exists. Efficient: SVM training cost is negligible at plausible staff-cohort sizes; efficiency is not a differentiator. Effective: The evidence does not show the stated problem (improved pharmacy security posture) is solved — the metrics classify a label whose construction and data source are undefined, making them a proxy at best and possibly an artifact. Scalable: Not tested and not meaningfully claimable; nothing indicates the pipeline was run on more than a hypothetical sample. Deliverable: paper only — no tool, dataset, model, or reusable artifact is released. Strengths: - Timely and well-scoped problem framing: pharmacy staff as a specific, underserved population in healthcare cybersecurity training research. - A reasonably organized literature review spanning five directly relevant works (pharmacy-specific training, the iCAT gamified/knowledge-graph approach, EHR-focused primers) plus broader security-culture literature (Bada et al., Amankwa et al.). - Correct identification of the field's consensus insight that awareness campaigns alone do not change behavior — only skill-based, feedback-driven training does. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that training effectiveness depends on engagement, relevance, and learners' prior knowledge, and that awareness campaigns alone are insufficient without targeted, continuous education. They do not acknowledge any limitation of their own empirical work — no mention of dataset size, data availability, generalizability, or validation. This non-confrontation of methodological limits is a credibility negative. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The empirical core appears fabricated or hypothetical: the dataset is described in conditional mood and no experiment log, sample count, or data source is given; the reported metrics (86.67%/92.1%/87.5%/89.7%) therefore cannot be traced to any evidence. - No baseline classifier, no ablation, no cross-validation results, no hyperparameter search results despite promising grid search in the methods text. - Internal inconsistencies (70/30 split in the algorithm vs. 80/20 in results; "filling" for "overfitting") suggest the empirical section was not carefully executed or reviewed. - The venue itself (Adolescencia e Saude, an adolescent-health journal publishing a pharmacy-cybersecurity paper with eight authors from Indian engineering departments) is a strong signal of publication-quality problems; peer-review confidence should be treated as minimal. - Remote-work training, highlighted in the abstract as a focus, is never analyzed anywhere in the paper. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains almost nothing from this paper — the literature review can be skipped in favor of the primary sources it cites (Bada et al. 2019; Alkhazi et al. 2022), and the SVM results are unverifiable and almost certainly not derived from real data, so any serious reader should look elsewhere for evidence on pharmacy cybersecurity training effectiveness.

Foundational Verification of Systems Software — avg: 72 (Innovative)

These papers share a common agenda of producing machine-checked, foundational correctness proofs for real systems software, all built on the Rocq (Coq) theorem prover with the Iris separation logic framework. "Corten - Foundational Verification of Rust Programs" and "Bringing Foundational Verification to Real-World Rust Code" target the Rust language specifically, with Corten establishing a THIR-level semantics and weakest-precondition calculus, while the RefinedRust extension focuses on scaling to idiomatic features like traits, closures, iterators, and unsafe code. "Modular Responsiveness Verification of Rust Async Runtimes" diverges in verifying a liveness property (eventual task progression) for async runtimes rather than functional correctness of sequential programs. "Extending concurrent separation logic to the hardware level to verify the xv6 OS kernel on RISC-V with AI agents" addresses a different layer entirely — C/assembly kernel code verified against sub-instruction-level RISC-V hardware semantics rather than a source language. Collectively, the trend shows foundational verification maturing from idealized benchmarks toward realistic, deployed systems code, pushing down to accurate hardware models and up to idiomatic high-level language features simultaneously.

These papers share a focus on the practical engineering challenges of the quantum era, though they approach it from opposite directions. "Towards Scaling Quantum Fine-Tuning of Foundational Time Series Models for Classification" leverages quantum resources, attaching parameterized quantum circuits to a frozen Chronos foundation model and studying how adding qubits affects performance on power-grid event classification. Collectively, they suggest a maturing research trend: treating quantum computing and post-quantum security as systems-level engineering problems with measurable constraints, moving beyond proof-of-concept demonstrations toward deployable hybrid architectures.

Verifier-Guided On-Policy Distillation — avg: 70 (Innovative)

These papers share a focus on improving post-training of reasoning-capable LLMs through on-policy distillation, self-distillation, and verifier-grounded signals, rather than pure RL or imitation. Most propose concrete training methods: Verification-Aware Training for Speculative Decoding aligns draft models with the verification step, Verify Before You Distill gates dense teacher supervision by a verifier audit, and Eliciting Weak-to-Strong Generalization and RISE both construct better teachers — via reverse policy-gradient amplification and teacher extrapolation, respectively — to strengthen dense supervision. Others critique or restructure the paradigm: One Symptom, Three Levers offers a critical review organizing the on-policy self-distillation literature around diversity collapse, Revisiting Complete Reasoning Trases shows trimmed traces beat full-trace SFT, and FlowBalance replaces pointwise RL with a trajectory-balance objective blending sparse and dense rewards. A common thread is that dense token-level supervision is powerful but fragile — teacher error, missing verification signals, or redundant traces cause failure modes like confidence collapse and diversity loss. Collectively, the trend points toward hybrid recipes that combine verifier grounding, adaptive gating, and self-improving teachers to make distillation more reliable and efficient than either RL or vanilla imitation alone.

A complementary thread focuses on efficiency and controllability: 'X-AuT' compresses audio encoders for latency-sensitive speech LLMs, 'Mask Forcing' improves distilled autoregressive video diffusion, and 'The Attention Triangle' training-free-steers cross-modal attention to fix prompt violations in audio-video generation. The approaches differ in level of intervention, spanning architecture pruning, distillation, inference-time steering, and new training pipelines with dedicated datasets (SCENEGES, SwDA-500), but all respond to the same gap between monolithic research models and real-world constraints. The collective trend suggests a shift from task-specific cascades toward unified, efficient, and controllable multimodal systems suited for real-time, embodied, and on-device deployment.

Skill-Based LLM Agent Efficiency — avg: 64 (Innovative)

These papers share a focus on improving the efficiency, robustness, and control of LLM-based agents, particularly for long-horizon or multi-agent tasks where naive per-step prompting is costly or unreliable. "Act More, Decide Less" and "SKILL.state" attack runtime cost directly, the former by amortizing LLM decisions across learned action chunks and the latter by replacing accumulated conversation history with mutable structured execution state. "Theory of Agent" provides the conceptual umbrella, framing these trade-offs as choices about internalizing competence in parameters versus externalizing it into tools, memory, and orchestration, while "Toward Latent Language Model Skills Steering" examines how skills can be represented and manipulated at the activation level. Collectively, the trend points toward treating agent competence as a first-class, transferable resource—distilled, steered, and provably coordinated—rather than relying on monolithic prompting at every step.

Security and Safety of Agentic AI — avg: 64 (Innovative)

These papers share a focus on the security and safety risks of LLM-based agents and agentic development environments. The Double-Edged Sword survey and HookPry examine threats in agentic coding ecosystems, but differ in method: one consolidates literature into taxonomies and defense architectures, while the other empirically demonstrates attacks via trojanized plugin lifecycle hooks that bypass prompt-level defenses. EvoSafeHarness and SchemeArena target agent safety evaluation and mitigation more broadly, with the former automatically synthesizing model- and domain-specific safety harnesses and the latter providing a benchmark for detecting scheming behavior. Collectively, the cluster reflects a maturing research trend: moving from documenting agentic AI vulnerabilities toward principled, evaluated defense mechanisms, monitoring systems, and benchmarks that treat agent safety as a first-class engineering problem.

Sparse Modeling and Efficient Transformers — avg: 53 (Moderately Innovative)

These papers share a focus on making models leaner and more interpretable, whether through explicit sparsity mechanisms or streamlined architectures. "Feature Permutation for Accelerating Vision Transformers Inference via N:M Sparse Activations" and "Sparsity in factor analysis" directly exploit sparsity—one via hardware-friendly N:M pruning of ViT activations using minimum-cost matching, the other by comparing sparse factor analysis penalties like SCAD and MC+ for interpretable loadings. "Neural Symbolic Regression Using Deep Learning and Sparse Modeling" likewise uses LASSO to distill networks into compact closed-form expressions, emphasizing interpretability over pure compression. In contrast, "FreeFlow: A Bias-free Hierarchical Transformer for Optical Flow Estimation" and "Marigold V2: Revisiting Diffusion Transformers for Monocular Depth Estimation" pursue efficiency by architectural simplification and accessible fine-tuning rather than pruning, removing task-specific heuristics or enabling single-GPU training for dense vision tasks. Collectively, the cluster reflects a trend away from heavier, hand-engineered pipelines toward sparsity, parsimony, and architectural minimalism as routes to efficient, deployable, and interpretable models.

Persistent Self-Sustaining Agent Architectures — avg: 52 (Moderately Innovative)

These papers share a focus on long-lived AI agents that maintain continuity of identity, memory, and authority across runtime changes and self-modification. "SUCCESSOR Ω v9.0.0 — Machine Civilization" addresses how a successor AI system can inherit mission and obligations while re-earning authority through proof-gated protocols, whereas "Runtime-Independent Persistent Agents" tackles the same continuity problem at the infrastructure level via a formal migration protocol that decouples an agent's persistent substrate from its execution substrate. "Dalek: A Constructive Agent Machine" differs by formalizing self-maintenance, self-evolution, and self-reproduction as intrinsic machine transitions rather than external operations, and "SUCCESSOR Ω — AEON Ω: The Continuity Estate" extends the framework into an applied economic analysis, candidly reporting a negative result that neural-symbolic continuity infrastructure loses to conventional baselines on cost. Collectively, the trend suggests a maturing research agenda moving from defining what persistent, self-modifying agents are toward rigorously specifying, verifying, and cost-justifying them for production deployment.

Autonomous Search Agents and Tooling — avg: 52 (Moderately Innovative)

These papers share a focus on agentic systems that navigate, search, and retrieve information in complex environments, whether on the web or within enterprise workflows. 'Iris: Climbing to the Search Frontier' trains large search agents (via SFT and RL) and evaluates them on benchmarks like BrowseComp, while 'Agent and Tool Search: Foundations, Techniques, and Open Challenges' steps back to survey the broader problem of discovering and selecting tools and agents themselves. The other two papers apply multi-agent architectures to concrete tasks: 'Enhanced Multi-Agent Framework for Predictive Process Mining' builds a 21-agent CrewAI system for open-source enterprise process mining, and 'Agent2UCB: Agentic System for Generative Engine Optimization' uses a bandit-driven multi-armed policy to optimize content visibility in LLM-based generative search. Collectively, they reflect a trend from raw search-agent capability (Iris) toward tooling and optimization layers around agents — including discovering the right agents (survey), optimizing for generative engines (Agent2UCB), and applying agent orchestration to domain-specific pipelines (process mining). Differences lie mostly in scope: two are system/benchmark contributions, one is a survey, and one is an optimization demo.

Automated Verification and Optimization of Complex Systems — avg: 50 (Moderately Innovative)

These papers share a focus on applying systematic, often learning-based automation to hard engineering problems in embedded and hardware design flows. 'Analysis of ZigBee Implementations Using Protocol State Fuzzing' and 'Simulation-Based Metamorphic Testing for System Verification of Cyber-Physical Systems' address verification of stateful systems with incomplete observability, using active automata learning and metamorphic relations respectively to cope with the absence of conventional test oracles. 'Advanced Debugging Strategies with Reinforcement Learning in Semiconductor SoC Verification' extends automation into the debug loop, applying multi-agent RL to failure triage in UVM-based verification. On the optimization side, 'LevelSyn: Physical-Aware Logic Synthesis via Level-Asynchronous Graph Neural Networks' and 'GLOW: Glitch Optimization with Retiming for Low Power' improve logic synthesis—one via GNN-predicted physical placement priors, the other via an exact MILP retiming formulation—while 'An enhanced seagull optimization algorithm for multi-dimensional internet of things routing under heterogeneity and mobility constraints' tackles network-layer optimization with an improved metaheuristic. Collectively, the trend points toward replacing manual heuristics and ad-hoc testing with formal, learned, or exact methods that exploit structure in state machines, netlists, and event streams, spanning the full lifecycle from synthesis and routing to verification and debugging.

Hybrid Machine Learning for Intrusion Detection — avg: 28 (Incremental)

These papers share a focus on machine learning–based network intrusion detection across diverse environments, including general networks, IoT, VANETs, smart cities, and cyber-physical systems. Most combine multiple techniques—such as One-Class SVM with GANs in 'Modern Cyber Threats: A Hybrid Intrusion Detection Model for Effective DDoS Mitigation', CNN–BiGRU hybrids, or CNN–LSTM with gradient boosting in 'RC-ADAPT: A Resilient and Continuous Adaptive Intrusion Detection Framework for CPS'—and report high accuracies (96–99%) on benchmark datasets like CICIDS2017, CICDDOS2019, and TON_IoT. They differ in their primary emphasis: some prioritize model architecture and imbalanced-data handling, others address label scarcity ('Weakly Supervised Learning for Cybersecurity Attack From Only Unlabeled Data'), privacy constraints via federated learning ('Smart Cities AVNs' and 'Explainable Federated Learning for Privacy-Preserving Cybersecurity in Industrial IoT and Smart Factories'), or operational resilience and network performance. A recurring theme is trustworthiness—several works incorporate explainability (SHAP, LIME) so security operators can interpret alerts. Collectively, the trend suggests the field is moving beyond raw accuracy toward deployable, interpretable, privacy-aware, and drift-resilient IDS solutions tailored to specific infrastructures.
